p.seg: Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The Mysterious is
the ultimate ancestor of nature,
and the great origin of all diversities.
Profound and obscure is its depth,
therefore it is called subtle.
Vast and remote is its distance,
therefore it is called wondrous.
In height it crowns the nine heavens,
in expanse it envelops the eight quarters.
It shines forth like the sun and moon,
swift as lightning’s flight.
Sometimes it flashes and vanishes like a shadow,
sometimes it drifts and darts like flowing stars,
sometimes it ripples in the clear abyss,
sometimes it floats as clouds in misty spray.
It becomes being by conforming to omens and forms,
and becomes non-being by resting in hidden stillness.
It sinks into the great depths below,
or ascends to roam the utmost heights of the stars.
Neither metal nor stone can compare with its hardness,
nor clear dew with its softness.
Square but unmeasured by rule,
round but untraced by compass.
Its coming is unseen,
its going cannot be pursued.
Qián is high through it,
Kūn is low through it,
clouds move through it,
and rain is dispersed by it.
It is womb and embryo of primordial unity,
molds and forges the Two Principles,
exhales and fuses the Great Beginning,
drives and tempers the myriad types.
It turns and whirls through the four sevens,
crafts the dim and obscure,
reins the mysterious mechanisms,
exhales and draws in the Four Breaths,
encompasses the secret and silent,
stretches forth in radiant display,
suppressing the turbid and raising the pure,
discriminating between the Huáng Hé and Huí Shuǐ.
If increased, it does not overflow;
if ladled, it never fails;
shared, it never is overgloried;
withdrawn, it does not exhaust.
Therefore, where the Mysterious abides,
its joy is inexhaustible.
Where the Mysterious departs,
the vessel decays and spirit flees.
As for the five tones and eight sounds,
the pure shāng and flowing zhǐ,
they injure the sense of hearing.
Brilliant hues and splendid colors,
dazzling and resplendent,
harm the sense of sight.
Feasts, ease, and indulgence,
fine wine and fragrant liquor,
disturb one's nature.
Flirtatious form and charming looks,
powder and fair complexion,
cut short destiny.
Only the Mysterious Dao
may be pursued forever.
Those who do not know the Mysterious Dao,
though they regard a glance as the instrument of life and death,
lips and jaws as the key to rise and fall,
behold splendid pavilions above the clouds and rain,
adorned chambers with luxurious greens in variegation;
curtains of patterned silk merge like mist,
gauze canopies part like clouds.
Western furs displayed in inner rooms,
golden cups pass in endless procession,
clear strings clash and sound together in unison,
Zhèng dances swirl and twist in confusion,
plaintive flutes rise to the clouds,
feathered canopies float on rippling water,
gather blossoms in the orchid grove’s enclosure,
play with red flowers at the pool of gathered pearls,
ascend heights to look afar and forget all cares,
lean over chasms to gaze below, forgetting morning hunger,
enter the splendor of feasts through a thousand gates,
emerge in vermilion chariots of magnificent form.
Yet, when joy reaches its height, sorrow gathers;
when fullness is reached, there must be loss.
Thus when the song ends, sighs arise;
when the banquet breaks up, hearts feel grief.
Such is the call of circumstances and principle,
like echoes that answer one another.
That which is borrowed and not real,
thus, when things depart, it is as if something remains behind.
The Mysterious Dao,
is obtained within,
kept by what is outside,
used by the spirit,
forgotten by the vessel.
These are the essential words for contemplating the Mysterious Dao.
Those who attain it are honored,
without relying on the awe of the yellow battle-axe.
Those who embody it are rich,
without needing rare treasures.
It is so high it cannot be climbed,
so deep it cannot be fathomed.
Ride upon fleeting light,
drive the flying shadow,
soar through the six expanse,
pass through and enfold all.
Go out above the utmost,
enter deep below the nadir.
Pass through the gate of vastness,
roam the mysterious and remote fields.
Wander free in dreamlike vagueness,
drift about beyond indistinct forms.
Swallow the nine flowers at the cloud's edge,
savor the six breaths in rosy clouds.
Loiter in the haze and dimness,
soar in the subtle and rare,
walk lightly across the rainbow,
pace around the turning sphere.
Such are those who have attained it.
Next are those who truly know contentment;
knowing contentment, one can modestly retreat and not be employed,
nurturing radiance in the forests and mountains.
Unfurl the wings of phoenix and dragon among the lowliest creatures,
cultivate vast spirit within humble thatched huts.
With coarse belt and hempen rope,
do not trade them for the dragon-decorated robes shining bright.
Bearing staff and walking stick,
do not exchange them for a team of fine steeds.
Hide night’s brilliance in the peaks of Sōng Mountain,
not accepting attack from other mountains.
Soak scales and armor in the profound abyss,
to escape the fire-drilling of disaster.
One’s every motion and pause knows its limit,
lacking nothing wherever one goes.
Abandon the splendid radiance of courtly mornings,
avoid the dangers of wrecked carriages on perilous roads.
Sing and whistle among azure cliffs,
while the myriad things dissolve into dusty vapors.
With cheerful face beneath lush branches,
while vermilion gates become simple doors of rope and wood.
Grasp the plow to till fields,
and banners are suddenly like holding a whip.
Sip bitter tea and rinse with spring water,
yet it is as though meat banquets and wild herbs are the same.
How abundant is the joy at the field of non-action,
gladly considering noble and base as equal where none contend.
Embrace purity and keep simplicity,
with no desires and no worries,
maintaining the true and the empty vessel,
living in calm and tastelessness.
Broad and vast,
in natural harmony with the undivided.
Floodlike and boundless,
matching the operation of creation in accord.
As if dark, as if bright,
as if turbid, as if clear,
seeming slow yet swift,
seeming vacant yet full.
How could one be willing to sit as a corpse shaman,
or relinquish the post of great craftsman,
vault past the wine-jar to act as an ignorant cook,
or forsake the cord and rule to assist clumsy artisans?
Not for the petty matters of stink rats
does one take the joys and sorrows of ordinary men.
Slight and unconcerned with the common praise,
upright and unafraid of slander in conformity.
No external thing confuses its utmost refinement,
no profit or harm sullies its pure essence.
So, poverty, riches, and the highest honors
are insufficient to lure such a one;
what else could delight them?
Naked blades and boiling cauldrons
cannot coerce them;
what is slander, that it should give them grief?
Always untroubled by common vexations,
and never mingling with the world.
As for those who use the Suí pearl to shoot at sparrows,
lick Qín’s hemorrhoids for a noble’s favor,
climb rotten strings to seek birds’ nests,
swim the Lüliáng to catch fish,
guests at dawn in a prince’s court,
at dusk reduced to remnants among foxes and birds.
Rafters bent, kettles overturned,
fallen and drowned beyond recovery,
these are what the world strains after with speed and longing,
yet the enlightened shudder and sorrow at them.
Thus, the perfected hide the shào and xià and conceal their talents.
They spread their six wings in the ruins of the Five Cities,
without troubling about the rush of the reed’s defense.
They shade their scales and horns in the realm of the useless,
trusting not in the defenses of crooked burrows.
Looking down, they do not cry out like proud hawks,
looking up, do not regret reaching the utmost height.
None among men can recognize them,
remote and distant indeed!”
Someone asked:
“The immortals do not die,
is this truly reliable?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“Even with utmost clarity,
yet that which has form cannot be fully seen.
Even with perfect hearing,
yet that which makes sound cannot be fully heard.
Even with the great feet of Dà Zhāng and Shù Hài,
what is usually trodden upon
is far less than what is not.
Even with the wisdom of Yǔ, Yì, Qí, and Xié,
what is known is far less than the multitude of what is unknown.
Amongst the myriad things,
what is not present?
How much more so the ranks of the immortals,
which fill the records written on bamboo and silk.
The way of not dying,
why should it not exist?”
At this, the questioner burst out laughing and said:
“What has a beginning must have an end;
what exists must perish.
Thus the sages of the Three August Ones and Five Emperors, Qiū Dàn’s wisdom,
the intelligence of Qì Jí and Liáng Píng,
the eloquence of Duān Yīng and Suí Lì,
the valor of Bèn Yù and Wǔ Dīng,
all of them have died,
this is the common course of human reason,
the inevitable grand principle.
I have heard of those who wither before the frost,
or fade their green while still in summer,
who bear ears but do not blossom,
or wilt away before setting fruit,
but have not heard of one who enjoys ten thousand years of life,
or a lifespan that endures without end.
Therefore, in antiquity, people who studied did not seek immortality,
nor did their words discuss the strange,
they rejected those heterodox doctrines,
and guarded what is natural,
regarding turtles and cranes as different types,
and seeing life and death as morning and evening.
If one labors the mind and restrains oneself,
to do things of no benefit,
chiseling ice and carving rotten wood,
in the end there will be no certain accomplishment.
Far better to set forth lofty strategies for aiding the world,
to summon the prosperity due in one’s own era,
let purple and green banners billow again and again,
let the dark stallion and dragon stand at the ready,
let the ornate chariot wheels hasten the steps,
let the meat in the cauldrons replace the plow,
is this not fine indeed?
Often I ponder the mockery in the poem “Fu Tian,”
and deeply consider Zhòng Ní’s mortality as proof,
not clutching at formless wind,
nor chasing shadows that are hard to grasp,
nor seeking what cannot be obtained,
nor treading a road that cannot be reached.
To abandon honor and bloom and enter hardship,
to cast aside what is easy and attack what is most difficult,
is like a mourner chasing after a wandering woman,
surely there will be regret for losing both,
as one-sided faith brings biased judgment,
bringing calamity within and without.
Bān Dī could not slice tile and stone into fine needles,
Ōu Yě could not forge swords from lead and tin.
Thus, when something cannot be done,
even spirits and deities cannot make it so;
when something cannot succeed,
even Heaven and Earth cannot complete it.
How could there be a miraculous method in the world
to make the aged youthful once more,
or the destined-to-die live again?
And yet you wish to extend the short life of a huìgū cicada,
and grant it the lifespan spanning ages and cycles,
or nourish the glory of a fleeting zhāojūn fungus,
and make it last through countless months,
is this not absurd?
I hope you reflect ninefold,
and do not stray too far in confusion.”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“Where hearing departs,
even great thunder cannot make it heard;
where sight is lost,
even the Three Luminaries cannot make it seen;
is it that ordinary sound is faint,
or the heavenly light is dim?
Yet the deaf call this ‘no sound’,
and the blind, ‘no objects’.
How much more so the harmonious music of pipes and strings,
or the brilliant adornment of the mountain dragon
—how could they appreciate the elegant charm
or the radiant scales and embellishments?
Thus the deaf and blind, hindered by their bodily instruments,
do not believe in Thunder Deity and the Celestial Phenomenon.
How much more so with things even subtler than these?
When the mind is dark and hindered,
they will not believe there was ever a Zhōu or Kǒng in ancient times.
How could one even try to tell them the way of the immortals?
Coming and going, beginning and ending,
truly this is a great rule.
But in their varieties and differences,
sometimes so, sometimes not,
infinite transformations,
myriad wonders without limit,
things and affairs seem at odds,
with equal origins yet diverging ends,
how can they all be made the same?
To claim that all that begins must end is common,
but to generalize so
is not sound reasoning.
To say summer must always be long—
yet wild radish and barley wither in it.
To say winter must always cause decay—
yet bamboo and cypress flourish.
To say that what begins must end—
yet Heaven and Earth are inexhaustible.
To say that what lives must die—
yet turtles and cranes endure.
In high summer one expects only heat—
yet summer days still bring coolness.
In deep winter one expects only cold—
but harsh winters still have moments of warmth.
Hundreds of rivers pour east—
yet some mightily flow north.
The earth’s way is utmost stillness—
yet at times quakes and collapses.
The nature of water is pure cold—
yet there are warm springs in valleys;
the nature of fire is fierce—
yet at Xiāo Qiū there are cold flames;
the heavy sinks by nature—
yet in the Southern Sea mountains of floating stone exist;
the light should float—
yet at Niú Yáng Kē, there are floating feathers that sink.
Of the myriad differing things,
one cannot judge all by the same measure—
it has always been this way.
Among the living, the most numinous
is none other than humankind.
Of all things noble by nature,
surely all should be the same.
Yet in wisdom and foolishness, uprightness and perversity,
beauty and ugliness, tall and short,
clarity and turpitude, chastity and wantonness,
slowness and haste,
leanings and aversions,
what ears and eyes seek—
the differences among these
are as far apart as heaven and earth,
as incompatible as ice and coals.
Why single out the immortals as odd
for not perishing along with ordinary people?
If you say all those who receive vital energy are fixed in form,
then how is it that the pheasant becomes a shèn,
the sparrow transforms into a clam,
the earthworm borrows wings,
the river frog takes flight,
the oyster becomes a dragonfly,
the water plant turns into a maggot,
the field mouse turns into a quail,
decayed grass becomes a firefly,
the alligator becomes a tiger,
the snake becomes a dragon—
are these not so?
If you say that humans alone receive true nature,
differing from all other creatures,
Heaven bestows fate impartially,
making no distinctions—
then how is it that the cow of Āi becomes a tiger,
the old woman of Chǔ becomes a giant turtle,
the zhīlí transforms into a willow,
the Qín girl becomes a stone,
life and death succeeded by rebirth,
men and women change form,
Lǎo Péng attains great longevity,
while a young child dies prematurely—
for what reason is this?
If differences exist at all,
then what limit can there be to their variety?
As for the immortals,
they nourish their bodies with medicines,
and prolong their lives through arts and calculations;
thus internal ailments do not arise,
and external troubles do not enter.
Even though they look upon the world for a long time without dying,
their old bodies do not change.
If one possesses the Way,
there is nothing difficult about it.
Yet the shallow-minded crowd,
constrained by custom and clinging to convention,
all say that since immortals are not seen among people of the world,
they immediately claim such things cannot exist in all under Heaven.
But is that which the eyes have seen
ever worthy of being spoken of as the standard?
Between Heaven and Earth,
there is no outside to their vastness;
within them, there are marvels beyond compare—
how could there immediately be any limit?
One lives under the dome of Heaven until old age,
yet does not know what lies above it;
treads upon the earth for a lifetime,
yet fails to recognize what lies beneath it.
The body and its form are what one naturally possesses,
and yet none understand the reason for their own heart and will.
Longevity and life belong to oneself,
yet none know how to attain their length or brevity.
How much less, then, concerning the distant principles of the shénxiān,
and the hidden profundity of Dàodé!
Relying on the short-sightedness of their senses,
they judge the existence or nonexistence of the subtle and wondrous—
is this not to be mourned?
Suppose there is a great and wise person,
who chooses seclusion and will not serve in office,
concealing brilliance and covering over purity,
discarding falsehood and removing desires,
holding onto pure jade within utter simplicity,
casting aside trivial affairs beyond the flow of the common world—
yet people in society are still rarely able to distinguish such a person,
and perhaps not a single one is able to achieve intention and conduct surpassing namelessness,
or to find spirit within a humble form.
How much less, then, the xiān rén of extraordinary paths and divergent ways,
who regard wealth and rank as misfortune,
consider glory and splendor as filth,
treat treasures as mere dust,
and see fame as but morning dew.
They tread fiery gales without being scorched,
step lightly atop profound waves,
beat their pinions in pure dust,
ride wind-harnessed chariots upon cloud-borne carriages,
look up and soar to the Purple Pole,
look down and nestle on Kūnlún.
How can worldly, living corpses
hope to see such people?
Even supposing they roam at leisure,
and at times pass through the human world,
hiding the true and veiling the strange,
appearing outwardly no different from the ordinary and mediocre,
shoulder to shoulder and walking side by side,
who could possibly perceive them?
If all men were like Jiāo and Xián, whose eyes are perfectly square,
or Qióngshū, with a pair of widely set ears
protruding from the crown of the head;
if Mǎ Huáng could ride a dragon,
and Zǐ Jìn personally drive a white crane chariot;
or some bore scaled bodies and serpentine forms,
or wore golden chariots and feathered garments—that alone would allow men to recognize them.
But since they are not such as these,
then if not those with penetrating vision, how could anyone behold their form?
If not those with thorough hearing, how could anyone hear their voice?
In this world, people choose not to believe,
and are quick to criticize and slander;
thus the zhēn rén detest this,
and all the more withdraw in secret.
Moreover, what ordinary people love
is precisely what the highest worthies detest,
and what the vulgar prize
is what the utmost men despise.
Great scholars of talent,
who nourish their vast and overflowing spirit,
are unwilling even to meet with shallow and superficial people,
or those stained by the world.
How much more so those shén xiān—
why would they with urgent haste
allow people as insignificant as straw dogs
to know of them, or even seek them out,
and what is strange in never having known them?
One whose sight discerns a hundred paces
still cannot see clearly,
and yet wishes to take what is seen as existence,
and what is unseen as non-existence—
how much, then, must be absent from the world!
It is as if one tries to measure the sea with a finger,
and when the finger reaches its end claims that the water is finished.
The mayfly compares itself to the giant āo,
or thinks to calculate the age of the vast chūn tree—
how could such be possible?
Emperor Wèi Wéndì exhausted all observation and gained vast knowledge,
claiming that among things, there was nothing he had not experienced;
he declared that in the world there was no knife that could cut jade,
and no cloth that could be cleansed by fire;
but when he compiled the Diǎn Lùn,
he once wrote of this matter.
Not long after,
both objects appeared in the world.
The emperor then sighed deeply
and hastily destroyed those writings.
It may well be that nothing in this world is fixed and certain;
such is possibly the reason.
Prince Chén Sī once composed the Treatise on Dispersing Doubt, saying:
“At first, regarding the Daoist arts,
I directly called them the empty, deceptive words of foolish men.
But later, when I saw Wǔ Huángdì test Zuǒ Cí and others,
keeping them without grain for nearly a month,
yet their complexion did not fade,
and their strength was as before—they often said they could go fifty years without eating—
who could doubt as before?”
He also related:
“Ordering Gān Shǐ to hold a living fish in his mouth with a medicinal pellet,
then boiling it in seething fat,
those without the medicine were cooked and could be eaten;
those who held the medicine sported all day,
as if they were in water.
Giving mulberry leaves dusted with the same powder to silkworms,
the silkworms did not grow old even by the tenth month.
Feeding chicks and newborn puppies with longevity medicine,
they all ceased to grow.
Giving whiteness-restoring medicine to a white dog,
within a hundred days its fur turned entirely black.
Hence it is known that the things of the world
cannot all be known,
and to judge by one’s own supposition
is not reliable.”
He lamented only that he could not wholly sever himself from sounds and sights
to devote his heart solely to learning the way of longevity.
Those two Cáo, as scholars, read all texts,
and in talent were heroes of their age;
yet at first both declared the Dao absent,
but late in life they investigated principle and exhausted their nature,
thus did they sigh.
For those not even their equal,
not to believe in shén xiān
is not surprising.
Liú Xiàng, in his broad learning, delved into the subtle and wondrous,
traversed deeply and widely through the classics,
and in his thinking clarified true from false,
investigating what is and is not;
in his compiled Lièxiān Zhuàn,
there are more than seventy entries of xiān rén.
If those stories were untrue,
what purpose would there be in fabricating them?
Affairs of remote antiquity
could not all be personally witnessed,
but are all handed down in records and hearsay.
The Lièxiān Zhuàn thus radiantly displays the certainty of their existence.
Yet, if books do not emerge from within Zhōu Gōng’s gates,
or matters are not handled by Zhòngní’s hands,
then people of the world end up not believing in them.
If so, then everything recorded in ancient history
would all be false—
why doubt merely one thing?
Common people crave honor and love profit,
striving restlessly for fame and gain.
They use their own hearts
to speculate on the people of antiquity,
unwilling to believe that there were once those who refused imperial abdication
and slighted high office—
thinking, regarding the likes of Cháo and Xǔ,
or the followers of Lǎo Lái and Zhuāng Zhōu,
that such things could not have been.
How much the more, then, in the case of shén xiān,
whose existence is even harder to know;
how could one expect that the people of today would all believe in them?
Many say Liú Xiàng was not a sage,
and that his records
cannot be solely relied upon—
and this above all makes people sigh.
The historians of Lǔ could not match the virtue of Heaven and Earth,
yet Zhòngní used their records as scripture.
Sīmǎ Qiān could not shine as radiantly as the sun and moon,
yet Yáng Xióng praised his work as truthful record.
Liú Xiàng was a renowned scholar and worthy of the Hàn era—
could his records so easily be cast aside?
The reason why people of the world do not believe that xiān can be learned,
nor believe that fate can be prolonged,
is simply because Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔ did not obtain it,
or that Shǎo Jūn and Luán Tài failed to demonstrate it.
But one cannot use the poverty of Qián Lóu and Yuán Xiàn
to claim that in ancient times there were no rich men as Tào Zhū and Yī Dùn;
nor cite the ugliness of Wú Yán or Sù Liú
to conclude there were no beauties like Nán Wēi and Xī Shī in the past.
Moreover, those who advance zealously sometimes fail to succeed in their aims;
farmers sometimes fail to reap a harvest;
merchants may sometimes suffer losses;
and soldiers may sometimes gain nothing from battle.
How much more so in seeking immortality,
which is the most difficult of undertakings—how can all who attempt it expect to succeed?
As for those two kings and two ministers,
it is natural that they sought but did not obtain,
or some were diligent at first but slothful in the end,
or did not meet with an enlightened teacher—
how could such cases determine that xiān do not exist in the world?
As for seeking longevity,
cultivating the utmost Way,
the secret lies in one’s will
and not in wealth or rank.
If one is not the right person,
then high office and abundant riches
are but heavy burdens.
Why is this?
The methods of learning to become an immortal
desire tranquility and calm detachment,
cleansing away desires,
turning the gaze inward, listening within,
dwelling like a corpse with an untroubled mind;
yet the emperor bears the heavy responsibility of the world,
manages the affairs of government with his own hands,
constantly toils over myriads of affairs,
his spirit roams across the universe,
if one minor official goes astray,
then the kingly Way is diminished;
if the people err,
it is said to be his fault.
Strong wine disturbs his harmony,
alluring beauty undermines his roots,
thus what cuts the essence, depletes thought, and saps pure simplicity
cannot be completely or exhaustively discussed.
If a mosquito bites the skin, one cannot even sit at ease;
if lice attack in swarms, one cannot sleep in peace.
How much more is this the case
with the affairs of the four seas!
How could he ever obscure his keen senses,
quietly retire for meditative breathing,
keep to a long fasting and cleansing,
personally tend to the furnace and fire,
rise early and retire late
in order to fly on eight stones?
Hàn Wǔ enjoyed his kingdom
with the longest life among rulers,
he obtained only a small benefit in the cultivation of his nature.
Yet with the aid of measures of medicine
he could not meet the expense of great mineral elixirs;
with channels and ditches supplying water,
he could not manage the outflow of large rivers.
The methods of the immortals seek stillness, serenity, and non-action,
forgetting even bodily form;
but the ruler strikes the thousand-stone bell,
beats the drums that sound like thunder,
clamor and noise resound,
startling the soul and disturbing the heart,
with a hundred skills and ten thousand changes,
exhausting his essence and blocking his ears,
flying swiftly and running quickly,
fishing for the hidden and hunting the lofty.
The methods of the immortals wish that compassion would reach even the smallest creatures,
doing no harm to those who breathe;
but the ruler has the furious anger of Hè Sī,
the exterminating punishments of wholesale slaughter,
with the yellow axe swung once
and the Qí sword swiftly bestowed,
corpses lie prostrate for a thousand li,
blood flows in torrents,
the punishment of beheading
is never absent from the marketplace.
The methods of the immortals wish to avoid all foul odors,
to rest from food and cleanse the bowels;
but the ruler cooks fatty meats and slaughters plump beasts,
slaughters and carves multitudes of living beings,
eight delicacies and hundreds of blended flavors
arrayed before him by the square yard,
decocts and boils medicinal herbs,
delights in and gorges on delicious fare.
The methods of the immortals wish to extend compassion to the eight directions,
to see others as oneself;
but the ruler annexes the weak and attacks the ignorant,
takes from the disorderly, destroys the perishing,
expands lands and extends borders,
wipes out the altars and societies of men,
drives and gathers the people,
casts them into the place of death,
lonely souls left in remote lands,
corpses exposed and rotting in the wilds:
south of the Five Ridges are armies stained with blood and blades,
at the northern towers hang the heads of Dà Yuān,
pits full of massacred prisoners,
in numbers reaching hundreds of thousands,
burial mounds heaped with corpses,
rising up to touch the clouds,
exposed remains as thick as weeds,
filling the mountains and choking the valleys.
Qín Huáng made it so that, in ten households,
in nine there was rebellion;
Hàn Wǔ made it so the whole realm groaned,
with the population halved.
Prayers for benefit,
curses bring harm as well.
If even grasses can repay virtue,
then false sacrifices will surely bring resentment.
The many troubles afflict his vital organs,
both human and ghost alike unite in bitter hatred.
Those two sovereigns had only the reputation of loving immortals
but did not truly practice the Way;
their knowledge was shallow, their pursuits superficial,
they could not fully put them into action.
The essential subtleties are deep and secret,
yet they had no way to hear of them.
They could not obtain men of the Way
to compound for them the completed elixir of immortality,
so they did not gain long life;
there is nothing strange in that.
We common folk,
moreover, are utterly exhausted,
at home as poor as Zhǎng Qīng standing upright against a wall,
hunger in the belly like Yì Sāng running out of food,
embracing the cold outside the northern gate like the Róng and Yí in winter,
in summer overshadowed within the narrow wall like Rú Zhòng,
wishing to travel far but lacking carriage or boat,
wishing to accomplish something but lacking anyone to relieve our toil,
inside, we have no pleasure of fine silk,
outside, no joy in outings and sightseeing,
delicacies never cross our lips,
bright colors never reach our eyes,
fragrance never passes our nose,
the eight sounds never touch our ears,
a hundred worries assail our hearts,
countless hardships beset our homes,
dwelling in the world like this,
how could one be attached to it?
Some may obtain the essential secret of the Way,
or encounter an extraordinary master,
yet still regretfully cling to their aged wife and weak children,
remain affectionate toward hills where foxes and hares live,
and drag out lingering days until their decline and death,
unaware of the aging caused by passing days and months,
knowing that immortality could be attained yet unable to cultivate it,
troubled by the corrupt customs of the vulgar world yet unable to discard them.
Why is this so?
Because the affection for familiar habits is ultimately hard to dispel,
and the resolve to cut off from the world is not easily firm.
All the more so for those like the two Emperors,
rulers of the four seas,
whose pleasures and diversions
are not just one or two,
whose favorites and close attendants
are truly innumerable.
Supposing they were made to observe austerities for ten days or a month,
or spend a few days in quiet retreat,
they would still find it impossible,
let alone giving up inner affection for gentle beauty,
and outwardly casting off dazzling honor,
cutting off delicious delicacies from the mouth,
severing desires from the heart,
turning their back on glory and riches to go alone,
and seeking immortality in distant solitude.
How could they possibly endure it?
Therefore, in looking back over the past,
those who obtained the Way of immortality
were mostly men of poverty and low station,
not people of power and rank.
As for what Luán Tài knows,
it is truly shallow and superficial;
hungering and thirsting for honor and wealth,
pursuing dishonest gains and bribes,
parading empty pretense in lascivious indulgence,
forgetting danger and disaster in idleness,
a petty youth’s trickery and falsehood—
how could this prove that there are no immortals in the world?
In ancient times, Gōu Jiàn trained himself through bitterness on the grindstone,
and his soldiers fought fiercely, even contending to walk through fire.
Líng of Chǔ loved slender waists,
so many people in his state starved to death.
Qí Huán delighted in strange flavors,
and Yì Yá steamed his own son.
The Lord of Sòng rewarded emaciated filial sons,
and the dead lay house by house.
Whatever the ruler of men desires,
there is nothing that cannot be achieved.
When Hàn Wǔ summoned and sought practitioners of esoteric arts,
he favored and rewarded them excessively,
thus causing such people
to dare utter emptiness and falsehoods.
If Luán Tài truly possessed the Way,
how could it possibly be extinguished?
The one who possesses the Way
views rank and title as boiling cauldrons,
regards seals of office as mourning strips,
sees gold and jade as dirt and dung,
looks upon splendid halls as prison cells.
How could such a one wring his hands and speak vain words,
seeking glory and wealth by luck and chance,
reside in grand pillared chambers,
accept inestimable gifts,
wear the seals of fivefold profit,
enjoy the high status of a princess’s spouse,
sink into the pursuit of power and profit,
never knowing contentment nor sufficiency?
Such a one truly has not obtained the Way;
this can be known for certain.
According to Dǒng Zhòngshū’s compiled “House Record of Lǐ Shǎojūn,” it says:
Shǎojūn had a recipe for immortality,
but his family was poor and had no means to purchase the medicines,
so he left Hàn,
used borrowed titles to seek wealth,
and, when his Way was fulfilled, departed.
Also, according to the Inner Court Diary of Hàn,
when Shǎojūn was about to leave,
Emperor Wǔ dreamed of ascending Mount Sōnggāo together with him;
halfway,
an envoy riding a dragon and carrying a scepter
descended from the clouds.
It was said that Tàiyǐ summoned Shǎojūn.
When the emperor awoke,
he told those beside him,
“Based on my dream,
Shǎojūn is about to leave me.”
A few days later,
Shǎojūn claimed illness and died.
After a long time,
the emperor ordered his coffin opened;
there was no corpse,
only his clothing and cap remained.
According to the Daoist scripture,
the highest adept ascends bodily into the heavens,
and is called a heavenly immortal.
The middle adept wanders among famous mountains,
and is called an earthbound immortal.
The lowest adept dies and then sheds the body,
and is called a corpse-liberated immortal.
Now, Shǎojūn must be one of these corpse-liberated immortals.
In recent times, Hú Gōng was about to go with Fèi Chángfáng.
Also, Daoist Lǐ Yìqī prepared to depart with two disciples,
all claimed to die,
and their families kept vigil and buried them.
After several years,
Chángfáng returned.
Also, acquaintances saw Lǐ Yìqī and his two disciples all present in Pí County.
Their families, each opening the coffins to look,
found in each a single bamboo staff,
inscribed in cinnabar on each staff:
all were those who had achieved corpse-liberation.
In ancient times, Wáng Mǎng cited the classics to embellish his heresies,
yet he cannot be called a Ruist;
all he did was usurpation and theft.
Xiàngrú used playing the qín to secretly win Wénjūn,
but we cannot say that refined music necessarily leads to licentiousness.
Those who choke to death cannot blame Shénnóng for sowing grains,
those who die by fire cannot resent Suìrén for drilling fire,
those who drown cannot hold Emperor Xuān responsible for making boats,
those who drink to excess cannot denounce Dù Yí for producing wine.
How then can we use the deceit of Luán Tài
to claim the immortal Way truly does not exist?
This is like seeing Zhào Gāo and Dǒng Zhuó
and at once asserting that in antiquity there were no Yī Yǐn, Zhōu Gōng, or Huò Guāng.
Seeing Shāngchén and Mòdùn
and saying that there were never Bójī or Xiàojǐ in ancient times.
Again, in the collected works on immortals, there are methods for summoning spirits and indicting ghosts,
and also techniques for enabling people to see ghosts.
When common people hear of these things,
they all call it empty talk.
Some say there are no spirits or ghosts in the world,
others say they exist
but cannot be summoned or indicted.
Some say those who see ghosts
are xí when male,
and wū when female,
and that it must occur naturally,
not something that can be learned or obtained.
According to the Book of Hàn and Sīmǎ Qiān’s Records, both state that Shào Wēng of Qí
was made General Wénchéng by Emperor Wǔ.
When Emperor Wǔ's beloved Lady Lǐ died,
Shào Wēng could make the emperor see her as if alive.
He also enabled Emperor Wǔ to see the Kitchen God;
these are explicit records in the historical texts.
If esoteric arts can make ghosts manifest in form,
and furthermore, cause those who could not see ghosts to see them,
then by this reasoning,
what could there not be among other such things?
Spirits and ghosts often produce strange lights and transform in the human world,
as also recorded in the classics,
which are replete with accounts of spirits and ghosts.
If the common man yet does not believe that there are spirits and ghosts in the world,
how much less so for immortals who dwell on high and far away,
pure and impure streams following different courses,
ascending afar and departing,
never returning to the world?
Those who have not attained the Way,
how could they see or hear such things?
The families of the Ruists and the Mòists know this is not something to be taught,
so in the end, they never speak of its existence.
That common people do not believe,
is it not as it should be?
Only those who recognize the truth,
who compare and test many arts,
gain verification of them,
and examine their certainty,
can know these things alone,
it cannot be forced.
Thus, though one does not see spirits and ghosts,
nor see immortals,
it cannot be said that there are no immortals in the world.
Whether wise or foolish,
every person knows within themselves that they possess hún and pò;
if hún and pò depart partially, the person falls ill;
if they wholly depart, the person dies.
So, when they partially depart, the technicians have arts to summon and record them;
if they fully leave, the rites contain meanings for calling them back;
these things are most intimately close to us.
Yet they are born with a person,
and remain lifelong,
but none have themselves heard or seen them.
How can it be, then, simply because one has not heard or seen them,
that he declares they do not exist?
If we consider, for example, the ghost to whom Fǔ Shì repaid a favor,
the spirit incensed by King Chéngtāng at Qí,
Shēnshēng conversing with Húzǐ,
Dù Bó avenging his resentment on Zhōu Xuān,
Péngshēng assuming the form of a black boar,
Rúyì assuming the guise of a blue dog,
Guàn Fū guarding Tián Fěn,
Zǐyì smashing Yān Jiǎn,
Rùshōu descending at Shēn,
Lord Luán halting at a villager’s house,
Sù Jiāng interpreting omens and portents,
Xiào Sūn composing writings,
Lord Shén speaking at Shànglín,
Luóyáng serving in the court of Wú,
all matters of spirits and ghosts
are recorded on bamboo and silk,
plainly set forth in this manner,
too numerous to count.
Yet those blinded still claim they do not exist;
how much less will matters of long life,
which are seldom spoken of in the world, be heard!
To wish for all to believe,
is like forcing mosquitoes and gnats to shoulder mountains,
or discussing the sea with a frog in a well.
Common people have never seen dragons, qilin, luan, or phoenixes,
yet claim these creatures do not exist in the world,
thinking that the ancients devised auspicious omens in vain
to make rulers urge themselves on unceasingly,
hoping to obtain such rarities.
How much more so in hoping people will believe in the existence of immortals!
People claim that since Liú Xiàng failed to produce gold,
therefore he indulged in hidden quests and strange ways,
fond of transmitting fantasies,
and that all the immortals he compiled in Biographies of Immortals
were but fabrications.
Alas!
This is what is called discarding a whole foot of luminous jade
for a flaw of an inch,
and casting away priceless pure copper
on account of a blemish as small as an ant's nose.
This is not the far-sightedness of Jīng Hé,
nor the true appraisal of Fēng Hú.
Thus Zhūgōng was disconsolate,
and Xuē Zhú sighed long in sorrow.
Now, all methods of gold-making are to be found in the collections on immortality,
which the King of Huáinán excerpted
for the Hóngbǎo Zhěnzhōngshū.
Although these writings exist,
all the essential formulas are kept secret,
requiring oral transmission,
explanation in person when consulting the text,
only then can it be accomplished.
Regarding the medicines used,
they often changed their original names,
so they cannot be used simply by referencing them.
Liú Xiàng’s father Dé obtained this book from the prison of the King of Huáinán,
not through a teacher's transmission.
Xiàng himself did not understand the arts of the Way,
but happened to see this book by chance,
and assumed its meaning was all on the page,
thus he failed to produce gold.
As for his compilation of the Biographies of Immortals,
he mostly excerpts what Qin official Ruǎn Cāng wrote,
or records only what he personally heard or saw,
then recorded it,
so it was not fabrication.
Folly and children's rhymes,
the sages sometimes select;
the words of shepherds and woodcutters
sometimes should not be discarded.
Gathering wild radish and mustards,
do not despise the lower parts;
how can we, for a single error out of many thoughts,
claim that the classics are unusable,
or, because the sun and moon once suffered an eclipse,
assert that the suspended cosmos is not shining bright?
Foreign lands produce crystal bowls,
in fact made from combining five kinds of ash.
Now in Jiāoguǎng there are many who, having obtained the method, cast them accordingly.
If one tells this to common folk,
they simply refuse to believe.
They say crystal is by nature a natural thing,
akin to jade or stone.
How much less, then, in this world,
should there happen to be naturally occurring gold,
would common people believe in the possibility of artificially making it?
The ignorant even disbelieve that yellow lead and hūfěn
are made by transforming lead;
they also disbelieve that mules and jùxū
are produced by the union of donkey and horse.
They claim each thing has its own type.
How much more so, then, regarding difficult-to-understand matters!
Where what one sees is little,
what one finds strange is much—
thus it is always so in the world.
Truly, this saying is trustworthy:
though the matter is as clear as heaven,
yet people are like living beneath an overturned basin,
how could they recognize the supreme truth?
Someone questioned, saying:
"Among people, there is Lǎo Péng,
just as among trees, there are pine and cypress;
having received this from nature,
how can it be learned?"
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"When it comes to shaping and transforming creation,
nothing is more spiritual than humans.
Thus, those who have mastered it on a superficial level
can make use of the myriad things;
those who have attained its depths
can live long and see far.
Knowing that superior medicines prolong life,
they take these medicines to seek immortality.
Knowing the tortoise and the crane live long lives,
they imitate their methods to increase their years.
Moreover, the branches and leaves of pines and cypresses
are distinct from other trees.
The bodies and appearances of tortoises and cranes
are different from other creatures.
As for Lǎo Péng, he was still just a human,
not of a different kind, and yet his lifespan alone was long;
this was due to attaining the Dào,
not by nature.
Other trees cannot model themselves after the pine and cypress;
other creatures cannot learn from the tortoise and crane;
therefore they are short-lived.
But a person of understanding and wisdom
who can cultivate the Way of Lǎo Péng
can achieve the same results.
If you say there are no immortals in the world,
yet among the ancient worthies' records
there are nearly a thousand individuals,
all with their family and given names,
along with accounts of their activities from beginning to end;
these are not empty words.
If you say they each only received unique endowments,
yet their transmissions all involved teachers and the practice of taking medicines;
it was not innate knowledge.
If the techniques of the Dào were impossible to learn,
then how are there those who can change their appearance,
swallow knives and spit fire,
sit and die or stand and disappear,
raise clouds and summon mist,
call forth insects and snakes,
gather fish and turtles together,
turn thirty-six kinds of stones instantly into water,
dissolve jade into terraces,
melt gold into syrup,
enter deep waters without getting wet,
tread on blades without being injured—
feats of transformation and illusion,
more than nine hundred in number;
when these are followed and put into practice,
none fails to prove effective.
Why, then, are you unwilling to trust that immortality can be attained!
The Way of Immortality is slow to achieve,
with many prohibitions and taboos;
without a will to surpass the ordinary,
and the talent for perseverance,
one cannot keep to it.
Some people, perhaps with a bit of fondness yet doubts in their hearts,
abandon it halfway,
and then claim that the Way of Immortality and long life
is truly impossible to gain.
The classic of Immortals says,
'Take cinnabar and guard the One,
your fate joined with Heaven;
refine the essence, nurture the breath,
and your lifespan will have no limit.'
All these are essential words of the highest Dào.
Among common gentlemen,
they do not deceive themselves inwardly,
nor feel shame before their own shadow without;
they do not cheat Heaven above,
nor break their word below—
how much more so the True Men of ancient times!
How would they invent empty words,
using what is said to be utterly unachievable
to delude future generations?
What benefit would there be!
If one has not the allotment of fate,
in the end they cannot be made to believe,
so how could they be forcibly made to have faith?"
Someone objected, saying:
“The long lifespans of the guī and hè are merely empty words passed down in the world;
who has ever accompanied these two creatures from birth to death and thus come to know this?”
Bào Pǔzǐ responded:
“If one grasps the essentials,
then what lies beyond the eight extremes
is as though it were on one’s own palm;
even things a hundred generations past
seem as if contemporaneous.
There is no need for them to be right beside porch or hall,
or to wait until they are visible to the eye
before one can know them.
According to the Yùcèjì:
The guī of a thousand years
has all five colors in full;
on its forehead, two bones rise like horns;
it comprehends human speech;
it floats upon lotus leaves,
or dwells beneath clumps of yarrow;
above it, at times, white clouds and coiling serpents appear.
The hè of a thousand years
calls forth in accord with the seasons;
it is able to perch in trees;
those that have not yet lived a thousand years
never collect upon branches;
their color is pure white, and the brain is completely red.
If one observes this,
then one can know.
Moreover, those creatures that are long-lived are mostly wise,
and generally dwell in deep and concealed places;
thus few people ever see them.
According to the Yùcèjì and Chāngyǔjīng,
it is not only these two creatures that are long-lived.
It is said the sōng tree of a thousand years
spreads wide on all sides,
yet its top does not grow longer;
viewed from afar,
it appears like a reclined canopy.
Within it are creatures
that may resemble blue oxen,
or blue goats,
or blue dogs,
or blue people;
all live ten thousand years.
It is also said
that serpents can live endlessly;
the xiǎnhóu lives eight hundred years and becomes a yuán;
the yuán lives five hundred years and becomes a jué;
the jué lives one thousand years.
The chánchú lives three thousand years;
the qílín lives two thousand years.
The ténghuáng horse
and the jíguāng beast
both live three thousand years.
Birds of a thousand years
and fowl of ten thousand years
all have human faces and birds’ bodies,
their lifespans matching their names.
The hǔ, lù, and tù
all live a thousand years;
of those whose lives reach five hundred years,
the fur turns white.
The xióng that lives five hundred years
can transform itself.
Foxes, jackals, and wolves
each live eight hundred years;
when they reach five hundred years,
they are skilled at transforming into human form.
The mouse lives three hundred years;
reaching one hundred years, its color turns white;
it is skilled at leaning on humans to divine,
called zhòng;
it knows the fortunes of the year and affairs a thousand li away.
To record all such cases in proportion
would be impossible in full.
But one who has broad knowledge and encounters a thing can name it,
while one who is widely heard is not confused by principle.
Why must one always consort with the guī or hè
before one can know?
If one does not know things,
then even among the grasses and trees of the garden,
or the birds and beasts of the fields and ponds,
many remain unknown;
how much more so with the extraordinary ones!
The Shǐjì, in the Guīcèzhuàn, says:
Among the common people between the Jiāng and Huái, when a child,
someone used a guī as the support of a bed;
afterwards, he grew old and died,
his family moved the bed,
and the guī was still alive.
This already accounts for no less than fifty or sixty years,
without eating or drinking,
lasting so long and yet not dying;
how vastly different it is from ordinary creatures,
so what doubt can there be about a lifespan of a thousand years?
In the Daoist scripture, one models breathing after the guī;
is this not for a reason?
Thus, Tàiqiū Zhǎng Yǐngchuān Chén Zhònggōng,
a man of profound discourse,
wrote in the Record of Strange Accounts:
There was a man of his commandery named Zhāng Guǎngdìng,
who, during turmoil, often sought refuge elsewhere.
He had a daughter four years old
who could not walk far,
nor could she be carried;
to abandon her would surely cause her to starve,
yet he did not wish her bones to be left exposed.
At the mouth of the village was an ancient mound,
in the top of which was an opening.
He placed her in a vessel and lowered her down,
leaving her in the mound
with several months’ supply of dried rice and water, and then departed.
When peace was restored
after three years,
Guǎngdìng was finally able to return home,
intending to gather his daughter’s bones from the mound
and rebury them.
Guǎngdìng went to see,
and the girl was still sitting in the mound;
she saw her parents,
still recognized them, and was greatly overjoyed.
But the parents, at first, feared she was a ghost;
her father descended to confirm,
and realized she was not dead.
Asked how she survived,
the girl said that when her provisions first ran out, she was extremely hungry;
she noticed, in a corner of the mound, a creature
stretching its neck and swallowing qi;
she tried to imitate it,
and quickly ceased to feel hunger,
doing this every day up until now.
The clothes left by her parents when they departed
remained in the mound;
she did not come and go,
and the clothing did not become worn,
so she was not cold or frozen.
Guǎngdìng then searched for the creature the girl described,
and it turned out to be a large guī.
When the girl ate grain outside,
at first she had stomach pain and vomited,
but after a while she became accustomed.
This is further proof that the guī has a method for not dying,
and that those who follow the Dao and imitate it
may attain the guī’s longevity.
Both Sīmǎ Qiān and Zhònggōng
were not men who spoke carelessly.
Of the myriad insects and birds in the world,
the ancients alone singled out these two creatures,
making clear that they alone are extraordinary among the many.
To see one corner is to comprehend the whole.”
Someone posed a difficulty, saying:
“The guī can burrow in the earth,
the hè can fly in the sky.
If a person were made to burrow for a short while,
or to fly for a brief moment,
yet even then he could not do it.
How then could their longevity be learned?”
Bào Pǔzǐ answered:
“There are many creatures that can burrow,
and many birds that are able to fly;
yet only the guī and hè are singled out for their long-lived ages.
The reason they do not die
does not lie in their burrowing or flying.
Thus, the zhēnrén merely teach to learn their Way of leading and nourishing life to extend one's years,
to model their consumption of qi in order to abstain from grains,
not to imitate their burrowing in the earth or flying in the sky.
Those who attain the Way,
above can raise their bodies to the clouds,
below can dive and swim in rivers and seas.
Thus, Xiāo Shǐ rode together with the soaring phoenix to traverse the void,
Qín Gāo rode a vermilion carp in the deep abyss—
these are the proofs.
Why restrict it merely to momentary burrowing
and brief flights alone!
Dragons, serpents, jiāo and chī,
monkeys, apes, tuó and lí—
all are able to go without eating for an entire winter,
and during the time they do not eat,
they are in fact fatter than when they do eat.
But one cannot gain their method.
Moreover, in those single particular excellences,
many creatures exceed man;
it is not limited to the guī and hè.
Thus Tài Hào learned from the spider to weave nets,
Jīn Tiān relied on the nine bù to regulate the seasons,
Emperor Xuān awaited the call of the phoenix to tune his musical pitches,
Táng Yáo observed the měng pod to understand the moon’s phases,
the tortoise knows the past,
the magpie knows what is to come,
Lord Yú recognizes the signs of droughts and floods,
the mayfly knows the location of hidden springs,
the white wolf knew of the rise of the Yin house,
the yuèzhuó beheld the flourishing of the Zhōu house,
the guī and hè alone understand cultivation and nourishment of life,
so it is nothing strange.
Moreover, the immortal writings on the Way to longevity
have several hundred methods,
differing only in speed and intricacy;
it is by no means necessary to follow the guī and hè in all things.
The superior man expands his thought to fathomless distances,
reaching natural and mysterious understanding;
it is difficult to use the shallow sentiments of the vulgar
to infer the far-reaching meaning of the shénxiān.”
Someone said,
“We do not know the principle of longevity for people today;
how could people of old alone have known it?”
“This is but a narrow discussion of the ignorant and benighted;
it is not the attitude of those who have attained understanding.
One who divines the mysterious principles of the heavenly patterns,
who measures the waxing and waning of the seven celestial directors,
discusses eclipses and conjunctions in past times,
discerns ascensions and declines of future ages,
gazes upward at auspicious omens among the clouds,
looks down to determine fortune and misfortune in oracle signs,
manipulates the three chessboards to decide success or failure in a campaign,
interprets the nine tokens to judge the regions of calamity and fortune,
calculates with multiplication and division
to exhaust the conditions of ghosts and spirits,
interweaves the six emotions
to deal with endless variations of good and ill—
the root and origin can be investigated,
forms and principles can be sought.
Yet ordinary talents and nearby instruments
still cannot penetrate the depths where learning is governed,
and as for the simple-minded,
they merely sharpen their thoughts on the dregs,
unable to fully probe the subtle and fine.
In the rough skills of mortise and tenon work
there is yet the untransmitted subtlety of the wheelwright;
in the meager art of snaring cicadas
there is the inspired skill of the stooped old man;
it lies in the person,
and comes from their utmost refinement.
How much more so is the Way of the shénxiān,
whose intentions are deep and far-reaching,
and whose roots and stalks are indeed not easily found.
The company of Sōng Qiáo,
even if they obtain the effect,
may not necessarily fathom the reasons for it,
how much less can ordinary men?
The practice can be learned,
and so the people of old recorded and passed it on
to hand down to those who can comprehend.
If the mind comprehends and the intention is attained,
then it is credible and one should cultivate it;
if suspicion remains in the breast,
it all comes from one's own destiny;
one should not press the ancients as to why they alone understood this
while I alone fail to know it.
Now I know that immortality can be attained,
I am able to abstain from food and not eat,
I guarantee that the floating pearl can indeed fly,
and the yellow and white elixirs can be sought.
But if you demand I seek their ultimate principles,
then I too in fact do not know.
If people of the world regard what their reasoning can achieve as real existence,
and deem whatever they cannot reach as non-existent,
then there would be few things under heaven indeed.
Thus, Lǎozǐ said,
to rely on the ferret’s head to fix rat leaks,
to use the woodpecker’s beak to remedy rotten teeth—
these too are examples for analogical seeking.
Conversely, the crab producing lacquer,
hemp spoiling wine—
such things cannot be inferred by reason.
Ten thousand differences swirl in confusion;
how can one’s intention ever exhaust them all?
Suppose one clings to a grave illness
and needs a good medicine for rescue,
yet is unwilling to immediately take it,
and insists on knowing the original intent behind Shénnóng and Qí Bó’s using this herb for this disease
—that would not avoid being foolish.”
Someone said:
“Life and death are determined by fate,
length or shortness of life set from the beginning,
not something
that medicines can alter for better or worse.
If a finger is already severed and then joined again,
it cannot be reconnected;
if blood is already spilled and swallowed,
it brings no benefit.
How much less so consuming those alien types like pine and cypress
in hopes of extending the brief span of one's years?
That is quite impossible.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“As for this argument,
it is only by what is of the same kind
that benefit can be obtained;
if so, then a severed finger
or spilled blood,
both originally of the same body,
not of different kinds—
why, having been severed, can they not be rejoined,
and when spilled, cannot be taken up anew?
I have several times seen men use snake-carried ointment to reattach severed fingers,
or mulberry beans to replace the feet of chickens and ducks;
the benefits of alien things
cannot be denied.
If you say one should not rely on other things,
should one then pound flesh and smelt bones
to make medicines for wounds,
or boil skins and cook hair
to treat baldness and hair loss?
Water and soil are not of the same body as the hundred plants,
yet the hundred plants all rely upon them to grow.
The five grains are not of the human kind,
yet humans must depend on them for life.
Fat is not of the fire’s lineage,
water is not the kin of fish,
yet when fat is exhausted the fire is quenched,
and when water dries up, the fish die.
Cut down trees and the mistletoe dies;
mow the grass and the dodder withers;
if river crabs do not return, the jí perish;
when the mulberry is felled, the wood-boring pests are wiped out.
By drawing analogies and extending them,
one can come to an understanding.
When gold and jade fill the nine orifices,
the dead do not decay.
When salted brine soaks through flesh and marrow,
dried meats and preserved foods do not rot.
How much more then with substances suitable for the body and nourishing to life
when they are taken into oneself—
why marvel that they can make a person long-lived?”
Someone questioned, saying:
“The writings on shénxiān methods
seem plausible yet are false;
surely they are fabricated by enthusiasts who make things up rashly,
and not necessarily written by Huáng Lǎo,
nor examined by Sōng Qiáo.”
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
“If your refined argument were true,
then the methods should not be effective,
but when trying even the minor ones,
none fail to produce results.
I have repeatedly seen people use these methods: seeking water by means of the setting moon,
drawing fire with a burning mirror from the morning sun,
concealing themselves so as to sink into invisibility,
altering their appearance to become different beings,
throwing a knotted kerchief to the ground and causing a rabbit to run,
attaching a needle to a scarlet belt and making a snake crawl,
melons and fruits ripening in a moment,
dragons and fishes swimming about in basins,
all just as the stories describe.
According to the Hànshū, Luán Tàichū appeared before Emperor Wǔ,
and was made to compete at chess;
the chess pieces moved on their own.
Moreover, the Later Hànshū records that Wèi Shàng could be sitting here while his wraith stood elsewhere,
and Zhāng Kǎi could summon clouds to rise and fog to gather;
these are all recorded by reputable historians
and are reliable and verifiable.
As for these techniques,
they all belong to the category of shénxiān;
it is thus clear they are not baseless fabrications.
If the minor arts are effective,
why should the way to longevity
alone not be so?”
Someone said:
“If it is truly possible to learn the shénxiān arts,
rise swiftly to the heavens,
turning away from the mundane world,
then who would continue the ancestral rites?
There would be no one to uphold and perform them.
If the spirits of the ancestors are aware,
would they not starve?”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“I have heard that to preserve the body unharmed is called the ultimate filial piety;
how much more so in attaining the way of the immortals,
gaining long life and enduring vision,
so that even after Heaven and Earth pass away,
one will have received true preservation and perfect return—
is this not the highest goal?
If one can ascend to the void and tread upon shadows,
ride in a cloud-chariot with a rainbow canopy,
partake of the rosy mists of dawn,
absorb the pure essence of black and yellow energy,
drink jade nectar and golden brew,
eat emerald fungus and vermilion blossoms,
reside in jade halls and rare chambers,
wander freely in the highest clear heavens—
then if the ancestral spirits are aware,
they will bask in my glory.
Perhaps I could aid and advise the Five Emperors,
or oversee and command the myriad numinous beings;
high rank would come without seeking,
my meals would be taken among splendid gems,
power would encompass the realms of Luófēng,
my majesty would make Liángchéng tremble;
truly, understanding such a way
yet not perceiving its mysteries,
there would be no one left unfed.
The highest in attaining Dao
is none other than Bǒ Yáng.
Bǒ Yáng had a son named Zōng,
who served Wèi as a general
and for his merit was enfeoffed at Duànqián.
Thus, students of immortality today
may all have descendants
to inherit sacrifices;
how then could the rites of sacrifice
ever be severed?”
Someone said:
“If one who has attained Dao
has fully mastered the arts of breathing
and thoroughly knows the essentials of ingesting elixirs,
can cover his ears and hear a thousand li away,
can close his eyes and see the future;
some abandon splendid carriages to drive dragons,
others leave the Divine Land to dwell on Péng and Yíng;
yet some linger among ordinary folk,
free and easy in the human world.
Why is it that some do not completely vanish in pursuit of mystery and void,
yet all seem to share the same aspiration,
though their dwellings or departures differ?
Why?”
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
“I heard from my former master:
Some immortals ascend to Heaven,
others remain on Earth,
but all pursue longevity;
each stays or goes as pleases him.
Moreover, in the methods for taking the elixir and golden liquor,
if one wishes to linger in the world
he takes only half a dose.
If later he seeks to ascend to Heaven,
he then takes the full dose.
The matter of not dying is already decided;
there is no longer any sudden peril to fear.
He might choose to roam the world,
or enter renowned mountains—
what is there to dread?
Péngzǔ said,
‘In Heaven are many high officials and great spirits;
new immortals have low rank,
and those they serve are many;
thus they toil and labor,
and it is not worthwhile to be anxious about ascending to Heaven;
better to remain in the human world for more than eight hundred years.’
It is also said,
‘Those in ancient times who became immortals
sometimes sprouted feathers and wings,
transformed and flew,
but lost their human nature,
taking on other forms,
as a sparrow becomes a clam,
or a pheasant a mirage;
this is not the human Way.
The human Way is to eat fine food,
wear light and warm clothes,
unite yin and yang,
hold office and rank,
have keen senses,
strong bones and joints,
a cheerful countenance,
grow old but not feeble,
prolong life and maintain clear vision,
come and go at will,
immune to cold, heat, wind, or damp,
unassailable by spirits and demons,
invulnerable to weapons or poisons,
untroubled by sorrow, joy, slander, or praise—
this is the true nobility.
If one casts aside wife and children,
dwells alone in mountains and marshes,
utterly severs human ties,
and sits solitary among trees and rocks,
what worth is there in that?
In ancient times, Ānqí Xiānshēng, Lóngméi Nínggōng, Xiū Yánggōng, and Yīn Chángshēng
were all those who took only half a dose of golden elixir.
They remained in the world
for nearly a thousand years
before departing.
Frankly speaking,
those who seek longevity
simply value their present desires;
they do not truly crave immediate ascension to the void
and do not consider soaring above as superior to living on earth.
If one could stay at home and not die,
why hasten to ascend to Heaven?
If immortality left no possibility to remain,
it would be only one more option.
Thus Péngzǔ’s remark
was made to accord with human feelings.”
Someone asked:
“Should those who practice the Dào first establish merit and virtue,
is this truly so?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“Indeed.
According to the middle section of the Yùqián Jīng,
establishing merit is the highest,
removing faults is next.
Those who follow the Dào, by saving people from danger and helping them avoid calamities,
protecting them from illness,
so that they do not die in vain,
this is the utmost merit.
Those who seek to become immortals
must take loyalty, filial piety, harmony, gentleness, benevolence, and faith as their foundation.
If one does not cultivate virtue and conduct,
but only pursues formulas and techniques,
he will not attain long life.
For great evil deeds,
the Controller of Fate takes away cycles from one’s lifespan;
for lesser faults, lesser portions are removed,
each according to the severity of the transgression,
thus the amount taken varies.
All people’s allotted fate and lifespan
already have a fixed number,
if their fundamental number is great,
then their years are difficult to exhaust, and their death is delayed;
if their original allotment is slight,
but their offenses are many,
their years run out quickly and they die early.
It is also said,
if a person desires to become an earthbound immortal,
he must establish three hundred good deeds;
those who seek to become celestial immortals
must establish one thousand two hundred good deeds.
If one has one thousand one hundred and ninety-nine good deeds,
but commits one evil out of nowhere,
then all previous good deeds are lost,
and one must start over to accumulate goodness.
Therefore, goodness does not depend on greatness,
nor evil on smallness.
Even without committing evil actions,
if by words or deeds,
or by demanding repayment for acts of charity,
one immediately loses the goodness of that deed,
though not all is lost.
It also says,
if accumulation of good deeds is not yet full,
even if one takes elixirs of immortality,
it is of no benefit.
If one does not take immortal elixirs,
but continues to perform good deeds,
though not yet attaining immortality,
he may avoid the calamity of sudden death.
I further suspect that the likes of Péng Zǔ,
whose good works were insufficient,
therefore could not ascend to Heaven.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
I have studied texts on nourishing life,
collected methods for attaining longevity,
the volumes I have perused
number in the thousands,
and without exception, all regard the Reverted Cinnabar and Golden Elixir as essential.
Thus, these two things
are, indeed, the ultimate in the Dao of Immortality.
If by taking these, one does not become immortal,
then since ancient times, there have never been immortals.
In the past, when the Upper Kingdom fell into chaos,
all scattered in flight.
I traveled through the various provinces of Xú, Yù, Jīng, Xiāng, Jiāng, and Guǎng,
and met and saw several hundred wandering Daoists.
Some were of established repute,
renowned beyond the clouds and sun.
Yet in general, they were all alike;
what they understood and experienced
ranged from deep to shallow, from possessing to lacking,
but none could outdo the others.
Though each had dozens of volumes of books,
not one could fully explain them,
but only copied and stored them.
Some knew the methods of moving qi, grain abstention, and taking various herbs,
and the medical texts they held
were mostly similar in content.
There was not one who did not possess the Dàojī Jīng on mechanisms of the Dao,
and all regarded this as the most secret,
saying it was authored by Jūn Xǐ,
but I told them,
‘It was authored by Wáng Tú, military inspector during the Wei era,
not by ancient sages.
Tú had no knowledge of the Great Elixir,
but simply wished to enter seclusion and seek immortality by practicing breath control,
thus he wrote the Dàojī,
thinking the Way was complete in this,
but this greatly misleads people.’
When I asked various Daoists about the Divine Elixir, Golden Fluid,
and about the Sān Huáng Nèiwén methods for summoning heavenly deities and earth spirits,
not one knew of them.
Nevertheless, they boasted and praised themselves, deceiving others,
claiming they had lived long,
and saying that most of them had journeyed with immortals.
Those who could discuss the most subtle matters were extremely rare.
Some had only vaguely heard of the Golden Elixir,
but did not believe that anyone in the present age could attain it,
all claiming that only immortals of high antiquity
could understand it.
Some had received exoteric teachings,
but not the true scriptures.
Some had acquired miscellaneous and fragmented alchemical recipes,
and then thought the entire teaching of elixir-making was contained therein.
In the past, Zuǒ Yuánfàng practiced in concentration on Tiānzhù Mountain,
and a spirit being bestowed upon him the scriptures of the Golden Elixir Immortal.
Caught up in the chaos at the end of the Hàn,
he had no leisure to practice,
so he fled to cross the Yangtze in the east,
intending to seek out a famous mountain to cultivate this Dao.
My granduncle Xiāngōng
also received it from Yuánfàng.
He obtained three volumes of the Tàiqīng Elixir Scripture, one volume of the Jiǔdǐng Elixir Scripture, and one of the Golden Fluid Elixir Scripture.
My master Zhèng Jūn
was the disciple of my granduncle Xiāngōng,
received it from my granduncle,
but as his family was poor, he could not afford to buy the medicines.
I served him personally,
diligently cleaning and tending him for a long time,
and on Mǎjì Mountain, set up an altar to pledge myself and received the transmission,
including all the oral formulas never set down in writing.
This book was previously unknown in Jiāngdōng,
it originated from Zuǒ Yuánfàng,
Yuánfàng transmitted it to my granduncle,
my granduncle to Zhèng Jūn,
Zhèng Jūn to me;
hence, no other Daoists know of it.
Yet it has been over twenty years since I received it,
but I have no possessions or resources,
nothing with which to carry it out,
and can only sigh in vain.
There are those with gold piling up in chests
and money amassed like mountains,
yet they do not know of this undying method.
Even if they heard of it,
there is not one in ten thousand who would believe it.
Why is this so?
Those who have drunk from the Jade Terrace know the blandness of duckweed soup;
he who has gazed upon Kūnlún perceives the utter lowliness of small mounds.
Having seen the Way of the Golden Elixir,
one no longer wishes to look at trivial medical formulas.
But the Great Elixir is not easily made;
for now, one must resort to medicinal minor ones in order to support oneself.
Yet, though one consumes myriad bushels of other medicines,
and may gain slight benefit,
ultimately they cannot bring one to true long life.
So the secret words of Lǎozǐ say:
If you do not obtain the Reverted Cinnabar and Golden Elixir,
your efforts are but in vain.
Even the five grains can sustain human life;
those who receive them live,
and those who are deprived of them die.
How much more so the supreme spirit elixir,
whose benefit for people must be a myriad times greater than the grains!
As for the Golden Elixir,
the longer it is fired,
the more marvelous its transformations.
Gold, when placed in fire,
remains undiminished even after a hundred refinings;
if buried,
it will not decay till the end of Heaven.
Taking these two substances,
they refine the body,
and can thereby keep one from aging and dying.
This is by borrowing external things to strengthen oneself,
just as fat feeds a fire and cannot be extinguished,
copper-green applied to feet
prevents corruption by water,
which is to use copper's strength to defend the flesh.
Let the Golden Elixir enter the body,
penetrating and nourishing the vital and protective energies,
this is never merely external application like copper-green.
In this world, many do not believe in the supreme Way,
and so the vast majority are just like this.
Yet, if by a thousandth chance, there are those with a liking for such things,
but who never encounter these methods,
and never meet an enlightened master,
how can they ever hear that such a marvelous thing exists in the world?
I now briefly copy the essentials of the Golden Elixir,
to show later students of like mind.
Those who diligently seek it
must not stick to shallow and superficial recipes,
thinking them enough to cross the ages.
If they never encounter it,
they should simply abandon limitless hopes.
By contemplating this teaching,
one will surely know what it is to emerge from filth to float on the open sea,
to turn one’s back on fireflies and candles and face the sun and moon,
to hear thunder and recognize the vulgarity of a drum,
to see a giant whale and know the minuteness of an inch-long shellfish.
If, however, one muddles about,
without pursuing what is primary,
and seeks to soar upward with inferior medicines,
how is this any different than flogging a lame donkey to overtake a swift wind,
or steering a basket-raft to cross a great river?”
Moreover, there are very many minor elixirs and pill formulas;
however, the making of them differs in depth and complexity.
Therefore, the strength and efficacy are not the same;
even though some are superior and some inferior,
they are so distinct as to be in different categories,
just like a wine of single fermentation
cannot be compared with the pure flavor of Jǐuyùn wine.
Yet even the lowest of the minor elixirs
is still far superior to the highest among herbs and plants.
For all herbs and trees, when burned, turn to ashes,
yet when Dānshā is burned, it becomes mercury,
and after many transformations, it returns again to Dānshā;
thus, its difference from common vegetation is vast indeed.
Therefore, it can make one live long;
the immortals alone clearly see this principle,
and their separation from ordinary people
—how exceedingly vast and infinite it is!
People of the world have little knowledge
and are full of suspicions;
some do not know that mercury comes from Dānshā,
and even when told, they simply will not believe;
they say Dānshā is originally a red substance,
so how could it ever produce this white substance?
They also say Dānshā is merely a stone;
yet when stones are burned, they all turn to ash,
so why does Dānshā alone act differently?
Even such simple and near-at-hand matters
cannot be explained to them;
as for hearing about the Way of Immortality,
they only laugh heartily at it—
is this not as one would expect?
In ancient times, the zhēnrén, out of compassion for those in future generations who could be taught,
created methods and formulas,
in every possible way wishing only that they might escape the disaster of death—
these can truly be called words of the utmost importance.
Yet ordinary people ultimately will not believe,
and say it is empty rhetoric.
If these are mere empty words,
how could it be that after nine purifications and nine transformations,
things are completed in a few days
and all precisely according to the formulas?
What the zhēnrén know
truly cannot be attained by the limited thoughts of the average.
Since youth I have loved methods and techniques;
carrying my provisions, I have gone to ask questions,
never shirking danger or distance.
Whenever I hear of something unusual
I am filled with joy.
Even when met with disparagement or mockery,
I do not feel distressed.
Who can know that those who come after will not surpass those today?
For this reason, I have written this for those of insight.
Is it that I merely admire the strange and rare,
or embellish empty words,
wishing only for my book to circulate in the world
and win the approval of worldly people?
Just as even great sunlight cannot rejuvenate withered wood,
and the wisest cannot change the ignorant,
a book is for the enlightened to transmit,
and a matter is valued by those with discernment.
The farmer receives a red bow to drive away birds,
while the southern barbarians use ceremonial robes as firewood;
those who do not understand—
how can they be forced?
People today eat their fill all day,
yet rarely devote themselves to the studies of the Rú or Mò,
or to cultivating virtue and progress;
rather, they seek only leisure and carefree wandering,
thus passing all their years.
Whatever they pursue
is either honor or profit.
Some go hunting for blue [horses] and yellow [dogs] on the Central Plains,
some idly linger with cups and steaming soup,
some waste away with beauties and music,
some drown in luxury silks,
some draw the bow to the point of exhausting their sinews,
some gamble and play games at the expense of honest effort.
Upon hearing words of the ultimate Way, they act as if drunk,
seeing discussions of the Way, they doze in daylight.
Possessing a body, yet they do not cultivate it;
they act to bring themselves to the place of death,
refusing to inquire into ways of nourishing life;
instead, they themselves wish to cut, pare,
boil,
and exhaust
and strain themselves to the last drop.
Those who have the Way treasure and guard their knowledge,
and do not seek from others;
how then could they force themselves to speak of it to all?
Common sayings among people
are all that attaining long life, if possible,
the ancients who were wealthy and noble
should have attained it,
and since none of them did,
therefore this Way does not exist.
But they do not realize that the wealthy and noble of antiquity
were only like the wealthy and noble of today;
likewise, none believed or sought after it,
and all took whatever their eyes desired as most urgent;
so then, how could they obtain it?
Suppose one cannot make up their mind
to believe that fate and life may be prolonged,
and immortality may be attained,
yet what is there to lose by trying?
If one makes an attempt and achieves but a minor effect—
even if only to gain two or three hundred years—
is this not better than the common man’s brief and early death?
Of all the matters under heaven,
the Way and the arts are the most difficult to understand.
How can one use an average mind
to decide that in the world there certainly cannot be a Way to longevity?
If it be simply because people in this age do not believe it,
and therefore say it does not exist,
then how could it be that wise people are so common in this age?
If so, how could there be so many among them?
Today, if there are those who know the meaning of the Way and still study and seek it,
are they necessarily the most foolish?
Must they always be worse than worldly people?
And sometimes people worry in seeking longevity,
that if they do not obtain it,
they fear others will laugh at them,
and think them deluded and confused.
But if, in making up one’s mind,
in one in ten thousand cases one fails,
and there truly exists such a Way to immortality in the world,
would one not then be the laughingstock of those who did obtain it?
The sun and moon cannot shine everywhere;
how can a human heart trust only itself?
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
According to the Huángdì Jiǔdǐng Shéndān Jīng,
the Huángdì took it [the elixir],
and thereby ascended to immortality.
