It also says:
Although breathing and Daoyin,
and taking herbal medicines,
may prolong life,
they cannot avert death;
but if one takes shéndān, one’s life will never end,
being coextensive with Heaven and Earth,
riding clouds and driving dragons,
rising and descending through Tàiqīng.
The Huángdì transmitted this to Xuánzǐ,
warning him:
“This Way is most weighty;
it must be entrusted to the worthy;
if someone is not such a person,
even if they have piles of jade a mountain high,
do not speak of this Way to them.
The one who receives it must cast a golden man and a golden fish into the flowing eastern waters as a pledge,
taste blood as a covenant;
if one does not have the bones of an immortal,
one also cannot attain to see this Way.”
To combine dān, one must be within famous mountains,
in places where there are no people,
joined by no more than three companions,
first fasting for a hundred days,
bathing in the five perfumes,
taking utmost purity and cleanliness,
avoiding filth and dirt,
and contact with common people;
and also not allowing those who do not believe in the Way to know of it,
nor slandering or belittling the divine medicine,
or else the medicine will not succeed.
If successful, the whole family may attain immortality,
not just one person.”
People of the world do not compound shéndān,
but rather believe in herbs and plants as medicines.
But herbs and medicines,
when buried, decay;
when boiled, become mush;
when burned, become charcoal;
they cannot reproduce themselves;
how could they grant life to man?
The Nine Dān [elixirs]
are the essentials for longevity,
not what common people ought to see or hear.
Thousands upon tens of thousands, teeming and ignorant,
know only to crave wealth and privilege;
are they not but walking corpses?
At the time of compounding, one must also make offerings;
there is a scroll containing the ritual diagrams for this.
The first dān is called Dānhuá.
First, make xuánhuáng;
use xiónghuáng water, fánshí water, róngyán, lǔyán, yǔshí, mǔlì, chìshízhī, huáshí, húfěn, each several tens of catties,
to create “six-one” mud;
fire it for thirty-six days, and it is complete.
Take it for seven days and ascend to immortality.
Also by using xuángāo to make pills with this dān,
placing them atop a fierce fire,
in moments, they become gold.
Also, by combining two hundred forty zhū of mercury with one hundred catties of water and firing it,
gold is produced.
When gold is formed, the medicine is finished;
if gold does not form,
again seal the medicine and fire it,
using the same number of days as before,
and there will never be failure.
The second elixir is named Shén Dān,
also called Shén Fú.
After taking it for one hundred days, one becomes an immortal.
One may traverse water and fire;
by applying this elixir to the soles of the feet,
one may walk upon water.
By taking three dāo guī,
the sān shī and jiǔ chóng are all instantly destroyed,
and all diseases are cured.
The third elixir is also called Shén Dān.
After taking one dāo guī,
in one hundred days one becomes an immortal.
If given to the six domesticated animals to swallow,
they too will never die.
It also wards off the five kinds of weapons.
After taking it for one hundred days,
immortal men and jade maidens,
the mountain and river spirits and deities,
all come to serve the person,
appearing in human form.
The fourth elixir is called Huán Dān.
By taking one dāo guī,
after one hundred days, one becomes an immortal.
The Vermilion Bird and Phoenix
soar and circle above,
while the jade maidens arrive to one's side.
If one dāo guī is combined with one jīn of mercury and fired,
gold is instantly produced.
If this elixir is applied to coins or objects in use,
everything is restored the same day.
If this elixir is used to write above the eyes of ordinary people,
a hundred ghosts flee in avoidance.
The fifth elixir is named Ěr Dān.
After taking it for thirty days,
one attains immortality.
Spirits and deities will come to serve,
and jade maidens will appear before you.
The sixth elixir is called Liàn Dān.
After taking it for ten days,
one becomes immortal.
If compounded with mercury and fired,
gold is also produced.
The seventh elixir is named Róu Dān.
By taking one dāo guī,
in a hundred days one becomes immortal.
If mixed with the juice of quē pén and taken,
even a ninety-year-old man,
can still have children;
if compounded with Jīn Gōng and fired,
it produces gold.
The eighth elixir is called Fú Dān.
By taking it, one becomes immortal on the same day.
Carrying this elixir, about the size of a date pit,
a hundred ghosts will flee from you.
By writing with the elixir above doors and gates,
myriad evils and all spirits dare not approach,
and it also repels thieves, tigers, and wolves.
The ninth elixir is called Hán Dān.
By taking one dāo guī,
in one hundred days one becomes immortal.
Celestial youths and jade maidens come to serve,
one may fly swiftly and rise lightly,
without the use of wings.
Of all these nine elixirs,
simply obtaining one brings immortality;
it is not necessary to make them all.
Making them depends on each person’s preferences.
For all who take the nine elixirs,
if they wish to ascend to Heaven, they may depart;
if they wish to remain in the human world, they are free to stay.
All may come and go unobstructed,
and cannot be harmed.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
There is also the Tàiqīng Shén Dān,
the method of which comes from Yuán Jūn.
Yuán Jūn
was Lǎozǐ’s master.
The Tàiqīng Guān Tiān Jīng consists of nine chapters,
which state that the upper three chapters must not be taught,
the middle three chapters are not suitable to be transmitted in the world,
and are always submerged beneath the Three Springs.
The lower three chapters
are precisely the Inner, Middle, and Lower texts of the Elixir Classic,
totaling three scrolls.
Yuán Jūn
was a great divine immortal,
able to harmonize yīn and yáng,
command spirits and control wind and rain,
ride with nine dragons and twelve white tigers,
all the immortals under Heaven are subordinate to him.
He himself stated that even he achieved all this through practicing the Way and taking elixirs,
not by nature.
How much more so for ordinary people?
The scripture says:
If a superior man attains the Way,
he ascends to become a celestial official;
if a middling man attains the Way,
he dwells in Kūnlún;
if an inferior man attains the Way,
he lives long in the world.
The ignorant do not believe this,
considering it empty talk;
from dawn until dusk,
they merely perform acts seeking death,
and do not seek life at all,
yet would Heaven force them to live?
Ordinary people know only to pursue fine food and clothing,
music, women, wealth, and rank,
indulging their desires to the utmost,
and are but those who fade away in the end.
Be careful not to tell them of the shén dān,
lest they laugh at the Way and slander the True.
To pass on the Elixir Classic to an unworthy person
inevitably brings misfortune.
If there is one who truly believes,
the medicine may be given and shared,
but never pass on the formula lightly.
For those who know this Way,
what need have they for lords or princes?
Once the shén dān is made,
not only does it bring long life,
it can also be used to create gold.
When gold is produced,
take one hundred jīn and first conduct a grand sacrifice.
The sacrificial rites are detailed in a separate scroll,
which is not the same as the rites for the nine tripods.
The offering should be labeled according to the type of gold.
Offer twenty jīn to Heaven,
five jīn each to the Sun and Moon,
eight jīn to the Běidǒu,
eight jīn to Tàiyǐ,
five jīn to the Well,
five jīn to the Hearth,
twelve jīn to Hé Bó,
five jīn to the Earth Deities,
five jīn each to the deities of gates and lanes and the Pure Lord,
totaling eighty-eight jīn.
The remaining twelve jīn,
should be placed in a fine leather pouch,
and on an auspicious day, when the market in the city is flourishing,
silently discard them in a place crowded with people,
then depart straightaway without looking back.
Only after using one hundred jīn in this way,
may one use the rest at will.
If gold is not first used to sacrifice to the spirits,
disaster or retribution will surely follow.
It is also said,
the Way of long life
does not lie in sacrifices to spirits and deities,
nor in breath exercises or stretching,
but the key to ascension to immortality
lies in the shén dān.
To know this is not easy,
and to make it is truly difficult.
If you can make it,
you may endure forever.
In recent times, at the end of the Hàn, Yīn Jūn of Xīnyě
compounded this Tàiqīng elixir and became immortal.
He himself was originally a Confucian scholar,
with talent and learning,
skilled at composing poetry and praising and prefaces to the Elixir Classic,
relating his initial study of the Way and the account of following his master from start to finish,
listing more than forty people whom he personally knew to have attained immortality,
in great detail.
When making this Tàiqīng elixir,
it is somewhat difficult and hard to prepare in the nine tripods,
yet it is the highest method for ascending to Heaven in broad daylight.
To compound it, one must first prepare Huāchí, Chìyán, Gěn Xuě, Xuánbái, Fēifú, Sānwǔ Divine Water,
and only then may the fire be started.
A single-refined elixir,
if taken for three years, confers immortality.
A twice-refined elixir,
if taken for two years, confers immortality.
A thrice-refined elixir,
if taken for one year, confers immortality.
A four-times-refined elixir,
if taken for half a year, confers immortality.
A five-times-refined elixir,
if taken for one hundred days, confers immortality.
A six-times-refined elixir,
if taken for forty days, confers immortality.
A seven-times-refined elixir,
if taken for thirty days, confers immortality.
An eight-times-refined elixir,
if taken for ten days, confers immortality.
A nine-times-refined elixir,
if taken for three days, confers immortality.
If you obtain the nine-times-refined elixir,
place it in the shén dǐng,
after the Summer Solstice,
blast the dǐng with heat,
place one jin of zhū ér under the lid.
Watch attentively,
awaiting the sun's essence to shine upon it.
In a moment, all will rise together,
glorious and radiant,
divine light in five colors,
it immediately transforms into the returning elixir.
Take it and ingest a single dāo guī,
and you will ascend to Heaven in broad daylight.
Also, regarding the nine-times-refined elixir,
it is sealed and smeared inside an earthen cauldron,
fired with rice-husk fuel;
first with gentle heat, then strong,
for each refinement from one to nine,
there are different durations for slow or fast,
which can be determined this way.
If the number of refinements is few,
the power of the medicine is insufficient,
thus more days are required to take it,
and attaining immortality is slow.
If the number of refinements is many,
the medicine is potent,
thus fewer days are required to take it,
and immortality is attained quickly.
There is also the Nine Lights Elixir,
which is a different method from the ninefold refinement,
but in general, it is similar.
In the method of preparation,
one combines all the medicines with fire,
refining five stones.
The five stones are:
dānshā, xiónghuáng, báiyù, céngqīng, and císhí.
Each stone, refined five times, produces five colors;
with five stones, there are twenty-five colors.
Each color yields one liang,
and is stored in a separate vessel.
If you wish to revive the dead
within three days of passing,
take a dao gui of qīng dān and mix with water,
and bathe the corpse with it.
Again, place a dao gui of the elixir in the mouth,
and the dead person will immediately return to life.
If you wish to summon a traveling kitchen,
take hēi dān and mix with water,
smear it on the left hand,
and whatever you request by mouth will come of its own accord,
all things under Heaven can thus be summoned.
If you wish for invisibility, or to know events before they occur or are yet to come,
or to remain unaging,
ingest a dao gui of huáng dān,
and you will immediately achieve long life and not grow old.
You will also be able to sit and see a thousand li away,
knowing good or ill fortune,
as if it were before your very eyes.
One’s destiny in life,
rise and fall, longevity or early death,
wealth and nobility or poverty and lowliness,
all will be known,
and the methods are all found in the Tàiqīng jīng, in one scroll.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
Next, there is one scroll of the Five Spirits Elixir Classic,
describing five methods.
It uses dānshā, xiónghuáng, cíhuáng, shíliúhuáng, céngqīng, fánshí, císhí, róngyán, Tàiyǐ yúliáng,
and also uses liùyī ní,
and is combined in ritual in the divine chamber,
completed in thirty-six days.
It also uses the seals of the Five Emperors,
written in five colors,
which likewise prevent death,
but do not equal the Tàiqīng and Jiǔdǐng elixirs.
There is also the Mínshān Elixir Method,
in which the Daoist Zhāng Gài Tàjīng concentrated on this formula in the stone chamber of Mínshān
and obtained this recipe.
In the method, yellow copper is smelted,
and cast into a square vessel,
to collect water from within the moon,
which is covered with mercury,
and the essence of the sun’s fire is brought within it.
Taken over a long time, it prevents death.
Also, take this elixir, place it in a xiónghuáng copper fire-striker,
cover with mercury and expose to sunlight,
after twenty days it matures and is processed,
ingest with jǐnghuá water, in the amount of a small bean,
for one hundred days,
and all the blind will be able to see,
all ailments will heal themselves,
white hair will turn black,
lost teeth will grow anew.
There is also the Wù Chéngzǐ Elixir Method,
using Báshā mercury placed in a copper tray eight inches wide and a clay furnace filled with charcoal,
propped on three ditches using a branch tray,
irrigated with sulfur water,
always kept as moist as mud,
taken for one hundred days, and death is prevented.
There is also the Xiànménzǐ Elixir Method,
mixing one jin of elixir with wine,
using three shēng of wine to blend,
and exposing it to the sun for forty days,
take it for one day,
and the three worms and all ailments instantly disappear;
take it for three years,
the Dao of immortality is achieved,
and two jade maidens will surely come to serve you,
who can be commanded to bring forth a traveling kitchen.
This elixir can ward off all kinds of ghosts,
as well as the disasters brought by corpses from the four directions that bring calamity to people’s dwellings,
and harm from earthworks disturbing the living,
hang it facing them,
and there will be no harm.
There is also the Instant Elixir,
which also has nine varieties,
similar to but not as effective as the Jiǔdǐng.
Its essential method says,
take cíhuáng and xiónghuáng, burn and smelt with copper,
cast into a vessel,
cover it for three years with pure mature wine,
after one hundred days,
red cream will form on the vessel,
several inches in length,
or there may be rainbow-colored gems,
collect and process these and take them,
and one will also attain long life.
It may also be combined with tùsī,
tùsī is the root of a new sprout,
shaped like a rabbit,
dig it up and take its juice,
and mix it with this elixir,
taking it immediately grants transformative powers,
allowing one to do as they wish.
It may also be mixed with zhūcǎo,
taking it once,
one can travel upon clouds through emptiness.
Zhūcǎo resembles a small jujube,
grows to three or four feet,
branches and leaves are all red,
stem like coral,
prefers to grow beneath the cliffs of famed mountains,
cut it and its sap flows like blood,
cast jade or any of eight stones, gold, or silver into it,
which will immediately become a pellet like clay,
over time it becomes liquid,
add gold into it,
it is called Golden Brew,
add jade into it,
it is called Jade Mead,
both grant immortality when consumed.
There is also a method for obtaining Concealed Elixir,
among all the waters under Heaven,
there are those named for dān,
such as in the Dānshuǐ of Nányáng.
Within them are always dān fish,
ten days before the Summer Solstice at night, watch for them,
the dān fish will surely float to the edge of the water,
red light shining upwards,
brilliant as fire,
use a net to catch them, and you will obtain them,
even if you get many,
do not take all of them;
cut their blood,
smear it on the soles,
and you will be able to walk on water,
and dwell long in the depths.
There is also the Chìsōngzǐ Elixir Method,
collect the juice of a thousand-year-old léi and of alum peach, marinate the elixir,
put it in a non-permeable vessel,
seal its mouth with refined honey,
bury it three feet underground,
after a hundred days,
squeeze the red fruit of líng mù,
mix the juice and take it,
and your face, hair, and eyebrows will all become red,
granting immortality.
In ancient times, the yellow-essence immortal had a red-bearded son;
was it not from taking this?
Furthermore, the dān method of Shí Xiānshēng:
Take an unfeathered chick of the crow,
swallow it with true dān mixed with beef,
until it matures,
and all its feathers become red.
Then kill it,
dry it in the shade for one hundred days,
pound it together with feathers and take one dāoguī in dose,
and in one hundred days you will obtain a lifespan of five hundred years.
Again, the dān method of Kāng Fēngzǐ:
Use sheep, crow, and crane eggs, and sparrow blood,
combine with the juice of Tiān Xióng from Shàoshì,
mix it with dān and lacquer it inside a swan egg,
then place it in mica water,
where after one hundred days it transforms into red water.
Take one hé,
and your life immediately increases by one hundred years;
take one shēng, and you gain one thousand years.
Again, the dān method of Cuī Wénzǐ:
Place dān inside the abdomen of a duck and steam it;
take it,
and it will make one live long,
taking it continuously, one does not die.
Again, the dān method of Liú Yuán:
Put cinnabar in xuánshuǐ liquid,
after one hundred days it becomes purple,
and it will not stain your hand when held.
Then mix it with mica water,
lacquer it inside tubes,
throw it into a well,
after one hundred days it becomes red water,
take one hé,
and you obtain one hundred years,
taking it for a long time grants immortality.
Again, the dān method of Lè Zǐcháng:
Use azurite, lead dān, mercury, and cinnabar,
put them in a copper tube,
seal it with dry tiles and white talc,
and steam it in white sand,
for eighty days,
take it in doses the size of small beans,
after three years you will become an immortal.
Again, the dān method of Lǐ Wén:
Wrap dān in white silk,
boil it with bamboo juice,
name it hóngquán,
then float it on the broth to steam it,
combine with xuánshuǐ,
take one hé,
in one year you will become an immortal.
Again, the dān method of Yǐn Zǐ:
Mix mica water with dān and seal it tightly,
place it in Jīnhuá Pond,
remove after one year,
take one dāoguī,
finish one jīn,
and you obtain five hundred years.
Again, the Tàiyǐ Zhāo Húnpò dān method:
Uses five minerals,
and seals with Liùyī clay,
all similar to the Nine Dāns.
It is especially effective for those who die suddenly within three days;
break a tooth and place one pill inside,
with a sulfur pill,
swallow them both with water,
and as soon as they enter the throat, life is restored.
All say they see a messenger carrying a warrant summoning them.
Again, the dān method of Cǎinǚ:
Mix rabbit blood and dān, steam with honey,
for one hundred days,
and take a dosage the size of a firmiana seed, one pill,
three times a day,
for one hundred days;
then two divine women will come to serve you,
and may be used as retainers.
Again, the dān method of Jìqiūzǐ:
Mix clear wine, hemp oil, Bǎihuá honey wine, and dragon ointment,
seal with Liùyī clay,
warm it with bran fire,
it becomes ready in ten days,
take a small bean-sized pill,
finish the full course,
and achieve a lifespan of five hundred years.
Again, the dān method of Mòzǐ:
Use mercury and five minerals liquid in a copper vessel,
boil with fire,
stir with an iron ladle,
for ten days,
it then becomes dān.
Take one dāoguī,
ten thousand illnesses are removed from the body,
take it long-term and you do not die.
Again, the dān method of Zhāng Zǐhé:
Blend lead, mercury, azurite water, and seal it,
steam in red millet,
ready in eighty days,
mix it with date paste to form pills,
take them the size of large beans,
in one hundred days,
a lifespan of five hundred years.
Again, the dān method of Qǐlǐ:
First fly to obtain five-shíng jade dust,
combine with cinnabar and mercury,
boil it in a large copper vessel,
for one hundred days,
it becomes five colors,
take it and you do not die.
With one hundred jīn of lead,
and one hundred dāoguī of medicine,
combine them with fire to produce white silver,
then mix with realgar water and fire it,
after one hundred days it becomes gold.
If the gold is too hard,
boil it with pork fat;
if too soft,
boil with white plum.
Again, the dān method of Yùzhù:
Combine Huáchí and dān,
cover it with azurite and sulfur powder, and offer it up,
place in a tube in sand,
steam for fifty days,
take it for one hundred days,
then the Jade Maidens, Liùjiǎ, and Liùdīng divine women come to serve you,
may be used as retainers,
and you will know all affairs under Heaven.
Again, the dān method from Zhǒuhòu:
Mix Jīnhuá with dān and seal with dry tiles,
steam for eighty days,
take pills the size of small beans,
place on a plate,
let them face the sun to activate,
their radiance connects with the sun,
take them the size of small beans,
and you will live long.
If thrown into Dānyáng copper,
fired, it becomes gold.
Again, the dān method of Lǐ Gōng:
Use true dān and water from the five minerals, one shēng each,
mix them until like mud,
fire them in a cauldron,
remove after thirty-six days,
combine with liquid sulfur,
take for ten years,
and you shall end together with Heaven and Earth.
Again, the dān method of Liú Shēng:
Use white chrysanthemum juice, paper mulberry juice, and chū juice to mix dān and steam it,
for thirty days,
grind and take it together,
in one year,
you will obtain five hundred years,
an old man taking it becomes unrecognizably young,
and a youth remains ever young.
Again, the dān method of Wáng Jūn:
Use bāshā and mercury, place them in a chicken egg,
lacquer it to seal,
let a hen brood three eggs,
and take them by taking auspicious days,
one’s years will cease to age.
Children must not take it,
otherwise they will not grow;
for newly-born chickens and dogs, if given,
they all will not grow large,
and so it is proven in birds and beasts alike.
Again, the dān method of Chén Shēng:
Use white honey mixed with dān,
seal in a copper vessel,
steep it in a well,
for one cycle,
take it for a year,
hunger will not arise,
consume one jīn,
obtain one hundred years lifespan.
Again, the dān method of Hán Zhōng:
Mix with lacquer and honey, boil the dān,
taking it can prolong life and keep the vision keen,
and one will have no shadow when standing in sunlight.
Beyond this,
there are dozens of further methods,
which cannot all be explained.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The Golden Elixir of Tàiyǐ is that which, when taken, one becomes immortal;
it is no less than the Nine Elixirs.
In its composition, ancient sources refer to using one jin of yellow gold,
together with Xuánmíng dragon balm, Tàiyǐ ten-day-head middle stone, ice stone, Purple Wandering Lady, Xuánshuǐ fluid, gold-transforming stone, and cinnabar;
these are sealed and become liquid.
Its canon says,
when the golden liquid enters the mouth,
then the whole body becomes golden in color.
Lǎozǐ received it from Yuánjūn,
Yuánjūn said,
“This Way is supremely important,
it appears once in a hundred generations.
Store it in a stone chamber;
when you combine it,
all observe purification and abstinence for one hundred days,
you must not associate with common people,
do this beside a famous mountain,
above eastern flowing water,
erect a separate hermitage,
in a hundred days it is completed,
taking one or two taels leads to immortality.
If you do not yet wish to depart from the world,
and desire to be an earthly and aquatic immortal,
only practice purification and abstinence for one hundred days.
If you seek to ascend to heaven,
first abstain from grains for one year,
then take it.
If you take half a tael,
you will have long life and not die,
ten thousand calamities and a hundred poisons,
none can harm you,
you may have wife and children,
hold official ranks,
do whatever you wish,
there are no prohibitions.
If you wish to ascend to heaven again,
then fast and purify,
take another tael,
and at once you will fly and become an immortal.
As for the Golden Liquid being the most formidable and victorious method,
take the Golden Liquid and mercury, combine and boil them together,
for thirty days,
take them out,
use a yellow earth bowl to contain them,
seal with six-one clay,
place over fierce fire and cook,
for sixty periods,
all transform into elixir,
take it in the size of a small bean and you become immortal.
With a knife’s-measure of this elixir powder,
and one jin of mercury,
immediately it becomes silver.
Again, take one jin of this elixir and place it on fire, fan it,
it transforms into red gold and flows,
this is called elixir gold.
Coat knives and swords with it,
and weapons are kept at bay for ten thousand li.
Make bowls and plates from this elixir gold,
eat and drink from them,
and one gains long life.
If you use it to receive the essence of the sun and moon,
just as Fāngzhū obtained water,
drinking it brings immortality.
Mix the Golden Liquid with yellow earth,
put it in a six-one clay bowl,
cook it with fierce fire,
it all becomes yellow gold,
which is usable,
cook it again with fire,
it all transforms into elixir,
take it in the size of a small bean and you may enter famous mountains and great rivers to become a terrestrial immortal.
With a knife’s-measure of this elixir powder and mercury, you immediately produce silver,
take one tael of that silver and combine with one jin of lead,
all becomes silver.
The Golden Liquid Canon says,
throw eight taels of gold into eastern flowing water,
drink blood to swear an oath,
only then may you be told the oral instructions,
but if you do not follow the original method,
and steal the recipe for your own use,
it will never succeed.
If among people there is one with utmost faith,
the medicine may be given to him,
but never lightly transmit the book,
for this brings misfortune to both parties,
the divine spirits watch people very closely,
people are just unaware of it.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Truly, the Nine Elixirs is the highest canon of immortal medicines,
yet in the preparation,
the various drugs required are very many.
If all four quarters are clear and accessible,
they may be procured in the market.
But if the nine domains are blocked and separated,
the materials cannot be obtained.
Also, you must keep up the fire day and night for many days,
watching and waiting for just the right heat,
never letting it miss its proper degree,
it is laborious and extremely difficult,
thus it cannot match the ease of preparing the Golden Liquid.
In making the Golden Liquid, only the gold is hard to get.
Whereas in antiquity, one jin of gold was so-called, today it means two jin,
usually costing only about three hundred thousand in value,
the other various drugs are relatively easy to assemble.
Moreover, there is no need to kindle fire,
simply place it in the Huáchí,
when the required days are reached it will be ready,
in total, forty thousand in value is enough for one batch,
enough for eight people to become immortals.
But if there is a little less in the mixture,
its potency will be insufficient for transformation,
just like fermenting several shēng of rice wine,
it surely cannot be accomplished.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Next is the method of ingesting gold in pellet form;
although it does not match the elixir of gold-liquid,
it is still far superior to other medicines.
Some refine it with pig hide fat and wine,
or prepare it with chū bark,
or dissolve it with jīng wine and lodestone,
or it may be drawn out as a cloth,
or immediately rendered into water and drunk.
Sometimes there are taboos,
and it is still not equal to gold-liquid.
Some combine realg ar and orpiment to make the pellets,
and it can be drawn out and stretched like leather,
but these are all methods of terrestrial immortals.
Silver and the large pearls from within oysters
can also be transformed into water to be drunk.
However, these require long-term consumption without interruption,
so they are not as good as gold-liquid.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
To combine this ninefold gold-liquid elixir,
it is necessary to use coins,
and also to enter famous mountains,
severing worldly affairs,
hence few are capable of achieving it.
Among thousands and tens of thousands of people,
perhaps one will obtain its essential method.
Therefore, in all books on the Way,
there is rarely any discourse on golden elixir.
The first prohibition:
do not allow commoners or those who do not believe in the Way
to slander or revile it,
otherwise it will certainly fail.
Master Zhèng said that the reason for this
is that when combining this great medicine, one must always offer sacrifices;
by offering sacrifices, Tàiyǐ Yuánjūn, Lǎojūn, and Xuánnǚ all descend to inspect.
If the maker of the medicine does not keep to secluded and remote places,
allowing common ignorant people to pass by and witness it,
then the various spirits will reproach the maker for not adhering to the prohibitions of the scriptures,
resulting in evil people uttering words of slander,
and they will no longer aid the person,
thus, evil energies intrude,
and the medicine will not succeed.
One must enter a famous mountain,
observe purification and abstinence for a hundred days,
avoid eating the five pungent vegetables and raw fish,
avoid meeting with common people,
and only then may one make the great medicine.
One must maintain fasting until the medicine is completed,
not just at the start of the process.
Master Zhèng said,
Master Zuǒ informed him,
saying that all small mountains
are not suitable for producing the golden-liquid divine elixir.
All small mountains lack a proper deity as their lord;
mostly they are spirits of wood and stone,
ancient creatures a thousand years old,
blood-consuming ghosts—
this class is all evil energy,
bearing no thought to bestow blessings upon people,
but able only to bring harm;
they like to test Daoists,
so Daoists must apply arts to ward themselves,
as well as protect their students and followers;
yet it is still possible that they ruin people's medicine.
Now among doctors,
whenever they compound good medicines and ointments,
they do not wish chickens, dogs, children, or women to see it.
If touched by such,
its effect is lost.
Furthermore, if it is seen by those with evil intent or bad eyes in the gathering and harvesting,
its good color is lost.
How much more so with the great medicine of the gods and immortals!
Thus, in ancient times Daoists
when compounding divine medicine,
would always enter famous mountains,
never merely stay in ordinary hills;
this was precisely the reason.
Also according to the Immortal Classics,
those who can earnestly and attentively prepare the immortal medicine

may do it in Huà Shān, Tài Shān, Huò Shān, Héng Shān, Sōng Shān, Shàoshì Shān, Cháng Shān, Tàibái Shān, Zhōngnán Shān, Nǚjī Shān, Dìfèi Shān, Wángwū Shān, Bàodú Shān, Ānqiū Shān, Qián Shān, Qīngchéng Shān, Éméi Shān, Ruí Shān, Yúntái Shān, Luófú Shān, Yángjià Shān, Huángjīn Shān, Biézǔ Shān, Dà-Tiāntāi Shān, Xiǎo-Tiāntāi Shān, Sìwàng Shān, Gàizhú Shān, and Kuòcāng Shān;
in all these there is a proper deity dwelling in the mountain,
and within them may be earthbound immortals.
All these mountains bear zhī herbs,
which can protect from great armies and calamities,
and are not only places to compound medicine.
If a person of the Way ascends them,
the mountain spirits will definitely aid and bless him,
ensuring the medicine's success.
If one cannot ascend these mountains,
then on the great islands and islets in the sea
one may also compound medicine.
Such as Wēngzhōu, Dǎnzhōu, Zhùyǔ east of Kuàijī,
as well as Xīnzhōu, Jǔzhōu, Tàiguāngzhōu, Yùzhōu in Xūzhōu—
all these are next best.
Now, among famous mountains in Zhōngguó, some cannot be reached,
but among those that can be dwelled in the eastern region,
there is Huò Shān
in Jìn’ān;
Cháng Shān and Tàibái
in Dōngyáng;
and Sìwàng Shān, Dà-Tiāntāi Shān, Gàizhú Shān, and Kuòcāng Shān
all in Kuàijī.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
I, though unworthy descendant of great ministers,
while my talent is insufficient to govern the state and manage affairs,
yet in the matter of like-minded friends,
and the pursuit of progress,
those whom I cannot match in knowledge
are many who spread their wings to the skies,
blazing brilliantly among the stars and heavens.
The reason I have severed ties of celebration and condolence with my local community,
and abandoned the glory and splendor of my times,
is out of the desire to ascend famous mountains,
complete the writings I have authored,
and next to that, to compound divine medicine,
seeking longevity as my goal.
There is no commoner who does not wonder at my abandoning home and kin,
turning away from the clear path,
to toil in the forests and wilds,
my hands and feet turning calloused,
thinking I must suffer from some madness or delusion.
Yet the Way and worldly affairs cannot flourish together;
if one does not abandon the business of the human world,
how could one fulfill such ambition?
Those who truly see this
and firmly abide by it,
what fear would they have of slander or praise,
how could they sway before encouragement or discouragement?
Let me briefly set forth my heart here,
to show it to comrades of like mind in the future.
In later times there are those who sever gold,
who cast aside worldly things,
behaving no differently from myself.
Recipe for the Little Divine Elixir:
Use three jin of true cinnabar,
beat and mix in six jin of white honey,
sun-dry, then simmer,
so that it may be formed into pills,
each morning take ten pills, each the size of a hemp seed,
not a year will pass
before white hair turns black,
lost teeth grow anew,
the body becomes moist and lustrous;
take it long and
an old man will become a youth,
attaining immortality.
Recipe for the Lesser Elixir:
One jin of cinnabar,
pound and sift,
add three shēng of thick bitter wine,
two shēng of lacquer,
combine these three ingredients,
allowing them to interact,
simmer gently over low heat to form into pills,
each dose being three pills the size of hemp seeds,
taken twice daily,
within thirty days
a hundred diseases in the belly are cured,
the three corpses depart;
after a hundred days' use,
skin and bones are strengthened and firm;
after a thousand days,
Sīmìng erases one's name from the register of death,
and you will join Heaven and Earth,
gaze upon the sun and moon,
change form and appearance,
shifting and transforming endlessly,
casting no shadow at noon,
and bearing a different radiance.
Lesser method for ingesting gold:
Refine gold and place it in clear wine,
about two hundred times,
immersing and removing so that it boils,
when squeezed it oozes from between the fingers like clay;
if it does not boil,
or does not ooze when squeezed,
then shave it down
and place it again in clear wine, the process without number.
When finished,
take a dose the size of a small pellet,
or make one pill,
divide it into smaller pills,
take them for thirty days,
feeling neither cold nor hot;
divine beings and jade maidens will serve you;
silver may also be ingested
using the same method as gold.
Taking these two substances,
if one resides in a stone chamber of a famous mountain,
within one year he will achieve levitation.
Even if taken among men, one will become an earthbound immortal;
do not transmit this recklessly.
Liǎng Yízi’s Method for Consuming Gold,
three jin of pig’s hide fat,
one shēng of pure bitter wine,
take five liǎng of gold,
place it in a vessel,
simmer it on an earthen stove,
place the gold in the fat,
bring it in and out a hundred times,
and do the same with the bitter wine.
If you eat one jin,
your lifespan will obscure Heaven and Earth;
if you eat half a jin,
your lifespan will be two thousand years;
five liǎng,
your lifespan will be one thousand two hundred years.
No matter the quantity,
simply consume it as an elixir.
This should be prepared on a day governed by King Xiàng,
and its efficacy is divine.
Do not transmit this to unworthy people,
for if shown to the undeserving,
the medicine will lose its effectiveness and spirit.
Should you wish to dispel corpse-transformation drugs,
you ought to take dānshā.
Bào Pǔzi said:
The subtlety is hard to discern,
and many are those who harbor doubts.
How could my wisdom and clarity surpass others?
It is only by chance I have a partial understanding,
like the crane knowing midnight,
and the swallow knowing wǔ-sì day,
but not necessarily understanding other matters as well.
There has also been examination and verification,
revealing that long life can be obtained,
and that immortals are not born from special stock.
As for the mysteries of the Way,
they cannot be fully written down,
and those that are near at hand,
are not worth discussing.
In days of old, Gēng Sāng with calloused hands,
and Wénzi, Xī and Yán,
long endured toil and hardship,
yet when they received the great secret teaching,
it surely had its reason.
For man’s round head inhales vital breath,
who does not rejoice in life and fear death?
Yet glory, rank, and profit entice their will,
fair faces and jade-like skin beguile their eyes,
pure shāng and flowing zhǐ music confound their ears,
the strife of love and hate, profit and harm, disturbs their spirit,
achievement, fame, and reputation bind their bodies,
all these arrive unbidden,
are completed without study.
Unless one is destined to become an immortal,
deep in reason and insight,
recognizing transformation outside of common affairs,
wielding clear discernment in the mysterious and obscure realm,
awakening to the closeness or distance of fame and self,
and lamenting the flash-swiftness of life like a passing gap,
how could one abandon relationships and break off distant affairs,
or suppress appetites and desires,
cut off the near-at-hand cravings before their eyes,
to pursue the distant accomplishments that are hard to achieve?
From existence is born by non-being,
form stands established by spirit.
That which exists,
is the palace of non-being;
the form,
is the dwelling of spirit.
So it is like a dike:
if the dike collapses, the water will not remain.
Or like a candle:
if the candle melts, the fire will not abide.
If the body is worn out, the spirit scatters;
when breath is exhausted, life ends.
If the root is depleted but the branches flourish,
then the green leaves will leave the tree behind.
When the vital energy is spent but desire prevails,
then essence and soul will depart from the body.
Those who depart do not return,
and once decayed there is no restoration of life.
Thus, the man who understands the Way,
truly has reason to grieve!
To value jade and devalue time,
how could there not be cause for this?
Thus, those who cultivate their nature in the mountains and forests,
those who withdraw from custom and find delight,
compare what is high to tumors,
and see all things as cicada wings.
How could it be idle boasting,
or forcibly disparaging worldly affairs?
Truly what they see is clear,
thus they cast it aside as if forgotten.
Therefore, they dwell afar in seclusion,
conceal their brilliance and cover their beauty,
shut their eyes to desires,
send away the colors that dull their brightness,
block thoughts of sounds from their ears,
banish disturbing noises from their hearing,
cleanse and clear the mysterious gaze,
maintain gentleness and embrace unity,
focus on gathering breath to attain softness,
calm themselves with tranquility and purity,
send away the false emotions of joy and sorrow,
externalize the honor and disgrace of gain and loss,
cut off the deep-seated poison of attachment to life,
avoid idle talk at critical moments,
listen only after reflection to understand thoroughly,
look within to find the traceless,
nourish the spiritual root in the mysterious depths,
remove the allure and envy brought by contact with things,
cut off shallow affairs,
defend with pleasure and harmony,
act by non-action,
so as to preserve heavenly principle entirely.
Then, one’s father inhales the precious radiance,
bathes the spirit in utmost clarity,
outwardly expels the five wandering stars,
inwardly guards the nine essences,
secures the jade key at the gate of destiny,
binds the North Pole at the Yellow Court,
draws the three lights into the Bright Hall,
causes the Primal Origin to fly and refine the form,
gathers the spiritual fluid at the Golden Beam,
drives the white to depart and retains the blue,
condenses the clear spring at the cinnabar Field,
draws the sinking pearl at the Five Cities,
the jade cauldron looks down upon the firewood,
aquatic birds raise their heads and sing,
rare flowers extend their tips,
heavenly deer cough up beautiful jade,
cherish the double circle in the Scarlet Palace,
hide the nine lights in the caverns of darkness,
clouds thickly entwine to join the sky,
deep valleys connect and cross as streams,
treading upon the qián and duì trigrams,
call upon the six Dīng spirits,
sitting or lying in the Purple Chamber,
chewing and absorbing golden blossoms,
glowing autumn mushrooms,
vermilion flowers and green stems,
bright precious ointment,
flowing and overflowing with celestial dew,
curing hunger and quenching thirst,
no hundred ills arise,
free and at ease on the wǔ-sì day,
the swallow is at peace and drinks harmoniously,
controlling hun and commanding pò souls,
bones are filled and the body lightened.
Thus able to spur wind and clouds to soar through the void,
board the immortal chariot and live forever.
Yet the dust upon the beams grows an inch thick,
it cannot be attained in a fleeting moment.
The mountain’s drip penetrates to its depths,
one cannot reach this in haste.
The trouble is that those who hear of it do not believe,
those who believe do not practice,
those who practice do not persevere.
Those who attain it are extremely few and hidden,
those who fail are exceedingly many and conspicuous.
The people of the world cannot perceive the hidden,
and see only the evident,
thus they say that in all the world there is truly no Way of Immortality.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
If the defenses are solid, there is no waste from water seeping through;
if there is plenty of fat, there is no danger of the fire subsiding;
the sword of Lóngquán remains sharp because it does not cut and is thus always useful;
the axe and hatchet, used daily, quickly wear out;
concealed snow defies heat and persists through summer;
stored ice, kept deep, endures intense heat;
a single layer of silk draped over a mirror shields it from scorching;
all sorts of plants, if covered on one side, survive the winter.
Clay soil is easily eroded,
but when fired into tiles,
it lasts as long as Heaven and Earth.
The zhuò and yóu oaks rot quickly,
but when burned into charcoal,
they can endure for hundreds of millions of years without decay.
The yuán tún, favored livestock, die late;
a fine horse, driven up steep slopes, dies early;
the cold insect, suited to its environment, lives twice as long;
southern forests, dwelling in warmth, grow lush;
when meeting baleful airs, they wither under frost;
when touched by spring sunshine, they flourish in leafy splendor.
The categories of things are one,
yet the means of thriving or withering differ;
is there truly a fixed limit for autumn’s harvest,
or a definite rule for winter storage?
And as for the fate of people,
the appointed time for life and death,
is less determined by winter chill than the lives of grass and trees;
and as for the principles of nourishing and extending life,
and the methods of remedy and restoration,
the benefits do not lie merely in warmth;
if these can produce the effect of long life,
why should this not be so?
Yet the people of the world adhere to shallow customs and narrow habits,
regarding the Immortal Way as empty fantasy,
and calling Huáng-Lǎo’s words delusions,
is this not to be lamented?
There are truly foolish men who will not trust decoctions, acupuncture, or moxibustion;
how much less will they trust things deeper than these?
They always say,
“Yú Fū, Biǎn Què, Hé Huǎn, and Cāng Gōng and the like,
are certainly able to cure illness;
why could they not also prevent death?”
And again they say,
“In wealthy and noble households,
can there truly be a lack of medical skill?
Yet even they are not longer-lived;
so it must be that destiny is determined by nature.”
To require such people
to trust in immortals is like
making an ox climb a tree
or a horse chase a bird.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
The “Summoning the Soul,” “Small Elixir,” and “Three Messengers” pills,
as well as minute preparations like the “Five Flowers” and “Eight Minerals” medicines,
can dissolve solid ice instantly,
or float upon entering water,
can cut off spirits and demons,
ward off tigers and leopards,
break up masses in the bowels,
drive out the “two bandits” from the vital organs,
raise the suddenly dead from where they lie,
and recall wandering souls already departed.
These are all ordinary drugs,
yet can restore the dead to life;
then as for the superior medicine,
how could it not make the living escape death?
The Yuèrén rescued the Prince of Guó at the point of death;
the foreign doctor saved the breathless Sū Wǔ;
Chún Yú could open the skull and treat the brain;
Yuán Huà could cut open the belly and cleanse the stomach;
Wén Zhì healed the critically ill despite delays;
Zhòngjǐng pierced the chest to insert vermilion pills;
these are mere lesser arts of physicians,
yet can achieve such feats,
how much more so the arts of the immortals,
for which nothing is impossible?
As for the reasons men die,
it is because desires deplete them,
old age besets them,
a hundred diseases harm them,
they are poisoned or injured by malicious things,
struck by noxious influences,
afflicted by wind and cold.
Now, the Dao involves cultivating and circulating breath,
restoring essence and replenishing the brain,
regulating food and drink,
having moderation in activity and rest,
taking medicines,
focusing the mind and guarding unity,
practicing proscriptions to support Heaven,
wearing and carrying talismans and seals,
and keeping far from all things harmful to life;
all these one must entirely avoid.
Practiced in such a manner,
one can avoid these six harms.
Now, physicians have pills to clarify and fortify the kidney qi,
powders to supplement the five networks within,
decoctions of gǒuqǐ to fill up the bones,
and huángqí “center-fortifying” soups;
those who use these
all become robust.
Lac leaves and qīngzhēn,
and all manner of withered grasses—
Fán Ā took them
and lived two hundred years,
with hearing and sight still clear.
He was still able to wield a needle and treat illness;
this is a recent fact,
recorded and annotated by reputable historians.
Again it is said,
there was Wú Pǔ,
who learned the Five-Animal Frolics from Huà Tuó,
and used it instead of the Daoist calisthenics,
thus attaining more than a hundred years of life.
All these are but the simplest medical arts,
yet such results are achieved;
how much more with the most marvelous ones?
Now if one tells ordinary folk
that the “Four Harmonies in the Center” can cure sudden disorders,
kuǎndōng and zǐyuàn
can treat coughing and breath reversal,
huánlú and guànzhòng can kill the nine worms,
danggui and sháoyào stop colicky pain,
Qínjiāo and dúhuó dispel the eight types of wind,
chāngpú and dried ginger stop damp obstruction,
tùsīzǐ and cōngróng supplement deficiency and fatigue,
gānsuì and tínglì eliminate phlegm masses,
guālóu and huánglián cure thirsting disorder,
jìní and gāncǎo resolve a hundred poisons,
lúlú and yìrè root protect many wounds,
máhuáng and dàqīng treat “cold damage”—
still, ordinary folk refuse to believe.
They would rather beg favors at the risk of their lives,
cast lots and divine for spirits,
than trust a good doctor’s diagnosis;
instead, they employ a jumble of mediums and shamans.
How much less would they believe it when told that the Golden Elixir transcends the world,
and zhī and yīng can prolong life?
In the past, Liúhóu Zhāng Liáng
produced astounding strategies
unmatched in his era;
in intellect and resourcefulness
he far surpassed common men,
yet he believed immortality was attainable.
Though surpassing others in wisdom and intelligence,
he said, “I will cast aside worldly affairs
and follow Chìsōng on his wanderings”;
he thus cultivated the Daoist way,
abstained from grains for a year
in pursuit of ascension,
but, pressed by Empress Lǚ,
he had to heed her plan to assist Prince Ān.
In desperation,
he plotted with the Four Elders of Shāngshān,
and, as he predicted,
Empress Lǚ appreciated this
but forced him to resume eating;
so he was prevented from completing the Way.
According to Kǒng Ānguó’s Secret Record,
Zhāng Liáng obtained from Huáng Shí Gōng the method of not dying,
not only strategies of war.
It also says
his original masters were the Four Elders,
and men like Lùlǐ Xiānshēng and Qǐlǐ Jì,
all were immortals;
Zhāng Liáng learned all their esoteric methods,
and though compelled by Empress Lǚ to eat and drink,
he soon returned to cultivating the Dao,
secretly transcending the world,
but people did not know
and so thought he had died.
Following Kǒng Ānguó’s words,
Zhāng Liáng thus attained immortality.
Also, Zhāng Cāng, Chancellor of Hàn,
by chance acquired a minor technique:
by sucking women’s breast milk,
he lived to a hundred and eighty years;
such was but a paltry Daoist method,
yet Zhāng Cāng practiced it
and gained triple the normal lifespan.
How much more so by employing the complete arts,
and carrying out all the subtle secrets—
how could one not attain long life?
These events are recorded in the Book of Hàn,
not mere empty words.
Bǎo Pǔzǐ said:
“Although taking medicines is the foundation of longevity,
if one is also able to practice the regulation of qì,
its benefit comes much more swiftly.
If one cannot obtain medicines,
but solely cultivates qì to its utmost principle,
this too can gain several hundred years of life.
Yet it is also necessary to know the arts of the bedchamber;
the reason for this is,
if one does not understand the method of yīn and yáng,
and repeatedly suffers fatigue and injury,
then it is difficult for the practice of qì to be effective.
People exist within qì;
qì resides within people.
From Heaven and Earth down to all things,
there is none that does not require qì for life.
One skilled in the practice of qì
nourishes the body within,
and wards off evil without,
yet the common people use it daily but do not know it.
Wú and Yuè have methods of spells and interdictions
which are exceedingly effective and manifest,
they are mostly just techniques of qì.
Those who understand them can enter among great plagues
and share a bed with the sick without being infected.
Moreover, by leading several dozen companions,
all can be made unafraid;
thus qì can avert disasters from Heaven.
Sometimes there are malevolent demons and mountain spirits
that invade people's homes,
and throw tiles and stones at them,
or set fire to houses with flame.
Sometimes their forms are seen coming and going,
or only their voices and speech are heard,
but those skilled at interdiction can restrain them with qì,
and they will immediately be cut off;
thus, qì can also restrain ghosts and spirits.
Entering forests and mountains with many poisonous serpents such as viper and moccasin,
when ordinary people briefly pass through,
none avoid getting harmed,
but those skilled in interdiction can repel them with qì,
protecting a region of several dozen lǐ,
so that companions suffer no injury.
One can also subdue tigers, leopards, serpents, and wasps,
making them all prostrate and unable to get up.
With qì, wounds from metal weapons can be checked,
and the bleeding will stop at once.
One can also mend bones and link tendons.
By using qì to restrain sharp blades,
one can tread upon them unharmed,
or be stabbed without the blade entering.
If someone is bitten by a snake or a huǐ,
using qì to restrain it, he is healed instantly.
In recent times, Zuǒ Cí and Zhào Míng
used qì to restrain water,
making it flow backward for one or two zhàng.
They would also set fire atop a thatched house,
boil food and eat it,
yet the thatch would not be scorched.
Again, by driving large spikes into posts,
making them enter seven or eight cùn deep,
and blowing upon them with qì,
the spike would immediately shoot back out.
Also, by using qì to restrain boiling soup,
tossing in about a hundred coins,
and having someone reach in to retrieve them,
the hand would not be scalded or damaged.
They could also restrain water and set it out in the courtyard,
so that even in intense cold it would not freeze.
They could also prevent all cooks within a lǐ from having their food properly steamed.
They could restrain dogs so that they could not bark.
Once, Wú sent General Hè to suppress mountain bandits,
among whom was someone skilled at interdiction;
whenever battle was joined,
the official army’s swords and knives could not be drawn,
arrows shot from bows and crossbows would return towards the archers,
causing repeated misfortune.
General Hè, possessing far-reaching wisdom and talent,
then said,
'I have heard that metals with blades can be interdicted,
as can insects having poison;
things without blades,
and insects without poison,
cannot be interdicted.
If he can restrain our army’s weapons,
he surely cannot restrain those objects without blades.'
So they made many strong wooden white staves,
and selected five thousand extraordinary and robust soldiers to lead the assault,
each wielding staves to attack the bandits.
The bandits, relying on their practitioner of interdiction,
were completely unprepared.
Thereupon, the official army struck them with white staves,
utterly defeating the bandits.
Indeed, the interdictionist’s magic could no longer be used;
those beaten to death
numbered in the tens of thousands.
Qì arises from the body;
through its use such effectiveness is attained—
so how can one doubt that one could cure diseases by abstaining from grain
and prolong life while nourishing one’s nature?
Zhòngcháng Gōnglǐ
was a man of talent and ability;
he wrote the Chang Yan,
where he too discussed, 'By practicing qì, one can be free of hunger and illness.
At first I did not believe it,
but once I practiced it myself,
I found it entirely so.
The method of nourishing life
is truly this straightforward,
yet I myself have not succeeded in it.
Is it not because my mind is distracted by worldly affairs,
and my thoughts are sharp concerning human matters?
What others cannot do,
must also be due to this same malady as mine.'
In the past there was an enlightened teacher
who knew the way to avoid death.
The Lord of Yān sent an envoy to learn from him,
but the envoy did not succeed, and the teacher died.
The Lord of Yān was angry at his envoy
and was about to execute him.
A remonstrator said:
'There is nothing to fear more than death,
and nothing more urgent than life.
Since he lost his own life,
how could he enable our lord not to die?'
Thus, the lord did not execute him.
Of remonstrations, these words are a fine example.
Yet if that teacher had possessed the method of immortality,
like the qì-practice I have heard of,
then those who said the teacher died
would not necessarily be ignorant of the truth;
it was only that they could not abandon worldly affairs to practice it,
so even if they knew it, it did them no good;
it was not that there was no method for not dying.”
He also said:
“In Hénán, Mìxiàn,
there was one called Bǔ Chéng;
he studied Dao for a long time,
and at last bid farewell to his family and departed.
At first his steps grew lighter and higher,
and then he entered the clouds and was seen no more.
This is what is called 'raising the form to fly lightly,
ascending to Heaven in broad daylight,
and being ranked above other immortals.'”
Chén Yuánfāng and Hán Yuánzhǎng,
both eminent men of Yǐngchuān,
were nearby in that region;
the reason these two men believed in the existence of immortals in the world
is because their own fathers and forebears, as well as what they witnessed of Bǔ Chéng ascending to immortality,
provided them further proof of the existence of immortals.
Bǎo Pǔzǐ said:
“What belongs together, once united,
needs no words to establish trust;
where paths and intentions diverge,
even loyal counsel arouses doubts.
For principles that are near at hand,
and everyday matters of human choice,
which are weightier or lighter than gold or feathers,
and as clearly distinguished as black from white or powder from ink,
yet there are still many puzzled people
who cannot discern them;
how much more when one speaks of things beyond worldly ways,
or shows the subtlest of principles?
The majority laugh at them,
and this has been so for a long time,
not only in our day.
Where clarity reaches,
though it be the depths of dark nights,
or things as tiny as a hair’s tip,
it is not considered difficult to see.
But where it does not reach,
even the sun and moon shining in the sky,
or lofty peaks thick with clouds,
cannot be perceived clearly.
The sages of the Yellow Emperor and Lǎozi,
deep in comprehension, rare in insight,
revealed the secret teachings on famed mountains,
and received the immortal scriptures from divine beings,
casting off dust and worldly ties,
ascending far away to lofty heights,
more steadfast than metals and stones,
and living longer than tortoises and cranes.
For those with aspirations for the future,
and who lament that true believers have no written guides,
they left methods and instructions behind,
clear and manifest;
a little cultivation yields small results,
great effort brings great effect.
Yet shallow-sighted people,
bound by narrow attachments,
are content with bitterness and cannot recognize honey,
drunken on thin wine and do not appreciate the heady brew.
They know they love life but do not know there are ways to nourish life;
they know they fear death but do not believe in methods to be undying;
they know that excess in food and drink causes illness,
yet they cannot restrain their desire for rich and sweet tastes;
they understand that indulgence in passion and desire brings weakness,
yet do not know to cut off cravings for what is desired.
Though I say that the attainments of immortals are possible,
how can I make people believe?”
Someone questioned, saying:
“You do not possess the penetrating understanding of Sānwǔ,
nor the talent for extraordinary things that permeates to the bone;
your years do not match the long life of Ānqí or Péngzǔ,
your eyes have never beheld any spirit immortals,
and your ears have not alone heard any wondrous doctrines.
How then can you know that long life can be attained,
or that there is evidence for nurturing one's nature?
If it is that you sense these profound subtleties within your heart,
or rely on a rare insight from solitary perception,
still I dare not accept it.
If a person lacks clothing to cover their skin,
and has no provisions for a single evening,
yet speaks loftily of the methods of Táozhū,
placing himself alongside Yī Dùn's strategies,
surely people who criticize and ridicule him
must have their reasons.
Someone with chronic illness talking about mastering the skills of Hé or Què in harmonizing essence,
or a person repeatedly routed north who claims to have mastered the stratagems of Sūn and Wú,
if people do not believe him,
it is because there is no proof.”
I replied, saying:
“A small shrimp drifting aimlessly in the water
thinks there is nothing wider than the four seas under heaven.
A little cricket twisting within a fruit pit
supposes that the bounds of the eight extremities are exhausted right there.
Even if you tell them of the enormous, shoreless expanse without end,
or describe to them the vastness of the universe,
they take it for empty words;
they will never believe it.
If I had square pupils in my eyes
or ears growing long from the top of my head,
and could therefore command flying dragons and ride on auspicious clouds,
soar upon the lightning and reach inverted realms,
how would you, sir, then still find cause to question me?
Supposing you did see me,
you would call me a heaven spirit, an earth deity, or one of another kind,
and never think that this is something attained by study!
For now, let me merely use my prior enlightenment to guide those of like mind;
why must I insist
that you and your followers all believe it?
If every household had an immortal,
standing shoulder to shoulder before your very eyes,
even if you were blinded,
still you would have no doubt.
But when those people attain the Dao,
they tread the blue heavens and roam the purple poles;
unless someone is spiritually connected,
no one may see or hear them.
You, sir, would surely say yourself without ears.
People of this world trust in their own conjecture,
relying on their limited vision,
assuring themselves that their judgment
is never mistaken;
they are accustomed to what is attainable,
and are astonished at what is rare.
Even if it is pointed out to them,
still they never awaken.
It has been this way for ages;
how could it be unique to today?”
Someone said:
“Having often received your fine discourse,
it is enough that I do not doubt the existence of immortals.
But I still regret that I am unable to become one myself.
May I dare to ask if there is some essential method
that can be practiced by itself?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“All who study the Dao should start from the shallow and proceed to the deep,
beginning with the easy and advancing to the difficult;
if the will is sincere and firm
then nothing will be unattainable.
If there is doubt, then there will be no achievement;
this is not just in a single matter.
If a root does not penetrate the earth,
but one seeks branches and leaves touching the clouds,
or if a spring is not deep or clear,
yet one asks for a river to flow a thousand miles,
such a thing has never been.
Therefore, if one has not accumulated hidden virtue and done good deeds,
it will not be enough to move the spirits;
if one's heart is not sincere and united,
it will not be enough to bond with teachers and friends;
without merit, one should not speak of great endeavours;
and if one has not yet met a clear-sighted teacher, seeking the essential Way
cannot succeed.
Of all elixirs, the Golden Elixir of the Nine Transformations
is held supreme among immortals.
Yet this requires great expense and effort,
and cannot be accomplished quickly.
Treasuring essence and cherishing qì
—this is what is most urgent.
Along with this, take minor medicines to prolong life,
and learn the practical arts to ward off evil;
then one may gradually ascend to subtlety and refinement.”
Someone said:
“Of methods and techniques, there are so very many,
truly it is difficult to master them all.
Setting aside the Golden Elixir,
among the rest that may be practiced,
which are best?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“If you have not yet attained the greater essentials,
then the lesser ones must be widely studied.
For it is by relying on a combination of many arts that long life is achieved.
To put it in grand terms:
it is like a worldly ruler governing a state;
civil and military affairs, rites and laws—
not one can be omitted.
In more specific terms:
it is like an artisan building a cart;
the pole, the frame, the axle, the linchpin—
none may be missing.
As for these techniques,
they cultivate the form and spirit within,
to prolong years and cure disease;
they also repel evil from without,
keeping harm and misfortune at bay.
As with a lute or harp,
you cannot seek all five notes from a single string.
With armor,
you cannot defend against blades with a single strip of leather.
Why so?
Because all five notes are needed together, none may be lacking;
and where blades fall, even a little protection is still needed.
All who nurture life
should strive to hear much and grasp the essential,
to see broadly and choose well.
To practice only one method
is not something surely reliable.
Again, there is the flaw of those enthusiastic for novelty:
each relies solely on their own specialty.
Those who know the esoteric arts
say that only inner chamber arts
can help one transcend the world;
those who understand the art of breathing
say that only circulating qì can prolong life;
those who know stretching and bending techniques
say that only physical exercises can ward off old age;
those who know the herbal prescriptions
say that only medicinal preparations can grant immortality without end.
The reason why those who study the Dao do not succeed
arises from such bias and one-sidedness as this.
There are those with shallow vision,
who happen to master just one thing
and think it sufficient,
yet those who lack true understanding
may have good formulas
but still seek endlessly for more,
wasting effort and squandering their days;
and when applying what they know,
their intent is never fixed,
so all these let slip both ways.
Some are by nature dull-witted
and what they know is quite shallow and crude,
yet they force themselves to enter famous mountains,
braving venomous insects and stings,
often injured,
yet too ashamed to admit defeat.
Some are eaten by tigers or wolves;
some are slain by demons and ghosts;
some starve, lacking the arts of self-sustenance;
or freeze without any method to keep warm;
to perish in cliffs and valleys—
is this not folly?
To devote effort to learning is not as good as carefully choosing a teacher.
If the teacher’s experience is meager,
and he withholds his full knowledge when teaching,
one hears only,
‘In the Way, quantity does not matter.’
Indeed, if one has that supreme method of the Golden Elixir,
nothing else is needed.
However, those who know this art are exceedingly rare;
how could one idly wait for some uncertain great matter
and not, meanwhile, cultivate smaller arts of mutual benefit?
This is like a householder
saying that he has no use for anything else
only because he has gold, silver, jewels, and jade
all in hand and in his breast,
enough to provide for generations.
But if he lacks these,
how could he not sow every kind of grain
and store up fruit and vegetables?
Therefore, abstaining from grain to ward off armies,
subduing demons and spirits,
resisting all poisons,
curing myriad illnesses,
causing wild beasts in the mountains not to harm one
and dragons and monsters at water not to injure one,
being unafraid in times of plague,
turning invisible in moments of danger—
these are all minor arts,
yet not to be neglected.
How much more, then, should one not ignore those that surpass even these?”
Someone said:
“May I dare to ask about the cultivation of the Way of Long Life—
what taboos and prohibitions are there?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“The most urgent prohibitions
are simply not to injure or harm.
According to the admonitions within the Yì, the Scripture of Chì Sōngzǐ, and the Hé Tú’s Record of Fate Talismans, they all say that
Heaven and Earth have spirits who are officials in charge of faults,
who, depending on the severity of one's transgressions,
diminish one’s allotted span.
When the span is lessened, a person becomes poor, wasteful, and diseased,
frequently encountering troubles and calamities;
when the allotted span is exhausted, the person dies.
There are several hundred actions that can lead to the loss of lifespan,
too many to discuss in full.
It is also said that within the body there are Three Corpses.
The Three Corpses,
though formless, are in fact of the order of souls, spirits, ghosts, and deities.
They wish to cause a person to die early;
these Corpses desire to become ghosts,
to roam and wander at will,
and to enjoy the offerings and libations of people.
Therefore, whenever the day of Gēngshēn arrives,
they ascend to Heaven to report to the Director of Destinies
the misdeeds committed by people.
Also, on the night of the end of the lunar month,
the Kitchen God likewise ascends to Heaven to report a person’s crimes.
For major offenses, a jì is subtracted.
A jì
is three hundred days.
For minor offenses, sùan are deducted.
A sùan
is three days.
I myself have not been able to ascertain whether this matter truly exists or not.
Yet the Way of Heaven is remote,
and ghosts and spirits are hard to fathom.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ and Qín Mùgōng both personally received golden tablets from the Supreme Deity,
with clear proof shown upon their lands.
Mountains and rivers, grasses and trees,
wells, stoves, and pools—
all still possess vital essences;
within the human body
there are likewise souls and spirits.
How much more so should Heaven and Earth, as the greatest of things,
naturally possess spirit and consciousness;
with spirit and consciousness, it is fitting to reward goodness and punish evil.
It is only because its substance is vast and its net is wide-meshed
that response need not be instant and obvious.
Nevertheless, reviewing all Daoist precepts,
none fail to say that for those seeking long life,
one must accumulate goodness and establish merit,
show compassion to all beings,
extend forgiveness to oneself and to others,
be benevolent even toward insects,
rejoice in others’ fortune,
pity others’ suffering,
assist those in urgent need,
rescue those in poverty and distress,
never with one’s hand harm life,
never with one's mouth encourage misfortune,
view others' gain as one’s own gain,
see others' losses as one’s own loss,
not value oneself too highly,
not boast of oneself,
not be jealous of those who surpass oneself,
not flatter insincerely or act deceitfully.
Such a one is truly virtuous,
receiving blessings from Heaven,
seeing all labors swiftly accomplished,
and having hope of attaining transcendence.
If, on the contrary, one hates the good and delights in killing,
speaks false words with a duplicitous heart,
betrays trust and utters contradictory speech,
opposes uprightness and correctness,
acts cruelly toward inferiors,
deceives and misleads superiors,
rebels against those whom one serves,
shows no gratitude for favours received,
abuses laws for bribes,
condones crookedness and suppresses the upright,
sacrifices the public for private gain,
punishes the innocent,
destroys others’ families,
seizes others’ treasures,
harms the bodies of others,
takes the positions of others,
encroaches upon and oppresses the worthy,
kills and subdues the surrendered,
slanders and reviles saints and immortals,
injures Daoist adepts,
shoots at flying birds,
cuts embryos or breaks eggs,
sets fires and hunts in spring or summer,
curses and abuses spirits and deities,
teaches others to do evil,
conceals others’ good deeds,
endangers others for one’s own safety,
takes credit for others’ merits,
ruins the good works of others,
takes what others love,
forces apart those who are close by blood,
insults others in pursuit of victory,
takes from others more in cash,
returns less in grain,
breaks dams to release floods or starts fires,
uses magic and arts to harm others,
oppresses the weak and crippled,
exchanges good for evil,
seizes by force and demands by threat,
amasses wealth by plundering,
acts unjustly and unfairly,
is wanton and perverse,
bullies widows and orphans,
takes and appropriates lost property,
deceives and defrauds,
delights in exposing others’ secrets,
holds over others their faults and strengths,
claims to invoke Heaven and Earth,
utters curses seeking vengeance,
borrows and does not return,
exchanges on loan and does not repay,
pursues desires endlessly,
hates and rejects loyalty and faith,
disobeys superior orders,
shows no respect to one’s teachers,
mocks others who do good,
destroys others’ crops,
damages others’ tools,
exploits the poor for one’s own needs,
gives others unclean food and drink,
uses light weights and small measures,
narrows widths and shortens lengths,
mixes false with the genuine,
seeks crafty profit in buying and selling,
coaxes others to take things,
steps over wells or stoves,
sings at dusk or mourns at the new moon—
for any one of these things,
it is a crime;
depending on its severity,
the Director of Destinies deducts from one's lifespan or allotted time,
and when these are exhausted, one dies.
If there is only evil intent but no evil deed, lifespan is deducted;
but if evil acts result in harm to others, the allotted time is taken.
If one's lifespan and allotted time are unexhausted but one still dies,
calamity will affect one’s descendants.
Those who forcibly take others’ goods or wealth,
may find that their wives or children or household are made to make restitution instead,
even to the point of death and mourning,
though it does not occur immediately.
If the evil conduct is not enough to kill family members,
after a long time, they will still meet with disaster by water, fire, robbers,
or loss of property;
or they will encounter litigation or disease,
requiring private medical treatment,
or expenditures on sacrifices with slaughtered animals,
which must in total equal the amount unjustly taken.
Therefore Daoist teaching says, ‘Those who kill unjustly
are forced to kill and be killed by arms and blades in return.
Those who obtain wealth unrighteously,
without considering resentment,
are like those who use leaky dried meat to appease hunger,
or poisonous wine to quench thirst—
even if they are momentarily sated, death will certainly come upon them.’
If anyone has once committed evil deeds,
but later repents and reforms,
if they have killed people unjustly,
they should think to save in return those about to die, in order to absolve themselves.
If they have wrongly taken the wealth of others,
they should think to give to the poor and distressed to make amends.
If they have imposed guilt on others,
they should be intent on recommending the worthy to atone.
In all cases, these must be repaid double to what one has done,
then one can receive auspicious fortune,
and this is the way to turn misfortune into blessing.
If one is entirely without violations,
one is sure to extend life and increase longevity,
and achieve success in learning the Way swiftly.
Heaven is high but listens below;
nothing remains unnoticed;
those who do good without slackening
will surely receive a fortunate reward.
Yáng Gōng accumulated virtue and gave generously
throughout his long life
and thereby received gold that fell from Heaven.
Cài Shùn, through utmost filial piety,
was moved by divine response.
Guō Jù killed his own son for the sake of his parents
and obtained the great gift of the iron deed.
However, good deeds are difficult to perform,
evil deeds are easy to do.
Yet foolish people still rely on the likes of Xiàng Tuǒ and Bó Niú,
claiming that Heaven and Earth cannot discern good and bad,
not knowing that those who have outward reputation
do not necessarily have inner conduct,
those with public praise cannot cancel hidden crimes.
If one were to judge the fate of coriander and wheat on their birth and death,
and thus doubt the great energies of Yin and Yang,
this is not enough to reach the distant goal.
Thus, those superior beings who are most circumspect can barely avoid disaster.
It is because of mediocrity that one cannot attain one’s desires.”
Someone said:
“Your Dàodé is not yet accomplished,
nor have you managed to retreat and lose all traces in the famous mountains;
furthermore, the world today is not as it was in ancient times,
and there are very many thieves and robbers;
how then can you ward off calamities morning and evening,
and prevent unexpected misfortunes?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Always, at the hour of Jírì,
take upper earth from the position of the sixth Guǐ day,
and blend it with herbal incense made from a hundred leaves,
and plaster it on the door and threshold, the size of one foot square;
then thieves and robbers will not come.
You may also take earth from the southern city gate,
and earth broken at the year’s end,
or earth from the month’s establishment,
blend these together as a person,
and place it at the position of the Vermilion Bird;
this too will suppress thieves.
If there is urgency, enter the ‘Living Ground’ and abide there;
there will be no trouble.
Within All Under Heaven there is ‘Living Ground,’
each province has its ‘Living Ground,’
each commandery has its ‘Living Ground,’
each county has its ‘Living Ground,’
each village has its ‘Living Ground,’
each hamlet has its ‘Living Ground,’
each residence has its ‘Living Ground,’
and each room has its ‘Living Ground.’”
Someone said:
“If even a single room has a ‘Living Ground,’
is this not rather restrictive?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The classic says,
at the direst extremity of urgency,
one hides beside the carriage crossbar.
In this way,
even within a single carriage,
there is also ‘Living Ground’;
how much more so a single room?”
Someone said:
“I have heard, in seeking the Way to preserve life,
one must understand the Two Mountains.
I am not clear on which mountains these are;
where exactly are they found?
I beg you to enlighten and resolve my confusion.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“These mountains do exist;
they are not Huá or Huò,
nor are they Sōng or Dài.
The Tàiyuán Mountain
is hard to know but easy to seek;
it is neither Heaven nor Earth,
neither sunken nor floating,
entirely cut off and remote,
steep and winding;
its harmonious qi is gathered and dense,
its divine power wanders freely;
the jade well is profound and deep,
its irrigation never ceases;
there are a hundred and twenty officials,
with offices overseeing one another;
Lí and Kǎn are arrayed in order;
there are ten thousand mystic ganoderma plants;
a vermilion tree grows there alone,
all its treasures are unique,
gold and jade stand in lofty peaks,
sweet springs flow from its corners.
The ones who can return their years
draw from its limpid stream;
if you can cultivate yourself thus,
you could be the equal of tall pines;
—this is one mountain.
The Chánggǔ Mountain
is dim and lofty,
its dark qi drifts lightly,
jade nectar misting down;
the golden pond and purple chambers
are found in its recesses.
Foolish people go there in vain,
and all perish there;
but those skilled in the Way
ascend it without decay;
they gather and ingest huángjīng,
thus attaining flight to Heaven—
these are the Two Mountains.
They have always been the secret of the sages of old;
take careful thought upon them.”
Someone said:
“I wish to hear the methods by which the True Person preserves the body and refines the form.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Profound indeed is this question!
Beneath the initial green, below the moon and sun,
the two halves ascend together and unite as one.
Emerge from the jade pond and enter the golden chamber;
it is as large as a pellet, yellow as an orange,
within there is a fine flavor, sweet as honey;
if you can obtain it, be careful not to lose it.
Once lost, it cannot be recovered, and your life will be extinguished.
Pure white qi, subtle and fine,
rises through the obscure passes, winding through three bends;
within, cinnabar blazes forth, unmatched in brilliance;
placed at the Gate of Life, the form will not perish.
Profound! Marvelous! Difficult to make clear.
This is the oral formula of the former masters;
those who know it do not fear ten thousand demons or five armies.”
Someone said:
“I have heard that in matters of the bedchamber,
one who fully comprehends its method
can, on their own, attain spirit immortality;
and also turn away disaster and resolve guilt,
transform misfortune into blessing,
rise high in government service,
and double profits in trade—
is this truly so?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“These are all words from the books of sorcerers and from deluded exaggeration,
arising from enthusiasts embellishing the subject,
resulting in utter falsehood.
Some are even forgeries and wild inventions,
in order to deceive the world,
concealing the origin,
seeking to attract followers,
