recruiting disciples,
all merely to grasp worldly profit.
As for the arts of yīn and yáng,
at best, they can treat minor disorders,
and at second-best, prevent depletion—nothing more.
Their principle has its limits;
how could it alone bring spirit immortality, turn aside disaster, and procure blessings?
People cannot, if their yīn and yáng do not combine,
but wait for illness to befall them.
If they seek only to indulge their desires and cannot moderate themselves,
they injure life-span and fate.
One skilled in these arts
can cause the galloping horse to halt, replenishing the brain;
return the yīn elixir, coloring the bowels red;
gather jade nectar at the golden pond;
draw in the three and five at the flowery bridge,
such that you will age with a beautiful appearance,
and live out your allotted years from Heaven.
But ordinary people, hearing that Huángdì ascended to Heaven with 1,200 women,
think that Huángdì gained long life by this matter alone,
without knowing that Huángdì, at the foot of Jīng Mountain
and atop Dǐnghú,
completed the ninefold elixir,
and only then rode the dragon and ascended to Heaven.
Huángdì could indeed have 1,200 women,
but not by that means alone.
If one takes a thousand types of medicine,
or even the best livestock,
and does not know the arts of the bedchamber,
they gain nothing thereby.
Thus the ancients, fearing people would lightly abandon self-restraint,
therefore praised this art greatly in words,
but it cannot entirely be believed.
The Xuánsù canon compares it to water and fire:
water and fire can kill,
yet they also give life—
it depends on one’s ability to use them.
In general, knowing the key methods,
the more women one manages, the more beneficial;
but if one does not know the method,
even one or two women will bring swift death.
The art of Péngzǔ
is the most essential;
the rest in other classics are mostly laborious and hard to practice,
and their benefits do not match their claims.
Few people today can actually succeed in them;
and the oral formulas contain but a few thousand words.
Those who do not understand them,
even if they take a hundred medicines,
will still fail to obtain long life.”
Someone said:
“The supreme spirit Huáng Qióng,
in conferring destinies, ought to be impartial.
Why then is it that a common man like Qiáo Sōng receives the longevity of immortality,
while Zhōu and Kǒng, the greatest sages, do not enjoy the blessing of long life?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“The length of one’s allotted lifespan
truly depends on what one encounters.
When the vital energies are received and the embryo forms,
each person has their own stellar influences.
The Way of Heaven is non-intervening,
and allows things to be as they naturally are.
There is neither partiality nor bias,
neither this nor that.
If a person’s fate is governed by the star of life,
then that person will surely love the Way of Immortality.
Those fond of the Way of Immortality
will inevitably attain it if they seek it.
If one's fate is governed by the star of death,
then such persons will not believe in the Way of Immortality.
Lacking belief in the Way of Immortality,
they will not cultivate it themselves.
Whether one delights in what is good or not
is decided by that which one has received.
Alteration and bestowal, gain and loss
are not within Heaven’s ability.
It is like metal and stone melting in the furnace,
or clay vessels being shaped in the kiln.
Though they acquire form through these means,
the hardness or softness of bronze and iron,
the rightness or crookedness of jars and urns,
depend on what they happen to encounter;
these are not matters for the furnace or the kiln.”
Another person challenged:
“All that a skilled craftsman makes
comes from his handiwork.
Since Heaven is divine and wondrous,
what is there that it cannot do?
How can it be said that each person’s fate is determined by circumstance,
rather than by the design of that vast blue Heaven?
I am deeply confused by this
and dare not assent to it.”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“When chaos was sundered,
the pure and the turbid were set forth.
Some rose to move,
others descended and grew still.
Even Heaven and Earth themselves do not know the reason for this.
All beings respond to vital energies;
everything too proceeds naturally;
along with Heaven and Earth,
each is but a thing among things.
Only the order of their formation differs,
and their bodies are merely greater or lesser.
Because there is the greatness of Heaven and Earth,
all other things seem small.
Because there is the smallness of myriad beings,
so the greatness of Heaven and Earth is perceived.
Though the abdomen and back enclose the five organs,
the organs are not made by the abdomen or back.
Though the skin enfolds the blood and breath,
blood and breath are not produced by the skin.
Though Heaven and Earth contain all things,
yet all things are not made by Heaven and Earth.
It is like grasses and trees sprouting luxuriantly by relying on mountains and forests,
but the mountains and forests do not act for their sake.
Or fish and turtles depend on marshes and waters for birth and growth,
but the marshes and waters do nothing for them.
Common people see the greatness of Heaven and Earth,
and the smallness of things,
and so they say that Heaven and Earth are the parents of all things,
and that all things are the descendants of Heaven and Earth.
Now lice are born upon my body;
are they something I have made?
Lice cannot be born without me,
yet I am not their parent;
lice are not my descendants.
The mèměng are produced in vinegar,
zhī nù grow from wood and stone,
jiéqū arise from filth and rot,
cuì luó flourishes on the pine branches;
none of these four things are produced by those things upon which they grow.
The myriad creatures fill the space between Heaven and Earth;
is there any difference from this?
Heaven has sun and moon, cold and heat;
man has sight and breathing.
By inferring what is near from what is far,
by extending this to that,
if humans cannot understand the causes of aging, sickness or pain in their own bodies,
then likewise Heaven cannot know why it waxes and wanes or suffers calamity or fortune.
Man cannot make his ears and eyes always keen,
nor keep his vital energies from ever ceasing or being blocked;
just so, Heaven cannot keep the sun and moon from being eclipsed,
nor the four seasons from losing their order.
From this it can be said
that the matter of great longevity
truly does not lie with Heaven and Earth;
whether one becomes immortal or not
is certainly not determined by fate.
My father gave me life,
my mother bore me,
yet even they could not ensure my body would always be fit and appropriate,
my appearance would certainly be striking and beautiful,
my nature would necessarily be harmonious,
my wisdom would certainly be high and far-reaching,
my strength much increased,
my life long-extended.
Rather, some are short, ugly, stooped and weak,
others are dark and homely,
some may be deaf, blind, stubborn, and ill-tempered,
or deformed and halting;
what is gained is not what is wished for,
what is wished for is not what is gained.
How much less can we expect this from the vastness of Heaven and Earth?
Even parents are already remote from the effects.
As for my own self,
I cannot cause myself to remain always strong and never grow old,
always healthy and never sick,
to never err in joy or anger,
or never regret or fret over plans.
Thus, it is my parents who bestowed on me my qi and shape;
but it is I myself who have received and possess them.
Beyond this, there is no one closer to me than myself,
nor anyone who can control or command it.
Even these two cannot increase or diminish me;
how could Heaven and Earth possibly know me?
If, indeed, all persons were made by Heaven and Earth,
then all would be good and none evil,
all completed and none ruined,
and there would be no living beings not fulfilled in their kind;
then Xiàng Yáng would never suffer the sadness of withering in spring!
You say that Heaven cannot grant Kǒng and Mèng the blessing of surviving the ages;
thus it is evident that what is received has its own nature,
and is not divided out by Heaven and Earth.
The virtue of the sage
is virtue perfected.
If Heaven could bestow perfect virtue upon them,
yet cause them not to know all things,
or fail to accomplish their work,
or not hold kingly power,
or not live a hundred years,
would this not show that Heaven is without intervention?
If the Sage’s death
is not by Heaven’s killing,
then likewise the Sage’s life
is not by Heaven’s giving.
The worthy are not necessarily long-lived,
the foolish not necessarily short-lived.
Goodness does not ensure nearness to blessings,
nor evil to disaster.
Life is not fixed in years,
nor is death fated to a certain time.
Steadfast virtue and wisdom
may appear yet not yield fruit;
Dòu Gōng, an ordinary man,
lived nearly two hundred years.
Bó Niú was disabled,
Zǐ Xià lost his sight,
Dào Zhí was resentful and cruel yet died with white hair,
Zhuāng Jué was supremely wicked yet lived to old age.
That Heaven is non-intervening
is clear in these matters.”
Someone said:
“Zhòngní claimed that since ancient times all have died,
while Lǎozǐ spoke of the possibility of learning to become an immortal.
The words of the sages
are trustworthy and evidence-based;
what the Dàojiā speak of
is exaggerated and difficult to apply.”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“Zhòngní
is the sage of the Confucians;
Lǎozǐ
is the sage who attained the Way.
The Confucian teaching is near at hand and easy to perceive;
thus, those who honor it are numerous.
The Dào is distant in meaning and hard to comprehend;
therefore, those who reach it are few.
The Dào
is the source of all variance;
the Confucians
are a branch of the great simplicity.
After the Three Sovereigns,
the world was governed by the Dào.
Since the age of Emperors and Kings,
Confucian teachings have prevailed.
All who speak of such things understand the lofty and sincere naturalness of former times,
and disparage the shallow dissipation of later customs;
why then value Zhòngní alone and belittle the teachings of Lǎo shì?
This is to admire the blossom and ornament at the tips of the tree,
yet not recognize that what bears them has its root.
How is this different from esteeming bright pearls but scorning deep pools,
loving the Heshibì but hating the Jīng Mountains,
not knowing that the deep pools
are whence the bright pearls emerge,
the Jīng Mountains
are where the Heshibì is born?
Moreover, nurturing one's nature
is but a remnant of the Dào;
rites and music
are the last of the Rú teachings.
The reason the Rú are honored
is because they transform customs and alter folkways,
not merely for their bows and ritual turning.
The reason the Dào is revered
is because without words, its transformation spreads;
it is not solely about nourishing life.
If truly there were precedence between Confucianism and Daoism,
then Zhòngní could not be completely trusted alone,
nor could Lǎo shì be singly used.
Zhòngní respectfully asked questions of Bóyáng,
and wished to be compared with Lǎopéng.
He also recognized that, though he knew fish and birds, he did not understand dragons,
thereby likening Lǎo shì to a dragon—
these were words of true admiration,
not empty speech.
What he said to Yánhuí—
‘Looking ahead, it is before me,
yet suddenly it is behind;
the more I bore into it, the firmer it becomes;
the higher I look, the loftier it grows’—
is no different.”
Someone said:
“Zhòngní personally met Lǎo shì, yet did not follow him to learn the Dào;
why?”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“Examining this,
it becomes all the clearer that what one receives is determined by innate mandate,
and what one esteems stems from an unalterable nature.
Zhòngní knew that Lǎo shì was profound, wondrous, and precious,
but could not draw from the clarity and emptiness,
the great source and ancestral root,
which emerges outside of form
and enters within the ultimate Dào.
What he sought to learn
was only matters among the people,
how could he possibly request the arts of immortality?
I assess that his heart was urgently devoted
solely to teaching and transforming the world,
and did not concern itself with specialized arts.
Although Zhòngní was sage-like in worldly affairs,
he could not be profoundly tranquil and mysteriously silent,
keeping to non-action himself.
Thus Lǎozǐ admonished him, saying:
‘A good merchant conceals his wealth as if he had nothing;
a gentleman, though full of virtue, appears foolish.
Give up your arrogance and excessive desires,
your affectation and licentious ambitions;
these do not benefit your person.’
From this, we know that Zhòngní could not escape worldly emotions,
and was not one who learned the arts of immortality.
Ever restlessly anxious—
his efforts were to set the age aright;
looking up, he grieved at the phoenix’s song;
looking down, he sighed over gourds growing wild;
he feared that what he sold would not be bought;
generous and eager, he wished for even a horsekeeper’s role;
how, then, would he abandon the deeds of ordering the realm
to pursue the remote and empty practice of nourishing life?”
Someone said:
“Of the Confucian and Daoist endeavors,
which is more difficult or easier?”
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
“For the Confucian,
it is difficulty within ease.
For the Daoist,
it is ease within difficulty.
To part with friends and associates,
leave wife and children,
renounce fame and glory,
diminish profit and emolument,
deny dazzling sights to one’s eyes,
repress lovely sounds to one’s ears,
be calmly content and retire to tranquility,
cultivate goodness alone and guard oneself,
endure slander without grief,
hear praise without joy,
see the noble without coveting,
live in humble station without shame—
these are the Daoist difficulties.
Outwardly, with no expectation of congratulation or condolence,
inwardly, with no requirement of attention;
not straining the mind with the Seven Classics,
not exhausting thought on calendars and calculations,
the will bears none of the hardships of theorizing,
the heart suffers none of the labors of literary composition;
once various worries are diminished,
harmony naturally increases,
with non-action and no concerns,
unfrightened and unalarmed—
these are the Daoist eases,
the so-called ease within difficulty.
What the Confucian cultivates
all conforms to established models and precedent;
whether to enter or retire, there are prescribed standards;
speech and silence follow the times;
for teachers, one can seek among the humble houses;
books, with their commentaries, serve to resolve doubts—
these are the Confucian eases.
But in probing the profound and reaching the distant,
intertwining the canons and tombs of antiquity,
encompassing the full corpus of the Hé and Luò texts,
broadly embracing the innumerable schools of the Hundred Masters;
accumulating virtue amid the lanes and alleys,
fully committing loyalty and integrity in service to the ruler,
looking upward, the spirit rides after the heavenly images;
looking downward, thought whirls upon the winds and clouds;
if he is ignorant of one matter,
his actions will be ineffective;
if a single word is incorrect,
praise and censure will not be properly apportioned;
the lift of his foot is what the world takes as a model;
the movement of his lips is what the world transmits—
these are the Confucian difficulties,
the so-called difficulty within ease.
In earnest discourse about the two,
the Confucian enterprise has more difficulty,
the Daoist, greater simplicity and ease;
I worry over that difficulty,
and will set it aside and follow the easier.
As for those in the world who criticize me,
many are such, side by side.
But those with whom I might share understanding,
I have not yet seen such a person.
If there are people of the same conviction,
surely they will exist in the future,
so I do not yet call myself rare.”
Someone said:
“I have read and met men of great fame,
widely learned eminent scholars;
indeed, many have thoroughly investigated the principles and exhausted the nature,
and inquired into existence and nonexistence,
yet none have ever spoken of the extension of life,
or that immortality can be attained.
The Master’s brightness cannot match the sun and moon,
his wisdom does not surpass all men,
yet he claims to possess the Way of longevity—
this I dare not believe.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“I am a mediocre man of slight talent,
my knowledge is shallow and my understanding scant;
how could I dare presume myself distinguished among men or surpass the world?
But I have indeed sought out the hidden by means of the manifest,
and attained the difficult through the easy.
By comparing its small effects,
I thus know its great efficacy;
by observing what has already occurred,
I thus understand that which has not yet been tried.
Moreover, as for those in the world who do not believe that there are immortals between Heaven and Earth,
they yet will not take guidance.
They generally possess conventional worldly talents,
appropriate abilities for their occupations,
and peruse books and instructional texts,
using them to weigh straightforward matters of human nature,
and to discern what cloud the ordinary.
Thus, when encountering the doubts common to the multitude,
they believe they alone can resolve them.
Before a portent arises,
they claim to foresee it.
Thus, they believe with the feelings of all creatures
there is nothing left unexhausted for them;
with the obscure and hidden,
nothing escapes their grasp.
They claim that if they speak of the nonexistence of immortals,
then there must be none;
from ancient times this belief has been so firm!
I so often see that commonplace scholars, busy with trivialities,
do not believe in ultimate matters,
and are all troubled by having some intelligence,
yet are one-sided, narrow, and self-bound,
burdened by small cleverness,
unwilling to be wholly in darkness
like those who cannot tell beans from wheat.
With the narrow vision of peering through a tube,
and closing themselves off from what their wisdom cannot reach,
how is this different from drawing water with a mere fathom-long rope
from a hundred-fathom deep well,
and, not realizing their tool is too short,
claim the well has no water?
There are those among the common people who, hearing the sound of fierce wind and raging fire,
say it is winter thunder from the sky;
seeing drifting clouds heading west,
claim it is the moon moving east.
Some may tell them otherwise,
but they remain utterly unconvinced—
this is the trust in their own knowledge.
Those who listen to sounds
believe only their own ears;
those who observe forms
trust only their own eyes.
Yet it may be that what they see or hear,
they declare true when it is false;
then, are our ears and eyes really trustworthy?
How much more so with the workings of the mind,
which has neither form nor sound—
all the harder to understand than seeing and hearing—
that people, relying upon what their own minds can reach,
then firmly reject matters most remote from worldly affairs,
call immortals a fiction—
is this not delusion?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Beauty and ugliness are each established,
yet love and hate are of different emotions;
thus the two eyes do not always see alike.
Refined and common music are established,
yet preference and aversion differ;
thus the two ears do not always hear as one.
True and false each have a substance,
yet preferences and aversions are at odds;
thus the two hearts do not always plan alike.
There are those who take the ugly as beautiful,
the turbid as clear,
the lost as gained;
these three are clearly contrary,
apparent to all,
yet still the sides can never be reconciled.
How much more is this true of the affair of immortals,
which is exceedingly subtle,
and yet one wishes all people to believe in it—
how can that ever be?
If all men could know,
what worth would there be in enlightenment?
If one waits for the common folk to cease their idle talk,
it is like waiting for the Yellow River to run clear—
not such a long wait, is it?
That I cannot remain silent,
is only in hope that those above or below,
might be attracted and drawn in.
As for those who cannot be moved,
what could even the ancients do for them?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Ultimate principle is not easily made clear,
and immortals are not readily believed in;
this has been the case for a long time—
is it only now?
The Supreme One naturally knows;
next to Him are those who are instructed and then comprehend;
as for those who, upon hearing, laugh loudly—
these are in the majority.
In discussing these matters,
I may well regret being defeated many times
and reproach myself for words misspoken!
When things lack support,
those who harm will come.
Even blazing sunlight cannot give glory to rotten wood;
spiritual brilliance cannot transform a nature mired in darkness;
Zǐ Gòng could not please the rustic who branded horses;
Lord Gǔgōng could not sway the desires of the Róng and Dí of the borderlands;
realities cannot reach everywhere,
nor good words be always followed.
Official hats cannot be sold among the Mányuè,
nor red shoes used by the barefoot Yí—
how could one force it?
To see jade and call it stone
does not mean the jade is not genuine—
only that it must wait for Hé Shì to distinguish it.
To see a dragon and name it a snake
does not mean the dragon is not numinous—
it only waits for Cài Mò to recognize it.
What makes the Way precious
is that it cannot be increased by addition
or diminished by subtraction.
What makes virtue valuable
is that it is not saddened by slander
nor delighted by praise.
If others truly hold that there are certainly no immortals under Heaven,
and I alone contend, knowing truly there are,
the longer we dispute,
the more tenacious their position becomes,
which only breeds endless confusion
and never brings resolution
—should I really pursue the logic of chained arguments?”
Someone asked:
“The human path has many branches,
and seeking immortality is most difficult.
Unless one abandons something,
one cannot manage all affairs together.
The pursuit of the arts and culture,
the duties of worry and joy,
the Way between ruler and minister—
how can these be set aside?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“The essential Way is not complicated,
what is to be done is simply few.
The trouble lies only in not establishing one’s will,
in insufficient sincerity of belief.
Why then worry about the abandonment of human principles?
Those with great talent can embrace and cultivate all these together—
what difficulty is there in that?
Inwardly, treasure the Way of nourishing life;
outwardly, harmonize one’s radiance with the world.
Cultivate oneself, and one’s life will endure with refinement;
govern the state, and the country will enjoy peace.
Use the Six Classics to instruct the common people;
use specialized arts to teach those who understand.
If you wish to linger a while, then remain here and assist the times;
if you desire to ascend and soar, then rise to the high heavens and lift yourself lightly—
this is the true gentleman.
Those who rely solely on their own talents and abilities,
unable to achieve all things together,
thus withdraw from the world of men,
and concentrate solely on cultivating the Way and virtue—
these are only secondary.
Of old, Huáng Dì bore the charge of the Four Seas,
yet it did not hinder his ascension at Dǐnghú;
Péng Zǔ served as a great officer for eight hundred years,
and then journeyed west to Liúshā;
Bó Yáng was the Pillar Historian,
Níng Fēng was the Chief Pottery Official,
Fāng Huí was the Village Gentleman,
Lǚ Wàng was the Grand Preceptor,
Qiú Shēng served the Yīn dynasty,
Mǎ Dān was an official in Jìn,
Fàn Gōng dominated Yuè and sailed the seas,
Qín Gāo held a ritual tablet at the court of Sòng Kāng,
Cháng Shēng humbled his aspirations while handling the whip,
Zhuāng Gōng concealed his abilities as a lowly clerk.
The ancients often attained the Way and aided the world,
cultivating it while hidden at court—
this was because their strength was more than sufficient.
Why must one practice only in the mountains and forests,
completely abandoning the affairs of the living—
only then to succeed?
There are also those whose hearts are content in quietude and silence,
whose natures dislike noise and clamor,
who take delight in freedom and ease,
and find sorrow in prestige and office.
Clad in rope and wearing ragged clothes,
eating herbs and wielding the plough,
they enjoy their three pleasures,
abide by the norm and await their end,
not striving for mere existence,
not fearing an early death,
refusing rewards of a thousand gold,
disregarding the honors of high ministers.
Even without any cultivation or striving,
they are always thus;
how much more so if, in addition, they know the Way of the immortals?
They surely would not consent to exert themselves for the world.
Each follows their own aspiration;
it cannot be summarized in a single assessment.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“It is said in the world that one good word
is more precious than a thousand gold—
but this only refers to the success or failure of armies and states,
or the praise and blame of conduct.
As for imparting to others the secret of long life,
or granting them the method of immortality,
this is not merely like the kindly words of ordinary people—
so how can it be accounted as worth only a thousand gold?
Suppose there is someone suffering, near death,
and another can save him and bring him recovery—
all would call this a great and weighty kindness.
Now, if according to the classic of immortals,
one can refine the Nine Elixirs,
transmute water, gold, and jade,
then all under Heaven could be made immortal;
such a benefit is not merely equal to saving a single life.
The virtue of Huánglǎo
is indeed immeasurable;
yet no one can comprehend it,
and they call it wild and deceitful talk—
this is to be lamented.”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“If one wishes to seek the shénxiān,
one must grasp only the most essential points,
and the most essential lies in preserving the jīng and practicing the circulation of qì;
taking only a single great elixir is sufficient,
and there is no need for more.
Yet even these three matters,
have their degrees of depth and shallowness;
if one does not encounter an enlightened teacher,
and does not persist with diligence and hardship,
one cannot expect to know everything in haste.
Though it is said to practice the circulation of qì,
yet there are several methods for circulating qì.
Though it is said the ‘arts of the bedchamber,’
yet within the arts of the bedchamber,
there are close to a hundred techniques.
Though there is talk of taking medicines,
yet of recipes for taking medicines,
there are roughly a thousand methods.
When first transmitting these to people,
all start from the shallow,
and those who have resolve and are not lax,
and are diligent and hardworking,
only then are told the essentials.
Therefore, circulating qì may sometimes cure a hundred illnesses,
sometimes enter pestilence unharmed,
sometimes ward off snakes and tigers,
sometimes stop wounds from bleeding,
sometimes allow one to dwell in water,
sometimes walk across water,
sometimes ward off hunger and thirst,
sometimes prolong one’s lifespan.
Its most important aspect
is ‘embryonic breathing.’
One who achieves embryonic breathing
is able not to breathe in and out with nose or mouth,
as if within the womb,
then the Dào is accomplished.
At the beginning of practicing the circulation of qì,
draw the qì through the nose and hold it,
secretly count with your heart up to one hundred and twenty,
then gently exhale through the mouth;
in both inhaling and exhaling,
do not allow even your own ears to hear the sound of qì coming and going,
always letting more in than out,
and placing a goose feather atop the nose and mouth,
if the feather does not move when exhaling, this is the sign.
As one gradually becomes more accustomed, increase the number counted in the heart,
in time reaching up to a thousand;
reaching a thousand, those who are old will become young again,
each day reclaiming another day.
One must circulate qì at the time of living qì,
and not at the time of dead qì.
Therefore it is said, ‘The immortal takes in the six qì’—
this is what is meant.
In one day and night there are twelve double hours;
from midnight until noon, the six double hours are living qì;
from noon to midnight, the six double hours are dead qì.
At the time of dead qì,
circulating qì is of no benefit.
Those skillful at using qì
blow on water,
and the water reverses and flows back several steps;
blow on fire,
and the fire is extinguished;
blow on tigers or wolves,
and tigers and wolves crouch and cannot move;
blow on snakes and huǐ,
and they coil and cannot depart.
If another is wounded by weapons,
blow upon them and the bleeding immediately stops;
if one hears of someone afflicted by poisonous insects,
even without seeing the person,
blowing and chanting spells toward one’s hand at a distance,
for a man one blows on the left hand,
for a woman the right hand,
and even if the afflicted person is a hundred lǐ away,
they are immediately healed.
Also, for those suddenly struck by fierce illness,
merely swallow the qì of three times nine,
and they too recover at once.
But human nature is often restless,
and few can calm themselves to cultivate this Dào.
Again, the main point in circulating qì
is not to eat excessively,
nor eat raw vegetables or rich fresh foods,
which make the qì too strong and hard to restrain.
Also, avoid anger;
frequent anger disorders the qì,
and if it cannot flow out,
may cause coughing,
so few are able to do this practice.
My paternal grand-uncle Xiān Gōng,
whenever greatly drunk or in the heat of summer,
would always enter the depths of deep pools,
and after a day would emerge—
this was precisely because he could cease breathing and practice embryonic breathing.
There are over ten family traditions of the bedchamber arts,
some to repair injury and damage,
some to attack and treat various illnesses,
some to gather yīn to benefit yáng,
some to increase age and to prolong life,
but their essential point lies in returning jīng to replenish the brain.
These methods have always been passed down from mouth to mouth by the zhēnrén,
and originally were not written down.
Even if one takes famous medicines,
if one does not know this essential,
one cannot achieve longevity.
Nor should one entirely sever yīn and yáng,
for if yīn and yáng do not unite,
one inevitably incurs blockages and stagnation,
thus those who are shut in and resentful outcasts
are often sick and do not live long.
Yet to indulge one’s desires recklessly
also shortens one’s lifespan.
Only those who attain moderation and harmonious regulation
can avoid harm.
If one does not understand the oral transmission of these techniques,
then of countless people not a single one will avoid harming or killing themselves through such practice.
Xuánsùzǐ, Dū Róngchéng Gōng, Péng Zǔ and their like
have recorded only their superficial practices,
and never commit the most essential things to writing.
Those who are determined to seek deathlessness
should diligently pursue and practice these things.
I have received the teachings of my master Zhèng Jūn,
therefore I record this to show future devotees of the Dào,
not as idle conjecture.
I myself have not yet fully grasped all these oral instructions.
Some Dàoist priests along the way
wish to devote themselves solely to the arts of sexual union
in order to seek the shénxiān,
yet do not make the great elixir of jīndān;
this is truly utter folly.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Of the Dào texts attributed to Huáng-Lǎo,
truly only a few are genuine;
most were composed by lovers of novelty in later generations,
each expanding according to their limited understanding,
so that the volumes eventually piled up like mountains.
The ancients were simple and unsophisticated,
and many lacked talent;
thus, their discussions of the principles of things
were neither thorough nor exhaustive,
and their demonstrations and verifications
were likewise not clear and explicit.
All lacked what was essential and were difficult to interpret,
and yet the interpretations themselves were not deep or far-reaching,
insufficient to elaborate and unfold subtle meanings,
to reveal and inspire those eager to learn,
to encourage and advance the determined,
to teach and admonish beginners,
or to enable understanding of the mysterious and wondrous path,
the origins and courses of calamity and fortune.
To recite them ten thousand times
yields truly nothing to be obtained.
Even if one wishes to read widely,
one should carefully select the good among them
before focusing attention.
As for the Dàoist texts that are unnecessary,
they are not worth searching out and tracing.
Some later students may not distinguish the shallowness or depth of the authors,
and, regarding all words named as those of the Dàoist school,
they merely transcribe and fill boxes and baskets,
exhausting their minds pondering the contents.
This is like seeking phoenix eggs in a swallow's nest,
or trying to catch eels at the bottom of a well.
Even if utmost diligence is applied,
it is not a thing to be possessed,
and cannot be necessarily put to use;
in vain are days and months wasted,
leaving only the toil of weariness,
and not a hair’s breadth of benefit is gained.
In advancing, one becomes neglectful of the affairs of the age;
in retiring, one attains no effect of longevity;
thus, none fail to point and say,
‘This one cultivates the Dào with such diligence,
and yet fails to transcend the world;
therefore, there can be no art of immortality beneath heaven.’
Yet they do not know that this person's quest for immortality
is like standing by a river longing for fish
but lacking net or trap;
it is not the river that is without fish.
Moreover, although the Five Thousand Words came from Lǎozǐ,
all are but general discussions and summaries.
In them, there is nowhere a matter wholly and thoroughly set forth from beginning to end
that could serve as a dependable guide.
Simply reciting the text by rote
without obtaining the essential Dào
is sheer futile labor,
how much more if one cannot even attain that?
As for the likes of Wénzǐ, Zhuāngzǐ, Guān Líng, and Yǐn Xǐ,
their writings and prose,
though they take Huáng-Lǎo as their model,
following the pattern of the mysterious and abstract,
only elaborate their general aims
and never reach ultimate words.
Sometimes they equate life and death,
regarding existence and survival as burdensome labor,
regarding death as rest,
which is a thousand billion lǐ from the way of immortals,
so how could one so indulge in them?
Their parables and analogies
indeed offer things worthy of adoption,
for minor applications,
to stave off occasional shortages;
but in the end, they let the depraved flatterers and dissolute sons of later ages
use Lǎo and Zhuāng as their lair and refuge—
is this not a pity?”
Someone said:
“When a sage and enlightened ruler governs the world,
only worthies are valued as treasures;
yet those who study immortality
are unwilling to enter officialdom.
If all people cultivate the Dào,
who then would assist in governing affairs?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Those who turn their backs on a sage ruler and dwell in mountains
are like Cháo and Xǔ, who are thus deemed noble;
those who, encountering a time of true Dào, yet withdraw from the world
are like Zhuāng and Bó, who are therefore esteemed.
When Xuānyuán ruled all under Heaven,
this was truly the summit of good governance,
yet Guǎngchéng did not join him;
when Táng Yáo possessed all within the four seas,
this was true peace and prosperity,
yet Wòquán did not assist him,
nor was virtue and transformation lessened thereby,
nor were men of talent lacking.
When Tiānyǐ overturned a dynasty,
Wùguāng carried a stone to drown himself in the river;
when Jī Wǔ destroyed Shāng,
Yí and Qí would not eat the grain of Xīshān;
when Qí Huán rose to power,
Shǎojì slumbered peacefully in a humble alley;
when Wèi Wén prospered,
Qiánmù let down his hair in Xīhé;
the Four Elders gathered like phoenixes at Shāngluò,
yet this did not hinder the abundance of worthies in the Great Hàn;
Zhōu Dǎng and Lín Zhì dwelt in the woods and marshes,
yet Gāngwǔ’s corrections were not diminished.
Their hearts could not be moved by honor and nobility,
nor could the utmost wealth alter their affections.
Washing their tassels in the Blue Waves,
they would not submit, would not be humiliated,
making fragrant forests their terraces and pavilions,
lofty peaks their great halls,
green orchids their brocade beds,
verdant leaves their curtains,
coarse garments in place of embroidered robes,
wild vegetables their fine cuisine.
If not by their own tilling, they had nothing to fill hunger;
if not by their wives’ weaving, they had no clothes against the cold.
Through a thousand ages,
at times such people have existed.
How much more those who also forsake their close kin and clans,
abandon their households and do not look back,
turn their backs on glory as if discarding footprints,
cutting off desire from heart and mind,
traversing lofty mountains in solitary wandering,
companioning only shadows among famed peaks,
contemplating within the formless domain,
listening within utter silence—
within the eight extremes,
how many such people could there truly be?
And yet you fear your lord will be without ministers—
is this not to be too anxious?”
Someone said:
“Those who study to become xiān,
purify only themselves and forget the disorder of the great relationships,
turn their backs on the rulers of their time, and display the arrogance of not being official subjects.
I fear that not only will they not succeed in attaining immortality,
but they will also come to suffer the net of guilt.”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“Among the people of the North, Shí Hù, Shàn Juǎn, and Zǐ Zhōu,
all were men of great talent,
yet they withdrew, retreated, and liberated themselves,
nurturing their abundant vital energy.
Their rising and falling did not bring them loss,
the grand transformation did not make them deficient.
How much more so with those who study to become xiān—
they do not necessarily have the talent to govern the state,
or the utility to serve at court;
whether society gains or loses them, it feels neither the benefit of dust nor dew,
nor the harm of a hair’s width missing.
Now, with the Nine Regions sharing one dwelling,
even those from remote wastes come to serve;
the qualified and accomplished pile up,
yet have nowhere to be employed.
There are scholars detained on the waiting list,
while there are no temporarily vacant offices;
those who toil long sigh at their slow acknowledgments,
those with high achievement are constrained by advancement by seniority;
so abundant is the crowd of the talented,
naught could surpass their excellence,
and the loss of a single individual
is not to be missed.
In ancient times, Zǐ Jìn left his duty of serving food,
and relinquished the heavy charge of being the reserve heir,
yet King Líng did not blame him for being unfilial;
Yǐn Shēng abandoned his office as girded official,
and resigned from an important position,
yet the Zhōu dynasty did not accuse him of disloyalty.
Why is this?
Because they truly demonstrated that they were not slighting the world or belittling their rulers;
it is simply that what they pursued differed,
for each person’s resolve
has something that cannot be changed.
A ruler possessing the Way
bears insults, excels at forgiveness,
and understands that people’s minds cannot be identical,
that their choice to appear or withdraw is by their natures;
he does not coerce nor prohibit,
thereby exalting and glorifying greatness.
Above, he has no partial heart of suspicion or resentment;
below, his people attain perfect joy.
Therefore, his illustrious reputation shines and spreads to boundlessness,
so that greedy men grow ashamed upon hearing of him.
I have heard that when the gentle wind rises, the cloaks and braziers are set aside;
when the times are peaceful, those of unusual ability withdraw.
Now that turmoil and chaos have been pacified,
cattle rest and horses are set free,
beacons are extinguished and cast no shadow,
weapons are returned to their cases,
the bow has been put away,
and the owl is ready for cooking;
Zǐ Fáng left the dark curtain and returned to the lanes among the people,
and Xìn Yuè put aside his armor and took up fishing.
How much more then for those who study to become xiān,
numbering less than one in ten thousand—
how could the nation begrudge so few people?
Moreover, their practice is focused on few thoughts and few desires,
their calling is in preserving the body and longevity;
they do not engage in the ugliness of competition,
nor do they injure custom or bear its burdens;
so what crime do they have?
Furthermore, Huáhuò is grand to the utmost,
and the vast ocean is boundless and wide;
its height does not await the coming of floating dust,
its depth does not draw on passing rainwater;
gathering a handful of earth cannot lessen its loftiness,
dipping a ladle of water cannot diminish its expanse.
In an entire age, there are but a few immortals,
how could they possibly diminish the enterprise of men?”
Someone said:
“If the Way of the Immortals could truly be attained,
why do the Five Classics not record it,
why do Zhōu and Kǒng not speak of it,
why did the sages not transcend the world,
why do the highest intelligences not dwell long among us?
If Zhōu and Kǒng did not know of it,
then they cannot be considered sages.
If they knew of it but did not practice it,
then there is no Way of the Immortals.”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“Men are under the influence of stars and constellations,
each has what befalls him,
and these have already been discussed in detail in another chapter.
You may be said to be wearing a basin upon your head and looking up,
unable to behold the brilliant shine of the Seven Luminaries;
you only briefly gaze across the great river,
unaware of the marvels in the deep.
What is not recorded in the Five Classics is countless,
and what Zhōu and Kǒng did not speak of is not small in number.
Let me briefly explain but one small portion to you.
Even if you laugh greatly and cannot stop,
and your restricted perspective is hard to open fully,
I still wish you to hear a rough summary.
Heaven and earth are the greatest of things.
Nine sages jointly created the Book of Changes,
enough to harmonize and encompass Yin and Yang,
and nothing could be added to it.
But now, if you ask those skilled in the Changes
about the number of degrees of the circuit of the heavens,
the breadth and narrowness of the Four Seas,
the distance across the universe,
how many lǐ in all these?
What is the utmost above,
what is the foundation below?
How is its rotation carried out,
who drives and pulls it?
The slowness or speed of the sun and moon,
the course traversed by the Nine Paths,
the waxing and waning of day and night,
the alternation of the seven stars,
the expansion and contraction of the five wandering stars,
the aureoles and eclipses,
the conjunctions and conflicts of the four and seven,
whence comets and meteors emerge,
the oddities of celestial omens,
the auspices of eclipses and portentous phenomena,
the fixedness of the celestial pole,
the lone eastward course of Zhènxīng,
Xīhé is bright without yet brings heat,
Wàngshū appears within and thus is cold,
the stars of the Milky Way can be seen providing the nature of moisture and descent,
the tides’ ebb and flow show great and small changes,
the five tones and six harmonies,
divining joy and anger,
the movement of clouds and arising of vapors,
portending auspicious or inauspicious events,
the stars Chán, Qiāng, Yóu, and Shǐ,
the sequence of times and their red and intertwining threads,
the four guardians and five diminutions,
Tiāngǒu’s return to the harmful,
sometimes showing completion,
sometimes correcting decline—
though familiar with the Book of Changes,
you cannot discuss these.
In turn, ask those of the Spring and Autumn Annals, the Four Divisions, Shījīng, Shūjīng, and the Three Rituals;
they too cannot answer.
They all say these are not recorded in the orthodox classics,
only Wū Xián, Gān Gōng, Shí Shēn, Hǎi Zhōng, Xì Méng, and the records of the Seven Luminaries contain these in full.
If I then ask:
Are the writings of these six houses
teachings of the classics?
They would reply: No.
And if I ask further:
Are the followers of Gān and Shí
sages?
They would again reply: No.
Thus, from birth we wear the heavens above,
and reaching old age tread upon the earth below,
yet if we seek them above what is written in the Five Classics, nothing is there,
and if we search the works of Zhōu and Kǒng, we do not obtain the answers.
Can we then wholly take them for falsehood and illusion?
The heavens and earth are extremely vast,
and even what meets the eye
cannot all be comprehended,
how much less the most profound of the mysterious and the subtlest of the marvelous?”
Again, I ask ordinary people:
“As for the nations that ride clouds in cocoons,
and the peoples whose livers and hearts do not decay,
living in nests and caves,
with a single eye and three heads,
horses at leisure and dogs with hooves,
long arms crossed with legs,
the Yellow Pool with no men,
pierced chest with side mouths,
Lord Lǐn who started with stone and floated a clay ship,
Shā Yī who struck wood and birthed a host of dragons,
Nǚwā emerging from the earth,
Dù Yǔ falling from the sky,
flying bricks and talking dogs,
mountains shifting and altars moving,
the armies of three divisions
in a single morning all transformed,
gentlemen turning into cranes,
petty men into sand,
the ugly woman leaning on a withered tree,
Èrfù embracing a shackle,
host-lodging insects,
shedding armor to step forth as flesh,
the double-headed serpents,
string for bows,
wood that will not burn,
fire that never grows hot,
the birds of Chāng and Shǔ,
beasts without eyes,
heads without bodies,
bodies without heads,
Jīngwèi filling up the sea,
succession of creatures giving way each to the next,
cloth cleansed by fire,
knives that cut jade,
flaming dragons hissing out fire,
mud ground and strained for water,
withered shrubs taking new shapes,
the mountain kuí with a foot in front,
the stone xiū with nine heads,
Bìfāng with a human face,
Shàoqiān’s impeachment of Bóshuài,
Shèngqīng’s service to Sùshuāng,
the Western Qiāng made powerful by the tiger’s shadow,
the Xiānbēi strong by riding turtles,
Línyì ruling by spiritual records,
Yōngshǔ with the Emperor of the Flowing Corpse,
the Salt Spirit brings forth children and insects take flight,
the wide-eyed ones transform the world amid the Jīng peaks,
the Five Dǐng dragging snakes and toppling heights,
and the mighty flesh flapping wings over the three seas.
Golden tablets and jade scripts
unearthed by the well of Yǔ.
Accurate devices and true balances
cut from fine stone.
All these strange events
number in the thousands,
yet are not recorded in the Five Classics,
nor explained by Zhōu and Kǒng.
Can one say none of them ever existed?
As for the southerners who can enter a pillar and exit through an ear,
Yǔkòu stopping his elbow in water as he draws the bow,
Bóhūn walking a hundred million rèn in one stride,
Lǚliáng chanting as he leapt across an abyss,
Duke Sòng carving shapes on leaves to confound reality,
Gōngshū building flying wood that hovered and soared,
Lízhū spotting a single hair’s breadth at a hundred paces,
Bēnhuò demonstrating his strength at ten thousand jūn,
the Yuè man reviving the dead by feeling for a needle,
Shù Hài leaping over thousands with his tracks,
the man of Yǐng brandishing an axe at his mud-plastered nose,
Zhòngdū baring his body in the depths of winter—
all these were beyond even Zhōu and Kǒng.
Can one say none of them ever existed?
If even the sages truly had things they could not do,
then it is not surprising if they could not become immortals;
not becoming immortals also does not prevent one from being a sage.
That there are things sages occasionally do not understand
is insufficient grounds for assaulting and challenging their wisdom.
The sages may well accept coming or going,
follow what is natural,
possess the body without selfishness,
possess life without pursuit,
leave existence and extinction to Heaven,
let length and brevity rest with fate,
thus not learning the art of Immortality,
and what is there to be surprised at in that?”
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
“The Dào encompasses Qián and embraces Kūn;
its origin is nameless.
If one discusses its non-being,
then its shadow and echo still count as being;
if one discusses its being,
then all myriad things are still as if not existing.
Lìshǒu cannot calculate its quantity,
Lí Zhū cannot discern its likeness,
Wú Zhà and Jìn Yě exhaust their hearing,
yet cannot seek its sound within the depths of obscurity;
Zhōu Xī and Bù Zhū run swiftly,
yet cannot trace its signs beyond the universe.
Speaking of it as nearby,
it effortlessly permeates the autumn down and has abundance to spare;
speaking of it as distant,
it envelops the great void and is not enough.
It is the sound of sound,
the echo of echoes,
the form of forms,
the shadow of shadows.
The square receives it and is at rest;
the round receives it and moves;
the descending receives it and bends low;
the ascending receives it and looks up.
To forcibly name it as Dào
is already to lose its reality,
let alone when it is divided a thousand ways and judged a hundredfold,
split a hundred million and analyzed ten thousand times,
so that its names and surnames reach to the boundless;
this is to depart from Dào to a vast distance—
is it not far indeed?
Common people cannot recognize its primordial root,
but cultivate only the final aberrant traces.
If people can be indifferent, quiet, serene, and at ease,
unstained and unshaken,
nourishing their hearts with absence of desire,
fostering their spirits with purity and simplicity,
cleansing away seductive hankerings,
gathering themselves with uprightness,
ridding themselves of the desire to seek what is hard to find,
sending away the burdens that harm the true,
slighting the unruly passions of joy and anger,
extinguishing the roots of love and hate,
then without asking for fortune, fortune comes;
without warding off misfortune, misfortune departs.
Why is this?
Destiny is within,
not attached to the external;
Dào dwells here,
and there is no need to await it from elsewhere.
The affliction is that ordinary men cannot keep the true,
and lack boundaries of restraint to block and check themselves;
love of tastes and pleasures stirs and carries them away,
they gallop wildly and flee,
lost in confusion, unable to return;
their feelings respond to things, and arise outwardly,
their intelligence attaches to affairs, and overflows on all sides.
Lured by desirable things,
the nature of Heaven is destroyed;
deluded by what is seen and heard,
they lose essential simplicity and unity.
The mind is bound by excess and extravagance,
feeling is muddied and disturbed by surging waves.
Thus come disasters of collapse and disorder,
and calamities from which they cannot recover.
In vain they slaughter fattened cattle and pigs,
pour libations of strong ale and sweet wine,
clash bells and beat drums,
sing and leap in song and dance,
bow down, prostrate, and knock their foreheads to the ground,
guard the empty seat and wait,
beseech and beg for blessing and favor,
hoping it must surely come;
to their dying day they remain unenlightened—
is this not lamentable indeed?
When the spirit is vexed by disturbances,
inner harmony is consumed by toil and labor,
the body and vital breath are boiled and tormented,
natural harmony is carved and diminished,
rest and exertion go to extremes,
and they dash their heads to the ground to beg for life,
their illnesses turn dire,
and so they sacrifice and pray seeking recovery;
they lie in the wind and sleep in the damp,
and then plead for pardon from the spirits;
gluttonous eating and drinking without moderation,
but blame their misfortune on ghosts and demons.
Their tiny bodies
bring these woes upon themselves;
how can Heaven, Earth, and the numinous powers
possibly deliver them?
Even if they slaughter the whole herd for sacrifice,
what benefit is there?
Blessing is not something gained by mere piety,
nor is misfortune dispelled by sacrifices and rites.
If destiny could truly be prolonged by repeated prayers,
if illness could be eliminated by abundant offerings,
then the wealthy would surely live long,
and the noble would surely never fall ill.
Spirits do not delight in sacrifices not of their kind,
ghosts do not partake in irregular offerings;
those in the alleys of humble station
cannot turn aside the golden-charioted coaches,
nor can plain-folk gates
move the six-horse teams.
Though all are human,
yet rank and lowness are worlds apart—
how much more so with the spirits of Heaven,
remote, lofty, and pure,
their kind utterly different,
their nobility absolute.
It is certainly not the stinking wines and humble foods,
nor the cringing bodies of the common folk,
that can move them to descend—
this is already clear.
For those who are disloyal and unfilial,
the gravest of crimes,
even if they accumulate gold by the thousand jin,
or the grand offerings of an imperial banquet,
and seek fair reputation from an enlightened sovereign,
or release from blame from their country,
one person seeking pardon from another
is still not always successful—
how much less can long life be obtained for a good name,
or serious illness be removed for absolution?
Ghosts and spirits are of a different order,
they ally themselves only with uprightness;
to expect them to grant partial blessings
has never been heard of.
Even a ruler ashamed of virtue
or a minister who endures disgrace
can still reward the good without asking a bribe,
and punish evil without acting on private feelings,
ensuring rules and standards are firmly maintained,
impartial and without party spirit;
how much more must it be so for ghosts and spirits,
who are far beyond this,
and cannot be moved by artful speech,
nor swayed by decorated bribes—
this can certainly be known.
Líng Wáng of Chǔ,
personally performed shamanistic rites,
spared nothing for sacrificial victims,
but could not turn back the punitive army of Wú.
At Guǎnglíng in Hàn,
they reverently honored Lǐ Xū,
emptied the treasury but could not avert the punishment for rebellion.
Emperor Xiào Wǔ believed especially in ghosts and spirits,
his sacrifices without lack of observance,
yet could not avoid death at Wǔ Zhà.
Lord Sūn esteemed Huáxiāng,
enfeoffed him with a king’s title,
yet could not prolong his life to its appointed limit.
It was not that the sacrificial animals were not abundant,
nor that the jade and silks were insufficiently fine,
nor that his faith was insincere,
nor his reverence lacking gravity;
there was damage like a mound of earth,
yet not a hair’s breadth of benefit.
Is this not due to missing what is near,
and instead striving after what is far?”
The Fifth Gōng executed and eliminated the heretical Daoists,
yet he lived long and was honored;
Sòng Lújiāng abolished the mountain sacrifices,
and his blessings and prosperity endured to the end;
Wén Wēng destroyed the temple of the spirit of the water,
and his person was fortunate and the people secure;
Wèi Wǔ prohibited the customs of licentious worship,
and great good fortune came forth.
Past events are not to be forgotten,
they serve as a mirror for what is to come.
Illustrious virtue is truly fragrant;
those without worries live long;
one who cherishes and protects does not die young;
much grief only brings on early aging;
thus it is the principle of nature,
why concern yourself with external things!
If one’s nurturing loses harmony,
and attacks are not resolved,
then a hundred ailments take hold wherever there is a gap,
and the vital essences are exhausted without realization.
Even with the grandest sacrifices of three animals,
how can they bring restoration?
What the common people speak of is mostly heretical and false,
they deceive and confuse one another in turn,
and this only grows more severe over time.
They can neither perfect the art of healing illness,
nor return from their deep delusion;
they do not pursue remedies in medicine and stone,
but devote themselves only to the erroneous ways of prayer and sacrifices,
praying endlessly,
inquiring of diviners tirelessly.
Sorcerers and ritualists of low standing
utter wild words of calamity and misfortune;
when illness becomes critical,
there is nothing they have not heard,
yet upon hearing, they immediately carry it out,
resulting in limitless expense;
wealthy households exhaust their storages,
the poor must borrow and then double their repayments,
their fields and houses are divided up until all is lost,
and trunks and chests are emptied with nothing left behind.
If by chance there is some slight recovery,
they at once claim it as a gift from the gods;
but if there is death,
they say it is because the ghost was not pardoned.
If by fortune one survives in error,
with wealth and property already depleted,
they end up dying of hunger and cold,
or turn to robbery and plunder,
or commit burglary and theft,
losing their lives beneath blades and arrows,
or becoming subject to shameful punishments,
all because of these causes.
Sometimes all their possessions are spent on sacrificial expenses,
silks and cloth are squandered on greedy and unscrupulous mediums;
when they are dead and gone,
they have no valuables for burial,
nor garments and covers to wrap them,
so that their corpses rot, filled with worms;
how lamentable indeed!
The blindness of the foolish masses
truly reaches such extremes!
Licentious sacrifices and evil spirits
are what the rites and laws prohibit.
Nevertheless, common people
can ultimately never understand.
Only the king should further strengthen laws and regulations,
punishing all offenders, great or small,
by sentencing them to capital punishment;
those who continue to employ sorcerers and mediums,
should be punished without pardon,
and exposed to the marketplace for public shame.
It will not be long before,
without a doubt, all such affairs will cease,
thus allowing the people to cut off the source of hunger and cold,
and stem the first stirrings of banditry and theft—
this is no small benefit.
In former times, there were the likes of Zhāng Jiǎo, Liǔ Gēn, Wáng Xīn, and Lǐ Shēn,
who claimed to be millennia-old immortals,
and pretended to petty arts,
presiding while others came and went,
changing forms and appearances,
bewildering and deluding the common people,
gathering crowds of the foolish,
seeking not to prolong life or increase span,
nor truly to relieve disaster or heal illness,
but only assembling villainous cliques,
stirring up rebellion and chaos in the name of unity;
those unaffiliated were destroyed in consequence,
sometimes causing the massacre of innocent men,
sometimes deceiving and enticing the people,
all to seize profit and gain,
amassing cash and silk in piles like mountains,
wealth surpassing that of princes and nobles,
indulging in extravagant living and debauchery,
wearing luxurious attire and eating delicacies,
with courtesans and concubines filling their rooms,
musicians arranged in rows,
employing assassins and death-defying followers
to serve their interests,
their power rivaling rulers of states,
their influence overwhelming the officials,
fugitives and criminals
using them as dens of refuge.
All this arose because the authorities did not prosecute and correct them,
so the calamity arose.
Tracing back to the cause,
one cannot help but sigh.
We, the common people,
even if we see the reason,
are not in a position of authority,
and have no way to change things.
The local magistrates in charge of the people
suspect that gods exist,
and fear prohibiting these activities,
lest they bring calamity and misfortune;
even if they do harbor doubts,
they cannot resolve them,
and this is not a pressing duty of their office,
nor an urgent matter in their performance evaluations;
furthermore, it is what their foolish wives and stubborn children cling to,
and the petty people around them
all declare it must not be opposed;
with so many dissenters,
and no true commitment themselves,
the few who dare criticize are drowned out by the rest,
thus doubts multiply,
and none dare to act.
This makes one clench their fists in anger and frustration.
Among those I have personally seen and known, several,
never venerated the spirits,
never once prayed or sacrificed in their lives,
yet lived to a great old age,
held high names and status,
with their descendants prosperous and flourishing,
both rich and honored.
As for me, I too have nothing to do with these things,
other than the four-season sacrifices to my ancestors.
In my travels by land and water spanning ten thousand li,
countless roadside shrines and temples
numbered in the hundreds,
yet when passing to and fro,
I never stopped at a single one,
yet neither wagon nor horse encountered overturning or misfortune,
nor when crossing waters did I face storms or waves,
though I often encountered epidemics,
it was through medicine that I regained health;
though frequently exposed to arrows and stones,
I was lucky to avoid wounding or harm.
All this further shows that ghosts and spirits have no real power.
Moreover, among the hundreds of kinds of heretical Daoism,
all slaughter living creatures for blood offerings—
only the Lǐ family’s Daoism, which emphasizes nonaction, is slightly better.
Yet even though they do not engage in butchery,
they constantly prepare banquets for fortune,
with no set limitation,
what is bought from the market,
must be rich and abundant,
and as for delicate and fresh ingredients,
cannot but be purchased;
sometimes enough for the kitchens of several dozen people,
so the expense is also great;
thus it still cannot be considered thrifty or pure,
and this too ought to be placed among those forbidden and abolished.
Someone asked when the Way of the Lǐ clan began.
I replied:
During the time of Wú Dàdì,
in Shǔ there was one named Lǐ Ā,
who dwelled in a cave and did not eat,
and was seen by people through generations,
being called the Lord of Eight Hundred Years.
People often went to inquire about things,
but Ā said nothing,
only divining by the expression on Ā’s face.
If the expression appeared joyful,
then all matters were auspicious;
if the countenance was mournful and sorrowful,
then all matters were inauspicious;
if Ā was smiling,
then great celebration would come;
if there was a slight sigh,
then there was deep worry.
Such portents
were never once mistaken.
Later, one day, he suddenly disappeared,
no one knew where he went.
Afterward there was a man surnamed Lǐ named Kuān,
who came to Wú, speaking the tongue of Shǔ,
could perform water incantations to heal illness with notable effect,
and thus people from near and far gathered,
calling Kuān by the name Lǐ Ā,
and so they all called him Lǐ Bābǎi,
though in truth he was not.
From the nobility and down,
none failed to crowd his gate;
later, as he became ever more proud and noble,
he was no longer easily seen,
guests and visitors would only bow outside his outer gate and then retire,
such was the strangeness.
Therefore, among officials and commoners seeking to escape conscription,
those who attached themselves to Kuān as disciples were constantly near a thousand in number;
and those who entered the hall and advanced in the practices,
at most attained the water incantation, the talismans of the Three Divisions, or guiding and drawing in the qi of the sun and moon—
altogether lacking essentials for refining the body, ingesting magical elixirs, extending life, preserving fate, or the arts of immortality.
They would swallow qi and abstain from grains,
but could only last for a hundred days or so,
and could not endure for long.
Thus, it is evident how shallow this method is.
Among those I personally know, there were many who saw Kuān,
and all reported that Kuān was frail with age and emaciation,
rising and sitting down with coughing and sighing,
his eyes dim and ears deaf,
teeth lost and hair white,
gradually more and more feeble,
sometimes forgetting even his children and grandchildren,
being no different from ordinary people.
Yet the people insisted Kuān only pretended to be ordinary to deceive people,
but how could that be true?
Once, a terrible epidemic struck Wú,
and more than half died.
The sanctuary where Kuān practiced the Way,
he called a hut.
Kuān too contracted a fever,
claimed he was retreating in the hut to fast and purify himself,
and so died in the hut.
Yet those who followed Kuān still claimed he had transformed and become an immortal by dissolving his corporeal body,
that it was not true death.
Now, the art of the immortals,
that which makes them different from ordinary people,
is precisely valuing agelessness and deathlessness above all.
Now, Kuān truly became old,
and truly died;
that he had not attained the Way
is clear and plain,
so what is there to doubt?
As for those who say that according to the immortal arts there should be dissolution of the corporeal body,
why then not remain among people for one or two hundred years,
preserving years without aging,
and then depart?
It is not that the Way of immortals does not exist in the world,
it is merely that Kuān was not such a man.
That I have explained the matter in detail
is because Kuān’s disciples in turn instructed each other,
spreading throughout Jiāngbiǎo,
their numbers ever into the thousands,
yet none sensed the superficiality of Kuān’s methods,
unworthy of adhering to and upholding,
hoping to transcend the world thereby,
so I wish by this to awaken people and dispel their delusion.
In the world, things that seem to be but are not
are truly without end.
Let me thus briefly recount some stories
to show those among later generations who do not yet understand.
In the past, someone in Rǔnán set up a snare in the fields to catch a deer and succeeded,
but the owner was yet unaware.
A traveler passed by and saw it,
took the deer in secret and left,
but still thought merely taking it was not right.
Above was an abalone,
so he placed one on the snare and left.
When the original owner came,
he found the abalone in the snare,
and was astonished, taking it for a spirit,
not daring to take it home.
Then the villagers heard of it,
and together built a house and established a shrine,
calling it Lord Abalone.
Later, ever more people venerated it,
with lacquered pillars and painted beams,
bells and drums without end.
If among the sick someone happened to recover,
they claimed it was the work of the spirit.
All who traveled past,
would offer sacrifices there.
After seven or eight years,
the original owner of the abalone later passed by the shrine,
and inquired of its origin.
People explained to him in detail.
The abalone’s owner then said,
"That is merely my abalone,
what spirit is there?"
Thus, the matter ceased.
Again, there was Zhāng Zhù of Nándùn,
who farmed at Báitián.
There was a plum sapling,
within his furrow and about to be plowed up;
Zhù pitied it,
wishing to take it home,
so he dug it out,
but did not immediately take it,
wrapped the roots in wet earth,
and placed it inside a hollow mulberry tree,
then forgot about it.
Later, Zhù left for a distant post and was not in the area.
Afterward, someone in the village
saw a plum tree growing inside the hollow of the mulberry,
and thought it was a spirit.
There was one with an eye disease,
who rested in the shade beneath the mulberry,
and prayed to it,
saying, "If Lord Plum can heal my eyes,
I will offer a pig’s stomach in thanks."
His eyes happened to recover,
so he killed a pig and made a sacrifice.
As the story was passed on,
people claimed this tree could make the blind see.
People from afar and near gathered alike,
all came to seek blessings,
and there were always carts and horses filling the place,
food and wine flowing in abundance,
for several years thus.
When Zhāng Zhù completed his post and returned,
he saw this
and said,
"This is merely the plum sapling I placed here years ago,
what spirit could there be?"
Then he cut it down and the matter ceased.
Again, near the highway by the tomb of the Péng clan of Rǔnán,
there stood a stone figure at the tomb’s entrance.
An old peasant woman, returning from the market with several cakes,
on a hot day
rested in the shade beneath the tree by the tomb,
and placed her cakes for a moment atop the stone figure’s head.
She suddenly got up and left,
forgetting to take the cakes.
A passerby saw the cakes on the stone figure’s head,
was astonished and asked about it.
Someone said,
this stone figure is possessed of a spirit,
can heal illness,
and those restored to health express gratitude by offering cakes.
Thus the tale spread from one to another,
that those with headaches should rub the stone figure’s head,
those with belly aches should rub its belly,
and afterward rub themselves,
and all would be healed.
People came from a thousand li to seek healing by the stone figure,
at first offering only chickens and pigs,
but later cattle and sheep,
erected curtains and canopies,
music and song unceasing,
for several years thus.
Suddenly, recently, the old woman who forgot the cakes heard the tale,
and explained the matter to people,
so that none went anymore.
Also, to the west of Luò there was an ancient great tomb,
which, having been broken through, held much water.
Inside the tomb was an abundance of lime,
and the juice of the lime was primarily used to treat sores.
In the summer months,
when travelers who suffered from sores were vexed by heat,
they saw that the water within the tomb was clear and pleasant.
Thus they washed and bathed themselves in it,
and, by chance, their sores were cured.
As a result, those who were ill heard of this
and all went there to wash themselves.
Some even went so far as to drink the water in hopes of curing internal ailments.
The people living near the tomb,
thus built a temple and lodgings at the site and began selling the water.
Those who went to buy it would always offer sacrifices in the temple,
so wine and meat were never lacking.
As yet more people came to buy the water,
the supply was exhausted.
Consequently, those selling the water would often steal water from elsewhere during the night to supplement it.
For those travelers from afar who could not come themselves,
all would take the opportunity when passing by or would send vessels with letters and money to purchase it.
Thus the sellers of water became greatly wealthy.
Someone remarked that there was no spirit here,
and when the officials prohibited the practice,
they filled up and sealed the place,
and it finally ceased.
Again, in Xìnggǔ, when the Prefect Mǎ was in office,
a relative or acquaintance came to him seeking relief.
Mǎ then ordered this man to live outside the city,
falsely declaring him to be a divine person or Daoist priest
who could cure any illness with his own hands, every patient recovering immediately.
He also sent persuaders to travel about,
spreading rumors on his behalf,
saying he could restore sight to the blind
and make the lame walk.
Thereupon people from all directions gathered together,
flocking to him as if to a marketplace,
and money and silks were already heaped up like mountains.
He further instructed those seeking cures
that, even if they did not recover immediately,
they were to tell people that they had recovered,
for thus, they would certainly recover;
but if they said they were not better,
then they would never recover afterward.
Such were the true ways of the Dao,
and must not be doubted.
Thus, when later patients inquired of those who had come before,
the previous patients always said they had been cured,
and no one ever dared to say they were not yet better.
In about ten days,
enormous wealth had accrued.
In general, people often show small cleverness and great folly:
when they hear of the methods for extending life and attaining longevity,
all consider them empty and absurd,
yet they are fond of believing in strange demons and ghosts,
letting themselves be stirred to prayer and worship.
As for what is called “spirits,”
all are of the sort of Mǎ, deceiving others.
I record a few such matters
as a warning for those who have not yet been awakened.
Someone asked:
“In the world there are those who have no knowledge of Daoist arts or medical skills,
yet live in peace to a ripe old age.
How is this so?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“For those such as these,
it may be that they had hidden virtue and good conduct,
and thus received fortune and protection;
or they may by nature have had a long lifespan assigned,
so that they were made slow to age and late to die;
or perhaps, by luck, they simply did not happen to encounter calamity or harm.
It is like the area where hunting takes place,
yet some birds or beasts escape;
or when a great fire has passed,
and there are occasionally some grasses and trees not burnt.
But, in the essential matter of protecting oneself and averting harm,
one ought to cultivate practices that safeguard the body
or wear talismanic swords and celestial amulets.
Sacrifices and prayers are of no benefit;
one should rely on the fact that I am inviolable,
and not on the hope that ghosts and spirits will refrain from harming me.
Indeed, focusing on the mysterious and holding to oneness,
carrying the essence of light around the body,
can ward off demons and evil,
and avert misfortunes,
but cannot extend longevity
or eliminate bodily illness.
Those who rely on nature and use no arts,
may yet live out their natural span,
but they cannot escape when struck by violent ghosts’ assaults
or widespread epidemics;
there is no way then to fend them off.
Those who store armor and helmets
and keep rain capes and hats,
do so in preparation for war or rain.
If they are fortunate enough to face no attack
and never see heavy rain,
then having them or not is just the same.
But when arrows and stones are flying thick,
and the clash of battle clouds the field,
then one will understand the plight of those without armor.
When flooding rains pour from the sky
and pure white snow fills the heavens,
then one realizes the hardship of standing bare in the elements.
It is not right, because of the petty details of rushes and wheat,
to doubt the great influences of Yin and Yang,
thus misleading late learners who roam at will
into thinking that arts and methods are of no benefit.”
Someone asked about the precedence between Rú and Dào.
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“Dào
is the origin of Rú;
Rú
is the end of Dào.
At first, it became the art of Yīnyáng,
with many prohibitions and taboos,
causing people to be constrained and fearful;
whereas the Rú are broad but lack essentials,
toil much and achieve little;
the Mò are frugal but hard to follow,
and cannot be universally adopted;
the Fǎ are strict but sparing of kindness,
harming and breaking rényì.
Only the teachings of the Dàojiā
enable people to focus their spirit,
to act in accord with the formless,
embracing the virtues of Rú and Mò,
encompassing the essentials of Fǎ,
adapting with the times,
responding to change,
directing concisely and easily understood,
requiring little yet achieving much,
devoted to preserving the great root of simplicity,
and guarding the true source.
Yet Bān Gù, in ranking Sīmǎ Qiān before Huáng-Lǎo and after the Six Classics,
deems Qiān mistaken.
Now, Qiān’s extensive learning,
comprehensive grasp of the hidden,
weeding through the good and bad of events,
investigating the correctness or depravity of the ancients;
his judgments,
truly originate from nature itself;
his praise or blame,
are all measured by ultimate principle;
never offering empty praise,
never concealing faults,
never echoing the commonplace merely to fit custom.
Liú Xiàng, an eminent man of his age,
called it a true record;
whereas the judgments of Bān Gù
cannot be relied upon.
Gù was indeed a pure Rú,
never pursuing the intent of Dào,
amused only by what he practiced,
hardly able to be impartial.
Now, what is called Dào—
is it merely a matter of nourishing life?
The Yì says:
Establishing the way of Heaven,
there is yīn and yáng;
establishing the way of Earth,
there is softness and firmness;
establishing the way of man,
there is rén and yì.
Also, it says:
‘The Yì has four ways of sagely men;
if they are not such men,
the Dào will not be vainly practiced.’
Also, when the world is well-governed and at peace,
it is called ‘there is Dào’;
when the state is in danger and the ruler is chaotic,
it is called ‘there is no Dào.’
Also, those who sit and discuss Dào
are called the Sāngōng;
when the state has Dào,
the poor and lowly regard it as shameful.
Whenever Dào is mentioned,
from the highest, the two primal forces,
down to all things,
none do not depend on it.
But Huáng-Lǎo grasped its root,
while Rú and Mò administered its end.
Now those in the world praised as having Dào
are surely learned in the past and present,
able to look above and observe below,
to traverse change and subtlety,
to understand the workings of rise and fall,
to discern the structure of order and chaos;
with minds unconfused,
able to answer all questions;
why must they study the arts of prolonging life
or admire the martial exploits of Sōng Qiáo?
Yet those of narrow vision,
making guesses and blind claims,
hearing of those who dwell among mountains and forests,
practicing the teachings of Bó Yáng,
slander them and laugh, saying,
‘That is but a petty path,
not worth counting.’
Alas!
Such are like those holding a firefly’s light within four walls,
not seeing the brilliance of the sky;
like those who dwell with minnows and shrimps in shallow waters,
never knowing the vastness of the four seas;
fixated on the depth of rivers,
but not realizing their source is Kūnlún;
treasuring crops of millet and rice,
but not perceiving the fertility of rich soil.
Now, if one only exalts Rú learning,
yet does not know that its fulfillment comes from Dào.
Dào,
is that which molds the hundred schools,
shapes the two primal forces,
nurtures all creatures,
ferments the five human relations.
In the world, the shallow are many,
the deep are few,
the few cannot outnumber the many—
so it has ever been.
Thus Sīmǎ Qiān, though long, was not praised,
while Bān Gù, though short, was not censured.
Yet things rare are valued,
the plentiful despised;
is it not so with human affairs?
Why would it be different?
Thus wormwood and beansprouts cover the fields,
yet ganoderma is rarely seen;
hawthorn and bramble fill the wilds,
but rare trees bear the finest shoots;
sand and gravel abound,
but pearls and jade are scarce;
wild geese and hawks flock in numbers,
but phoenixes rarely arise;
vipers and lizards fill the marsh,
but dragons are seldom seen;
if Bān’s partisans are many,
it is only to be expected.
Now, Dào
cultivates the self within,
orders the state without,
can make the seven offices follow regular measure,
the two vital forces harmonize,
the four seasons not lose their proper intervals of cold and warmth,
winds and rain not bring disasters,
jade candles signal signs of peace,
clear wine shows the sign of pervasive virtue,
fiery wheels and rainbows subside in their omens,
crumbling clouds and one-legged birds fold their wings,
the sun shines radiantly above,
fine grain ripens fully,
plagues do not spread,
chaos does not arise,
fortifications are not built,
arms are not used,
there is rightness without argument,
trust without pacts,
stability without bonds,
success without plotting,
encouragement without reward,
discipline without punishment,
gain without seeking,
cessation without prohibition,
ruling from above without being considered oppressive,
leading from the front without being resented,
before commands are given, the customs shift,
before orders are enacted, the ways change—
this is indeed the rule of Dào in times of order.
Thus, when Dào flourishes,
even Yuánshì, Yáo, and Shùn rule effortlessly with surplus;
when Dào is in decline,
then in the lesser ages men strive and achieve little.
Only when there is abundance
