can non-action transform the world to goodness.
When there is lack
there is strict punishment and much corruption.
The people grumble below,
the august spirits are angered above.
Sometimes floodwaters run wild,
sometimes drought scorches the earth,
mountains and valleys change form,
thunder in winter, snow in summer,
blood flows drifting oars,
corpses pile into mounds,
prisoners slaughtered by the ten thousand,
bones divided and children exchanged,
the higher the walls, the more skillful the siege engineers,
the deeper the moats, the cleverer the scaling ladders,
the clearer the laws, the more thieves,
the more covenants, the greater the treachery,
like troubled waves disturbing fish and turtles in the deep,
fine nets disturbing birds in the marsh,
wolves multiplying, beasts rampaging in the woods,
fires blazing and fish in the pan wasted away.
There have been those who reversed the roles of ruler and minister,
fathers who wielded blades against their sons;
only then did loyalty and righteousness gain renown in troubled states,
filial sons find praise in ruined homes.
When pestilence arises, shamans and doctors are esteemed;
when morals are lost, Rú and Mò are valued.
From this perspective,
the precedence of Rú and Dào
can be determined.”
Someone asked:
“In former times, Chì Sōngzǐ, Wáng Qiáo, Qín Gāo, Lǎo Shì, Péng Zǔ, Wù Chéng Yù Huá were all perfected beings.
They all served in worldly offices,
and did not withdraw into remote seclusion.
But since the middle ages,
those who follow the Way
all remain aloof, disappearing into hidden solitude.
Why is this?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“In ancient times, customs were pure and simple;
craftiness and falsity had not yet arisen.
Those who believed in the Way
diligently studied it;
those who did not believe
simply remained silent and that was all.
Words of slander and disparagement
never left their mouths;
thoughts of harming others
were not kept in their hearts.
Therefore, perfected beings moved slowly and easily among the people,
and did not hasten to withdraw on high.
But in later generations, customs became lazy and shallow,
falsehoods became ever deeper;
the transforming power of mystery and simplicity waned,
while the factions of depraved customs multiplied.
No longer believing in the Way,
people delight in ridicule and slander,
regarding truth as heresy,
and immortals as fabrications.
Some say it confuses the masses;
some say it disrupts society.
Therefore, those of highest attainment are ashamed to dwell among them.
Of old, the enlightened ones
cut off misdeeds and prevented evils at their source;
at the slightest sign they would leave,
not waiting for night to become dawn;
seeing the hint, they would act,
not lingering till day’s end.
Therefore, when Zhào brought harm to the calf,
Zhòng Ní turned his carriage;
when sweet wine was not offered,
Mù Shēng traveled as swiftly as the stars.
When the multitude is against the few,
Huá Yuán departed from among them.
How much more so must those of wisdom and clarity,
whose pursuits are different in nature,
have nothing to long for in staying among such people?
When the deep pool dries up
the jiāolóng no longer swim there;
when the nest tips and eggs are gathered,
the fènghuáng do not alight there.
When words reside only in rooms,
even the soaring gull will not descend.
When weeds are plucked in spring,
zhīmíng will not sprout luxuriantly.
When the common people dislike what is upright,
and insult and disgrace draw near,
how can those who possess the Way
not soar aloft and shake their wings beyond the winds and clouds,
and secretly conceal their path at the edge of mystery and emptiness?
The mountain forests in themselves do not possess the Way,
but those who practice the Way must enter mountain forests,
truly wishing to distance themselves from the filthy and foul,
and approach purity and clarity.
Those who enter the nine chambers to concentrate their thoughts,
and keep to the One to summon spirits,
do not delight in noise or in mingling with the impure;
when combining the great elixir of jīndān,
gathering the flying essences of the eight stones,
they especially avoid the foolish and sharp-tongued,
and the perceptions of ordinary people.
The bright spirits will not descend,
and the elixir of immortality will not be achieved,
if these taboos are neglected.
If one remains among people,
there may be those with shallow understanding who denounce him to the authorities,
adding charges of offense or merit;
there may be friends and relatives coming and going,
entangling him with celebrations and condolences.
It is better to hide away from it all,
and thus escape these verminous troubles.
As for their remote and solitary journeys,
finding contentment in lofty peaks,
is there not a reason for this?
Some say:
the highest adept attains the Way amidst armies;
the middle adept attains the Way amidst the marketplace;
the lowest adept attains the Way amidst the mountains and forests.
All of these refer to those who have already accomplished the immortal elixir,
and have not yet wished to ascend to heaven;
even among armies,
blades cannot harm them;
even in the market,
calamities cannot befall them.
But the lowest adept has not yet reached this level,
so he must remain in the mountains and forests.
It is not that those of the highest rank,
when first beginning the Way, ought to remain among armies and the market to attain it.
If that were so, then Huáng Lǎo could have remained with us until today.”
Someone asked:
“The Way is the source and foundation;
the Ru is the subsequent stream.
Now I have heard your explanation;
but the differences in the present times,
to what do they all amount?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“The teachings of rise and fall, looking up and down,
the rituals cycling through three thousand occasions,
strategies of offense, defense, and progress,
upholding one’s body lightly and righteousness as weighty,
affairs of joy, sorrow, ritual, and music,
methods for governing and benefiting the world—
these are what the Ru devote themselves to.
Casting aside external objects and abandoning cleverness,
cleansing away calculation and manipulation,
forgetting wealth and distinction,
blocking encouragement and discouragement,
not worrying about poverty,
not glorying in success,
not grieving over slander,
not delighting in praise—
these are the practices of the Daoists.
The Ru pray in sacrifices to seek blessings;
the Daoists walk in rectitude to expel evil.
What the Ru value is power and profit;
what the Daoists treasure is freedom from desire.
The Ru strive after name and gain;
the Daoists embrace unity and perfect themselves alone.
What the Ru discuss
are the texts and records mutually examined;
what the Daoists practice
are teachings and precepts to free the emotions.
As for the Daoists,
in what they do,
they are good at refining themselves to accomplish things;
where they dwell,
they are good at taking what others do not contend for;
in governance,
they are good at cutting off misfortune before it arises;
in what they bestow,
they are good at assisting others without taking credit;
in action,
they are good at observing the people and applying the heart;
in stillness,
they are good at dwelling with caution and without discontent.
Thus they are leaders among the Hundred Schools,
and the ancestors of benevolence and righteousness.
The principle of difference
is as clear as this;
from beginning to end, high and low,
it has not changed.”
Someone said:
“The scholars of Rú,
that is, Zhōu and Kǒng,
their canon is the Six Classics;
these are the means by which order is preserved in a well-governed age,
the standard and rule for establishing one’s person and conduct;
their application is far-reaching and their profession honorable,
their matters are great and their words beautiful,
a constant system for state and household.
As for men of the Dào,
they do not concern themselves with rites and teaching,
nor heed great ethical norms,
they consort with foxes and badgers amidst marshes and wilds,
and pair with apes and monkeys among forested slopes,
towering and cast aside,
dwelling as neighbors with trees and rocks—
this, too, is a deluded wandering to the east,
forgetting the sweetness of mugwort.”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“Unfurling ornate words and displaying dazzling beauty
is not what those who value honesty and straightforwardness esteem.
To rectify ignorance and dispel confusion
was what satisfied men of former times.
Truly, I do not wish to again dispute with you over what is good or bad in the principles of things,
nor weigh gains and losses at the tip of the tongue.
Yet, observing a child fall into a well
is not the intention of a benevolent man;
to witness a blind man strike a pillar
is what is called ‘universal love’, is it not?
Let me again present a general outline
and briefly contend for one corner.
Those who embody Dào to order things,
and who treasure virtue for longevity,
are the school of Huáng-Lǎo.
Huángdì could govern the world and bring great peace,
and further ascended to immortality;
thus, he cannot be considered inferior to Yáo and Shùn.
Lǎozǐ not only encompassed and synthesized rites and teachings,
but also attained long vision;
so he cannot be said to fall short of Zhōu and Kǒng.
Thus, Zhòngní had sighs of humble comparison,
but was never heard to slander or revile them.
Yet in later ages, mediocre people,
being unable to enter their gate,
adopted the doctrines of the Ru and Mohist schools and vilified those of Dàojiā;
how is this different from descendants cursing and abusing their ancestors?
They do not recognize their own origin;
this is most excessive indeed.
The hand of a dwarf
is not enough to topple Sōng or Huá mountains;
the shrunken shank of Jiāo or Jiǎo
cannot fathom the great ocean.
Often I see ordinary, conservative scholars of the Rú,
tirelessly practicing what they have learned,
but not broadly understanding the principles;
they instruct the obstinate and order the unruly,
exalting and embellishing malicious words,
slandering and interrogating the Daoist school,
expounding on the dregs and refuse;
when it comes to the fleeting glance of a fine horse passing through a crack,
or crossing the depths of spirit and essence,
they are lost and confused.
Like a quail flapping its short wings
trying to ride the waves with great wild geese,
like a feeble fly with exhausted strength
attempting to cross the heights where agile apes traverse—
they are not equal to the task,
and only hasten their own exhaustion.
Yet, ensnared in their narrow confines,
their hearing has not experienced spaciousness,
their vision has not penetrated distance,
yet they wish to stand on tiptoe to encompass the Three Luminaries,
and drum their bellies to rouse thunder spirits—
is this not delusion?
Indeed, when ascending the remote heights of the rotating celestial sphere,
one understands the utter baseness of wells and valleys;
seeing the blazing sun radiant in the heavens,
one realizes how paltry is gilded gold.
I was not born knowing this,
nor did I believe it from youth;
at first I was ignorant,
just like you.
Having beheld the vastness of hidden mysteries,
I regret that I did not earlier escape my former limitations.
The matters of the Five Classics
are plainly revealed in their commentaries,
even beginning students
may still fail to understand them.
How much more so, then, the golden tablets and jade slips,
the scriptures of the immortals,
whose most essential words
are often left unwritten.
One mounts the altar and pledges with blood,
then is entrusted with oral instructions;
if not the proper person,
even if the land could be torn up and cities linked,
and halls filled with gold and jade,
they will not be shown to him recklessly.
Their principles are deep and their teachings distant;
even if one obtains the texts but does not receive instruction from a master,
one looks up and cannot see the head,
looks down and cannot find the feet—
how could you possibly be thoroughly aware of them?
As for those who attain immortality,
some ascend to the Supreme Clarity,
some soar in the Purple Empyrean,
some reach the Mysterious Isle,
some rest among phoenix trees,
listening to celestial music,
enjoying the feast of the nine ganoderma,
going forth to stroll with pines beyond the shadowy world,
returning to banquets in everlasting sunlight within jade chambers—
why should they consort with foxes and badgers or pair with apes and monkeys?
This is what is called speaking without knowledge.
For the Dào
wanders freely amid rainbows,
soars in the vermilion clouds,
to the cliffs of the Great Goose and the six voids,
and reaches wherever the heart desires.
To tower in isolation and be cast aside
is not to be grieved.
Though cattle and swine gather together,
even if draped in brocade,
in considering joy,
how can it compare with the exultant qilin departing the herd to journey alone
or the auspicious light, tearing from the multitudes and enjoying abundant blessings?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The Shénnóng Four Classics says,
“The supreme medicines bring peace to the body and extend life,
rising to become heavenly spirits,
roaming freely above and below,
commanding ten thousand spirits,
the body grows hair and feathers,
and the Kitchen of Action arrives at once.”
It also says,
“The Five Zhī, as well as the ingestion of dānshā, yùzhà, céngqīng, xiónghuáng, cíhuáng, yúnmǔ, and Tàiyǐyǔyúliáng,
each may be taken alone,
all enable one to fly and achieve longevity.”
It further states,
“The middle medicine nourishes nature;
the inferior medicine removes disease;
it can make venomous insects not attack,
fierce beasts not harm,
evil vapors not move,
and all demons are repelled.”
Also, the Xiàojīng cites the Shénqì:
“Pepper and ginger ward off dampness,
chāngpú increases intelligence,
jùshèng prolongs life,
wēixǐ wards off soldiers.”
All these are the utmost words of the highest sages,
and the true records of formulaic arts;
the clear text shines brightly,
yet people of the world ultimately do not believe,
which is truly lamentable.
Among the utmost of immortal medicines is dānshā;
next is gold;
next is silver;
next is the various zhī;
next are the five jades;
next is yúnmǔ;
next is luminous pearl;
next is xiónghuáng;
next is Tàiyǐyǔyúliáng;
next is yellow seed from stone;
next is shíguì;
next is shíyīng;
next is shínǎo;
next is shíliúhuáng;
next is shítái;
next is céngqīng;
next are sōngbǎizhī, fúlíng, dìhuáng, màiméndōng, mùjùshèng, zhònglóu, huánglián, shíwěi, chǔshí, xiàngchái,
also called tuōlú.
Some say Immortal’s staff;
some say Xī Wángmǔ’s staff;
some call it tiānjīng;
some call it quèlǎo;
some call it dìgǔ;
some call it gǒuqǐ.
Tiānméndōng,
also called dìméndōng,
or yánméndōng,
or diānjí,
or yínyángshí,
or guǎnsōng,
grows in high places;
its root is short and sweet in taste,
and the fragrant ones are best.
Those that grow beside water in lower ground,
have fine leaves like yùn and are slightly yellow,
the root is long and very bitter in flavor,
and those with foul odor are inferior,
but they may also be ingested.
However, they are apt to cause qi to descend,
thus the benefit is especially slow.
Taken for a hundred days,
each produces a flat belly and doubles the strength compared to shù and huángjīng,
so upon entering the mountains one may steam it,
or cook and eat it,
and if enough is taken one can abstain from grains.
If one has strength, one may make it into pills,
or also make it into powder,
and even extract its juice to make wine,
which is especially excellent for taking powder.
The people of Chǔ call tiānméndōng “bǎibù,”
but there is a genuine bǎibù herb,
whose root also has about a hundred segments,
very similar in appearance,
but its shoots are slightly different.
The true bǎibù shoots look like báxiā,
and are used only for treating cough and killing lice,
not suitable for ingestion,
so they must not be mistaken.
For example, huángjīng is also called báijí,
yet it is not the báijí used for paste.
According to the Běncǎo, many medicines share names with other herbs,
and only the most knowledgeable can distinguish them,
so this must not be overlooked.
Huángjīng is also called tùzhú,
also called jiùqióng,
and chuízhū.
Consuming its flowers surpasses its fruit,
consuming its fruit surpasses its root,
but the flowers are hard to find in quantity.
If one obtains ten hú of fresh flowers,
when dried, just five or six dǒu remain,
and the daily dosage is three hé,
so only those with great labor can obtain it.
Only after taking huángjīng for ten years
can one greatly benefit from it.
All stop taking grains, but not as well as shù;
shù pills make one fat and strong,
capable of bearing heavy loads and traversing dangers,
but are not as sweet and easy to eat as huángjīng.
In years of famine it can be used for the elderly and children to avoid grains,
and people cannot distinguish it,
calling it “grain jerky.”
The five zhī are:
stone zhī,
wood zhī,
grass zhī,
flesh zhī,
and fungus zhī,
each with about a hundred varieties.
Shí zhī,
also called "shí xiàng zhī," grows on the famous mountains at the edge of the sea
and at the ends of islands where rocks accumulate.
Its form resembles flesh, looking like a creature with a head, tail, and four legs;
it truly appears as if alive.
It adheres to large rocks,
preferring the high and precipitous places,
or sometimes clings upside down.
The red kind resembles coral;
the white kind is like cut animal fat;
the black kind is like black lacquer;
the blue kind is like the feather of kingfisher;
the yellow kind is like purple gold.
All are bright and translucent like solid ice.
In the darkness of night, from three hundred paces away,
one can already see its light.
The large ones weigh over ten jīn,
the small ones three or four jīn.
Unless one has fasted for a long time to utmost purity,
and wears the Lǎozǐ Rùshān Língbǎo Five Talismans,
one cannot obtain sight of these.
Whenever one sees any zhī,
one must first lay the Kāishān Quèhài Talisman upon it,
so that it may not hide or transform and vanish.
Choose an auspicious day with care,
set offerings and sacrifices of wine and dried meat,
pray and then take it,
approaching always by walking in the Yǔ-step from the direction of the sun, holding the breath.
Should one obtain shí xiàng zhī,
pound it thirty-six thousand times,
take a fāngcùn spoonful,
three times a day,
consuming a full jīn,
and one attains a thousand years of life;
with ten jīn,
one attains ten thousand years.
It may also be divided among people to take.
Also, Yùzhī zhī
grows on mountains with jade,
always dwelling in precarious hanging spots,
where jade sap flows out;
after more than ten thousand years,
it congeals and forms zhī,
oftentimes resembling the forms of birds or beasts.
Its color does not have a constant hue,
but is mostly like xuán jade of the mountains or blue-green water jade.
It is also bright and clear as rock crystal;
once obtained, grind it,
and mix it with the juice of wúxīncǎo,
and in a moment it becomes water.
Drink one shēng,
and gain a thousand years of life.
Qīmíng and Jiǔguāng zhī
are all stones;
they grow among the rocky cliffs of high mountains beside water.
Their form is like a plate or bowl,
no more than one foot in diameter or less;
with stalks or pedicels connected beneath,
rising three or four cùn,
those with seven holes
are called qīmíng,
those with nine holes are called jiǔguāng.
Their light is like stars;
within a hundred paces,
at night one can see their radiance.
Each light is distinguishable,
dispersible but not able to be combined.
Always wait for the autumn equinox to pursue and obtain them,
grind and take a fāngcùn spoonful,
upon entry, the body flushes with heat,
and the five flavors are sweet and beautiful;
taking a whole jīn gives a thousand years,
causing one's body to emit light,
illumining dark places like the moon,
and allowing one to see at night.
Shímì zhī
grows in the stone chamber of Shǎoshì,
where within the chamber lies a deep ravine
that cannot be crossed.
If a stone is thrown into the ravine,
its sound can still be heard half a day later.
Ten or more zhàng outside the gate stands a stone pillar,
atop which is a rock like a reclining cover,
tall and wide, about one zhàng in each direction.
One can see the mì zhī falling from atop the stone chamber into the reclining cover.
After a long time,
only a single drop forms,
like the last drip from a roof after a rainstorm,
dropping now and then.
Yet the mì zhī falls without ceasing,
and the reclining cover never fills up.
On top of the gate is engraved in seal-script:
"He who obtains and takes one dǒu of Shímì zhī shall live ten thousand years."
All the Daoists ponder this place together;
it is impossible to reach.
One must only affix a bowl or vessel to a sturdy bamboo or wood pole to catch it,
yet no one has yet succeeded in doing so.
According to the inscription above the stone chamber,
there must surely have been those who obtained it in ancient times.
Shíguì zhī
grows in stone caves on famous mountains;
it looks like the guì tree, but is actually stone.
It is about one foot high,
as wide as a foot in diameter,
bright and pungent in flavor,
with branches and twigs.
Pounding and consuming one jīn grants a thousand years.
Shízhōng huángzǐ
can be found everywhere,
but is especially abundant on Qìnshuǐ Mountain.
When it is inside a large stone,
the stone always remains moist and not dry.
Striking the stone may take dozens of layers before obtaining it.
Only then is it retrieved.
When inside great rocks,
it is red-yellow and melting,
like an egg within its shell.
It must be drunk immediately;
if not, it will harden into stone,
and can no longer be taken within.
The correct method is to drink it before it solidifies;
once congealed, it must be ground and consumed in powder.
Breaking open a single stone,
it may contain a shēng at most,
or only a few hé at minimum,
and can be taken in one dose.
Even if one cannot obtain much,
take it in succession,
tally the total taken before and after,
and when it adds up to three shēng,
one attains a thousand years of life.
If one wishes to consume more,
it is only difficult to obtain.
Shínǎo zhī
grows in huáshí,
resembling shízhōng huángzǐ,
but is not always present.
Breaking a thousand great huáshí,
only then might one obtain a single piece.
When first broken open,
within the stone,
it shines with five colors and moves of itself.
Take one shēng and a thousand years are attained.
Shíliúhuáng zhī
is found in all the Five Sacred Peaks,
but is most abundant on Jīshān.
Local tradition says that Xǔ Yóu partook of it here and attained long life,
so he no longer let wealth and rank weigh down his mind,
nor accepted Yáo's abdication.
Shíliúdān
is the red essence of stone—
it is a kind of shíliúhuáng.
All ooze out among the cliffs and riverbanks;
those that are moist and soft can be formed into pellets and consumed;
those that have already solidified can be ground and taken as powder.
In total, there are one hundred and twenty such varieties;
all are shí zhī;
matters relating to them can be found in the Tàiyǐ Yùcè and Chāngyǔ Nèijì.
It is impossible to record them all here.
As for the mù zhī,
when the resin of Sōngbǎi seeps into the earth for a thousand years,
it transforms into fúlíng;
after ten thousand years,
a small tree grows atop it,
in appearance like a lotus flower,
named mù wēixǐ zhī.
It glows at night,
is extremely slippery to the touch,
and cannot be burned;
wearing it wards off weapons.
If one ties it to a chicken and mixes it with twelve other chickens, placing them together in a cage,
then withdraws twelve paces,
and shoots twelve arrows,
all the other chickens will be injured,
but the one bearing wēixǐ zhī will never be harmed.
Harvest it from above the gate of life,
and dry it in shade on the day of liùjiǎ,
for one hundred days.
Grind it and take a spoonful the size of a fāngcùnbǐ,
three times daily,
until a whole specimen is consumed,
then one attains three thousand years of life.
The kuò mù of a thousand years,
its lower root resembles a seated person,
seven inches long,
when cut, it bleeds;
with its blood one anoints the soles of the feet,
thus can walk upon water without sinking;
if smeared on the nose and entering water,
the water will part,
and one can remain at the bottom of the abyss;
if smeared on the body, one becomes invisible,
to become visible again, wipe it off.
It can also heal illness;
for diseases within the abdomen,
scrape and take a bladeful the size of a dāoqī;
if the swelling and pain are external,
scrape a dāoqī from the corresponding area,
and rub it on the afflicted area,
it will be cured immediately by hand;
if, for example, the left foot is diseased,
then scrape and apply it on the left foot of a person.
Moreover, if scraped and mixed with jùshèng to make a torch,
at night it illuminates the ground everywhere;
if there is hidden gold or jade treasure,
the light turns blue and droops down;
dig it up with a spade and you shall obtain it.
If ground into powder,
taking ten jin in total grants a thousand years of life.
Furthermore, the branches of a Sōng tree three thousand years old,
in the bark there is gathered resin,
shaped like a dragon,
called fēijié zhī;
the large ones may weigh ten jin,
grind and take it,
when ten jin are consumed,
one obtains five hundred years of life.
Additionally, there is fán táo zhī,
its trunk like a soaring dragon,
its flowers and leaves like cinnabar silk,
its fruit like a kingfisher,
not exceeding five feet in height,
growing on the shaded sides of famous mountains,
in lands watered by east-flowing springs;
if sought at the time of the Beginning of Summer,
and obtained and powdered for consumption,
after consuming the whole plant, one attains five thousand years of life.
There is cān chéng zhī,
red and luminous,
if tapped, its twigs and leaves
sound like metal or stone;
if broken then joined,
it will return to its original state.
There is mù qú zhī,
parasitic upon large trees,
like a lotus blossom,
with nine stems in a cluster,
its taste sweet and pungent.
Jiàn mù zhī grows in Dūguǎng,
with bark like the yīng snake,
its fruit like a luán bird.
If one gains and consumes any of these three zhī,
they may ascend to the heavens in broad daylight.
Huáng lúzi, xún mù huá, and xuán yè huá,
these three zhī grow in the secluded villages of Tàishān and Fènggāo;
if one obtains and consumes them,
each can grant a thousand years of life.
As for huáng tán huán zhī,
the thousand-year-old yellow,
beneath the tree the roots form a shape like a three-hǔ container,
one or two zhàng away from the trunk,
linked by fine roots like threads,
if the powder is obtained and consumed,
after a whole specimen is finished, one becomes a dìxiān, not dying.
There are another one hundred and twenty kinds of these,
all with their own diagrams.
Of the grass zhī, there is dú yáo zhī,
which moves on its own without wind,
its stem as thick as a finger,
red as cinnabar,
with white leaves resembling amaranth,
its root bearing a great cluster as large as a dǒu,
with twelve smaller ones the size of hen's eggs,
surrounding the large root on all sides,
like the twelve double-hours,
a zhàng apart,
each connected by fine roots,
like white hair linking them together,
growing atop high mountains and deep valleys,
with bare ground left and right where nothing else grows.
If the large cluster is powdered and consumed,
when finished, a thousand years is obtained;
if a small one is consumed, each gives a hundred years,
and may be shared with others.
Holding the large root grants invisibility,
to appear again, turn left and let it go.
Niújiǎo zhī,
grows on Hǔshòu Mountain and above Wúbǎn,
resembling scallions,
but grows singly like an ox's horn,
three or four feet long,
blue-green in color,
grind and take a fāngcùnbǐ,
three times a day,
up to a hundred days,
to gain a thousand years.
Lóuxiān zhī,
resembles two ascending dragons entwined,
with leaves as scales,
its root like a coiled dragon;
one specimen grants a thousand years.
Má mǔ zhī,
resembles hemp but has a red stem,
and purple blossoms.
Zǐ zhū zhī,
with yellow flowers,
red leaves,
fruit like a plum and purple in color,
twenty-four branches connect,
hanging down like a string of beads.
Bái fú zhī,
four or five feet tall,
resembles a plum,
always flowering after heavy snow,
bearing fruit in the last month of winter.
Zhū cǎo zhī,
having nine bends,
each bend giving three leaves,
each leaf bearing three fruits.
Wǔ dé zhī,
shaped like a tower or palace,
with square stem,
leaves in five colors, each distinct, not mixed,
top like a reclining canopy,
always holding sweet dew in the center,
with purple vapors rising several feet.
Lóng xián zhī,
always grows in pairs in mid-spring,
having three joints and twelve branches,
the lower root like a seated person.
All of these grass zhī,
there are also another one hundred and twenty types,
all dried in the shade and consumed,
then one may complete cycles with Heaven and Earth,
or attain one thousand or two thousand years of life.
The ròuzhī,
refers to the Wànsuì Chánchú,
which has horns upon its head,
and beneath its jaw bears, inscribed in cinnabar, eight characters twice over.
If it is taken at midday on the fifth day of the fifth month,
and dried in the shade for one hundred days,
then using its left foot to trace upon the ground,
there will immediately flow running water.
If its left hand is worn on the body,
one is protected from the five weapons.
Should an enemy shoot at one,
then all bows, crossbows, and arrows will return, turning back upon those who fired them.
The Thousand-Year Biānfú,
pure white as snow,
hangs upside-down when gathering together,
due to the weight of its brain.
If these two creatures are obtained and dried in the shade, then ground and taken as powder,
one’s lifespan will be forty thousand years.
The Thousand-Year Língguī,
bears all five colors upon it;
the males have two bones protruding from the forehead resembling horns.
Bathe it in sheep’s blood,
then extract its shell,
roast it over fire, pound it, and take one square inch–sized spoonful,
three times each day,
until one shell is finished.
This grants a lifespan of a thousand years.
Traveling in the mountains,
if you see small people riding in carts or on horses,
standing seven or eight inches tall,
these are ròuzhī;
seize and ingest them, and you will become immortal.
The Fēngshēng Beast resembles a marten,
is blue in color,
and as large as a wildcat.
It dwells within the great forests of the southern sea.
Set nets to catch it,
and stack several carts of firewood to burn it.
When the firewood has burned away, this beast, in the ashes, will remain unburned;
its fur does not scorch,
stabbing and piercing do not penetrate,
and when struck, it is like beating upon a leather sack.
If one forges its head with an iron hammer dozens of times, it finally dies.
Dead, if its mouth is placed facing into the wind,
in an instant it revives and bolts upright to flee.
Stuffing its nostrils with chángpú grown on rocks, it dies.
Take its brain and blend it with chrysanthemum to ingest;
once ten jin are consumed,
one obtains a five-hundred-year lifespan.
Also, the Thousand-Year Yàn,
whose nest entrance faces north,
whose color is mostly white and whose tail is split,
should be taken and shade-dried,
and taking the powder of a single head yields five hundred years of life.
Altogether, there are another one hundred and twenty kinds
—all are ròuzhī.
The jùnzhī
may be found in deep mountains,
or under great trees,
or beside springs.
Their shapes may resemble palaces and chambers,
or carts and horses,
or dragons and tigers,
or human forms,
or flying birds—
their five colors are ever-changing.
There are likewise one hundred and twenty types;
there exist diagrams of these as well.
Always approach to gather them by walking with the Yǔ Step,
and cut them with a bone knife,
shade-dry and powder them, taking a square inch spoonful;
this will cause one to ascend as an immortal,
the best will grant several thousand years,
and the lesser a thousand years.
If you seek zhī herbs,
enter famed mountains;
always do so in the third or ninth month,
for these are the months when the mountains yield divine medicines.
Do not go on fierce mountain days,
but only at times auspicious due to Heaven's aid.
When three auspicious stars converge, it is especially favorable.
Depart through the fortunate gate of the Three Auspices, then reach the mountain,
and choose a day of Six Yin,
at the hour of the Mingtáng,
carry a Língbǎo talisman,
lead a white dog,
hold a white rooster,
bring a dǒu of white salt,
and the Kāishān talisman proclamation.
Place these upon a great stone;
carry a handful of Wú Táng grass to enter the mountain.
The mountain god will be pleased,
and you will surely obtain the zhī.
Furthermore, when gathering or ingesting zhī,
seek the days ruled exclusively by Wáng Xiàng Hé,
when stems and branches ascend and descend in mutual generation, which is best.
These various zhī are found in abundance on renowned mountains,
however, common Daoist practitioners,
whose minds are not focused and pure,
whose conduct is impure and virtue shallow,
and who know nothing of the arts of entering mountains,
though they obtain the diagrams,
not knowing their forms,
ultimately will never obtain them.
No matter a mountain's size,
spirits and deities are present,
who will not grant the zhī to people.
Thus, even if a person treads upon it,
it cannot be seen.
Again, as for yúnmǔ, there are five types,
but people mostly cannot distinguish them.
The proper method is to hold them up towards the sun,
and observe their color,
scrutinizing them in detail,
then one can know.
If viewed only on shaded ground,
their variegated hues are not visible.
The one with all five colors but predominantly blue is named yúnyīng;
it should be taken in spring.
The one with all five colors but mostly red is called yúnzhū;
it should be taken in summer.
The one with all five colors but mostly white is called yúnyè;
it should be taken in autumn.
The one with all five colors but mostly black is called yúnmǔ;
it should be taken in winter.
The one with only blue and yellow colors is called yúnshā;
it should be taken in late summer.
The bright, pure-white one is called línshí,
and can be taken for all four seasons.
As for the method of ingesting the Five Clouds,
sometimes combine them with cinnamon, scallion, and jade, transforming them into water;
or expose them to dew in iron vessels,
then boil them in black water to make a potion;
or mix them with niter in a tube and bury them to make a solution;
or mix with honey to make a paste;
or soak in autumn dew for a hundred days;
pound them in a leather bag into powder;
or combine with wúdiān grass and āi blood as food.
After taking them for a year,
all illnesses are eliminated;
after three years of persisting in taking them,
an old man may become a youth again;
after five uninterrupted years,
one may command ghosts and spirits,
enter fire without burning,
enter water without being wetted,
walk among thorns without harm to the skin,
and stand in the presence of immortals.
Moreover, other things when buried decay,
and when put to flame are scorched,
but when casting the Five Clouds into fierce fire,
though time passes they are never burned;
buried, they never rot or decay,
and so they can bestow long life.
It is further said,
that after ten years of ingesting them,
clouds always linger above one's head.
Consuming the female to produce the male,
this is the natural principle.
If viewed toward the sun,
when a dark, fully black color arises,
it is not suitable for ingestion,
for it can cause strangury and sores.
Even if taking them in water or as food,
always use water dripped from the eaves of a thatched cottage,
or water from eastward-flowing streams or dew,
soaking for a hundred days,
and sifting away the earth and stones;
only then may they be used.
Wèi Shūqīng of Zhōngshān took them,
and after a long period could ride upon the clouds to travel;
following the method, he sealed them in a jade casket,
and after ascending to immortality,
his son, named Shì,
and the Hàn emissary Liáng Bó,
obtained them and compounded and took them according to the method;
all ascended to immortality.
Moreover, the best xiónghuáng must come from the Wǔdū Mountains;
it is pure and without admixture,
its red is like a rooster’s comb,
shining with radiant brilliance.
Only this kind may be used.
If it is only pure yellow, resembling the color of xiónghuáng,
but lacking the red luster,
it is not suitable for making elixirs of immortality;
it can only be used as an ordinary medicine to treat illness.
Methods of ingestion:
sometimes it is steamed or boiled,
sometimes taken with wine-leaven,
or first dissolved into water with xiāoshí, then solidified,
or wrapped in xuándòngcháng and steamed under red clay,
or mixed with pine resin,
or refined with three ingredients,
drawn out like cloth,
white as ice.
Consuming it causes long life,
cures all diseases,
expels the Three Corpses,
eliminates scars,
turns white hair black,
causes lost teeth to regrow.
In a thousand days, a yùnǚ will come to attend upon you,
whom you may employ,
even bringing forth the traveling kitchen.
Moreover, the yùnǚ always bears a sign of huángyù,
as large as a millet grain,
on the top of her nose;
this is a true yùnǚ.
If she lacks this sign,
she is a demon sent to test people.
Yù is also an elixir of immortality,
but simply hard to obtain.
The Book of Jade says:
Whoever ingests gold has a lifespan like gold;
whoever ingests jade has a lifespan like jade.
It also says:
Whoever ingests xuánzhēn
has a life without limit.
Xuánzhēn
is another name for jade.
It makes one’s body light and able to fly,
not only a terrestrial immortal.
However, its effects are slow,
requiring ingestion of a hundred or two hundred catties
before anything can be known.
Jade may be dissolved in wūmǐ wine or dìyú wine into water,
or melted with green onion juice into a paste,
or made into pills and ingested,
or burned to make powder.
After more than a year’s ingestion,
one may enter water without becoming wet,
enter fire without being burnt,
blades do not injure,
and a hundred poisons cannot harm.
Finished jade artifacts must not be used,
as they harm people without benefit;
uncarved jade should be obtained,
only then may it be used.
White jade from the State of Yútián is especially good.
Next in quality is jade from Xú Shàntíng District in Nányáng, as well as jade from the Lú Róng River in Rìnán; these are also fine.
Chìsōngzǐ uses the blood of the xuánchóng to soak jade, making it into water for ingestion;
thus he could ride the vapors up and down.
Jade powder, whether taken directly or with water-leaven,
both cause one not to die.
The reason it does not equal gold
is that it causes frequent fever,
similar to the symptoms of the Cold-Food Powder.
If consuming jade powder,
every ten days one should take each a dāoguī of xiónghuáng and dānshā,
loosen the hair and bathe in cold water,
walk facing the wind,
and then fever does not arise.
Dǒng Jūnyì once gave jade liquor to a blind person,
and his eyes recovered in about ten days.
There was a man Wú Yánzhì,
who wished to ingest jade;
but though he obtained a recipe from the Book of Jade, it was incomplete,
completely ignorant of the proper procedure and taboos.
Thus he gathered together guī, zhāng, huán, and bì,
and many sword pommels and ornaments,
intending to make and take them as medicine.
Later I told him that this was useless,
at which he sighed and said,
“One must be meticulous;
not only is there no benefit,
but it nearly brought disaster.”
Silver only falls short of gold and jade;
it can bestow terrestrial immortality.
The method is:
dissolve it with wheat gruel,
or use zhūcǎo wine-leaven,
or refine with dragon fat.
However, after three doses,
each as large as a pellet,
yet even this is not attainable by humble and poor Daoists.
Pearls more than one cùn in diameter may be consumed;
ingesting them grants long life.
Soaking them in curdled milk all transforms to liquid mercury;
or dissolve with fúshí water or bees’ nests,
mix with tōngshéhuáng,
can be drawn out to three or four chǐ,
made into pills and taken,
abstaining from grain,
and so one will not die and will have long life.
Pure lacquer that does not adhere,
if consumed, allows communication with spirits and long life.
The method:
sometimes with dà wúcháng gōngzǐ,
or some say with large crabs,
ten thrown into it,
or with mica water,
or combined with jade water and ingested.
All the nine worms will be expelled,
bad blood will leave by the nose,
and in one year the traveling kitchen will arrive every sixty days.
Cassia may be steamed with green onion mucus into water,
or with bamboo sap and taken as medicine,
or with xiānzhījūn brains—
or some say tortoise—
and ingested together.
In seven years,
one can walk on water,
achieving longevity and immortality.
Jùshèng, also called húmá,
when taken prevents aging,
resists wind and dampness and
rejuvenates the old.
Peach resin soaked in mulberry ash juice,
when taken cures all illnesses,
and after long use makes the body light and luminous,
as if in the dark of night, one rises like the moon.
Taking much enables grain abstention.
If the fruit of níngmù is red,
ingest it for one year,
and the old become young again,
able to see spirits and demons clearly.
In the past, the Daoist Liáng Xū, at seventy years old, began to take it,
yet became ever younger,
until at one hundred forty years,
he could write at night,
walk as fast as a running horse,
and later entered Qīnglóng Mountain and departed.
Huái seeds placed in a new jar and sealed with mud,
after more than twenty days,
their husks rot away,
and they are washed until they resemble large soybeans.
Consumed daily,
this substance mainly nourishes the brain.
Prolonged use
causes the hair not to whiten and grants long life.
Xuánzhōng mǎn recipes—
such as chǔ fēilián, zéxiè, dìhuáng, and huánglián,
—over three hundred kinds in all,
can all prolong life
and may be taken singly.
Língfēi Powder, Wèiguài Pill, Zhìmìng Pill, and Goat's Blood Pill—
these all keep one’s years constant and ward off old age.
In the mountains of Lìxiàn in Nányáng, there is the Gāngǔ spring water.
The reason the spring water is sweet
is that on both sides above the valley, sweet chrysanthemums grow,
and the chrysanthemum flowers fall into it,
accumulating over generations for a long time.
Thus, the taste of the water has changed.
The people dwelling in this valley,
do not dig wells at all;
all of them use the Gāngǔ spring water.
All who drink it grow old and live long,
the oldest reaching one hundred forty or fifty years,
the least living no less than eighty or ninety.
There are no people who die young;
this comes from the power of the chrysanthemum.
Therefore, Sīkōng Wáng Chàng, Tàiwèi Liú Kuān, and Tàifù Yuán Kuí
all served as Governors of Nányáng,
and whenever they arrived at their posts,
they would always order Lìxiàn to send forty hú of Gāngǔ spring water every month for their food and drink.
These eminent officials often suffered from wind paralysis or dizziness,
but all were cured.
Yet they could not obtain the full benefit,
as those residents who were born in the upper valley
and had drunk this water since childhood did.
Also, chrysanthemum flowers resemble yì flowers;
the difference is only in taste, one being sweet and the other bitter;
chrysanthemum is sweet and yì is bitter,
which is what the saying “bitter as yì” refers to.
Today, genuine chrysanthemum is found in many places,
but only in small quantities.
It generally grows by the water’s edge,
most abundantly on Gōushì Mountain and in Lìxiàn.
The immortal formulas refer to it as “the essence of the sun, newly grown,”
with each patch forming a single chrysanthemum,
while roots, stalks, flower, and fruit have different names.
The explanations are splendid,
but in recent times, those who take it have found little effect;
precisely because they have not obtained genuine chrysanthemum.
Though the Gāngǔ water indeed receives the flavor and essence of chrysanthemum,
what need is there to say more?
Yet the residents above
all achieve longevity thereby;
how much more so if one were to use fine medicines,
how could there be no benefit?
My late ancestor, Hónglú Shàoqīng, once served as Magistrate of Línyuán,
and said that in this county there was a Liào family
whose generations were all long-lived,
some reaching a hundred years,
others eighty or ninety.
Later, when they moved away,
their descendants more frequently died young.
Others who moved into their former house
again lived as long as before,
for several generations with long lives.
From this it became clear it was due to the location of the house,
though the cause was not known.
It was suspected that the well water was unusually red,
so they dug around the well,
and found dozens of hú of cinnabar buried there by people of old,
several feet from the well.
The juice of the cinnabar seeped into the well through the spring water over time;
thus, drinking the water brought longevity,
how much more so if one were to refine and ingest cinnabar directly?
I have also heard that in Shàngdǎng there was a man called Zhào Qú
who suffered from leprosy for many years;
the treatments of many could not cure him,
and he was on the verge of death.
Some said he could not be saved
and cast him out,
and later his descendants continued to pass him on between themselves.
His family provided him rations,
and placed him in a mountain cave.
There, in the cave,
Qú lamented his misfortune,
weeping day and night,
his tears flowing for more than a month.
An immortal happened to pass by the cave,
saw him and took pity,
asking in detail after his condition.
Qú knew this was no ordinary man,
so he knocked his head on the ground and begged for mercy.
The immortal then took a pouch of medicine and bestowed it on him,
instructed him in how to take it.
Qú took the medicine for about a hundred days;
his sores completely healed,
his complexion became radiant and joyful,
his skin glowing with the luster of jade.
Later the immortal came by again to see him,
and Qú gave thanks for the kindness of saving his life,
and begged for the recipe.
The immortal told him:
“This is merely pine resin;
there is much of this in these mountains.
Refine and take it,
and you may live forever without dying.”
Qú then returned home,
his family at first took him for a ghost,
and were greatly frightened.
Qú began to continuously take pine resin,
his body became ever lighter,
his strength many times greater,
he could scale cliffs and cross dangerous places,
going all day without tiring.
He lived to one hundred seventy years,
his teeth did not fall out,
his hair did not turn white.
One night as he lay sleeping,
he suddenly saw in his house a light as large as a mirror;
he asked those around him,
but all said they saw nothing.
The brightness gradually increased
until the whole room was bright as daytime.
On another night he saw, upon his face, two maidens gathering herbs,
two or three inches tall,
with complete features and bodies,
just very small;
they played about his mouth and nose,
in this way for about a year,
gradually growing larger,
and at last appeared at his side.
He would often also hear the sound of qín and sè,
and would be delighted, smiling to himself.
He lived in the world some three hundred years,
his appearance like a young boy,
and finally entered Bàodú Mountain and disappeared;
surely he became an earth immortal.
At the time, when it was heard that Qú had such effects from taking pine resin,
many began to take it in competition.
Those with much physical labor
hauled it in carts or on donkeys,
piling it until it filled their rooms;
those who took it in distant places
lasted at most a month,
and, finding no great benefit, soon stopped.
It is difficult to find one with such determination.
Again, in the time of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
a hunter in Zhōngnán Mountain
saw a person without clothes,
his body covered with black hair.
When the hunter saw him,
he wanted to capture him,
but the person leapt across ditches and valleys
as if flying,
and could not be caught.
They then secretly watched for his location,
encircled and captured him;
it was determined to be a woman.
When questioned,
she said, “I was originally a palace woman of Qín;
hearing that rebels from east of the Pass were coming,
the King of Qín went out to surrender,
the palaces were burned,
and in fear I fled into the mountains.
Hungry and with nothing to eat,
about to starve to death,
an old man taught me to eat pine needles and pine nuts.
At first they were bitter and astringent,
but later I gradually became accustomed to them,
so that I neither hungered nor thirsted,
felt no cold in winter,
and no heat in summer.
It is reckoned that this woman must have been a palace woman of Zǐyīng, King of Qín,
and by the time of Emperor Chéng,
she was more than two hundred years old.
She was then brought back,
and fed on grains;
at first on smelling the grain she vomited,
but after several days was all right.
After about two years like this,
the hair on her body fell off,
she gradually aged and died.
Had she not been discovered,
she would have become an immortal.
The Wén family of Nányáng
relates of their ancestor
that at the end of the Hàn, during the great chaos,
he fled into the mountains,
hungry and weak, about to die.
Someone taught him to eat shù,
and so he was no longer hungry.
After several decades, he returned to his village,
his complexion even more youthful,
his strength surpassing before.
He said that when he was in the mountains,
his body felt light enough to leap,
he could climb high places and walk dangerous paths,
and could go for days without fatigue.
Walking through ice and snow,
he did not feel cold at all.
He often saw on a high rock
several people sitting together playing games,
some reading books;
they would look down and see the Wén man,
then he heard them asking each other,
“Shall we call this young fellow up or not?”
One replied, “Not yet.”
Shù is also called shānlíng,
or shānjīng.
Therefore the Divine Medicine Classic says,
“If you would attain longevity,
constantly take shānjīng.”
In ancient times, eight immortals,
each took a different substance,
by which they attained terrestrial immortality,
each for several hundred years.
Only then did they combine the divine elixir, the golden liquid,
and ascend to Tàiqīng.
If a person combines the eight substances,
refines and takes them,
yet does not obtain their potency,
it is because the medicinal powers overcome and restrain one another.
Hán Zhōng took acorus for thirteen years,
and his body grew hair;
each day he read ten thousand words,
remembered them all,
could bare his arms in winter without feeling cold.
Moreover, acorus must be obtained growing on stone,
with at least nine joints in one inch,
and those with purple flowers are especially good.
Zhào Tǎzǐ took cassia for twenty years,
grew hair on the soles of his feet,
could travel five hundred lǐ a day,
and lift a thousand jīn.
Yí Ménzǐ took schisandra for sixteen years,
his complexion resembled that of a jade maiden,
water did not soak him when he entered it,
and fire did not burn him.
Chǔ Wénzǐ took rehmannia for eight years,
could see with light at night,
and held a crossbow in his hand.
Lín Zǐmíng took Chinese yam for eleven years,
his ears grew five inches long,
his body became as light as if flying,
and he could leap more than two zhàng across ravines and valleys.
Dù Zǐwēi took asparagus cochinchinensis,
could attend to eighty wives,
and had one hundred thirty children,
traveling three hundred lǐ a day.
Rèn Zǐjì took poria for eighteen years,
and immortals and jade maidens came to follow him;
he could vanish and reappear,
no longer needed to eat grain,
scar marks from moxibustion all vanished,
his face and body shone with the luster of jade.
Língyáng Zǐzhòng took polygala for twenty years,
had thirty-seven sons,
never forgot anything he read,
and sitting he would forget to stand, standing he would forget to sit.
The Immortal Canon says:
“Though one takes the leaves of grasses and trees,
one can already attain several hundred years;
but if one becomes lax regarding the divine elixir,
one will never become immortal.
Accordingly,
grass and wood only prolong life,
they are clearly not medicines for immortality.
If you have not yet produced elixirs,
for now you may take them
merely as support for yourself.
Someone asked:
‘When taking medicines,
is there an appropriate time, before or after eating?’”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“According to the dietary practice of Zhōng Huángzǐ,
medicines for treating illness
should be taken before meals;
medicines for nourishing life
should be taken after meals.
I consulted Zhèng Jūn:
‘Why is this so?’
Zhèng Jūn said:
‘This is easy to understand.
If you want the medicine to attack illness,
it ought to be taken before eating,
when the interior is empty,
so the power of the medicine can move readily.
If taken after meals,
then the medicine simply attacks the grain and its strength is spent.
But if you wish to nurture life,
and take medicine before eating,
its strength has not yet emerged,
but is driven downward by the grain and cannot remain,
so there is no benefit.’”
Someone further asked:
“When one takes medicine to nourish life,
is there an appropriate match,
is it really so?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“According to the Jade Register and the Kāimíng Classic,
both use the five tones and six associations
to determine a person’s year destiny.
Zǐ and Wǔ belong to gēng,
Mǎo and Yǒu belong to jǐ,
Yín and Shēn belong to wù,
Chǒu and Wèi belong to xīn,
Chén and Xū belong to bǐng,
Sì and Hài belong to dīng.
Those whose destiny falls under one word
are palace and earth.
Three words,
zhī and fire.
Five words,
yǔ and water.
Seven words,
shāng and metal.
Nine words,
jué and wood.
If your original destiny is earth,
you should not take green medicines;
if metal,
do not take red medicines;
if wood,
do not take white medicines;
if water,
do not take yellow medicines;
if fire,
do not take black medicines.
This follows the logic of the five phases:
wood overcomes earth,
earth overcomes water,
water overcomes fire,
fire overcomes metal,
metal overcomes wood.
As for the great medicines of golden elixir,
no consideration is given to appropriate or inappropriate matches.
One word is palace:
gēngzǐ, gēngwǔ,
xīnwèi, xīnchǒu,
bǐngchén, bǐngxū,
dīnghài, dīngsì,
wùyín, wùshēn,
jǐmǎo, jǐyǒu.
Three words are zhī:
jiǎchén, jiǎxū,
yǐhài, yǐsì,
bǐngyín, bǐngshēn,
dīngyǒu, dīngmǎo,
wùwǔ, wùzǐ,
jǐwèi, jǐchǒu.
Five words are yǔ:
jiǎyín, jiǎshēn,
yǐmǎo, yǐyǒu,
bǐngzǐ, bǐngwǔ,
dīngwèi, dīngchǒu,
rénchén, rénxū,
guǐsì, guǐhài.
Seven words are shāng:
jiǎzǐ, jiǎwǔ,
yǐchǒu, yǐwèi,
gēngchén, gēngxū,
xīnsì, xīnhài,
rénshēn, rényín,
guǐmǎo, guǐyǒu.
Nine words are jué:
wùchén, wùxū,
jǐsì, jǐhài,
gēngyín, gēngshēn,
xīnmǎo, xīnyǒu,
rénwǔ, rénzǐ,
guǐchǒu, guǐwèi.
The Yǔ Steps method:
First raise the left foot,
the right passes over the left,
and the left joins the right.
Next, raise the right foot,
the left passes over the right,
and the right joins the left.
Next, raise the right foot,
the right passes over the left,
and the left joins the right.
Doing this for three steps
should cover two zhàng and one chǐ,
leaving behind nine footprints.
The “Minor Divine Formula”:
take three jīn of true cinnabar,
one jīn of white honey,
combine and dry in the sun, then boil it,
making it possible to form into pills.
Each morning take ten pills, each the size of a sesame seed;
within a year,
white hair turns black again,
lost teeth regrow,
the body and limbs become moist and lustrous,
if taken long-term,
an old man will return to his youth,
taking it constantly brings long life and immortality.
The Minor Elixir Yellow Gold Recipe,
melt the gold with fire and add it to pure wine,
remove it two hundred times,
immerse it two hundred times,
then it will boil.
Grasp it and take it out between the fingers,
so that it is like clay.
If it does not boil, or when grasped does not come out between the fingers,
then remelt it and return it into the wine countless times.
When completed, take it in the size of a pellet, one piece.
Or press its juice into a pellet and divide into small pellets,
take it for thirty days,
with no aversion to cold or heat,
the shénrén and yùnǚ descend.
Also, silver may be used as an elixir,
by the same method as gold.
If you take these two substances,
you may dwell in the stone chambers of famous mountains;
in one year, you will ascend lightly.
If people in the human realm take it,
they are called dìxiān;
do not transmit this recklessly.
Liǎngyízi’s Elixir-Melting Gold Recipe:
take three jin of pig’s hide fat,
one dǒu of strong bitter wine,
and five liǎng of gold;
place it in a vessel and boil it,
remove from the furnace,
put the gold into the fat,
a hundred immersions and a hundred removals,
the bitter wine as well,
if one eats a jin of gold,
their lifespan will outlast Heaven and Earth;
if one eats half a jin of gold,
their lifespan is two thousand years;
for five liǎng,
one thousand two hundred years;
regardless of amount,
it may be used as an elixir.
It should be made on the day of the wángxiàng,
then it is numinous and efficacious,
do not transmit this to others,
for if you do,
the medicine will neither be completed nor will it be numinous.
If you wish to consume a corpse-expelling medicine,
then you should take cinnabar.
The method for taking cinnabar as an elixir:
one jin of cinnabar,
pound and sieve it,
add three shēng of strong bitter wine,
two shēng of pure lacquer,
mix the three together,
make sure they combine properly,
simmer over gentle fire,
until it can be formed into pellets,
take three pellets the size of sesame seeds,
twice daily.
In forty days,
all diseases in the abdomen are cured,
the three corpses are expelled;
take it for a hundred days,
the flesh and bones become firm and strong;
take it for one thousand days,
the Sīmìng will remove your name from the register of death,
and you will be safeguarded with Heaven and Earth,
the sun and moon look upon you,
your form and appearance will change,
transforming without limit,
in the daylight there is no shadow,
and another radiance will appear.
Someone asked:
“If immortality can truly be attained,
the sages should have already practiced it,
but Zhōu and Kǒng did not pursue it;
this shows there is no such Dao.”
Bàopǔzi replied:
“Indeed, a sage need not be an immortal,
nor must an immortal be a sage.
Sages receive their destiny,
not encountering the path of longevity,
they simply wish to eliminate cruelty and banditry,
level dangers and quell violence,
establish rites and compose music,
formulate laws and impart teachings,
alter unrighteous customs,
reform harmful trends,
rectify imperiled lords,
support declining states,
edit poetry and books,
compile the Yellow River and Luo records,
compose classics and admonitions,
harmonize yǎ, sòng, and sì courts,
educate the young and ignorant,
respond to invitations from various states,
always on the move,
their mats never growing warm.
Their affairs are endless and without limit,
to the end of their years without rest,
how could they close their hearing and conceal their sight,
introspect and listen within,
practice breath guidance,
observe long fasts and purity,
enter chambers to refine the body,
ascend mountains to gather herbs,
count breaths and meditate on spirits,
abstain from grain and purify themselves?
As for immortals,
they need only earnest resolve and utmost faith,
diligent and unflagging,
able to be tranquil and calm,
then it may be attained,
without the need for many talents.
Those among the highest perfected who enter the mundane world,
become a heavy burden for practitioners of the Dao.
Obtaining the Great Medicine of the One,
knowing the key to guarding the One and nurturing spirit,
then they live long and see for ages,
how could it compare to the limitless actions of the sages?
Moreover, what the world calls “sages,”
are all sages of governing the world,
not sages who have attained the Dao,
the sages who have attained the Dao,
are the likes of Huángdì and Lǎozǐ,
as for sages who govern the world,
they are Zhōu and Kǒng.
Emperor Huángdì first governed and then ascended as an immortal,
he alone had the ability to combine the two.
The ancient kings,
inscribed on Tàishān,
there are seventy-two schools whose writings may be abbreviated,
the rest have mostly perished,
they are beyond count,
yet only the record of Huángdì attaining immortality is preserved,
thus its authenticity is clear.
People of the world, that which an individual excels at,
which others cannot match,
they call that person a “sage.”
Thus, one who is peerless at the board game of wéiqí,
is called the “sage of chess,”
and thus Yán Zǐqīng and Mǎ Suímíng are called chess sages even today.
Those who surpass their era in calligraphy,
are called “sage of writing,”
and thus Huáng Xiàng and Hú Zhāo even today have the name “sage of writing.”
Those skilled at painting beyond others,
are called “sage of painting,”
so Wèi Xié and Zhāng Mò are called “sage of painting” even now.
Those exceptionally skilled at carving and shaping,
are called “sage of woodwork,”
for Zhāng Héng and Mǎ Jūn are now called “sage of woodwork.”
Thus Mèngzǐ said Bóyí,
was the sage of purity;
Liǔ Xiàhuì,
the sage of harmony;
Yī Yǐn,
the sage of service.
If I try to set them forth and discuss them,
“sage” does not denote a single matter.
Bān, Shū, Chuí, Dí,
were the sages of machines;
Fù, Biàn, Hé, Huǎn,
the sages of healing disease;
Zǐ Wéi and Gān Jūn,
the sages of divination by astrology;
Shǐ Sū, Xīn, Liáo,
the sages of divining by milfoil stalks;
Xià Yù and Dù Huí,
the sages of sinew and strength;
Jīng Kē and Niè Zhèng,
the sages of courage;
Fēilián and Kuāfù,
the sages of fleetness;
Zǐyě and Yán Zhōu,
the sages of musical discernment;
Sūn, Wú, Hán, and Bái,
the sages of military strategy.
“Sage”
is merely the ultimate term for human affairs,
not restricted to literature alone.
As Zhuāng Zhōu said:
“Thieves have five qualities of the Way of sages.
To judge a man’s hiding place by wild guessing,
is wisdom;
to enter first and not doubt,
is courage;
to leave last and not fear,
is righteousness;
to know what is feasible and what is not,
is knowing;
to divide spoils evenly,
is benevolence.
Without these qualities one cannot become a great robber in the world.”
Someone said:
“The Way of the sages
cannot be branched and scattered like twigs and leaves,
it must be comprehensive and all-embracing,
then one is truly a sage.”
I replied to him, saying:
“The disciples of Kǒngzǐ,
those who attained understanding numbered seventy-two;
each acquired an embodiment of one aspect of the sage,
thus the affairs of the sage have their distinctions.
It is further said:
Yán Yuān embodied the Way in a subtle manner,
thus the deeds of the sage have their degrees of depth and shallowness.
Also, the Yì says:
There are four ways of the sage:
those who express through words value their rhetoric;
those who act value their transformations;
those who make implements value their symbols;
those who divine by oracle value their prognostications.
This is clear evidence that the way of the sage can be divided.
Why, then, should those skilled in Dào and Dé, who thereby attain to shénxiān,
alone not be called sages who have attained the Way?
If there were not sages who attained the Way,
would Zhōu and Kǒng not be permitted to be sages ruling the world?
Since they are not one and the same,
why should they be required to encompass all at once?
According to the Xiān jīng, it is held that all who attain immortality,
it is because, at the moment of receiving their destinies, they coincided with the qì of shénxiān,
and received it naturally.
Therefore, within the womb,
they already possess the innate nature of sincerity towards the Way.
When they come to awareness,
their hearts naturally delight in these matters,
and they will certainly encounter an illumined teacher and acquire the methods;
if not,
then they will neither believe nor seek;
even if they seek, they will not obtain it.
The Yùqián jīng, in the chapter on the origin of destiny, states:
A person’s fortune or misfortune
is determined on the day when the embryo is formed and receives the vital breath;
all gain the essence of one of the constellations above.
If one encounters the sage constellation, one becomes a sage;
if the worthy constellation, worthy;
if the cultured constellation, cultured;
if the martial constellation, martial;
if the noble constellation, noble;
if the rich constellation, rich;
if the base constellation, base;
if the poor constellation, poor;
if the long-lived constellation, long-lived;
if the immortal constellation, immortal.
Moreover, there are constellations of shénxiān sages,
constellations of sages who rule the world,
constellations of those who possess both,
constellations of the noble but not wealthy,
those wealthy but not noble,
those possessing both wealth and nobility,
those wealthy first then poor,
those noble first then base,
those both poor and base,
those whose wealth and nobility do not last,
constellations of loyalty and filial piety,
constellations of evil and misfortune.
Such cases cannot be exhaustively enumerated;
their general outline is as discussed.
Thus, for a person’s life, destiny is originally fixed;
this is the doctrine of Zhāng Chēzǐ.
If one does not receive the mandate of shénxiān,
he will certainly lack a heart that delights in immortality,
for never has there been one who did not value it in his heart yet still sought the matter,
nor one who did not seek and yet obtained it.
From ancient times to the present,
there have been those of high talent and great clarity
who do not believe in the existence of immortals,
and ordinary people who study and attain immortality;
some, though experienced in many matters, are nevertheless blind to immortality,
while others, though lacking broad understanding, grasp this particular principle;
is this not commanded by Heaven’s decree?”
The Dàojiā treasure their secret arts of immortality;
among disciples,
selection is especially careful,
transmitting only to the most refined and over long years,
and only then are they told the essential method.
How much more is this the case with common people?
Luckily, most do not believe or seek it themselves;
why should one insist on telling them by force?
If one cannot transform them to make them believe,
it will only bring mockery and quick slander.
Thus, those who have attained the Dào,
therefore walk a different path from the people of the world,
and settle in different places;
their words do not seek mingling with others,
their persons do not wish to be mixed among them.
Even separated by a thousand lǐ,
they still fear this may not be distant enough to avoid the attacks of toil and trouble;
even by breaking all contact and tracks,
they still fear it is not enough to be spared slander and disgrace.
Honor is insufficient to lure them,
wealth is insufficient to sway them;
how could they willingly flaunt themselves before worldly men,
and claim to possess the arts of immortality?
This is why Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ had no connection to understanding the Way of immortality.
Moreover, Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ
were simply men of high talent and profound learning;
even small arts and minor skills
many of which they hardly knew well.
If they were to try spinning balls, wielding swords,
leaping through blades, or throwing into narrow spaces,
climbing banners,
threading pans or traversing cases,
hanging by the heels from thousand-rèn-high precipices,
swimming across unfathomable rivers like Lǚliáng,
lifting weights of a thousand jūn by hand,
or stepping on raging winds,
fighting tigers bare-handed and leopards in cages,
catching arrows flying swiftly through the air—
these are all feats others can perform,
but even Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ could not;
how much less those surpassing even these?
What others ponder over,
that lice and fleas first approach,
the red and purple behind walls,
the weeds below the groves,
the books in chests and cases,
the treasures buried in the ground,
the birds and beasts in dense forests and deep marshes,
the fish and turtles in the heavy depths and broad pools—
if Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ were made to classify their colors,
to discern their names,
to list their number,
to verify their presence or absence,
they could hardly know them all—
how much less, then, things more distant than these?
Sages, if they do not eat, become hungry;
if they do not drink, become thirsty;
if burned, suffer heat;
if frozen, feel cold;
if struck, feel pain;
if cut, are wounded;
after years, they grow old;
if injured, they grow sick;
when breath ceases, they die.
In these, they have very many ways in which they do not differ from ordinary people,
and very few in which they are distinct.
That in which they surpass others utterly
lies only in having greater talents and broader vision,
an agile tongue and able writing,
complete virtue and pure conduct,
and mastery of study and broad learning.
How, then, could they be expected to excel in all things without exception?
Having already compiled writings and classics,
set the ruler above and governed the people,
is it yet desired that they also both know the Way of immortality,
and achieve undying life?
To demand this of sages—
is this not excessive?
I have heard: the utmost words go against convention,
and the true words must contradict the crowd.
If the Ruist scholars suddenly glance through this book of mine,
they will certainly say that I am slandering the sages.
How could I be so?
I only wish to exhaust the principles of things.
When principle is exhausted and matters are exhausted,
it then seems as if I slander Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ.
People of the world claim the sages fell from Heaven,
numinous spirits,
knowing everything,
capable of everything.
They revere and fear the name to such a degree,
they dare not examine them by worldly matters:
what the sage does not do,
no person can do;
what the sage does not know,
no person can know.
Is this not laughable?
Now let us fully compare recent events,
and perhaps understanding can be gained.
The birds of Mount Wán,
their cries selling life and delivering death—
Kǒngzǐ did not understand them;
can it then be that Yán Huí alone was able to grasp their meaning?
He heard the wailing of a woman from Mount Tài,
questioned her,
and only then learned that a tiger had devoured three members of her family;
but did not know why this woman did not move away,
and had to be told the reason to realize it.
Seeing one snaring birds and taking solely chicks,
he did not discern the meaning,
and had to ask to know.
When wishing to bury his mother,
he did not know where his father's grave was,
and had to have someone tell him;
when the decided grave collapsed,
again he did not know,
and his disciple had to tell him,
whereupon he wept bitterly.
He even doubted whether Yán Yuān might be stealing food,
and thus invented words about sacrificing to his forebears,
guessing at the truth of whether the dust was false.
When the stable burned,
he did not know whether men or horses had been hurt.
When Yán Yuān was gone,
he deemed him to have died.
He journeyed through more than seventy states,
and yet could not foresee that people would certainly refuse to employ him,
so he roamed with anxious haste,
unable even to warm his seat.
He did not know the people of Kuāng were going to besiege him,
and still went by that road.
He asked Lǎozǐ about ancient ritual,
being unclear himself on the rites;
he questioned Tánzǐ about bird officials,
not knowing those official duties.
On the road, he did not know the fords,
and had others inquire,
not knowing that those he asked
would inevitably take offense and not tell him the way.
Had he known, he would not have asked.
He got down from his carriage and chased singing phoenixes,
not realizing they would not stop for him.
He saw Nánzǐ and did not know it would be of no benefit.
Such examples as these,
are too many to list.
That he did not know the arts of immortality,
what is there to wonder at in this?
Yet common Ruists say:
What sages cannot do,
no one else can do.
But then, the people of Dàng live upon water;
Lady Liáng is transformed by fire;
Bozǐ endures extreme heat;
Zhòngdū endures deadly cold;
Zuǒ Cí escaped armies and did not die;
Gān Shǐ went without grain for years;
Fàn Yì was struck but was not wounded;
Governor Biē floated dead yet came back to life;
Shǎo Qiān commanded a hundred ghosts;
Zhǎng Fáng shortened the veins of the land;
Zhòng Fǔ took the form of a morning duck;
Zhāng Kǎi summoned clouds and mists by breathing;
never have we heard of Zhōu Gōng or Kǒngzǐ performing such feats.
Some common people say:
‘Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ were able to do all this,
they simply did not do it.’
I replied to him, saying:
"If one must not seek this from clear written records,
but instead points to it with empty words,
then I could just as well claim that Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ were able to shake their wings and soar aloft,
gliding through the eight extremes,
raising clouds to bring about rain,
moving mountains and uprooting wells,
but simply chose not to do so.
Once we no longer rely on accounts found in written records as evidence,
then what cannot be asserted?
If it is as you claim,
then I too can say that Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ have all already ascended as immortals,
only that this method cannot be used to instruct the world,
for fear that all people would come to know that immortality can be attained,
and would surely all dedicate themselves in service,
abandon offices and climb dangerous, remote, and deep places,
to cultivate this Way.
In such a case, families would no longer have children and descendants,
and states would no longer have officials and ministers,
loyalty and filial piety would both be lost,
the great bonds of society would be thrown into chaos.
Thus Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ secretly practiced it themselves,
and kept it hidden, not telling others,
outwardly attributing it to the semblance of dying in the end,
while inwardly possessing the reality of attaining higher immortality.
If this is so,
then what criticism can you raise against me?
It might not necessarily not be the case.
The Língbǎo Jīng contains three sections: Zhèngjī, Pínghéng, and Fēiguī Shòuzhì,
all are arts of immortality.
At the time when Wú Wáng quarried stones to build his palace,
among the joined stones,
was found a book written on golden tablets with purple characters,
but he could not read it.
He sent an envoy to ask Zhòngní about it,
but deceived Zhòngní, saying:
'The King of Wú, while at leisure,
saw a red sparrow with a book in its beak and set it on the palace hall,
not knowing its meaning,
and thus sent it far away for consultation.'
Zhòngní looked at it
and said:
'This is in fact a prescription from the Língbǎo tradition,
a method of long life,
practiced by Yǔ,
who concealed himself in the realms of water,
living as long as Heaven and Earth,
attending court in the Purple Chamber.
When Yǔ was about to become an immortal,
he sealed the scripture within a stone box on a famous mountain,
and now the red sparrow bears it—
surely this is a gift from Heaven.'
On this evidence, this means that Xià Yǔ did not die,
and Zhòngní also knew of it;
how can one know whether Zhòngní did not also secretly cultivate this Way?
Even granting that sages did not practice such things,
one cannot assert there are no such effects.
What people like or dislike,
each differs from the other,
to persuade by argument,
is it not credible?
If something truly fits one’s mind,
even if it is small, one will surely do it;
if it does not accord with one’s spirit,
even if it is great, one will not pursue it.
Some love bitterness and hate sweetness—
both types exist;
some crave advantage and discard righteousness—
they are without number.
'The great treasure of the sage is called office,
what gathers people together is called wealth.'
It is also said:
'Wealth and noble rank—
these are what people desire,'
yet in ancient times there have been those who relinquished the imperial throne and did not use it,
entrusted with the wealth of all under Heaven and did not wish for it,
despised high officialdom,
refused lavish jade and silk for service,
went off to the purity of mountain and forest,
content with the humble work of fishing—
such people cannot be counted.
It is also said:
'Men and women, food and drink—
the great desires of humanity are contained therein.'
Therefore passion for beauty cannot be admonished,
fine flavors can make one forget sorrow.
Yet there were those who abstained from grain and gave up delicacies,
kept neither wife nor concubine,
strode forth alone,
free of constraint and content at heart,
glanced at their own shadow in joy,
rinsed their mouths in streams and forgot the taste of food,
whose number again defies record.
Human feelings are such that all love fine beauty and radiant grace,
light and pliant forms,
yet Huáng Dì courted the unlovely Mómǔ,
Lord Chén cherished the unappealing Dūnqià.
No one's nose does not delight in fragrance,
thus frankincense and turmeric, ganoderma and orchid or suhe, mysterious balsam, pure glue, river reed and jiēchē, spring fennel and autumn orchid,
are priced like jade and pearl,
yet women by the sea
follow men with dreadful stench,
and do not cease.
King Wén of Zhōu relished pickled greens of poor flavor
and would not trade them for the taste of the grandest meats.
Wèi Míng delighted in the sounds of hammer and chisel
and would not trade them for the harmonious music of strings and pipes.
Each person has their own inclinations;
how can one demand that this should be as that?
If Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ themselves happened to be skeptical,
and did not believe in the way of immortality,
the sun and the moon do not shine everywhere,
and the sage does not know everything;
how then can one, on account of what the sage did not do,
assert that under Heaven there are no immortals?
This is like blaming the three heavenly lights for not illuminating the inside of an overturned bowl."
Someone then asked, saying:
"The immortals of old,
did they all obtain it through study,
or did they possess special endowments by nature?"
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"What sort of talk is this?
None failed to shoulder their satchels and follow a teacher,
compiling merits through diligent effort,
enduring frost and braving danger,
combed by the wind and washed in rain,
personally laboring in cleaning and sweeping,
toiling in hardship,
first meeting with credibility because of their conduct,
in the end subjected to trial in adversity,
their disposition steadfast and practice upright,
their minds free from complaint or double-mindedness,
only thus entering the hall and advancing into the chamber.
Some grew weary or discouraged and stopped midway,
some became resentful and withdrew,
some were enticed by glory and profit
and returned to pursue mundane affairs,
some were led astray by heterodox doctrine
and lost their aspiration for simplicity,
some practiced in the morning and hoped for success by evening,
some cultivated while seated yet expected results while standing.
As for those who see wealth or beauty and remain unmoved,
who hear common talk but whose will is undiminished,
among ten thousand,
even one is a rare thing.
Thus, those who attempt are as numerous as ox hairs,
but those who succeed are as rare as unicorn horns.
A bow that is drawn taut,
finds its effect in launching the arrow;
one who crosses a great river
achieves safety when the journey is done;
if a well does not reach the spring,
it is as if it had not been dug at all;
if a step falls short,
it is as if no journey has been made.
The burdens of a long road
cannot be completed in the turning of a sundial;
to reach the heights of the sky
is not achieved by a single basketful.
