Those climbing steep heights are hindered when just near the summit by failing strength,
practitioners of the Way are troubled when on the point of attaining success their will is not fulfilled.
A thousand granaries and ten thousand chests
do not come from a single harvest;
a tree that reaches the sky
is not grown in ten days;
unfathomable depths
begin with trickling waters;
the fortune of Táo Zhū
was amassed only by gathering over hundreds and thousands.
When others retreat and one advances,
Yīnzi thus exhausted the utmost Way.
Persisting to the end as at the beginning,
Xiànmén thus attracted dragons amidst clouds.
My will is truly firm,
what kind of man is he?"
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Ordinary people are not able to nurture life,
but instead are intent on ways to harm life.
If there is a finite thing,
it cannot supply the endless expenditure;
the flow of the Jiāng and Hé Rivers
cannot fill a bottomless vessel.
If a person's income is small but their expenditure is great,
still it will not suffice;
how much more so if there is not an ounce coming in,
while a thousand or a hundred go out?
People, whether young or old,
all have illnesses;
it is only a matter of degree.
Each person receives a different amount of vital energy:
for those who have more, it is depleted slowly;
for those who have less, it is exhausted quickly.
Those who understand the Dao make up for and remedy this,
necessarily first returning things to their original state,
and then seeking further benefit in measured increase.
If one were to take medicinal substances all day long,
then flesh would fly and bones would soar;
if one practiced breath control and guiding exercises to the utmost,
then feathers and wings would grow unevenly;
then there would be no person in the world who does not believe in the Dao!
The problem is that the gain from ladles and scoops is not yet solid,
while the expense of bushels and stones comes one after another;
the foundation is not yet firm,
when the poisons of frost and ice come together to attack.
Not knowing that the fault lies with themselves,
instead they claim that the Dao is unprofitable,
and so they discard pills and powders, and abandon breath cultivation.
Therefore it is said: it is not that immortality is hard,
but that hearing the Dao is hard;
it is not that hearing the Dao is hard,
but that practicing it is hard;
it is not that practicing it is hard,
but that persevering in it to the end is hard.
A fine craftsman can provide people with compasses and squares,
but cannot make people skillful by necessity.
A wise teacher can teach people the formulae,
but cannot make people act on them for certain.
Cultivating the Dao is like sowing grain,
and completing it is like harvesting and storing;
even if the fields are fertile,
and the waters and marshes are fine,
if the timing of Heaven is missed,
and plowing and hoeing are not thorough,
and crops are left withered in the ridges,
and not reaped or gathered,
though there are many acres,
yet there is still no harvest.
Ordinary people not only fail to know that gain is gain,
but also fail to know that loss is loss.
Loss is easy to know and comes quickly,
while gain is hard to know and comes slowly.
People do not yet wake up to what is easy,
how could they recognize what is hard?
That which causes loss is like the lamp's flame consuming oil,
no one sees it,
but suddenly it is all gone.
That which gives increase is like seedlings and grains being sown and growing,
none notices it,
but suddenly they are lush.
Therefore, to nurture the body and cultivate one's nature,
one must be careful with the smallest things;
do not dismiss small gains as trivial and thus not cultivate them,
do not take small losses as harmless and thus not guard against them.
All accumulation of small things is done so as to reach greatness,
by accumulating one, one can reach a hundred million.
If one can value things in their subtlety,
and accomplish them when they are manifest,
then one is close to knowing the Dao."
Someone asked:
"In ancient times, was there anyone who did not practice any method,
yet happened to attain immortality?"
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"No.
Some followed enlightened teachers,
accumulated merit and toiled diligently,
and thus were granted the medicine that enables perfection.
Some received secret formulas,
and prepared elixirs themselves,
their affairs unconnected to the world,
their words not burdened by custom,
and recorded histories retain only their names,
but cannot fully know how they attained immortality,
so details are lacking.
In ancient times, Huáng Dì could speak from birth,
commanded all the spirits,
and could be said to have been born by the endowment of Heaven,
yet still could not sit quietly and thereby gain the Dao.
Thus, he ascended Wángwū to receive the Cinnabar Sutra,
reached Dǐnghú and flew forth shining pearls,
climbed Kūngtóng and consulted Guǎngchéng,
went to Jùzī to serve Dàwěi,
traveled to the East Dài to venerate Zhōnghuáng,
entered Jīngǔ to seek advice from Juānzǐ,
for nurturing the Dao he relied on the two maidens Xuánsù,
for refining calculations he visited Shānjī and Lìmù,
for divination he consulted Fēnghòu,
for diagnosis he received instruction from Léiqí,
for military strategies he took counsel in the arts of the Five Notes,
to fathom deities and treachery he recorded the words of Bǎizé,
for geomancy he wrote the teachings of Qīngwū,
for healing and injuries he collected the arts of Jīnyě.
Thus he was able to possess all the essential secrets,
and exhaust the Dao and attain truth,
ascending on a dragon to lofty heights,
united with Heaven and Earth in infinity.
Yet according to the Scriptures of the Immortals,
all say that Huáng Dì and Lǎozǐ served Tàiyǐ Yuánjūn to receive the essential teachings;
how much more, then, those who fall short of these two sages—
how could there be anyone who spontaneously achieved immortality and transcended the world?
I have not heard of such a case."
Someone said:
"If Huáng Dì truly became an immortal,
then what of the tomb on Qiáoshān?"
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"According to the Jīngshān Classic and the Longshǒu Record,
both state that after Huáng Dì consumed the divine elixir,
a dragon came to welcome him;
his ministers and subjects longed for him,
unable to know where to go or what to think;
some took his couch and staff,
established a temple and sacrificed to him;
others took his clothing and hat,
buried and guarded them.
The Biographies of the Immortals says:
Huáng Dì chose his day of departure,
left for seventy days,
returned for seventy days,
was buried at Qiáoshān,
and then suddenly the mountain collapsed,
the tomb was empty with no corpse,
only a sword and shoes remained.
Although these accounts differ,
they all agree on his becoming an immortal.
Accounts of Huáng Dì becoming immortal
are numerous in Daoist writings and among the various schools,
but the Confucians do not wish to propagate miracles,
nor open up alternative paths,
but focus on ritual teachings.
As for the affairs of the immortals,
they cannot be used to instruct the common people;
therefore they say he died,
simply to block the thoughts of the populace.
Zhū Yì and Luán Bā as ministers,
brought merit and benevolence to the people,
and the commoners in life built temples and shrines for them;
also in ancient times, persons of great virtue,
after their bodies perished,
their ministers engraved their achievements on imperishable vessels.
Even today, when rulers relocate,
officials and people remember them with longing,
and often erect stelae in praise of their virtues;
such things frequently occur,
and this too is comparable to Huáng Dì having a temple and tomb.
How could this be sufficient to prove he truly died?"
Someone asked:
“Péng Zǔ lived eight hundred years,
Ānqī lived three thousand;
their longevity surpassed that of others.
If indeed there is a way to avoid death,
why did they not simply become immortals?
Is it not that allotment of fate and reception of qi
naturally determine length or brevity of life,
and those people happened by chance to gain the greater share,
but in principle it cannot be extended,
so they could not escape decline and perishing?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“According to the Jīng of Péng Zǔ,
he assisted Yáo on behalf of Emperor Kù,
served as a minister from the Xià through the Yīn dynasties,
and when the Yīn king sent a gathering woman to learn the techniques of the bedchamber from him,
he practiced them with effect.
The king wanted to kill Péng Zǔ
in order to cut off his methods;
Péng Zǔ became aware and fled.
When he left, he was over seven or eight hundred years old,
and it was not because of death.
According to Huáng Shí Gōng’s record,
over seventy years after Péng Zǔ’s departure,
his disciples saw him west of Liúshā,
showing clearly that he was not dead.
Moreover, among Péng Zǔ’s disciples,
Qīngyī Wūgōng, Hēixué Gōng, Xiùméi Gōng, Báitù Gōngzǐ, Lí Lóu Gōng, Tàizú Jūn, Gāoqiūzǐ, and Bùkěnlái—seven or eight people,
all lived for hundreds of years,
and during the Yīn dynasty each became an immortal and departed;
how much less likely, then, that Péng Zǔ himself would willingly die?
Furthermore, as Liú Xiàng notes in his Biographies of Immortals, he also says Péng Zǔ was an immortal.
As for Mr. Ānqī,
he sold medicines along the seashore,
and people from Lángyá transmitted sightings of him for generations;
it has amounted to over a thousand years.
Qín Shǐ Huáng invited him to converse
for three days and three nights.
His words were lofty,
his purport far-reaching,
broad and well-evidenced.
Shǐ Huáng was amazed by him,
and bestowed gold and jade objects
worth several tens of millions.
Ānqī accepted them and placed them in the Township Pavilion of Fùxiāng,
and in return sent a measure of red jade slippers.
He left a letter saying,
‘In several thousand years,
seek me on Pénglái Mountain.’
In this way,
it is clear he was already a thousand years old when he saw Shǐ Huáng,
and it was not by death.
Moreover, Shǐ Huáng was harsh, violent, and proud,
the last in the world to be willing to believe in immortals.
Nor is he someone who could be satisfied by false answers.
Yet when he questioned Ānqī about the matters of attaining long life,
Ānqī answered him appropriately;
Shǐ Huáng was awakened
and believed there certainly must be the Way of Immortality in the world.
Having thus richly rewarded him,
he was sincerely willing to seek to learn the art of not dying,
but simply lacked an enlightened teacher,
and was deceived by the likes of Lú Áo and Xú Fú;
thus he could not obtain it.
If indeed the words of Mr. Ānqī had been without foundation,
in three days and nights,
it would have sufficed to exhaust his arguments,
and Shǐ Huáng would surely have boiled and slaughtered him,
unable to escape disaster at the cauldron and chopping board;
how could he have received great rewards?
” Someone asked:
“There are people who ingest medicines,
practice breathing and guiding exercises,
yet do not avoid death—
why is this?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“If one does not obtain the Golden Elixir,
but only takes herbs from plants and trees or practices minor arts,
one may prolong life and delay death,
but cannot become an immortal.
Some know only to take herbal medicines,
but do not know the essential arts for returning one’s years,
then in the end, there is no way to achieve long life.
Some do not understand wearing divine talismans,
performing prohibitions and precepts,
contemplating the body’s spirits,
and guarding the true One;
then at best, they can only keep internal diseases from arising,
and avoid invasions of wind and dampness.
But if suddenly attacked by malignant ghosts or powerful evil,
or mountain spirits or water poisons harm them,
then they will die immediately.
Some have not obtained the methods for entering the mountains,
causing the mountain gods to bring them calamity,
so that monstrous ghosts test them,
fierce beasts injure them,
river poisons strike them,
and serpents or vipers sting them,
resulting in many causes of death,
not just one.
Some begin cultivating the Way late in life,
but have already deeply damaged themselves beforehand,
making recovery difficult.
The benefits of recovery
are not firmly established,
and the illness soon returns,
so with matters of overcoming and correcting,
how can they attain long life?
There are some who become immortals by practicing the Way when already old,
and some who fail though they start young;
why is this?
The former, though old in years, originally received much qi,
and having received much qi, their injuries and losses are shallow,
and being less depleted, they are easy to nourish,
thus they can become immortals.
The latter, though young, originally received little qi,
and with little qi, the injuries are deep,
and with deep injuries, rescue is difficult,
therefore, they cannot become immortals.
Consider the hibiscus and willow trees:
when their roots are cut off, they regrow,
if overturned, they still grow,
if laid sideways, they still grow.
Of things easy to revive,
none surpass these trees.
Yet, if they are buried too shallowly,
and not left there long,
sometimes carved or peeled,
sometimes shaken or pulled up,
even if heaped with fertile soil,
and soaked with spring water,
still they cannot escape withering and devastation,
because their roots are not secure,
and they have no time to send forth shoots,
nor can their sap nourish their vital force.
The human body
is easily harmed and hard to nourish;
compared to the two trees,
it falls far short.
And what damages and destroys it
goes beyond carving and peeling,
being even worse than shaking and pulling up.
Those who help it are few,
those who harm it are many,
so death is only natural.
As for expelling the old and taking in the new,
it is through qi that qi is lengthened,
yet when qi is already greatly depleted, it is hard to extend it.
In taking medicinal substances,
it is through the blood that blood is replenished,
but when blood is nearly exhausted, it is hard to restore it.
Those who run about and pant in rebellion,
or cough or feel bloated,
or use their strength and exhaust their bodies,
or labor anxiously and easily tire,
show the signs of qi depletion.
When the face loses its lustrous color,
the skin is withered and sallow,
the lips are parched and pale,
and the tissues shrivel and decline,
these are the signs of blood reduction.
When these two signs have shown external decline,
then the spiritual root within also withers.
In such a state,
even the highest medicine
cannot save.
All who practice the Way but do not succeed,
or struggle for life but die nonetheless,
it is not that they have no qi or blood.
Yet that which constitutes their qi and blood within the body,
the root and source is already lost,
and only the outflowing branches remain.
It is like embers entering water:
when the fire is extinguished, the smoke does not immediately stop;
or a felled tree:
though the branches and leaves still remain green,
in both cases, it is not that there is no smoke,
nor that there are no leaves,
but that which makes the smoke and leaves
has already perished.
People, on the day they notice sickness,
only then do they begin to call it illness,
just as on the day qi is cut off
they consider that the sign of bodily death.
They only blame wind-cold or summer-dampness,
not knowing that wind-cold and summer-dampness
cannot harm robust persons;
they only afflict those whose bodies are weak and qi is insufficient,
who cannot withstand them,
and thus are affected.
How can this be proved?
Suppose there are several people,
of equal age, whether old or strong,
and consume the same diet in equal amounts,
all travel together to the desert,
and spend the night in severe cold,
with pure snow falling above,
black ice freezing below,
cold winds break branches and howl at night,
and coughs and saliva freeze on the lips;
among them, someone will surely fall ill with the cold,
but not all become sick.
This is not because the cold is partial,
but simply because human bodies differ in endurance.
Thus, though all eat the same thing,
sometimes only one develops an illness,
not because that substance is especially poisonous.
Though the same cup is filled, all drink equally,
yet some become sober and some drunk,
not because wine is of two natures.
In the same summer heat,
sometimes only one dies of sunstroke,
not because the heat favors or disfavors people.
When all take the same medicine,
some may become dizzy or troubled,
not for the drug loves or hates anyone.
Thus, when storm winds sweep the forest,
dry branches break first;
when great waves strike the cliff,
the cracks fall first;
when blazing fire sweeps the plain,
the dry grass burns first;
when a dragon bowl falls to the ground,
the brittle one breaks first.
Observing thus,
when people are without the Way,
their bodies are already diseased by nature,
then wind, cold, summer, and dampness merely trigger the condition.
If one can preserve true qi from declining,
and have form and spirit protect one another,
then nothing can harm him.
All practitioners of the Way
generally suffer from being too late,
not from being too early.
Trusting in youth and vigor,
and bodily strength at its peak,
they overtax themselves,
a hundred sicknesses ensue,
and their lives hang as precariously as morning dew;
if they cannot obtain the great medicine,
and only take plants and herbs,
they may be better off than ordinary people,
but cannot greatly prolong their lifespan.
Therefore the Immortal texts say:
‘Nourishing life takes not harming as its foundation.’
This is an essential saying.
Shénnóng said:
‘If the hundred diseases are not cured,
how can one attain long life?’
Truly, these are trustworthy words.”
Someone asked:
“Those things which are said to harm one’s life,
are they not merely matters of excessive desires?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“Why should it be only this?
Yet the essential point of long life
lies in the method of rejuvenation.
If a superior person understands this,
they may extend their years and ward off sickness;
next in degree are those who do not damage themselves.
If one, while still young and strong, knows the way to restore youth,
takes yīn elixirs to nourish the brain,
gathers jade nectar from long valleys,
does not take medicines,
and yet does not fail to attain three hundred years,
though they may not become an immortal.
Those who do not acquire these arts,
the ancients compared to one who puts hot soup into an ice cup,
or stores fire within a feather bag.
Moreover, if one pursues what cannot be attained by their ability
and exhausts themselves in thought,
this causes harm;
if one attempts what surpasses their strength
and forces themselves to lift it,
this causes harm;
grief and emaciation,
cause harm;
excessive joy,
causes harm;
restlessly striving after desires,
causes harm;
lengthy talking, laughing,
cause harm;
sleeping and resting at the wrong times,
cause harm;
drawing bows and crossbows,
cause harm;
intoxication and vomiting,
cause harm;
eating one’s fill and then immediately lying down,
causes harm;
jumping, running, and breathlessness,
cause harm;
whooping with joy or weeping,
cause harm;
when yīn and yáng do not mingle,
it causes harm;
when many harms accumulate fully, early death ensues
—early death is not the Way.
Thus, the methods of nourishing life are as follows:
do not spit far,
do not walk rapidly,
do not strain the ears in listening,
do not gaze for a long time,
do not sit for too long,
do not lie down from exhaustion,
clothe oneself before becoming cold,
remove clothing before feeling hot,
do not eat only when extremely hungry,
do not eat until overfull,
do not drink only when extremely thirsty,
do not drink in excess.
If one eats too much, it forms lumps and accumulations;
if one drinks to excess, it creates phlegm and congestion.
Do not labor too much, nor be too idle;
do not get up late;
do not sweat excessively;
do not sleep too much;
do not gallop in carriages or on horseback;
do not gaze too long or too far;
do not eat much raw or cold food;
do not drink alcohol in a draft;
do not bathe too frequently;
do not set ambitious, far-reaching desires;
do not scheme to create strange and ingenious things.
In winter, do not seek excessive warmth;
in summer, do not pursue extremes of coolness;
do not sleep exposed beneath the stars;
do not sleep unsheltered with your shoulders seen;
great cold and great heat,
strong winds and heavy fog,
should all be avoided.
Of the five flavors entering the mouth,
none should be consumed to excess;
for too much sour injures the spleen,
too much bitter injures the lungs,
too much pungent injures the liver,
too much salty injures the heart,
too much sweet injures the kidneys;
this is the natural principle of the five elements.
As for harm,
it is not immediately perceived,
but over time life is shortened.
Therefore, those skilled in preserving life
lie down and rise in accordance with the four seasons’ timings,
their activity and repose follow the constant rule of supreme harmony;
to moderate and benefit the sinews and bones,
there is a method of stretching and relaxing;
to ward off illness and intrusive evils,
there is the art of swallowing and breathing;
for the circulation of vascular energies,
there are methods of supplementing or draining;
to regulate work and rest,
there is an essential doctrine of giving and taking.
Restrain anger to preserve yīn energy;
restrain excessive joy to foster yáng energy.
Only then should one first take plants and herbs to remedy deficiencies,
and later take golden elixirs to achieve limitless stability;
the principle of long life
is thus exhausted.
But as for those who cherish their own inclinations and ambitions,
deeming themselves wise and knowing fate,
not clinging to heterodox doctrines,
indulging their feelings and exertions,
and not seeking long life—
hearing these words,
though it is like wind passing their ears,
like lightning flashing before their eyes,
it cannot persuade them.
And even as their bodies wither amid indulgence,
their breath ceasing in fine silks and brocades,
yet they are content,
so how could one speak to them of nourishing life?
Not only do they not accept it,
they even call it witchcraft and deception.
To hope that they would believe is
like giving a bright mirror to the blind,
or entertaining the deaf with strings and flutes.”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The greatest virtue of Heaven and Earth is life,
and life delights in things.
Therefore, what the Daoists hold most secret and precious,
none surpasses the method of long life.
Hence the blood oath is transmitted,
but if transmitted to the wrong person,
heavenly punishment is to be feared.
The former masters did not dare to lightly teach people,
but waited for those who sought it with utmost diligence;
even then, they would carefully select the most excellent before instructing them.
How much less for those who neither like nor seek it,
or who are not earnest in their pursuit—
how could one advertise and peddle it to them?
For those not ordained to immortality,
even if they saw immortals daily, groups in the world,
they would still say they are of a different stock,
that there is some other thing in the world,
or call them the transformations of ghosts and spirits,
or say they just happened by chance in nature—
who would ever admit it was attained by cultivation?
Indeed, if the heart does not believe,
even if Chìsōng and Wáng Qiáo spoke into their ears,
they would also regard it as heretical deception.
Yet at times there are those who discern and believe,
but again they struggle to diligently seek out an enlightened teacher.
Those who understand the essentials and attain the true Dao
are indeed extremely rare,
and cannot be encountered suddenly.
Yet those who know of it
are merely few in number,
but have never disappeared from the world.
Because those who seek are neither broad nor sincere,
only those with the mandate of immortality
are certain to encounter each other naturally.
There have been those who sought but did not obtain it,
but never those who did not seek and did obtain it.
In the world there are always cunning and false young men scheming for money,
who steal the name of Daoist,
and are innumerable.
Yet these still cannot be said to be utterly ignorant,
all of them have roughly pried open the basics,
some peddle false reputations,
and further cover themselves with hidden evil and feigned skill.
Then, among those eager for such things,
those who cannot discern true from false
go to question them in great numbers,
thereby deceiving and deluding themselves,
binding themselves up
and preventing themselves from acting,
seeking widely for exceptional men,
and telling them:
'The Dao ends with us.'
In this way, not a few earnest seekers are misled—
it is lamentable and infuriating.

Some have heard of those who understand the transmutation of five clouds, soaring with eight stones, revolving the nine elixirs, refining yellow and white, the watery jade of qióngyáo, transforming cinnabar and jasper, condensing frost and snow in the divine furnace, or harvesting lingzhī on Sōngyuè—
then most will slander them, saying,
'Only Chìsōng and Wáng Qiáo know these methods.
If people today claim to know them,
it is all a lie.'
Thus, those of shallow insight
do not sense the trick in such words,
and immediately give up their desire to seek afar.
Alas,
it is cause for grief and sighing!
Time hastens by like wind,
aging comes in the blink of an eye;
in its furious swiftness,
there is nothing to compare it to.
A lifespan of a hundred years
is but a little over thirty thousand days.
In childhood, one knows nothing;
in old age, joy and pleasure both are gone.
Childhood ignorance and senile confusion—
subtract a few decades,
then dangers, hardships, anxiety, and illness
come one after another in succession.
Of the years spent in the world,
roughly half are spent.
For those who count on living a hundred years,
the years of happiness and peace
are no more than fifty or sixty years.
In a flash, these all disappear,
and the days of grief and confusion
are but six or seven thousand.
Looking back, everything is already over;
how much rarer is one who attains a full hundred years—
perhaps one in ten thousand?
Consider it deeply,
and one cannot but remember the summer insects and morning mushrooms.
Indeed, the ignorance of Daoist principles is most pitiful.
There is a saying among the people:
A person in the world
loses a day each day,
like leading cattle and sheep to the slaughterhouse,
with each step forward,
one step closer to death.
Though this comparison is crude,
it is the truth.
The reason why the wise do not worry about death
is not that they do not wish to seek it,
but because they truly do not know the art of avoiding death,
so they worry in vain
to no benefit.
Thus it is said: Those who are content with fate and understand destiny
therefore do not grieve—
it is not that they do not wish for long life.
Jī Gōng offered to die in Wǔ Wáng's stead;
Zhòngní dragged his staff and grieved at heart.
Thus we know the sages also did not delight in an early death.
Common men, seeing Zhuāng Zhōu's metaphor of the great dream,
then hasten to elaborate on the doctrine of the equality of life and death.
Such are clever and forced arguments,
feigning statements of denial and restraint,
all matters that even Zhòngní would break the laws to dispel.
Now consider those who speak thus:
when ill, they hasten to moxibustion and acupuncture;
when facing danger, they greatly fear death.
But in these decadent later ages,
people no longer value true faith,
turning away from the classics and studying only the sub-commentaries.
If one does not spout clever contrarian arguments,
one is called rustic
and not a student of Lǎo and Zhuāng.
Therefore, men without backbone, seeking to blend in with the crowd,
drift upon false doctrines
and cannot return to themselves.
Lǎozi took long life and clear vision as his career,
whereas Zhuāng Zhōu valued wagging his tail in muddy waters,
not becoming a turtle caught in a net,
nor an ox adorned with embroidery,
nor begging for grain from the River Lord;
by this we know he could not make life and death equal.
Today's students cannot scrutinize the truth,
but seize blindly upon one phrase—
is this not erroneous?
Moreover, sinking into the depths of the Nine Springs,
endless are the long nights;
at first one becomes food for ants,
in the end merges with dust and earth.
It makes one tremble with dread,
and sigh unconsciously.
If your heart has the will to seek life,
how can you neglect urgent matters
in order to cultivate the subtle and mysterious pursuit?
If you do not believe, then so be it;
if you do believe,
then again you may be troubled by not thoroughly cleansing yourself of worldly affections,
and cannot wholly devote yourself to nourishing life,
but only take it up in idle moments after attending to worldly affairs—
thus, of those who try,
most begin late and mostly do not succeed.
What all men anxiously strive after
are power, profit, indulgence, and desire.
If my body is not whole,
then even high office and great power,
gold and jade piled in mountains,
beauty in uncountable forms,
are not truly mine.
Therefore, superior men first undertake matters of long life;
with long life, all desires can be fulfilled.
If one does not yet ascend to the mysteries and leave the world,
one can at least dwell among the earthly immortals.
If like Péngzǔ and Lǎozi,
living among men for several hundred years,
without losing the joy of human relationships,
and only then gradually departing to distance,
it is also a splendid thing.
But it is absolutely necessary to have a good teacher;
if the teacher is inadequate,
there is no way to succeed.
In olden days, the Han Empress Dowager studied the Shūjīng with Xiàhóu Shèng,
rewarding him with a hundred catties of gold,
and other gifts beyond number.
When Shèng died,
again she rewarded his family with two million coins,
and observed mourning in plain clothes for a hundred days.
When Chéng Dì was Crown Prince,
he studied the Lúnyǔ with Zhāng Yǔ.
When he ascended the throne,
he awarded Yǔ the title of guān nèi hóu,
a fief of a thousand households,
made him Senior Great Master of the Imperial Court,
and gave him a hundred catties of gold.
Later, he was promoted to Chancellor,
and elevated to ānchāng hóu.
In old age, when requesting retirement,
he was granted a carriage and four horses,
a hundred catties of gold,
and tens of thousands of coins.
When Yǔ fell ill,
the Emperor himself visited him,
and solemnly bowed beside Yǔ's bed.
When Zhāng Dì was Crown Prince,
he studied the Xiàojīng with Huán Róng.
When he became emperor,
he made Róng Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
The Emperor visited Róng's mansion,
had Róng sit facing east,
and set up a desk and staff for him.
He gathered all the officials and Róng Ménsēng’s disciples, numbering in the hundreds,
and the Emperor personally held the text and lectured.
Róng was bestowed the title Guān Nèi Hóu,
with a fief of five thousand households.
When Róng fell ill,
the Son of Heaven honored his household in person,
and upon entering the lane, descended from his carriage,
embracing a scroll and hurrying forward,
observing the courtesy due to a disciple.
When Róng passed away,
the Son of Heaven wore plain garments in mourning for Róng.
All those lords,
though unable to besiege cities and fight in open battle,
break resistance and expand the borders,
hang banners and demonstrate loyalty,
pacify dangerous regions,
and transfer great achievements,
or display valor in distant lands,
yet solely by mastering a single classic,
expounding on its chapters and verses,
were they held in respect,
honored so greatly,
though they were but able to speak the lingering words of the dead.
The exaltation of emperors and kings,
still they humble themselves to revere them.
In the world, some there are who wish to seek and cultivate the Way of Long Life,
yet refuse to humble themselves before one who can be their teacher,
strutting arrogantly,
seeking the essentials directly,
how can they possibly attain it?
If a student only performs superficial courtesies,
what benefit is that to the teacher, even by an inch?
If it is not so,
then his heart is not fully engaged;
if his heart is not fully engaged,
then in teaching him, one is not diligent;
if teaching is not diligent,
how can one possibly impart all the secret methods?
With no choice, one must reveal only the superficial,
how can that suffice to achieve the accomplishment of immortality?
There are also those who outwardly delight in this Way,
and whose professed faith in the Dao
is not rooted in heart and spirit,
pursuing their desires,
feigning humility in appearance,
but after several days,
neglect and indifference appear.
If they meet a wise and perceptive teacher,
eager to carefully observe the nuances of the seeker,
testing with prolonged delay,
thus does not instruct him,
to gauge his intention.
As for such people,
their false and true behavior is exposed,
thus they ultimately cannot be taught,
and even if taught, cannot be told everything honestly;
if words are incomplete, then teaching is of no benefit.
Chén Ānshì,
at age thirteen,
was but a guest of Guàn Shǔběn,
yet first attained the Dao of immortality.
Shǔběn, at age seventy, his hair white,
would morning and evening bow to Ānshì, saying,
“The Dao is supreme and virtue exalted;
he who first attains the Dao is the teacher,
I dare not neglect to follow the courtesies of a disciple.”
Therefore Ānshì revealed the essential methods to him,
and so attained immortality again.
At birth, man first receives essence and spirit from Heaven and Earth,
and later receives qi and blood from his parents,
yet if he does not obtain an enlightened teacher
to instruct him in the Way of crossing over the world,
then there is no means to escape death;
a chiseled stone may still have remaining embers,
but one’s lifespan is already withered and fading.
Judging from this,
the grace of an enlightened teacher
truly surpasses that of Heaven and Earth,
and far outweighs that of one’s parents,
so can it not be revered?
Can it not be sought?
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The ancients were sincere and upright;
they valued action and despised words.
Therefore, those who governed did not esteem ornate argument,
and those who cultivated the Dào did not revere flowery speech.
With customs declining and growing thin,
outward ornament has become ever more elaborate.
Thus, written strategies pile up like mountains in the halls of the Rú,
and internal manuscripts also fill the hands of the shù experts.
For the beginner,
it is not suitable to impart them the essential principles at once.
Moreover, it is human nature to take pleasure in abundance of detail rather than essentials.
Therefore, those who later came to know the Dào,
such as Qián Jí, Róng Sōng, Guì Bó, and others,
each composed works numbering in the thousands,
yet mostly fill them with exhortations and admonitions;
they are unwilling to clearly reveal for others the essential destination and guiding direction.
As for the true formulas,
some are only transmitted orally,
or recorded no more than on a slip of cloth a few feet long,
worn at the waist,
and unless one serves their teacher for a long time,
laboring diligently and testing repeatedly,
it cannot be obtained.
Various and mediocre disciples
each according to the diligence or laxity of their intent,
and the duration of their arduous pursuit,
as well as the reach of their intelligence,
and what their will and strength can discern,
each receives some teaching.
In the span of a thousand or even a hundred years,
sometimes there appear those who entirely impart from their own bags and pillows,
and from under their arms,
the essential points of the secret.
Some only take these to prepare medicines;
when the medicine is complete, they divide it,
sufficient only to make others avoid death, and nothing more,
and never once record their formulas or texts and transmit them.
Therefore, among Daoists in the world,
those who truly know the matters of the elixir are one in ten thousand,
if that.
Yet those narrow in sight
believe that immortal techniques must be exhaustively set forth in writings full of confusion
or in the intervals of rituals and prostrations.
Yet the control of long life lies solely in the Great Medicine;
it is not something to be obtained by sacrifices and offerings.
In former times, during the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
they made great displays of prayer and supplication,
and offered sacrifices to Tài Yǐ and the Five Gods,
and laid out treasures for the Eight Spirits and the like,
expending cattle, sheep, grain, and silk,
and spending money by the millions,
but there was no benefit at all.
How much the less so among commoners,
whose virtue is incomplete,
whose bodies are not nourished,
yet who hope through the offerings of three animals, wine, and delicacies,
praying to ghosts and spirits,
to seek an extension of life—
such delusion is extreme indeed.
Or there are those with a penchant for such affairs,
who truly wish to practice the Dào,
but lack the persistence to seek enlightened teachers,
or to prepare wondrous medicines;
instead, they merely recite day and night unnecessary books,
numbering in the thousands and hundreds of volumes,
but gain nothing even into old age;
then declare that in all the world truly there is no method of immortality.
Some knock upon their thresholds,
bow toward empty seats,
slaughter sacrificial animals,
burn incense and pray for good fortune,
yet the sick are not healed,
death and mourning follow one after another,
families go bankrupt and property is exhausted,
and nothing extraordinary occurs;
still they do not repent and awaken,
but attribute it to their own lack of devotion.
If with as much effort
one sought teachers who knew the formulas,
and used as much expense
to purchase ingredients for medicines,
surely one could attain transcendence and long life!
How is this different from the elderly who vainly till a field of stone,
and hope for a harvest of a thousand granaries?
Even if all their strength is used,
they will not obtain what they seek.
This is what is called traveling toward Yān when intending to go to Chǔ:
though the horse be swift, it will not arrive,
not because the journey is slow,
but because the road is lost.
Some are naturally credulous and delight in trusting others,
but lack the wit to distinguish the genuine from the false,
and to judge depth and shallowness;
their experience and breadth are narrow,
unable to discern true merit.
In later times, the foolish and shallow
seize upon finding a single person,
self-praise him as their master,
and proclaim possession of secret books,
and steadfastly serve him.
Yet most commoners and ignorant youths
claim the name of having the Dào
far beyond the reality.
This stems from boasting and deceit;
within, they are grasping and corrupted,
seeking only profit,
and whatever is requested of them,
they forcibly groan and mumble,
lowering or raising their tone as if
their knowledge were genuinely deep treasures, unobtainable.
When anything is asked of them,
whatever is requested,
they lower their head and smile,
or give vague promises for the future,
thus causing the unwary,
wishing to give up yet unable,
to think it is only due to their own insufficient diligence
or to offering too small a gift.
Therefore, those of firm faith
become all the more deferential,
presenting rare trinkets as bribes,
acting as servants,
never shirking burdens or distant travel,
not avoiding risks or perils,
hoping to repay them with accumulated toil,
enduring hardship and plaintively begging,
in the hope of hearing something unusual.
All the while years slip by in vain,
while they neglect the support of their elderly parents,
abandon their wives and children with no remorse,
braving frost and treading on ice,
year after year following such people,
to the ruin of their finances and waste of their effort,
yet in the end attain nothing at all.
Some may have intended to deceive from the start,
in the end feel some shame,
and stand bewildered in body,
knowing themselves to be utterly empty and short of substance,
lacking any competence or method to instruct others;
with what means can they help anyone achieve fulfillment?
I have seen many such people with my own eyes,
not less than ten or more.
Some style themselves with lofty names,
living long among the populace;
the world may claim they are three or four hundred years old,
though they have only changed their name,
and fraudulently assert themselves as sages,
mingling among men,
with many serving them.
As for myself, I simply dislike recording their names.
They often roam among the common people,
whom the ordinary man cannot judge as genuine or false,
but unite to praise and proclaim them,
thus increasing deception and delusion,
lending their skill in fraud,
to falsely create a reputation for brilliance,
and as this custom grows widespread,
no one can discern truth from falsehood.
Therefore, sometimes even superior men, not paying particular heed or discernment,
simply rely on hearsay,
and thus mislead earnest learners.
This always comes from such people,
and invariably leads others to sigh and lament.
Each time I see such types,
deceiving the world,
seeking power and profit,
whether quick or slow, all receive retribution;
even though Heaven’s net is vast
it never misses anything in the end.
Yet it is the misguidance of those with true aspiration that is most lamentable.
People of the world mostly pursue empty rumors,
rare are those who thoroughly examine reality.
When they hear that someone, A or B, has many disciples,
even numbering over a hundred,
they are certain there must be something extraordinary,
and so they race and compete,
flocking to become that person’s followers,
wasting their time and effort to exalt those who are ignorant and crude.
Yet they never further investigate,
and these impostors then benefit from the labor of their followers.
Some thereby amass wealth,
and though exposed and driven off repeatedly,
there is still no way for true completion.
Fools do not realize these people are not worth serving;
how can it be that none ever wake up to the truth?
This is truly lamentable!
It is as if one searches the ridges of a single zhang for
a tree that reaches the heavens;
or sifts in ox-hoof prints
for scales of a fish that swallows boats;
even with prolonged effort,
how can success be expected?
Alas!
For learners to come,
even though it is right to make seeking teachers one’s duty,
it is also urgent not to neglect careful selection.
If a person is narrow and crude,
their conduct shallow and virtue thin,
their merit minor and their connections few,
It is insufficient to fulfill the Way of becoming a true person,
nor is it any achievement to requite the weighty kindnesses of others.
Deeply contemplate its meaning,
and do not let yourself labor in vain.”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“As for those so-called Daoists with empty reputations,
they are skilled at deception
and use it to mislead students;
moreover, they often conceal their shortcomings and hide their ignorance,
ashamed of what they do not know.
Outwardly, they feign that their breadth of knowledge is sufficient,
never willing to seek out and humbly inquire of those better than themselves;
foolishly they cling to stagnation,
standing as if facing a wall.
Nor is their silence all;
they even come to envy and slander those who truly possess the Way,
fearing their fame will surpass their own.
How could such people possibly care about the methods of attaining long life?
Their purpose is only to gather disciples,
seek their wealth and strength,
and satisfy their own desires—nothing more.
Yet they do not understand that the heavens are lofty and hear even the lowly,
and in the end, they will surely suffer disaster because of this.
A poor man cannot recklessly claim that he is rich,
nor can a base man falsely assert that he is noble;
how much less should one, who truly lacks Dao and virtue,
raise up disciples in vain?
Even common people
should not harbor jealous thoughts toward the virtuous,
how much more so for Daoists,
who ought to take loyalty and trustworthiness as the very joy of their lives.
How then can they make a chest full of this foul envy?
Men themselves cannot perceive the spirits and gods,
yet it is easy for spirits and gods to perceive men.
How is this different from someone standing outside a silk curtain,
unable to see inside the chambers
yet displaying arrogance,
thinking others do not see him?
This is like one who tries to steal a bell by striking it,
causing it to ring out,
fearing others will hear,
so he covers his own ears—such is their kind.
As for those spiritually deaf and blind,
they desire only to monopolize fame,
to gather followers to themselves,
to seek external reputation,
and to scheme for internal profit.
They are anxious lest anyone surpass them,
and are even more contentious than commoners striving for power.
They make their lips and tongue into the edge of a blade,
take praise and blame as parties and factions,
are verbally affectionate yet inwardly estranged,
outwardly united but inwardly divided,
publicly expressing camaraderie,
while secretly harboring the poison of bees and scorpions.
Such conduct is abhorred by both heaven and man,
a summons for disaster.
When reading the Five Classics,
one still ought not be ashamed to ask those beneath oneself,
in order to advance in virtue and cultivate one’s endeavors,
so that there is daily progress and illumination.
When it comes to the crude arts of archery and charioteering,
the shallow skills of calculation and writing,
the overt practices of farming and silk-raising,
and the minor crafts of rules and measures,
even these require a teacher’s instruction to be fully mastered;
how much more so for cultivating the methods of long life,
desiring to extend one’s years to benefit the world,
which is no different from saving those about to die.
How could one be reluctant to seek instruction,
and thus endure forever the misery of ignorance,
growing old without change,
facing death without regret?
Such are the most deeply benighted among the people under heaven.
They inspire shame and dread in others on their behalf,
yet the ones who act thus never reflect even on their own forms and shadows.
For Confucian scholars, it is still considered proper to steadfastly guard their simplicity,
to outwardly maintain honesty and integrity,
to know while seeming not to know,
to possess while seeming not to possess,
so that mediocre children cannot judge them completely;
even if judged, they neither question nor respond;
if they must respond, they do so with humility before speaking.
How much the more, then, should those calling themselves Daoists
not stubbornly pretend to know what they do not know,
or to have what they do not have,
vainly flaunting themselves
in pursuit of wicked profit?
Those who are lost and do not know to turn back
become ever more deluded;
if there are any who can practice the Way,
one would hope they are not ashamed to amend themselves.
I do not say these words recklessly;
truly, there is a reason for them to arise.
I am tormented by what I see and cannot keep silent.
I only feel pity for the foolish,
unable to bear seeing babes thrown into wells.
If anyone reads this and awakens,
that is like one plant out of the myriad ingredients of the elixir of immortality;
what more could I seek!
If they do not accept these bitter words of advice,
their peril is truly imminent,
and this can be known without feeling their pulse.”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“Suppose someone faced a death sentence,
and there were a person able to save him,
he would certainly not begrudge hardship or fear to be humble in his words,
for by doing so, he would surely attain the benefit of continued life.
Now, as for this motley crowd of so-called Daoists,
if they do not obtain the Great Law of the Golden Elixir,
then surely it is evident that they cannot attain long life.
Though they may cure illnesses with effects even of reviving the dead,
abstain from grain and not be hungry for years,
command ghosts and spirits,
sit and perish or stand and die at will,
see a thousand li in the distance,
know others’ ups and downs,
discover hidden disasters in the shadows,
and discern fortune and misfortune before it arises,
still none of this is beneficial for longevity.
Yet they are ashamed to seek out instruction,
embarrassed to serve those who preceded them,
regretting a moment’s humility,
yet content to suffer endless pain;
such is one who fails to see the reality of affairs.
The ancients had a saying:
‘Life, as it pertains to me,
is of great benefit indeed.’
As for discussing the value of this,
even if ennobled as emperor or king,
it is not enough to compare to this method.
As for its weightiness,
even if one possessed the whole world in wealth,
it is not worth exchanging for this technique.
Thus there is the parable of the dead king preferring to be a living mouse.
To govern a state well and have peace,
to govern oneself and attain life—
these do not come of themselves;
they are all brought about by a means.
Yet people cherish empty fame despite their shallowness and lack,
are ashamed of the fleeting trouble of being instructed by a teacher,
and even if they are not outwardly foolish,
I cannot believe they are truly wise.
Now, if someone were to be saved from certain death and delivered from punishment,
he would surely rejoice to be relieved of the heavy and accept the light,
to escape roasting and preserve his breath,
and would gladly endure pain,
even if it surpassed being given a new life.
People only do not feel temporary distress
because they do not know the day they will die.
If they truly knew it,
and if undergoing amputation or mutilation
could delay it,
they would surely do so.
How much more, then, to simply attend to sweeping and cleaning oneself,
to bear a towel and exhaust one’s strength in serving a superior,
in order to be taught the Way to avoid death—
how could such things be suffering,
yet the deluded fear it?
Suppose there were a person
too proud to run and waits for a wildfire to consume him,
ashamed to flee the wind and so drowns in deep waters—
surely the world would call him oblivious to reality,
and all would laugh at how he does not avoid disaster,
yet none would wonder why he does not fear real calamity.
Why is this so?”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“In former times, there were many writings on Dao,
none of which failed to seek out flowery and clever expressions,
to elevate the principles of mystery and emptiness,
but none thoroughly explored the steps and paths to long life
or prescribed remedies for the pains and maladies of the Dao,
with the diligence I have shown.
I truly wish to make the deluded know to turn back,
that a loss in the east can be recovered in the west,
that one who falls in a well can be pulled out with a rope,
better than letting him drown.
But those who cherish a beautiful disease and shun the harsh stone
can only be left to their fate.
Who among men is without fault?
To have faults and be able to change—
such is like the sun and moon in eclipse
and is the hope of the worthy sons of the Yán clan.
Again, I wish that those who in future value the Way of life
will be discerning in those they depend upon,
and so I pour out my loyal counsel and excellent strategies,
without ornamenting my words with lascivious eloquence.
When I speak, my meaning is pointed;
when I write, my words are severe;
my care is only for long life and for suppressing the crooked—
what more could I ask?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Those who deeply think about learning the arts of the Dao to nourish life,
if they follow masters but do not find the right person,
in the end achieve nothing,
causing later aspirants
to see their failure to attain long life,
and thus say that there truly are no immortal methods in the world.
Generally, those who consider their own lives,
and certainly cannot bear hardship and restrain themselves to cultivate the profound mysteries,
will vainly advance, failing in their pursuit of official rewards,
and retreat without attaining the achievements that avert aging,
inwardly harming themselves,
and outwardly discouraging those who come after.
As for the possibility of learning and attaining immortality,
it is like the possibility of sowing millet and rice and obtaining a harvest,
perfectly clear indeed.
Yet there has never been a case of reaping good grain without tilling,
nor has anyone gained long life and transcended the world without diligence.”
Someone said:
“May I dare ask, can those who abstain from grain attain long life?
In general, how many methods are there,
and which is the best?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“Those who abstain from grain can merely save on the expense of food and provisions;
they alone cannot achieve long life.
When I questioned those who have abstained from grain for a long time, they said,
they were rather less afflicted by ailments
compared to when they ate grain.
If one practices certain arts or takes huángjīng as a medicinal food,
as well as Yǔ Yúlíang Pills,
taking them twice daily,
after three days,
one gains much vitality and strength,
enabling one to bear loads and travel far,
the body feels light and unexhausted.
As for those who take various mineral medicines,
some take a dose that maintains their center for ten or five years, as well as those who swallow breath, ingest talismans, or drink spirit water:
these only serve to stave off hunger,
but their bodies are not capable of labor.
Although the Daoist texts say that if one wishes to achieve long life,
the intestines must be made clean;
to attain immortality,
the bowels must be without dregs.
They also say,
those who eat grass are good runners but unintelligent,
those who eat meat are strong but fierce,
those who eat grain are wise but short-lived,
those who eat qi become spiritual and undying.
This is merely a one-sided theory of the practitioners of cultivating qi,
and cannot be adopted in isolation.
If one wishes to take the Grand Elixir of gold and great medicines,
it is best to first stop eating for a hundred days or so.
If one is unable,
then simply go ahead and take it,
one’s attainment of immortality will only be a little delayed,
with no great harm.
If you encounter a time of famine,
or must hide away in the mountains and forests,
those who understand these methods
may avoid starving to death.
If not,
then there is no urgent need to abstain;
even if forced, it will bring no great benefit.
Also, even among people who have ceased eating meat,
upon smelling the scent of fat and fresh foods,
none can avoid desiring it in their hearts.
If one is not prepared to wholly forsake the world and give up one’s family,
and dwell in cliffs and caves,
one will not in fact be able to completely forgo the five flavors,
and there is no need to bring hardship upon oneself;
it is better not to abstain from grain, but to moderate hunger and fullness.
Recently, there have been about a hundred such methods;
some people take several dozen pills of medicines that maintain the center,
and immediately go forty or fifty days without hunger.
Training in pine and cypress, as well as shù,
may also maintain the center,
though not as effective as the great medicines,
and over a long period will not last more than ten years or so.
Some avoid hunger for one hundred, even two hundred days;
some have to take it every day
in order not to grow hungry.
Some first eat delicacies in abundance to satiety,
then take medicine to preserve what was eaten,
ensuring it does not digest,
thus avoiding hunger for three years.
If one wishes to resume eating grain,
one should take a decoction of kuízǐ and pork fat to expel it from below,
thus all the delicacies eaten previously will be eliminated,
without harm, as before.
In Luòyáng, there was a Daoist Dǒng Wēiliǎn,
who always dwelled in the Bái Shè;
he did not eat at all.
Chén Zǐxù attended and served him,
and through long years of learning the Way,
he obtained this method:
he said to grind about ten kinds of herbs such as gāncǎo, fángfēng, xiànshí into powder,
first take a spoonful the size of a square inch,
then swallow twelve pebbles the size of sparrow eggs,
which suffices to stave off hunger for one hundred days.
Afterwards, take more of the scatter;
his strength and complexion remained as before.
Wishing to return to eating grain,
one should take a decoction of kuízǐ to purge the pebbles,
and then food may be eaten.
There is also the Red Dragon Blood and Green Dragon Paste,
using cinnabar and cupric water,
placing stones within them,
wait a short while,
until the stones soften and can be eaten.
If not taken out promptly,
they will dissolve and disintegrate.
Eating these stones brings a sense of fullness,
making one robust and vigorous.
There is also the Attract-Stone Powder,
whereby a measure the size of a square inch is thrown among a dǒu of white pebbles,
mixed with water and boiled,
and they become soft at once, like taro roots.
These may be eaten as a substitute for grain.
Zhāng Tàiyuán, with his whole family and several dozens of disciples,
living in seclusion at Línlǜ Mountain,
has lived over ten years eating these stones by this method;
all are fat and healthy.
The catch is, white stones must be procured,
and this is not as convenient as the Red Dragon Blood and Green Dragon Paste,
since suitable stones can be used directly,
though boiling is still required,
so there is the trouble of firewood.
Some use talismans,
some use water,
some combine talisman water.
Some use dried jujubes,
nine per day,
with one or two shēng of wine.
Some eat according to the twelve seasonal qi,
starting from midnight,
proceeding from 9x9 down to 8x8, 7x7, 6x6, 5x5 and stop there.
Or, in spring, facing east, they eat the blue qi of Jupiter
to let it enter the liver;
in summer, they ingest the red qi of Mars
to let it enter the heart;
in the four-season months, they take the yellow qi of Saturn
to let it enter the spleen;
in autumn, they eat the white qi of Venus
to let it enter the lungs;
in winter, they take the black qi of Mercury
to let it enter the kidneys.
Also, the Zhongyue Daoist Chī Yuánjié eats the essence of the Six Wù,
and this is also highly effective.
Suppose, in the ten-day cycle starting with jiǎzǐ,
there is a wùchén day;
through the ten days of the cycle,
always face the direction of chén and swallow qi,
upon the next jiǎ, again face that cycle’s wù.
The Gānshǐ method
summons the Yùnǚ of the Six Jiǎ and Six Dīng,
each with their own names;
invoke them over water and drink it,
and this can make oxen and horses likewise not feel hungry.
Or, contemplate the spirit-name in the spleen,
named Huáng Shāngzǐ,
simply close the mouth, keep breath inside, and absorb qi.
All these methods have true effects.
Elsewhere, I have often met people who have abstained from grain for three years, two years or so;
their bodies are light, their complexions good,
able to withstand wind, cold, heat, and dampness,
but, by and large, none are fat.
Although I have never seen anyone go without eating for several decades,
yet people who stop eating grain for barely ten days will die,
while these people persist for years as if nothing had changed—
so why doubt that long abstention is possible?
But if all those who abstain from grain became emaciated,
I have often worried
it might not be sustainable for long.
Yet, asking those practicing it,
all say that initially there is little strength,
but afterwards gradually become robust,
improving month by month,
year on year,
indeed,
it can be sustained without worry.
Those who attain the Way and long life,
none have achieved it without taking medicines or breathing qi;
those who succeed do not act recklessly.
Those who take medicines and abstain from grain,
none fail to try the utmost at first.
But those using only talisman water or merely breathing qi,
all become thin and weak in forty days,
but after this, regain their strength.
Zhèng Jūn said:
by nature, I have never drunk much alcohol;
in olden times, while at Tóng Mountain,
I abstained from grain for about two years
and could drink several dǒu of wine without getting drunk.
By this reasoning,
not eating makes a person more tolerant to poisons,
and such tolerance is an omen for resistance to severe illnesses.
Because of this, I asked: ‘How does one obtain wine on the mountain?’
Zhèng Jūn said,
first brew a good cloud liquor, do not press or strain it;
then mix it with powdered guì, fùzǐ, gāncǎo, five or six kinds, to make pills,
dry them in the sun;
with each pill about the size of a chicken egg,
throw it into a dǒu of water,
and it immediately becomes fine wine.
There is also Huángdì’s Cloud Liquor Spring method:
combine sprouted rice and seven or eight kinds of medicines,
take a shēng,
drop a shēng of water into it,
as one does for thousand-year bitter wine.
It never runs out,
and the flavor remains good and unchanged;
drinking it greatly benefits a person.
Also, for talisman water to abstain from grain,
though it first causes emaciation,
one should still be aware:
should one suddenly encounter a year of famine,
and lacks time to concoct medicines,
then talisman water is best.”
There was a man named Féng Shēng,
who merely practiced swallowing qì,
and had abstained from grains for three years.
Observing his steps as he climbed mountains,
carrying a burden of about one hú in weight,
he was never weary throughout the day.
He also often drew the bow,
and hardly ever spoke;
when he did speak, he was unwilling to raise his voice.
When questioned, he said,
"Abstaining from grains consumes essence and drains qì;
this is the greatest taboo."
I have also often seen shallow and superficial Daoist priests,
who, desiring to vainly display their marvelous and strange ways,
seek the reputation of not eating food,
yet actually do not understand the method;
they merely pretend not to consume soup or rice.
But when it comes to drinking wine,
they consume more than a dǒu a day;
with dried meats, preserved foods, dates, chestnuts, eggs, and such,
they never stop eating.
Some gorge themselves on meat, swallow its juices,
and expel the dregs;
throughout the day, dozens of catties pass through their mouths,
this is nothing but creating new delicacies for themselves.
Any wine drinker, if he but drinks wine and eats dried meats but not grains,
can endure for half a year or a year without collapse,
yet this cannot be called true grain abstention.
In Wú there was a Daoist named Shí Chūn,
who, whenever he regulated qì to treat illness for others,
would immediately stop eating,
and wait until the patient recovered;
sometimes a hundred days,
sometimes a month before he ate again.
When Wú Jǐng Dì heard of this, he said,
"This will not last long;
surely he will starve to death."
He thus summoned Shí Chūn and locked him up,
placing people to guard him thoroughly.
Shí Chūn only asked for two or three shēng of water,
and in this manner, for over a year,
his complexion became even more radiant and cheerful,
and his strength was as before.
Jǐng Dì questioned him,
"How much longer can you endure?"
Shí Chūn replied, "There is no limit;
I could endure for decades,
but I fear only dying of old age,
not hunger."
At this, he was dismissed and released.
Judging by Shí Chūn's words,
it is thus evident that abstaining from grains does not lengthen lifespan.
Even today, there are those who obtain Shí Chūn's method."
Someone asked about the method for not feeling cold.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Some, on the day of the Beginning of Winter,
wear talismans for Liù Bǐng and Liù Dīng,
or close the mouth and circulate the qì of Five Fires twelve hundred times;
then throughout the twelfth month, they do not feel cold.
Some drink Tàiyáng wine;
some take purple quartz and cinnabar lacquer powder;
some take one male pill,
then two female pills afterwards,
and so may endure a day and a night without cold.
The female pill uses orpiment, azurite, alum, and lodestone.
The male pill uses realgar, cinnabar, and copper sulfate.
However, these do not benefit the matter of prolonging life."
Someone asked about the method for not feeling heat.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Some, on the day of the Beginning of Summer,
wear talismans for Liù Rén and Liù Guǐ,
or circulate the qì of Liù Guǐ,
or take the pill of Black Ice,
or take the powder of Flying Frost.
But these use the bark of trees on Xiāo Qiū mountain,
and the blood of a black snake captured at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month while traveling north,
so very few can obtain all the ingredients.
Only Yòu Bózǐ and Wáng Zhòngdū,
these two people, wearing heavy furs,
would expose themselves to the summer sun,
surrounded by ten braziers of fire,
yet never claimed to feel hot,
nor did their bodies sweat,
no doubt from using this formula."
Someone asked about the method for warding off the Five Weapons.
Bào Pǔzǐ answered:
"I have heard that Wú Dà Huángdì once received the essential method from Jiè Xiānshēng, who said:
One only needs to write the characters for the Northern Dipper and the sun and moon,
and then one need not fear sharp blades.
The emperor tested several dozen men from his retinue in this way;
they always took the lead charging into battle formations,
and none were ever injured throughout their lives.
Zhèng Jūn said:
Even merely reciting the names of the Five Weapons is efficacious.
The saber is called Dàfáng,
governed by the Xū star;
the bow is called Qǔzhāng,
governed by the Dī star;
the arrow is called Fǎnghuáng,
governed by the Yínghuò star;
the sword is called Shīshāng,
governed by the Jiǎo star;
the crossbow is called Yuǎnwàng,
governed by the Zhāng star;
the halberd is called Dàjiàng,
governed by the Shēn star.
When going into battle,
one should always softly recite these names.
Some, on the fifth day of the fifth month, make the Red Spirit talisman
and place it over the heart.
Or at noon on a bǐngwǔ day,
make the Yànjūn Dragon-Tiger Three Sachets talisman.
The year talisman is renewed annually,
the monthly talisman monthly,
the daily talisman daily.
Some wear the talisman of the Western Queen Mother's military trust;
some wear the talisman of Yínghuò and the Vermilion Bird;
some wear the Nánjí gold-melting talisman;
some wear the Talisman Against Blades;
or the Zhùróng talisman.
Some apply jade slip powder;
some bathe with forbidden scallion decoction;
some take chaste tree and make the Talisman of the Six Yin Spirit Generals,
and point the talisman at the enemy.
Or, during a lunar eclipse,
take the blood under the throat of a three-year-old toad displaying eight characters,
and write on the edge of one's sword or saber.
Some carry the Martial Prowess talisman or Yínghuǒ pill.
Or at the moment when blades cross in battle,
tread on Kuí and step on Gāng,
and invoke the four regional lords;
these too have manifest efficacy.
Even now,
there are those who have obtained the method to prohibit and ward off the Five Weapons,
and such persons are not rare."
Someone asked about the art of invisibility.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"The shén-dào is fivefold,
with its numbers present while sitting and gone while standing.
Yet it has nothing to do with the extension of life;
for one to practice this among men without cause,
is only to invite suspicions of the strange;
it is not worth acting recklessly.
It may be used for defense in times of war and urgent peril,
and if compelled to use it,
it can avert calamity.
Zhèng Jūn said:
Taking the Great Concealment Talisman for ten days,
if you wish to vanish, turn to the left;
if you wish to appear, turn to the right.
Or apply the Jade Terrace Pill over the body;
or use Snake-Foot Powder;
or keep with you lí mǔ herb;
or break off the Qīnglóng herb
to hide beneath the Liù Dīng;
or enter the bamboo fields
and hold the soil of Heaven's Pivot;
or visit the Stone Chamber of the Hé Dragon
and conceal yourself under the shade of the cloud canopy;
or crouch by the clear and cool abyss
and pass through the path of the ghostly gate;
or ride the Heaven-One Horse to wander the Purple Chamber;
or scale the Bright Hall of Heaven-One;
or enter the Golden Casket of the Jade Maiden;
or turn your back to the assistant and face the magistrate,
standing beneath the Three Canopies;
or throw down scarf and remove shoes, with gall ointment and a child's clothing talisman;
Zi Jū Mēng,
with blue sap and cinnamon stalk,
Liù Jiǎ parents,
the adhesive from secluded corners,
Piebald Horse Clay Pill,
the wood demon's child,
the wormwood of Jinshāng;
thus one may become a child,
or may become an old man,
or may become a bird,
or may become a beast,
or may become grass,
or may become wood,
or may become one of the six domestic animals,
or become wood beside wood,
or become stone beside stone,
water beside water,
fire beside fire.
This is what is called changing form and altering appearance,
but it does not allow complete concealment."
Someone asked:
“Wèi Wǔdì once captured Zuǒ Yuánfàng and shackled him,
yet he was able to escape naturally.
By what method did he do so?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“I cannot know exactly what strategy Lord Zuǒ employed.
However, after examining various books on techniques,
some mention taking yìyǐ seeds three times a month,
combining them with three or five doses of yīn dān,
or using the paired fangs from a yáng bāo,
or leaping off with a脱虫 heading east on the seventh day of the seventh month,
or wearing a single garment made from a dragon child found on a stone on the fifth day of the fifth month,
or with a thunderbolt wedge on the summer solstice,
or with twenty-one talismanic characters of celestial patterns,
or by withdrawing oneself and discarding father’s blood,
or with the leftover grain of jade eggs,
or combining with the eyes of the mountain lord,
or the remnants of Hé Bó’s stored grain,
or smearing with the dregs of floating clouds,
all can enable escape on one’s own.
Yet Lord Zuǒ’s transformations have no fixed method,
and may not have been achieved by any of these.
Using the transmutations of liùjiǎ,
his true form could not be grasped.”
Another asked:
“Can those who practice the Way avoid illness?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Those who fully understand the principles of nurturing life,
not only take divine medicines,
but also diligently practice breath regulation,
guide and exercise every morning and evening,
to circulate and activate the nutritive and defensive energies,
so that there is no stagnation or obstruction,
in addition to arts of the bedchamber,
moderation in food and drink,
avoiding wind and damp,
not overexerting what one cannot do—
in this way, one may avoid illness.
The trouble, however, is that people living among others
cannot keep their resolve undivided,
practice without constancy,
and moreover suffer from sloth and lack of diligence,
thus inevitably illnesses arise.
They bitterly have only faith in the Dao,
but lack any practices that benefit themselves;
their lifespan is beneath emptiness and solitude,
their body is at risk of harm and injury,
so that the three corpses, taking advantage of declining months and dangerous days,
when entering the territory of deadly afflictions,
summon inharmonious qi,
recklessly draw in ghosts and spirits,
which cause disaster and harm.
When all six calamities converge,
when the three punishments align,
the disaster is necessarily great.
Even those still in their prime
will fall ill with various diseases;
those already ill with rashes
will have them triggered again.
Therefore, in ancient times, those who first pursued the Way
all studied medicine as well
in order to avert imminent disaster.
As for common Daoists,
who do not understand these principles,
relying only on what they have heard,
and that has little to do with methods of treating illness.
Also, they cannot sever themselves from the world and dwell in seclusion,
single-mindedly practicing inner disciplines,
so as to ward off illness.
When sickness and pain come,
they have no means of treating them,
and are then even less than ordinary people who rely solely on decoctions and medicines.
This is what is called advancing without acquiring the gait of Hándān,
while retreating they also lose the meaning of Shòulíng.
I have seen the Golden Coffer, Green Satchel, Cùi Zhongshu’s Yellow Silk Prescriptions, and various miscellaneous formulas collected by Dài Bàhuá and others, amounting to some five hundred scrolls.
Gān, Hú, Lǚ, Fù, Zhōu, Shǐ, Gān, Táng, Tōng, Ruǎn, Nánhé and so on,
each compiled formulas for sudden death and emergency aids—
some numbering a hundred and ten,
some ninety-four,
some eighty-five,
some forty-six.
People of the world all consider them thorough,
thinking nothing can be added.
I have studied and observed them,
and found them still greatly lacking;
many urgent maladies are not yet fully covered,
and they are jumbled and confused,
without logical arrangement;
if one searches for a case,
one cannot easily find it.
For treating sudden and violent conditions,
they all use expensive medicines;
often several tens of kinds.
Unless one is from a wealthy family living in the capital,
one cannot keep them in store,
nor prepare them in haste.
They also often have people use acupuncture,
but their cautery methods do not specify the precise locations and measurements,
and only mention the names of the body’s acupoints.
Unless one is an experienced doctor who has thoroughly examined the diagrams of the Mingtang with notes and illustrations,
how could one understand this?
The hundred scrolls I have compiled,
titled Jade Case Formulas,
are all sorted by disease name,
arranged by category in order,
not jumbled together;
the emergency treatments volume,
all use straightforward and simple methods,
concise and easily effective—
in the alleys and paths,
whatever one glances at can serve as medicine.
For all urgent diseases,
nothing is omitted or lacking;
if every household possesses this book,
there is no need to call a doctor.
Most doctors inherit a family profession,
have a name but not substance,
only keep up a shallow reputation
to seek profit.
For those impoverished and disengaged from office,
doctors are not obtainable;
if obtained, they often cause more mistakes,
so it is better to understand the essentials oneself
than to rely on ignorant doctors who are summoned.
Doctors cannot quickly be found,
and if found are not willing to serve promptly,
so that minor ailments of the flesh
become grave misfortunes in the vitals,
sometimes beyond rescue.
And when emergencies arise,
if one has to travel and inquire at a distance,
often one dies in vain.”
Someone asked:
“Regarding future fortune or calamity,
safety or danger, whether to go or stay—
if these can be known, can one preserve life?
Is there a Way for this?”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“Looking up to observe the celestial patterns,
looking down to examine the geography of the earth,
divining through the winds,
arranging counting rods for calculation,
pushing the three chess pieces,
stepping the nine palaces,
inspecting the eight trigrams,
investigating where the flying and hidden spirits gather,
diagnosing disputes and errors among types of things,
casting fortunes of fortune or misfortune with tortoise shell and milfoil,
all these are inferior techniques and common skills,
exhausting and unreliable.
If one can sit within curtains and yet see the world,
then this enters into the realm of the spirit.
Some use the celestial patterns of the Three Augusts,
summon Sīmìng, Sīwēi, the lords of the Five Sacred Mountains,
the spirits of Liùdīng who are guardians of crosspaths and village leaders,
making all of them visible to people,
and ask them questions about various matters,
so that fortune and misfortune are made clear,
as though holding them in one's palm,
regardless of distance or depth,
all can be known beforehand.
Some summon the six yin jade maidens,
with the method being fulfilled in sixty days;
once fulfilled, they can be commanded at will for a long time.
Some perform sacrifices to bring forth the Eight Scribes;
as for the Eight Scribes,
they are the essence of the Eight Trigrams,
and are likewise sufficient for foreknowing the yet-unformed.
Some take géhuā, autumn awn, hemp, bō, dāoguī, in a square-inch spoon,
and suddenly feel as if desiring to sleep,
and then hear someone speak about unresolved matters,
and the outcome of fortune and misfortune is immediately determined.
Some use a clear mirror over nine inches to reflect upon themselves,
keeping something in mind with focus;
after seven days or upon the Double Seventh Festival, one can see spirits or immortals,
whether male or female,
old or young;
at a single showing,
one’s mind naturally knows matters coming from a thousand li away,
events yet to come.
With the clear mirror sometimes one is used,
or sometimes two,
called the sun and moon mirror.
Or sometimes four,
called the four-directions-mirror.
The four directions,
when using them for viewing,
one is placed before, behind, left, and right.
Using the four directions shows many arriving spirits.
Some are glaring-eyed,
some ride dragons or drive tigers,
dressed in colorful robes and hats,
different from worldly people,
each following a patterned image.
If you wish to cultivate this method,
you must first silently recite the names, ranks, and titles of the gods outwardly summoned to appear,
and be familiar with their dress and appearance.
If not,
then when suddenly confronted with the spiritual presence, you will forget who they are,
or become startled and afraid;
if so, harm will befall you.
As for practicing these,
it is generally best to seek quiet and secluded forests and foothills,
so that external forms do not reach the eyes,
and external sounds do not enter the ears—
then the Dao will certainly be achieved.
If Sāntóng, Jiǔnǚ, Jiéshòu-jūn,
the nine-headed snake-bodied chancellor of one hundred and twenty offices,
appear, do not gaze upon them intently.
If anyone asks you,
or scolds you in anger,
do not answer.
If there are attendants or followers gleaming or resplendent,
strongmen or armored guards,
riding dragons and driving tigers,
with the music of flutes and drums,
do not lift your eyes or speak to them.
Only intently recall the true form of Lǎojūn;
when the true form of Lǎojūn appears,
then rise and bow twice.
As for the true form of Lǎojūn,
contemplate this:
his surname is Lǐ, his personal name is Dān,
style name Bóyáng,
his body nine feet tall,
yellow in color,
a bird’s beak,
high nose,
elegant brows five inches long,
ears seven inches long,
three lines run across his forehead from top to bottom,
his feet bear the mark of the Eight Trigrams,
he uses a spirit tortoise as his bed,
a golden tower and jade hall,
stairs of white silver,
robes made of five-colored clouds,
a tiered crown,
a sword of pointed blade,
attended by one hundred twenty yellow-haired children,
with twelve green dragons to his left,
twenty-six white tigers to his right,
twenty-four vermilion birds before him,
seventy-two black turtles behind,
twelve ferocious Qióngqí monsters clearing the road in front,
and thirty-six Bìxié following behind,
with thunder and lightning above,
glittering and dazzling—
all these are described in the scriptures of the immortals.
On seeing Lǎojūn, one’s lifespan is extended,
the heart is like the sun and moon,
and there is nothing that is unknown.”
Someone asked about the way to strengthen the teeth.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“If you can nourish them with huáchí,
steep them in sweet liquor,
and gently tap your teeth three hundred times at dawn,
they will never be loose.
Next best is to hold in the mouth decoctions of dìhuáng,
or xuándǎn broth,
and pills of snake fat, alum, or jiǔjí powder.
Then teeth already loose will become firm again,
and those with worms will be cured at once.
Also, taking língfēi powder
can make lost teeth grow back again.”
Someone asked about the way to sharpen hearing.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“If you can practice dragon-guiding and tiger-leading,
bear-circulation and tortoise-swallowing,
