swallow-flying, snake-bending, bird-stretching,
heaven looking down, earth looking up,
so that the red and yellow rays
never leave your secret chamber,
with gibbon posture and startled-rabbit stance,
reaching one thousand two hundred times,
then the hearing will not be diminished.
For those already deaf,
smoke the ears with black tortoise,
or stuff them with the heads of thorn bushes, sheep dung, cinnamon fuzz, and sparrow cinnamon;
or use wolfbane-cooked gě,
or aconite and green onion juice,
mixed and put into the inner ear,
or instill by steaming the brain of carp,
all will be cured.”
Someone asked about the way to brighten the eyes.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“If you can lead up the ascending essence of the Three Burners,
summon the great fire from southern Lí,
wash them with clear stone,
soothe them with the sunlight,
and burn bǐng-dīng open-sight talismans,
wash with wine mixed in,
then the ancients were able to write at night.
Alternatively, cook turnip seeds in vinegar until mature,
dry them in the sun,
powder them and take a square-inch spoonful,
three times a day,
and after finishing one dǒu,
you will be able to see things at night.
Or boil dog gall with green sheep, turtle-dove, shíjuémíng, chōngwèi, and bánhuā powder,
or simmer with jīshéxiāng, huánglián, and milk and apply it.
For all manner of hundreds of diseases of the eyes, there will be a cure,
and the vision will be even sharper than before.”
Someone asked about climbing steep heights, traversing dangerous places, and traveling unendingly far distances.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“Only by taking the Grand Elixir
will the body become light and the strength vigorous,
tireless despite toil.
If one has just entered the mountains and forests,
and the body is not yet fully strengthened,
one should wash the feet with yúnzhū powder, bǎihuá sweet brew, and xuánzǐ soup,
as well as take hǔdǎn pills, zhūmíng wine, tiānxióng hèzhī pills, fēilián autumn grass decoction, chēqián, and zéxiè powder.
Using these for ten days,
not only will one be able to walk far without limit,
one’s pace will quicken,
and it may be three times faster than normal.
If one is able to ride on qiào,
then one may travel throughout the world,
unrestricted by mountains and rivers.
There are three methods for riding on qiào:
the first is called dragon qiào,
the second tiger qiào,
the third lùlú qiào.
Some take talismans and practice concentrated visualization;
if one wishes to travel a thousand lǐ,
then visualize this for one period.
If one visualizes for twelve periods, day and night,
then one can travel twelve thousand lǐ in a single day and night.
One cannot exceed this;
to go further, one must visualize again
as per the previous method.
Or use jǒuxīn wood to make a flying cart,
and join rings of ox hide to swords to operate its mechanism;
or store the thought of forming five snakes, six dragons, and three oxen entangled in the Great Dipper, and ride it,
ascending forty lǐ upward—
this is called Tàiqīng.
Within Tàiqīng,
its qi is extremely gangdāo,
surpassing that of humans.
The master said that when a kite flies ever higher,
it simply stretches both wings
without flapping or shaking, and advances by itself
because it gradually rides the gangdāo qì.
When a dragon first ascends the steps, it is said:
if it travels upward forty lǐ,
then it will move on its own.
These words come from the xiānrén,
and have merely been passed down among commoners;
they are truly not known by ordinary people.
Moreover, to ride on qiào, one must observe long-term abstinence,
eliminate pungent vegetables,
cease from eating blood foods;
after a year,
one may then ride these three qiào.
Even if one again takes talismans,
visualizing the five-dragon qiào to travel the farthest,
the rest do not go beyond a thousand lǐ.
The ascent, descent, advance, and retreat
each have their methods;
do not act arbitrarily.
If one does not abide by its prohibitions,
then one must not rashly ride on qiào,
for there is misfortune of falling.”
Someone said:
“In Lǎozǐ’s chapters and in the Guīwénjīng,
it is recorded that after the war of medicines,
in the years of metal and wood,
there will certainly be a great epidemic,
with only one in ten thousand surviving.
Dare I ask the method of warding it off?”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“The immortal’s secret prohibitive method for entering pestilence
is to visualize one’s body as five jades.
The five jades
correspond to the colors of the four seasons:
in spring, blue;
in summer, red;
in the four interim months, yellow;
in autumn, white;
in winter, black.
Also visualize wearing a golden turban,
and visualize the heart like a blazing fire,
as large as a dipper,
and then there will be nothing to fear.
Another method:
visualize the hair spreading to cover the body,
with each tuft of hair
adorned by a great star.
Next, visualize forming the seven stars of the Northern Dipper,
with the kuí hanging over the head,
and the gang pointing forward.
Then visualize the qi of the five organs
emerging from both eyes,
encircling the body like clouds and mist:
the liver’s blue qi,
the lung’s white qi,
the spleen’s yellow qi,
the kidney’s black qi,
the heart’s red qi,
the five colors mingling together—
then one may share a bed with those afflicted by pestilence.
Or, walk with the stepping of Yǔ, invoking the Direct Sun Jade Maiden;
or, hold the breath and visualize a strong man
wielding a thousand-jīn golden hammer,
and a hundred twenty men defending oneself.

Or use shèguǐ pills, chìchē shǐzhě pills, guànjūn pills, xú chángqīng powder, yùhán refined powder, qīngnián dàoshì sanitizing pills, cuī wénhuáng powder, cǎoyù wine, huángtíng pills, huángfú talisman, Lǎozǐ’s collar talisman, chìxūzǐ peach blossom talisman—
all of these have excellent effects.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The “Divine Immortals Classic on the Yellow and White Arts” consists of twenty-five juan,
containing more than one thousand sections.
“Yellow”
means gold.
“White”
means silver.
The ancients treated these methods as secret and of great importance,
and did not wish to speak of them directly,
so they concealed them thus.
Some chapter titles are called “Gēng” and “Xīn”;
“Gēng” and “Xīn” also mean gold.
Yet for the most part the methods are profound and subtle, difficult to know,
and only a few can be clearly explained.
Many people in the world doubt these matters as fantastical,
just like those who do not believe in divine immortals.
In the past, I studied the “Nine Elixirs” and the “Classic of Gold and Silver Elixirs” from Zhèng Gōng,
and then again sought and received five juan of the “Yellow and White Middle Classic”.
Zhèng Jūn said,
he had once, together with Zuǒ Jūn, tested the method in the copper mountains at Lújiāng,
and were successful each time.
However, the diligence required for purification and ritual prohibitions
is no different from that for the divine elixirs of immortality.
Common people often mock me for pursuing heterodox teachings,
saying that I desire to forcibly communicate things in the world that cannot be united.
But why should I be like this!
If I wished, by means of these things,
to display my literary skills for posterity,
then my “Outer Chapters” and miscellaneous writings in more than two hundred juan
would be enough to express my intentions to later generations,
and I would not still need these.
Moreover, these “Inner Chapters”
are all direct speech alone,
without embellishment.
Also, I know that discussing these matters,
not one person in the world does not call them impractical and of no urgency,
and rather that discussing common, immediate principles
is what can harmonize the minds of the many.
Yet the reason I cannot cease with these matters,
even knowing they do not enter the ears of people,
and still discuss and write them,
is because I have truly seen their efficacy,
and my teachers from whom I inherited them were not men of false speech.
But I have suffered poverty and hardship, lacking resources,
and encountered times of great difficulty,
with relentless misfortune,
furthermore with roads blocked,
and medicines unobtainable,
so in the end I had no chance to practice them.
Now when I tell others
that I understand the making of gold and silver,
yet suffer hunger and cold myself,
how am I different from a man who cannot walk,
but sells medicines to cure lameness,
asking others to trust him?
Truly, it cannot be.
Yet just because the facts do not accord with wishes,
one should not entirely dismiss things in one sweep.
Therefore, the reason I diligently record these in writing
is to let future men who love the marvelous and value the genuine
see my writings and understand my intent in discussing the Way.
As for the arts of transformation,
what is there they cannot do?
The human body is naturally visible,
but there are methods to conceal it.
Spirits and deities are naturally hidden,
but there are methods to make them manifest.
There are often many who can practice them.
Water and fire are in Heaven,
yet one can obtain them from fire-drills.
The nature of lead is white,
yet it is turned red to make cinnabar.
The nature of cinnabar is red,
yet it is made white to become lead.
Clouds, rain, frost, and snow,
are all qi of Heaven and Earth,
and when made by medicines,
are no different from the genuine.
As for creatures who fly and run,
and those that crawl,
they receive forms by natural transformation,
and are already fixed as such.
But when, suddenly, they change their form,
and become different things,
there are a thousand types and myriad kinds,
beyond count or discussion.
Of all things among men,
the most precious is that human nature is most spiritual,
yet men and women can swap forms,
becoming a crane or stone,
a tiger or gibbon,
sand or turtle;
there are many such instances.
As for high mountains becoming depths,
deep valleys becoming hills,
this too is transformation of great things.
Transformation,
is simply the natural way of Heaven and Earth,
so why suspect that gold and silver cannot be made from different things?
If we compare, for example, the fire gained from the burning mirror,
or the water obtained from condensation,
with ordinary fire and water,
how are they different?
A snake becoming a dragon,
chaff turning into grease,
also does not differ from those naturally born.
However, regarding the sources and causes of these,
all come from spontaneous responses of nature;
if one does not exhaustively investigate principles and fully realize one’s nature,
one cannot know their destination;
without knowing the origin and seeing the end,
one cannot grasp their real circumstances.
A narrow, shortsighted view,
bound up in one’s own nest,
measures profound subtlety as unknowable,
assumes divine transformation to be fiction,
and since Zhōu and Kǒng did not discuss it,
nor are they recorded in the classics,
simply declares all of it to be untrue—
is this not narrow-minded?
Further, common folk, because Liú Xiàng could not make gold,
immediately claim that the Way does not exist in the world,
which is like seeing a farmer suffer crop failure due to flood or drought,
and then saying that grains cannot be grown at all.
Wú Dàwén, Prefect of the Capital at Chéngdū,
was broadminded and learned,
and once recounted that in former times he served the Daoist Lǐ Gēn.
He saw Lǐ Gēn refine lead and tin,
throw in a little medicine the size of a large bean into the cauldron,
stir it with an iron spoon,
and as it cooled, it turned into silver.
Dàwén obtained the secret formula,
but when he wanted to make it himself,
even after one hundred days’ purification and fasting,
being tied up with official duties,
he was never able to do it,
and often sighed that there is no leisure in human affairs.
Also, Huán Jūnshān said that Chéng Wěi, an Imperial Secretary of the Hàn,
loved the Yellow-White arts,
and married the daughter of a family expert in the arts.
Wěi, frequenting court duties without proper seasonal clothes,
was greatly troubled.
His wife said,
“Let me obtain two lengths of silk.”
At once, the silk appeared before them out of nowhere.
Wěi, referencing the Hongbaǒ in his pillow,
tried to make gold but was unsuccessful.
His wife then went to see him,
as Wěi fanned coals to heat a bamboo tube,
which contained mercury.
His wife said,
“Let me try showing you something.”
She then took medicine from her pouch,
and put in a little,
and after a short while,
it turned into silver.
Wěi was greatly astonished, saying:
“The Way was close to you,
yet you did not tell me sooner,
why is that?”
His wife said,
“One must have the destined person to receive it.”
So Wěi pleaded daily, persuading her,
selling houses and estates to provide fine food and clothing,
yet still she would not tell him.
Wěi then plotted with others to tie her up and beat her.
His wife sensed it at once,
and said to Wěi:
“The Way must be transmitted to the right person;
when I meet such a person,
even on the road, I will teach him;
if it’s not the right person,
if one’s words and intentions do not agree,
even if I were chopped to pieces,
the Way would still not come out.”
Wěi kept pressing,
so his wife went mad,
ran about naked,
smeared herself with mud,
and died in the end.
Recently, Huà Lìngsī, former Prefect of Lújiāng,
a man of great talent and learning,
and widely informed,
yet did not believe in things that are not canonical.
Later, a Daoist spoke to him of the Yellow-White arts,
so he had him tested.
He was told to melt lead in an iron vessel,
throw in a powdered medicine,
and instantly it turned into silver.
Then, by melting the silver again,
and adding another medicine,
it then became gold.
He also learned from this Daoist the art of “penetrative vision,”
and before a hundred days had passed in practice,
when sleeping at night, he could see the constellations in the sky and all his neighbors clearly,
as if there were no walls or fences between houses.
Furthermore, a concubine named Yáo Huá had already died,
but appeared in visible form,
conversing with him just as when she was alive.
Moreover, if one does not obtain the oral instructions of an enlightened master,
it is truly inadvisable to undertake this lightly."
The medicines of the medical tradition
are exceedingly superficial and obvious,
yet their commonly effective formulas
are often still kept secret.
Thus, formulas include things such as palace maids from the inner chambers,
glues from obscure or eccentric origins,
Fēngjūn níwán,
Mùguǐ zǐ,
Jīnshāng zhī,
Fēijūn gēn,
Fúlóng gān,
Báimǎ hàn,
Fúyún zǐ,
Lóngzǐ dānyī,
Yèguāng gǔ,
Bǎihuā lǐ,
Dōng Zōu zhāi and their ilk—
these are all things close at hand,
but without the oral instructions,
one still cannot understand them.
How much more so, then, with the arts of transmuting yellow and white!
Now, those capable of accomplishing this
do not keep it secret merely because it is valuable,
but because, once this Way is achieved,
it enables long life.
The Way of long life
is the ultimate attainment of the Way;
thus, the ancients valued it greatly.
Of all the medicinal substances named in formula books,
sometimes there are those that share a name with common medicines but are not actually those things.
For example, Héshàng Chànnǚ
is not a woman;
Língyáng Zǐmíng
is not a man;
Yǔyúliáng
is not rice;
Yáo jiāng
is not water.
As for common people, when they see formulas using dragon gall and tiger palm, chicken head and duck foot, horse hoof and dog blood, mouse tail and ox knee,
they all assume these are substances pertaining to blood and qi;
when they see things like quēpén and fùpén, fǔjīn lì dàjǐ, guǐjiàn and tiāngōu,
they call them implements of iron or tile;
when they see things like Húwáng shǐzhě, Yǐgū xīnfù, Yě zhàngrén, Shǒutián gōng, Dài Wén yù, Xú Chángqīng,
they think these are people’s names.
As for grasses that are nearby and easy to find,
some still do not know them.
As for formulas that are profoundly mysterious,
who could fully interpret them?
Liú Xiàng tried to create gold but failed;
this is no cause for surprise.
Once one obtains the essential oral instructions,
then it is no longer necessary to rely on the great talents of sages and worthies;
anyone may accomplish it.
Was Liú Xiàng a fool?
He simply failed to obtain the oral transmission.
Now I will record its essentials and those who have succeeded with it,
to present it to future fellow practitioners.
First, obtain Wǔdū xiónghuáng,
which is red in color, like a rooster’s comb,
shining and free of impure stone,
any amount as you wish,
but do not let it be less than five catties.
Pound it into powder,
mix it with ox gall,
and boil it till dry.
Take a red clay kettle holding one dǒu,
first put on the bottom powdered Róngyán and shídǎn,
to a thickness of three fen;
then place the powdered xiónghuáng inside,
to a thickness of five fen,
and add more Róngyán above.
In this way,
repeat until all is used up.
Then, add crushed charcoal the size of date pits
to a thickness of two cun.
Use earth from earthworms and Róngyán to make mud,
smear it on the outside of the kettle,
cover with another kettle,
seal all around with a layer of mud three cun thick,
so that no vapors escape.
Let it dry in the shade for one month,
then heat it with horse dung fire,
for three days and three nights;
let it cool,
open it,
tap out the bronze at the bottom,
which will flow out like molten copper or iron from a smelter.
Then cast this bronze to make a tube,
and when the tube is formed, use it to hold cinnabar water.
Again, heat it with horse dung fire,
after thirty days, open the furnace,
and tap out the gold,
which is then also used to make a tube,
again to contain cinnabar water.
Once more, use horse dung fire to heat for thirty days,
open and take out, pound and process it.
Take two parts of cinnabar,
one part of mercury,
mercury
is quicksilver,
it will instantly solidify into gold.
It will be bright and lustrous in color,
able to be hammered with a nail.
Method for making cinnabar water:
prepare one catty of cinnabar,
place it inside a fresh bamboo tube,
add two liǎng each of shídǎn and xiāoshí,
cover above and below,
seal the mouth of the tube,
by plugging with lacquered bone pellet,
wait for it to dry,
then place it in pure bitter wine,
bury it in the ground,
to a depth of three chi,
after thirty days it becomes water,
red in color and bitter in taste.
The method for making gold received by Jīnlóu xiānshēng from Qīnglín zǐ:
First, forge tin,
so that it is six cun square,
and one cun two fen thick;
mix red salt with ash lye,
make it into a mud,
and coat it on top of the tin,
making sure it is uniformly one fen thick,
then stack it in a red clay kettle.
For every ten catties of tin,
use four catties of red salt,
seal all the edges tightly,
heat with horse dung fire,
for thirty days,
then open the fire and inspect,
all the tin inside will appear as ash,
and within it there will be clusters like beans,
which are gold.
Gather them together in an earthenware bowl,
blast with charcoal,
refine ten times and it will all become gold.
For every ten catties of tin,
you will obtain twenty liǎng of gold.
Only clay kettles from Chángshā, Guìyáng, Yùzhāng, and Nánhǎi can be used.
The people of those regions
use earthen kettles for cooking food,
so they are readily available.
Method for preparing red salt:
use one catty of cold salt,
then prepare one catty of hánshuǐshí,
then one catty of hán yǔniè,
then one catty of báifán,
combine them in an iron vessel,
burn with charcoal,
until all are dissolved and turn red,
then remove, ready for use.
Jiǎolǐ xiānshēng, taught by Jìqiū zǐ, method for transmuting gold:
First, take two parts of fánshuǐshí,
place in an iron vessel,
add charcoal fire to boil,
then add mercury as needed,
stir so that they combine,
boil six to seven times,
pour onto the ground to produce silver.
Then, take cinnabar water and zēngqīng water, one part each,
two parts xiónghuáng water,
add to a copper pan and apply light fire to boil,
stir several times,
so they combine,
then heat again with charcoal to boil,
insert this silver within,
as much or little as you wish,
boil six to seven times,
pour onto the ground to solidify,
then this will become highest grade purple-refined gold.
Method for preparing xiónghuáng water:
take one catty of xiónghuáng, place in fresh bamboo tube,
add two liǎng of xiāoshí,
cover above and below,
seal with lacquered bone pellet,
place in pure aged vinegar,
bury three chi deep,
in twenty days it will transform into water.
Method for preparing zēngqīng water,
the same as for fánshíshuǐ,
but each is placed in a separate tube.
Method for making gold for children.
Make a large iron tube,
its interior one chǐ two cùn,
height one chǐ two cùn.
Make a small iron tube,
its interior six cùn,
polish and smoothen it.
One jīn of chìshízhī,
one jīn of xiāoshí,
one jīn of yúnmǔ,
one jīn of dàizhě,
half a jīn of liúhuáng,
four liǎng of kōngqīng,
one jīn of níngshuǐshí,
combine all finely pounded and sifted,
mix with xī,
plaster it inside the small tube,
to a thickness of two fēn.
One jīn of mercury,
half a jīn of cinnabar,
half a jīn of liángfēi.
Take liángfēi, use ten jīn of lead in an iron cauldron,
place on the furnace, exposed to heating,
melt the lead,
add three liǎng of mercury,
that which first comes out is taken with an iron spoon,
this is called liángfēi.
Stir so they are fully combined,
when the mercury is no longer visible, this is the sign,
place inside the small tube,
cover with yúnmǔ,
seal with an iron lid.
Take the large tube and place on the furnace,
melt lead and pour into the large tube,
immersing the small tube inside,
leaving half a cùn at the top,
wait for the melted lead as a signal,
intensely fire it,
after three days and nights it is completed,
this is called zǐfěn.
Take ten jīn of lead, melt it in an iron vessel,
over twenty days or so,
then transfer into a copper vessel,
when the lead is melted,
add seven fāng cùn spoonfuls of zǐfěn,
stir it,
it immediately becomes gold.
If you wish to make silver,
take mercury and place into an iron vessel,
add more than three cùn of zǐfěn,
fire until fully combined,
pour into water,
immediately becomes silver.
The Method of Wù Chéngzǐ:
Make an iron tube nine cùn long,
five cùn wide,
pound three jīn of xiónghuáng,
earthworm castings and ant-hill soil in equal parts,
make into a mixture to form a mud,
coat it to make a diameter of three cùn,
with an opening of four cùn,
add two hé of cinnabar water,
cover and place above a mǎtōng burner,
make it thoroughly dry,
place into a copper tube,
seal firmly with a copper cover,
heap yellow sand on top,
cover with moist earthworm soil,
so the top is fully sealed,
place in a furnace with charcoal,
with three cùn of charcoal,
when the tube’s mouth turns red,
let cool before taking out,
all the xiónghuáng will have entered the copper tube,
take out and operate as previously.
The essence of three jīn of xiónghuáng,
all placed into the tube below,
draw off and mix with yellow sand in equal amount,
combine to make a furnace,
the furnace may be of any size.
When you wish to use it,
place the furnace on burning charcoal,
when the furnace is red hot,
add mercury,
when the mercury moves, put in lead,
yellow arises from the side meeting at the center,
pour it on the ground,
it immediately becomes gold.
Whenever you make fifteen hundred jīn,
the furnace’s potential is spent.
Take this gold and soak it in mǔjīng and chìshǔ wine,
for one hundred days,
then it becomes soft and blendable.
It is like small beans,
take one pellet as a dose,
three doses daily,
when one jīn is finished,
the three sìwǔ worms are subdued,
a hundred illnesses entirely leave,
the blind see,
the deaf hear,
the aged return to the vigor of thirty,
enter fire without being burned,
hundreds of malevolent spirits and poisons, cold wind, summer heat, and dampness cannot invade;
when three jīn are finished,
you may walk upon water,
the spirits of mountains and streams,
all come to serve as guardians,
and your life will end together with Heaven and Earth.
Boil one pellet with zhù blood and zhū cǎo,
rub it on the corners of the eyes,
you will see ghosts and things within the earth,
and can write at night;
coat one pellet with white sheep blood,
throw it into water,
fish and dragons immediately rise up,
and can be caught;
coat one pellet with blue sheep blood and cinnamon chicken blood,
hang it above the city gate,
for one lǐ there will be no epidemic;
if you coat the foreheads of cattle, sheep, and all livestock,
none will suffer from disease,
and tigers or leopards will not attack;
coat one pellet with tiger gall and snake fat,
on a jiàn month day, throw it into an enemy army,
and at once the army will fall into confusion without cause,
wounding and killing each other and fleeing;
coat one pellet with ox blood and throw it into a well,
the well water will immediately boil,
if thrown into flowing water,
the water will flow backward for a hundred paces;
coat one pellet with white dog blood,
throw it into a shrine or temple,
the spirits and gods will appear,
and can be employed;
coat one pellet with rabbit blood,
place in a yīn land (of Six Yins),
the xíngchú yùnǚ will appear at once,
able to serve sixty or seventy people;
coat one pellet with carp fish gall,
carry it into water,
the water will open one zhàng for you,
allowing you to breathe underwater and move,
when covered by rain, the garment will not become wet;
boil one pellet with purple amaranth,
hold and swallow its juice,
you can go a hundred days without hunger;
boil one pellet with císhí,
place it in your hair knot,
when fighting enemies,
swords and arrows will not strike you,
those who shoot at you,
their arrows will turn away by themselves;
combine one pellet with the "six ding" and "six ren" earth,
hold it to conceal a person and render them invisible,
hold one pellet,
face north and blow fire,
the fire is extinguished;
on a gēngxīn day at the time of shēn or yǒu,
facing west, throw one pellet at a tree,
the tree will wither the same day;
again with one pellet,
make a yǔbù and throw it at tigers, wolves, snakes, or vipers,
they all die at once;
grind one pellet to write on stone, it enters the stone,
write on gold, it enters gold,
write on wood, it enters wood,
all inscriptions penetrate the fiber,
filing and scraping cannot remove them.
If someone dies suddenly but the night has not passed,
take one pellet and place it in water under a jiàn month day,
let it enter their throat,
hold water in their mouth and spray onto the dead person’s face,
they will immediately revive.
Coat one pellet with fox blood and crane blood,
place it inside the fingernail,
point at anything,
it changes as you speak,
mountains walk, wood moves,
all witness it,
but in truth nothing actually moves.
Whenever yellow or white [metals] are made,
erect an altar to Tàiyǐ, Xuánnǚ, and Lǎozǐ and perform offering rites,
as with the method for the nine cinnabars,
always burn five kinds of incense,
the aroma must not be interrupted.
Again, once gold is made,
first throw three jīn into deep water,
one jīn into the marketplace,
after that you may then use the rest as you wish.
Someone asked about the Dao of mountain ascension.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“All those who practice the Dao and compound elixirs,
or who seek to avoid chaos and live in seclusion,
without exception enter the mountains.
Yet, not knowing the correct method for entering the mountains,
many encounter disasters and harm.
Therefore, there is a saying,
‘Beneath Tài Huà,
white bones lie scattered.’
This refers to knowing only part of the matter,
and being unable to prepare comprehensively;
even with the desire to live,
they instead hasten their own deaths.
Mountains, regardless of size,
all possess spirits and divinities;
if the mountain is great, the spirit is great,
if the mountain is small, the spirit is small.
If one enters the mountains without skill,
there will inevitably be calamities.
One may suffer sickness or injury from thorns,
or be frightened and unsettled;
one might see strange lights and shadows,
or hear unusual sounds;
it may happen that great trees, without wind, collapse and break on their own,
or cliffs and rocks fall for no reason,
striking and killing people;
or one may be bewildered, running madly,
falling into pits and valleys;
or face attacks from tigers, wolves, or poisonous insects;
so, one must not rashly enter the mountains.
One should enter in the third or ninth month,
for these are the months when the mountains “open”;
moreover, within these months, one should choose an auspicious and favorable day and time to enter.
If circumstances require more time and one must enter slowly, only in one of these months,
then simply select a suitable day and time.
Whenever a person enters the mountains,
he should at first observe abstinence and purification for seven days,
avoid filth and defilement,
wear the Ascending-the-Mountain Talisman when leaving home,
and make the three-and-five protection around his whole body.
Also, the Wǔ Yuè may at times be subject to misfortune during certain years,
just as the Nine Provinces each
have times of decline and fortune,
subject to flying calamity talismans and baleful energies,
at such times, the chief of that region should not take action.
According to the Zhou Duke’s Register of Cities,
the world’s domains are divided,
and where calamity strikes,
one may avoid it but not dispel it by ritual;
this is true also for dwellings,
as it is for mountain ranges.
Furthermore, it is an especially dire taboo, in the years of jiǎ, yǐ, yín, or mǎo,
and in the first or second month, to enter the Eastern Mountain;
in years of bǐng, dīng, sì, or wǔ,
and in the fourth or fifth month, to enter the Southern Mountain;
in years of gēng, xīn, shēn, or yǒu,
and in the seventh or eighth month, to enter the Western Mountain;
in years of wù or sì,
in any of the four seasonal months, to enter the Central Mountain;
in years of rén, guǐ, hài, or zǐ,
and in the tenth or eleventh month, to enter the Northern Mountain.
One must not enter Tài Huà, Huòshān, Héngshān, Tàishān, or Sōnggāo Shān
during these years;
in all regions of each of these peaks,
the same prohibitions apply.
Moreover, among all things, the aged of any kind
are able to temporarily assume human form,
in order to mislead human eyes and constantly test people;
but only in a mirror can they not alter their true form.
Thus, in ancient times, Daoist practitioners entering the mountains
all hung behind their backs a bright mirror, at least nine inches across;
carrying it suspended behind them,
and then old goblins dared not come near.
Should any come to test a person,
he should look in the mirror;
if it is an immortal or a benevolent spirit of the mountains,
the reflection in the mirror will look just like a human.
If it is a bird, beast, or malignant spirit,
its real form will definitely appear in the mirror.
Moreover, when such old goblins arrive,
they always leave walking backwards;
one may turn the mirror toward them as they go,
and observe from behind;
if it is an old goblin,
it will certainly lack heels;
if it has heels,
then it is a mountain spirit.
In the past, Zhāng Gài and Ōu Gāochéng,
both cultivated with pure intent in a stone chamber on Yúntái Shān in Shǔ,
when suddenly there appeared a man clad in a plain yellow robe and hempen headscarf,
who approached them and said,
‘You Daoists labor,
such hardship in secluded retreat!’
Then the two turned to look in the mirror,
and saw that it was a stag.
They asked,
‘You are an old stag of the mountain,
how dare you masquerade in human form?’
Before the words were finished,
the visitor immediately became a stag and ran away.
At the foot of Línlǜshān, there was a pavilion,
which housed a ghost;
all who stayed there overnight
either died or fell ill.
At night, there would always appear several dozen people,
their clothes were yellow, white, or black,
some male, some female.
Later, a man named Zhì Bóyí passed by and stayed there;
he lit a bright lamp and sat reciting scriptures;
after midnight, over ten people came,
and sat opposite Bóyí,
playing dice games among themselves.
Bóyí secretly used a mirror to look at them,
and saw that they were a pack of dogs.
Bóyí then took the lamp and rose,
pretending to accidentally drop a burning wick on their clothing,
which caused a smell like burnt fur.
Bóyí held a small knife,
seized one of them and stabbed it;
at first it cried out as a human,
but on dying became a dog,
and the other dogs all fled.
Since then, it ceased;
thus was the power of the mirror.
When a superior adept enters the mountains,
he carries the Three Sovereigns’ Inner Text and the True Forms Chart of the Wǔ Yuè;
everywhere he summons the mountain spirits,
and consults the Ghost Register,
calling forth local deities and mountain stewards to question them;
therefore, the monsters of wood and stone,
and the spirits of mountain and stream,
do not dare to come and test him.
Next in rank would be to establish the seventy-two perfected sealing talismans,
to subdue all malignant influences,
together with the Vermilion Official Seal, the Wrapped-Primal Twelve Seals,
to seal the four directions of the dwelling;
thus, all evils dare not come near.
Next in rank, one carries the Eight Powers Scepter,
wears Lǎozǐ’s Jade Talisman,
so that the mountain spirits become at one’s command,
how then could they dare to cause harm?
I have heard Zhèng Jūn speak thus,
but in truth, I am unable to know the matter completely.
My master often told his disciples:
‘Those who seek the Dao,
if their longing is like that of a man anxious for his poor household,
or worried for his lowly position,
how could they not obtain it?
The only trouble is the will is not firm,
pursuing what is near and forgetting the distant,
delighted when they hear of it,
eagerly moving forward,
but not long after,
they abruptly seem to forget it;
when small gains are not secured,
then great losses accumulate without rest,
how, then, can one hope to fathom the subtle marvels of ultimate words,
and achieve the supreme elevation of infinity?’”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The gravest taboos for entering mountains are:
the Horse day of the first month,
the Pig day of the second month,
the Monkey day of the third month,
the Dog day of the fourth month,
the Goat day of the fifth month,
the Rabbit day of the sixth month,
the Jiǎzǐ day of the seventh month,
the Shēn and Zǐ days of the eighth month,
the Tiger day of the ninth month,
the Dragon and Goat days of the tenth month,
the Jǐchǒu day of the eleventh month,
the Tiger day of the twelfth month.
Auspicious days for entering the mountains:
Jiǎzǐ, Jiǎyín, Yǐhài, Yǐsì, Yǐmǎo, Bǐngxū, Bǐngwǔ, Bǐngchén—
all these are most auspicious days.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“According to the Nine Heavens Secret Record and Tàiyǐ Dùnjiǎ:
Major month taboos for entering mountains are:
the 3rd, 11th, 15th, 18th, 24th, 26th, and 30th days;
Minor month taboos:
the 1st, 5th, 13th, 16th, 26th, and 28th days.
If you enter the mountains on these days,
the mountain spirits will surely test you.
What you seek you will not obtain;
what you attempt will not succeed.
And not only for Daoists,
but for any person entering the mountains on these days,
there will be misfortune and harm,
and they will encounter tigers, wolves, and venomous creatures.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The nature and form of Heaven and Earth,
the auspicious and inauspicious of Yīn and Yáng,
are vast and difficult to describe in detail,
so I need not insist that they exist,
yet I also dare not guarantee that they do not exist.
However, Huángdì and Tàigōng both placed their trust in them;
in recent times, illustrious men such as Yán Jūnpíng and Sīmǎ Qiān both relied on them as well,
and the classics record the calculations of the calendar and the days of firmness and yielding.
Ancient sayings state,
‘The auspicious day is the wù day.’
This has been passed down from the past.
When a king establishes the office of Grand Astrologer,
for the purpose of bestowing honors and setting up institutions,
for making sacrifices in ancestral temples,
and for performing suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
all select favorable moments;
yet in recent times, mediocre men,
presuming themselves to be free from common customs,
in all their speech and actions,
are ashamed to select auspicious days.
Is this not foolish and ignorant?
Whenever I prepare to enter the mountains nowadays,
if one does not obtain the proper times,
the effects will manifest below,
and one should not enter lightly.
According to the Yùqián Jīng,
if you wish to enter famous mountains,
you must not be ignorant of the secret techniques of Dùnjiǎ,
yet these are not fully explained for others.
But the Língbǎo Jīng states,
when entering mountains, you should select bǎo days and yì days;
if only zhuān days are used, it is greatly auspicious;
if one uses zhì days or fá days, one will surely die;
these are not enumerated one by one either.
From my youth, I had the ambition to enter mountains,
so I studied the books of Dùnjiǎ,
which number over sixty rolls,
and the matters cannot be fully mastered at once,
so I have extracted the essentials,
so that they may be ready at hand,
yet not to be passed on in writing.
Now I briefly discuss them,
supposing that those eager for such things and wishing to enter the mountains
should seek out those who know,
as such people will certainly not be absent from the world.
The Dùnjiǎ Zhōngjīng says:
To seek the Way,
use tiānnèi days and tiānnèi times
to expel demons,
and apply talismans;
use tiānqín days and tiānqín hours to enter famous mountains,
so that all evils, tigers, wolves, poisons and thieves
do not dare to approach a person.
Depart through the ‘celestial storehouse,’
enter through the ‘terrestrial door.’
The six guǐ days are the ‘celestial storehouse;’
the six jǐ days are the ‘terrestrial door.’
It also says:
To flee a chaotic age
and hide away in famous mountains without worry,
use the dīngmǎo day of the Upper Prime;
this is called the time of hidden virtue,
also called the Heavenly Heart,
in which one can dwell in concealment;
this is what is meant by ‘white daylight on solid ground,
sun and moon have no light,
humans and spirits cannot see.’
Also,
those who seek the Way of Immortality and enter famous mountains
should use the six guǐ days and hours,
called the tiāngōng day,
and will surely achieve deliverance from the world.
It also says:
When going into the mountains and forests,
one should take with the left hand a blade of the Qīnglóng grass,
break it in half and place it at the Féngxīng spot,
proceed through the Míngtáng and enter the Yīnyīn,
walk in the Yǔbù fashion,
and recite a triple invocation:
‘Nuògāo Great Yin,
General, hear me alone,
Zēngsūn Wángjiǎ,
do not open to outsiders;
if one who sees the armor is human,
let him take it as firewood;
if he does not see the armor,
he is not human.’
Then place the halved grass on the ground,
take earth with the left hand and apply it under the nose,
hold the grass with the right hand as a cover,
wave the left hand in front,
walk in the Yǔbù manner,
when reaching the ‘six guǐ’ position,
hold your breath and remain still,
and humans and spirits cannot see you.
The six jiǎ are the Qīnglóng,
the six yǐ are the Féngxīng,
the six bǐng are the Míngtáng,
the six dīng are the Yīnyīn.
☵☲ correspond to the Bǐ and Jìjì hexagrams;
the initial first and second steps do not match the count of nine steps,
but each step thereafter is seven feet.
It also says,
one foot equals two zhàng and one foot,
look back at the nine steps.
Another Yǔbù method:
Stand upright;
right foot forward,
left foot back,
then right foot advances again,
with left foot joining the right,
this is one step.
Then right foot forward,
then left foot forward,
with right foot joining the left,
this is the second step.
Then right foot forward,
with left foot joining the right,
this is the third step.
Continue as such,
and the method of Yǔbù is completed.
In all practices and arts under Heaven,
it is best to know Yǔbù;
it is not only for this matter.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The Língbǎo Jīng says,
the so-called bǎo day
refers to the day when the Earthly Branch engenders the Heavenly Stem,
such as on the jiǎwǔ and yǐsì days.
Jiǎ
is Wood,
wǔ is Fire;
yǐ is also Wood,
sì is also Fire,
for Fire is born from Wood.
Again, a yì day
is when the Earthly Branch engenders the Heavenly Stem from below,
such as on rénshēn and guǐyǒu days.
Rén is Water,
shēn is Metal;
guǐ is Water,
yǒu is Metal;
Water is born from Metal.
A zhì day
is when the Heavenly Stem overcomes the Earthly Branch,
as on wùzǐ and jǐhài days.
Wù is Earth,
zǐ is Water;
jǐ is also Earth, hǎi is also Water;
by the principle of the Five Elements, Earth overcomes Water.
A fá day
is when the Earthly Branch overcomes the Heavenly Stem,
as on jiǎshēn and yǐyǒu days.
Jiǎ is Wood,
shēn is Metal;
yǐ is also Wood, yǒu is also Metal;
Metal overcomes Wood.
All others follow these models;
by extending the examples,
all can be understood.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“When entering famous mountains,
on the jiǎzǐ kāichú day,
take silk of five colors, five inches each,
and hang them on a large rock,
then your request will surely be fulfilled.
It is also said,
when entering mountains, one should know the secret invocations of the six jiǎ.
The invocation is:
‘Approaching soldiers and fighters,
all line up in front and march onward.’
There are nine words,
and one should always recite them secretly,
for there is nothing they cannot repel.
The essential method is not complicated—
that is what this means.”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“In the mountains, there are mountain spirits,
their form is like a small child with only one leg,
they run backwards,
and delight in harassing people.
When people enter the mountains,
if at night they hear human voices speaking loudly,
this being is called Qí,
and if you recognize it and call its name,
it will not dare to harm you.
It is also called Rènèi,
and you may call it by that name as well.
There is another mountain spirit,
red in color like a drum,
also with one leg,
its name is Huī.
There is also one that appears like a human,
nine feet tall,
wearing a fur cloak and a bamboo hat,
named Jīnlèi.
There are some like dragons, with five colors and red horns,
called Fēifēi.
If you see them, call them by their names,
and they will not dare to do harm.”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“In the mountains there are great trees,
some of which can speak,
but it is not the tree itself that can speak;
its spirit is called Yúnyáng,
and if you call to it, it is auspicious.
If at night in the mountains you see firelight,
it is always produced by long-dead wood;
do not be alarmed.
If at night you see a Hú person in the mountains,
it is the spirit of bronze or iron.
If you see Qín,
it is the spirit of a hundred-year-old tree.
Do not be alarmed,
for none of these can do harm.
If you see an official between mountains and streams,
that is called Sìjiào,
and if you call it by name, that is auspicious.
If in the mountains you see a great snake wearing a crowned headdress,
it is called Shēngqīng,
and calling to it is auspicious.
If in the mountains you see an official,
or only hear a voice but do not see its form,
and it calls out to you without stopping,
throw a white stone at it and it will cease;
another method is to use a reed as a spear to stab at it, and that is auspicious.
If in the mountains you see a ghost coming to call for you,
persistently asking for food,
throw white mugwort at it and it will die.
If mountain ghosts often confuse and cause people to lose their way,
throw a reed staff at them and they will die.
On the Yín day in the mountains,
if one claims to be a yú official,
it is a tiger.
If it claims to be a master of the road,
it is a wolf.
If it claims to be a prefect,
it is an old raccoon dog.
On the Mǎo day, if someone claims to be an elder,
it is a rabbit.
If it claims to be the Eastern Wangfù,
it is an elk.
If it claims to be the Western Wángmǔ,
it is a deer.
On the Chén day, if it claims to be Yǔshī,
it is a dragon.
If it claims to be Hébó,
it is a fish.
If it claims to be Wúcháng Gōngzǐ,
it is a crab.
On the Sì day, if it claims to be guǎrén,
it is a snake of the altar.
If it claims to be Shíjūn,
it is a turtle.
On the Wǔ day, if it claims to be the Three Excellencies,
it is a horse.
If it claims to be an immortal,
it is an old tree.
On the Wèi day, if it claims to be the master,
it is a sheep.
If it claims to be an official,
it is a roe deer.
On the Shēn day, if it claims to be a ruler,
it is a monkey.
If it claims to be a Jiǔqīng,
it is a gibbon.
On the Yǒu day, if it claims to be general,
it is an old rooster.
If it claims to be a thief-catcher,
it is a pheasant.
On the Xū day, if it claims to be a human surname and given name,
it is a dog.
If it claims to be Chéngyáng Gōng,
it is a fox.
On the Hài day, if it claims to be Shénjūn,
it is a pig.
If it claims to be a woman,
it is metal or jade.
On the Zǐ day, if it claims to be Shèjūn,
it is a rat.
If it claims to be a divine being,
it is a bat.
On the Chǒu day, if it claims to be a scholar,
it is an ox.
If you just know its real name,
then it cannot harm you.”
Someone asked about the method for avoiding snakes and vipers when living in seclusion among mountains and marshes.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“In ancient times, the Yuanqiū area had many large snakes,
and also produced excellent medicinal herbs.
When Huáng Dì was about to ascend there,
Guǎngchéngzǐ instructed him to wear realgar,
and all the snakes left.
Now, if one wears Wǔdū realgar,
with a color like a rooster’s crest and weighing at least five liǎng,
and enters the mountains and forests amid trees and grass,
then one need not fear snakes.
If bitten by a snake,
apply a small amount of powdered realgar into the wound,
and it will heal immediately.
Though there are many varieties of snakes,
only the fù snake and the qīngjīn snake are truly perilous when they bite humans:
if untreated,
they will kill a person in a single day.
If a person does not know the technique for treating them,
and is bitten by either of these two snakes,
he should cut away the flesh around the wound with a knife and cast it to the ground;
the flesh will boil as if seared by fire,
and in moments will be scorched away,
but the person will survive.
During the seventh and eighth months, when these snakes are most poisonous,
if they do not bite people,
their poison has nowhere to go,
so they bite great bamboo and small trees with their fangs,
causing both to wither and die instantly.
Nowadays, when Daoist practitioners enter the mountains,
they may only know broad principles,
but not the proper ways to avoid these dangers;
this is no small matter.
Before entering the mountains,
one should prepare in advance at home,
and first learn forbidden rituals.
Meditate upon the sun and moon, the Vermilion Bird, Black Tortoise, Azure Dragon, and White Tiger,
to protect oneself.
Only then should one venture into the forests, grassy places, and mountains.
On the left, take three breaths of qì and hold them,
then blow them into the grasses and hills,
visualizing the qì as a red mist or cloud,
filling tens of lǐ all around.
If there are companions,
no matter how many, have them line up;
then blow the qì for them too.
Even if they step on snakes,
the snakes do not dare move,
or they hardly ever encounter any snakes at all.
If by chance a snake is seen,
face the sun, and on the left take three breaths of qì and hold them;
press the tongue to the palate,
pinch the Dūguān point with your hand,
and also close the Tiānmén,
seal the Dìhù;
then press down the snake’s head with something and wind it with your hand,
draw a prison on the ground to contain it,
and one can play with it as one likes.
Even if it winds around your head or neck,
it does not dare bite.
Unless the binding spell is released,
breathe qì and blow at it,
and it can never escape from the prison.
If another person is bitten by a snake,
on the left, take three breaths of qì and blow at him;
at once he is healed and the pain ceases.
If the person is tens of lǐ away,
you can still create qì at a distance for him,
calling out his surname and given name:
for men, bless with your left hand;
for women, bless with your right hand;
he or she will also recover.
According to the method of Jiè Xiānshēng:
when living in the mountains,
visualize five snakes of different colors, one of each,
then gather qì, bend green bamboo and small wooden boards to prick them,
move to the left in the steps of Yǔ,
visualize several thousand centipedes on the boards,
covering your body,
and thus depart.
In the end, you will never encounter snakes.
Or one may tie dry ginger or fù zǐ at the back of the elbow,
or burn horns of cattle, sheep, or deer to fumigate the body,
or wear one of Wáng Fāngpíng’s realgar pills,
or place swine ear wax and musk pills in the nail bed of the toes,
all are effective.
Moreover, musk deer and wild boars both eat snakes,
so these things repel them.
It is also said that the rì bird and yī turtle
also eat snakes.
Therefore, southerners entering the mountains
all carry the tail of the yī turtle,
saying the beak of the rì bird can repel snakes.
If bitten,
scrape a bit of either substance and apply it to the wound,
and it heals at once.
The rì bird
is another name for the zhèn bird.
Moreover, southerners entering the mountains
always use bamboo tubes to keep live centipedes;
the centipede, sensing the presence of snakes,
will move within the tube;
when this happens, they carefully examine the grass,
and will surely find a snake.
If the snake is larger than a zhàng in length,
with a body more than a wéii in circumference,
when the centipede sees it,
it is able to subdue it with qì,
and the snake will die at once.
If the snake sees a centipede on the banks of a river or cliff,
the big snake will flee into ravines or deep underwater;
the centipede simply floats on top of the water to subdue it;
people can see something truly blue,
as big as a silk sash,
go straight down into the water to where the snake is;
in a moment, the snake will float up dead.
This is why southerners use powdered centipede to treat snake wounds,
with unfailing success.”
Someone asked:
“In the valleys of Jiāngnán,
there are many kinds of poisons and evils.
Is there a way to avoid them?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“The central plains and highlands,
have pure and harmonious earth energy.
In the famous mountains of the upper regions,
there are none of these sorts.
Now in the lands of Wú and Chǔ,
with heat and dampness steaming and stifling,
even the proper mountains of Héng and Huò,
still abound with poisonous stingers.
There is also the duǎn hú,
also called yù,
also called shè gōng,
also called shè yǐng.
In truth, it is an aquatic creature,
shaped like a cicada in sound,
and in form like a three-sided cup.
It has wings and can fly,
has no eyes but keen hearing.
Inside its mouth is a crosswise object like a horned crossbow;
when it hears the sound of people,
it uses the horned crossbow-like thing in its mouth,
and with its breath as an arrow,
it shoots people from the water.
When it hits a person's body, sores break out immediately.
If it strikes a shadow, sickness still follows,
though sores do not instantly appear.
Those who do not understand how to treat it will die from it.
Its illness is like a severe cold;
within ten days all are dead.
There is also the shā shī,
found both in water and on land.
After fresh rains and before morning and dusk,
when passing through such places it will surely attach to a person.
Only when the sun is fierce and grass is dry,
is it somewhat rarer.
It is as small as the tip of a hair.
At first attachment to a person,
it immediately burrows under the skin.
The spot will feel like being stabbed with an awn,
with great pain from a minor prick.
It can be picked out with a needle,
appearing bright red like cinnabar,
and will crawl upward with its claws.
If it is not picked out,
the insect will bore to the bone,
then travel through the body.
It is similar to the shè gōng,
and both are deadly.
Those who travel in areas where these insects are found,
whenever returning to their residence,
should always use fire to scorch and burn their whole body,
then these insects will drop to the ground.
If one carries any of the following: shèxiāng wán, dù shì wán, hù mìng wán, yù hú wán, xī jiǎo wán, qī xīng wán, or jì nǐ,
all ward off shā shī and duǎn hú.
If one suddenly cannot obtain any of these medicines,
it is also good simply to carry pure shèxiāng.
Take equal parts of realgar and garlic, pound them together,
and carry a pill about the size of a chicken egg—it is also effective.
If already afflicted,
apply this medicine to the sores and they will also heal.
Chewing chī xiàn juice,
drinking it and applying it will also heal.
The roots of wǔ qié and xuán gōu cǎo fú téng—
these three things may be used individually,
pound them and ingest one or two shēng of their juice.
Also, the shè gōng insect hibernates in the valleys in winter;
when there is heavy snow, search for it,
and where this insect is found,
the snow will not accumulate,
and vapor will rise as if scorched and steaming.
Dig there,
and it will not be deeper than one chi into the ground before it is found.
Dry it in the shade and powder it to carry,
and in summer it naturally wards off shè gōng.
If a Daoist knows a single prohibition formula,
or has mastered a hundred prohibitions,
and always keeps to prohibitions and preserves true unity,
then a hundred poisons will not dare approach,
with no need at all for these medicines.”
Someone asked:
“When a Daoist dwells in the mountains,
perched on cliffs and sheltered by caverns,
there is need neither for layered warmth,
yet I have no fear of wind and dampness.
May I dare ask the method?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Jīn bǐng sǎn, sān yáng yè, chāng xīn wán, hūn cǎo nài dōng jiān, dú yáo gāo, yīn yù xuán huá sǎn, qiū dìhuáng xuè wán,
all can be taken for no more than fifty days,
and for ten years one need not fear wind or dampness.
If one takes the Great Elixir of Golden Cinnabar,
even if not yet ascending to the emptiness and flying lightly,
the body will not receive illness,
even though sleeping in wind and on wet ground.
One cannot be harmed.
Of these seven medicines,
all are said for those who have just begun cultivating the Way.
Master Yáo only took sān yáng yè,
and could bare his chest and lie on ice,
feeling no cold at all.
These same methods were tested by Master Jiè and Liáng Yǒudào, lying on rocks,
in autumn and winter, facing wind and cold,
and all have been tested and found effective,
as secret methods.”
Someone asked about the method for crossing rivers and seas to ward off snakes and dragons.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“When a Daoist must cross great rivers,
one must first, by the water’s edge,
break one egg,
mix a little flour and powdered incense with it,
and stir them together in water,
using this to wash oneself,
then one need not fear the winds, waves, jiāo dragons or long.
Also, wear the Eastern Sea Young Boy Talisman, the Water-Controlling Talisman, or Pēnglái Staff,
all of which ward off the hundreds of water dangers.
There are also the Six Jia Three Gold Talisman, or the Five Woods Prohibition.
Also there is the method:
at the river, first recite this prayer:
‘Rolling reeds, rolling reeds,
Hébó leads the way, warding off jiāo dragons;
all disasters are wiped away, heaven shines clear.’
The Jin Jian Record says,
on the wùwǔ day during midday in the fifth lunar month,
pound five stones,
and place their copper below.
The five stones are:
realgar, cinnabar, orpiment, alum, and azurite.
All are powdered,
bathe them in the Jīnhuá Pond,
place them in the Six-One Spirit Furnace and stoke the fire,
burn with cinnamon wood,
when copper forms, refine it with hard charcoal,
use boys and girls to feed the fire,
take the male copper to forge the male sword,
take the female copper to forge the female sword,
each five inches and five tenths long,
taking the number of earth,
to suppress the water essence.
When carried on journeys by water,
then jiāo dragons, giant fish, and water spirits will not dare approach.
If you wish to know the male and female of the copper,
have a boy and girl each pour water on the copper
while it is in the fire, as it turns red;
then the copper will divide by itself into two pieces—
the piece with a protrusion is the male,
the one with a hollow is the female;
inscribe their names on each.
When entering water,
wear the male on the left,
the female on the right.
If only traveling by boat and not entering water oneself,
then on yang days wear the male,
on yin days, the female.
There are also great celestial texts,
with the Northern Emperor's script,
write them on silk to wear,
and these also ward off wind, waves, jiāo dragons, and water creatures.”
Someone asked:
the method for warding off the hundreds of ghosts in mountains, rivers, and temple halls.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“A Daoist always wears the Heavenly Water Talisman, the Supreme Sovereign Bamboo Messenger Talisman, Lǎozǐ's Left Contract, and one who practices the True Unity Mind with the three generals;
then ghosts will not dare approach.
Next best is to study the Register of Hundreds of Ghosts,
know the names of all ghosts in the world,
and consult the Baizé Map and Jiǔ Dǐng Record;
then the multitude of ghosts will retreat of their own accord.
Next best is to take the quail’s-egg red stone pill, or the azurite night-light powder, or the onion-seed black-eye pill, or swallow the white quartz Qímǔ powder;
all these allow a person to see ghosts,
and thus the ghosts will fear him.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“There is the Lǎojūn Yellow Court Central Embryo Forty-Nine Perfected’s Secret Talisman;
when entering mountains and forests,
on the jiǎ yín day inscribe it in cinnabar on white silk,
at night place it on the desk,
facing the Dipper in offering,
with wine and dried meat, each a little,
announce one’s name,
bow twice to receive it,
wear it inside the collar,
and it will ward off a hundred ghosts, ten thousand spirits, tigers, wolves, insects and poisons in the mountains and rivers.
Why must you be a Daoist?
In troubled times, those fleeing into the mountains and forests
should also know this method.”
Entering the Mountain Talisman
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The upper five talismanic texts
are all the Rǒujūn Entering the Mountain Talismans.
Write them in cinnabar ink on peach wood tablets,
inscribe the script largely,
so as to completely cover the surface of the tablet,
and enjoin them to doors and entryways,
as well as at the four directions and four corners,
and at important places along paths,
within
fifty paces of the residence,
to ward off mountain spirits, ghosts, and demons.
On beams and pillars within the house,
all may have them affixed.
Whenever people dwell in forests and mountains or enter temporarily,
all may use these,
and then all beings will not dare to harm them.
Affix three talismans in succession onto one tablet.
This is advised especially to you, not to the Gě clan.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“This talisman is also the Rǒujūn Entering the Mountain Talisman,
and may be affixed on beams and pillars within the house.
Whenever people dwell in forests and mountains or enter temporarily,
it is always suitable to use these.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“This is the Entering the Mountain Tiger and Wolf Warding Talisman as transmitted by the immortal Chén Ānshì.
Write it in cinnabar ink on silk, making two talismans,
each distinct.
Always wear them at your residence,
four for each place.
When traveling, be sure to gather and take them along.
This is a greatly powerful secret.
The Mountain Opening Talisman, with the name of ‘Millennium Bramble Mountain Gate,’
opens the Precious Book of Ancient Script in gold and jade,
all are kept secret.
The above is one method,
there are only minor differences in others.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“This talisman is worn by Rǒujūn,
and marks his power over all ghosts, as well as snakes, vipers, tigers, wolves, and spirit seals.
Carve it on a two-inch square piece of jujube heartwood,
bow twice in reverence and wear it,
it possesses great efficacy.
This is the talisman of the immortal Chén Ānshì.”
Entering the Mountains—talisman to be worn:
These three talismans
should also be placed on the left, right, front, and rear of cattle and horse sheds, as well as pigsties,
to ward off tigers and wolves.
Someone once asked:
“In former times we have heard the stories of Tán Chāng,
who could walk upon water,
or dwell long within water.
By what method was this achieved?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“By mixing green onion juice and cassia,
form pills as large as the seed of a parasol tree, making seven each time,
taking three doses each day,
until three years have passed,
then it is possible to walk upon water.
Lord Zhèng stated that one only needs to practice breath-holding to a thousand breaths;
after prolonged practice, it is possible to remain within the water for about a day.
If one obtains a genuine Tōngtiān xī (Heaven-Penetrating Rhino) horn of more than three inches,
carve it into the shape of a fish,
and hold it in the mouth when entering the water,
then the water will always open for the person,
three feet square,
thereupon one can draw breath and dwell within the water.
Moreover, on the Tōngtiān xī horn there is a red stripe like a silk thread,
which passes from the base to the tip.
If grain is filled in the horn and placed among flocks of chickens,
the chickens will try to peck at it,
but before coming within a few inches,
they are startled and retreat.
Therefore, people of the south sometimes call Tōngtiān xī the ‘Frighten-Chicken Rhino.’
If this rhino horn is set on a granary,
no birds dare to gather there.
On nights of heavy fog and thick dew,
if placed in the central courtyard,
it will never get damp or wet.
This rhinoceros dwells deep within the mountains,
and on dark and cloudy nights,
its brilliance is just like blazing torchlight.
Using its horn as a forked stirring rod,
stir poison decoctions,
if the horn fork is used to stir them,
white bubbles immediately arise,
and the poison loses all potency.
When used to stir non-poisonous substances,
no bubbles appear.
Thus is knowledge of its properties attained.
When traveling in foreign lands with sorcery and poison,
whenever eating or drinking at another's house,
always stir with the rhino horn first.
If a person is wounded by poisoned arrows and faces death,
stab the wound with the rhino horn fork,
then the wound will emit foam and heal.
The reason why Tōngtiān xī can kill poisons
is that this beast feeds exclusively on all poisonous plants,
and all trees with thorns,
never consuming soft and smooth vegetation.
Each year it sheds its horn among rocks in the mountains,
if someone finds it,
it is necessary to carve wood resembling the color, pattern, and shape,
so as to replace the original horn,
and the rhino cannot discern the substitution;
in later years it will again shed its horn at that place.
Other rhinoceroses also ward off poison and evil,
but none can match the marvelous powers of the Tōngtiān kind.
Some people consume the Six Wù talisman for a thousand days,
or mix the red-banded spider and the seven-layered water horse,
to compound with Féng Yí Water Immortal Pills and take them,
and they too can dwell in the water,
or simply apply to the soles of the feet,
and thus walk on water.
Dandruff from the head is enough to make gold and iron float on water—
how much more so these subtler arts!”
Someone asked:
“Those who practice the Dao frequently dwell in forests and mountains,
but these places are infested with tigers and wolves,
how may one ward them off?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The ancients who entered the mountains
all wore the Seal of the Yellow Deity Yuèzhāng,
four inches square,
with one hundred and twenty characters upon it,
affixed with clay seals at each of the four boundaries, a hundred paces from the residence.
Thus tigers and wolves do not dare to come near.
If traveling and encountering fresh tiger tracks,
imprint the seal on them in the same direction,
the tiger will depart;
if pressing the seal in the opposite direction,
the tiger will return;
when wearing this seal to travel through forests and mountains,
one need not fear tigers and wolves.
It not only wards off tigers and wolves,
but if there are evil spirits from mountain rivers, shrines, temples, or blood-feeding deities who bring fortune or harm,
seal them with clay using the seal,
to block their paths,
and they will no longer be able to act as spirits.
Once at Shítóu Waters there was a great turtle,
residing always in a deep pool,
so people named this pool ‘Gui Pool.’
This creature could bewitch people,
inflicting illness.
Wú had a Daoist named Dài Bǐng,
who happened by,
and with Yuèzhāng made several hundred mud seals
and threw them throughout the pool from a boat.
After a time,
a great turtle over a zhang in length
surfaced, not daring to move.
He struck and killed it,
and all those afflicted recovered.
Also, many small turtles floated out and piled up dead on the islet.
In the mountains, if one suddenly encounters a tiger,
immediately perform the Three-Five Prohibition,
and the tiger will also immediately withdraw.
The Three-Five Prohibition method
must be transmitted orally,
as it cannot be fully written down.
One method:
just visualize oneself as the Vermilion Bird,
making it three zhang tall,
standing atop the oncoming tiger’s head,
then hold your breath,
and the tiger will go away.
If spending the night in the mountains,
secretly take the hairpin from your head,
hold your breath and stab at the White Tiger,
then there is also nothing to fear.
Another method:
with the left hand grasp a knife, hold your breath,
and draw a square on the ground,
recite:
‘The shady side of Mount Héng,
the sunny side of Mount Tài,
thieves do not arise,
tigers and wolves do not roam,
city walls are not completed,
sealed with the Golden Pass.’
Then pass the knife horizontally across the White Tiger in the Sun’s meridian,
and there is likewise nothing to fear.
Or use the great prohibition:
swallow three hundred and sixty breaths,
draw from the left to the right to command the tiger,
the tiger will not dare to rise.
Using these methods to enter the mountains,
one need not fear tigers.
Or use the Seven Stars Tiger Steps,
as well as the Jade Spirit Talisman, Eight Powers Five Victories Talisman, Lǐ Ěr Peace Talisman, Central Yellow Canopy Seal Script, and Stone Flowing Yellow Powder,
burn cattle and sheep horn,
or establish the Xīyuè Gōng Prohibition Mountain Talisman,
all are efficacious.
These four talismans are missing here.”
This talisman is the Rǒujūn Entering the Mountain Talisman,
explained below as in the text.
It may also be affixed to beams and pillars within the house.
Whenever people dwell in the mountains and forests or enter temporarily,
all may use it.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"I have heard from my teacher,
if a person can know the One,
all matters are completed.
To know the One
is to have nothing one does not know.
To not know the One
is to be incapable of knowing anything.
The Dào begins with the One;
its nobility is without peer,
each dwells in its own place,
corresponding to Heaven, Earth, and Humanity;
thus it is called the Three-Oneness.
Heaven obtains the One and thus becomes clear,
Earth obtains the One and thus becomes tranquil,
Humanity obtains the One and thus comes to life,
Spirits obtain the One and thus become numinous.
Metal sinks while feathers float,
mountains stand while rivers flow;
look for it and you will not see,
listen for it and you will not hear,
keep it in mind and it will be present,
neglect it and it will vanish;
face it and it is auspicious,
turn away and it is inauspicious;
preserve it and blessings will be boundless,
lose it and destiny will wither and vitality perish.
Lǎojūn said:
Suddenly and vaguely—
within there is form;
vaguely and suddenly—
within there is substance.
This is called 'the One.'
Thus, the Immortal Scriptures say:
If you wish for long life,
guard the One and be enlightened;
long for the One until hunger,
the One gives you food;
long for the One until thirst,
the One gives you drink.
The One has a surname, a given name, and clothing of a certain color;
for men it is nine parts long,
for women six parts long;
sometimes it is two cùn and four fēn below the navel, in the lower dāntián;
sometimes it is below the heart, in the Crimson Palace, in the Golden Citadel, the middle dāntián;
sometimes it is between a person's eyebrows,
one cùn back is called the Bright Hall,
two cùn is called the Cavity Room,
three cùn is called the upper dāntián.
This is what the Dàojiā value most,
and from age to age it is transmitted by blood oath and in secret, passing down only its names.
The One can generate yīn and bring forth yáng,
it moves and calculates cold and heat.
Spring obtains the One and thus sprouts,
summer obtains the One and thus grows,
autumn obtains the One and thus gathers,
winter obtains the One and thus stores.
So great that it cannot be measured by the six directions,
so small it cannot be compared even to the tiniest hair.
In former times, Huángdì traveled east to Qīngqiū,
passed Mount Fēng,
and saw Zǐfǔ Xiānshēng;
he received the Inner Scripture of the Three Sovereigns,
by which to summon myriad spirits;
then went south to Yuánlǒngyīn and Jiànmù,
viewed the ascent of all numinous beings,
gathered flowers from Ruòqián,
and drank water from Crimson Peaks;
in the west he saw Zhōnghuángzǐ,
received the Method of the Nine Multiplications,
passed through Kōngtóng,
and from Guǎngchéngzǐ received the Scripture of Spontaneity;
north he reached Hóngtí,
climbed up to Jùcí,
met Dàwěijūn and Huánggài Tóngzǐ,
received the Diagram of Spirit Fungus;
he returned and ascended Wángwū,
and obtained the Record of Golden Formula for Divine Elixirs.
He arrived at Éméi Mountain,
saw Tiānzhēn Huángrén in the Jade Hall,
and asked about the true Dào of the One.
The Huángrén said:
Since you already rule the four seas,
and yet still seek long life,
is this not greed?
Its shifting aspects cannot be fully spoken,
I only set forth a corner of it.
As for the elixirs of immortality and long life,
only the Golden Elixir exists;
as for guarding the form and repelling harm,
there is nothing but the True One,
thus the ancients esteemed it highly.
The Immortal Scriptures say:
Ninefold Elixir,
Scripture of Golden Nectar,
the Secret of Guarding the One,
all are within the Five Cities of Kūnlún,
stored in jade boxes,
inscribed on golden slips,
sealed with purple mud,
impressed with the Zhongzhāng seal.
I have heard from my former teacher:
the One is in the Great Abyss of the North Pole,
before which is the Bright Hall,
behind which is the Crimson Palace;
grand is the Canopy of Splendor,
the golden towers arch high;
to the left Guāng, to the right Kuí,
waves surge and rise to the sky;
black fungus strews the cliffs,
vermilion grasses cover their peaks;
white jade rises steeply,
the sun and moon cast their rays;
passing through fire, crossing water,
traversing black, crossing yellow;
city walls and towers interlace,
canopies and tents are of precious jade;
dragons and tigers guard in ranks,
divine beings stand at either side;
not giving nor taking,
the One rests in its place;
neither slow nor hasty,
the One settles in its abode;
capable of leisure and contentment,
the One will not depart;
guard the One and keep to the true,
then you can commune with spirits;
lessen desires and eat sparingly,
then the One remains;
even when the white blade touches the neck,
recall the One and gain life;
to know the One is not difficult,
the difficulty lies in persevering to the end;
guard it without letting it slip,
and you can be unending;
on land, repel fierce beasts,
in water, drive away jiāolóng;
do not fear evil spirits,
nor venomous insects;
ghosts dare not approach,
blades dare not wound.
This is a general outline of the True One."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"I have heard from my master
that among the scriptures of Dào teachings,
the practices and mindful contemplation,
which can ward off evil and protect the body,
number in the thousands of methods.
For example, 'Holding the Shadow and Hiding the Form,'
'Guarding the Form, Being Without Life,'
the 'Nine Transformations,' 'Twelve Metamorphoses,' 'Twenty-four Lives,' and so on,
methods to contemplate and perceive the various shén within the body,
and methods of internal visualization to see them,
are beyond counting,
and each is effective.
Yet some involve imagining or performing several thousand actions to protect oneself,
and for the most part are complicated and difficult,
sufficient to greatly weary the mind.
If one knows the Way of 'Guarding the One,'
then all such things may be entirely set aside,
hence it is said: 'He who can know the One completes all affairs.'
In receiving the oral transmission of the True One,
there is clear written instruction;
one sips the blood of a white sacrifice,
and receives the teaching on the auspicious day determined by the king’s augury;
using white silk and white silver as tokens of covenant,
cutting a contract in metal and separating it,
if one lightly speaks or recklessly transmits it,
its numen will not function.
If a person can guard the One,
the One will also guard that person.
Therefore, a sharp blade has no place to display its edge,
a hundred harms have nowhere to contain their inauspiciousness.
In defeat one may succeed,
in peril remain uniquely secure.
Whether in a guǐ temple,
beneath mountains and woods,
in a land of plague,
among tombs and graves,
in the lairs of tigers and wolves,
in places rife with snakes and vipers,
if you faithfully guard the One without slacking,
all evils scatter far away.
But should you suddenly and by chance forget to guard the One,
you may be harmed by the hundred ghosts.
Or if, lying down, you suffer night paralysis,
immediately go out to the central courtyard and gaze at the Fǔxīng star,
clench your fists and guard the One,
and the鬼 will instantly depart.
In times of overcast or rain,
only remain indoors,
face north and contemplate a vision of the Fǔxīng star, and that suffices.
If surrounded by armies or bandits,
with no avenue for escape,
quickly enter the shade of the Six Jiǎ,
crouch and guard the One,
and the five armies will be unable to do harm.
Those who can guard the One,
travel ten thousand lǐ,
join military campaigns,
cross great rivers,
need not divine days or select times,
begin building work or move residence,
enter new houses,
need no further consultation of geomancy or stellary calendars,
and need not avoid the spirts of Tàisuì, Tàiyīnjiāngjūn, Yuèjiàn, Shāhào,
nor the taboos of the natal year,
and will never again meet misfortune or blame.
It is a method proven by repeated testing of former worthies."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The Way of Xuányī
is also an essential method.
It leaves nothing unshielded,
and has the same efficacy as the Zhēnyī.
In my Inner Chapters, the very first is entitled 'Smoothly Following the Xuán',
precisely for this reason.
Guarding Xuányī is yet easier than guarding Zhēnyī.
The True One has surname, given name, stature, attire, and features,
whereas the Xuányī only appears thus.
At first, seek it under the midday sun;
this is what is called 'know the white, guard the black,
desiring death but unable to gain it.'
But beforehand one must practice purification and abstinence for a hundred days,
then one may quietly await and seek to obtain it;
in no more than three or four days will it be obtained,
and once obtained and guarded,
it will never depart.
Guarding the Xuányī,
imagine your body
dividing into three people;
when three are visible,
then further increase them,
and may reach several tens of persons,
all like your own body.
Whether hidden or manifest,
each has its own oral method.
This is the so-called Way of Dividing the Form.
It is because of Zuǒ Jūn, Jìzǐ, Xùn Gě Xiān Gōng being able to be at tens of places in a single day,
and when guests arrive at the hall,
one master converses with the guests,
at the doorway another is there welcoming,
and by the waterside yet another master fishes,
so that the guests cannot distinguish which is the true master.
The master says: those who combine guarding the One with the cultivation of the 'Bright Mirror,'
when the way of the mirror is perfected, can divide the form into several tens of persons,
with attire and countenance,
all exactly alike."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The master says: if you wish for long life,
devote yourself diligently to the great elixirs;
if you wish to attain spirit communication,
practice the division of the form with metal and water.
Once the form is divided, one can naturally see within one's own body the three hún and seven pò;
and the tiānlíng and dìqí,
all become accessible to meet,
and the spirits of mountains and rivers,
all may be ordered and employed."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Life is precious,
death is to be feared.
Yet those who attain long life, nourish their nature, and avert death,
invariably begin with diligence
and finally accomplish it through protracted contemplation.
After attaining the Way,
there is virtually nothing further to do.
While it is yet unfulfilled,
there is nothing that is not requisite.
Gathering and delving for the medicinal herbs of grass and wood,
toiling and laboring in the mountains and marshes,
preparing and refining medicines,
all require physical effort;
climbing heights and crossing dangers,
industrious by day and night without sloth—
unless one has utmost resolve,
it cannot be maintained long.
Even when the golden elixir is about to be achieved and ascent to Heaven sought,
yet the great medicinal substances
must all be bought with coin,
and cannot be secured in one stroke.
Therefore, one must still resort to farming or trading to acquire resources,
accumulate years of industry,
and only then may they be combined.
On the day of the actual composition,
one must again be pure and clean with abstinence,
breaking off worldly entanglements.
In each stage there is difficulty,
and one must further augment these with spiritual cultivation and guarding the One,
to ward off evil and protect the body,
always as a sovereign rules his state,
as a general keeps watch for the enemy,
thus is one able to achieve the merit of long life.
If endowed with great wisdom and intelligence,
possessing ability to govern the world and aid the common people,
and cultivate these arts,
one can surely attain them.
Those who are simple and mediocre,
though they aspire and delight in these,
will be unable to persevere to the end.
Thus, a single person's body
is the image of a nation.
The location of the chest and belly
resembles the palace chambers;
the arrangement of the four limbs
resembles border territories;
the articulation of bones and joints
like a hundred officials;
the spirit like a ruler;
the blood like ministers;
the qì like the people.
Thus, he who knows to govern his body,
can govern a nation.
Loving the people is thus to secure the state,
nurturing the qì is thus to perfect the body.
If the people are scattered, the nation perishes;
if the qì is exhausted, the body dies.
The dead cannot live again,
the lost cannot be preserved.
For this reason, the perfected person averts calamity before it arises,
treats illness before it develops,
applies remedies before there is trouble,
and does not pursue it after it is already gone.
The people are hard to care for and easy to imperil;
the qì is hard to purify and easy to befoul.
Thus, scrutinize power and virtue to protect the altars of state,
curb passions and desires to preserve the blood and qì.
Only then does the True One remain,
the three and the seven are guarded,
a hundred harms are repelled,
and the span of years is extended."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The masters say that consuming the golden elixir and great medicines,
though one has not yet departed this world,
all malevolent forces will not draw near.
If one merely consumes herbs, plants, or minor ‘eight stones’ medicaments,
it may suffice to remove illness and increase one’s lifespan,
but it is not enough to ward off disasters from without.
One may be harassed by ghosts,
or scorned by the great mountain gods,
