or invaded by spirits and demons;
only by guarding the True One
can one fear nothing from such beings.
Next is to wear divine talismans.
If one entirely knows nothing of these two matters and yet seeks long life,
how dangerous indeed!
It is as if four gates are closed but three,
and thieves may yet enter;
how much easier if all are left open!”
Someone said:
“I, a crude person, faced the wall,
confined and fettered by Confucian teaching,
knowing only the words of the Five Classics, the Three Histories, and the Hundred Schools,
and the flowery poetry and prose,
frivolous writings of no benefit,
striving solely to keep to these,
now for many years.
Born in a time of much misfortune,
chaos without respite,
weapons raised everywhere,
arts and literature are not valued,
my labor is wasted,
suffering in thought and exhausting my mind,
pursuing the subtle and seeking the obscure,
yet ultimately unable to acquire rank thereby,
and escape working the fields.
Moreover, it harms deep thought,
and brings no benefit to longevity;
my hair two-toned with age,
my long-held aspirations waning,
I truly wish to renounce delusion,
and seek the way of life.
But hurried and at a loss,
I know not where to turn,
as if crossing a great river,
and not knowing where to ford.
Sir, you have thoroughly studied the classics and records
and comprehensively gathered the marvelous and the secret;
I do not know, among Daoist texts,
just how many scrolls there are.
I beseech you to inform me of the titles.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“I too am one afflicted by these same woes.
In the past, I was fortunate to meet the eminent teacher Zhèng-jūn,
yet I regret that as a disciple I lacked wisdom,
and could not penetrate to the utmost depths and heights.
At that time, although I had the privilege of sweeping and tidying as a disciple,
since my talent and knowledge were shallow,
and my age was still young and vigorous,
my mind was not focused,
worldly feelings yet remained,
and thus I was unable to achieve great gain,
which I counted as a great regret.
Zhèng-jūn at that time was over eighty years old,
his hair at the temples mottled white,
but after a few years, it turned black again,
his complexion full and joyful,
able to draw a strong crossbow and shoot a hundred paces,
walk several hundred li in a day,
and drink two dou of wine without getting drunk.
Whenever climbing mountains,
his body was light and nimble,
ascending danger and crossing peril,
younger men gave chase
and often could not overtake him.
His food and drink were no different from commoners,
nor was he seen to sever grain.
I asked his former disciple Huáng Zhāng,
who told of how Zhèng-jūn once returned from Yùzhāng,
and in Jué Gōu Pǔ,
he encountered a great wind.
Having also heard that there were many brigands ahead,
his companions urged Zhèng-jūn to stay,
waiting for those behind.
All said their rations were scant,
but Zhèng-jūn apportioned his rice to relieve the others,
and did not eat himself,
yet for fifty days did not grow hungry.
Nor was he seen to employ any magic,
and no one knew how he did this.
He wrote fine script by firelight,
surpassing young men.
He had a natural grasp of music,
was skilled at the qín,
and when he sat at ease,
with several seated in attendance,
he would answer questions,
his words never ceasing,
and his ears took in all,
listening to those on both sides plucking strings,
teaching when to lengthen or shorten,
never erring by a hair’s breadth.
I was admitted as a disciple to Zhèng-jūn in later years,
requesting to see his formula books.
He told me:
‘The essential Way need be written on no more than an inch of silk;
at the highest it suffices to cross the world,
there is no need for great quantity.
Yet after broad study,
it is far better than never having seen it.
Once you understand,
you may also obtain the simpler arts,
to guard against the various ailments that plague beginners.’
He first showed me nearly a hundred volumes of Daoist exhortations and admonitory books,
showing them to me little by little.
I too had read widely before,
and often asked him about things within that I found doubtful.
Zhèng-jūn said:
‘You have a talent for discerning truth,
and may be taught.
Yet what you know,
although much, lacks refinement;
and your interest lies also in outside learning,
so you cannot focus on one thing,
and have not deeply surveyed the classics.
Now, I shall show you fine books myself.’
He further permitted gradual access to short books and those written on plain silk,
and over the years,
I gathered what I saw,
which amounted to about two hundred volumes,
yet in the end, I could not acquire them all.
The other disciples all personally served as attendants,
gathering firewood and plowing fields;
only I was frail and weak,
unable to perform such labor,
yet I had no way to make myself useful,
so was always close at hand, sweeping and cleaning,
dusting his bed and desk,
grinding ink and holding candles,
and copying out old books along with Zhèng-jūn, and nothing more.
The way I was treated was the same as the senior disciples,
and he said to me:
‘Among the Daoist books, each contains fine matters,
but you should compare their merits,
and choose what to practice;
do not aim to thoroughly memorize them all,
lest you waste your days and trouble your mind.
Once the golden elixir is accomplished,
all of these will be unnecessary.
Or if you are to teach others,
you should know the fundamentals,
and the order from shallow to deep,
to encourage and advance the learners,
without setting up fixed models and steps for them.’
Zhèng-jūn also would not permit others to copy his books in advance,
all awaiting his decision;
even if borrowed for long,
none dared secretly transcribe a single character.
Zhèng-jūn was originally a great Confucian scholar,
and in later years loved the Way,
and continued to teach the Lǐjì and Shàngshū without cease.
His demeanor was lofty and bright,
his character upright and proper;
all who met him were awed.
When there were questions,
one always waited for his warm countenance,
never daring to be hasty or sharp.
As for books that remained with me,
if it was as long as a month,
it was enough for ample copying,
but there was no secret transcribing,
precisely because Zhèng-jūn was so astute
that, should he discover it by chance,
losing his favor would mean a small loss causing a greater one.
Yet at the beginning of my studies,
I truly did not dare,
and only occasionally made requests as circumstances allowed.
Thus I merely knew the taste of drinking from the river,
but never filled my belly.
Of over fifty disciples,
only I received the Jīndān Scripture as well as the Sānhuáng Neiwén, Zhěnzhōng Wǔxíng Jì,
while the rest never even saw the title page of these books.
Other books, though I did not obtain them all in completeness,
I still took note of their names,
and now I will recite them for you;
later generations who love books
may search far and wide for them.

If there is no number of scrolls mentioned,
each is a single scroll.
Next are the various talismanic scripts.

These include the Zìlái Talisman, Jīnguāng Talisman, Tàixuán Talisman in three scrolls, Tōngtiān Talisman, Wǔjīng Talisman, Shíshì Talisman, Yùcè Talisman, Zhěnzhōng Talisman, Xiǎotóng Talisman, Jiǔlíng Talisman, Liùjūn Talisman, Xuándū Talisman, Huángdì Talisman, Shào Qiān Sānshíliù Jiāngjūn Talisman, Yánmìng Shén Talisman, Tiānshuǐ Shén Talisman, Sìshíjiǔ Zhēn Talisman, Tiānshuǐ Talisman, Qīnglóng Talisman, Báihǔ Talisman, Zhūquè Talisman, Xuánwǔ Talisman, Zhūtāi Talisman, Qījī Talisman, Jiǔtiān Fābīng Talisman, Jiǔtiān Talisman, Lǎojīng Talisman, Qī Talisman, Dà Hàn’è Talisman, Xuánzǐ Talisman, Wǔxiào Jīng Yàn Jūn Lónghǔ Sān Náng Bìbīng Talisman, Bāoyuán Talisman, Shěn Xī Talisman, Yǔqiāo Talisman, Xiāozāi Talisman, Bāguà Talisman, Jiānqián Talisman, Léidiàn Talisman, Wànbì Talisman, Bāwēi Wǔshèng Talisman, Wēixǐ Talisman, Jùshèng Talisman, Cǎinǚ Talisman, Xuánjīng Talisman, Yùlì Talisman, Běitái Talisman, Yīnyáng Dàzhèn Talisman, Zhěnzhōng Talisman, Zhì Bǎibìng Talisman in ten scrolls, Yàn Guài Talisman in ten scrolls, Húgōng Talisman in twenty scrolls, Jiǔtái Talisman in nine scrolls, Liùjiǎ Tōnglíng Talisman in ten scrolls, Liùyīn Xíngchú Lóngtāi Shíshì Sānjīn Wǔmù Fángzhōng Talisman altogether five hundred scrolls, Jūnhuǒ Zhàozhì Talisman, Yùfǔ Talisman in ten scrolls.
All these are great talismans.
As for the lesser ones,
they are too numerous to record in detail.”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“Zhèng Jūn says that talismanic scripts come from Lǎojūn,
and all are of celestial pattern.
Lǎojūn is able to commune with the spirits and numina,
and all talismans are granted by the numina.
As for the fact that today people rarely find them effective in use,
it is because so much time has passed since they emerged,
and through much copying many errors have crept in.
Furthermore, faith is not sincere,
and so their application does not bear results.
Analogous to characters in writing,
if the talismanic characters are in error,
not only do they not benefit,
but they can even cause harm.
People understand written characters,
yet still make many mistakes when copying.
Hence the saying,
‘Copy a document three times,
and a fish becomes a lǔ,
while xū becomes a hǔ’—
such is what is meant.
‘Seven’ and ‘shì’
differ only in the slight variation of their hooks and lines.
But now, the characters upon talismans are unreadable;
even if mistaken, it cannot be detected;
thus, no one knows their instability.
In the world there are even those who gain efficacy from talismans by natural affinity,
and find them effective used alone—
just as some people, using musk, are naturally able to emit fragrance;
it cannot be transmitted to others.
Even so,
one must obtain talismans without error,
and apply them with upright mind.
They will merely be less efficacious than those who possess true affinity for their use,
but will certainly provide benefit.
In general, for Daoist practitioners who seek long life,
their aim is truly in the elixirs;
talismans and swords can only keep demons and evil spirits at bay.
As for those who claim that with these great talismans one can attain immortality through practice,
this too cannot be solely relied upon.
In the Wu era there was someone named Jiè Xiàng,
who could read talismanic script
and distinguish errors from correctness.
Someone once took various talismans for healing a hundred ailments as well as talismans for exorcising and restraining,
removed their labels and showed them to Xiàng;
he could identify each and name them one by one.
Those that were in error,
he could immediately correct for people.
From that time on,
no one else could discern such things.”
Someone asked:
“Among the supreme elixirs for immortality,
none surpasses Jīndān.
I have now heard your teaching.
May I ask: of the various talismanic scriptures,
are any truly the most numinous and divine?”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“I heard Zhèng Jūn say:
Among the Daoist writings,
none is more valued than the Three Sovereigns’ Inner Text and the Five Sacred Peaks True Forms Diagram.
In ancient times, transcendents and immortal officials
treasured and kept these teachings secret;
those without a transcendent’s name
could not be entrusted with them.
They are transmitted once every forty years;
when passed on, there is a blood covenant,
pledging sincerity as a bond.
All the renowned mountains and the Five Sacred Peaks
possess these writings,
but they are kept hidden in stone chambers in secluded places;
when one destined to obtain the Way seeks them,
and enters the mountains with utmost sincerity,
then the mountain spirits themselves open the mountains
and allow the person to see them.
For example, Bó Zhònglǐ
obtained such a text in the mountains,
built his own altar and offered silk,
and always drew a copy before departing.
Having the text,
one always keeps it in a pure and clean place.
Whenever one undertakes anything,
one must first make declaration to it,
as if serving lord or father.
The classic says:
‘Within a household possessing the Three Sovereigns’ Text,
evil and wicked spirits are repelled,
the vapors of pestilence,
sudden disasters and flying calamities.
If there are those sick and near death,
whose faith in the Dao and sincerity are utmost,
and they hold this text,
they will certainly not die.
If a nursing woman is distressed or ceases to breathe and holds it,
the child will certainly be born safely.
If a Daoist wishes to seek long life,
keeping this text and entering the mountains,
can keep away tigers, wolves, and mountain spirits,
the five poisons and myriad evils,
none will dare approach them.
It is possible to traverse rivers and seas,
ward off dragons,
and calm storms and waves.
By obtaining its methods,
transformations and enterprises can be accomplished.
No need to select auspicious earth or days,
no disaster or calamity will befall the household.
If desiring to establish a new residence or tomb,
then one writes dozens of passages from the Earth Sovereign’s Text,
and lays them upon the ground;
next day one observes,
where yellow color appears,
there one may begin construction,
and the household will certainly prosper.
Also, when others are burying the dead,
write passages from the Human Sovereign’s Text,
inscribe one’s own name upon paper,
secretly place it within the person’s tomb,
not letting others know,
and no flying disaster or theft will befall the person.
If anyone plots against oneself,
the ill will return upon themselves.
Furthermore, before using these texts, one should observe a hundred days’ purification,
then it is possible to summon the Heavenly Gods in charge of destiny and Tàisuì,
who daily tour the Five Peaks and Four Rivers,
the gods of shrines and temples,
all appearing in human form.
One may query them about fortune or misfortune, safety or danger,
and the source of disaster and affliction in the sick.
There are also eighteen characters to be worn within one’s clothes,
so that when traveling over rivers and seas,
one never need fear storm or wave.
If the household possesses the Five Sacred Peaks True Forms Diagram,
it can avert soldiers, violence, and rebellion;
should others seek to harm one,
all such harm will rebound upon themselves.
Whenever a Daoist obtains these,
if they cannot practice benevolence, righteousness, and compassion,
and have no purity or uprightness,
then disaster will arrive and exterminate their family.
One should never take this lightly.
Of the arts of transformation,
the greatest are only the Mòzǐ Wǔ Xíng Jì,
originally comprising five scrolls.
In the past, when Liú Jūn’ān had not yet departed for immortality,
he selected its essentials
and made it into one scroll.
Its methods employ medicines and talismans,
thus enabling a person to fly up and down,
to disappear and become invisible at will,
to become a woman with a mere smile,
to appear as an old man with a furrowed brow,
to turn into a young child by sitting on the ground,
to become a forest tree by holding a staff,
to plant things and have gourds and fruits grow edible at once,
to draw a river on the ground,
to pile up earth and form a mountain,
to summon a portable kitchen while seated,
to raise clouds and kindle fire,
there is nothing it cannot produce.
Next is the Yùnǚ Yǐnwēi, one scroll,
which also transforms shapes into flying birds and running beasts,
as well as into gold, wood, jade, and stone.
It can raise clouds and cause rain over a hundred li,
and similarly with snow;
it can cross great waters without need of boat or bridge,
divide one's body into a thousand forms,
ride the wind and soar high,
passing in and out without hindrance,
breathe forth air of seven colors,
see the eight extremes while sitting,
and see beneath the earth,
emit radiance thousands of fathoms long,
illuminate the dark chamber by itself—
it is also a great art.
However, one must follow the motions of dozens of stars,
the methods being winding and difficult to discern,
few are able to record them.
As for the Huáinán Hóng Bǎo Wàn Bì,
none can match these books.
There is also the Báihǔ Qī Biàn method,
which takes the head skin of a white tiger killed on the third day of the third month,
fresh blood from the tiger and from a screen,
purple ribbon,
woven sandals,
drifting duckweed,
and mixes them all on the third day of the third month.
The first grass that grows resembles sesame,
it bears fruit,
and one takes this seed and plants it,
each generation brings forth a new distinction.
After planting it seven times,
one uses its fruit in combination,
and it also enables the shifting of forms and altering of appearances,
flying and sinking at will,
much like the Mòzǐ and the Yùnǚ Yǐnwēi,
anything beyond this is not worth discussing."
The intention of the Xiálǎn zhě
is to let those devoted to the Way know the names of rare books.
Master Zhèng not only was versed in the Five Classics and in the immortal Way,
but also mastered the Jiǔgōng Sān Qí methods, deduced astronomy, the Héluò prophecies,
without exception, he delved into them all.
In the first year of Tài’ān,
understanding that the last age was in turmoil,
that Jiāngnán was soon to boil over,
he carried his book box and the pouch of immortal medicines,
intending to become a disciple,
fleeing east to Huòshān,
and no one knew his whereabouts.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"If you seek a bright pearl,
not in the depths of Hépǔ,
you cannot obtain the luminous pearl of the black dragon.
When gathering fine jade,
if not from the cliffs of Jīngshān,
you cannot secure the flawless tablet worth a walled city.
To receive the teachings and seek the Way from a master,
if you do not find the right person,
yet hesitantly hope for gain,
but persist in following, you will end with nothing accomplished,
merely wasting effort and time;
even if you regret it bitterly after,
it is already too late.
Even in worldly, shallow matters,
one cannot gain knowledge by merely waiting;
how much less so regarding the ways of immortals?
However sage or wise,
no one can understand them by their own insight;
it cannot be reached by pondering,
nor attained by drawing analogies.
Truly, one must have a master,
and his knowledge must be deep and broad;
it is like drawing water from the blue sea,
or chopping wood in a vast forest:
the trouble comes from weakness of strength,
not from lack of material.
What the tiger and leopard leave behind,
the wildcat and rat struggle over.
What Tàozhū has discarded,
Yuán and Yán have never possessed.
If the ones from whom you learn
do not know the gate of deep pools and marshes,
but encounter those ignorant and narrow-minded,
with naturally limited understanding,
their source is meager, their flow short,
they pass on what they themselves have haphazardly assembled,
and yet guard it jealously, unwilling to let go;
even if they impart it in small, damaged portions,
it is shallow and lacking in wonder;
the treasures they possess are already impure,
if they further teach others from the dregs,
how could you hope for any accomplishment?
It is like borrowing grain at the gate of Yí and Qí,
or pleading coldness at the home of Qián Lóu:
what you obtain is nothing but acorns and plain hempen garments,
there can be no hope of grand feasts or brocade and fox furs.
Some serve affairs as mediocre teachers,
but in the end, never awaken to the truth.
Some are fortunate to meet a true knower,
yet fail to seek diligently;
this is a loss that arises from unconsciousness,
one that cannot be recovered.
To know a person’s depth or shallowness
is, in fact, never easy.
The difficulties of the ancients
indeed have their reasons.
White stone resembles jade,
deceitful flatterers resemble the worthy.
The more virtuous, the more they hide themselves;
having it is like not having it.
The more treacherous, the more they boast and display;
being empty, they seem substantial.
If not for the truly discerning,
how can one tell the difference?
Those who cling to mediocre teachers and do not leave,
it is not that they know their teacher to be ignorant and choose not to stop,
but truly think them sufficient and accomplished.
Those who meet the discerning and cannot serve them,
it is not that they know the master is profound and yet do not ask,
but truly see nothing different.
Those who know the essential Way,
desire nothing from things,
seek not after worldly reputation,
how could they be willing to openly display themselves among the common crowd?
Yet shallow and superficial followers
usually boast extravagantly and praise themselves,
adopting severe expressions, seeking reputation, to embellish their hollowness,
sufficient to dazzle and confuse lesser students,
yet dare to make grand claims.
They say,
‘I have already ascended the famous mountains
and seen immortals in person.’
Those hearing it suddenly
and unable to carefully verify it
rarely detect the falsehood.
I have often seen among scattered and mixed Daoist priests
those who hasten to the gates of wealthy men,
commanding their followers only to create empty reputations for them;
claiming themselves to be four or five hundred years old.
When people ask their age,
they pretend not to hear,
smiling and nodding,
saying ‘eighty or ninety.’
Presently they will declare,
‘I once fasted from grain in the Huàyīn Mountains for fifty years,
then stayed in the Shàoshì of Sōngshān for forty years,
then also in Tàishān for sixty years,
then again with so-and-so in Jīshān for fifty years;
telling all their companions of their travels;
in this way,
if one calculates,
they would have lived for several hundred years.
And thus, among those who seek them,
smoke and mists coil and gather,
their doors crowd with visitors."
There are also some practitioners who, by coincidence, receive bodies that are naturally endowed;
they can see ghosts and spirits,
are somewhat able to divine inwardly,
know people's futures as well as past events,
but in truth they cannot increase or diminish fortune or calamity.
This is like using milfoil stalks or tortoise shells.
When ordinary people observe their minor successes,
they immediately call them "divine men,"
claiming that there is nothing they do not know.
Otherwise,
some are adept in the techniques of talismans, incantation water, and spells,
and have some efficacy in treating harmful influences,
but are by no means knowledgeable about the Way of Immortality.
Others practice miscellaneous arts,
can see ghosts and monsters,
but this is of no benefit to one's lifespan or fate.
If you ask them about the Way of the Elixir,
almost none of them knows.
Because of this, if one scrutinizes them in detail,
most go about deceiving the people of the world,
gathering wealth and profit,
stopping at nothing.
These kinds of people and those thieves who tunnel walls or break through windows,
though their paths are different, end up at the same destination.
To rely upon empty words
is not as good as adhering to conduct that can be verified,
so as to serve as an awakening warning to those who come later,
describing these sorts of cases,
as a means to expose false things.
In ancient times there was a certain Qiáng, a person of great strength,
who took herbal and plant remedies,
and somewhat practiced the methods of Róngchéng and Xuánsù,
living to about eighty,
and still retained keen intelligence, not greatly weakened or aged,
so people of the time called him an immortal,
or sometimes the Old Man of a Thousand Years.
The Administrator Jī of Yángzhōu heard of him and invited him to Yídū.
When he arrived,
he would speak with hoarse cries and with a drawn manner,
as if what he knew was actually vast,
but had not yet poured out all that he knew.
Thus, those fond of such things
gathered to listen to his words as echoes gather to a sound,
looking upon his form as shadows follow a shape,
like clouds converging or mist collecting,
all competing to praise and marvel at him,
offering gifts in succession,
so he always had more than enough money.
Though Lúan and Lǐ were highly esteemed in the Former Hàn,
they could not surpass him.
He regularly took asparagus root and did not stop,
so it is clear his body never had the Great Medicine of the Golden Elixir.
Yet Qiáng had casually studied some documents,
and had some knowledge of ancient affairs.
He claimed to be four thousand years old,
and dared to utter empty words,
speaking them without shame.
He said he had met Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng,
and retold stories about them as clearly as if they were real.
The world says Yáo’s eyebrows had eight tufts,
but that is not so—
just the two brows at the ends stood very upright,
resembling the character "eight."
Yáo was a tall man with beautiful beard and whiskers,
and drank more than two hú each day,
so people later exaggerated this by claiming he drank a thousand zhōng,
but in truth he could not,
for I myself saw him deeply drunk many times.
Even though he was a sage,
yet in old age governing affairs,
he was not as capable as in his youth and vigor.
When he banished the Four Evildoers,
installed Yuán Kǎi,
and relied on Shùn’s employment.
Shùn was but an orphan from an obscure and humble family,
yet was of extraordinary talent;
he tilled in the hidden fields of Lìshān,
fished at Léizé,
and made pottery by the seashore,
but at that time no one was able to appreciate his remarkable nature.
I saw how he transformed the people through virtue wherever he went,
and his eyes had double pupils,
a sign of great nobility,
so I always encouraged and supported him.
I told him to excel in exalted virtue;
not to worry about being wealthy or noble,
for the era of the fire virtue had ended,
and the yellow essence was about to rise;
you shall receive the Mandate of Destiny,
who but you could fulfill it!
Yet his father was extremely stubborn,
his brother was especially wicked,
always plotting to kill Shùn.
I often admonished him, saying,
“This son will bring glory to your house and clan;
the four seas will receive his blessing,
not just your family,
do not treat him lightly.”
Shortly afterward, Shùn received the abdication,
and I often recalled how my words were verified.
Again he said:
“When Kǒngzǐ’s mother was sixteen or seventeen,
I observed that she was destined to bear a noble son.
When Zhòngní was born,
he truly was an extraordinary person,
nine feet six inches tall,
with a forehead resembling Yáo,
a neck like Gāo Yáo,
shoulders like Zǐchǎn,
but from the waist down fell short of Yǔ by three inches.
Even so,
despite his poverty, hardship, and lowly background,
as a child he delighted in ritual matters.
I knew he would surely accomplish much.
When grown,
his lofty speech astonished others,
and people from near and far came to learn from him,
with thousands recorded as his students.
I enjoyed listening to his words,
often went to see him,
but regretted that I was unlearned
and could not discuss texts with him.
He often urged me to study the Yìjing, saying,
'This is a fine book.'
Qiū (Kǒngzǐ) privately cherished it,
and the leather binding broke three times,
and the metal clamp broke three times as well;
only then did he attain great enlightenment.
In the fourteenth year of Lord Āi of Lǔ,
a unicorn was caught while hunting to the west,
and the unicorn died.
Kǒngzǐ asked me about it,
and I told him
that this was not an auspicious omen.
Kǒngzǐ was deeply grieved and wept.
Later he had a terrible dream,
and wished to see me.
It was the height of summer in the fourth month,
and I could not go.
Soon after, I heard he was ill for seven days and passed away.
To this day I can vaguely recall his countenance.
Again he said:
Qín Shǐhuáng brought me to Péngchéng,
and drew out a tripod cauldron from the Zhōu era.
I told Qín Shǐhuáng
that this cauldron was a spirit object.
With virtue, it would emerge of itself;
without the Way, it would be lost and perish.
You must only cultivate yourself:
then it will surely come of its own accord,
it cannot be forced by human power.
At the time, Shǐhuáng was greatly puzzled by me,
and in the end could not draw it forth.
He then apologized to me, saying,
‘You truly have far-seeing insight in governing people.’
He also recounted Hàn Gāozǔ and Xiàng Yǔ in clear detail—
there were so many such matters
they could not all be recorded.
The people of the time all recognized him
and treated him as an object of amusement.
And yet, whenever ordinary people heard such things,
they all believed his words.
Later, Qiáng grew increasingly muddled and senile,
almost completely forgetful.
Administrator Jī once gave Qiáng a jade goblet,
but after some time Qiáng suddenly told Jī,
‘In the past, Ānqí Xiānshēng also gave me this thing as a gift.’
Later on, Qiáng fell ill at Huáng Zhěng’s house in Shòuchūn and died.
Zhěng suspected he had transformed and departed.
About a year later,
they tried opening his coffin,
but his corpse was still there as before.
Such as these have only the name, not the reality:
they cause people in the world not to believe there are immortals in the world,
and it is all due to these kinds falsifying the true with the false.
The Prefect of Chéngdū, Wú Wén,
spoke of a certain Cài Dàn from Wǔyuán,
who sought the Dao but could not find an excellent teacher for essential matters.
He abandoned his family affairs,
spending day and night reciting and chanting the "Huángtíng", the "Tàiqīng Zhōngjīng", and the "Guān Tiān Jié Xiáng" and related works,
various families’ books of no urgency,
his mouth ceaselessly reciting,
claiming the Dao was exhausted within these texts.
Yet in the end, he knew not how to apply what he learned,
merely admiring their florid words to deceive the ignorant.
He also instructed others to simply read them a thousand times,
and the meaning would be naturally gained.
By this, over a long accumulation,
his household grew troubled and distressed,
resources for clothing and food were consumed sitting idly,
yet nothing unusual came of it.
He himself was ashamed and angry,
unable to explain himself,
so he abandoned his family,
saying, “I have attained the immortal Dao.”
Thereupon he fled into otherworldly deep mountains,
yet did not know how to gather or extract the herbs and trees that could enable abstention from grain.
He merely gathered and sold firewood to exchange for clothing and food.
In this way, three years passed,
suffering hunger, cold, and hardship.
When people recognized him,
he would feign ignorance of them.
Unable to endure any longer, he returned home,
blackened and emaciated, bones standing out,
scarcely resembling a person.
His family questioned him,
“Where have you come from?
Did you finally become an immortal or not?”
Thus he deceived his family, saying,
“I have not yet ascended to Heaven,
but rather have become an earthbound immortal.
At the outset I achieved a low rank,
so I must serve those immortals who advanced before me,
and thus gradually ascend in status.
Formerly, Lǎojūn assigned me to herd several dragons;
among a class of dragons, those of five colors were the best,
and these were those Lǎojūn himself regularly rode.
He ordered me to watch over them,
but I was not diligent,
instead spending my time gambling with younger immortals.
Suddenly I lost one of these dragons;
the dragon then disappeared without a trace.
For this crime I was blamed,
and sent beneath Kūnlún Mountain
to weed and till three or four qǐng of land,
all growing very fine,
but much overgrown with wilderness,
and managing it was indescribably toilsome.
According to the rules, only after ten years could I be released.
Then Yùquánzi, Wáng Qiáo, and other immortals came to inspect,
so I appealed to them;
they together labored on my behalf,
and I was also temporarily released to go home;
but I must labor again before I can depart freely in the future.
Thus, in the end, I grew old and died.”
At first, when Dàn returned, he said,
“I have come from Kūnlún.”
All his relatives and acquaintances vied to ask him,
“What is Kūnlún like?”
He replied:
“Heaven’s height is not measured in lǐ;
the main thing is that, looking up toward it,
it is little more than a dozen zhàng from the sky.
On top there is the Mùhé tree,
forty-nine chǐ tall,
its ears of grain fill up a carriage.
There are trees of pearls and jade, shātáng, lánggān, and bìguī,
jade plums, jade melons, jade peaches,
whose fruits look like peaches and plums in the world,
only they are radiant, translucent, and hard,
and must be washed with water from the jade well,
then they become soft and edible.
Whenever the wind arises,
the trees of pearls and jade,
their branches, flowers and leaves,
strike and brush each other,
producing naturally the five notes,
clear and plaintive, stirring the heart.
When I, punished and dispirited, heard these, I could not help but grieve within.
Also on Kūnlún Mountain,
each side has four hundred and forty gates,
each four lǐ wide.
Within are five cities and twelve towers,
beneath which are blue dragons and white tigers,
serpents more than a hundred lǐ long,
their mouths and teeth as large as three-hundred-hǔ boats,
great bees a zhàng in length,
their poison able to kill elephants.
There are also divine beasts,
such as shīzi, bìxié, sānlù, and jiāoyáng,
copper-headed, iron-browed, with long fangs and chiseled teeth,
thirty-six kinds in all;
if one knows all their names,
then the malicious ghosts and beasts of the world
dare not harm people.
As for the deities: there are "Headless Master", "Lord of Reversed Light", "Duke Xīlù", "Teacher Zhōnghuáng", and the "Six-Gate Ministers".
Zhāng Yáng, styled Zǐyuān,
thoroughly furnished the Jade Palace,
and unless one carries Lǎojūn’s bamboo envoy tally and side contract,
one may not enter.
All five rivers emerge from the foot of the mountains,
and the Weak Water circles it,
which cannot support even a wild goose feather,
and over which not even birds may fly;
only immortals may cross it.
Above are divine birds and divine horses:
the likes of Yōuchāng, Jiāomíng, Ténghuáng, Jíguāng,
all able to speak human language and immortal;
truly a flourishing, joyful palace of immortals.
I only regret that I could not freely roam above it.
At that time, when Cài Dàn had spoken all this clearly,
many believed him.
Also, in Púbǎn of Hé​dōng, there was a certain Xiàng●dū,
who, together with his son, entered the mountains to seek immortality,
and after ten years returned home.
His family asked the reason.
Xiàng●dū said:
“After three years’ concentration in the mountain,
an immortal came to invite me,
and together we rode a dragon and rose to Heaven.
After a good while,
I looked down at the earth:
it was deep and dark,
and above, we had not yet arrived;
but we were already far from the ground.
The dragon moved swiftly,
head raised, tail lowered,
leaving me upon its back,
trembling with peril and fear.
When we reached Heaven,
we first passed by the Purple Palace,
with gold couch and jade table;
dazzlingly radiant,
truly a noble place.
The immortal only offered me a cup of rosy clouds;
drinking it, I no longer felt hunger or thirst.
Suddenly, longing for home,
I came before the Celestial Emperor,
but, failing in proper etiquette,
I was rebuked and sent back,
told that only by cultivating myself again would I be able to return.
Formerly, when King of Huáinán Liú Ān ascended to Heaven and met the Supreme Lord,
he sat cross-legged, speaking grandly,
calling himself ‘the lonely one’,
so he was punished to guard Heaven's kitchen for three years.
What kind of man am I?”
Thus the people of Hé​dōng called Xiàng●dū ‘the banished immortal’.
There are many such people in the world,
of more than one type;
one should examine them closely.
As for such absurd words,
yet there are still those who do not realize their falsity.
How much more, when these fabrications are vague and deceiving,
and especially when they are made to resemble real events in certain particulars;
unless one is supremely clear-sighted,
how could one suddenly discern the truth?
Furthermore, there are those who feign or claim to be famous Daoist masters of past generations,
like Bái Hé,
who is said to be eight thousand seven hundred years old.
From time to time he appeared among common people,
then suddenly left,
and none knew where he went.
In Luò, there was a Daoist
erudite in many affairs,
broad and refined in arts and numbers;
he would ask Bái Hé all sorts of perplexing questions,
and Bái Hé would respond with explanations to whatever he heard,
leaving no more doubts or obstacles,
hence was revered as far-sighted.
People knew not his age or longevity,
but believed it must approach a thousand years or more.
Later, suddenly he disappeared,
and none knew his whereabouts.
A man in Héběi claimed to be Bái Hé;
thus people from near and far contended to serve him,
and he gained much wealth and honor.
But Bái Hé’s disciples,
hearing that Bái Hé had reappeared,
rejoiced greatly,
and went to see him,
but determined he was certainly not the real one.
This man thereupon fled and vanished.
The Wǔjīng and Sìbù,
together are but the chaffed dogs already set forth,
the dregs of what has passed.
That which is called “traces,”
is merely what feet leave behind, and not the feet themselves.
“Books” are things authored by sages but are not themselves holy,
yet the Rù scholars cross ten thousand li carrying their satchels to seek their teachers;
how much more so the Way of Longevity,
which Zhēnrén value so highly,
can it be but indifferently sought or casually asked after?
Yet, one must with utmost precision distinguish the true from the false!
I fear that those like Gǔ Qiáng, Cài Dàn, Xiàng Dōudū, and Bái Hé have not vanished from the world,
and those who delight in such matters, if they examine this book of mine,
may be able to cull and filter its merits to some extent.
Moreover, in the Xiān Jīng it is said:
“The pupils of immortals are all square.”
When Bái Zhònglǐ saw one such in Luòzhōng,
he told me his pupils were indeed square,
so it must be a man of the extraordinary indeed.”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
There was one called Mister Huái Bīng,
who disdained the harried engagements of traveling the world,
and grieved at the bitter labor of “spitting and grasping.”
Yielding rich soil by river and sea,
he made his home to till in wild saltlands.
He kept the Six Marvels hid in his pouch,
containing jade-like gems but refusing to reveal them.
When his pure voice resounded softly, none could hear it,
when he covered the brilliance of his elegance, the world could not behold him.
He turned his back on the glory of vermillion gates,
preserving quiet and solitude in a thatched hut.
He cast aside the tracks found in the alleys of Jīn Zhāng,
to cultivate exuberance among recluses in obscure places.
He reckoned glory and rank as misfortune,
and prized jade and silk as mere earth and grass.
He raised his spiritual model above the clouds,
alone contravening the present and pursuing the ancient.
He sheltered beneath lofty, towering peaks,
and rested on the fragrant mats of green orchids.
He rinsed his mouth with the clear essence of flowing clouds,
and ate of the purest grains of the Eight Stones.
His thoughts soared unseen, as though living at the tips of rainbows,
his mind fluttered aloft as if neighboring the mirrored sun.
The myriad things could not disturb his harmony;
the four seas could not vex his spirit.
At this there was Fùshì Gōngzǐ, who heard of him,
and, filled with emotion, sighed, saying:
“That there are fine steeds with slender necks in empty valleys
is a shame to Sūn Yáng;
that Tàipíng loses to the world one of such talent
is a charge against those who honor the genuine.
How could one permit worthy men to keep their virtue alone,
and let the august court lack the service of such exceptional men?
Thus, he approached and spoke, saying:
“Merely hearing of one stretching wings and raising his body,
but unable to soar among the nine heavens,
or leap to the mystery’s utmost,
or set in order ritual bonds,
is not fitting for the truly heroic.
Now you, sir, wield the cutting edge of decision,
outshine all in brilliance and writing,
peruse records in the thickets where no tracks are found,
and draw forth elegant rhetoric among birds and beasts,
display the emblem of the dragon amid the dark of night,
submerge treasures in bottomless depths,
lie dormant through the height of summer,
and conceal your flowers even as spring arrives.
Though you may lower your curtain and ponder deeply,
exhaust your brush and gallop through literary embellishments,
secretly aid the Supreme Ultimate,
and expound on primal origins;
when speaking joyfully, your wooden features beam with a skillful smile,
when lamenting, your brows crease and tears pour down;
in contempt you are like swan feathers adrift in weak waters,
with gravity, like jade and stone tossed by flying waves;
in separation your gall and liver are distant as Hú and Yuè,
united you make ten thousand differences converge into one harmony;
in stern debate, as autumn frost and spring’s austerity,
in gentle words, as ice twigs sending out blossoms;
in toppling the lofty, you drive down what’s at its peak,
raising the lowly, you make the deep pond soar high;
if you find fault with clarity, then you depend on dim light at night,
if you save the muddy, you restore brightness to the Huáng Hé.
And yet you cannot bestow great benefits on all creatures,
nor establish your grand merit in the imperial house;
your fame, with the morning dew, will all evaporate,
your body will perish as mayflies do;
suddenly exalting yourself above what sages treasure,
forgetting the flowing river while lamenting your old age,
I privately believe, sir, that you do not follow the right way.
“I have heard the greatest things are Heaven and Earth,
next in order are lord and vassal.
The sages of old worried for their times,
wishing to act on their Way;
if there is no ruler for three months,
they are as anxious as can be.
They are ashamed if today’s wise sovereign is not one with Yáo and Shùn,
and distressed that the people cannot have each household enfeoffed alike.
Thus, some bear the cauldron and their dragon leaps,
some strike their horns and sing the phoenix’s song;
they do not wait for the chariot of reeds before setting out,
nor await King Wén to begin their cause.
Those who first hide themselves, take flight at the right moment,
rise and fall with the times;
in advancing, they go when there is benefit;
in retreat, they are not burdened by regret;
the wise and discerning preserve themselves,
extending their influence to aid the world.
They let those who incline to the orchid’s breeze bow their branches,
those who wash in clear waves cleanse away impurities;
as the shrouded reflection responds to the bright mirror,
as the straight and round answer to compass and square.
Thus, their merits reach high and low,
their blessings flow to the eight directions.
This is why the House of Táng stands grand and tall,
why Zhònghuá was reverent in self-conduct,
why Xībó divided the realm in three,
why Jī Fā revolted and renewed,
why Huán and Wén unified the lands,
why Hàn Gāo responded to Heaven;
never was it so that they did not make the worthy their six wings,
nor trust heroes as the beams of their boat.
If each were only to guard his fitting withdrawal,
or each only shared in the labors of plowing with a partner,
then the transforming influence of learning from antiquity would not arise,
the glory of wisdom would not shine,
the songs of bright rulers would not be sung,
and the all-embracing net of Heaven would not be spread.
“For this reason, those who hide their talents find value in adaptation to the times,
the brilliant and outstanding are precious for presenting wonder and restoring order.
If the shining spirit obscures its radiance amidst the clouds,
then the splendor of the heavens does not appear;
if the roaring tiger hides his fangs and clutches his claws,
then the rapidity of his strike is unseen;
if the Tài’ē sword buries its edge and does not thrust,
then the resoluteness of quick action does not appear;
if the fleet horse twists its hooves and does not gallop,
then the speed that chases the wind is not manifested;
if all are silent, then Zigòng’s mouth is no different from that of the speechless,
if all are in darkness, then Lí Zhū and the blind differ in nothing.
For you, Sir, to preserve your purity and neglect the disorder of human relations,
for you to be content with your own insight and forget the duty of serving above,
to remain with ties to the mechanisms of the world,
and to die without leaving a sound as lasting as metal or stone,
even ordinary people would be indignant at this,
how could true greatness be so indifferent!
“If the rule is set straight, then the wood is straightened,
when uprightness grows, the crooked withers,
when Yǒuyú is in power, the Four Fiends are executed,
when Xuānní is employed, Shàomǎo is cast out;
just as, when thunder crashes, the signal drums fall silent,
when the morning sun rises, fireflies and candles grow dim.
If you do not save the sickness of summoned souls,
then you will not be imitating the master of medical arts from Yuè;
if you do not bestow aid in troubled times,
then there is no way to discern exceptional farsightedness.
Watching others drown with arms folded,
is not the benevolence of one who treads not on others;
cherishing the Dao while the nation is in chaos,
is not the work of one who would act.
If you wait for mid-Táng to cultivate auspicious plants nourished by the sun,
wait for the song of the phoenix to fill the morning,
for the one-horned beast to appear at the outskirts,
or for groves of conjoined trees to gather in the wilds;
if long banners are rolled up and never hung,
and shields and spears are set aside and not found,
if Shǎobó is ready to retire after achievement,
then who can ever promote the likes of Lù and Shěn?
I earnestly hope you, Sir, will not stand aloof in confusion and will return!”
Thereupon, Huáibīng Xiānshēng gazed out in tranquil solitude into the distance,
his spirit wandering along the heavenly thoroughfares,
his emotions and mind reaching far and wide,
as if there were nothing beside him.
Bowing his head, he replied:
“Alas!
Is there truly such talk?
Indeed, the man who has attained the utmost is without striving;
he dwells in serene emptiness,
does not enslave his ambition for rank or gain,
so that harm and disgrace cannot touch him.
He does not stand on perilous paths,
thus fall and ruin cannot afflict him.
Though served weeds and wild beans,
yet his mind finds ease in a single room;
ranked among commoners,
yet his heart rejoices in having the land.
He sleeps content in an official’s lodging,
closes the gate of a thatched door,
takes Zhūang Lái as his friend,
keeps to a humble lane for his dwelling,
stands firm as a towering mountain, unshaken,
how could he ever be anxious over rising or reclining?
If desires grow large, then harmony grows murky;
thus he casts aside worldly affairs without a backward glance.
To those who reach the heights of office, concern runs deep;
therefore he turns away from power and profit, free of lingering doubt.
His worth is not in rank,
nor his wealth in property.
He travels high with companions like yún and péng,
and so does not let his wings be tangled among decaying rats;
taking Fan Wǔ as a great warning,
he does not abandon his joy in simple food and drink.
“Moreover, the universe is vast and distant,
but human life is but a fleeting moment;
as brief as light passing through a crack,
set amid the boundless void,
swift as a passing star’s sudden appearance,
drifting like an arrow’s flash through the air.
It is enough to wander at ease and find self-contentment,
how could one bitterly struggle for outward things!
The luán is not caught in nets,
the lín does not fall into traps;
look at those birds and beasts—
even they know what brings harm.
How much more should men of the world—
have they ever truly cared for such things?
As for Yào Lí destroying his own family to achieve merit,
Jì Xìn entering the flames to deceive Chǔ,
Chén Jiǎ slitting his throat to prove his younger brother’s case,
Zhòng Yóu giving up his life and being made into mincemeat,
Yíngmén falling on his sword to show his resolve,
Niè Zhèng, moved by kindness, being butchered,
Jīng Qīng sacrificing his leg to repay Yān,
Fán Gōng delivering his head in sorrow—
all are the deluded madness of base men,
how could they be models for the wisdom of the highest sages!
“Those with abundant salaries bear heavy responsibilities,
those with noble titles labor in spirit.
Therefore, Qī Yuán angled his line in retirement,
never coveting the prestige of high ministers;
Bǎi Chéng guided the plow,
scorning the lofty places of feudal lords.
Yáng Yuè found peace in the butcher’s shop,
Yáng Zhū begrudged even a single hair from his body.
The seekers after fortune,
blind to what is truly desirable,
gather without choosing the right tree,
serve without judging the times,
greedily pushing forward without worrying about the calamity of being crushed beneath their own ambitions,
accepting commissions without reckoning the disasters of failure.
When discussing glory and honor, they invoke Yī and Zhōu to rescue the drowning;
when debating disasters and regrets, they hush up Fù Sù and will not recall them.
They wait for the river dragon to sleep in order to steal its pearl;
they enjoy the ruler’s favor yet hope to remain free from harm.
They indulge in fleeting comforts,
blinded to impending peril;
without the splendor of the morning mushroom,
they hope instead for the longevity of the grand chūn tree;
it is like treading thin ice waiting for the summer sun,
or climbing rotting branches while expecting a sturdy wind.
Like the deep fish lured by fragrant bait,
or the marsh pheasant swallowing poison seed;
they chew spoiled meat to stave off hunger,
and drink strong poison to quench their thirst.
“In former times, Jīzǐ wept at the sight of ivory chopsticks;
Nífù gave a long sigh on hearing of paired burials;
delving into subtlety, they foresaw the obvious,
tracing the beginning, they discerned the end.
Yet the ignorant man steps into snares without awareness;
how difficult it is to have foresight,
and how deep the bondage of self-interest!
Even Zhōu Chéng was a worthy man but believed rumors,
Gōng Dàn was a sage yet fled to Nán Chǔ,
entrusting his sorrow to the owl,
only escaping with his life thanks to the Jīn Téng.
And as for a ruler who is truly wise,
such appear but once in an age;
slanders that displease him,
are never for a moment absent.
Virtue does not come by fierce winds that kill the crops,
nor is talent displayed through wealth of jade and gems;
sighs and tears avail nothing,
and so it must be.
“If the soaking is long,
then even glue and lacquer lose their strength;
if the saturation continues,
then even flesh and bone are torn asunder;
when dust and feathers accumulate,
they can sink a boat and break its axles;
if rumor is repeated thrice,
the marketplace will believe there are tigers.
Thus, Jiāng Chōng, though base and lowly,
had no kinship with the Crown Prince;
the stepmother, though only a foster,
had no intimacy with Bó Qí.
Yet through the slanders of a digging stick,
the affection of father and son was destroyed;
by the trick of carrying bees in the sleeve,
the natural love of kinship was broken.
How much more so with others!
How can anyone be certain?
Alas!
Wǔ Yuán, because of his loyalty, was left to float as a corpse;
how tragic!
Bái Qǐ, for upholding righteousness, slit his throat.
Therefore, looking clearly brings dread to the heart,
and even the wise craftsman is bewildered.
“Some would set little talent as the standard, and judge all alike;
rely on narrow rectitude to condemn the faults of many.
Yet they do not see that though metal conquers wood,
an awl or gimlet cannot fell a large forest;
though water overcomes fire,
a small jug cannot put out a burning mountain.
An inch of glue cannot clear the silt of the Yellow River,
a foot of water cannot drive off the heat of Xiāo Hill.
Thus, it is exceedingly rare for both reputation and body to remain intact,
and there are many who laugh first and wail after.
Fearing remorse yet never quenching their hunger for glory,
shunning disgrace yet unable to rid themselves of rivalry;
it is like disliking wetness yet diving into a deep abyss,
hating one’s own shadow yet not seeking shade,
boring holes in a boat to stop its leaks,
or throwing more fuel on a fire to stop it boiling over.
“The seven-foot frame
is endowed by life,
it must not be given back in ruins;
the inch-square heart,
its governance is within me,
it must not be cast aside to wander aimlessly.
I should till fields for food,
dig wells for drink,
wear coarse cloth for warmth,
live in a hut of thatch as shelter,
sing and play for amusement,
breathe in and out to prolong my days,
roam freely with bamboo slips and silk thread,
let my feelings rest on mysterious brushwork,
keep to the eternal, awaiting my end—
this too is enough.
Others: so long as the Way abides, one gains honor;
when virtue prevails, one attains worth.
Firing fine pearls at sparrows—
no wise person would do that.
Why must one rely on influence to stand out,
or wait for official salary to be fed?
Moreover, the one who is content in poverty regards lack of wealth as abundance,
and the one who enjoys humility considers not holding office as honor.
Thus, Yòu Ān floated upon the sea to purify his spirit,
while Húzǐ was content to retreat and farm.
Féng Bǐ suffered the crime of possessing admirable virtue,
and Xìn Bù fell into severe punishment for great merit.
A single branch is enough to fold the wings of the luán bird—
what need is there for a rich forest?
A mere pool is enough to carry the scales of a dragon—
why care for the vast ocean?
Coarse herbs are more delightful than the Eight Delicacies;
cold spring water more flavorful than fine wine;
cloth shoes are better than red slippers,
a wadded robe more splendid than ceremonial attire;
holding a staff is more fitting than a mighty axe,
the song of sticks is more joyful than strings and pipes;
a thatched dwelling is lovelier than painted pillars,
plain rafters more precious than carved beams;
climbing a high peak becomes a grand terrace,
a rocky cliff a splendid mansion;
piling up writings forms treasured granaries,
and cherishing profound discourse is gold and jade;
forsake the shallow affections of petty people,
abandon the desires of the lowly and servile;
wander the nine marshes, harboring joy,
send off cleverness to cut off the world.
Like the inchworm bent in its retreat,
hiding one's light and preserving authenticity;
displaying clumsiness and appearing hesitant in speech,
knowing where to stop and ever being content.
Only then can one chew the fragrant zhī herb,
float with the winds and drifting clouds;
bask in the radiance of the nine suns,
soar high with borrowed wings;
looking up, nest in the wutóng tree,
looking down, gather at the mystical isles.
Who would wish to wear the bridle and lie tied in the stable,
or be adorned with embroidery like the sacrificial ox? ”
Gōngzǐ Fù Shì said:
“Those who enter and do not come out
are said to wallow in favor and forget to retreat;
those who go and do not return
are said to be incapable and without principle.
Thus, the enlightened regard their body as not belonging to themselves,
but follow where circumstances take them.
Whether hidden or manifest, silent or spoken,
they have no unyielding insistence.
When the times require stillness, then be still,
when the time is for action, then act.
When gifts of silk are gathered,
and ceremonies are performed in the court,
the gentleman's way ascends,
and fortune appears from heaven.
But if slander prevails and peril abounds,
do not step beyond door or courtyard,
tie up your pouch and do not make use of it.
The dragon rises and the phoenix folds its wings—
follow what suits the time.
This is why ancients would sometimes avoid chaos and not enter;
or, though present, would not stay the day—
out of fear the fire of Wūshān might befall,
or the rare herbs might both burn.
Now, the Sagely Emperor rules and conducts the world,
the age is peaceful, the Way is prosperous,
benevolence extends to all creatures,
favor reaches afar with gentle winds,
authority inspires awe as far as the land of ghosts,
and his grace blesses the farthest frontiers;
he models the earth’s virtue to carry all thickly,
matches Heaven in its lofty spread;
by divine transformation, clouds move and rain is bestowed,
by mysterious beneficence, mists gather in abundance;
the four gates are tranquil and wide open,
the ruler selects the worthy to govern well.
This is a rare chance of a thousand years,
a singular meeting in time.
Yet you, sir, admire the one-sided withdrawal of the recluses,
and do not notice the harm in narrow seclusion;
you strive for the inner cultivation of Dān Bào,
but have not seen the external threats faced by the fierce tiger.
This is like hearing some drown while crossing water,
and then believing all those in boats must fail;
or, because of Shāng Chén’s cruelty and rebellion,
saying that all heirs are unworthy. ”
Mr. Huái Bīng replied:
“The prosperity of sagely rule
is indeed as you have eloquently stated.
But in matters of office or retreat,
each person has their own inclination.
Thus, while Yáo and Shùn were above,
there were still guests nesting among Jī and Yǐng;
when Lord of Xià ruled the world,
there were nevertheless worthy men tilling their fields in remote marshes.
Could this be out of fear of danger?
It is simply each associates with what gives them peace.
Therefore, some cherish lofty ideals,
refusing to serve lords or princes,
preserving the symbols of change,
holding fast as commoners,
maintaining integrity in Yánzhōu,
and are thereby praised by the Sages.”
“As for my own wandering in gardens and fields,
withdrawing to the wilds and marshes,
it is truly because my talents are not fit for politics,
and my endowments lack what is needed to govern people;
yet talented men arise in crowds,
and outstanding figures gather like scales;
civil and martial men fill the court,
all affairs are well-managed,
so I do not wish to bring forth dim light to compete with sun and moon,
to tap a pot beside the great bell,
to offer a light fan in the depths of winter,
or display a fur cloak in the heat of summer—
I would certainly be discarded as useless,
and mocked for ill-timed acts.
If one embraces the classics and writing,
this can preserve authenticity and establish a name,
and contribute to refining the culture;
but if one forces what one cannot bear,
then disgrace and failure surely follow,
with regret like the timid fox.
Thus, I dwell where I am strongest,
and thereby preserve what I lack.
Though I have no achievements in court,
and no merit in war;
nevertheless, by guiding later generations,
promoting the Way and cultivating what is right,
we all reach the same end by different paths,
and do not harm the people.
The lesser man preserves his humble self,
but how could I compare to Xǔ Yóu?
In this sage age, there is tolerance and acceptance,
like those widely exempted in the era of Yǒu Táng;
is this not fitting?”
Gōngzǐ Fù Shì was suddenly embarrassed,
and respectfully changed his demeanor,
saying:
“Sir, your words help instruct and edify,
your writings denounce the treacherous,
you uphold withdrawal and tranquility to restrain a competitive world,
and promote Confucian teaching so subtle words are not lost;
if there were no one to withdraw,
who would establish the norms?
If there were no one to hide away,
who would instruct the young and ignorant?
Everywhere under heaven and upon the land,
all are subjects and people.
Why must only those who hang tassels and hold tablets be commendable,
while those content and hungry behind a modest gate be condemnned?
Those who lose their way in the clouds and mists
must have a guide to show the way;
those wandering the vast sea
must look to the pole star to return.
Now, hearing your fine instruction,
I perceive my own blindness.
I will don robes and cap,
spur on my slow horse to follow the swift,
spread love and strive to advance,
not shunning any choice.”
The master Bào Pǔzǐ said:
In the past I traveled to the mountain of Yúntái,
and met a recluse,
encountering an office-holder also there.
The office-holder said:
“The enlightened are above,
ruling over all under Heaven,
attracting both Huá and Yí,
and even distant lands submit;
yet you, sir, wander in faraway Bǎichéng,
mixing with birds and beasts.
Now, times change and customs differ,
and worldly affairs are not rigid,
so living on nuts and nesting in mountains,
casting off worldly burdens,
were once high and pure,
now are fugitive outcasts.
The gentleman is wary of danger before it forms,
and cuts off disaster as it approaches;
why avoid the inward heat of Zhāng Yì,
just to suffer external harm like Dān Bào?
Fearing excess and overthinking,
forgetting the near worries of disorder in the crowd,
avoiding the shallow dangers of cattle tracks,
only to fall into abysses a hundred fathoms deep;
fleeing the muddy waters that dampen the feet,
only to stumble unawares into fire and furnace?”
The recluse replied:
“He who strives with the baby mouse
knows nothing of the true intent of the zōuyú beast;
busy with grains in the courtyard,
how could he understand the far-reaching flight of mandarin duck and luán bird?
It is like the scorched worm laughing at the great roc,
or the morning mushroom doubting the giant chūn tree,
the well frog suspecting the sea turtle,
the well snake mocking the responsive dragon.
You are moved by encouragement or criticism,
but how could you recognize the lofty note of boundless mystery!
I am fortunate to live in the time of Yáo and Shùn,
why worry that I cannot fulfill the aspirations of this man!”
The official said:
“In the past, wild and reclusive Huá shì, in their loyalty, refused to serve their superiors,
and hid at the margins of the sea,
yet Tài Gōng put them to death.
Now, if you, Master, follow Shěn’s retreat,
is this not also dangerous?”
The recluse replied:
“Lǚ Shàng excelled at warfare,
but was lacking in statecraft;
he could not govern the primeval forces to nurture the world,
nor embrace sea and mountains to widely accept all kinds,
to honor the worthy and esteem virtue,
and delight in cultivating talent;
instead, he found satisfaction in punishment and killing,
and did not cultivate benevolence and righteousness.
Therefore, the disaster of his violence and killing
began from the time he received his fief.
When Zhōu Gōng heard of this,
he knew that Lǚ Shàng could not long keep his state.
Attack and defense are different in form,
and the Way values an understanding of change,
yet Lǚ Shàng had not mastered the art of cooking fresh fish,
nor of distant governance,
but only promoted the methods of battle
and harmed men of high integrity.
One may say he relied on armor to complete the blade,
and moreover floated upon the currents,
using the technique of shooting at running targets,
desiring always to seek after the mark.
If you overturn the nests of common birds,
then the numinous phoenix will not gather there;
if you drain the pond of fishes and turtles,
then the divine dragon will journey far away;
if you pierce the wombs of ordinary beasts,
then the qilín will not tread on your outskirts;
if you harm even a solitary worthy,
then heroes will not set foot in your land.
Lǚ Shàng founded a great line,
leaving it as an example to later generations,
but he set the beginning for cruelty,
and opened the path for violence;
he only succeeded in driving the talented to benefit other realms,
expelling the worthy to become the legacy of rival enemies.
For those who sought horse bones in the market to entice fine steeds,
or used a humble alley to persuade Qín’s army to retreat,
how far apart these attitudes are!
Do you judge Lǚ Shàng as the equal of Zhōu Gōng?”
The official said:
“I am not able to judge.”
The recluse replied:
“Zhōu Gōng was a great sage;
he honored the lowly while being noble himself,
spitting out his food and grasping his hair in haste,
fearing to lose talented men.
He followed seventy men from humble houses,
and among men of plain clothing, he personally received ten who brought their tokens to learn from him,
and made friends with another twelve,
without compelling any of them to serve at court.
If, for example, Lǚ Shàng had held the place of Zhōu Gōng,
these people would have become corpses exposed in the marketplace or court,
their flesh decaying in ditches and streams.
It was not that Táng Yáo could not attract Xǔ Yóu and Cháo Fù,
nor that Yú Shùn could not coerce the virtuous Zhèng Shíhù,
nor that Xià Yǔ could not pressure Bǎi Chéngzǐ Gāo,
nor Chéng Tāng fail to detain Biàn Suí and Wù Guāng,
nor Wèi Wén king unable to overbear Qián Mù,
nor Jìn Píng king unable to make an official of Hài Táng.
And yet, they respected and studied under such men,
valuing them highly and giving them honor—
was this mere weakness of the Six Lords?
Truly, it was because they held myriad virtues in esteem,
and recognized how silent attainments are hard to match;
they longed for the noble reputation of honoring the worthy,
and were ashamed of the ugly traces left by harming the good.
To appoint such men would not in itself enhance authority;
to let them be would not, in fact, make the government empty.
To let their will have free course promotes culture and morality,
brings prosperity to humility and deference,
chastens those greedy for advancement,
and affects those of frivolous and rash temper;
even if their abilities do not serve immediate needs,
even if their talents are not those of successful courtiers,
is this not better than hunching shoulders and bowing brows,
flattering the men of power,
presenting gifts in secret,
consorting with dust and dirt,
scrambling for crossings and rushing for gain,
buying and selling names and reputations,
abandoning the foundation of virtue and study,
and running eagerly to ruin as at the end of the Zhōu?
Those Six Lords were unwilling even to criticize recluses harshly—
how then would they put them to the sword?
The way of sages and worthies is truly something to learn from,
and Lǚ Shàng was clearly mistaken.
Hàn Gāodì, though his minor conduct was often lacking,
and he was not versed in classical arts,
yet he was broad-minded and magnanimous,
skilled in forgiveness and accepting of many,
unconcerned with petty matters—
truly open in spirit.
Even though he hungered for Sì Hào’s service,
still he did not coerce them.
Later, the Crown Prince spoke humble words to bring them in,
desiring to have them as his wings,
then he respected virtue and restrained his own feelings,
valued what was most important,
sang the sad song of ‘Yellow Swan,’
and blocked the longing of concubines like Du Wǎn,
treasuring the worthy and cherishing recluses
to the utmost degree.
Therefore he could, as a man of humble birth, rule all under heaven;
his magnanimity was truly extraordinary.
Now, as for Lǚ Shàng’s killing of the wild and reclusive,
it was out of fear that they might weaken the masses.
Yet what troubles society
is only the frantic pursuit of advancement,
and the neglect of virtuous conduct.
It is not that there are too many who are content with poverty and delight in lowliness.
Even if recluses everywhere attract notice,
when it comes to pursuing profit and position,
and if one’s ambition knows no limit,
in the end one will never be able to cast off these common desires,
nor truly admire those who retire into quietude.
Since the beginning of time,
there have not been few men,
yet those who could forget wealth and fame,
could not make up even one in ten thousand.
Even Zhòngní studied directly under Lǎozi,
yet could not practice non-action;
Zǐgòng and Yuán Xiàn studied together,
yet could not emulate his purity and humility.
The Four Villains lived at the same time as Cháo Yóu,
Wáng Mǎng was contemporary with the Two Gōng,
yet could not follow their example.
Even if all the people were whipped and harried,
menaced and humiliated,
and made to pursue wild and reclusive Huá shì,
still they would never be willing;
how then could it be feared that they corrupt the common customs?
Lǚ Shàng could not see this;
he ruled peaceful times with military law,
wrongfully harmed the worthy,
and his cruelty was a grievous error!
Only thanks to his great achievements
did he not meet with disaster straightaway.
Moreover, before Lǚ Shàng met King Wén,
he, too, lived in obscurity and poverty,
and all men slighted him,
old women drove him away,
his labor was unsold,
he was unsuccessful at fishing and butchering,
and not a single person admired him.
In his retreat from the world,
was he the only one who feared wild Huá shì might undermine the masses?
If, for example, King Zhòu of Yīn had driven Lǚ Shàng to flee,
and then captured and gathered him in,
and when Lǚ Shàng faced death,
would he have said that he truly deserved punishment?
Wèi Wǔdì, too, enforced harsh laws,
was resolute in killings,
but in his heart wished to employ Kǒngmíng;
Kǒngmíng himself claimed he took no pleasure in entering office.
Wǔdì excused and dismissed him, saying:
‘It is not right to compel a man of such lofty character
to be humiliated by serving in a corrupted court.’
Though he scourged the realm
and founded imperial rule,
even so, he was not reckless.
“Over long years of turmoil,
the pursuit of gain has become the custom:
some use wealth and bribery to leap like a dragon,
others rely on party ties to rise like a phoenix,
the wind of such manners spreads,
and the great Way grows overgrown;
later generations are ignorant,
and the teachings of the scholars are thereby buried.
Now, those who wish to establish themselves
see wealth as the only means.
If there is anyone truly outstanding,
unwilling to step outside his threshold,
hiding his ambition and savoring the Way,
they truly ought to be specially sought out,
to promote humility and self-effacement.
When Sūn Wú and Wú Qǐ brandished their weapons,
it was but the strength of one man;
yet if their plans were employed,
they were worth more than ten thousand men.
Now, if great scholars are made into officials,
it is not necessary that they fit every practical need;
set them free among mountains and forests,
and they can mold and educate the young,
spreading the way of propriety and respect.
Why must we harness great elephants to catch mice, or use the bellows of phoenixes?
“Yet as for those who waste away in swamps and marshes,
living in vain and dying in obscurity,
how can they ever be valued?”
The yìmín replied:
“You might be called one who guards anthills,
amuses himself on Fox Mound,
but has not yet ascended Làngfēng to overlook the clouds and rainbows;
you play by clear islets,
wander through muddy pools,
but have not floated upon the Southern Sea nor crossed the Celestial River.
In general, those who are called men of aspiration
do not necessarily depend on rank and position,
nor must they rely on merit and conquest.
The highest have no self;
next best have no name;
able to spread their wings and soar beyond the flock,
set their traces far from common tracks,
accomplish what ordinary people cannot do,
cast aside what mere talent cannot part with,
care not for scarcity or abundance as judged by common folk,
pure and serene, untainted by reputation or rank,
their honest character can cleanse a hundred generations of corruption,
their lofty conduct can inspire future ages to purge defilement.
Why must one trail red or drag purple,
wear ceremonial caps and ride state carriages,
don the embroidered robes patterned after sacrificial oxen,
swallow the fragrant delicacies of Zhān Hé,
burn in the blazing heat of Zhāng Tiān by day,
and become cold ashes of frigid night by evening?
The shrike does not give up the heights of the clouds for brambles and thorns,
the great king tuna does not trade the vast ocean for a secluded cave,
tigers and leopards entering a grand hall feel grief,
wild swans and great birds atop lofty mountains harbor sorrow.
All creatures possess their own spirit,
content in fulfilling their strengths.
None are not at ease when finding fulfillment,
yet are distraught when displaced.
Men who manage the world,
all are like this,
for even a single day without a ruler,
they are restless and anxious.
It is as though, like the heaps of jade at Lántián,
or the abundant timber of Dènglín,
the skilled artisan and great craftsman
use them as they wish.
Why must fish roost in trees or birds immerse in water?
Lofty withdrawal and noble reclusion
are what the revered sages approved;
whether emerging or retiring,
each follows his own inclination.
“What the gentleman values
is to establish virtue and words.
As for filial piety, friendship, benevolence and righteousness,
noble conduct and pure mind,
these may be called establishing virtue.
Exhaustively studying the Fén and Suǒ,
producing distinguished writings,
these may be called establishing words.
Shàn Zhèng may not have ruled the people,
but cannot be considered inferior to vulgar officials;
Zhòng Ní gained no merit in conquest,
but cannot be said to fall short of Hán and Bái.
To preserve both body and reputation,
this is called the highest.
Living in reclusion, pursuing one’s will,
was commended by the ancients.
Yí Qí and Bóyí, though lone individuals,
refused to conform and change,
ancient men sighed and admired,
praising them for not lowering themselves to disgrace.
To say they did not lower themselves
shows the high value of reclusion;
while to say they were unashamed
indicates that to be fettered is base.
The purest among sages
was admired by Mèng Kē,
who also said the nobility of Heaven’s rank surpasses the jade seal and purple ribbon.
To cultivate virtue and leave behind worldly glory
was esteemed by Sūn Qīng;
when the Way and righteousness are complete,
one may slight princes and dukes.
Yet what worldly people fear is only power,
and value only profit.
If one of great virtue is kept back,
he is called a commoner;
if one of small talent is in high office,
he is hailed as a worthy man.
There are some who risk danger and brave peril,
throwing away their lives and forgetting death,
casting away their bodies beneath ten-thousand-foot cliffs,
to seize glory and wealth in a single morning,
but compared with those who dismiss All-under-Heaven and cherish even a hair of their shin,
how remote they seem!”
The official asked:
“Those who retire and withdraw,
finding fulfillment in mountains and marshes,
not relying on the honors of the world,
roaming at ease with wanton abandon,
not employed by the age,
and showing contempt for rank and profit,
are in truth the most useless things under heaven;
how should they be regarded?”
The yìmín replied:
“The qílín does not bark as a watchman,
the fènghuáng does not act as a cockcrow,
the flying yellow horse does not pull the plough,
corpse-bearers and sacrificers do not tend the kitchen.
Further, spreading great brilliance to all without exception,
what ought to nurture with warm, gentle wind
is the sun;
for shining lamps in the dark night,
working metal and stone to produce utility,
it is fire.
The world cannot go long without the sun,
nor even a day without fire,
yet their scale
cannot be compared.
Beyond rivers and seas,
encompassing the two fundamental forces,
rising as clouds and rain,
falling to become a hundred rivers;
for daily use
they do not match a many-fathomed well,
to irrigate fields and gardens,
are not as useful as ditches and channels.
Comparing their greater and lesser
which is vaster?
Jié and Zhòu
were emperors;
Zhòng Ní
was a mere subject.
If compared to Jié and Zhòu,
none would fail to be outraged;
if likened to Zhòng Ní,
none would not be delighted.
Thus, nobility and baseness truly are not found in offices.
Therefore Mèngzǐ said,
Yǔ, Jì, and Yán Yuān,
placed in different stations, would act the same.
Zǎi Yǔ also said
Kǒngzǐ far surpassed Yáo and Shùn in worthiness.
Ordinary men measured as equals with kings,
Confucian scholars reaching the heights even of Táng and Yú,
it is due only to virtue,
why care about office?
“Furthermore, when one’s spirit communes with creation,
holding heaven and earth in the embrace,
the affairs of the world never settle in his heart,
honor and disgrace cannot sully his pure whiteness,
what the vulgar desire
cannot taint his spirit,
what ordinary men are deluded by
cannot shift his intention.
Wealth and honor
are but warts and extraneous growths;
the myriad things
mere cicada wings.
For such as these,
how could they bend their limbs,
humble their bearing,
bow to things they despise,
seek out what they have rejected,
smile in order to advance,
stoop to avoid dismissal,
fearing the displeasure of common people,
anxious lest their bodies be tormented,
using the treasured sword of Lóngyuān as a drill or awl,
repressing the sacred drum Língfén to play trivial war music,
taking the grand axe Huángyuè and using it as a sickle,
lowering the splendid banner Huáqí to the bottom of a thicket?
Gǔgōng cast aside his staff as he retired,
Yuè Yì took to hiding underground to escape,
Jìzǎ withdrew to farming and left office aside,
Lǎo Lái watered his garden to stay away,
each following what he loves,
nothing could equal this.
Therefore, pure and unmixed,
this is true wealth;
if the body is not subject to coerced service,
this is true honor.
As for those assigned grants and lands,
that is merely called rank and profit,
not wealth and honor.
Furthermore, those in high office bear heavy burdens,
the accomplished are envied by all,
but only one who is poor and low
has none to contend with,
may secure lasting treasure,
and have no worries.”
"Washing furs and wearing cloth quilts,
picking amaranth and ceasing to weave,
piglets not covering the beans,
vegetables and coarse grains for meals,
yet still incurring the forced slander of accepting baseness and falsehood;
trees block and overturn the wine stand,
thrice returning to jade meals of royalty,
the wealth of Ráng Hóu,
the peace and comfort of Ānchāng,
then there comes the burden of overstepping one's station and polluting murk.
It is yet not as good as letting the spirit wander through canonical texts,
discarding the old and welcoming the new,
seeking fullness at the ends of the plow handle,
searching for warmth among the loom's shafts,
with the belly gazing at the river and thus satisfied,
the body gathering on a single branch and the rest at peace,
while all things teem and bustle,
transforming to dust and ashes.
Eating a little to barely survive,
wearing coarse cloth and woolen robes,
being indifferent and open, letting the will roam,
neither worried nor joyful,
this is noble delight,
comparable to nothing else.
"As for serving as an official,
is it to seek fame?
Then refining a single stroke is enough to vent resentments,
and composing texts is enough to leave behind one's name;
why rely on a good historian?
Why trouble with inscribing tripods!
Mèngzǐ did not take merit in arrows and stones,
Yáng Yún did not count ruling people and benefiting the age,
seeking benevolence and attaining it—
is that not enough?"
The official then said:
"The hermit,
is he not thereby disloyal?
Is it fitting for him to reside in the ruler's land
and eat the ruler's grain?"
The recluse replied:
"Why do you say so!
In the past, when Yán Huí died,
Lǔ Dìng Gōng intended to personally mourn,
and sent someone to inquire of Zhòngní.
Zhòngní said:
'All those within the state
are subjects.
' Then Dìng Gōng ascended by the eastern stairs,
performing the rites of a ruler.
From this, it can be seen that
'To the shores of the land,
none are not royal subjects.'
Those within the court offer their strength to manage affairs,
those in the mountains and forests cultivate virtue to admonish greed and impurity,
so though their paths differ,
both are subjects.
For the king there is nothing outside his domain,
the world is his household,
wherever the sun and moon shine,
wherever dew and rain reach,
all is his territory.
How could one hang suspended in empty space,
dine upon drifting clouds,
