and claim not to dwell upon the earth,
nor eat the ruler's grain?
"The gold and jade in the mountains,
the pearls and shells in the waters,
though not stored in the treasuries,
nor used daily,
are all the ruler's wealth.
The recluse not joining the ranks of the meat-eaters,
is like the things of mountain and water,
are these not the country's wealth?
Xǔ Yóu did not hide beyond the four seas,
Sì Hào did not flee past the Eight Wildernesses.
Thus it is said:
All the peoples of the myriad states offer tribute,
and together are subjects of the emperor.
The withered tree does not bear arms to guard borders,
nor build ramparts on the frontier,
yet accomplishes the duty of defending the realm.
Now, if the recluse keeps pure conduct within a thatched hut,
and sings the Way of the former kings,
making the people know how to retreat and concede,
upholding Confucian and Mohist teachings without letting them lapse,
this too is what Yáo and Shùn approved.
Of old, Yí and Qí would not eat Zhōu's grain,
Bào Jiāo died atop the bridge,
their stubborn rigidity,
what is worthy there to be a model?
"In former days, Emperor Ān sent black and red silks and jade to invite Zhōu Yǎnzǔ.
Emperor Huán sent black and red silks and jade to invite Wéi Xiūmíng,
Emperor Shùn with black and red silks and jade invited Yáng Zhòngxuān,
and offered him the post of Attendant-in-Ordinary,
but he did not come.
Wèi Wén Dì summoned Guǎn Yòu'ān, but he did not appear,
and offered him Director of the Imperial Household,
yet still he did not come;
thereupon an edict was issued for every locality to present a sheep and two measures of wine each eighth month.
Emperor Huán sent black and red silks and jade to invite Píngjiè Rúzǐ,
offering him the posts of Prefect of Tàiyuán and Chancellor of Dōnghǎi,
but he did not come.
Emperor Shùn sent black and red silks and jade to invite Fán Jìgāo,
who did not come;
so every eighth month the local authorities were ordered to present a sheep and two measures of wine,
and also bestowed table and staff,
treating him as a master and mentor.
In the time of Emperor Xiàn,
Zhèng Kāngchéng was summoned by the province for the roles of Worthy and Upright and Talented,
fourteen times by the main government,
but did not accept;
the Ministry of Personnel summoned Zuǒ Zhōngláng, Court Academician, Zhào Xiàng, Attendant-in-Ordinary, and Minister of Finance,
but none responded.
During Emperor Zhāo's reign, Hán Fú was summoned by the Ministry of Personnel,
he arrived,
and was rewarded with fifty bolts of silk and sheep and wine.
Fǎ Gāoqīng was recommended twice for filial and honest conduct,
summoned five times by his native province,
eight times by the main government,
nine times for Worthy and Learned,
thrice summoned,
but refused all.
Emperor Huán sent black and red silks, a ceremonial carriage and wheels to invite Hán Bóxiū,
but he did not come.
(He) sent black and red silks, and a ceremonial carriage and wheels to invite Qiè Bóyǎ,
offering him the posts of Senior Grand Master and Prefect of Jiānwéi,
but he did not take up office.
Yet all were given high regard,
and were not coerced or threatened.
If the various emperors' honoring of recluses was never mistaken,
then Lǚ Shàng's slaying of Huáshì was surely wicked cruelty and excessive wrong,
this is certainly known."
The official then looked dejected and lost,
and with a deep sigh said:
"Now at last I understand the transcendence of the doctrine,
not something the ordinary or petty may see."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Learning is that by which one clarifies purifies one's nature,
winnows away dust and filth,
carves and refines rough jade,
grinds and tempers the dull and simple,
awakens and leads to brilliance,
colors and polishes the plain,
discerns the past and understands the future,
broadly immerses and offers encouragement and restraint,
gazes upward and observes below,
in this way lies the method;
regarding human affairs and the kingly Way,
all is thus fulfilled.
Advancing, one can serve the country;
withdrawing, one can preserve oneself.
Thus the sages and worthies are invariably diligent and earnest,
exerting themselves night and day,
only at the end of their days do they rest,
never ceasing even in hunger, cold, danger, or distress.
Could it have been that they sought anything from their age?
They truly delighted in the natural course.
As for the meager arts of carving, shaving, and drawing,
the simple accomplishments of archery and charioteering,
they all require practice,
and only then can be done well,
how much more so for the vastness of human reason,
the remoteness of Dao and virtue,
the transformations of yin and yang,
the feelings of spirits and ghosts,
all of which are remote, subtle, profound, and obscure,
truly hard to be innately understood.
Even if something is said to be white,
if not dyed, it is not lustrous;
and even if sweet in taste,
if not harmonized, it is not delicious.
Thus, if precious jade flowers are not carved,
their night brilliance will not shine;
if red and green are not attended to,
the power of the fine hook will not forthcome.
If fire is not drilled, it does not appear,
if not fanned, it does not blaze;
if water is not released, it does not flow,
if not accumulated, it is not deep.
Therefore, though the substance is in me,
its achievement depends on others.
Only after ascending Làngfēng
and reaching the limits of dawn,
does one realize the narrow confinement of the well and ravine;
only after studying the Seven Classics,
delighting in the Hundred Schools,
does one sense the utter struggle of facing a wall.
Now, to seek knowledge without study
is like wishing for fish but lacking a net;
though the mind is diligent, there is nothing to gain.
To be broad and exhaustive in investigating principle
still requires the wind as its support;
the body does not labor, yet attains what is far.
When cosmetics arrive, they make Xī Shī even more beautiful,
while they hide the ugliness of those with old tumors.
When mastery of the classics is profound, the highly talented will comprehend thoroughly,
while the dull and blunt will be awakened.
Fine timber reaches the heavens in height,
but cannot be called a tower or a pavilion
because it lacks the handiwork of Bān Lún in construction.
One may be naturally straightforward and bright,
but cannot be called a gentleman
if he does not understand the great principles of right and wrong.
If one wishes to travel a thousand miles in a single morning,
he must rely on the feet that chase the shadow.
If one wishes to cross great waves and reach distant shores,
he must depend on the vessel and oar.
If one wishes to see the world beyond without leaving his hall,
he must rely on books and records.
If one wishes to fathom the profound and subtle without wearying the spirit,
he must gain it from an enlightened teacher.
Thus, vermilion and green dyes transform raw silk;
instruction serves to remove ignorance and obscurity.
If one spreads out mysterious clouds and manifests great illumination,
then all things have nowhere to hide their forms.
If one unrolls bamboo and silk records to examine the past and present,
then heaven and earth have nowhere to hide their truths.
How much more is this so for spirits and ghosts?
And how much more for human affairs?
Can mud and clay ever compare in hardness to gold and jade?
Can crooked wood be carved to meet the rule and compass?
Can all wild beasts be taught to form lines in war?
Can livestock be trained in advance and retreat?
Can aquatic creatures be stirred to action by sound?
Can inanimate stone be moved by sincerity?
How much more so for those endowed with the five constants and possessed of the utmost spirituality!
The team of horses that bows and rears,
is the result of training.
The fierce birds of prey,
are tamed through practice.
As for the ordinary horse and wild hawk,
by nature they are of the same kind;
it is this one who is made noble by refinement,
and that one who is base by its plainness.
If one directs his waters to flow ceaselessly,
they will surely merge into the vast sea;
if he keeps adding baskets of earth without rest,
he will surely reach the heights of the steepest mountain.
When great rivers surge in waves,
dragons and water-spirits gather and swim;
if one makes daily and monthly progress,
virtue is established and the Way becomes complete.
Thus one can attain correctness.
When dreaming at night and awakening at dawn,
how could one only escape bondage and ignorance!
In the past, Zhòng Yóu wore a rooster cap and a pigskin belt,
jade pendants like chirping cicadas,
he held a sword and danced,
praising the sturdy bamboo of Mount Nán,
wishing to rely on natural strength;
Confucius skillfully led and guided,
infusing him with moral education,
thus making the crude refined,
and producing the worthies of the four categories.
Zǐ Zhāng was a rustic,
and exceedingly coarse and cunning,
but gradually soaked in the teachings of the Way,
becoming a famous scholar by transformation,
and gained rank among lords and princes—
how could he have merely escaped mediocrity and vulgarity!
Thus, the worthy lament the fleeting nature of life,
and are pained by extinction and being left without renown;
they are moved by the grand teaching heard in the morning,
and awakened by the subtlety of penetrating understanding;
they fear the warning of those who fell,
and are shocked by the madness of aimless thought;
they do not pass the day sated with food,
nor abandon their efforts for one brief moment;
they are inspired by the swift passing of the river,
and grieve the lightning speed of the sunbeam through a crack;
they cut off idle passions,
reduce the trivial pursuits of the world,
cleanse the heart of worries over poverty,
dispel the taint of boundless desires,
cease the frivolous amusements of hunting and gambling,
and correct the slackness of napping and idly sitting in the daytime;
knowing that empty pondering is useless,
they thus set forth on the path of the sages.
Study is to accumulate it,
questioning is to discern it;
advance in virtue and cultivate one's work,
review what is old to know the new.
Zhōu Gōng, though of the highest sageliness,
read a hundred chapters a day.
Kǒngzǐ, endowed with heavenly talents,
wore out the bindings of his books three times.
Mò Dí, a great worthy,
filled carts with books.
Dōng Zhòngshū, destined to instruct his age,
never glanced beyond his garden gate.
Ní Kuān wore his classics at his waist as he weeded,
Lù Shēng cut reed stalks to make books,
Huáng Bà received learning while wearing shackles,
Nìng Zǐ labored from dawn to night, doubling his efforts;
thus they could fully explore the mysteries of the Way,
exhaustively discern subtle sayings,
gaze upon ten thousand ages as if it were a single day,
know the realm of the Eight Desolations as if it were their own courtyard,
examine the waxing and waning of the Seven Luminaries,
track the changes of the Three and Five,
discern the ebb and flow of prosperity and decline,
verify the good and bad through the past,
understand mysteries as if held in the palm,
distinguish things not yet come as if accomplished.
Thus they attained great virtue and grand achievements,
becoming the foremost of their age,
their clear brilliance and fame
spread boundlessly.
Furthermore, those who heard of the single-legged shāngyáng would take precautions against floods,
hearing of the bird nǔ they harmonized the east,
consulting the floating duckweed, they spoke of flavors and colors,
inquiring about earth-dogs, they learned about graveyard sheep,
studying the “Lingbao” to know about mountain recluses,
discussing chariot-parts through broken meat-trays,
gazing at the constellations Lì and Bì to understand the signs of yin and yang,
learning from winter grasshoppers to understand the errors of leap years—
what magic is in this?
It is only study.
Even children's chants aided the sages' senses;
how much more so the vastness of the “Fén” and “Suǒ” texts!
Abilities and nature differ in excellence,
thought and understanding in depth and brevity.
Some have innate knowledge and early achievement,
some must be admonished repeatedly before they understand.
Those who are quick to comprehend and learn at the right time
are as the feet of a fine steed;
those who are slow to grasp and realize late
are as the wings of a quail or magpie.
Though the latter may seek to fly over great distances,
if they stop and do not proceed,
their steps will not surpass others;
though the former may advance little by little,
if they go on without stopping,
even mountains and marshes can be crossed.
Such is the study of the clear-sighted and the dim-witted—
is it not so?
Indeed, when young, one's will is focused and difficult to forget;
when grown, the mind is scattered and easy to lose;
so learning must be engaged in early,
while still able to concentrate;
practice and nature merge,
becoming no different than the natural.
If one is talented above all others,
yet loses his prime years for some reason,
even if he misses the sun at the eastern valley,
he can still catch it at the western abyss.
Then one knows that good fields sown late
are still better than letting the years go to waste.
The analogy of the sunlight
is especially apt.
The ways of the world are beset by troubles,
the teachings of the scholars are in decline;
the tracks of civil and martial virtue
are on the verge of withering away.
Some drown in sounds and sights,
others are driven along paths of competition.
Those poor and solitary who refine the six arts
with the endowment of Yóu and Xià,
are still forced down to the underworld;
while those who catch the wind and ride the phoenix’s wings,
though mediocre by nature,
still drift about beyond the clouds.
Those who forsake the essential to pursue the trivial
are called diligent students;
those who cling to the classics for their own sake
are called pedantic and impractical.
Thus, all are exposed to dust and rain,
wearing frost and treading ice;
some clutching yellow, gripping white,
picking the pure and choosing the fat,
they all pursue the quick and easy by-paths,
thinking to plant in the morning and harvest in the evening.
As for drawing down the curtain and resting one's head on a lofty pillow,
letting the spirit wander through the Nine Canons,
delving deeply into the subtle and hidden meaning of principle,
tasting the Way while dwelling in tranquility,
firmly establishing an unshakable resolve,
exalting evergreen virtue after the coming of harsh winters,
not conforming to the world to shape one's conduct,
not drifting with the crowd like duckweed upon water—
such people are indeed rare.
Those who are anxious in their pursuit of advancement,
or dejected when hindered by misfortune,
how could they forsake the broad and easy avenue that swiftly reaches its goal,
to guard instead the blocked path that is so arduous and certain to lead to exhaustion?
This is why, by the river's edge, there are none to be found,
and thus was the “Zǐ Jīn” composed.
Those who grieve for the vulgar ways of the age feel pained in their hearts and sigh unceasingly;
those who worry for the Way harbor sorrow and are weighed down by melancholy.
Truly, cold and heat replace one another in turn,
misfortune, when ended, becomes prosperity,
Wén and Wǔ rise to prominence in succession;
such is the constant law of things.
I hope that the bandits may be thoroughly swept away,
that restoration might come in our own time,
the seven visible lights follow their courses,
the ancient state is made anew,
brandishing Heaven's great comet to sweep widely,
stirring the mighty furnace of the Nine Suns,
moving the great regulator at the imperial center,
opening the heavenly pattern to set things in order.
Refining and transforming the many kinds,
the artisan forms those who excel and stand out,
washing away accumulated dust,
removing perversion and returning to the correct.
Arms are stilled,
bows and arrows are kept in their quivers,
the academies of Bì Yōng flourish anew,
the young of the state are gathered,
culture and virtue refined,
golden tones resound,
and jade notes reverberate.
Let the gracious winds and clouds descend upon the hidden beginnings,
the bundles of silk be brought to the village fields,
let the phoenix with folded wings,
soar aloft in the pure emptiness;
let the noble steed with raised neck,
gallop for a thousand li.
May those with hidden talent, long constrained,
and those who have broadened their sight and learning,
the likes of Shēn Gōng and Fú Shēng,
unfurl their dark and brilliant banners,
ascend in carriages of woven rush mats,
utter words with conviction,
set forth and present their honest intentions,
make their persons manifest,
walk the Way,
so that the enlightened age may follow the lofty path of Yáo and Shùn,
and traverse the broad way to peace and plenty,
the mysterious current spreading to the nine limits,
the benevolent wind pervading everywhere without boundary.
When the five punishments are set aside and songs of praise rise,
when harmonious energy abounds and auspicious grain is born,
is this not most excellent!
In the past, at the time of Qín’s Second Emperor,
he did not value the Confucian arts,
abandoning the Way of the former sages,
and practicing laws of punishment and prisons.
The people saw no virtue,
only executions reached their ears.
Thus, befuddled, they did not know the way to return from confusion,
defeated, they did not know how to rescue themselves,
eventually tumbling from the heights of the clouds,
and were trampled beneath unfathomable depths as if ground like chives into powder.
To honor the exalted and the humble—
can this be done without discernment?
Bào Pǔ Zǐ says:
One who examines only the tip of an autumn hair
does not see the brilliance of the heavenly constellations.
One who indulges the mind in trivial matters
is not aware of the vastness and profundity of the Confucian Way.
One who dallies with shellfish forgets orchids and sweet-smelling herbs,
one who is lost in the great cannot find his way back.
Wood that is measured with line and ink will have no crooked or hollow pieces;
those who are steeped in the teachings of the Way are not people who are wrong or perverse.
Of all the arts by which order is perfected,
none excels learning.
The breadth of learning lies in not growing weary,
and not growing weary lies in the firmness of will.
If the will is not firm,
then the poor and lowly are anxiously bent on their livelihoods,
the wealthy and noble are sunk in indulgence and pleasure.
Thus, those with broad views and deep knowledge
have been rare throughout the ages;
while the followers who face the wall in ignorance
are as numerous as those who stand shoulder to shoulder.
If one is of humble station, then by day he toils at the plow to keep from hunger,
at night he gathers firewood to pursue his studies;
if in office, then in the intervals after lavish banquets,
he occasionally takes time to counsel and exhort.
If this were so, then there would be no need for those who regard learning as useless,
nor would there be lack of disciples such as Yóu and Xià.
There are also those who are pressed by hunger and cold,
for whom even coarse greens are insufficient,
their skin suffering from wind and frost,
their mouths deprived of rough grain and husks,
lacking resources to learn from a teacher,
with urgent needs in their households at dawn and dusk;
if they lay aside the plow, farmwork is neglected,
if they take up the book, their duties of support fall short.
Though their studies are thus incomplete,
who could blame them?
The so-called steed that can run a thousand li
is hindered beneath the salt cart;
ore fit for the blades of Chì Dāo
never makes it to the gate of the master smith Ōu Yě.
As for princes and lords' sons,
at leisure in noble enjoyment,
swaggering among fine silks and damasks,
not knowing the hardships of planting and harvest,
their eyes weary of colors dark and bright,
their ears worn out by Zhèng and Wèi music,
their noses sated with orchid and musk,
their mouths indulging in delicacies,
in winter wrapped in furs of sable and fox,
in summer clad in light gossamer and silk,
going out they ride in the light chariots of Qìng and Fēng,
coming home they feast amidst splendor and elegance,
decorating pillars with vermillion and kingfisher,
filling chests and cupboards without end,
displaying alluring ornaments to amuse the mind,
carousing in strong wine until deeply drunk,
leaders of drinking parties in action,
chiefs of the gambling tables at rest.
They know nothing of literary works,
regard scholars as mere weeds,
their words and writing lacking sound citation,
yet they forcibly draw the wrong analogies.
In debate, they surrender before the battle is won;
when faced with doubt, they grow haggard before they are old.
Even possessing the powers of advocacy of Shū Mài,
how are they any different from the blind?
Bào Pǔ Zǐ says:
I have heard that the heir to the Emperor
must enter the Tài Xué,
receive teaching from masters and inquire into the Way.
Those counted among the students of the state
must learn to care for the state before they can serve as ministers;
only then may they one day be rulers.
They must know how to fulfill the role of the son,
only then may they one day be fathers.
Therefore, it is by establishing learning that one enters government service;
not by learning how to govern.
He who wields the blade and yet wounds where he cuts
is what Zhèng Qiáo lamented.
To indulge the emotions and abandon oneself to desires
is called being less than human.
And for the sons of the noble,
born within the deep palace,
raised in the hands of women,
never having known worry or hardship,
nor ever having wearied their own thoughts,
some may not even have left the swaddling bands,
yet are given offices adorned with blue and purple rank;
their distinction outmatches their attire,
and they reside in clear and eminent positions.
They wield the power of life and death,
hold the authority to demote or promote,
honor and disgrace depend on their grant or denial,
profit and harm are settled by their lips and tongue,
fondness and aversion never cease for even a moment,
praise and blame thunder constantly at their ears.
Suspicion and doubt take countless forms,
resembling what is right but being wrong,
seizing upon opportunities to manufacture endless troubles,
borrowing old trusts to set clever traps,
the transformations of intrigue,
thousands upon thousands of threadlike schemes,
the craftiest reckonings cannot fathom them all,
nor ink and brush ever record them to the end.
Without art or learning,
how can one discern the true from the false, the right from the wrong,
and comprehend the deeds of ancient and modern times?
If one relies only on personal enlightenment,
without recourse to inherited wisdom,
can one truly avoid a disaster as total as the nest overturned or the cart capsized?
The former sages occupied lofty positions,
yet did not dare to forget the danger;
when loving their sons and wishing to teach them rectitude,
they carved and polished, shaped and refined,
and did not admit them to perversity or falseness.
They selected enlightened masters to model and complete them,
chose good friends to gradually nurture them,
supervised them in broad reading,
showed them examples of success and failure,
let them examine the past to comprehend the future,
observe the other to know themselves,
urge them onto the straight path,
restrain them within rules and discipline,
and kept them vigilant, as if standing with heels hung over ten thousand fathoms,
trembling, like riding a galloping horse over ice.
Thus they were able to avoid much regret and shame,
and preserve their chastity and good fortune.
In the past, all the Dòu and Méng obtained blessings from legacies of instruction,
while Huò and Yǔ suffered misfortune from following their own impulses;
Zhōngshān and Dōngpíng found security through loving antiquity,
while Yān and Lì were put in danger by facing the wall.
Forgetting not past events
is the best mirror for the present.
Tāng and Wǔ were influenced by Yī and Lǚ,
and thus their prosperity surged forth;
Xīn and Guǐ were influenced by flattery,
and so their downfall came suddenly.
As for friends and teachers,
it is most necessary to select and simplify.
One must choose men of humble means and virtuous conduct,
who establish themselves through purity and hardship,
and are feared for not following the crowd.
Those whose classical learning resembles Zhōngshū or Huán Róng,
whose strong integrity resembles Gōng Suì and Wáng Jí,
who can discuss day and night the ultimate paths of loyalty and filial piety,
whose upright demeanor confirms the traces of survival or demise,
to cleanse away filth and grime,
to separate the wicked and correct the crooked,
who must suppress emotion and follow the laws,
such are those who instruct in virtue.
At the end of the Hàn,
and during the later years of Wú,
it was not so.
Expecting carriages and caps to choose men for office,
entrusting nominees' reputations among factions of friends,
there were names of teachers and associates,
but without substance in correcting omissions.
Not only were they without benefit,
but actually became harmful.
Thus what they discussed and explained,
was not about morality;
what they presented and offered,
was not loyal or beneficial.
They cared only for fresh music and seductive beauty,
for graceful forms and exquisite skills,
criticizing the clarity or turbidity of singing,
judging the length and shortness of pipes and strings,
appraising hounds and horses for swiftness or dullness,
debating places for roaming and amusement,
comparing differing preferences in paths,
weighing the refinement or coarseness of carvings,
competing in the skills and blunders of board games,
calculating victory and defeat in fishing or hunting,
judging the charm or homeliness of courtesans and concubines,
finding fault with the vulgarity of dress,
disputing the worthiness of horses and vehicles,
and discussing the range and fit of bows and swords.
They attracted novelty and difference,
to no limit,
overflowing in excess,
increasing with each day and month.
When they discussed palaces,
they distantly compared them to Yáotái and Qióngshì,
or nearby imitated Àfáng and Línguāng,
finding even a thousand gates and ten thousand rooms constricted,
regarding Kūnmíng and Tàiyè lakes as shallow and crude,
mocking thatched houses as unworthy,
considering earthen steps as base and rustic.
The people's strength was exhausted by labor,
their savings squandered on frivolities,
raising earthen mounds to rival Sōng and Huò mountains,
diverting canal waters to resemble the Nine Rivers;
ascending flowery towers that reached the clouds,
and opening ornate windows touching the sky.
Licentious music clamored and confused the ear,
gauzy sleeves fluttered and dazzled the eye,
Púshàng and Běilǐ,
alternately performing and rising;
sometimes wailing, sometimes shouting,
turning day into night.
Lingering among feathered cups,
immersed beside music and rhythm.
Sometimes raising green canopies,
sometimes shooting bold birds in the fields,
racing light-footed atop steep heights,
exposing servants under the blazing sun,
departing with torches,
returning under the stars,
neglecting public duties and leaving them untended,
ignoring rewards and punishments, allowing disorder.
Sometimes launching painted boats on broad waters,
spreading fine nets in verdant streams,
dropping fragrant bait in rippling pools,
releasing singing girls by clear deeps,
letting tall wires drop for light wild geese,
drawing deep lines to catch hidden fish;
or setting traps in the forests and foothills,
closing encircling hunts on the marsh's edge,
lining up grooms in the lush grass,
racing noble horses on the plain,
letting spotted hounds chase cunning beasts,
sending hawks to strike flying birds,
strong crossbows to fell mad rhinoceros,
long spears to slay bears and tigers.
Such amusements,
continued for years without fatigue,
passing from year to year without end.
Moreover, adding the gatherings for the four seasons,
farewells and congratulations,
calling on frequent secret guests,
entertaining distinguished visitors with gifts.
Affairs among men,
became ever more secret and boundless.
Therefore, uprightness and propriety gradually disappeared,
while indulgence and dissipation grew ever stronger.
Their distance from Confucian learning,
became remote and vast.
Those who alone could discern the principles of rise and fall,
pull themselves out of disaster and mire,
forsake the hazardous path of ruined virtue,
and walk the great and lasting Way—
such men were indeed very few.
Alas!
Those who could truly safeguard the state and bring security to their families became extremely scarce,
while those who brought disaster and wept blood were without number.
Now sage and enlightened rulers are on the throne,
studying antiquity to aid the people,
strengthening dikes and defenses to prevent flooding and overflow,
making clear praise and blame to highlight encouragement and warnings;
so that the imperial clan and noble families,
and those of wealthy houses and youthful years,
must necessarily strive for excellence in Confucian learning,
restrain extravagance in arts and literature,
set aside the non-urgent ideas of Shì, Lǎo, and Zhuāng,
(the character yì is extraneous)
and devote themselves to the correct Way of the Six Classics.
According to Bào Pǔzǐ:
Pure and mysterious rises above after separation,
while turbid and yellow sinks below after division.
Therefore, the ranks of noble and base and their respective authorities
become evident.
The ancient sages took from the two principles,
thus establishing the path between ruler and subject;
they set up offices and assigned duties,
thus fostering a harmonious and flourishing transformation.
Those who govern must surely cultivate themselves first to precede all within the Four Seas,
eliminate factional bias to make the kingly Way impartial,
cast aside personal feelings to set a standard for utmost fairness,
embracing the universe to encompass all diversity.
When truth and falsehood are distinguished beyond the realm of things,
one can also show oneself accordingly;
when hearing and receiving are keen through broad connection,
one can also make one's own voice heard.
Open sluices to advance the good,
break the taut string to dismiss the evil,
illuminate virtue and block deviation,
always draw near and cherish the worthy,
so that the compass fulfills its circle,
the square reaches its sides,
the line is fully straightened,
the axe discloses its cut.
Vessels are not assigned tasks for which they lack measure,
and talents are never employed amiss.
Examine titles and verify substance;
frequently review and labor with care and compassion;
establish teachings and precedents to show the utmost to the people;
scrutinize praise and blame to manifest encouragement and discouragement;
clarify regulations to prevent usurpation and excess;
analyze right and wrong to avoid obscurity and stinginess.
When bestowing benefits,
let there be no undeserved fortune through perverse governance;
when taking something away,
let there be the concealment of a hundred schools.
Craft skills by the Six Arts;
set rules by loyalty and trustworthiness;
administer by kindness and harmony;
keep order by propriety and law.
Expose the mean and narrow to urge restraint and suppression;
stir the pure current to clarify good and bad.
Let there be no deceitful ways among things;
no transgression of bounds in affairs.
Those who stand at court and govern the people
must not encroach upon offices or overstep their jurisdictions;
those who push the axle and take up arms
must not shrink from danger or disobey orders.
Win over those near to cherish those far;
cultivate culture to attract and bring in the estranged.
Enrich the wealth and grain of the people;
broaden the wide path of advancing virtue;
shut off the many affairs of intrigue and deceit;
then make punishments clear and laws strict;
judge cases with compassion and reverence.
When customs are pure and harmonious,
flaws and ailments are hidden;
benevolence reigns in leniency throughout the Five Teachings.
Outwardly, gather many scholars in civil and military ranks;
inwardly, build harmonious kin within as the fortress of stability;
let close and distant relations hold each other mutually;
the tail serves as the support of the body.
Branches may be luxuriant, but there is no fear of harming the root;
streams may be plentiful, but there is no trend of turning from the source.
Rocks are firm and mountains stand tall;
thus restrain covetous desires.
Noting the fall and extinction of the Sānmiáo,
one understands that river sources cannot always be relied on;
beholding that Yèyōu could not defend itself,
one realizes that mere precipitousness cannot be depended on.
Even when the Jiāng and Hàn Rivers remain,
the strong state of Chǔ suffered humiliation;
though Jiàngé passes endure,
Zǐyáng's clan was destroyed.
The Four Peaks and the Three Mounds of earth
are not the domain of a single surname;
metal-walled fortresses and moats of boiling water
are not as good as harmony among men.
If the defense lies overseas,
it is not the mountains and rivers that secure it.
Therefore a worthy ruler holds fear as at times insufficient,
and sees correcting his faults as possibly still not enough.
When planning for profit,
he yet ponders danger and never rests;
after victory in war and the expansion of territory,
he still fears excess and keeps vigilant by night.
He emulates the round heavens in far-reaching protection;
models the earth's thickness in broad nurturing.
He sets the weighty lights to make the subtle plain;
projects distant thoughts to what is yet unmanifest.
Draws on the spring's warmth to nurture and soothe;
follows autumn frost to make things solemn.
Consults the provinces to verify sameness and difference;
balances and weighs the words of the multitude.
Empties his own mind to fully receive lower opinions;
assigns merit to encourage those yet to come.
If governed only by techniques,
then the beginning and the end can be exhausted;
if regulated by proper measure,
then what is uneven can be made harmonious.
He stands lofty as Làngfēng soaring up to the sky,
and subordinates cannot measure him by lightness or weight;
profound as the abyss of ten thousand fathoms,
those nearest cannot estimate him by smallness or largeness.
Thus the flow of the ruler's virtue is inexhaustible,
and the talents of all the hundred officials are fully displayed;
the limits of my domain have no outside,
and the weight of theirs can be set with limits.
When orders are issued,
then chariots rumble like the reverberating thunder,
and will not be swayed from correctness by crooked debate.
When laws are drawn and systems established,
they shine forth like the seven luminaries adorning the sky,
and are not bent by personal like or dislike.
When he plans grand strategies with distant foresight,
it is like thick clouds high overhead.
In holding steadfast and completing tasks,
he is as firm as the roots of Mount Sōng and Dài.
Weighing possibilities before their sprouting,
judging praise or blame from the mouth of clever speech.
He does not let honest simplicity be scattered by artifice;
does not let unity be corroded by duplicity.
Even if able to judge alone,
he certainly welcomes broad advice from the lowliest;
though keen to be inclusive and generous,
he keeps his ear pure from insidious influence.
If the people are cold and hungry,
he pities them and blames himself;
if the people commit crimes,
he claims the fault is with himself.
If auspicious signs arrive,
he credits the help of the spirits;
if he encounters Heaven's wrath,
he thinks of the Sānglín ceremony, taking blame upon himself.
He is not reluctant to change strings to a more suitable tune;
does not feel shame in retracing the path of morning errors.
He glances like a tiger to guard secrets;
stands like a qilín to connect with both close and distant.
If along the road there are no elders beating the earth in contentment,
he is ashamed to hear music of harmony being played;
if the people lack grain to eat,
he regrets partaking of banquets.
Dwelling in lofty pavilions reaching the sky,
he fears the exhaustion of the laborers;
tasting the deliciousness of choice delicacies and the color of the moon,
he worries for those who suffer from late harvests;
hearing the music of pipes and strings at feasts,
he grieves that comfort and pleasure may go to excess;
beholding the brilliance of ornate speech,
he is concerned for the hardships caused by taxes and levies.
He follows the coarse furs of Fàngxūn;
models after the great cloths of Wèi Wén;
recalls the humble palaces of the Xià;
remembers the unfulfilled grand tower;
reflects on Zhānghuá's calamity-summoning;
understands Āpáng's quickly incurred disaster.
In announcements and oaths, he recalls the loss of trust through untimeliness.
In indulgences, he is alert to the bewitchments of Bāo and Dá.
In campaigns, he weighs strength and times,
not letting the people of a hundred li lament in sorrow;
in executions, he lets feeling go and follows justice,
preventing a Chī Yí from dying with grievances.
Reflecting on Dù Bó's loyalty at Cāo and Tóng;
admiring Rén Lì's denunciation as "calling out the pig."
When abolishing an heir of rank, cautions against Jìn Xiàn's great delusion.
When establishing a secondary heir, recalls Liú Biǎo's extinction of his sacrifices.
In hunting, rejoices at losing game but gaining worthy men;
recognizes the pursuit of the distant as a cause for delight.
Partial favor provokes anxiousness over Huì Fēng's slander;
Dài Yàn's monopoly on favor.
Monopoly in power prompts reflection on the deer-and-horse confusion of authority;
Kōng Xiǎn's malice toward honesty.
When accepting remonstrance, thinks of Hànzǔ spitting out his food;
Xiào Jǐng's execution of Cuò.
When offered delicacies,
becomes distant from Yí Dí.
When indulging and appeasing,
is reminded by Shěn Luán's admonitions.
Removes Zhēngzǐ's flattery;
draws close to Fàng Mí's benevolence.
Reflecting on Báilóng curbs frivolity;
considering Léiguàn restrains greed.
Prevents human and swine disasters inside the inner palace;
halts the search for blood-sweating steeds beyond distant borders.
Removes vicious dogs to prevent the perils of drunkenness;
buys the bones of horses to attract the fleet.
Endures the wrath of frogs to encourage bravery;
avoids the praying mantis to inspire martial valor.
Hears the frank admonitions of Gōng Lú;
embraces the integrity of Bǎojiǎ.
Removes useless hair from back and belly;
grasps all six wings for use in soaring.
Scalds the tongue like a reed pipe to heed the warnings of Sīyuán;
breaks with Yuǎnruò to follow Liáng Bó's merits.
Lets Dān Jī go to end enchantment;
dismisses Zǐxiá to halt the Peach of Temptation.
Keeps the fish hidden in the depths;
grasps the handle of sharp tools.
Does not shun the trouble of moving firewood,
to reduce the costs of scorching and burning.
Beats the drum of honesty and shame to mold character;
clarifies fair standards for examination and assessment.
In anger, he does not overstep the law to inflict cruelty;
in joy, he does not transgress the statutes to bestow excessive gifts.
He suppresses his feelings toward those he loves,
yet, should they offend, there is no pardon;
he discerns merit in those he dislikes,
and, if they have merit, he does not neglect to reward them.
He lowers himself to receive loyal counsel from subordinates,
listens to unpleasant words without concealment.
He broadly seeks advice even from slander,
though put down and pressured, never refuses it.
He overlooks minor flaws to employ those of great use,
forgets recent faults to remember distant achievements,
causing those like Cáo Guì and Mèng Míng to excel in effecting good on arrival,
and Wèi Shàng and Zhāng Chǎng to establish feats of removing disgrace while standing in the snow.
Corrupt ministers who ensnared themselves,
are entrusted with grand tasks that bring union and rectification;
left-hand charioteers once bound,
now display the highest strategies for ending war.
Thus, even owls and night-hawks are transformed into mandarin ducks and luan birds,
and the devious and false become loyal and upright.
Wild grasses flourish upon barren ground,
and luminous jewels arise from mire and mud.
Cutting sharpness rides the tide,
the nine meritorious achievements are all harmoniously realized;
he faces west with respectful hesitation,
to invite talent among teachers and friends;
he honors and serves the old men,
to promote acts of filial piety and brotherly love.
Thus, those who hid in the depths look up and come forth,
those who dwelt in the mountains bow down and assemble.
Illustrious and flourishing are his inner aides,
nine tigers watch fiercely to defend the outer gates.
The government is well-managed above,
and the people are devoted below;
kindness springs forth near at hand,
and its benefit extends far away.
The wise and sagacious exert their strength in whatever they govern,
and the common folk yield their borders in the marshes and swamps.
Then you cleanse and enrich the statutes and decrees,
arouse the pure wind of great harmony.
Reeds wheels and jade silks,
draw forth the worthy people from hamlets and fields;
all talents gather together,
to thoroughly discuss the gains and losses of the Dao.
The number of herders of sheep is lessened,
you return to unmixed spirits not to be sold,
spread the gates of benevolence and humility,
block the ferry of competition for honors,
signal the conduct of righteousness and rectitude,
uphold the standards of the Dao and simplicity.
Those who cling to virtue rejoice like sprouts basking in the sweet rain,
and those who come to submit are like streams flowing toward the great river.
The common people find peace in it,
like green leaves attached to tall branches;
those who wear their robes the left way look up in admiration,
like the multitude of stars circling the Pole Star.
Thus, the seven agencies do not disrupt the celestial order at the dark pole,
cold and warmth align with their proper seasons and assemble in order.
The four divine creatures are all seen,
and the rare fungus shines brilliantly.
Sweet dew drips down and attaches to the sky,
fine grain sways delicately and fills the granaries.
The red demon is driven off by the divine pool,
the dark curse is restrained in the vast expanse.
All rivers show no sign of boiling or turbulence,
the southern Dipper calms and flattens the tempest upon the crops,
no creature withers out of season,
no man voices a sigh or complaint.
Prisons stand empty,
the five punishments are suspended and laid aside.
Where the calendar does not reach,
where caps and sashes are absent,
where felt coats and fur garments are worn,
where people dwell in mountains and float upon seas,
none fail to wear glad looks and change their hearts,
moved by harmony and translating gratitude many times over;
spirit birds are sent as tribute to the Vermilion Court,
jade rings are presented from the farthest west.
Those who formerly were rebels suddenly become good,
like mist yielding to the steady wind;
those at earth's edge respond to the summons,
like resonant echoes harmonizing with rare sounds.
Truly, this is the height of prosperous ascension,
the pattern of Sān Wǔ ages.
Therefore he is able to secure temples and ancestral shrines for all eternity,
and cause his lineage to flourish for a hundred generations.
For when the roots are deep, the branches are luxuriant;
when those below are content, those above are secure.
If the horse is untrained,
even Zào Fù cannot make it gallop a thousand li;
if the people do not submit,
not even Táng Yú can produce a world of perfect harmony.
When the horse reaches its limits, strange behaviors arise,
and overturning and failure give all cause for dread;
when the people are distressed, division and rebellion multiply,
and disaster must surely sweep through.
Should one not be ever vigilant, awaiting each dawn?
Should one not be ever wary, thinking on peril?
If the ruler does not clarify his thoughts regarding order and disorder,
does not deeply reflect on omens of destruction,
then though his eye discerns the hair of an autumn rabbit at a hundred paces,
and his ear distinguishes the subtleties of the eight tones,
in letters, the luster of fine jade may pour from his brush,
in martial affairs, his hooks and spears may snap between his fingers,
his mind may store the recitation of ten thousand scrolls,
and his mouth utter waves of debate,
still, it is of no use against the collapse of the land,
and cannot rescue the crumbling of tiles.
Why is this?
Because he does not dwell in the great things,
but busies himself with the petty,
gets stuck in the undertakings of those beneath,
and loses sight of the original source.
If truly he can attend to affairs beyond the multitude,
approach depth and tread on ice,
while living in security not forget the admonition of runaway steeds,
while secure in existence not forget the fear of perishing,
managing the main threads to order the details,
holding firmly to the Dao to repel subordinates' ambitions,
with Hán and Bái giving their utmost to shatter the enemy,
with Xiāo and Cáo exhausting their ability to govern the state,
the solitary one's heart bringing forth his determination,
and advisers combining their thoughts to advance superior strategies;
then, even if the ruler lounges at ease within the jade chamber,
and strolls freely atop the cloud terrace,
while feathered cups go moldy amid sweet wine,
and musicians are worn out by endless performance and dance,
he can still govern by resting his arms and entrusting the worthy,
lean back on his pillow, commanding success.
Why must he dwell in a thatched hut's narrowness,
eat thin broths of plain gruel,
personally oversee the labor at the gate,
harbor bitter toil and risk shortening his lifespan,
only thereby to spread grace among the common people,
and extend the Dao overseas!
As for a muddled and deluded ruler,
he is not so.
His governance is such that
sometimes he is kindly but indecisive,
red and purple mingle in confusion,
the upright are not rewarded,
the wicked are not punished.
Sometimes he is harsh, fierce, and cruel;
sometimes only his authority is present, with no kindness.
Penalties are excessively heavy,
without mercy and not reaching their target.
The roots are exposed and the foundations crumbling,
perilous as a nest beneath a canopy,
yet he compares himself to the sun and sky,
and supposes his solidity like Tài Shān.
He thinks it is not difficult to equal the brilliance of the truly virtuous,
or that those who are careful and cautious are not worthy of consideration.
Thus, the innocent and blameless,
are victims of licentious punishments,
people see no virtue,
and hear only of executions.
In appointing officials, he takes only those who follow his will as worthy,
in promoting talent, gives precedence to those near him in habit.
High ministers fill the court,
entrusted to the kin of the Empress Dowager;
power and decision-making
rest with sycophantic attendants.
Those they recommend are distant relatives beyond the nine degrees of kinship,
without properly examining their abilities;
those they trust and rely on are petty talents skilled in flattery,
while upright men are detested;
those they suppress and dismiss are chosen for their conformity,
without discerning their true hearts;
those they promote and favor are judged by fair speech,
without assessing their actual achievements.
Those presiding over key government posts,
and marshals in charge of warfare,
may plunder and corrupt their stations,
may seek self-interest and disrupt the court,
may display weakness and ruin all affairs,
may be cowardly and lose military advantage.
In the end, no one perceives it,
nor has the heart to dismiss and expel them,
even continues to personally entrust them,
hoping for some late improvement.
Petty men are put in charge of great matters,
so calamity ensues.
Good talents of broad vision and unsupported men,
may wear coarse garments and hide in the court,
may sink and vanish into hardship and adversity,
harboring the Way and sealing their mouths,
the people's efforts have no outlet,
and disaster and decline
therefore often happen.
Again, though the canons and scriptures offer admonitions,
they are neither heeded nor read;
instead, one indulges in frivolity and extravagant feasts,
devoting oneself entirely to such pursuits.
From high towers, one looks down upon Dàodé,
with broad parks yet a narrow approach to the acceptance of people;
deep ponds and pools but shallow in grace and faith;
delighting in dogs and horses but disliking those who are honest and direct;
valuing pearls and jade but despising wisdom and strategy;
having rich brocades and fine silks but being stingy in acts of kindness;
slow to give relief but quick to amass taxes;
diligent in hunting and fishing but neglectful of agriculture;
emphasizing annexations but disregarding the lives of the people;
promoting entertainers while dismissing the refined and scholarly;
favoring favorites and confidants while treating soldiers with contempt;
chasing after pleasures and beauties while forgetting state affairs;
feasting first and only then hearing legal cases;
frequently assigning harsh labor and rarely granting rewards;
craftsmen spend heavily to create unnecessary objects,
and animals are kept penned and fattened for their meat, wasting grain.
If so, then disaster and destruction cannot be blamed on Heaven,
nor weakness and decline on other people.
For fortune and misfortune arise from oneself;
how could Tāng and Wǔ have been the same?
In ancient times, Zhōu Wén covered the bones of the unburied dead,
and all under Heaven praised his benevolence.
Yīn Zhòu split the heart of Bǐ Gān,
and the realm detested his cruelty.
Reputation rests in clear view,
and blame or praise comes swiftly.
Acts that bring gain or loss
do not depend on their multitude.
If praise accumulates, even the Mán and Mò will come in allegiance,
yet it cannot be demanded in vain;
when slander accumulates, even Huáxià will lose heart,
and words cannot save it.
Thus, even small good deeds, though lacking great benefit,
must nonetheless be done;
minor evils, though bringing no immediate harm,
still should not be ignored.
If one abandons restraint and gives way to desires,
without sharing their pleasures with the world,
then sorrows arise for which none show concern.
To undermine one’s own foundations and despise their height,
without realizing that collapse starts from below and then the top falls,
means that when the state totters, none will support it.
At that point, the reins and whip depart from my hand,
the spirit of Heaven withdraws and does not return;
efforts multiply, yet resources are exhausted;
the people cannot bear their fate;
resentment rises below,
Heaven’s wrath descends above;
Tián Chéng becomes a thief, and Quán Qí commands from his tent,
Jī Chāng gains two states from his western neighbor,
the followers of Chén Wú,
brandish swords and shout aloud,
the likes of Liú and Xiàng,
wield halberds in a tempest of fury;
siege ladders scale the walls a hundred battlements high,
gleaming blades cross beneath elephant defenses.
Assaults rush from within,
the guards break apart from without.
Then, in grief and sorrow, they long for the sages of old,
holding a broom they invite reclusive wise men who dwell in the cliffs,
admiring Yī and Lǚ in the peaks of Sōng,
calling for Sūn and Wú from the wild thickets,
respecting wise discourse but finding none to heed,
longing for good counsel yet asking no one.
This is like when a grand mansion is already ablaze,
yet one tries to fetch water from the distant sea;
the house is flooded,
but one builds boats on the high terrace.
Exalted praise
should not make one arrogant or covetous in building;
the sacrifices at the Dōngyuè
are not so easily used to indulge desire or expansion.
Even the highest sages press forward and ride fast,
still fearing they will not match those before them;
yet ordinary rulers proceed slowly and rein their horses,
believing themselves capable of exceeding the ancients.
Some, in times of peace, think on danger;
others, in peril, find comfort in themselves.
Some, having succeeded and stabilized order,
remain neither idle nor negligent;
others, with their cap dangling and fate balancing like stacked eggs,
remain unaware and unawake.
If not for the downfall of Xīn and Guǐ,
why would the worthy and prudent be needed to aid in crossing high waters?
Let this ever be remembered,
let it ever be!
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
Long ago, in the times of Tāng and Yú,
they reverently considered the past and were prudent and wise,
yet still awaited assistance from all the feudal lords
to achieve their most eminent deeds.
Therefore, they could gloriously uphold the celestial mandate,
and all undertakings were harmonious and steadfast,
the four gates in dignified order,
the hundred officials acting in due sequence,
the southern and eastern tribes had no rebellions to threaten Huá,
and phoenixes nested in palace eaves.
As the head is to the body,
as arms and legs to the trunk,
though there is a difference between high and low,
in truth, they function as mutually dependent parts of a single body.
A ruler who always matches positions to abilities
is prepared against the disaster of someone unfit attempting to serve;
a minister who always weighs his talents as he accepts office
will have no fear of exile or calamity.
Those who obey like shadows and echoes,
who bow and submit completely,
are nothing more than idle corpses given shelter.
Those who defy commands and speak frankly,
risking themselves for the public weal,
are the true wings of the people.
Those who anticipate the ruler’s wishes and intentions
are merely flatterers and sycophants;
those who correct mistakes and dissuade wrongs
are the backbone of the state.
Only by risking the executioner’s axe and speaking upright admonitions,
speaking forthrightly even when suffering severe punishment,
can one be called loyal and honest,
and if frank advice is not accepted,
it is proper to withdraw;
for to die without benefit
only increases the ruler’s faults,
and so it is better to depart.
If one acts,
let it never be contrary to canon or precedent;
if one abstains,
let it never be in violation of the constitution or statutes.
Personal requests find no place,
the law is strictly applied, not favoring kin.
Punishments are enforced with clarity, but do not fall upon the hated rashly;
rewards are given justly, not lavished on favorites.
Never monopolize orders to seize power,
never conceal filth and claim purity.
In office, one should speak exhaustively to correct errors;
in retirement, one should promote the worthy and not obstruct them.
Rise early and sleep late,
ever anxious for the welfare of the people;
economize in self and check desires,
as if treading on thin ice.
Accepting advice and men of merit,
one does not boast about it;
profits gained unethically,
one does not harbor them in the heart.
In court, one must maintain resolute integrity like a whetstone and arrow;
at home, gentle and pure like lamb’s fleece.
In times of crisis and difficulty,
one forgets family and does not spare one’s own life.
Holding the seals of office and weights of justice,
be impartial, showing no preference.
Emulate the management of Xiāo and Cáo,
admire the outstanding strategies of Zhāng and Chén,
pursue the unyielding loyalty of Zhōu Bó,
model after the uprightness of the two Bào,
tread the path of Yīng and Hóng’s steadfastness,
maintain Tián and Yì’s constancy to the end,
be willing to face hardship and burning punishment,
guard against Hán Yīng’s disaster for failing in loyalty.
Outside, do not shrink from toil;
inside, do not count your achievements;
upon returning with merit, claim responsibility for faults;
yield precedence to the lowly;
devote yourself with sincerity and awe,
always as if the awe of Heaven is upon your face;
be vigilant night and day,
as if boiling caldrons waited by your side.
In shouldering heavy charges,
take Yī and Zhōu as your examples;
when exerting yourself in all directions,
let Jí and Zhào be your models;
in sending off the departed and attending the present,
exhaust your loyalty and never falter;
when striking down traitors to the code of kingship,
be fierce as the eagle or hawk chasing sparrows;
defending the frontiers,
admire the noble footsteps of Wèi Jiàng and Lǐ Mù;
governing and consoling the people,
aspire to the virtuous transformation of Wén Wēng and Xìnchén.
Those most loyal have nothing more to offer for the state,
much less then can the confused wise contribute.
Those most dutiful to righteousness suffer disaster unflinchingly,
how much less will they shrink from disgrace?
Thus they preserve their toil and honor and glorify their families,
entrusting their renown to be sung in carriages.
The bronze vessels of Kūn Wú
bear the inscriptions of the meritorious.
Gāo Yáo and Hòu Jì,
who, after all, were but men!
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If the achievements of a ministerial subject are not extensive,
then he will be ashamed of receiving an unmeritedly generous salary;
if his accomplishments are not outstanding,
then he will feel shame for being granted a rank or title that is unjustly high.
If he acts with sincerity and seeks harmony,
Heaven and men will together aid him;
if he fears excess and maintains humility,
then in the end he will surely have good fortune.
When he lifts his feet, he steps according to the Way and its measure;
when he raises his hands, he follows the standard and the rule;
though praise and elevation may be slow in coming,
yet regret and disgrace will certainly be kept at a distance.
If one diminishes the ruler to curry favor with inferiors,
neglects public duty to pursue private gain,
flatters and bends to others’ wishes,
tries to mix water with water,
and even if the ruler’s actions are mistaken,
yet mocks, flatters, and commends him as good,
frequently presenting playthings and trinkets,
thereby leading the lord into evil,
employing clever words to undermine right governance,
using pleasing expressions to curry favor,
thus obstructing the ruler’s insight above,
and sealing off the path of worthy advancement below;
making external ties outside the borders,
and forming cliques of factional opposition within—
though one’s talents suffice to cover up wrongs,
and words suffice to embellish faults,
exercising sole authority like Zhào Gāo,
monopolizing power at court like Dǒng Zhuó,
there has never been one who did not perish beneath sharp blades,
whose family did not become scorched by boiling water or fire.
Yet the ignorant and blind abandon righteousness and follow evil,
shun truth and consort with falsehood,
witnessing collapse and ruin in person,
yet not altering their course,
so when disaster and calamity befall them,
it is not because Heaven has sent it down.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If ministers are likened to the arms and legs,
then they are the hands and feet of the state.
When walking on ice or handling something hot,
one cannot refuse the task.
For this reason, the ancients compared ministers to the earth:
if you dig it, springs of water emerge;
if you plant in it, a hundred grains flourish;
the living stand upon it,
the dead are laid within it.
Achieving much but not seeking reward,
laboring to exhaustion without daring to complain—
discerning this duty
is the essential way to safeguard oneself.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If ministers keep to their proper responsibilities, there is good governance;
but if duties are too broad, many affairs will be obstructed.
Without the strength of Bēn Huò,
one cannot bear the heavy load of replacing another;
without exceptionality surpassing ten thousand men,
one cannot take charge of offices with diverse demands.
Thus, Lord Hán was punished for overreaching duties,
and Zǐ Yuán feared the misfortune of not being able to bear the burden.
If, however, one’s talent and strength are unparalleled,
both literary and martial virtues fully present,
with profound plans at home which are the ruler’s confidants,
with distant strategies abroad to resolve conflicts,
then even heavy responsibilities will be handled with greater success,
both internal and external matters will be managed well together;
if such a person is withdrawn, the moral order is disrupted;
but if such responsibilities are delegated, and there is no such person,
then combining offices is allowable;
if not of this capacity,
one should examine oneself and withdraw,
for a cart yoked to too much weight
rarely reaches its destination.
Most people crave honor,
not considering future disasters;
once their own persons are already ruined and submerged,
disaster reaches their ruler and kin,
is this not pitiable!
Everyone declines to wield the axe and adze where the path is not yet cleared,
but none refuse to temporarily assume offices for which they are unfit.
Alas!
It was for this reason that Chén Lǐ gave warning against striving beyond one’s strength,
and Zǐ Fáng withdrew and relinquished his post to avoid overstepping.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Birds that fly and perch without choosing the tree
are surely those that will fall into nets and snares.
Those who begin their careers without considering the times
are surely the men who will meet with peril and disgrace.
When the time is favorable,
then one soars as the yìnglóng surveys the swirling clouds;
when the time is lost,
then one is as a great fish stranded and withered upon high ground.
For this reason, the wise one conceals his talent and waits for the right moment,
hides his person to be able to act when the time comes.
A high precipice about to tumble
cannot be held up by a mere thread;
the boiling waters at Lóngmén
cannot be barred by handfuls of earth.
Thus, one does not rashly work for profit and disappear from view;
one does not cast oneself into danger in hope of fortune.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When Zhōu Gōng assumed the royal throne,
Yī Yǐn deposed Tài Jiǎ,
Huò Guāng removed Chāngyì,
Sūn Lín forced the Young Emperor to retire,
these are called abandoning the norm and using expediency
for the peace of the state and temples.
Yet when Zhōu Gōng exiled unruly nobles,
slander filled the roads;
Yī Yǐn was finally executed,
a great fog lasted three days;
Huò Guāng was nearly implicated himself,
his family soon perished as well;
before the mulberry tree had shifted its shade,
Sūn Lín’s head and feet were separated.
Before the laughter of the crowd had stopped,
cries and lamentation had already arisen.
When danger is not contained,
what use is having such a minister?
If there are seven disputing ministers,
there is no way to rescue the state.
Thus, men like Wáng Mǎng
fostered their cunning and deceit,
outwardly citing old precedents to disguise their wrongs,
inwardly harboring wolfish treachery,
and though the foundations lay with Yī and Huò,
that is where the chaos began.
In the future, those of worth
would do well to consider this deeply.
As for enthroning and deposing rulers,
in petty submission it is great rebellion,
and must not be allowed to continue.
The deceptions of King Zhào
have already met with disgrace;
how much more so for deposing the ruler—
how could this be acceptable!
All these cases follow the logic of acting to gain success,
and soon after suffering disaster.
As for those whose secret plans are betrayed by the greedy,
their whole clans are exterminated;
yet in other families who were enfeoffed,
there were not a few.
If sycophants help bring about arrogant disorder,
like how Jié was assisted by Gān Xīn and Tuī Tuō,
Zhòu by Chóng É Lái,
or the factions of King Lì,
replacing the loyal and good
is all too easy.
Purging the many villains near the ruler,
exiling fierce clans to far-off borders,
gathering troops to defend the domain,
upholding the Way and adhering to the law,
wielding the axe and handle strict in duty,
standing upright and maintaining the carpenter’s line,
clarifying rewards and certain punishments,
punishing all offenses without pardon,
appointing the worthy and using the able,
associating only with the loyal,
never usurping matters by private authority,
acting only after consulting the ruler;
if the ruler errs,
admonishing with reason and correcting him;
anxious and reverent at all times,
never forgetting to be respectful,
making the state forever stable above,
and ensuring himself is without trouble below—
if, after achievement is accomplished,
one does not linger but
requests retirement to return one’s body,
recommends loyal and capable men,
and advances them to take one’s place,
is not this truly more than sufficient?
Why must one seize the imperial seals,
and endanger the one whom one was to serve?
The ruler
is Heaven,
is father.
If the ruler may be overthrown,
then Heaven may be changed,
and father replaced.
Those whose merit covers the world are not rewarded;
those whose power shocks the ruler imperil themselves.
Even those who won wars and took cities,
and whose achievement and labor were beyond comparison,
are like birds—when hunted out, the bow is cast aside;
when the rabbit is gone, the hound is boiled.
How much more so for those who depose their ruler,
and hope for the love of the next!
Is this any different from a son discarding the parent who gave him life into the mountains and valleys,
then taking up another to nurture him,
and saying he could fulfill the filial piety of Bó Yú or Zēng Sān,
only his own parents were unfit to be served,
so he abandoned them?
Even if he daily offered the three sacrificial animals,
and attended morning and night,
how could he hope to receive real affection and trust?
The followers of Huò Guāng,
though in their time were promoted in rank and ennobled,
their rewards and gifts without measure,
all were elevated through schemes,
but was this the true sincerity of such men?
To accept a cast-off wife and then discuss the evils of her former husband,
to buy a slave and then condemn the cruelty of his previous master,
even the most ordinary people,
still find it unjust.
Why is this?
Because it deeply wounds their own kind—
this is natural feeling.
Thus Lè Yáng was shunned for his cruelty,
while Qín Xī was favored for his excessive kindness.
Yet people of the world truly say that Tāng and Wǔ were justified,
and Yī and Huò were worthy;
in fact, this is encouraging one another to rebellion.
Moreover, as for those rulers who were deposed,
they were not necessarily wholly in the wrong.
Sometimes those who assist a young ruler
wield power for their own benefit,
committing great crimes and accumulating evil,
causing fears of future trouble;
and while still holding power,
someone may overthrow them,
thus extending disasters close at hand.
When establishing merit and devising plans,
their calculations were for self-interest,
not necessarily for the state.
Having already seized great authority,
they decided life and death as they pleased.
When the deposed ruler is seen,
the object of rulership is gone,
and all guilt of decline and failure
is ascribed to him.
Even though people know it so,
who dares to speak it openly?
Without the efforts of Dōngmóu and Zhūxū to put forward calculations,
without Nánshǐ and Dǒng Hú to prove offences,
in times to come, even today,
who will judge it again?
Only those who see clearly are able to recall that the wickedness of Jié and Zhòu was not as great as it is said,
nor the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ as splendid as they appear.
In the strategy books,
none fail to honor the ruler above the subject,
to strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches.
According to the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Heaven must not be wronged.
The great sages in their classics
base the conduct of a son toward his father, and of a subject toward his lord.
Of the three foundations of human existence,
this one is served as if it were the whole.
Yet to allow the business of deposition and enthronement
opens the gate to lawlessness;
the lower tramples the higher,
and instruction becomes difficult.
Common scholars are steeped in the merchant stalls,
confused by sophistry;
some criticize Tāng and Wǔ for feasting on horse's liver,
and, censuring such acts,
believe they do not understand the changes of expediency,
and value arising in goodness without violating order,
not calling it a reversal of reason and rightful duty.
Yet those who wrote in past ages,
did not distinguish this with grand principle,
so that those with such feelings add the sharp point to the blade,
and ascend the crumbling mountain,
which is no way to prolong the years and sustain the generations,
nor to keep danger afar.
Even if power and mandates temporarily flourish,
rewards generously showered,
it is no different from a sacrificial ox adorned with embroidery,
a deep-pond fish loving a field of wheat,
the thirsty seeking to quench themselves with wine from clouds or sun,
the hungry seeking fullness from spoiled meat or pickled rations.
But all who write about it compete in praise,
considering it a fine story,
regarding crimes that should not be punished as discernment of change,
leaving men troubled and forever sighing.
Some have reproved me, saying my words hurt the sages,
and I will surely be slandered and disparaged.
I reply:
“Shùn and Yǔ endured trials at home and abroad,
before finally taking on the legacy from Wénzǔ.
Although there are those fond of criticizing,
how could the sages be harmed!
In ancient times, Yán Yánnián in the court impeached Huò Guāng for lawlessness,
and everyone was awe-struck,
none could refute him.
Much less when I admonish as a warning to the age,
without specific accusation,
why fear the common sayings!”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
One who fulfills his duty without concealment,
this can be done.
But as for words always being accepted and oneself always secure,
one must wait for the time.
If the time is wrong—
the treacherous and violent are envious of what they cannot reach,
holding down the high and oppressing the low,
hating the direct, detesting the upright,
anxious and afraid that the upright will expose the crooked,
thus endeavor to rid themselves of those better, to relieve themselves of blame.
An enlightened ruler is rare in the world,
the mediocre are confused about right and wrong,
thus cannot accept the use of loyal counsel,
sometimes even spread extreme sayings.
Thus men like Hóng Gōng and Shí Xiǎn,
embellished cunning words to concoct semblance and shadow,
and feigned highest fairness to sell private evil.
So those who offered methods for longevity,
instead received capital punishment;
those who proposed plans for the ruler’s security,
soon met with disaster themselves.
Hence it is said:
It is not that words are hard to speak,
but that it is hard to speak at the right time.
When speaking to the wise and sage,
still acceptance is not assured,
so Yī Yǐn advised Tāng,
and it took seventy times.
When telling the wise to the foolish,
it will surely not be accepted,
so when Wén admonished Zhòu,
it was never admitted in the end.
If one’s words are not believed,
this may well be borne.
But as when Lǐ Sī executed Hán Fēi,
Páng Juān hamstrung Sūn Bìn,
Shàngguān slandered Qū Píng,
Yuán Àng trapped Cháo Cuò—
examples too many for record.
To serve as a minister is not easy,
how could there be just one path!
Those who went and did not return,
thus their merit endures after death;
while those who concealed their talents and awaited the right time,
rarely find one chance in a hundred.
Ministers of lofty achievements appear only once in an age;
while those who fall into disaster
are heaped in the records of history.
Alas!
How hard it is to encounter the right time—
how extreme it truly is!
Therefore, in speaking thus,
I know that those like Lǚ Shàng on the banks of the Wèi,
and followers of Fù Yuè among the cliffs,
holding within them the talents to aid a king,
and carrying abilities rare for the age,
grasping rods and handling earthworks,
dying among laborers and children,
never meeting Wén Wáng or Gāo Zōng,
certainly cannot be disparaged.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The galloping of Lù’ěr over far tracks
was due to Zào Fù’s reinsmanship;
the regulation of the realm by Yǔ and Jì,
was because of the rulers Tāng Yú.
Thus they could, without toil, travel a thousand miles,
civility and yielding arousing praise.
But if Zāng and Pǐ rode the sùshuāng,
or Yīn Xīn sat over the Three Gudemen,
hoping to run unrestrained and fast,
then the reins would tighten and the shafts squeeze;
hoping to give all their counsel and exhaust their loyalty,
disaster would spring upon them like a triggered mechanism.
Thus carriages overturn on perilous roads,
states perish and do not rise.
So fine steeds fail due to clumsy drivers,
wise men stumble in dark ages.
Zhòngní could not stop the Marquis of Lǔ from departing,
Yàn Yīng could not prevent the disorder of Cuī Zhǔ.
Their ability was present,
but the rulers were lacking.
A ruler is like a vessel,
a minister like a thing;
if the vessel is small and the thing is large,
it cannot contain it.
A child may carry gold worth a thousand, yet chase butterflies;
a man of Yuè discards the eight delicacies, but relishes frogs and toads.
Thus, they suffer not to reward the good,
and further fail to recognize what is bad.
If not used,
then though rare, it is not valued;
if none give it,
then one who harms it will surely come.
Formerly Wèi Líng, hearing sage advice, was frequently alarmed;
Qín Xiào, hearing lofty discourse, would sleep;
yet they wished to keep the rule in peace,
and reap the merit of the able;
just as one walks backward to chase a racer,
or seeks the road to Yān while heading for Chǔ.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The southern seas draw in all rivers, achieving unfathomable depths;
the Xuánpǔ raises its root of stone, reaching the utmost heights of heaven.
The great Xià soars above the clouds,
relying on the accumulated beams;
its wheels are curved and axles straight,
lacking no essential part.
Thus when Yuán Kǎi aided in ascending,
he enabled harmonious transformation to reach heaven;
when those skilled in strategy and compromise were broad,
the cunning among the deer-chasers faded away.
This is why Shùn and Yǔ possessed the world without dispute,
and why Wèi Líng, though arrogant and indulgent, was not endangered.
When many forces are united,
even ten thousand jūn cannot be lifted;
when many minds are put to use,
all tasks are easily handled.
Thus the centipede dies but does not lose its vigor,
and a host of scholars in turmoil does not bring the state to ruin.
Yet swords and halberds are not better for sewing,
awls and drills cannot hack things apart,
oxen and horses cannot bark and guard,
chickens and dogs are not fit for the chariot.
Use each for what it excels at,
and nothing fails to achieve results;
avoid what they lack,
and no talent in the world will be discarded.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
To abandon a light boat and set out across the boundless sea
is no guarantee one will reach the other shore;
to covet order without good ministers
has never yet brought success.
The wild flight of the hóngluán
is due to the strength of its six pinions;
the dragon that soars to the heights
is accompanied by clouds and mist.
Thus to recruit the worthy
is the chief business of the ruler;
to achieve works and found enterprises
is what the gifted strive for.
To enjoy peace and order but neglect the wise
—how is this different from wishing to travel far, yet abandoning fine steeds?
To lift up those stuck in low places,
to draw out the secluded and neglected,
to make men serve according to their talents,
to grant honors according to their merit—
such is how the ruler treats the worthy;
to labor early and late for the public’s sake,
to exhaust heart and strength on a hundred affairs,
to promote good and remove evil,
withholding nothing within one's knowledge or capacity—
such is how ministers repay their benefactor.
In the world, there are recluses,
but no sovereigns who stand alone;
scholars may be glad to retreat without anxiety,
but rulers cannot bring order without ministers.
It is thus that Fù Yuè and Lǚ Shàng did not strive for fame,
and when their virtue was complete, they cared little for kings and lords.
Yet the High Kings of Yīn and the Civil King of Zhōu only dreamed of finding the worthy,
and establishing great achievements depended on excellent counselors.
The trouble lies in being born within deep palaces,
raised by women's hands,
unacquainted with the toils of cultivation,
never knowing the cause of worry or fear,
inheriting the house and dynastic body,
blinded by the ebb and flow of favor.
What they hasten for is extravagance,
their urgent affairs are feasting and pleasure,
busy with hunting and hawking,
addicted to revels,
quick to listen to lewd sounds,
eye caught by suggestive beauty.
Their hearing and sight are put to use
for these two pursuits alone.
When examining men,
they do not judge by principles and spirit,
but only know how to find amusement to delight their will,
never realizing that able men can secure the state.
Rhinoceros, elephant, pearls and jade,
though without legs, come from ten thousand miles away;
tilted vessels,
though able to move, nonetheless sink within the boundaries.
When disease grips both sides but one finally seeks good physicians,
when roof beams are rotten but then one seeks schemers,
why wait until a fire to dig a well,
or experience hunger and then measure out fields?
Even common laborers are not to be managed without being mollified and guided to exert their utmost,
how then can one, without preparation, suddenly gain their effective use?
Someone says:
"When the tail is larger than the body,
it cannot be wagged;
when ministers are worthier than their lord,
they are not to be entrusted.
Thus if the mouth is too small and one forces food in, he chokes;
if talent does not match but one trusts it, he is disdained."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"How perverse
these words are!
In the past, when the Prince of Jīng was a child acting as Prime Minister,
he truly relied on twenty-five elders
to achieve good governance.
Zǐjiàn, rising from humble origins, ruled a great state,
because he had many better than himself
and sought their extensive assistance.
Qí Huán killed his brother and took the throne,
his conduct like that of birds and beasts,
hair disheveled, never sober,
three hundred women in his women's quarters,
all government left to Zhòng Fù,
thus he became paramount leader;
when Yíwú died,
disorder and calamity quickly followed.
Lǔ employed Jìzǐ for over twenty years,
with no misrule inside,
no encroachment or loss outside;
when the great man was gone,
ruin came quickly.
Was it not due to insufficient talent
that his achievements were thus;
insisting on personal rule
brought disaster of such a kind."
"Emperor Gāo of Hàn planned his strategy within the curtained tent,
and won victories over a thousand miles,
yet he was not as good as Liáng Píng;
his military was vast and ever victorious,
invincible wherever he went,
yet not as effective as Xìn and Bù;
by combining all their abilities,
the imperial enterprise was completed.
Therefore, to hurry on foot
cannot equal riding a swift steed;
to chase birds and animals by hand
cannot equal using hounds and hawks.
A strong crossbow is hard to draw,
yet can shatter armor and reach far;
a great vessel is hard to steer,
yet can carry heavy loads across deep water;
a fierce general is hard to control,
yet can repel attacks and open territory;
a high sage is hard to serve,
yet can order the rites and relationships."
"In olden days, Duke Āi of Lǔ was a mediocre ruler,
while Zhòngní was a supreme sage,
yet he dared not give less than full loyalty;
Jǐng of Qí was of limited ability,
but Yàn Yīng was greatly virtuous,
yet he dared not give less than perfect sincerity.
When have ministers been expected to compare wits and strength with their lord,
or gauge their abilities against him,
