so that only a Yáo or Shùn would merit their service?
What matter is not the ruler's?
What office is not served by the people?
To be ashamed that one's ruler does not equal Táng or Yú
is just how those who understand employ their heart."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Yóu Yú was with the Róng,
while Qín Mù worried over him;
Chǔ killed Déchén,
and Jìn Wén rejoiced;
when Lè Yì left, Yān was ruined;
when Zhòng Lì entered, Yuè became hegemon.
Countries destroyed, families lost,
all for want of able men.
Is it only that possessing them makes one honored,
while lacking them brings disgrace?
Liǔ Huì's tomb,
could still blunt the invaders' edge,
how much more so if he were alive and at court?
Qián Mù's seclusion,
could still deter border aggression,
how much more if he were placed at one's right hand?
The image of Zhì Dū
could make fierce enemies tremble;
the corpse of Kǒng Míng
could still cause great states to lay down arms.
With such as these to resist insult,
one's territory would never be invaded;
with such men to lead armies,
the ruler would never be humiliated.
So it is that enlightened rulers send bundles of silk to remote alleys,
raise humble feathers in withered forests,
dispatch feathered carriages to river bridges,
open all four gates tirelessly,
not begrudging gold or jade,
not shunning a journey of a thousand miles,
not resenting lowering themselves,
not ashamed to speak humbly,
but take recruiting the worthy as their first task,
and obtaining talent as their greatest treasure.
Those who recommend such men receive the highest reward,
those who conceal them are considered usurpers.
Thus, Gōng Dàn offered tribute in a humble abode,
Qín Shào paid homage to Chāng at Zhāng Shēng’s place.
When Zōu Zǐ crossed the border,
the Lord of Yān took up a broom;
Zhuāng Zhōu went unfed,
yet Zhào Huì stood tall in respect.
Jìn Píng greeted Hài Táng,
sitting with numb feet, not daring to sit upright;
Qí Rènzhī visited Jìqiū,
though frequently, he never declined the labor.
The King of Chǔ received a flogging at Bǎo Shēn,
Jiǎn removed his armor in Gōnglú;
though they humbled the lofty and suppressed arrogance,
and with nobility stooped to the lowly,
in the end, they nonetheless combined their sight to extend their vision,
and borrowed the ears of others to broaden their hearing.
Dragons soaring, tigers crouching—
this is as it should be.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"There is none who does not value benevolence,
but none can be purely benevolent so as to bring about good governance;
there is none who does not despise punishment,
but none can abolish punishment and still keep the people in order.
Some say:
‘When an enlightened ruler faces the world,
the wind bends the grass.
When the Way is widespread and transformation pure,
what need is there for punishment?’
I then discuss this, saying:
‘The teaching of virtue
is like the ceremonial dress adorned with embroidery;
punishments
are like the armor wielded against blades.
If one tries to curb cunning malice through virtue and teaching alone,
it is as if one resists sharp weapons with robes and embroidery;
to apply punishments to a peaceful age
is like bringing armor into the ancestral hall.
Therefore, benevolence is the vessel for nurturing things,
while punishment is the tool for restraining misconduct.
I wish to benefit others,
but others wish to harm;
if benevolence is added without change,
then only punishment can bring things to a halt.
Punishment aids benevolence—
this much is clear.
Consider maintaining a hidden breath,
inhaling and exhaling, taking in and expelling,
encompassing illumination and gazing within,
stretching as bears and birds do—
these are arts of long life.
Yet difficult and slow,
those who practice rarely succeed;
those who master them
are but one in ten thousand.
When the illness is severe and pain extreme,
the body exhausted and life in peril,
one cannot but attack it with needle and stone,
and treat it with potent poisons.
If, abandoning Héhèquè’s methods,
one admires Sōng Qiáo’s way instead,
many will surely perish.
To govern through benevolence
is not unworthy;
yet the common people are crafty and deceitful,
pursuing profit and forgetting righteousness.
If not regulated with authority,
corrected with punishment,
and yearning for the custom of Xī and Nóng,
then disorder cannot be stopped,
and calamity will be deep and grave.
To end killing with killing—
is this out of joy?
‘In the creation of the Eight Trigrams,
they exhaust reason and fully express human nature,
making punishment and lawsuits clear
as recorded in the Shìkè Hexagram;
binding with ropes and cords
is preserved in Xí Kǎn Hexagram.
The use of punishment has come from ancient times.
Even in the time of Xuānyuán,
whose sacred virtue was especially lofty,
he himself led campaigns,
fought a hundred battles,
corpses lay at Zhuōlù,
and blood flowed at Bǎnquán,
yet he could not cause an age without rebellion,
nor put away weapons for good.
How, then, could he make all people good,
and have a people free of crime without governing them?
This has never been.
In the prosperity of Táng and Yú,
punishments were used as the heavens did,
banishment and execution were employed,
thus the world submitted.
Hàn Wén was silent and mysterious,
compared to Chéng and Kāng,
yet still judged four hundred cases,
and many died from flogging.
As Carpenter Shí does not set aside the line and ink,
so there is no crooked wood;
an enlightened ruler does not abolish punishment,
so politics does not decline.
‘The Way of Heaven and Earth
cannot be of pure kindness;
thus Qīngyáng brings forth the harmony of nurturing,
while Sùqiū upholds the severity of killing.
When warm winds blow, the withered flourish;
when white dews congeal, abundant blossoms wither.
Therefore, the multitude of things grows abundantly,
and the year’s work is accomplished.
If there is warmth without cold,
then insects do not hibernate,
and trees put forth leaves in winter.
If there is leniency without severity,
then villainy will prosper together,
and sharp tools guarded constantly.
Thus, clear rewards preserve the upright,
punishments must root out the wrong.
Of the means to encourage or restrain,
none is more essential than this.
In observing the people and establishing teaching,
one must balance leniency and severity,
so that the timid will not be taken lightly,
and the resolute will not harm kindness.
Of offenses for which the Five Punishments are applied,
three thousand have been counted—
thus the cord must not be bent;
if the Sīkòu carries out punishments,
and the ruler does not intervene,
thus the law must not be abolished.
If the cord is bent,
then villainy is fostered;
if law is abolished,
then disorder increases.
‘The downfall of a state is not for lack of statutes,
but because statutes are numerous and not enforced;
the defeat of an army is not from lack of prohibitions,
but because prohibitions are set and not upheld.
Thus evils spread the more,
and subordinates defile their superiors.
Rewards are valued when they match merit, not because they are heavy;
penalties are effective when attached to guilt, not because they are harsh.
If caning is abolished at home,
the servants become lazy;
if campaigns cease in the state,
then the people become irreverent.
Affection must be treated with respect and not spoiled,
thus rites are established to honor it;
virtue must have authority to endure,
thus punishments are established to make it austere.
Bān Chuí did not let go of compass and square,
thus forms were made neither too square nor too round;
an enlightened lord does not discard statute and rule,
thus guile cannot display its cleverness.
Táng and Yú were as benevolent as heaven,
yet did not pardon the four crimes;
Jī Gōng was friendly with his brothers,
yet did not pardon the two uncles.
Zhòngní executed Zhèng Mǎo,
Hàn Wǔ put to death his nephew;
though tears were shed in pity for the law,
truly, it could not be helped.
‘Therefore, punishing one to shake ten thousand,
lessening the few to save the many:
as combing the hair,
most are benefited;
as cutting away an ulcer,
much is preserved.
Thus, the pain of cautery or acupuncture cannot be stopped
because it cures disease;
the severity of punishment and penalty cannot be abolished
because it saves from harm.
Though the Six Armies are dense as forests,
not all are truly brave.
To dash at the vanguard or plunge into fire—
this is what people fear.
But if encouraged with gentle faces,
few hazard their lives;
if threatened with execution,
none fails to fight.
Thus, to urge with laughter
cannot match the swiftness of the stern shout;
to lead with pleasure
is not as effective as discipline and execution.
Thus, Ān Yú could move the people of Gǎn Gǔ by severity of the law,
Wèi Zǐjí inspired awe by discarding ashes and making his commands strict.
By what they fear,
one prohibits what they toy with;
make severity unbreakable,
that is the art of preserving all.
The one who is skilled at treating diseases
blocks illness before it arises;
the one who understands the principles of governance
forestalls trouble before it comes.
If one uses light punishments to deter great crimes,
mild laws to guard immense profit,
and publishes statutes abundantly,
yet offenses increase,
it is like digging a pit on the road ahead—
not the way a benevolent man would hold in his heart.
“One who is skilled in governance,
must first set his own affairs in order to lead others;
manage those near to put those distant in order;
do not twist the law to fulfill personal intentions,
one must require guilt to be punished without pardon.
As Shí Shíxī once cut off his affection to root out his kin,
and Jìn Wén endured his feelings to execute Xié.
Thus benevolence
is the powder and rouge of governance;
punishment
is the bridle and whip controlling the world.
Powder and rouge are not urgently needed by the body,
but bridle and whip must not be lacking even for a moment.
If solemnity and respect slacken a little,
then slowness and indolence quickly follow;
if authority and sternness relax even for a moment,
then all manner of evil is born in men's hearts.
When one should be angry but is not,
treacherous ministers become tigers;
when one should kill but does not,
great thieves then emerge.
Water, if left unchecked, destroys the riverbanks,
mountains may rise just a foot away.
To seek a tree a thousand zhang high,
it begins from the tiniest sprout;
a fire kindled by striking flint,
a ladle of water can extinguish;
before a swan's egg hatches,
it can be crushed between the fingers.
But once it rides the rushing wind burning the vast plains,
and soars with six wings through the morning clouds,
then even the wise and brave cannot bring it under control.
Therefore, a wise ruler addresses difficulty in its ease,
removes evil when it is slight,
does not boast of good deeds thereby increasing disorder,
nor takes up the axe-handle and hesitates.
Thus, punishment
is the sacred implement of the state,
something the ruler must personally wield,
not something to be delegated to another,
just as a long sword must not be grasped by the blade,
a giant fish must not be taken from its abyss.
It is the source of rise and fall,
the origin of security and danger.
Tián Cháng usurped Qí,
the six ministers divided Jìn,
Zhào Gāo murdered the Qín ruler,
Wáng Mǎng usurped Hàn—
walking on frost leads to ice,
such changes have always happened in gradual steps.
Some sigh forever on the seashore,
some beat their hearts at Wàngyí,
calamity extends to their ancestral temples,
serving as caution to those who come after,
because they admired empty fame from ancient times,
and forgot the real disaster facing themselves.”
Someone said:
“The rise of punishments
occurred only in later generations.
The way of establishing people
lies solely in benevolence and righteousness.
If I am pure and quiet, the people will naturally be upright;
if I am without desire, the people will naturally be simple.
The caution for cooking fresh fish
is not to make it complicated.
Broad-mindedness and loving people gathers the masses;
delighting those you use brings their allegiance.
Therefore, Mèngzǐ considered embodying benevolence as true security;
Yángzǐ said that Shēn and Hán were but butchers.
Elaborate rules and harsh bridles
are not the driving methods of Zàofù;
severe punishments and harsh penalties
are not the ways of the Three August Ones and Five Emperors.
Thus, the Ruler of Yǒuyú merely sat, hands not commanding,
mouth not busy with words,
sat respectfully at the southern mat,
and all became peaceful and harmonious.
Fùshēng ruled by setting customs,
played the zither and sang the Odes,
without stepping down from the hall,
yet the fishermen in the night grew respectful.
Only by giving ample favors and light taxes,
helping the needy and promoting the stuck,
raising the worthy and appointing the talented,
encouraging farming and frugal use,
treating the estranged with ritual,
cherishing the distant with virtue,
nurturing them with Chéngjūn,
governing them with schools and academies.
When customs become good at the top and good people arise,
it must be as grass bending to a sudden wind;
when hearts are washed and faces are renewed,
it must be like clear waves washing away light dust.
In court, the lords yield to virtue,
in the fields, there is no violation of rituals or rules.
So great states can be left empty and wild,
Chǔ's drums can forever sound,
so why must rewards and punishments be the means to govern the state?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“‘The Yì’ says, ‘Clearly set punishments and command the law’;
‘The Shū’ speaks of ‘sorrow and pity in judging cases.’
Honoring men in the court,
punishing men in the marketplace—
such things have always existed,
how could they have begun with later generations!
When there is too much benevolence, law cannot stand;
when there is too little authority, inferiors defy superiors.
If law cannot stand,
then all affairs become confused;
if inferiors defy superiors,
then rebellion is clear.
The utmost purity was already diluted by the Three Dynasties,
the great simplicity later scattered under Qín and Hàn,
the Dao has withered in past eras,
and customs are shallow in our own time;
yet you would try to use knotted cords to restrain cunning and deception,
and teach without speaking to transform the crafty and sly,
abandoning bridle and whip yet galloping a running steed on a dangerous road,
discarding the rudder and oar yet floating an empty boat to ride the waves;
spinning around to chase fleeing thieves,
yielding politely to stop raging fires,
cutting down Cháo Cuò to repel the Seven States,
dancing with weapons to pacify the Red Eyebrows—
never have I seen such things succeed!
“The Three August Ones walked slowly, but with the Five Constants things moved at a trot;
from the time of the feudal overlords,
it has greatly accelerated.
In its decline,
officials deceive, the people grow cunning,
robbers are rampant,
shaving heads and chaining criminals do not deter the shameless,
clan execution does not forbid covetousness.
Heavy eyes expand vision,
piled ears extend hearing,
holding a torch solves troublesome matters,
burning with anxiety only lessens the source of wickedness,
yet in the marketplace and court still there are cries of pain,
and in border regions injustice goes unheard.
Those who wield power and luck
may arise from the lowest places;
households that ruin families and endanger states
may be bred within the inner walls of the home.
Yet you wish to use the Dao of Tài Hào
to govern people whose customs are lazy and corrupt;
to use the songs of Huà Yī
to rescue disorder boiling like a cauldron:
such cannot be done without understanding when to adapt and change,
and clearly discerning the flexibility of loss and benefit.
This is like carving a mark on a moving boat to find a lost sword,
aiming at the heavens to shoot something five paces away,
smashing through the armor of rhinos and wild bulls,
in order to cross an unfathomable abyss;
stripping off a winter coat
to guard against sweltering summer heat,
kicking at it to remove it,
scratching the chin to relieve an itch on one’s back:
of all confusion and folly,
nothing is worse!
“One must only issue orders before punishing,
find the truth but do not rejoice in it,
so that the elder brother is not resentful at losing his fief,
and Yú and Ruì know shame and cease their lawsuits.
But if the violent cover their faces,
those holding the law fear nothing,
seduced by those who swallow insults,
and weeds are left unpulled,
trusting in boasts of hidden disease,
forgetting the pressing urgency of fatal illness,
what is this but like someone parched with burning thirst,
yet points to the distant sea a myriad li away,
when floodwaters are already upon him,
and only then tries to make a boat from forest trees by the river,
how can he escape the calamity of Kuāfù,
or the disaster of being lost in the flood!
People of this age disparage the real practices of Shēn and Hán,
and praise the wild talk of Lǎo and Zhuāng.
Yet in governance, none can do without punishment:
those who kill are pardoned their death,
those who wound are excused their crime,
which is like offering half-rotten food,
unable to save those hungry in the morning.
The teachings of the Daoists,
lofty indeed as they are,
when applied become a failure;
far-fetched and impractical,
like the Sword of Gànjiāng unsuited for stitching clothes,
or a giant elephant unable to act as a mouse,
a golden boat unable to float on the waves of Yánghóu,
a jade horse unfit to run a thousand li.”
If one were to act on such words,
then shackles and manacles would be burned,
prisons cast down,
officials abolished,
the penal codes destroyed,
arms and armor melted down,
city walls leveled,
state treasuries scattered,
seals and tallies smashed,
gates and bridges dismantled,
scales and measures broken.
The eyes of Jiāo Lízhū would be glued shut,
the ears of Zǐ Yě blocked.
All would float about, untethered,
returning to the herding of Heaven;
without instruction or management,
mutually forgetting each other in lakes and rivers.
The court would be empty as if void of people,
the people, until death, would not communicate or come together.
Such things may be discussed,
but are difficult to put into practice.
“Common scholars have only heard that Zhōu rose by benevolence,
Qín perished by severity,
but have not realized that what Zhōu attained was not solely due to benevolence,
nor was Qín's failure solely due to severity.
In ancient times, Zhōu employed corporal punishments,
severing feet, cutting off noses.
At the order of Méngjīn,
those arriving late were beheaded,
rewards and punishments enforced with all their might,
oaths bore threats of family extermination.
Examining their actions,
they were not completely benevolent.
In its late generations,
laws were neglected and the letter of statutes was exploited,
rulers became harsh and cruel,
proclamations did not venture beyond palace walls,
rituals, music, campaigns,
no longer decided by the ruler himself.
Subordinates vied for dominance,
turning to become a great serpent.
They cut the root and blocked the source,
destroyed coronets, tore apart crowns.
Some were drowned in the Hàn,
some were exiled to Yīzhì.
The loss of power and failure
was due to a lack of severity.
At the rise of Qín,
officials were selected for talent.
Wèi Yāng and Yóu Yú and their kind
modeled the laws within;
Bái Qǐ and Wáng Jiǎn and the like
waged conquests without.
Absorbing the weak and striking the benighted,
they won prestige and established supremacy,
devouring the four neighbors,
chewing up the competing lords,
expanding territory and expelling the Rong tribes,
changing and scanning like a dragon,
all relying on clear rewards and certain punishments
as the foundation of imperial undertakings.
But reaching the final decline,
they grew arrogant in their success,
plunged into lavishness and extreme excess.
Adding cruelty to threat,
they built walls over ten thousand lǐ,
raised more than a thousand detached palaces,
assembled bells, drums, female entertainers,
all for extravagant displays.
The conscripted labor at Lí Shān,
a heavy taxation burden,
border garrisons by the common people,
the brutality of burying Confucian scholars,
northern campaigns against Xiǎn Yǔn,
southern campaigns against Bǎi Yuè,
mustering a million troops,
this lasted several decades.
Throughout the realm, there was the grief of parting,
in every household the sigh of bitterness and separation.
White bones piled into mountains,
empty sacrifices spread across the fields.
Xú Fú departed, compounding the resentment of a thousand mouths;
Zhào Gāo entered, gathering a band of wolves and jackals.
The world began to rebel,
ten households out of nine lay deserted.
As for the cause of ruin,
could it really be simply due to harsh punishments?
This is an example of Qín attaining power through severity,
not losing it because of severity.
“Moreover, punishment comes by the blade,
the skillful use it to fulfill themselves,
the unskilled bring harm upon themselves.
If, when governing the state with proper Way, one supplements by punishments,
he can prevent mischief and falsehood,
and cause the wicked to reform their intentions.
But if the net’s thread is severed and the web is in disorder,
offending against Heaven,
using punishments inappropriately,
disaster will come quickly.
It is like water and fire, with which one can save life,
but also kill;
it depends on whether one can use them well.
“If tumors and swellings are not removed,
and one does not practice the techniques of Yuè Rén,
it will be hard to hope for the longevity of Lǎo Péng.
If criminal gangs proliferate,
and there is no strict system for indicting and reprimanding them,
I have yet to see such people enjoy long-lasting fortune.
One should select from those like Jiǎn and Zhāng,
and entrust them with governing the world by law;
choose those akin to Zhào and Chén,
and have them investigate misconduct on occasion.
If an enlightened ruler attends keenly to what is above,
loyal and good ministers exhaust their sincerity below,
evil is dealt with as a hawk or falcon seizes sparrow or finch,
disorder rooted out as weeds in a millet field are cut away.
If rewards are never wrongly given,
and executions are never unjustly made,
then the path to great peace will not be far.
When commands are not violated,
perhaps punishments may be abolished and governance attained,
but I dare not say this could truly be so.”
Someone said:
“If punishments are indeed meant to assist instruction and promote good,
then how have their forms gone astray?
As for the corporal punishments of antiquity,
could these be restored?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Why would this not be possible!
In former times, Zhōu used corporal punishment
for seven hundred sacrifices;
the House of Hàn abolished it,
and its times have not matched those of old.
As for replacing it with flogging and beating,
the number who died became very great.
Outwardly it bore the name of lighter penalties,
while in reality it killed men.
When a crime was committed,
not quite enough to warrant death,
the offender was only sentenced to penal servitude, exile, or beating with sticks;
but if there happened to be an amnesty,
their body would be left unharmed;
furthermore, their shaven hair would regrow,
their wounds from beating would heal,
scarcely enough as a deterrence to those deserving of death.
Now, with the abolition of corporal punishment,
below the capital penalty, there is no longer an intermediate punishment,
and so those whose crimes below capital deserve more than penal servitude, exile or flogging,
there is no proper degree between light and heavy penalties.
Those who commit crimes are now rare and occasional,
but when executed, people regret it as too harsh,
while when flogged, people think it too lenient;
this offense thus becomes more common.
Now, with corporal punishment unused,
those crimes just below the death penalty
are often not suitably punished.
“Now, excepting the gravest crimes like treason and plotting rebellion,
those who violate ruler or parent,
those who, when facing the enemy, break military law,
those who murder with their own hand,
if corporal punishment were substituted for the death penalty,
this would be sufficient to warn and deter the wicked.
Punished offenders would continue with forced labor,
able to perform useful work,
yet not suffer the loss of continuation of their kind,
though mutilated for life;
all the people, seeing this,
would shudder in their hearts,
and it would inspire awe and warning in those not yet offenders,
serving as a clear warning for the future;
it would be even more effective than execution.
To kill is
not without gravity.
But after three days, the corpse is buried or abandoned,
the ignorant are many,
those who do not see are numerous.
But corporal punishment serves as a more visible warning.
In the era of Wèi, this matter was discussed repeatedly,
all the great scholars and erudite men,
thorough in Yīn’s ancient systems,
all said corporal punishment should be restored,
but those with differing opinions disputed it,
there was no agreement.
Even Emperor Wèi Wǔdì thought so.
But as the two borders were not pacified,
and those distant peoples who could not understand our highest laws
heard rumors that in China men had their limbs lopped off,
ears and noses cut,
they would straightaway condemn us as cruel,
so it was provisionally suspended,
awaiting the unification of the four quarters.
Yángzǐ, the broad-minded man, also thought corporal punishment should be restored.
But as it has been abolished for a long time,
those who sit and discuss the Way
do not consider its restoration urgent.”
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
The reason why Huá Huò can reach the utmost heights of heaven
is due to the profound depth of its foundation below;
the reason why Táng and Yú could attain majestic achievements
truly depended upon the excellence of their ministers and aides.
Even if one possessed the hands of Sūn Yáng,
without the feet of a qíjì (thoroughbred),
one could not cover a thousand li.
Even if one had the ability of a sage who studied antiquity,
without assistants to manifest his strength,
no one could carry out the many affairs of state.
Even if a ruler’s enlightenment rivaled the sun and the moon,
and his divine insight was unmatched,
yet he still could not govern myriad affairs alone,
nor could he personally oversee every detail;
he must rely on eyes to observe far,
and borrow ears to hear widely.
Truly, he needs officials,
to aid and support his good governance.
Therefore, all sagely rulers have been diligent in seeking out the worthy,
taking the selection of talent as their chief concern,
extending gifts of jade and silk to recluse scholars in the fields,
sending swift chariots to the mountains and marshes,
exerting themselves in seeking people,
and finding ease in employing the able.
From those of noble ancestry,
down to attendants and servants,
all were employed as appropriate in the governance of the state,
without exception entrusted to their roles.
By being respectful and practicing non-action,
order was established and punishments were set aside;
thus, transformation reached everywhere,
and all the realms enjoyed peace.
Assigning offices and dividing duties
is like constructing a house;
if even one thing is unsuitable,
then collapse and ruin will ensue.
As for the men recommended to office,
they were evaluated according to four categories;
the Three Matters and the Nine Ranks
were all selected from among them.
They always chose those who stood out for excellence,
yet in the final years of the Hàn,
in the eras of Huán and Líng,
authority passed from the imperial house,
and power fell into the hands of treacherous ministers.
The net of law had gaping holes, and safeguards collapsed;
the winds of custom were decadent and education was obstructed.
Pure virtue was suppressed while flattery and sycophancy were exalted;
those who acted with upright conduct were dismissed, while those with wealth and property were promoted.
Striving for advantage became the custom;
those who sought gain did so without shame.
Some offered rare treasures to sell themselves;
some sold letters of recommendation from important men;
some relied on the prominence of their fathers and elder brothers,
obtaining appointments simply by approaching the gates of the powerful;
others bowed their heads and bent their knees,
and through habitual obsequiousness were employed.
If the standards for weighing talent are unbalanced,
the proper distinctions of worth and weight are confused;
if the measures are not correct,
too much and too little are thrown into chaos;
if compasses and rules are not employed,
crooked and straight cannot be distinguished;
if the standards are tilted,
dross and impurity will abound.
If such people are set to govern others,
cruelty and greed will ensue,
and they will extort and amass wealth
to compensate for the money spent bribing their way into office;
if set in the court,
the disorder will be even worse than tangled silk.
When mediocre men are hired,
gathered for mutual partisanship,
and they yield to every changing wind,
how can the affairs of the state prosper?
This is no different from hanging pebbles and demanding they gleam like jade,
or plucking out-of-tune strings and demanding pure notes!
How can one not clarify muddied waters and distinguish the worthy from the unworthy,
eliminate the bad and promote the good,
strictly enforce the methods for evaluating candidates,
and raise high defenses against the greedy?
Ruin is never far,
and how could one not fear it?
In ancient times, feudal lords presented men of talent;
if the man chosen was suitable, he was said to have merit,
and those with merit were advanced in rank and title;
if the recommended man was unsuitable, he was said to be at fault,
and those at fault were demoted and lost their lands.
Yet even so they could not silence the satirical verses of the Shījīngrén mocking the great chariots and those who ate without labor,
nor did the mountains and forests lack those virtuous men lamenting “Do not cut sandalwood” and “Let the hares be.”
How much more so when all recommendations fail to choose for talent,
and acceptances breed no fear of consequences!
When the standards of measurement fail even once,
what hope is there to recover the difference?
The solitary and outstanding
hide their talents, waiting for a fair price;
the frivolous and shallow
busy themselves with currying favor to get ahead swiftly.
Precisely because the talented await just recompense,
they sink into distress and obscurity;
precisely because the shallow scheme for quick gain,
they leap and dance, utterly unrestrained.
When the owls fly in flocks,
the yuān and fèng (mandarin ducks and phoenixes) gather in seclusion;
when jackals and wolves block the way,
the qílín flees afar.
If good is promoted and taught,
then the unrighteous will be driven far away;
when treachery and falsehood attain honor and glory,
heroes and the talented will vanish in hiding.
Those of lofty character disdain the company of the vulgar,
and men of purity are ashamed to be among the gluttonous.
When all appointments and assignments are in error,
then the worthy withdraw in silence;
when the worthy keep their talents folded away,
the wicked draw one another in;
as the wicked gather,
the way of petty men prevails;
when the way of petty men prevails,
the wicked stand shoulder to shoulder.
Thus commendations cease to be voiced,
and complaints and laments fill the air.
Those with lofty aspirations and great talent,
confident in their own abilities,
whether they act or stay silent,
resign themselves to fate’s decrees;
in fortune or adversity, gain or loss,
they leave it to circumstance,
and thus are invariably outstripped by those with powerful factions
and reside beneath those with influence.
Men who outclass others,
move only according to propriety,
stand like mountains and are still as deep pools;
yet those who truly know them are few,
while the crowd that chases after office
slanders and attacks them.
So it is that rulers who desire the worthy
do not know where exceptional talent lies;
men who cherish the Way
wish to serve, but find no place to apply their strength.
Though they have the capacity of Jì and Xuè,
and the breadth of vision to transcend the world,
they are left stuck and die in obscurity,
never given rank or recognition.
Meanwhile, those with factions and power,
throng together like scales on a fish,
and though the supply of men is exhausted and offices go unfilled,
those who attain office are still lauded,
so how could such an opportunity not be seized and exploited?
In the era of Líng and Xiàn,
eunuchs controlled affairs,
and bands of villains held power,
endangering and harming the loyal and good.
Selections in the central government became corrupted,
and recommendations from the prefectures became lax.
When central selection is corrupt,
the governors and guardians are unworthy men;
when recommendations from below are lax,
the xiùcái and xiàolián are not the virtuous.
Thus, men of the time would say:
"Those recommended as xiùcái
do not know how to read;
those chosen as xiàolián
have fathers living separately.
The poor and pure are as muddy as silt,
while those who score high and are good generals are timid as chickens."
They also said:
"In ancient times, men studied diligently to advance and recited the classics;
today, people seek office merely to escape toil."
Such was the depth of the malady.
At that time, ranks of nobility were hung up for sale,
just like stalls displayed in a marketplace;
those vying for passage bought them,
much like people in a market.
Those with money had no barriers and advanced straight ahead,
while the empty-handed gazed at the road and withdrew their steps.
Those with plentiful goods had high office,
while those with little wealth held low position.
Thus, Dōngyuán accumulated the money from selling offices,
and Cuī Liè was mocked for the stench of copper.
What was done above, those below emulated;
the ruler acted and the ministers did so even more.
Thus, flatterers and sycophants found favor,
and lone speakers enjoyed intimacy and acceptance.
The elders of Sāngzǐ discussed who should rule,
those in charge of selecting officials at Zhōngzhèng and Lìbù
all became brokers,
each demanding their own price.
The pure and poor scholar,
how could he expect any prospect at all!
This was already the case.
Moreover, the crooked and the upright were not alike,
just as ice and burning coals;
those who disliked upright people
were hateful to those not of their clique.
Those whose knife and yardstick were crooked,
feared what others might say of them;
those who advanced not by the right path
worried that their reputation would not be fair.
So they conspired together to fabricate slanders,
striking at the clear and virtuous,
blemishes and accusations sprang up everywhere,
and none dared to rescue them.
Thus Zēng and Mǐn suffered the slander of Shāng Chén,
Kǒngzǐ and Mòzǐ bore the defilement of Dào Zhí.
Those who cherished integrity and dwelled in honesty
were pressed and mired in filth,
while the crafty and deceitful
soared high amid the rainbows.
Yet the shallow-sighted common folk
could not distinguish the crooked from the upright,
mistook those who held to the Way for stagnant waters,
and called those who took shortcuts clever in adapting to change.
Those among the common people who moved with the wind
and followed the currents of the waves,
how could they ever devote themselves to virtue and conduct,
or labor deeply in study and learning!
Thus, none failed to cast aside the ordeals of discipline and restraint,
and rushed towards the swiftness of bribery.
Truly, this was why the house of Hàn was overthrown,
and what subsequent generations ought to take as a deep warning.
Someone said:
“Sir, in your discussion of the system of recommendation and selection at the end of Hàn,
you have truly grasped its ills.
Now, if one truly wishes to warn against past errors,
avoid the path of the overturned chariot,
change the tune of the present age,
guard against abuses of the law and transformations thereof,
cause the singing at Púshàng of the ‘Bārén,’
to return to the correct tones of Ānlè;
if disease is in the skin’s channels,
and there is no lingering stasis for it to retreat,
is there a method?
Among scholars, some are graceful and imposing in appearance,
with lofty reputation in excess,
but their minds are empty and hollow,
dry roots without substance;
if we judge by looks,
we need not necessarily obtain the worthy;
but if we take time and first examine them slowly,
this cannot be done in haste.
What should be done?”
Bǎopǔzǐ replied:
“To know men is wisdom,
and even the highest sages found this difficult.
If we now require all governors to discern talent before employment,
guaranteeing their nature and conduct from beginning to end,
this is truly not easy.
But if all simply set aside their private feelings,
exert all their intelligence,
are not swayed by profit or desire,
nor bend for connections and influence,
and whomever they intend to recommend,
must thoroughly reflect and examine him,
widely consult and inquire in detail,
investigate his reputation and scrutinize his deeds,
compare similarities and differences to guard against false adornment,
so that his relatives commend his filial piety and friendliness,
and his community affirms his trustworthiness and righteousness—
if he has held minor office before,
and shown loyalty and purity,
and handled affairs capably,
then an inch of brocade suffices to show skill,
and piercing a rat lets one observe his courage.
“Also,
Xiù and Xiào should all, as formerly, be tested on the Classics and essays,
guarding against the evil of fraudulent answers;
it must be ensured that those who wholly fail are not approved,
and officials should add penalties and imprisonment.
If those recommended in documents are not suitable,
the Cìshǐ or Tàishǒu should be dismissed;
if unsatisfactory, demoted.
If the qualified outnumber the unqualified,
no further promotion beyond the previous rank should occur.
If anyone accepts bribes to recommend the unworthy,
and this is exposed and confirmed, his name should be struck out,
and he imprisoned for life,
and not pardoned even by amnesty;
the recommended and the recommender share the same guilt.
Were this law now applied,
and enforced for a year or two,
those Xiù and Xiào candidates who fail would be numerous,
clearly showing that the selection system has long lacked rigor.
After this,
surely many will cultivate virtue and diligently study.
“Furthermore,
for all officeholders,
those who commit public crimes
should be dealt with according to the law;
those who are guilty of greed and corruption, though not capital offenses,
but less than death,
when the sentence is served or a pardon occurs,
should all be barred from office for life,
the lighter for twenty years.
If this were done,
dishonest officials
would surely be transformed into Yí Qí.
But if, when in office, they accept bribes,
and gold and money pile up like mountains,
yet when discovered, they manage to escape,
and if dismissed, within days are reinstated—
then even loyal historians will turn into Dào Zhí.
In such a case,
even if all recommended candidates are qualified,
one cannot blame the senior officials for not being upright.”
Someone said:
“Skill in words does not necessarily equal skill in conduct;
now, though one’s essay answers are exceptional,
how could this guarantee talent in governance?”
Bǎopǔzǐ replied:
“The ancients even selected men by their skill in archery—how much more so the Classics and essays!
If such methods are set aside,
then I have not seen another method more worthy than this.
Luxurious grass does not flourish on barren ground,
nor do giant fish grow in shallow waters;
an aphorism does not emerge from a fool’s mouth,
nor a lofty essay from a dullard’s pen.
Therefore, by studying the ‘Hóngfàn’, we know that Jīzǐ had the capacity to manage the world;
by reading the ‘Nine Strategies’, we see that Fànshēng harbored the plans for governing a state;
by examining the writings of Yíwú,
we learn he had the capacity to restore order;
by perusing Bù Hài’s works,
we see his proficiency in the way of kings and hegemons.
Now, if honesty candidates must pass the test in the Classics without error,
and xiùcái must answer the policy questions without missing the intent,
then they cannot remain hidden or obscure.
Even for top-ranking generals, their courage is tested,
yet essays and discourse are again used for selection—
how much more for scholars!
Suppose it cannot always ensure all are worthy and capable,
yet it is certainly better than having no examinations at all.
If now all those subject to recommendation throughout the realm
dare not neglect their studies,
then at least this one change
will in itself be a great benefit for public morals,
and not a small matter.
If all within the seas fear the consequences of false recommendation,
and all men cease striving for undeserved appointments,
turn from the branches of competition
and return to the root of learning,
then the Confucian Way will greatly flourish,
private bribery will gradually disappear,
exceptional talent will be available for employment,
and most offices will not go unfilled.”
Someone said:
“Sir, you would make the law of recommendation strict,
with only the penalty of lifelong banishment,
which is both severe and heavy,
and many would fear it.
But holding the reins tight and using many whips
is something even Bólè would not do;
a system of harsh prohibitions and severe laws
is something for which a government of virtue should feel shame.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"The medicines that fill the bones and supplement the flesh
excel in nourishing the body and increasing longevity,
but they cannot rescue someone drowning in urgent peril.
Pursuing the politics of tolerance and bearing slander
may help govern with honesty and preserve simplicity,
but cannot save against the calamity of decline and ruin.
If tigers and wolves come pressing in,
and one does not brandish spear or draw sword,
but instead plays the qín and chants poetry,
I have yet to see his life be preserved.
If fire blazes and reaches the house,
and one does not run about to throw water and douse it,
but instead exchanges bows and yields, circling about,
I have yet to see the fire extinguish itself.
Now if one debates these matters with those who wish to sell strategies,
it is like debating how to catch thieves with Zhí."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Now under all heaven there is unity,
with the nine regions sharing one culture;
the king issues governance and decrees,
thus it is right that they be regulated and unified.
Smaller measures and balances,
even these cannot be allowed to differ here and there;
how much more the standards for people,
which must not be irregular and without restraint.
Although Jiāngbiǎo lies distant,
and closely borders the coastal corners,
yet being infused by Dao and civilization,
it follows ritual and teachings,
and this has already been so for over a thousand years.
In the past, although there was temporary separation,
not even a hundred years in total,
nevertheless the matter of Confucian learning
was never wholly abandoned.
Only because its territory is narrower than the Central Plains,
therefore the number of scholars
is not as plentiful, nothing more.
As for those of noble virtue and exceptional learning,
disciples such as Zǐ Yóu and Zhòng Rèn,
have not been surpassed by those of the upper country.
In the past, when Wú was newly annexed,
the tribute scholars offered were dismissed without examination.
Now peace has lasted nearly forty years,
yet examinations are still not held—
thus the Ru tradition of the southeast has declined compared to former times.
This is to regard them the same as those who wear their garments left-lapped,
which is not the way to distinguish them.
Moreover, if the junzi still cherishes others with propriety,
how much more so as their kind and gentle fathers and mothers!
Laws can invite calamity,
ordinances may harm transformation;
this is what is meant.
Now when tribute scholars are not examined,
all will certainly resort to embellishment and pursuit,
competing for empty fame,
and who will still open their books and receive instruction?
This is what is meant by excessive reward bringing only their ruin.
"There are those with a natural fondness for antiquity
whose hearts delight in arts and literature;
they study not for stipend,
relish Dao and forget poverty,
like Fǎ Gāoqīng and Zhōu Shēngliè.
As for those who have refined study but do not seek glory and gain,
such are one in ten thousand.
As to followers like Níng Yuè, Ní Kuān, and Huáng Bà,
whose reason for driving themselves to diligence in the classics
was not natural disposition,
it came from hardship, bitter struggle, and exhaustion,
wishing to pull themselves out of hardship by classical expertise.
If it had not been the age of Hàn Wǔ,
people like Zhū Mǎichén and Yán Zhù
would not necessarily have studied.
Nowadays, if the way to wealth and rank
is easily achieved without learning,
and they also lack natural preference for it,
how could they willingly toil in vain,
sweeping the floors as junior students,
or traveling afar to seek teachers and inquire into Dao?
In an age of war,
military matters are honored and letters neglected;
common people view Ru scholars as slaves and servants,
and see the classics as so much dirt and chaff—
why is this?
Because fame and reputation run contrary to them.
Not employing them is like selling formal caps in Yí and Yuè,
or offering bearded snakes to Huáxià.
If now all, far and near, are treated with the same rules,
and examinations are clearly administered,
then surely many will shoulder their satchels for a thousand li
to seek out teachers and friends,
shifting what they would have spent on gifts and bribes
to purchase books,
not even waiting out the day."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Among men of talent and learning, those worthy and filial
are already hard to find.
Suppose even in the age of Huán and Líng,
appointing officials was never based on wealth,
and those who presided in the grand towers and ministries
could explain all the classics thoroughly,
and answer every question without fail,
even so, injustice and slander would befall them,
and they would still not pass through.
I have always lamented that those in power at the time
did not set proper safeguards.
My view is that when it is a new year and the tribute-examination is to be held,
this year, the Ru officials and talented scholars
can be made to write various policy answers in advance,
sufficient for all uses.
They are submitted and prohibited from being kept in the palace halls,
sealed and closed;
at the time of examination,
they are quickly assigned.
Human plotting and contrivance thus ceases.
When answering the policies,
all can be gathered in one place,
with chosen high officials supervising personally.
Also, strictly forbid all collusion and entering or exiting;
only after affairs are finished may they depart.
Anyone violating this is guilty without pardon.
If it is done like this,
the wings of sycophancy and private connections are clipped.
An enlightened ruler relies on himself being un-deceivable,
not on others not deceiving him.
Why should one be ashamed to make such rigorous regulation?
If the examination system is established,
then all under heaven can do without official schools,
and people will study diligently of themselves.
According to the Four Divisions, there are also provisions for those adept in the laws and ordinances;
yet people in office today,
regardless of rank,
all do not know the laws.
Some passages are subtle and hard to grasp,
yet petty officials are often obstinate,
and are made to judge cases—
how can matters of life and death be entrusted to them,
and the fate of the people treated carelessly,
and placed in the hands of the ignorant?
As for bureaucrats who do not know the law,
deceived by subordinates without realizing it,
and those who settle matters by mouth and pen
are indignant, unable to know the letter of the law;
some neither know nor inquire,
nor refer to the responsible supervisor.
Some judge cases by their own opinion,
stumbling and careless with laws and ordinances;
so upright and capable officials,
let them all be examined in the statutes just as in the classics,
and those most proficient, promote them according to merit.
If such is done,
officials who twist the law
and wrongful cases in court will be few under heaven.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"As for my interactions with friends,
they should not be superficial or mixed.
Appearing close yet not sincere—
Yáng Xióng censured such men.
Thus, though men hold high position and fair name,
are of like family and equal years,
if our pursuits and actions are different,
and our interests divergent,
I have never joined with them.
Some are proud of their former achievements,
walking with lofty steps and far-seeing gaze;
some forget or neglect old acquaintances fallen from favor,
some slight and cast off those of common taste;
some judge men by their office and not by virtue.
Those who do not meet someone who understands them,
and languish in the fields and hills,
though richly talented and far-seeing,
and noble in conduct and principle,
this cannot be;
but those who happen to be promoted,
hold high rank and accessible office,
even if mediocre or dull,
they will assuredly join with.
Such persons,
though able to make earthworms soar among the clouds
and the sparrow-hawk reach heaven,
wielding knife and ruler in hand,
and dispensing fortune or calamity with their mouths,
when they gain favor, they display brilliance,
but losing it, wither even in spring.
For me to take their place or speak for them
would be shameful to share their world."
Poverty and success
cannot be sought after.
Yet the frivolous and insubstantial,
the sons without standing,
never have any sudden moments of honest refusal or indignation,
but in the space of a single night, hasten to seek an audience,
guard the entrances and courtyards,
eagerly flattering with simpering smiles,
words humble, faces pleasing,
bearing jars and holding gifts,
constantly seeking to ingratiate themselves;
with toil and effort accumulated over a long time,
still they meet with aversion and rejection,
then turn to rely on elder patrons to create connections for them.
If they are accepted,
then their elation surpasses that of a prisoner who, confined in darkness, suddenly receives pardon;
if they are refused,
then their dejection is worse than that of one struck by disaster or illness.
Whether one finds access or obstruction is decreed by fate,
and the Way esteems rectitude;
adversity and prosperity are entrusted to the natural course of things—
why need one ask so much about the fords and crossroads of life?
Alas for such petty men,
are they not contemptible indeed!
Human feelings are not the same,
how distant and strange they can be!
I am always moved with deep emotion,
pitying and even aiding them in their shame.
In the past, Zhuāng Zhōu saw that Huìzǐ’s carriages were many,
yet he cast away the extra fish he had.
I regret that men of the age do not eagerly strive for advancement.
Looking at those there,
galloping through dust and wind,
they do not excel in establishing meritorious achievements,
pursuing the essentials in themselves,
but are bent solely on lofty associations,
to form cliques,
thinking that the most urgent matter in human affairs,
the greatest urgency in the world,
is to favor those who stand tall and alone like mountains
and regard them as awkward, stingy, remote, and clumsy;
whereas those of servile demeanour, fawning like slaves and maidservants,
are thought to be the ones who understand the ways of the world.
Customs form and practices are adopted,
none do not pursue superficialities,
the current constantly drifts away,
this is something to lament.
Some possess scant virtue but high office,
vessels full and ambitions overflowing,
are startled and moved by talk of riches and profit,
yet when they see exceptional gentlemen, they doze quietly.
Those in tattered clothes, leaning on staves,
wearing coarse garments and carrying satchels,
even if their writings are brilliant in rivalry,
and their learning is deep and abstruse,
are treated no differently from dust or grass,
no one extends them a helping hand.
Yet as for the likes of Chéng, Zhèng, Wáng Sūn, and Luó Póu,
riding fine horses and wearing light silks,
carrying gold and concealing jade,
even if they cannot set pen to paper,
cannot distinguish beans from wheat,
people still rush out barefoot to greet them,
stop eating and clutch their hair in their haste to welcome them.
I only regret not being in such a position,
having an axe but no handle,
unable to prevent the filth and dregs of the realm from spreading to all corners,
or to cast them away into the wilds of the north.
Even though their power blazes bright,
their blades and rulers cut with influence enough to move mountains and drain seas,
their very breath can cause a clay idol to ascend the clouds,
if I were to approach their gates and courtyards,
I would still not have time for them.
Yet there are many who humble themselves, smiling pleasantly,
walking on their knees,
seeking friendships with such men
in hope of some advantage.
Alas!
How uneven are the minds of the people;
how remote and lacking in nobility!
That I, though born in a sage’s era, suffer poverty and lowliness,
turning back, see nothing behind me,
now looking ahead, fail to catch up—
is there not some reason for this!
Yet if one’s nature truly cannot bear something,
each follows his own heart’s desire;
by this shall one survive or perish—
I cannot change it.
But someone may object and say:
“Times change and the world changes,
the occupations of past and present are different,
action is based on oneself,
but one’s reputation is made by others.
For gold and jade to cross unknown dangers,
they must rely on a light boat;
for the numinous crow to reach the dark firmament,
it relies on a soaring wind;
for the fragrant orchid to spread its scent intensely,
it is by the merit of the pure breeze;
even a worthy in seclusion arising from the fields,
it is through the aid of a sympathetic confidant.
Now you, sir, your friendships must all be with those pure in conduct,
your intimates pass only the most rigorous selection of mind and nature;
standing alone with but one mouth,
abandoned by those of name and rank,
making enemies everywhere,
attracting resentment from the crowd—
is this in harmony with the highest ideal of adapting your brightness to things and gently encompassing all?
Does it accord with the loftiest principle of the Law?
If one forms friendships only with equal wisdom,
then the pauper would never have received the favor of Gōngdàn;
if one roams only with those of equal talent,
then Master Ní would have had no guest worthy of entering his private chambers.”
Bào Pǔ Zǐ said:
“I have heard that those who are careful in their friendships never lose good men,
but those who form bonds indiscriminately often regret it later.
Thus the wise of old always chose before befriending,
never befriended before choosing.
What you speak of
is the calculation of worldly men;
what I uphold
is the aspiration of a reclusive scholar.
You speak of gems afloat and birds soaring high,
all relying on something;
truly, this is another interpretation and a distinct argument.
But I believe it is better to be an uncarried treasure,
an unmoving roc,
an unswayed orchid,
a man without cliques—
what
(harm?)
is there to the brilliance of the night-shining gem,
the greatness that reaches Heaven,
the fragrant plant that holds sweet scent,
the undying orchid?
Moreover, when fame exceeds substance,
and rank surpasses talent,
those in such positions can scarcely escape disaster or humiliation;
so how can association with such be cause for glory or good fortune!
“By this reasoning,
to form connections and by them to meet with success,
even if one achieves distinction, it is not truly to be valued;
to rely on others but be led astray,
is like being shaded by a rotten tree and suffering its collapse.
They cannot even stop their own downfall,
how could they save me from destruction?
I have heard that the true gentleman, content in himself and unconcerned with externals,
in relation to ordinary men
only endures external association out of pressure and necessity,
even if there be thousands,
they are no more than lice crowding on the clothes,
or warts clustered on the body.
To lose thousands of such friends,
is like dust flying from Sōng and Dài,
or dead branches falling from the Dèng forest.
Can there be any benefit in their presence,
or any true loss in their absence?
“And as for friendship itself,
one must select those who are upright, trustworthy, and broadly learned,
who correct faults and expose falsehoods,
speak their minds unbidden in life,
do not cover up excuses in death,
whose trust lasts throughout,
unchanged by heat or cold.
Yet such a person is truly hard to find,
and sometimes silence and words take separate paths,
resentment and love dwell in different hearts,
they gather in prosperity and part in decline,
see gain and forget trust.
Their present condition
is like birds and fish flocking together,
or ice and coals kept in the same vessel;
that they remain long in union—
how can it be possible!
Between father and son the nature is Heaven-bestowed,
their likes and dislikes should be equal,
yet Zǐzhèng and Zǐjùn
could not reconcile different judgments;
or the youth Boqí of South Mountain—
there was still dispute and contention.
Face to face but hearts at variance,
this has ever been so.
To force all together into one—
is this not most difficult!
“As for people in the world,
their friendships do not concern intentions,
they pursue reputation and follow the prevailing trend,
coming when things are hot, leaving when they cool;
seeing faults but not correcting,
seeing confusion but not rescuing;
when there is profit, each hoards it for himself and does not share,
if there is harm, each seeks to avoid it and does not care for others;
when a matter is advantageous, each seizes it first without yielding,
when opportunity arises, they sell out the other to secure themselves.
Whenever it is thus,
having such friends is worse than having none at all.
“In all under Heaven, it is not that there are none wholly unworthy of friendship;
but among those who bring benefit, the few are led, while those who become burdens are many.
True discernment of people
is something even the highest sages struggle to attain.
Yet if one wishes to vigorously encourage those with near talent,
but is lacking in discerning ability,
striving to broaden one’s friendships
and wishing that all would turn out well,
hoping for companions who will traverse ease and danger without changing their hearts,
and endure hardship together, each bearing the burdens of the other—
I have yet to see such companions being easy to find in large numbers.
Even if you search for fine jade among ant hills,
or seek for phoenixes in the nests of wrens,
it would not be more difficult.
Nor do I dare assert that on the southern slopes of Lántián,
or in the caverns of Dānxué,
these things do not exist!
I only say that they are exceedingly rare.
“For people’s conduct and aspirations are not the same,
just as gold sinks and feathers float.
When aims and tastes diverge,
it is like fire rising and water descending.
If it is impossible to come together,
even with the magic of Creation,
or the skill of the Grand Craftsman,
it cannot make them united;
how could it be forced!
What I have received is the sluggishness of a blunt horse,
compounded by a nature innately earnest yet deeply lazy.
All amusements and tricks,
such as playing chess and gambling at dice,
are things I dislike to witness;
as for racing, dashing about quickly,
roaming in hunting or arrogant sightseeing,
these I never partake in;
I have no enjoyment in mocking or jesting.
All these few things
are what the world presently prefers,
all are obsessed with them,
and I entirely lack such pursuits;
thus my personal friendships are especially distant.
Moreover, I am upright in temperament,
inclined to speak sincere and faithful words,
like bitter medicine prescribed,
yet those willing to accept are few.
Again, if I would urge them in learning and knowledge,
admonish them against frantic striving,
restrain their gambling,
moderate their drunkenness,
this again is what ordinary people cannot rejoice in.
“To force together things of different forms,
to violate one’s feelings and conform to the vulgar,
is a burden to which people’s love cannot endure;
how could I ever endure it?
Wishing for genuine improvement with every day,
how could it be obtained!
Knowing it is so and not changing,
could this not be said to be blind to the present age,
and clumsy in employing what is great?
When a friendship does not reach the end,
when a union is followed by separation,
then both are called lacking in magnanimity,
and both lose the beauty of seeing things through.
If thick [affection], then intimacy and love are born;
if thin, then dislike and discord accumulate;
such is the order of nature—
should one not carefully select?
For those who can drink from the cup together and pat each other’s back,
gripping each other’s hand for a moment,
wanting to have many in number and necessarily to have them whole—
that is what I fear most.”
Someone asked:
“In that case, can one do without friendship altogether?”
Bào Pǔzi replied:
“How could it be so!
If one who fears water gives up on boats and oars,
or one wary of wounds casts aside axe and adze,
such thinking would not do!
The way of friendship
is of ancient origin.
If Heaven and Earth do not unite, there is no harmony;
if high and low do not relate, their ambitions are at odds.
When there is no harmony, the two qi are sundered;
when ambitions are at odds, under Heaven there is no state.
Yet the beginnings are easy,
but carrying it through to the end proves hard.
Trouble lies in forming ties with those not suited,
and failing over trifles, forgetting what is great.
The Yìjīng praises many orchids,
the Shījīng sings of hundreds of friends;
though one may have brothers,
none match friends in life.
Closely considering the Three Benefits,
the greatest sages have praised them;
it is why disciples deepen their intimacy,
and why harsh words do not come.
It is by the power of friendship that Guǎn Zhòng escaped execution and established hegemony,
and Zǐ Yuán left his constable’s post to drive the Vermilion Chariot.
“A single string cannot sound the harmonies of the Sháo and Xià music;
a single color cannot form the brilliance of the yǎnlóng dragon;
one flavor alone cannot complete the sweetness in Yī’s cauldron;
one tree cannot create the lushness of Dènglín forest.
The Mystic Orchard reaches to the sky,
due to the accumulation of many stones.
The vast Southern Ocean
is filled only by the gathering of all streams.
When a bright mirror is raised, one’s tilted hat is seen;
when Xī Hé shines, every crooked shadow is exposed;
when a whetstone is used, blunted points are soon sharpened;
when worthy friends are joined, the path of virtue is greatly extended.
Those who attain virtue know it is so;
those they seek as companions are those surpassing themselves;
those they befriend lower must share the same ideals.
In company, they discuss the Way and advance in virtue;
when apart, they join in heart, advancing together.
In prosperity, they share the order of the world;
in decline, they join to manage affairs.
In safety, they refine their moral principles;
in danger, they mutually aid one another.
They would be ashamed to let Tán Kěn monopolize steadfastness to the ground,
nor let Wáng Gòng alone possess the beauty of brushing the hat.
Thus,
the way of friendship is precious indeed.
“Yet it truly is not easy to comprehend;
power and profit cause people to come and go,
accumulated slander destroys close-tied alliances,
and gradual soaking weakens what was once as solid as glue and lacquer.
Thus come lamentations for the loss of original feelings;
at times, with a glare, one forgets all thought,
so that the bond between Yuán Bó and Jù Qīng
is famed only in the past,
while the strife between Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú
is seen again and again today.
Pushing the past to trace the present,
it is truly to be lamented.
The phoenix does not share a branch with owls and kites;
the qílín and unicorn do not herd with wolves and jackals;
pure springs do not mix with muddy run-off;
kind and enlightened do not dwell with cruel and dark.
Why is this?
For by gradual influence, righteousness is changed;
by violent coercion, harm is born.”
Someone asked:
“May I respectfully ask to hear the Way of perfect friendship?”
Bào Pǔzi replied:
“When a gentleman breaks off a friendship, he yet speaks no evil words;
how could he ever dispute with those who differ?
He would risk even his life to grant favor to a friend;
how could he vie over fame and position?
In good friendship, there is intimacy without disrespect,
harmony without uniformity;
when seeing faults in the other,
one corrects with honest speech and admonishes him;
if the other warns me of my faults,
I amend myself quickly and humbly.
One does not keep silent out of fear of hurting the other’s feelings,
nor refuse to accept because it jars my ears;
one does not use clever words to dress up what is wrong,
nor flowery speech to cover their faults;
not conforming outwardly while inwardly conflicted,
not faking agreement with one’s mouth while false in feelings,
not assenting to the face while resenting behind the back,
not resenting another’s surpassing oneself,
but shielding their defects and drawing forth their strengths,
hiding their shortcomings and declaring their virtues;
not engaging in schemes and disputes without,
nor accumulating rivalries and burdens within.
Only thus can the delight sung in ‘Lù Míng’ be preserved,
and the stings of ‘Fá Mù’ be silenced.
But if, from a trifling beginning there is a careless breach;
it is easy to deepen but not to lessen;
it starts as body and shadow,
but ends as distant as the stars;
great joy turns to deep hatred,
aid transformed to enmity;
such regret from lack of discernment,
there is nothing more to be done.
In times when, near the end of the Hàn dynasty, things were declining,
the imperial reins slack,
the public virtue abandoned,
and contentious customs took hold;
where diverging from the times was called purity,
and saving the world was seen as self-dishonor;
with order of rank and etiquette broken,
the great relations in chaos;
those in office
do not strive to fulfill their duty
but neglect the root and seek the branches,
turn away from reality and seek reputation.
Those who neglect state affairs gain praise for virtue,
the more wicked their accumulation, the greater their achievement claimed.
None fail to combine rapid advance with intrigue;
speaking fast, feigning sleep,
enduring cold or heat,
to run to powerful doors,
to trade vain fame by the words of those in control,
to buy undeserved office from sellers of rank.
Or, competing for what they desire,
they turn and mutually slaughter one another.
Thereupon Gōngshū Wěicháng was gravely displeased with such conduct,
but lacked the strength to rectify it;
unable to bear witnessing it,
he thus became indignant and composed a critical treatise,
secluding himself and severing social ties.
This was truly a response aroused by strong feelings and the desire for action.
Yet, to straighten what is crooked by going beyond what is just,
is not an enduring norm or lasting instruction.
What is truly required is to steer clear of the parties of those who differ in kind,
and be cautious of the source of flattery and wantonness.
Why must one bare his chest to feign opposition to others,
or cut off food to reproach those who eat delicacies!
If, in relations with others,
there is repeated remonstrance but no cessation,
it necessarily leads to great disorder.
Therefore, what ritual and righteousness have cast aside
may be utterly severed.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The xiāoniǎo horse can strain its fragrant sinews to outstrip shadows,
but cannot step on ice to ford the depths;
the fierce tiger may roar like thunder and pounce to devour,
but cannot leap into clouds and mist to fly through the void.
The great guānɡhún bird cannot spread its wings within a cage's cover,
nor can the nimble hawk strike like lightning beneath canopies and mats.
Since things are thus,
so too with men.
Thus one who can harmonize yin and yang
may not necessarily be able to master every discipline or edit records;
one able to travel the five great rivers and nine provinces
need not be able to pursue all the tiny fastidious paths in canonical details.
Huìzǐ—
model among top ministers—
could not row a boat to cross the Yánghóu river;
Hàn Gāo—
hero of martial spirit—
could not manage properties or keep accounts incisively;
Huáiyīn—
a model general—
could not maintain agriculture and commerce to avert hunger or cold;
Zhōu Bó—
pillar of the altars of state—
could not answer financial claims or plead legal cases.
If one discards strengths for the sake of weaknesses,
then talents surpassing their peers and standing out will go unused;
if one insists on practical performance and minute ritual,
then the feats of those who shape the world and save the people will remain unrecognized.
Heaven cannot level its northwest corner,
earth cannot raise its southeast,
sun and moon cannot shed light into every crevice,
nor can rising winds create waves in the bottom of a well.
If one plucks teeth, young catalpa trees won't cover a mat an inch wide;
if one picks ears, great beams are no better than a wren’s feather;
when shooting birds, a thousand gold coins are less effective than a clay pellet;
for sewing and mending, a long sword cannot compare to a small needle.
Why must one crouch a great elephant to catch a mouse,
or yoke a massive roc to announce the dawn?
Thus, Jiāng Yá’s peddling of warm drinks
(some think "warm drink" should read "broth") had no buyer,
yet he became instructor to Wénwǔ.
Jiǎng Shēng was slighted among the hundred lǐ,
yet walked alone in the grove of three locust trees.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Resplendent chapters and ornate language
are not toys for the blind;
extraordinary talent
is not recognized by the shallow and brief.
If one’s vision cannot discern things,
then a jade dragon and a coarse robe are equally valued;
if insight is lacking to recognize,
then the superior person and the commoner are viewed the same.
If the eye does not see,
beauty does not enter the spirit;
if none respond to it,
then those who wound it will surely come.
Moreover, the things people love or hate, admire or despise,
have never been the same in past and present;
as times change, customs change,
and even the same thing assumes different values.
It is like the huáng-jade of Xià Hòu;
formerly worth a walled city,
if sold today,
it would be less valued than copper or iron.
Therefore, in old times a man who sought resolve in reclusion was called a worthy scholar,
now a Confucian living in the wilds is deemed unworthy.
Thus those who were upright pillars in a sage age
may well be seen as criminals in a decadent time;
those formerly upright and pure
are considered weaklings in decline.
Lofty and distinguished men,
men who follow the Way,
their noble faith is not just the lofty city wall,
their deep virtue not merely the depth of Lǚliáng;
so the short-sighted cannot appreciate them,
and the shallow cannot fathom them.
Hence, they are looked down upon for being different,
and hated for not seeking one’s favor;
if unused abilities are not valued,
what more need be said?
Then comes the scattering of dust on pure jade,
or ulcers being born on fine skin;
they are slandered with uniform blame,
attacked for standing alone;
Meng Yǐng endured the filth of robbery and violence,
Cháo Xǔ suffered accusations as a secret thief.
If one is not as luminous as the suspended constellations,
or possessed of deep discernment that perceives the subtle,
how can one extract sunken jade from the mud,
or pick out a fine pearl from the river?
Thus pure jade and precious stones may be unsold in the market,
how much more so if obscured among ordinary pebbles?
A rare gentleman knocks at the gate and is rejected,
how much more so if hidden in the grove of four-horned sheep?
Sūn Bìn wished to display his secret strategems,
but Sīmǎ left him maimed;
Hán Fēi wished to establish achievements in governance,
but Lǐ Sī killed him;
Jiǎ Yì was impassioned
and held plans to govern the realm,
but martial men drove him away;
Zǐ Zhèng was loyal and upright,
fit to rescue from peril,
but Gōng Xiǎn entrapped him.
So the man of Hé clan clutched his uncarved jade and wept blood,
and Qín Xī’s anguish brought him to shatter his own head.
It is far easier to distinguish jade from stone than the worthy from the unworthy,
and love for precious treasures is fiercer than love for men of talent;
if it is so with treasures easy to distinguish,
and so with objects much prized,
yet one still risks punishment and mutilation
and suffers slander for generations.
How much more so with the worthy, who are hard to know and not regarded as urgent;
with slanderers who paint details on the unseen,
treacherous ministers who fear the upright might endanger them,
crooked men who envy those who follow the rule,
and those who wander naked at night who hate the coming of the bright lamp!
Thus, high praise for virtue
is suppressed and not exalted,
and baseless slander
arises before form casts a shadow.
There is no one to recommend them even like the Chu people who wailed on another’s behalf;
one chance in ten thousand is no chance at all.
So it is only natural.
If jade is treated as mere stone,
eventually stone will be treated as jade;
if the worthy are regarded as fools,
eventually fools will be regarded as worthy.
Mistaking stone for jade
causes no real harm;
but regarding fools as worthy—
that is the calamity of a dying state.
For diagnosing the dying, even if he survives, he will still die;
just as a dead pulse means death even if the body linger on.
Should this not be cause for caution?
Alas!
How sad!
None give it a thought.
In former days, Zhòngní, greatest of sages,
was encumbered in the east by Qí men,
and in the south blocked by Zǐ Xī.
Wén Zhòng, a great worthy,
was at first unranked by the customs of Chǔ,
and in the end wandered together with Jūn Rú.
To compete and establish merit in an age of strife—
is this not difficult?
Green jade and deep black stone
cannot be sold except by Táo Yī;
a weight of a thousand jūn
cannot be carried except by Bēn Huò.
The melody "Báixuě" on the strings
cannot be harmonized save by Líng Sù;
unmatched talent
cannot be put to use save by an enlightened sovereign.
And yet, the gleaming night pearl
does not lose its essence for want of a buyer,
nor sell itself cheaply for base profit;
the great bell of Zhōu and the Chime Stones
do not diminish their substance by being neglected,
nor seek appreciation from dwarfs;
the Yiyáng melody and Cloud Chant
do not cease their song for lack of an audience,
nor compete for fame amidst lewd cacophony;
supreme virtue
does not abandon principle to keep to common paths,
nor compromise in the face of the vulgar.
Thus, the Hé-jade becomes a blocked commodity,
pliant timber lies unused,
the raw ore of the Crimson Sword
never sees Ōuyě’s forge;
the fields of Yuán Kǎi
will never see the gates to the world opened.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Among my friends there is one named Jū Líng xiānshēng,
serene, joyful, calm, and pure,
his body and spirit are as if mutually forgotten.
Outwardly, he does not display a manner meant to startle or feign before the foolish;
inwardly, he does not keep a heart fixated on appearances.
He wanders among the profound mounds and ancient proclamations,
delighting to the point of forgetting his worries.
By day, he appreciates the last rays of Xīhé,
and in the evening, he admires the lingering glow of Wàngshū.
There is no path, however distant, which he does not investigate;
no subtlety in language that he does not scrutinize.
Yet the tracks of his carriage do not enter the powerful and influential domains,
nor do his letters pass through the halls of the mighty.
Thus, his name does not extend beyond the thatched hut,
nor does his person leave the furrows of the fields.
At this, Yì Liàng dàfū paid him a visit and reproached him, saying:
'I have heard that when the deep dragon stirs, dark clouds gather;
when the Way brings transformation like rain, outstanding talents rise up.
Thus, in the public way there are voices like the music of antlered choirs;
the cauldrons bear the marks of winds that soar above.
When measured, such things fetch a price beyond estimation;
when hurled upwards, they leap to the heights of heaven.
They shine with distant brilliance in Yánggǔ,
and spread their great light across the nine realms.
Their exploits shelter the age,
their fame resounds without end.
Thus, one who will not travel a path though it is close at hand,
even if he has the feet of the wind, cannot reach it;
one who does not move from beneath the low rafters,
even if he had the wings of the great hóngkūn, could not attain it.
How much the more when one lies at peace beyond the outer wilds,
folding his wings on the branches of hidden paulownia—
how can he hope to make swift pursuit to seek out light?
How can he soar lightly into the blue sky?
The span of years quickly fades and does not last,
one's sojourn in the world is fleeting, not to return.
The wise, treading on frost, know that hard ice is sure to follow;
maintaining awareness from the beginning, they know all things must end.
The Six Dragons drive their chariots through the great void;
the flowery pinnacle swiftly turns to dusk.
Thus, the ancients, journeying downstream, looked back with sighs,
gazing at the fleeting gap and were moved to sorrow.
Sir, you possess the transcendent talents of an epoch-making sage;
you embody excellence, far above the common run.
Your sharp pen surges and billows like waves;
six rare gifts pent up, accumulating in deep reserves.
Yet you cannot ride the ascending winds to soar high;
nor spread your pure radiance in the ninefold heavens.
Your talents are not displayed among the finest sacrificial vessels;
your person is not spared the toil of carrying firewood.
It is like performing harmonious music in a deaf world,
or selling caps of formal rank in a land where the hair is worn unkempt.
In vain, you forget yourself in the groves of letters;
you fix your will to exhaust the spirit;
exalting jade-like purity within your bosom;
uttering gems at the tip of your brush.
Your person faces recurring poverty;
your spirit is wearied amidst persistent loftiness.
It is as if a perfect jade disk were buried deep beneath heavy soil,
or embroidered silks sealed within chests of bundled documents;
in the end, there will be no wealth from trading,
who then will appreciate the treasures hidden in obscurity?
A dragon-horse when lashed and fettered,
cannot be distinguished from a lame donkey;
a crimson blade sheathed,
how is it different from a leaden knife?
The zhan and wei fishes do not dwell in the tracks of oxen;
the great péng bird does not linger in the mugwort thicket.
May you, Sir, abandon the dens of dragons and snakes,
and ascend the paths that lead to manifest benefit;
set aside the solitary purity of a tranquil gate;
learn from the two mice and be alert in the face of danger;
cross the desolate valleys to mount the heights;
don the red robes to transform your plain appearance;
strive to meet the rushing winds in the clear morning;
do not circle and hesitate, missing the right time;
gather renown and honor in lofty places;
