resonate with the joys of great bells and cauldrons.
Is Bǎi Chéng, but a mere common man,
to be much admired merely for knowing the difference between bramble and vetch? '
Jū Líng xiānshēng replied:
'I have heard that the working of the spirit is dark and remote,
mixed and dim, vast and indistinct;
fortune and misfortune interchange between latent and explicit,
rise and fall tangle together at the meeting of fullness and emptiness.
The swift traveler cannot escape the shadow dogging his body,
the one who rejoices in accomplishment cannot evade the failure of circumstance;
To redirect the flow at the end is
not so good as correcting things at their first, signless beginnings;
Regulating the already-formed
cannot compare to returning to the root beyond the primeval plainness.
Thus one who understands the inchworm
willingly endures constraint to preserve extension;
one who knows the ways of opening and blockage
is not distressed or elated by fortune or misfortune.
Moreover, the vast potter shapes things,
the Great Image gives them form;
agitation and tranquility embrace different values,
soaring and sinking reveal opposed tendencies.
Gold and jewels prize their heaviness,
feathers boast of their lightness.
The confined-minded cling to defilement and mud, while the one who achieves the subtle wanders free in the mysterious clarity.
The stagnant pool, collecting the runoff, overflows;
the vast Bohai Sea swallows a hundred rivers but is never full.
The goby shrimp leaps with joy in the mud;
the crimson chi dragon soars fiercely in lofty heights.
Those who gnaw fragrant bait
eagerly pursue their appetites unto death;
those who savor plainness
hold Heavenly Harmony and incline toward life.
One who discerns the workings of fate
beholds what has no sign and remains unconfused;
the one who is blind to rest and misfortune
blunders into the drawn crossbow without alarm.
Each follows what he loves,
how could he easily change his course?
I have heard: the five jades cannot split themselves open in the Sōng mountains,
the flying serpent cannot summon lightning without mist,
the famed Dragon Abyss sword cannot sever horn and rhino without being wielded,
the great bell cannot sound unless it is struck.
The golden fungus awaits the autumn wind to shine,
the oriole waits for the fires and the summer sun to sing;
the qílù horse will not gallop heedlessly into peril;
a true gentleman does not debase his name for expediency.
When times are oppressive, one sinks into neglect;
when the age is right, one soars to heaven's court.
The scholar thinks self-display is not true elevation;
a woman who seeks her own marriage loses her chastity.
Why must I pursue the lofty reclusion of Xiǎn Yǐ?
Or imitate Zǐqū's empty glory for bearing sacrificial meats?
When poverty comes,
then even Yǒuyú danced as he fished,
Shàngfù was pursued by foolish old women,
Master Fàn endured humiliation, carrying baskets of manure,
Hóng Shì hid his talents as shepherd and ploughman;
but when fortune arrived,
then Huái Yīn cast aside his rod and became a king,
Wén Zhòng took off his sandals and wore blue robes,
Fù Yuè gave up his trowel and spoke on the Way,
Guǎnzi slipped off his shackles and became Chief Minister.
Thus, the noble person conceals his talents waiting for the right moment,
accumulates virtue in preparation for achievements,
if the time is not right, he does not appear;
if the ruler is not fit, he does not serve.
Poverty or success depend on what one encounters;
advancement or withdrawal are not fixed.
When tranquil,
he is the model recluse;
when active,
the exemplar of heroes.
Some pursue merit through writing,
others inscribe their achievements upon national vessels.
The paths are different but the end is one.
The principle is unified.
A scholar may perform deeds worthy of esteem,
but cannot compel the world to esteem him;
he may possess abilities worth employing,
but cannot force the world to employ him.
If clothed in coarse clothes and eating herbs while trapping rabbits,
then the heart is happy and the mind at ease,
as if this would last for life.
If wearing official robes, riding in a carriage,
adorned in vermillion and purple,
it seems entirely appropriate.
Consistently dwelling as a commoner:
this is the true person’s practice.
If the treasures upon my mat are not amassed,
or the actions within my thatched cottage are not refined,
that is my fault.
Those who understand are few;
name and position do not arrive;
jade is mistaken for stone;
the phoenix is deemed a quail—
this is not my wrongdoing.
To strive fretfully for recognition,
and brood over being overlooked,
is the disposition of the common;
but to cultivate one’s energy spaciously,
to be bland and without desires,
is the will of those without regret.
When the time arrives and the Way is practiced,
the truly great feel no special delight;
within heaven and earth,
those who know fate have no worries.
If one pursues riches of ten thousand in search of an extra hundred,
he will lose many core things,
and I have no time for that.'
A disciple asked:
'I have heard that at the end of the Hàn,
in the time of Líng and Xiàn,
ranks and judgments were confused and disorderly,
the outstanding fell into distress and neglect,
the greedy and gluttonous held power,
fame did not match the reality,
worth was not based on substance,
those who were connected were deemed worthy,
those who were poor were considered foolish.
Why was this?'
Bǎo Pǔ Zǐ replied:
“The rumble and crash of thunder chariots,
and yet there are those who do not hear it;
the seven luminaries traverse the heavens,
and yet there are those who do not see.
Is it only the bodily vessels that can be deaf or blind?
When the mind-spirit is obscured,
it is just the same.
Thus, those who hear lofty words but do not grasp them,
it is not that they lack ears;
those who see outstanding talent but do not recognize it,
it is not that they lack eyes;
it is because their hearing does not reach the subtle,
and their sight does not attain the extraordinary.
Those whose wisdom and magnanimity reach far,
stand steadfast like a mountain;
those of small ability and petty ambition,
drift on the wind like thistledown, float on the water like duckweed.
Only the mountain stands,
thus none can move it;
only the duckweed floats,
thus it drifts and does not settle.
In comparison to goods,
those locked away, waiting in silence for a buyer,
are always of the utmost rarity and difficult to sell;
those proclaimed with drums and announced to all,
though common and trivial, are easily exhausted.
In comparison to timber,
those rooted on Sōng and Dài,
though their canopies soar a thousand rèn high,
and cast shade over ten thousand mǔ,
yet none know of them;
those staked at roadside crossings,
though hooked, twisted, crooked and fragile, soon to rot,
yet they are often used.
Thus in ancestral halls there may be goblets and sacrificial vessels of withered willows,
while deep valleys abound with untouched catalpa and oak.
Thus, those who steal resplendent reputations,
ant or lizard may rise to the clouds;
those who neglect genuine value,
the emerald dragon is lost to the nine springs.
Thus, the sparrowhawk soars high on the wind,
while the spirit-phoenix folds its wings and withdraws in stillness;
leaden blades fill the sheaths of treasured swords,
while dogs and sheep become the capital of tigers and wolves.
Flatterers beat precious gifts into strong wings,
then there is nowhere high they do not reach;
boarding cliques and factions as boat and oar,
then there is nowhere distant they do not cross.
If they hold fast by rising early and standing attentively,
and couple that with anticipating intentions and responding to gestures,
their glib tongue and flattering speech seem persuasive,
their hearsay from roadside talk seems learned,
their cunning hearts and gentle looks seem humane,
their base deeds and refined words seem honest,
their habit of exposing others’ faults seems loyal,
their ignorance of taboos seems upright,
thus they often find success.
Moreover, those who look to me for favor,
wish me to add to them;
those who do not seek from me,
I cannot cherish;
this is the way of Nature.
“The worthy are ever few, the foolish always many;
the many form cliques and conceal each other's flaws,
the few are solitary and weak, lacking any help;
flatterers help each other and block the proper path,
while the talented and wise dwell in lowly places, unrecognized;
the righteousness of pulling up misdeeds breaks down,
while crowds of those who bear others arise;
high-flying dragons fall from the sky,
shedding tears of blood in streams.
Thus Zǐ Xī exiled Zhōng Ní, the greatest sage,
and Zāng Cāng slandered Mèng Kē, a genius for the age.
If even those two could not escape such harm,
what is there to say of lesser men!
This calamity was born with the opening of the world,
and its pain is not of one age alone.
Looking across all antiquity,
many have suffered the same sickness.
Thus, the slow and lame raise their heads at the carriages of kings and lords,
while fine steeds are abandoned in wild pastures,
these men living off unearned salaries,
the states consumed to exhaustion,
the low intimidating the high, the superiors abandoned,
truly all from this cause.
Some scatter and cannot be gathered,
some flee into exile,
some are hung by the sinews from temple beams,
some meet death at Wàng Yí;
it is always because those promoted are not true,
and loyal ability is unused.
“Thus the enlightened ruler is diligent in seeking worthies,
and urgently selects the exceptional,
guides the blocked to flow on,
and strictly prevents obstruction and concealment.
If the talent is truly reliable,
he does not restrict them to butchers or fishermen;
if their words are clearly practicable,
he draws them from border garrisons.
Some are raised from beneath an ox's mouth,
then elevated above all officials;
some are chosen from among those in chains,
and entrusted with the weight of the state.
Thus he can achieve grand undertakings,
expand territory and subdue the distant,
gain power and establish merit,
and transmit the lineage far into the future.
“A straight line is what crooked wood detests;
a just official is the enemy of the wicked.
If a ruler cannot use mysterious discernment to seek out the hidden,
he must rely on those advanced along the way.
Yet whenever one looks at the power-holders of former dynasties,
invariably those they recommend are ones attached to themselves,
and those they promote are for self-interest first.
They slander those they fear and advance those they favor,
what they fear is those of perfect impartiality,
what they love is mutual self-interest.
If the perfectly impartial are employed, the villainous cliques are broken;
if networks of private interest are established, the ruler’s authority is lost.
When villainous cliques break, it opens the way to flourishing times;
when the ruler’s authority is stolen, it marks the beginning of downfall.
When slandering those they fear, they dread that the attack is not severe enough,
even to the point of mutilation or cutting off the nose,
still not content,
only when utterly removed do they feel satisfied;
as for advancing those they love, they begrudge if the praise is not glowing,
even if their rank surpasses others,
still they are not gratified,
so only by endangering others can they find security for themselves.
Thus, there have always been those who suffer wrongs and die,
or are dismissed with no cause.
“Therefore, the reason for embodying the Way and uniting with Truth,
standing out alone in all clarity,
having talent broad and ambition lofty,
cherishing purity like frost and walking on ice,
thinking far as heaven and earth,
possessing capacity to match Yuán and Kǎi,
holding to the classics behind humble gates,
deep as an abyss, upright as a mountain.
Such a one would rather keep oneself pure and remain in obscurity,
ashamed to stoop and seek easy accord.
Joyful in hunger in humble alleyways,
to maintain lofty character;
hiding one’s talents, keeping one’s essence intact,
to await the end of Heaven-given years.
Not stepping forth at the wrong time,
not acting against propriety.
Clad in coarse dress, chewing wild greens,
yet never dejected;
living to old age in fortune’s disfavor,
yet never sorrowful.
How could one wish to compress the height of Tài Shān,
to squeeze into what fits only mortise and tenon;
gather heaven-reaching wings,
to become mere servant in the pre-dawn hours?
To be ranked among officials,
and suppressed among mediocrities?
To abandon the groves of phoenix and luan,
to enter into the wilds of thorns and brambles,
to compete for moldy scraps with crows and owls,
and bend a foot-rule to fit a straight yard!
“Moreover, great sages appear most awkward in form,
their taste is most bland,
quietly self-sufficient,
calmly unknowing,
known by few, yet not concerned,
not troubled when not employed by the times.
Even if for day after day they lack even coarse meal,
they would not exchange that for unrighteous banquet;
though wearing shabby robes that fail to last the year,
they would not delight in the furs acquired through wrongdoing.
They alone can let their hair down and rest easy,
guarding only their own integrity,
never stooping and lowering their eyes
to seek what is not truly needed.
When virtue is meager but position is lofty,
do not associate with such a person;
when reputation and reality are at odds,
do not be intimate;
when one pursues glory and splendor,
do not make it your endeavor;
when a person is extravagant, chivalrous, cunning, or wields sinister power,
do not connect with them;
when worldly speech is finely debated,
do not respond;
when others rush to act out of peer pressure,
do not follow.
With a foolish appearance but distant ambition,
a soiled face yet pure conduct.
Steadfast as Sōng Shān and Tài Shān,
beyond what scales and balances can measure;
vast as the blue sea,
beyond what bushels and pecks can compare.
Stern in lofty virtue rising a hundred paces,
obscured in the abundance of ministers and officials.
If you observe those who are frivolous and thieving,
they are like weeds in the wild.
The resolve belongs to a faraway world,
surpassing even the heights of the autumn clouds;
the spirit, left behind by custom,
distantly dwells at the edge of the ninefold depths.
Even in poverty and lowliness,
he cannot be coerced by threat;
even amid danger and hardship,
he cannot be moved by profit.
“What he practices and esteems,
can be heard but never fully known;
what he adheres to and maintains,
can be seen but not discussed.
Thus those who hate him
join voices and glare sidelong;
those who love him
are few and feeble, and bring no benefit.
It is as if gathering handfuls of earth cannot fill a broken river,
carrying water up cannot extinguish a prairie fire.
At such times, drums and gongs stifle the sound of thunder,
drums and tamtams indulge in the clamor of the gao drums.
The fragrant hui grass is cut down,
while stinking salted fish is worn as ornament.
Dark and fragrant wine is poured out without shame,
thin whey is dedicated at the Round Mound.
Sweat-blood horses are driven away, their heads lowered,
while the lame and halt gallop in imperial carriages.
This is why the people of old would carry sand and bear rocks,
throwing themselves into rivers to be buried with the fish,
unable to bear living in the same world as such people.
Alas!
How sorrowful!
“Yet to cast pure black jade into mud
is not because the luminous gem is not genuine,
but because none recognize it;
to shoot the red Lu bow without bending it
is not because the strong Fan Ruò bow lacks strength,
but because none value its worth.
Thus, jasper waits for Jīng Hé to reveal its price equaling a city,
the black-feathered arrow awaits Mén to manifest its power in piercing the hardest armor,
the flying hare waits for Zǐ Yù to cause it to soar in storms,
the talented wait for those who recognize them to display their full strength.
If fine jade never leaves the deep ravine,
a fine bow never looses a hundred arrows,
a superior horse never harnessed to a crimson chariot,
a world-shaping man never set foot in a position of rank and influence,
then who can know that he could unfurl his dazzling brilliance,
strike down the heavenly birds from a thousand fathoms,
race like the wind,
promote the work of the hundred ministers?
If he is unrecognized,
at least he avoids mixing with tiles and stones,
being valued alike with rotten wood,
lined up with the lowest horses,
regarded the same as the trivial and ordinary!
Alas!
To take a wide bow with thorny arrows and wish to surpass the best archers at Qúguǎng,
to ride an exhausted nag and seek to follow the tracks of Zhōu Mù Wáng,
to lay down axe and adze and wish to match the skill of Bān and Mò,
to ignore the excellent and still hope for order and proper relationships—
is this not difficult?
Though one’s name and substance may go unrecognized in one age,
his virtue and reputation may be sought by those to come.
Taking joy in Heaven, knowing fate—
what worry, what anxiety need there be?
At peace with the times, accepting what comes—
what resentment, what sorrow is there?”
Bào Pǔ Zǐ says:
All say that those whose courage and strength are unparalleled
are fit to be great generals;
those widely learned in order and chaos
have the talent of the Three and Nine Dignitaries.
Yet Zhāng Fēi and Guān Yǔ, match for ten thousand men each,
both lost their lives and shamed their lord,
their deaths in vain;
Kǒng Róng and Biān Ràng, outstanding in literature yet removed from custom,
were unable to manage affairs of governance,
and were defeated wherever they went.
Dèng Yǔ and Mǎ Yuàn, scholars from the fields,
were adept at waging war;
Xiāo Hé and Cáo Cān did not study the classics,
but excelled as prime ministers.
Thus, to recognize people is never easy.
If one would try only after testing them,
I fear all would end up with broken legs and spilled food;
if one listens to words and observes appearance,
often it seems true but is actually false,
truth and deceit are jumbled together.
Yet the people of the world think it exceedingly easy,
once heard or glanced at,
they claim to fully understand.
I am most suspicious,
and dare not approve.
Distinguishing good and bad,
perceiving form and seizing the spirit,
depends on the person,
it cannot be forced.
Unless one is as clear as the sun and moon,
and hears the inaudible,
I wish he would clarify and observe carefully,
proceed step by step,
and not delegate authority all at once.
If you lightly lend out sharp implements,
it is exceedingly difficult to get them back,
and much may be lost thereby.
Do not blindly trust a person for one achievement,
those similar to oneself
may not necessarily be suitable;
those different from oneself
may not necessarily be cast aside.
Someone objected, saying:
“All that is in the heavens casts signs,
all that is on earth has form,
so for distant mountains and deep waters,
you can infer their height and depth;
from wind rising and clouds flying,
you can reckon fortune and disaster.
A wise man, seeing that trees are not withered,
understands that fine jade is within the mountain;
beholding a riverbank not dried up,
knows that bright pearls lie deep in the abyss.
If a comet appears,
we know that the sturgeon is about to die;
if the sun and moon are eclipsed,
we realize that the qilin are battling each other.
Huá and Huò need not be named,
yet their infinite value is known;
the Yangtze and Yellow River need not be measured,
but their fathomless volume is already definite.
The wings of the swan,
the legs of the fine steed,
even if they have not yet flown or run,
their speed can be assured.
The sword of Háo Cáo,
the dagger of Master Xú,
even if not yet wielded,
their ability to cut is undoubted.
The ox-bodied bózi has the look of swallowing an ox,
the mighty hawk owns the visage of rending prey.
If plants flourish, the soil must be rich;
if the fish are large, the waters must be broad.
A tiger’s tail cannot be on the body of a fox,
an elephant’s tusks do not grow from a rat’s mouth.
The insatiable heart of Shū Yú
shows in his nature at birth;
the sign of ‘devour me and destroy my line’
is evident from the start of the womb.
Shēn Tóng recognized the sorcery of the wife-thief Wūchén,
Zhāng Fù knew that Chén Píng would rise high in future.
It is because King Fàn cut off all ties with the Five Lakes
that he saw the keen eye and bird’s beak of Gōu Jiàn.
It was for this reason that the people of Zhào ceased vying against others in war,
because Bai Qǐ’s head was sharp and his vision direct.
King Wén’s meeting with Lǚ Shàng,
before the shade of the mulberry tree had shifted,
he recognized him worthy to be his teacher.
When Xuán Dé met Kǒng Míng,
before the sundial’s shadow moved,
he had already entrusted him with all his heart.
Guō Tài was of moderate talent,
yet he could still discern men.
Thus, when he entered Yǐngchuān, he befriended Lǐ Yuánlǐ;
when he arrived at Chénliú, he bonded with Fú Wěimíng;
upon entering Wàihuáng, he grew close to Hán Zǐzhù;
reaching Púhēng, he studied under Chóu Jìzhī;
residing in the scholars’ quarters, he received Wèi Dé Gōng;
seeing men plow, he singled out Máo Jìwěi;
he recognized the outstanding Mèng Mǐn among those bearing burdens,
and forewarned Yuán Ài of his inevitable defeat.
In the end, all was as he had said,
not a single error.
He must have been able to swiftly distinguish the bright and dull by their customs and signs,
analyze the slow and hasty through their tone and manner,
discern the hidden and apparent by examining their bearing and behavior,
observe the pure and impure from their wealth and desires,
watch their taking and giving in what suits and what fits,
determine truth and falsity from words and deeds,
examine their conduct within household chambers,
compare beginnings and endings through trustworthiness and results,
test for goodness or badness—
is it not easy?
Bàopǔzǐ answered,
“I do not say that men are wholly unknowable,
but the principle of discerning men lacks fixed form.
This art is only preserved because of great clarity,
not as something one should lightly claim for oneself.
Yet each person in the world claims ability in this,
and thus there is a saying,
merely to warn those entrusted with such matters.
One whose appearance is lofty and grand is not necessarily worthy,
and one whose form is withered and thin is not necessarily foolish.
Those who roar angrily are not necessarily brave,
those who are simple and bland are not necessarily timid.
Sometimes outward signs are the same, but intentions differ;
sometimes temperaments are unlike, but their pursuits match.
It is not, as with Heaven and Earth, that there are fixed patterns;
nor as with mountains and rivers, that there are definite bounds.
Some things are distant yet easy to understand,
while those close are hard to fathom.
For example, the eyes can gaze upon the heavenly road,
but cannot survey the space between the nape and shoulders;
the ears can hear thunder,
but not distinguish the sounds of insects or lice.
In Táng, Lǚ, Fán, and Xǔ were skilled in judging men’s appearances,
yet could only know longevity or short life, wealth or poverty, official rank and social standing,
and could not truly discern the generosity or severity of nature,
nor the height or lowness of aspiration and conduct.
Even an emperor finds it difficult,
how much more so ordinary men!
You have raised a discussion based on outward form,
and questioned the matters of spirit,
yet not cultivated the root,
thus missing the true point.
“As for a lost arrow,
it may split a hair;
yet hitting the mark consistently does not make one a master.
Shūxiàng’s mother,
and the son of Shēn—
though they might be correct once,
they cannot always be so.
Táotáng sought antiquity and erred in his appointments,
Jī Gōng was wise yet assigned authority wrongly.
Confucius foresaw the rise and fall of men from afar before its signs showed,
yet failed to assess Dàntái from his appearance nearby.
Yánzhōu could determine purity or impurity across a thousand years,
yet failed to see the hero at merely an arm’s length.
To know a man is,
thus, extremely difficult.
Were all those judged by Guō Tài
truly men surpassing sages?
Rather, those he recognized
were prominent and easy to perceive;
those he missed
none could record.
“What is valued
is discovering uncommon talent among the nameless,
measuring swift feet among the hills of Wú,
plucking the pearl-holding oyster from the depths of the nine abysses,
pointing out the brilliant gem hidden among the piled rocks.
Just as Bó Jiē recognized the rare instrument in the ashes,
and Píngzǐ selected the unique bamboo before it was employed.
Among the assembled armies,
in the crowds of the market,
with but a glance,
one remains unconfused,
probes the innermost plans of hearts,
assesses the actions from beginning to end:
this is truly the wondrous and unique insight of the few.
But if, as you say,
we must wait to see all of a man’s conduct fully revealed,
judge his goodness or ugliness by what he achieves,
it is like weighing threads after they’ve been measured,
or measuring cloth already stretched by the yard,
then slowly stating its weight,
or length;
anyone can do this,
what need is there for insight or wisdom?”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
To emulate the encompassing of Xuánhuáng,
to elevate the manifest so as to reveal the subtle;
for literary brilliance to reach its fullest form like Rì Bǐng,
yet to perceive with pure clarity and enter the divine realm,
that is the sage.
One who possesses lofty brightness in complete purity,
raises himself high above the vulgar world with an imposing standard,
is subtle and ingenious yet appears simple,
does not repeat mistakes nor flatter for gain,
such a one is the worthy.
Dwelling in seclusion, doing nothing,
walking uprightly and maintaining impartiality,
that is the person of the Dào.
Utmost devotion in honoring ancestors, whether present or gone,
cherishing bodily appearance to bring honor to the name,
that is the filial one.
Extending compassion to all living beings,
constantly forgiving oneself to connect with others,
that is the benevolent one.
Holding oneself upright and offering one's life for the state,
staying true through perils and ordeals without wavering,
that is the loyal one.
Perceiving subtleties that are hard to detect,
foreseeing hidden threats yet to come,
that is the discerning one.
Measuring reason and disorder to open or close,
judging what to accept or reject in order to preserve oneself,
that is the wise one.
Navigating fortune and adversity with a constant mind,
entrusting fate and not becoming stuck,
that is the accomplished one.
Not bending a foot to straighten a fathom,
not lowering oneself for expedient accord,
that is the refined one.
Basing motion and stillness on proper measure,
always clear and thorough, without regret,
that is the weighty one.
Having the purity of ice and frost,
unsullied by desire for advantage,
that is the pure one.
Remaining steadfast from beginning to end through heat and cold,
not doubting even in danger and ruin,
that is the righteous one.
Holding to a promise through long difficulty,
remaining unchanged through decline,
that is the faithful one.
Weaving keen ornament in establishing words,
whose expressions are brilliant and sincere,
that is the literary one.
Rising with courage and determination to heroic deeds,
employing weapons to subdue difficulties,
that is the martial one.
Discerning the profound depths of Fén and Suǒ,
mastering the words of the ancients to understand principle,
that is the Confucian.
Sharpening the mind toward essential meanings,
treasuring every moment to advance virtue,
that is the improving one.
Knowing the value of accumulation and concealment,
facing profit as if it were nothing,
that is the incorrupt one.
Not altering conduct with gain or loss,
not inclining the will toward desirables,
that is the steadfast one.
Pitying others in adversity and forgetting one's own toil,
taking others' worries as one's own duty,
that is the sincere one.
Upholding purity to the end,
not evading hardship for mere survival,
that is the principled one.
Displaying brilliance of exquisite wit,
speaking concisely yet fluently, resolving obstacles,
that is the eloquent one.
Always humble, yielding merit to others,
remaining ever more respectful even in honorable positions,
that is the modest one.
Promoting harmony among the nine kindred,
always upright when pursuing the right,
that is the obedient one.
Able to decide when faced with hesitance,
managing standards without bias,
that is the steadfast one.
Selecting the worthy in the midst of discord,
resolving doubts appropriately,
that is the reasoned one.
Observing the waxing and waning of the seven luminaries,
inferring the course of rise and fall,
that is the skilled one.
Facing deadly blades without regard for life,
confronting wild beasts in mountains and valleys,
that is the courageous one.
Maintaining dignity to awe the multitude,
upholding law impartially,
that is the strict one.
Inventing clever devices to aid practicality,
mastering music and calculation with precision,
that is the artisan.
Defying strength without fear,
undaunted even in danger or urgency,
that is the cunning one.
Persevering tirelessly day and night,
forgetting exhaustion amidst steep challenges,
that is the diligent one.
Bearing slanderous words calmly,
unafraid when faced with threats,
that is the resolute one.
Unaffected by praise or honor,
unchanged despite grief and hardship,
that is the prudent one.
Knowing what must be done and acting upon it,
without hesitating among doubts,
that is the decisive one.
Following standards precisely in action and restraint,
not seeking fortune through chance,
that is the cautious one.
Practicing propriety with fear and trembling,
blameless among relatives,
that is the virtuous one.
Upholding the Dào naturally and without desire,
unchanging though times may shift,
that is the simple one.
If none of these virtues
are possessed at all,
and cannot ascend to the path of the good,
that is the base one.
A disciple respectfully asked:
“Of the conduct of good men,
I have already heard its general categories;
as for the deeds of the wicked,
those which may serve as warnings to common morals,
I wish you would set them out in writing so as to admonish us.”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“One who does not provide for those who gave him life,
who diminishes the Way and endangers his own person,
is a rebel against others.
One who harbors deceit and falsehood to steal honor,
who seeks personal profit in advance and forgets his own life,
is an enemy of men.
One who turns his back on the right path of benevolence and righteousness,
who jeopardizes others for his own safety,
is a cruel man.
One who delights in contention and is endlessly grasping,
who focuses solely on blaming the upright and harming the just,
is an evil man.
One who sets up cords and rules to torture others with harshness,
whose heart delights in killing and is steadfast in cruelty,
is a tyrant.
One who adorns perverse sayings to seep in corruption,
and heaps slander upon the loyal and upright,
is a slanderer.
Though his words are skillful, yet his deeds contradict them,
whose actual conduct is filthy though he feigns purity,
is a sycophant.
One who never examines the root of right and wrong,
who recklessly hungers for victory and freely indulges his anger,
is a violent man.
One who displays trifling virtues to gain trust,
yet harbors poison in secret and forms no true ties,
is a treacherous man.
One who adapts himself to the winds for easy acceptance,
who divines his lord’s intentions and supports the wrongful,
is a flatterer.
One whose words take no account of repetition and reversal,
who lightly makes promises without truth,
is an empty man.
One who, seeing a land of profit, forgets righteousness,
and abandons integrity and shame for gain,
is a greedy man.
One who, beholding beauty and indulgence, has his heart unsettled,
who embellishes himself with fine clothes and indulges wicked thoughts,
is a lustful man.
One who, faced with accomplished deeds, is always perplexed,
who is forever miscalculating and repenting,
is a dark-minded man.
One who turns away from instruction and classics and relies solely on himself,
who is ashamed to ask advice from his betters,
is a harmful man.
One who knows virtuous deeds but does not reach them,
who does much but achieves nothing,
is a poor man.
One who discards virtue and fails to cultivate it,
who serves the powerful to curry favor,
is a base man.
One who treads shortcut paths for quick gain,
who pushes goods and bribes to contest for profit,
is a depraved man.
One who is haughty and unruly without courtesy,
who delights in humiliating those better than himself,
is a fierce man.
One who, when oppressed, slanders himself,
who, with no real hardship, is struck with fear and dread,
is a coward.
One who pursues petty arguments in crowded gatherings,
who voices all his thoughts before unworthy men,
is a shallow man.
One who is blind to the differences between what is appropriate or not,
who, though aspiring, never attains,
is a dull man.
One who knows his affairs are wrong yet does not change,
who, hearing good advice, only increases in wickedness,
is a deluded man.
One who lacks a compassionate heart to offer relief,
who lightly severs ties with close friends,
is a cold man.
One who begrudges what he cannot attain,
who delights in others’ misfortunes,
is a jealous man.
One who amasses grain and money but scorns righteousness,
who observes others’ hardship without lending help,
is a miser.
One who rushes heedlessly into danger seeking luck,
who plants the seeds of disaster without regret,
is a fool.
One whose nature is petty and partizan,
whose ambition lies only in profit,
is a petty man.
One who chases beasts with hounds and falcons,
who is addicted to gaming and cannot stop,
is a deluded man.
One who forgets the distinctions of rank and power,
who takes joy in ostentation and displaying luxury,
is a lavish man.
One who indulges in music and color at feasts,
who neglects social rituals of celebration and condolence,
is a dissipated man.
One who has no mind for cultivation and aspiration,
and is also lazy in tending household affairs,
is a lazy man.
One lacking dignity and authoritative bearing,
who is ever careless and thoughtless,
is a frivolous man.
One who, seeing the Way and righteousness, behaves drunkenly,
who is unsettled at word of profit and wealth,
is a sullied man.
One whose knowledge is shallow and often in error,
who is blind to right and wrong in what he accepts or rejects,
is a dullard.
One who hates the worthy and does not honor them,
who hearing noble words remains deaf,
is a haughty man.
One who sees brilliant colors but cannot distinguish them,
who remains unenlightened though ears are tugged,
is a benighted man.
One who wavers from the Way in indecision,
who disregards ritual and law without concern,
is a disorderly man.
One who at every movement is laughed at,
whose words always contradict principles,
is a clumsy man.
One who serves powerful chiefs as a slave,
who in times of decline turns his back on kindness,
is a wicked man.
One who discards old friends in poverty and low rank,
who scorns gentlemen and acts arrogantly,
is a proud man.
One who forsakes what has lost its luster and widens desire,
who wanders far though neither an official nor scholar,
is a dissipated man.
One who lacks steadfast loyalty and trust,
who turns his back on gratitude and seeks profit,
is a traitor.
One who, when dealing face to face, appears submissive,
but, at separation, turns to slander and harm,
is a hypocrite.
One who is accustomed to force and self-assertion,
who rejects loyal counsel and refuses to accept it,
is an obstinate man.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“A person’s talent is not easily known,
true and false may sometimes look alike.
There are scholars of handsome appearance,
elegant bearing and poise,
at first sight dazzling to the eye,
agreeable in all dealings,
whose bearing is like dragons or tigers,
their every movement fitting and rule-abiding.
Yet their hearts are clouded and their spirits lacking,
no talent fits them for anything,
all that fills their mind,
remains at the surface.
Their mouths cannot utter a single striking remark,
their pens cannot compose half a line;
at home they cannot govern people,
abroad they cannot lead troops;
what affairs they handle end in ruin,
what duties they are entrusted with are disgraced.
In movement and stillness, never appropriate,
in all situations, ineffective.
This is the first kind that is hard to distinguish.
There are scholars whose looks are plain and withered,
appearance frail and unattractive,
voices feeble,
movements awkward and stiff.
Yet they conceal brilliance, treasure virtue,
their learning is clear, their conduct exalted,
achieving more than Yuán Kǎi,
writings lush as a spring grove.
In office, they prosper all affairs;
in war, they conquer and win alone.
This is the second kind that is hard to distinguish.
There are scholars of profound schemes and deep understanding,
whose strategies verge on the divine,
whose wisdom encompasses success and failure,
whose thoughts reach into the mysterious and hidden,
whose talents embrace all abilities,
and who are suited for all offices;
yet their tongues cannot express their hearts,
their pens cannot set forth their minds,
in hurried encounters,
they seem no different from the common.
This is the third kind that is hard to distinguish.
There are scholars brilliantly quick and perceptive,
whose eloquence is ornate and resplendent,
who cite examples and analogies,
their words deep and forceful as the wind;
yet what their mouths discuss,
their bodies cannot practice;
strong in knowing the past,
weak in managing the present,
their rule brings disorder,
their governance breeds resentment.
This is the fourth kind that is hard to distinguish.
There are scholars whose outward appearance is fully respectful,
whose bearing is modest and whose speech is reverent,
yet whose spirit is distant and whose heart is careless,
whose inner thoughts are unrestrained and scattered,
who receive duties without worry,
and who, residing in their position, do not govern well.
This is the fifth type that is hard to distinguish.
There are scholars who, when drawing the bow, strike the mark,
who enter the white (target) with bare fists,
who can ride and stand reversed in the saddle,
and have mastered all five weapons;
yet whose bodies are light and whose deliberations are shallow,
whose hands are swift but whose hearts are timid,
who when tested in emptiness find no response,
and when put to actual use, yield no proof.
They flee at the sight of dust (enemy's approach),
and upon hearing of the enemy, lose their nerve.
This is the sixth type that is hard to distinguish.
There are scholars of upright character and plain simplicity,
whose words are few and appearance unadorned,
whose small deeds have flaws and omissions,
and who do not display minor bravery,
whose speech halts, whose posture is constrained and restrained,
who are offended but do not retaliate,
who clutch their claws and droop their wings,
and are called weak-willed.
Yet their courage is strong and their hearts are upright,
unafraid of a powerful adversary,
and when righteousness is clear,
they face death as if returning home,
even when dismembered and cut to pieces,
they do not change their resolve.
This is the seventh type that is hard to distinguish.
There are scholars who are filial to their parents and friendly to their peers, gentle and kind,
sincere, calm, and elegant,
trustworthy in conduct and thoughtful to follow,
who do not step where ritual forbids,
who are content in hardship and keep their aspirations pure,
and whose integrity is as pure as ice and frost;
yet who are inattentive, sluggish, and overly detached,
unable to grasp the essentials of affairs,
who see opportunities but do not act,
whose undertakings result in nothing,
who remain aloof even when alone,
and when given responsibilities, fail to carry them out.
This is the eighth type that is hard to distinguish.
There are scholars who conduct themselves with lofty simplicity,
whose demeanor is imposing and steep,
who whistle and act arrogantly,
look down upon their peers and disdain the common,
do not maintain respectful self-control,
do not guard against minor faults,
indulge their feelings and act according to their own will,
acting as if no one is around them,
who are shunned and censured by factions and parties,
whose speech alienates all debaters,
whose friends do not attach themselves to them,
and whose character is overlooked by those who assess talent.
Yet, when standing in court, they are upright in countenance,
do nothing contrary to knowledge,
faithfully serve those above,
and clearly instruct those below.
This is the ninth type that is hard to distinguish.
There are scholars who possess magnanimity and broad-mindedness,
who are open to receiving all things,
who conceal others’ faults and hide their own flaws,
who are warm, respectful, honest, and pure,
industrious, humble, yielding, and retiring,
who rescue the endangered and uphold trustworthiness,
who entrust their lives without doubt,
and who can be relied upon to safeguard the orphaned;
yet, for all their pure benevolence, they are oblivious to power and influence,
kind but indecisive,
unable to reward the good,
unable to punish evil,
so faithful and constant as to have excess,
but insufficient in practical administration,
hesitant to wield authority, still doubting;
abandon the law and follow heterodoxy,
confuse the crooked with the straight,
and in the end are burdened with defeat.
This is the tenth type that is hard to distinguish.
Thus, there are things that seem similar but are in fact not the same,
that appear so but actually are not.
Analyze them without confusion,
observe the form and grasp the spirit,
even the sage may err in this;
how much more so ordinary people?
Therefore, in employing talent and selecting scholars,
in making friends and choosing companions,
one must choose with great care,
and diligently examine and test them.
As for the perplexing changes of temperament and conduct,
beginning upright yet ending depraved,
like Wáng Mǎng, who at first surpassed Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng in virtue,
but later surpassed Zhào Gāo in wickedness—
such outcomes are beyond the capacity of ordinary men to foresee.
If distinguishing scholars were as easy
as telling the wren from the wild goose,
the fox or rabbit from the dragon or qilin,
then the Four Villains would never have held office in the court of Yáo,
and Guǎn Shū and Cài Shū would not have nearly endangered the House of Zhōu;
Zhòngní would never have erred concerning Dàntái,
and Yánlíng Zǐ would have no regret over the loss of gold;
Yī Yǐn would have been spared seventy-fold toil,
and Xiàng Yǔ would never have had remorse over his suspicions of Fàn Zēng.
The trouble lies in the confusion caused by Shí Wǔ and Shí Fū obscuring the beautiful jade,
the wryneck resembling the phoenix,
congealed ice being taken for crystal,
the smoke mistaken for clouds;
therefore, those who never go wrong are rare indeed.
Only the emperor finds it hard,
how much more so those among common men!
Thus, only with great clarity
and mystic discernment of hidden subtleties,
with spirit attuned to weigh and examine things,
with thought that can penetrate the obscure and ambiguous,
by gazing at mountains to recognize uncut jade,
and approaching the river to know its pearls,
can one, amid such hard-to-distinguish men,
be free of regret in accepting or rejecting them,
so that assessment is distinct,
and praise and criticism are both just.
Wǔ Dīng and Jī Wén would not alone have governed,
nor would Fù Yuè or Lǚ Shàng have been abandoned for long,
nor would Gāo Mǎng or Zǎi Pǐ have succeeded in their evil,
nor would Hóng Gōng or Shí Xiǎn have found a place for their deceit.
Such is a brief outline of how to select scholars,
and the general principles of choice.
To seek the subtle and profound,
it must depend on the person himself;
this cannot be fully addressed in a mere writing brush.
Now, Zǐ Liú Jūn's discourse on marriage says:
“The fundamental relationship of mankind begins with husband and wife,
dividing and joining in imitation of heaven and earth.
Thus, the great ceremony of marriage
was highly valued by ancient people,
to unite two surnames and
continue the foundation of their ancestors.
The host bows and greets at the door,
listens to the mandates at the ancestral temple,
with gifts of black and red silk,
personally presenting the harness,
where the groom, in mourning for three years,
informs the lady’s family,
and the lady accepts, never daring to alter the agreement.
After the great mourning has ended,
the lady consults the groom,
and if the groom has grounds for refusal,
only then does she remarry.
Such was the way to exalt reverence and deference.
How could there be talk of suing before marriage proposals?
But in later ages, customs grew lax,
damaging civilization and corrupting society,
all upright conduct cast aside,
agreements made but not fulfilled,
disputes and quarrels leading to shame and insult,
and lawsuits clogging the offices.
Now let all those contesting marriages,
before they have shared the wedding feast,
be permitted to ritually end the arrangement,
returning double the wine-ritual gift,
and restoring all gifts of silk and money.
If the contract has been broken once before,
one further double payment of the betrothal gift is required.
If broken three times,
then again double the payment.
In this way,
one who breaks the promise will not take pleasure in lawsuits,
and the greedy and miserly will have no profit in repeatedly receiving gifts.
This is an essential method for royal governance,
an unchanging and eternal law.”
Bào Pǔ Zǐ replied:
“Jūn Liú pities the decline of virtue and yielding,
and laments how the people’s disputes damage morality.
Even if I hasten lawsuits,
families are not at peace;
the value lies in harmony,
otherwise the result would be constant turmoil.
He sets forth upright views to recover what society has lost,
and establishes good counsels to rescue those adrift;
with such confused and contentious ways,
may these measures effect a change,
and shift the unashamed customs thereby.
Indeed, the interweaving of true and false
is hard to distinguish.
Truly, it is an eternal law of the state,
and a profoundly beneficial doctrine.”
Hóng, being lacking in discernment,
does not understand the ultimate principle.
In rashly seeking instruction,
I secretly harbor doubts.
As for the binding of marriage agreements,
it is a matter of righteousness, without force or coercion.
The other party thus selects and seeks,
while this party consents only if it pleases their wish.
If a promise is lightly made and later regretted,
the fault lies with the woman’s family.
Breaking one’s word and abandoning trust,
granting or withdrawing according to one’s feelings—
though strict prevention and severe regulations are employed,
it cannot yet be contained.
If, now, one indulges such conduct,
the only concern is that the added bridal gifts may be a burden to the poor,
while for those abundant in wealth,
it simply gratifies their wishes.
If the suitor later becomes prosperous,
perhaps able to amass wealth,
and thereby assists with the bride price,
surely the woman’s heart will be content.
In this case, the previous family must simply remain silent,
having nothing to say.
If the matter is discussed according to feelings,
how can there be no resentment or sighing?
For one who will not submit,
facing death is as returning home;
the calamity of blood and blades
is bound to arise from this.
If now, merely to avoid minor embarrassment in litigation,
one precipitates a great enmity hard to bear,
this is like fretting over the trouble of showing a rented house,
while forgetting the bitter suffering of loss and death.
When one buys goods at the market,
and another outbids him and snatches them away,
there are few who can endure it without anger;
how much more so when one’s betrothed wife is taken before the eyes and after formal notice!
If this law is thus applied,
it will cause those entering marriage
—even after offering tokens of respect and going to personally welcome the bride—
still to harbor fear of the wife being taken away.
Why so?
Liú-jūn’s argument
is to make sharing a meal together the final binding,
which is solid.
Now, if the woman’s family receives the gifts and years pass,
they constantly wield the threat of regret,
relying on the possibility of repeated annulment,
they will surely grow careless in choosing a son-in-law.
If for any slight dissatisfaction with the groom,
they may at once change their minds and repent,
and thus enmity and calamity will be bound together;
nothing is more severe than this.
Former lawgivers
considered both the beginning and the end,
stopped minor faults and guarded against latent troubles;
their thinking was indeed thorough.
Yet they did not open the road to indulgent annulment.
Those who would sever ties with a rule to return the bride price,
how could any decision be firm?
Suppose a woman is of peerless beauty,
surpassing all in the city,
and by chance is noticed by the likes of powerful houses or officials,
they would gaze upon her enchanting looks,
forget ritual and measure within their hearts,
command resources worth a thousand pieces of gold,
and restrain no desire.
To pay tenfold the bride price
would not deter them,
let alone just double it.
Huá-shì found it no difficulty to kill Kǒng-fù and seize his wife;
the people of Chǔ, when fetching a bride for a son,
because of her beauty, took her for themselves.
Judging by this,
who would shrink from exhausting all property to assist a woman’s family in returning a bride price to her previous family?
Petty people are frivolous and shallow;
even the slightest offense becomes a grudge.
They also delight in abandoning the weak for the strong,
treading on the cold to seek the warmth.
If this law is enacted,
it is certain there will be many cases of the poor and lowly having their wives taken and given to the rich and noble.
I do not know how, my lord,
you will prevent this abuse!
Someone said:
Let the woman’s family receive a bride price without excessive agreement;
all should be finalized with an immediate written receipt,
afterward requiring contemporaries to sign their names on a separate board,
with no fewer than ten people,
to account for distant travel or death.
Also, the woman’s father, elder or uncle
should reply in writing to the groom’s family,
in handwriting on one sheet,
and if there is a clear change of mind and evidence,
then the woman’s parents and brothers
should all be held responsible and punished.
In this way,
perhaps there will be no litigation!
Bào Pǔ-zǐ said:
What pleases the eye
may not be followed;
what delights the ear
may not be obeyed;
what pleases the nose
may not be indulged;
what the mouth craves
may not be pursued;
what the heart desires
may not be given free rein.
Thus, what beguiles the eye
must be alluring looks and fine features;
what beguiles the ear
must be seductive sounds and wanton voices;
what beguiles the nose
must be the fragrance of herbs and orchids;
what beguiles the mouth
must be rare delicacies and fine flavors;
what beguiles the heart
must be power, profit, and fame.
When all five have led one astray,
some calamity will surely befall the person,
is this not truly so!
Therefore, the wise carefully restrain themselves in accordance with principle,
not indulging their spirit in pursuit of things;
they regulate themselves through tranquillity and contentment,
and enhance it with far-reaching calculation.
As for suppressing feelings,
it is like shoring up a dike against a great flood;
as for restraining nature,
it is like riding a swift steed with rotted reins.
Therefore, they can preserve their years within,
and remain unblemished without.
Hunger and cold are hard to endure,
yet the pure and principled will not accept unrighteous grain or silk;
poverty and lowliness are hard to abide,
yet the noble-minded will not reside in dangerous, chaotic glory.
If one calculates gain, then the will to endure is whole;
if the Way prevails, then harmful actions are abandoned.
The near taste of wine and sweet liquor
are poisons that produce disease;
they bring not the smallest benefit,
but cause harm as great as hills and mountains.
Gentlemen are ruined in virtue by it,
petty folk hasten to crime with it;
those engrossed and beguiled by it
are few who avoid calamity.
Scholars of the world
also know it is so,
yet none can utterly abstain,
nor are they willing to moderate;
giving free rein to the fleeting desires of heart and mouth,
easily summoning the very root of disaster;
like slaking one’s hot thirst with cold water,
though it may be pleasing, the body is endangered.
Great and small disasters alike,
are almost never without wine.
Yet the common people rejoice and indulge in it;
at the outset of a drinking feast,
they are restrained and orderly,
their speech seeking propriety,
chanting "Yan Yan" from "Zhan Lu,"
singing "Kai Le" from "Zai Hao,"
raising cups in the "Ten Thousand Longevity" toast,
embodying the meaning of "Wen Ke."
Before the hour is much advanced,
limbs are light and ears are hot.
Vessels of crystal and conch are both used,
full cups and games of punishment urged in haste.
Drunkenness unchecked,
they pull out the door bolts and throw them in the well.
Thereupon, the mouth overflows, the nose spills,
soaking heads and causing confusion.
Repeatedly they dance in a swaying manner,
abandoning seats and wandering about;
shouting and quarreling,
as if boiling or stewing.
Some contend for words, striving to best one another;
some guffaw alone;
some talk with no one in reply;
some vomit beside the mats;
some, encountering a fine singer,
let their hats fall off and belts come undone.
The upright and good receive coquettish glances from the likes of Huá Dū;
the timid and cowardly imitate the nimble ways of Qìng Jì;
the slow and heavy whirl about like tumbleweeds on stormy waves;
the orderly and stern leap like deer and dart like fish.
Those slow of speech in cold or heat,
all clap hands and sing;
those modest and never contending,
all rush to make high connections.
The forms of integrity and shame are destroyed,
and wild disorder breaks out;
the vulgar and lazy nature is exposed,
and the arrogant, stubborn demeanor emerges.
When essence and impurity are confused, and spirit is disordered,
when good and bad are inverted,
some will race with carts or gallop on horses
to plunge into pits and valleys without fear,
regarding the ninefold-winding slope as just an anthill;
some climb to perilous heights and tread upon crumbling places,
yet do not sense it even when falling or tumbling down,
seeing the depths of Lüliáng as mere cattle tracks.
Some vent their enmity upon utensils,
some rage with wine before wives and children;
some add injustice and cruelty to their ministers and servants,
some use sharp blades on the six kinds of livestock;
the flames burn fiercely in their houses,
treasures and playthings are smashed into flowing streams;
they take out their authority and anger on passersby,
inflicting violence and harm upon friends and gentlemen.
Those who disgrace their dignified lord through vulgar slaughters
do indeed exist;
those who provoke fierce men and suffer disaster
exist as well.
Though their words may be ornate,
they trouble and betray reason;
their bowings and prostrations are many,
but their efforts and sorrows are not of respect.
Ministers and sons are discourteous before their sovereigns and fathers,
the young and base are rebellious and arrogant in the presence of elders.
They call pure discourse insult,
and take loyal admonition as a personal attack.
At this, they draw naked blades, forgetting the difficulties they might face;
clubs and staffs fly, with no regard for before or after.
Thus feuds of blood are created,
and disasters of summary execution are attracted.
When the weak oppress the strong,
the village and community heap heavy blame;
when one insults another's father or elder brother,
their sons and younger brothers will draw blades against them;
when one exposes others' taboos,
even the bravest cannot endure;
when one deeply calculates to take advantage,
even the sober cannot forgive.
Thus, in but an instant, multitudes of troubles arise,
and many illnesses are tied to the very essentials of life.
Even a speeding team of four horses cannot overtake regrets for what’s past,
and wishing to change, they have no way to retrace their steps.
These are what the wise deeply guard against,
yet what fools cannot avoid.
The harm and losses
are beyond reckoning.
Yet when gatherings are joyful,
none will restrain them;
everyone raises brimming cups,
not considering who is able or not.
Deliberations over mere droplets prolong into lengthy drinking,
treating slow drinking as belittling oneself.
Pouring out wine before those they respect,
earnestness turns to indifference.
If urged, they do not hold back;
if pressed, they do not stop.
Hence, anger and ugly words inevitably arise.
When wind passes through the government storehouse,
it causes people to feel faint and confused;
those severely afflicted
are filled with pain and apprehension about themselves.
If someone is struck by this illness,
all are anxious and afraid,
swallowing bitterness and enduring pain,
wishing only for a swift recovery.
As for the illness of drunkenness,
how is it any different?
One will stay alone in secret to avoid the wind,
yet cannot sever emotion to moderate wine.
If only one feared wine as one fears the wind,
loathed drunkenness as much as disease,
then the blame for ruin and heedlessness would be halted,
and the failures of indulgence would cease.
As for wind as a disease,
it can still be treated and subdued;
as for the transformations caused by wine,
it comes with every breath.
When drunk and confused,
the mind wavers between existence and oblivion,
viewing Tàishān as a mere pellet,
seeing the blue sea as a washbasin,
shouting upward as if the sky might fall,
calling downward as if the earth might collapse,
lying in wait for tigers and wolves,
plunging into wells or rushing into fire,
and never seeing evil in it.
One who treats their own body so lightly,
how can they treasure the rites of respect and reverence,
or restrain the transgressions of joy and anger?
In ancient times, Yí Dí first brewed wine,
and Dà Yǔ found it cause for concern.
The mound of lees and wine pools led
Xīn and Guǐ to ruin.
Lord Fēng was punished
for bearing cups and nurturing wine in his heart.
Jǐng Shēng fell to ruin and decay
by indulgence in the “three noble” vessels.
Liú Sōng’s intestines rotted
from drinking wine to escape the heat.
Guō Zhēn went mad
from never passing a day without being drunk.
Xìnlíng’s savagery and short life,
Lord Xiāngzǐ’s chaotic rule,
Zhào Wǔ’s loss of the people,
Zǐ Fǎn’s slaughters,
Emperor Huì of Hàn’s weary destruction,
Guàn Fū’s extermination of his clan,
Chén Zūn’s murder,
Jì Bù’s banishment,
Zǐ Jiàn’s dismissal,
Xú Miǎo’s prohibition from speaking,
all came from this thing.
In this world, there are many who love and enjoy it,
and few who warn and fear it.
They are many and I am one—
how can true admonition be applied?
So I only wish you would temper it and nothing more.
Formerly, in years of famine and expensive grain,
there were those who, drunk, killed each other;
therefore, governors often imposed prohibitions on wine,
issuing strict orders time and again,
sending officials to investigate,
arresting and parading offenders who shamed each other,
and of those flogged to death, more than half perished.
The more strict the prevention,
the more offenders there were.
Some even dug pits to brew,
others hid wine in oilskin bags.
The people’s love for this
could truly be called deep.
I, though a mere commoner of low rank,
commit this talk to writing,
not knowing what else to do.
Even those who govern, though they establish laws,
cannot themselves break from this substance;
lenient with themselves and harsh with others:
though the order is issued, it is not obeyed.
If the officials do not enforce it personally,
the common people do not believe it.
Teaching through this,
how can instruction be carried out?
Banning through this,
how can prohibition succeed?
When wine-sellers
give up their trade, they face hardship;
thus they resort to bribes and gifts,
relying on those in power;
subordinate officials dare not question them.
Only the powerless abstain,
while those with influence monopolize the marketplace.
Those who set up their brewhouses monopolize profit,
even doubling their prices;
people buy and sell at will,
all openly and without fear.
Law is light, profit is heavy—
how can this be stopped?
Some might object, saying:
“The downfall of Xià Jié and Yīn Zhòu and
the cruelty of Xìnlíng and Emperor Huì of Hàn
stemmed from excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures—
so is it only wine that is to blame?
If troubles arose from antiquity,
should we thus cut it off today?
That would be like blaming the downfall of Zhōu on Bāo Sì,
wishing rulers to abolish their harems;
or taking Qín’s fall at Āfáng as cause,
requiring kings to live in thatched huts.
Moreover, I have heard that the august Heaven marked the Wine Banner among the stars,
and Earth's spirit produced the hollow mulberry tree;
at the grand sacrifices on Yuánqiū,
at burials in Qízé,
on pouring sacrificial wine or presenting ritual vessels,
when inviting the spirits to descend,
wine was employed for ritual.”
A thousand zhōng and a hundred gū—
this was the drinking of Yáo and Shùn.
Only with wine is there no measure—
such was the ability of Zhòngní.
Jī Dàn kept food and wine ever at hand;
therefore he was able to establish ritual and compose music.
Hàn Gāo, swaying about in great drunkenness,
was thus able to behead the serpent and gather his army.
Yú Gōng, draining a full dǒu at a time,
rendered judgment with increasing clarity.
Guǎn Lù would tip and lift three dǒu,
and his eloquence became ever more brilliant.
Yáng Yún never let wine leave his mouth,
and thus the Tàixuán was completed.
Zǐ Yǔ drank to the point of unawareness,
yet achieved hegemonic deeds.
When the wine of a single vessel was poured out,
the multitudes of the Three Armies rejoiced.
To hand about the cup that dispelled poison,
even the horse thieves were moved.
To dispel sorrow and accomplish ceremony;
to drink upon the conferral of merit;
to summon spirits and unite people—
none of this can be done without it.
Within, it brings together the elders;
without, it welcomes the honored guests;
it flows like the Huái, like the Miǎn—
that is what the Spring and Autumn Annals esteem.
Speaking from this,
how could one warn against it?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
“As for the constant presence of wine-flags,
this has always existed.
It is like the hanging image that gives light—
nothing surpasses the sun and moon;
water and fire, their origins,
also lie therein.
Yet if they are used in moderation,
they nurture life and establish merit;
but if their use goes astray,
they bring burning and drowning, and death.
Can one rely on the sun and moon being in the heavens,
and then say that water and fire cannot kill people?
Of all things that benefit life,
none surpasses food;
but if one overeats,
illness and disease result.
How much more with wine, which is a poisonous thing!
When the likes of Xià Jié, Yīn Zhòu, Xìnlíng, and Hàn Huì yielded themselves to the debauched reputation of ruined states,
and sank amidst the chaos of captivating beauty,
all was due to wine clouding their nature,
drunkenness shaping their course;
thus they lost all restraint in following passion,
and forgot the art of self-cultivation.
I discuss the root,
but you recognize only the surface;
if not for the disaster of wine,
whence comes the calamity?
Such a one knows only that heavy rain wets the clothes,
but not that it is clouds that make it;
worries when dust flies into the eyes,
but does not perceive that it is the whirlwind's doing.
Talk of a thousand zhōng and a hundred hǔ—
words lacking basis,
things that are not so—
the wise do not believe them.
The Sage’s distinction lies in talent and understanding;
as for their physical bodies, they are not greater than others.
Have they, then, the stature of seven chǐ or three zhàng,
or are they thousands of times larger?
How could the drinking of a single day
reach such extremes?
Zhòngní, fearing the changeability of one's nature,
dared not approach disorder.
Zhōu Gōng in a whole day paid a hundred obeisances,
the food gone, the wine settled.
Even the highest sages trembled with caution;
being thus,
how much more for ordinary people,
who can escape regret?
Hàn Gāo responded to Heaven,
received the Mandate and established a new era;
even if he had not been drunk,
he still would have slain the serpent.
Yú Gōng was wise and discerning,
clear in judgment;
from the smallest to the greatest he judged by feeling,
neither favoring nor failing in justice.
Thus punishments were not inflicted wrongly,
and the world had no resentful subjects.
Only, as for his strong drinking,
it never interrupted his affairs.
But speaking of utter drunkenness,
all become equally oblivious.
The talent for resolving doubts,
how does it depend on wine?
Never have I heard that Gāo Yáo, Fǔ Hóu, or Zǐ Chǎn would let it pass,
and that only in drunkenness could they decide cases!
Guǎn Lù, in his youth,
often had to face intense debate,
so he borrowed the force of wine to strengthen his courage.
But if he exceeded his limit,
he too would be confused.
When it came to piercing minute measurements in just a single line of hexagrams,
investigating the transformations of spirits,
divining prosperity or decline by reading Qi-color,
learning the directions from the calls of birds,
forecasting fortune or disaster from watching the wind and clouds,
reading fate by observing steles and cypresses—
did he still need wine
before he could perceive these things?
Yáng Yún, a man of broad knowledge,
wonderful talent and far-reaching thought,
endowed with noble insight,
this endowment was from Heaven;
how could he rely on external things
to aid his writings?
If he often drank,
it was from occasional pleasures;
or perhaps, he had ailments,
for which wine suited as medicine.
Zǐ Yǔ gave free rein to his will,
but this was his innate disposition;
even had he not been drunk,
the result would have been the same.
The tale of the vessel of wine pleasing the masses,
is a figurative expression.
Truly, if one can bestow rewards and punishments justly,
balance authority and benevolence,
lay long-term plans with flexibility,
adapt always and in all ways,
then men become determined and resolute,
people gladly give their service.
Otherwise,
even wine flowing like a deep abyss,
how could it aid in victory or defeat?
Miù Gōng’s drinking with thieves,
a hasty expedient,
was to abandon law and foster evil;
what merit is there to praise in this!
How can it compare to being cautious?
Bàopǔzǐ said:
The ways of the world continue in succession,
but ritual and teaching have gradually decayed.
Respect and humility are not upheld,
arrogance and rudeness become the custom.
In gatherings and drinking parties with their peers,
some squat, some sprawl.
In the hottest summer months,
they bare heads and strip their bodies.
Their main business is only in dicing, shooting, and chess,
discussion reaching its height in music and women;
with every step, they do not leave silks and fine boots for a moment,
nor do they stray away from the doors of those wine-sellers who chase after profit.
Never do they hear refined talk or words on the Way;
their sole concern is trading base jokes and mockery.
They consider such behavior lofty and profound,
and those who do otherwise to be foolish and rustic.
So it is that commoners who run after fashion,
those who keep to the ordinary crowd,
pursue these like moths flocking to a flame,
or like feathers tossed by a wild wind.
In their banter and ridicule,
sometimes it is aimed above at ancestors,
or below, even at wives and women.
Those speaking first strive ever to be more excessive,
those replying, for fear of being considered weak, go to even greater lengths.
Those who start the exchange do not consider the trouble it may bring afterwards,
those who join in are ashamed if their responses are not sharp enough.
Just as in reaping wheat or cutting barley,
or in harvesting ripened wheat,
so is vengeance sought:
it cannot be stopped.
The glib-tongued support the strong and form factions,
the quick-witted borrow slander to sting others.
Those who do not reply are deemed clumsy and inept,
those who stop first are judged to have lost.
In this way,
hostile and hateful words,
how can they be silenced?
When those of talent and wit engage in it,
they are skilled in finding just the occasion,
adapting the form and style,
drawing on the past to illustrate the present;
their words subtle and their thought perceptive,
refined and amusing,
pointed but not hurtful,
not touching what people are sensitive about,
nor offending what people hold dear.
But if the clumsy at it engage in such things,
then crookedness and uprightness are jumbled together,
leaving people astonished and appalled;
beauty and ugliness,
where they ought to be kept apart,
how could it be not only useless, but even harmful!
Thus there are guests who indulge in wine,
who, when encountering an unyielding disposition,
cannot endure it,
shake their sleeves and pull at thorns,
and come to blows with hands and feet.
Foul words are added to those they should respect;
joyful hearts shift and become enmity;
ties are severed, self ruined,
discord is sowed, disaster results.
There are those who fling cups and shells at one another,
and those who expose each other's private matters.
In ancient times, Chén Líng was struck by an arrow,
and the Guàn family was wiped out;
these did not descend from heaven,
but were brought about by careless words.
The movement of pivotal matters,
is the master of honor and shame.
The warning of sealing the two gates,
how could it deceive me!
Not even a peal of thunder can recall an already uttered misspoken word;
Bān Lún cannot polish away stains already affixed by these statements.
Though one cannot ponder three times before each word,
still it is possible to restrain jesting and banter to prevent the sprouting of calamity.
Honor one's speech,
respect one's bearing,
ensure words contain no errors of the tongue,
and one’s posture no signs of arrogance;
to be worth emulating and observing,
to be both respected and loved,
this is truly the fine art of avoiding humiliation,
and the essential way to preserve friendships.
Moreover, those who treat others with disdain,
are the ones who do not cherish those close to them;
those who make light of fighting,
are the ones who do not value their own bodies.
These are all lapses into unfilial conduct;
should these not be examined carefully!
Yet those deluded by confusion lack the clarity to see themselves;
those who are emotional shun the admonitions that grate on their ears.
They are envious of virtue but lack the uprightness to correct it;
together they remain confused, with no guidance to reflect upon themselves.
Flatterers who fawn over petty men
praise their “virtues” with laughter;
those who outwardly comply
clap their hands to acclaim their deeds.
This only causes the deluded further to sense no wrong,
believing themselves to possess the surpassing eloquence and wit of Duān Yàn,
yet not awakening to the fact that these are the very banners that summon disaster, the tallies delivering misfortune, the stations of slander, and the chariots that overturn themselves.
How can it be merely the loss of a reputation for upright counsel,
or a tarnishing of one’s posthumous virtue!
Indeed, even if one is always as cautious as if growing old together,
one cannot make amends for a single offense in one morning;
even with the wealth of Táo Zhū,
one cannot ransom the error of a single rash word.
Hence, the slightest misstep
can result in miles of error;
words that wound others
cause pain sharper than sword or spear.
Minute harms accumulate into the manifest,
shallow faults pile up into depth,
the feather of a swan can sink a dragon boat,
the mass of trifles can break a strong axle,
a tiny gust can set fire to a house a hundred spans tall,
termites and scorpions can topple trees that two embrace.
Why did the sages of old restrain their tongues and act with such caution,
while people today are brash and arrogant in this way!
Therefore, gentlemen of lofty character
turn back at the first trace of dust;
frivolous men
rush in like echoes, flocking like shadows.
In making plans, they have no help from the wise;
in times of danger, they gain no benefit from mutual guidance.
The good historian lifts his brush
but finds no virtue worth writing;
commentators purse their lips,
finding nothing praiseworthy to transmit.
Good reputation is not established;
disgraceful talk spreads widely.
It leaves naught but ruin,
and bequeaths ridicule to posterity;
at the start, there is nothing worth emulating,
and in the end, nothing worth recording,
which is also a shame for the man of resolve.
How could anyone bear to do this!
To persist in one’s faults,
is truly to abandon the right road and plunge into thorns,
to reject fair food and swallow hooks;
is it not as they say, to consider small good deeds as useless and thus not perform them,
to think small evils do no harm and so not restrain them,
until evil accumulates and cannot be concealed,
and guilt grows so great it cannot be resolved!
I wish that people of the world would amend their undisciplined conduct,
eliminate their faults of arrogance and stinginess,
remove their tendency to boast and to compete with others,
and rid themselves of mockery and unlawful words;
then the gate of Zhào Shèng would have no departing guests,
and the staff of Huáng Zǔ would have no use.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Some do not cultivate pure virtue to earn respect,
but rely on strength and intimidation to inspire fear.
When entering a crowd,
they stand upright, refusing to sit,
vying for the place of honor,
altering their expression and pitch of voice,
moving among people as if content,
and if frustrated,
they stew in resentment, not letting go.
When walking out,
on narrow paths,
they are ashamed to yield,
brandishing their staff as they advance,
pushing others into danger,
and if others do not immediately make way,
they act with even greater displays of impatience.
Alas,
this is wrong!
Consider how in antiquity there were those so humble none could surpass them:
yielding shade and giving up the road,
respectfully greeting and lowering themselves before even humble men;
they did not contend with others,
standing as if unable to bear the weight of their robe,
walking as if there were no room for their body—
how excessively modest were they!
When virtue is abundant and conduct pure,
though one may greatly humble oneself,
people still esteem him.
If conduct is not upright,
then even domineering ways
do not earn respect.
Suppose one outwardly imitates worthies,
but inwardly loses the goodwill of people:
what is seen is aversion,
not true esteem.
In ancient days, when Zhuāng Shēng had not eaten,
King Zhào stood at his side;
when Zōu Yǎn entered the border,
the ruler of Yān swept the path for him;
at Kāngchéng’s home,
the barbarian rebels greeted him reverently;
in Línzōng’s court,
none failed to be humble and respectful.
This was not due to force.
To acquire wealth by robbery,
though one becomes immensely rich, is not praiseworthy;
to use evil to intimidate others,
though one inspires dread, brings no honor.
And yet the common people do not consider it repugnant.
When people hear such a person’s words,
it is like the screech of an owl;
to see his face
is as to behold a ghost.
Wherever he goes,
it is as if demons gather;
whenever he is on the road,
it is even more terrifying than meeting a group of tigers.
Fools who follow such ways
pride themselves as heroes;
petty men imitate it
as though it were the path to greatness.
Disorder never finds stability—
truly because of these people.
Yet those who dare act thus
are not necessarily innately stubborn;
most are descendants of those with carriages and caps,
born of powerful families,
and have previously performed some good deeds,
thereby stealing an empty reputation.
Once their name is somewhat established,
their true nature is revealed.
Some use wealth and beauty to befriend the powerful and noble,
some ride the times to climb to exalted stations,
some form marital ties with the distinguished,
some manipulate reputation and slander to join in wielding influence.
With vessels full and ambition overflowing,
arrogance and illness erupt;
their parties grow, their influence widens,
their connections extend, their stature rises.
Pure discourse can no longer restrain them,
nor law and justice call them back;
thus they become the snare for eagles,
the rats of temple walls.
As for those they have not reached,
they bow their heads and sweep the ground in anticipation;
when among their inferiors,
they wield power and grant favors to manage them.
Thus, to those more virtuous than themselves, they do not listen—
or if they hear, pretend not to know;
with those less than themselves, they do not permit speech—
or if there are words, block them.
When pests destroy the crops,
a frost destroys them completely;
when ambitious villains disrupt society,
the arrival of strict times brings their downfall.
Those who preserve their own integrity
can only decline to serve such men,
simply refraining from imitating them.
To have an axe without a handle—
what can one do!
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The Shī praises the sūijiū bird,
valuing its distinction.
In the rites,
if men and women lack a proper matchmaker,
they do not meet each other,
do not sit together,
do not inquire after one another,
do not share clothes or belongings,
do not deliver objects hand to hand,
when sisters return after marrying out,
brothers do not sit with them at the same mat,
words from outside do not enter in,
words from inside do not go out,
women do not cross the threshold to see off or receive guests,
when walking, they must shield their faces,
on the road, men go on the left,
women on the right.
Such is the Sage’s clear law of valuing separation and cutting off impropriety at its source.
Moreover, between husband and wife,
intimacy can be said to reach its utmost,
yet men, unless ill, do not dwell indoors during the day,
and at the end do not die in the hands of their wives;
how much more so with others!
Long ago, a woman of Lǔ would not seclude herself deep within her chambers,
and so trouble with Hù Luò was caused;
Kǒng’s wife did not quietly stay behind closed doors,
which brought about the disaster of Huá Dū;
Shǐ Jī was careless in his restraints,
and regretted the matter of Hàn Zhǒng;
Wángsūn was not strict,
and suffered the disgrace of Dùmén.
But now, the women of common custom
cease their work of reeling silk,
abandon their duties of dyeing,
do not spin hemp,
but loiter about the market.
In the home, neglecting tasks of preparing food,
they instead pursue seeking gifts.
They constantly visit relatives together,
starting before dawn, carrying torches,
never ceasing their outings,
always going with attendants,
rare ornaments fill the street,
with maids, servants, and officials,
mingling in confusion like a marketplace,
joking with each other on the way,
provoking loathing and disgust.
Some sleep at the homes of others,
or return home late at night,
play in Buddhist temples,
watch fishing and hunting,
climb high or go to watersides,
