travel outside the city for weddings or funerals,
open carriages and lift curtains,
hurrying about the towns.
Cups and goblets are set out and drunk on the roadside,
stringed songs and music played on the way,
they constantly try to outdo each other,
and what is wrong becomes the custom.
For the sake of selfish desires,
nothing is refused.
This is the source of licentiousness,
a crisis all the more urgent,
if penalties strike the wife,
then family and state may be set aright.
Therefore, I hope that all gentlemen,
can restrict and forbid as much as possible.
If women have no business outside,
then the beginnings of impropriety will be prevented.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Frivolous and shallow men,
though their traces reach lofty ranks,
though friendships yield material abundance,
though fame and rank are roughly achieved,
then at once they discard propriety and separate from the teaching,
claiming they follow their natural disposition,
yet their talent is not extraordinary,
they force themselves to act unrestrained,
taking arrogant, unbridled men with no self-restraint as great-spirited,
and those who are scrupulous in guarding integrity as churlish and petty.
Then at year’s end, when the drum sounds, the unreliable sons linger,
drunken and flushed after wine,
gathering in cliques,
associating regardless of character,
with extraordinary men and great scholars,
some refuse to even hand things over a fence,
yet everywhere they act recklessly,
no matter how far, they must arrive,
taking hands and linking sleeves,
roaming and gathering,
entering others’ halls and chambers,
looking at people’s wives and daughters,
pointing out their flaws or merits,
discussing their beauty or ugliness;
who knows what such people seek?
Some, not familiar with the host,
simply break in together,
before the household is properly arranged,
not even bothering to listen or look,
breaking doors and forcing their way in,
leaping over walls or squeezing through cracks,
it is like a robber’s invasion.
If concubines and handmaids cannot hide away in time,
they are even searched for in hidden, secluded places,
seized and dragged out,
which is indeed monstrous.
As for the dwelling of a gentleman,
even there one does not take advantage of the women’s unpreparedness,
so entering, one raises one’s voice,
mounting the hall, one looks down,
so to intrude rudely into another’s home—
how can this be justified?
Yet idle, dissolute youths,
spineless and eager to follow corrupt custom,
take familiarity as intimacy,
and reserve as disrespect.
Truly, this age cannot be without such conduct.
So, calling and confusion follow,
entering a room to look at the wife,
sitting side by side, knees touching,
sharing drinks at arm’s length,
playing seductive and wanton music,
so that, as in the story of Wén Jūn, words provoke desire,
shouting and clamoring,
indecent jokes and coarse jesting,
going to extremes of vulgarity and debauchery,
thus you mock the great bond of men and women,
and follow the formlessness of “Xiàngshǔ.”
Jié’s downfall and Zhòu’s destruction,
Zhōu’s collapse and Chén’s ruin,
all came from lack of propriety,
how much more so among ordinary folk!
If trust does not come from within,
then many oaths are of no use,
if spirit and intent are pure,
then formalities can be forgotten.
The friendships of gentlemen,
are united by principle and righteousness,
and joined by kindred aims,
therefore they are deep yet enduring.
The associations of petty men,
are bound by advantage and gain,
and close through familiarity and indulgence,
therefore they are sweet yet ends in ruin.
Why must there be private gatherings and banquets,
and then only reveal sincerity,
with wives and concubines drinking together,
and thus form intimacy and attachment!
The ancients, as a warning from the ruin of debauchery, set up severe barriers,
and thus stopped little faults from growing into great evils;
truly, theirs was the utmost.
Those who follow it are gentlemen,
those who go against it are offenders.
Yet if prohibitions are too lax, then even in the palace there will be men who climb in and out,
and if the net is too loose, in the mulberry woods there will be women who elope.
To let it go without restraint,
is like setting a fierce fire in Yún Mèng,
or freeing a great flood through ten thousand fathoms;
can it be swept away with a mere broom,
or checked with a handful of earth?
Yet custom has grown habitual,
and all say:
This is the capital city,
it is what the ducal sons, royal grandchildren, and nobles all do.
I always refute them, saying:
The Central States
are the source of rites and propriety.
Are the rites truly thus?
These are the beginnings of decline and disorder,
not the old customs of an ordered world!
Lǎo Dān,
who achieved the utmost clarity and emptiness,
still dared not meet those whom he desired,
so as to guard against disturbance of the mind.
Were someone like Liǔ Xià Huì, high in integrity,
to take part in repeated wanton banquets,
even he could hardly refrain from feeling emotion within
and revealing it in appearance without;
how much more so when those with mild feelings are one in ten thousand,
and those who can restrain their feelings are rare indeed!
Such things as these—
what is there to value or perpetuate?
Although an impoverished scholar knows that these customs are not worthy to be promoted,
yet being destitute of both reputation and influence,
how could he correct them!
He always laments over this,
and thus is often despised by this faction,
and is seen as a rustic and boorish person,
unable to adapt to the times.
I only hope to trust myself,
and why should I, being unable myself,
follow what others consider acceptable!
There are countless sighs over this,
and it has always been so.
Enough of this,
what more can I do!
Those who are tainted by degenerate customs
and are utterly ruined,
how would they ever accept frank and unpleasant admonitions
and turn back from their distant paths!
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Among the common people there is a method for mocking women;
in the midst of a crowd,
before their relatives,
they are questioned with ugly words,
rebuked with disrespectful replies;
these are base and obscene acts,
which cannot be borne or discussed.
Sometimes they are pressed with cruel beatings,
or hung upside down by the feet.
Drunken revelers,
not knowing their limits,
cause injuries and bleeding,
or even broken limbs,
all truly lamentable.
The ancients grieved when parting, yet did not extinguish the candles;
they mourned in place of their elders, yet did not perform joyful rites.
As for rites,
bridegrooms felt shame and did not receive congratulations.
Now, since old codes of conduct can no longer be practiced,
yet if virtue is respected by the village,
and words are trusted among men of talent,
one ought in earnestness to correct and rebuke these things,
how can one go along with the current
and perpetuate these corrupt customs!
But as among the people, this has endured for a long time,
no one senses it as wrong.
Pointed and pure discourse cannot prohibit it,
only strict punishments can stop it.
Thus Zhōu and Kǒng are humbled and criticized,
and acting aloof is said to be transcending the world.
Some, due to change in circumstances,
slyly attain glory and rank;
some rely on influential support,
and rise above others;
and then they become arrogant and boastful,
their pride soaring to the clouds,
walking high and gazing far,
complacent and self-satisfied;
they look down on the unfortunate and those estranged from the group,
even if those men are truly exceptional,
they are regarded as mere weeds.
Sometimes they recline on pillows to receive guests,
sometimes feign illness to refuse visitors,
desiring that only notable men may establish themselves and assemble,
so that chariots and cavalry fill the alleys,
and they may be hailed as honorable and noble,
believing it cannot be otherwise.
If one considers position and rank,
even Zhōu Gōng would humble himself to spit and grasp another’s hand;
if one compares reputation and prestige,
even Zhòng Ní was mild and excelled as an instructor.
All considered diligence and humility to be their duty,
not arrogance as something noble.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
things became different.
Hair disheveled,
belts worn askew or not at all.
Some received others in indecent dress,
or were bare-chested, sprawling as they sat.
At gatherings of friends,
and social meetings,
none earnestly sought to improve their virtue;
family talk and talk about one’s occupation,
critiquing faults and correcting errors,
discussing the Way and subtle meanings
—all these ceased.
On meeting,
they no longer asked about time apart
or inquired after each other’s well-being.
If a guest arrived, he would enter and call for the servants;
the host would look out at guests and call for dogs.
If one did not act so,
it was not regarded as sincere friendship,
and one would be cast out, never to be included.
At banquets,
they crouched like foxes and drank like cattle,
fighting over food and snatching and tearing at it,
without any sense of shame or propriety.
To act likewise was considered honorable;
to not do so was seen as inferior.
All day not a word about righteousness,
all night no words of admonition or proper rule.
They forcibly cite Lǎo and Zhuāng,
exalting spontaneity;
that the great man does not heed petty rites,
and the perfected man ignores prohibitions and constraints,
whistling and strutting, unrestrained and willful—
and claim this is the True Way.
Alas,
how pitiful!
Is it not to be mourned!
Thus they mock their clansmen to express joy in companionship,
and engage in utter obscenity to form close bonds.
Those who slouch and extend their legs are regarded as dashing and outstanding;
those whose demeanor is upright and dignified are regarded as simple peasants and stupid nags.
Those who ridicule and point fingers are deemed bold and independent leaders;
those whose words are properly ordered are deemed slow and awkward.
All these frivolous fellows,
though quick to pander to common ways,
make broad connections and join circles,
constantly praising and promoting each other,
and so they quickly find advancement;
yet for the most part, their clever polish is only skin-deep,
while their minds are empty and sterile.
It is like the Sìchuān man's gourd:
inside, not a single sheet of written learning;
their knowledge never exceeds matters of drink and roast meats.
So those who are arrogant toward virtue,
are deaf to correction and benighted;
greedy for wealth,
and gluttonous for food and drink,
as recorded by Zuǒ Shēng,
they are sons lacking in ability.
If you ask them about the subtle sayings of the Fén and Suǒ,
the nature of ghosts and spirits,
the transformations of all things,
the wonders of far-off lands,
the great rituals of court and temple,
the rites of suburban sacrifices and ancestral ceremonies,
the roots of the three calendrical corrections and four beginnings,
the methods of yīn-yáng and calculation,
the precedents of state and altar,
the differences and similarities of ancient and modern reform,
they are confounded and lost,
mumbling and looking up and down,
bewildered,
ignorant.
Though inwardly they perceive the embarrassment of facing a wall,
yet outwardly they defend their shortcomings,
unwilling to admit fault,
and forcibly put on empty arguments,
saying:
“Those are trivial old stories;
such things are only for pedants in back alleys writing on slips,
chanting to withered bamboo slips,
crawling to guard yellowed scrolls; these are what they should know,
it is nothing to ask of us.”
Truly, they know the evil of ignorance,
the value of great scholars,
the error of traditions they inherited,
the folly of what they rashly despised,
yet are forever deluded and do not return,
because wildness and excess are not a hindrance to advancement.
If a man of eminence, with maxims and rebuke, censures them,
and there are some not fearing authority and persisting in evil,
then if their reputation is taken away,
they should be filled with fear, melting like ice, and change their ways,
quickly turning back onto the proper path.
Bǎopǔzǐ said:
Clarity and turbidity are separated,
and myriad things transform and are born.
Among familiar species, some can respond accordingly;
among the feathered and the hairy, some can understand speech.
The yuè recognize the past,
the guī know the future.
The xuánqín understand yīn and yáng;
insects—how could they stray far from springs and streams?
Yarrow stalks and turtle shells cannot surpass them,
Gān and Shí are not better than they.
Only those without propriety
fail to be placed among the esteemed.
In the very beginning, in antiquity,
people had no ranks.
Shàngdì lamented the utter baseness of confusion,
and pitied the contemptibility of living in nests and holes.
Thus, houses were built to separate from the flocks of birds and beasts,
and rituals and measures were established to distinguish the grades of dignity and awe.
They were taught to move in circles,
instructed in bowing and yielding.
When standing, they bent at the waist;
when raising their hands, they embraced as if holding a drum.
The movements of walking, ascending, and descending were regulated;
the bearing of gaze and interaction was observed—
these reached three thousand in number.
These served as dykes to control excess,
and are of pressing urgency in the governance of people.
Thus, dignified as with the guān in Qu Lǐ,
appearance and bearing were first among the Five Matters;
on leaving one's door, there was the solemnity of meeting guests;
in private residence, the admonition of respect in solitude.
Yán Shēng arrayed his attire after night bathing;
Zhòng Yóu braided his cords when facing destiny.
If respectful posture is briefly set aside,
idleness and arrogance creep in.
To secure the ruler above and govern the people,
nothing surpasses this.
Indeed, for people to have propriety
is like fish having water.
If fish lose water,
though they may briefly rest elsewhere,
their drying up and death can be certainly expected.
If people abandon propriety,
though they may still appear in person,
it is the threshold of disaster and ruin.
Lǔ upheld the Zhōu rites,
and violent troops did not descend upon it.
Wèi modeled itself on the qián mù,
their sharp-tipped caps and swirling banners standing out.
Great Chǔ, with an army of a million armored men,
still had the pale countenance of one struck by frost;
mighty Qín, with delicacies from Hán and expeditions over difficult terrain,
still lacked the steadfastness of Zhéliǔ.
Is this not because they abandoned the three fundamentals and thus called forth the loss of their roots?
Moreover, now, giving free rein to comfort and desire,
with turmoil and disorder enduring long,
customs are battered, instruction is discouraged,
and the forms of restraint are discarded.
A slovenly, lax ethos has formed;
and recently, the people are subject to chaotic governance,
while ordinary folk are caught up in the dissolving and disordered net of the Way;
as if fish lose their water to the casting net,
or beasts, when encircled, are driven onto dry land.
Since the onset of disorder,
affairs and things have changed repeatedly:
hats and footwear, clothing,
sleeves and hems, forms of wealth—
all these transform with sun and moon,
with no fixity or standard.
Now longer, now shorter;
now wide, now narrow;
now high, now low;
now coarse, now fine—
what is adorned is never constant,
and uniformity is sought as pleasure.
Those who delight in such things
imitate and release themselves day and night—
as the saying goes: "In Jīng and Liǎn, grand eyebrows are esteemed;
in distant lands, all imitate with half-foreheads."
As for myself, an ordinary person,
I am clumsy at following custom.
The constant changes in attire and objects are more than I can endure,
so I do not change,
yet lose nothing thereby;
I have never changed my ways.
Though I am pointed at and laughed at,
I pay them no mind.
Could it be that I mindlessly wish to oppose the crowd?
Truly it is because I consider it unnecessary.
In the great states, there are many reasons
why they surpass the southern realms,
yet there is much in them both to accept and reject.
The gentleman practices propriety—
not seeking to change custom,
but, when departing from his own state to another land,
does not alter the laws of his native hamlet.
How much more, when dwelling in one’s parents’ home,
why should one discard the old ways and forcibly study new ones?
Among the skilled calligraphers of Wú,
there are Huáng Xiàng, Liú Zuǎn, Cén Bórán, and Zhū Jìpíng—
all unsurpassed in their generation,
as in the Central States, there are Zhōng Yuáncháng, Hú Kǒngmíng, Zhāng Zhī, and Suǒ Jìng,
each brilliant in their own region.
All employ the ancient forms,
and all are fully fit for practical use.
I say, to abandon one’s already-learned hand
and exert hardship to study the characters of Zhongguó
is something that need not be insisted upon;
how much less should one go so far as to alter their pronunciation
to imitate the northern tongue,
which achieves neither fluency nor grace,
but rather is laughable and shameful?
Such are those who, failing to master the gait of Hándān,
end up crawling on all fours in ridicule.
Yet even this is a small matter.
Some, having suffered loss,
study the methods of mourning of Zhongguó,
and so abruptly lose any true feeling of remembrance.
In olden times, Zhōng Yí and Zhuāng Xī
did not forget their native speech;
the ancients approved of this.
Confucius said:
When one loses a parent,
it is like an infant losing its mother.
Could the cry then be the sound of ordinary times?
Better to let grief be in excess and propriety fall short,
for weeping expels grief.
What place is there for beauty or clumsiness?
To polish and refine its sound
is not the sign of searing pain.
Again, I have heard that men of rank, when in deepest mourning,
or stricken with illness,
consume powdered minerals to stimulate appetite,
turn to drink as if it were life itself;
though gravely ill and weakened,
unable to endure wind or cold,
ensconced in curtained beds and thick quilts—
these are left to their comfort.
Thus, among petty men with wealth and means,
none remain at the place of mourning,
always staying in separate rooms,
lying high on thick bedding,
eating richly and drinking deeply,
sometimes with close guests,
filling their cups and emptying them,
even to the point of drunken stupor.
They say:
"This is the way of Jīng-Luò."
Is this not to be regretted!
In my own village,
the upright men of former virtue—
even when living in hardship,
some already stricken with age or infirmity—
by propriety, only the coarse hemp mourning garment was required on the body;
those who did not allow their grief to ruin themselves
all fasted to the point of extreme sorrow and consumed only gruel,
never letting sweet flavors enter their mouths.
Of the people of the time, even the unworthy,
none failed to look up to them and urge themselves on.
But now, people voluntarily behave otherwise—
how far have they departed from the ancient ways!
Furthermore, people in general do not understand,
and say that the people of Zhongguó, in mourning, are mostly extravagant and excessive.
This is not so.
I have heard that among the four emperors of Jìn—Xuān, Jǐng, Wén, and Wǔ,
all, when mourning parents, grieved and withered beyond what was prescribed;
they did not adopt the rules of twenty-five months' mourning of the Wáng clan,
but all observed seven months of mourning.
At that time, all throughout the realm, those in deepest mourning
regarded the Four Emperors as the model.
Why do people of the age alone fail to hear of this
and instead baselessly slander the worthy?
Is this not delusion!
Bǎopǔzǐ said:
Those born in wealthy families of the age,
dwelling in intense and lively contexts,
though not setting out to be arrogant, nevertheless arrogance arises.
Unless one has a vessel surpassing the crowd,
one cannot distinguish or avoid the excesses of fullness and overstepping bounds.
Indeed, tireless humility and self-effacement
gathers many supporters;
pride, arrogance, self-importance
leaves one with but few in company.
When followers are many,
it is a sign of stability;
when followers are few,
it is a sign of peril.
The pivot of survival and destruction,
lies herein.
To act lightly in such matters—
is that not sheer folly!
There are also those who arise from lowliness and insignificance,
beginning in obscurity and becoming renowned,
only by hunching their shoulders and hiding their traces,
standing obsequiously to the side,
lowering their brows and bending their knees,
attaching themselves to powerful and influential men,
relying on chance and circumstance,
swiftly surpassing others out of order,
their feathers grow, their wings lengthen,
casting off as a cicada molts in spring’s earth,
they become self-important,
neither casting a look nor setting foot among others,
vessels full, desires satisfied,
regarding others as no more than grass.
Some gather in crooked company,
pipes and strings clamoring with noise,
late guests filling their doors,
no longer extending hospitality.
Or, among those of their own standing,
they show partial favor to some,
yet may not obtain them fully.
Simply by seeking,
making extra efforts and frequently catering to their feelings,
bearing gifts in succession,
and keeping their wine cups constantly filled.
That which Mèng Kē called “affection without respect,”
treating others as swine and livestock.
Yet many carry out such behavior,
claiming this as the way of self-respect.
The way of self-respect
lies in exalting the humble even when noble,
maintaining lowliness in conduct,
and not in such actions.
These are the notorious customs of decadent times,
a chronic and incurable malady,
to accept and pursue such ways
is truly lamentable.
As for great men and extraordinary vessels,
possessing liberality and distant refinement,
treading lofty paths and journeying alone,
tranquil in their self-contentment,
their bodies floating in the currents of the world,
their spirits ascending to the highest heavens,
their Dao complete within,
leaving things behind without,
their hats askew, shoes torn,
clothes patched, belts of rope—
how could they compete with the world’s petty men for advantage in currying favor and pursuit of gain,
or cultivate the fawning countenance of sycophants and favorites,
or imitate the loquacious stewards of Shànglín,
becoming clamorous as spring cicadas and summer grasshoppers!
To judge by appearance,
to demand beauty,
the ordinary man only sees the simplicity of their external form,
and cannot perceive the depth and remoteness of their spirit.
Focusing only on the skin,
failing to grasp the mind and resolve.
So even if one harbors outstanding talent and rare gifts,
surpassing all and outstripping the world,
and by their actions might enlighten the world’s arts,
and by their words resolve the confusions of past and present,
their talents concealed and purse tied,
speaking nothing outside propriety—
yet thatched huts cannot stir the mighty resonance of a thousandweights,
nor can dwarfs fathom the grand beauty of heights.
Thus, they mock them,
calling them commonplace and muddled.
Unless one is a person from Hàn Bīn,
one cannot discern the bright pearl among the muddy worms of the mire;
unless one weeps blood,
one cannot recognize the luminous gem on the sheer cliffs of night.
Worms crowd among scorched millet and the brows of gnats,
yet laugh at the vast Ròcpéng of heaven;
tiny minnows swimming in cattle tracks,
do not value the great scaled fish that cross the seas.
Thus, the calling of the Way is insufficient to bring them together,
and cleverness fails to make them meet.
Their principles naturally differ,
so there is little cause for wonder.
Yet the reason one rails against such, unable to remain silent—
it is my hope that those in office, the jūnzǐ,
do not judge others by appearance,
strive for humility and modesty,
and thereby preserve Heaven’s order forever.
Bào Pǔzi said:
“People of the world, upon hearing that Dài Shūluán and Ruǎn Sìzōng scorned convention and set themselves free,
considered them men of great magnanimity,
failing to realize that their abilities and character were not fit matches for those of the proud ones,
yet longed to imitate them.
So some went about with twisted necks and bare heads,
some bared their arms and squatted like barbarians,
some washed their feet amid crowds,
some urinated in public,
some dismissed guests and ate alone,
some only served wine to those nearest them.
These are the ways of the Left-garmented barbarians,
and not the fine conduct of the Huá peoples.
Even with the talents and learning of Dài and Ruǎn,
they themselves complained that self-indulgence brought them regret,
gains and losses ill matched,
suppose these two, in life, had reverently upheld restraint,
engaged others modestly,
served diligently in office,
would they have come only so far?
How much more for those far beneath them,
if they follow their example,
how quickly would they court danger and destruction,
not even for the space of a shadow,
and not only would noble character go unrecognized!
In the past, Xīshī was wracked with pain and lay by the wayside,
her form and features ravishing in beauty,
fragrant with orchids and musk,
those who saw her all admired her appearance and pitied her suffering,
none passed by without compassion.
Then a neighbor girl envied her,
and feigned illness, lying by the roadside,
but her form was ugly,
and she stank intolerably,
all passersby detested her looks and loathed her stench,
not one failed to turn away and cover their nose,
hurrying past.
Now there are those in this age with none of Dài and Ruǎn’s nature
yet imitate their arrogance—
truly the like of the ugly girl blind to her own limits.
Even emperors uphold the etiquette of sons toward the elders Sān Lǎo and Wǔ Gēng,
to lead the people by reverence.
If a person has no ritual,
such a failing is deep indeed.
One who slights others is certain not to respect their own kin,
for if one would have others respect him,
he must show self-respect.
If one does not cultivate good conduct,
he becomes a wicked man;
if he does nothing of worth,
he becomes a petty man.
Zhòu, for lacking the Way,
was called a solitary tyrant;
Zhòngní, though a subordinate,
was acclaimed as a true king.
Thus, nobility is found not in wealth and rank.
Now to behave in transgression of ritual,
yet shrink from hearing criticisms of an untimely death,
is to carry a pig on one’s back and hate to be told it stinks,
to wallow in mud but resent others’ talk of filth.
Formerly, Xīn Yǒu saw those going disheveled to sacrifice,
and knew war was about to break out.
I survey these troubled times,
customs extol arrogance and disrespect,
and people treat themselves like barbarians;
thus later, Qiāng and Hú ravaged Huá,
invading and plundering the capital.
Only then awakened to these affairs,
it was but a forewarning of calamity.
Now that All Under Heaven tends toward peace,
with a renaissance at hand,
how could we not strive together to correct past errors,
and cultivate true excellence?
Only after entering a pack of tigers and wolves
does one realize Bēn Yù’s tremendous courage;
only while dwelling among rites-shattered customs
does one understand the steadfastness of the cultivated man.
The Dao is battered and delayed,
drifting to ever greater remove,
so it should be all the more cherished by worthies and scholars,
who must cherish it together,
reflect sincerely, and feel alike this earnestness,
correcting custom’s deviation.
If one lacks the strength,
and nothing can be done,
then at least act as bamboo and cypress—
remaining unchanged though winter comes.
Why should anyone chase after and compete with those who flaunt their gaudy sheepskins,
merely to curry favor with the likes of them!
This is to leave the Way all the more distant,
and truly lamentable indeed.
If someone stands proudly and holds fast to righteousness,
firmly unwavering,
not drifting like tumbleweed to follow the crowd,
nor altering his refinement to fit into Zhèng,
none can hate him while all recognize his goodness,
yet precisely because he differs from others,
they ally to become his enemies and do not count it as excessive.
Alas,
is it truly possible that decline and decay have come to this?
The gentleman can thus make himself upright and forthright, square and unbending,
not forming factions with the vulgar,
raising pure waves to stir the turbid current,
grasping a strong arrow to inspire the many who are crooked,
at the most, he may not be accepted or tolerated,
and may not obtain wealth and honor, that is all.
If the heavenly rank yet resides within my being,
to thus stand alone and unaccomplished,
what hardship, what regret is there?
And yet one at once chops at the root to form a fragile union,
feeds on dregs and clutches at mud,
cuts the foot to fit the shoe,
destroys what is square to force it into what is round—
is this not grievous indeed!
A man of integrity cannot make people respect him, but his resolve cannot be taken;
cannot make people not hate him, but his path cannot be bent;
cannot prevent others from humiliating him, but his honor remains with him;
cannot prevent others from rejecting him, but his conduct cannot be altered.
Therefore, with divisions set and plans decided,
encouragement or discouragement cannot sway him.
At ease with Heaven and knowing fate,
worry and fear cannot enter.
When beset by hardship, he only grows firmer;
when in dire straits, he does not regret.
Truly, one who can employ his heart thus,
how could he ever bend like grass, low and floating,
to seek connection by forceful matching,
and imitate what the rites have cast aside!
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
I have heard that at the end of Hàn, those without conduct
judged one another, arranging themselves in order,
all arrogant and insolent,
not abiding by the rules of the Way,
setting themselves up as leaders and chiefs,
with paths open in all directions.
All rebelled against ritual and teaching to pursue wanton perversity,
slandering and destroying what is true and right,
hurting those not in their faction,
daily using vile words,
personally engaging in corrupt deeds,
all they said and did
was unbearable to discuss.
Now, what the ancients called “open and accomplished”
meant to be open to Dào and Dé,
accomplished in Rén and Yì—
how could it mean to be open in lewdness and accomplished in depravity!
There was someone like Dào Zhí,
who claimed he had five ways of sageship.
Such social ills damage human relations
worse than the coming of bandits and thieves,
and cannot last long;
how could the harm be just the loss of a single domain!
As for the sons and grandsons of noble families,
and those officials in office,
they scorn laws and punishments,
all baring their heads and exposing their bodies,
lounging while receiving guests,
already disgracing the celestial office,
and further influencing the common people.
Late-born youth, newly coming of age,
see that some have already obtained high office,
or gained a reputation by shallow trickery,
and so imitate them in person;
thus ordinary folk say that to establish oneself in the world,
nothing is more beautiful than this.
To keep the rites and guard against transgression is bitter and difficult,
and those who do so are mostly poor and lowly,
while the self-indulgent and unrestrained find it joyful and easy,
and all who follow such ways quickly rise.
Thus, common people without exception abandon the former and incline to the latter.
Among men there may be some with slight purity and integrity in youth,
but in maturity purchase office and gain wealth and honor;
perhaps their own knowledge is enough to decorate themselves,
their partisans are enough to draw each other,
and the sons lacking conduct
then point to them as evidence,
saying:
“That person gives free rein to desire and is not hindered from brilliance;
this person controls himself and follows the Way but does not escape poverty and lowliness.”
Yet they do not realize that the honored and illustrious are fortunate,
and those who are cast aside are merely unfortunate,
which is not because of their conduct.
As for those so-called ‘paths open in all directions,’
they prefer to help only those close to themselves;
their shoes are not fully worn,
sashes not tied in time,
hand in hand to ascend the hall,
sleeve to sleeve entering the room,
when going out, knees pressed together,
in gatherings they go straight in,
whatever favours there are, they receive the most,
entrustments are always heard,
their wishes are always met,
their words are always indulged,
should trouble arise, they are sheltered,
in recommending someone, even a stumbling donkey obtains the price of a dragon steed,
when vilifying, even a filial son suffers the slander of Shāngchén.
Therefore, the rush of petty men
is like breaking a dike a myriad fathoms high to release pent-up water,
or setting wild fire to the withered grass of Yún Mèng.
If you wish for Xiāo and Yōng to be orderly and harmonious,
and the younger generation to take them as models,
it is like roasting ice to make it dry,
or piling up ashes to make them blaze.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
In the Three Terraces and Nine Ranks,
one sits and discusses the Way;
the provincial governors and district administrators,
hold the reins and lead;
the greater the office,
the more excellent are the affairs,
yet all toil and hardship accumulates at the county level.
Among them, it is the magistrate’s;
public duties issue from there,
where exactions and levies gather,
though the governors and prefects may be worthy, if the magistrates and chiefs are unfit,
then government cannot be carried out,
state affairs are neglected,
how could the harm stop at just one territory!
Therefore, the appointment of magistrates and chiefs all the more requires talent,
and is of more urgent importance than the officials of the central ministries.
If used yet the right man is not obtained,
the reason is nothing else,
for impartial justice is not acted upon,
and private interest is never set aside.
There are those whose fathers and brothers are honored,
thus, their sons and younger brothers are given office by reputation;
or high-ranking men favor and recommend those of common stock and no ability;
sometimes it is an old friendship;
sometimes they are close relatives, nothing more;
knowing full well that these are unfit, yet they use such.
Of course, there are at times those who succeed,
not that none at all are suitable,
but for the most part they are lacking in refinement.
Those who can rise by their own merit,
exhort themselves to purity and frugality,
devoted to public duty from dawn to dusk,
seeking the praise of the many,
fearing their conduct might not be commendable,
ashamed that their friends might have nominated the wrong man—
these are rare indeed!
The vulgar and ignorant
are shallow in capacity, near in ambition,
obsessed with wealth and profit,
pursue only riches,
indulge their desires without restraint,
knowing no limit or sufficiency.
When they hold official posts,
knowing there is more to be taken,
they rely on the local lords to accuse and impeach,
until finally they are removed from office;
yet fearing enmity will result,
and retaliation return upon them,
they do not dare to oppose them;
therefore, greed and cruelty go unchecked.
So it is,
how could the common people not suffer poverty and estrangement!
When there are many estranged,
they inevitably join together and become bandits.
A room a hundred armspans in size
may be consumed by a gust only inches wide;
an embankment a thousand zhang tall
may collapse through the hole of a single ant.
How could one not be deeply vigilant!
How could one not adapt and improvise!
Yet some who measure with weights
may abandon the scales and yield to their own inclinations;
some who wield the axe-handle
may bend the line and ink in favor of themselves.
Those who select candidates do not choose men for office,
and those who seek office never claim themselves unworthy;
thus, those who govern bring chaos to administration,
those who shepherd the people scatter them,
and there are those who are filthy, arrogant, and extravagant, oppressing the commoners;
some are harsh, cruel, and severe, earning much resentment;
some are ignorant and muddled, causing disorder in all affairs;
some are dispirited and lax, bringing about ruin and decay;
some pursue unnecessary projects and exhaust the people's strength;
some harbor fugitives and act with violence;
some, ignorant of laws and decrees, are deceived and cheated;
some indulge in music, wine, and sensual pleasures, falling into dissipation;
some waste time on weiqí and chūpú, neglecting state business;
some hunt, travel, and feast, forgetting public affairs;
and some, failing to hear lawsuits, throw prisons into confusion.
The people cannot endure it,
and rise up as bandits and thieves.
Disasters and crimes erupt and become known,
ending up amid thorns and brambles,
dimming the ruler's brilliance,
increasing the complexity of penal codes,
and the suffering of the people
grows ever deeper!
To employ the wrong person
is like putting ornate reins on a wooden horse—
how could it ever gallop with the wind?
Or like expecting a lump of earth to take the place of a dragon amid the clouds and rain—
how could it ever shine upon the highways of heaven?
If one who holds the balance of the nation,
who issues and receives the king’s commands,
scrutinizes like an experienced judge of medicine,
not letting the lame be yoked with fine steeds,
not recklessly and carelessly accepting,
nor blind to self-measure,
but anticipates pitfalls on the way,
never harnessing the weak to pull the carriage of phoenixes,
then what fear would there be that all enterprises would not prosper?
What worry that the Four Evil Ones would not be driven out?
Would the Three August Ones be insufficient to make four,
or the Five Emperors scarce to become six!
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If a hero of outstanding ability encounters an enlightened sovereign,
then before the mulberry’s shade has moved,
the bond of gold and orchid is already firm.
If a man of great talent meets one of deep discernment,
he need not undergo lengthy trials,
for mutual understanding is already clear.
He soars like a wild goose riding a strong wind,
flits like a flying fish leaping onto startled clouds.
If suppression and neglect could be lightly regarded,
then Jiāng Gōng would have gone unused in Zhōu;
if humble status were sufficient to reject,
then Máo Shēng would not have been honored in Zhào;
if one required a lifetime’s good conduct before entrusting government,
then Níng Qì would not have become renowned in Qí;
if high lineage alone determined who was empowered,
then Chén Hán would not have been recorded by Hàn.
The wise select broadly yet with attention to detail,
harbor neither envy nor greed;
thus can they inspire awe, accomplish great deeds,
bring order to heaven and balance to earth.
How could they deign to count firewood before cooking,
or number grains before making porridge?
Discard flaws and neglect trifles,
peel fur to hunt for blackness—never!
Someone says:
"The authors of antiquity,
being greatly talented and deeply thoughtful,
made their writings subtle and hard to comprehend.
People today have shallow minds and limited abilities,
so their works are open and easy to see.
This ease of comprehension,
compared with the difficult works of the past,
is as gutters to rivers,
as insects and molehills to Sōng and Dài mountains.
If water does not rise from Kūnshān,
it cannot send mighty floods toward the east;
if books do not come from heroes and worthies,
they cannot contain the grand resonance that reaches far. "
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"Those who discuss tubes and burrows
cannot be asked about the boundlessness of the Ninth Heaven;
those long accustomed to constraints
cannot be compelled to understand the unique insights of the exceptional.
Indeed, the scholars of antiquity
were neither ghosts nor gods.
Though their forms may have faded long ago,
yet their spirit
is spread throughout their writings.
Their intent is revealed in their words;
their aim can be discerned.
Furthermore, it is not true that all ancient writings are intentionally obscure—
not that those of former times wished to make them hard to understand,
but rather that the world has changed, language has evolved,
dialects differ,
calamity and disorder have been frequent,
texts have lain buried and neglected for ages,
bamboo strips and books have decayed and broken,
much has been lost,
some are confusingly continued from fragments,
others have lost their chapters and lines—
thus they are hard to grasp,
and only seem to be extremely deep.
Therefore, the Shàngshū,
which is a collection of government affairs,
does not match, in clarity and richness, the memorials, edicts, military books, and reports of near times.
The Máo Shī,
though a flowery and colorful text,
does not compare to the richness and abundance of 'Shàng Lín,' 'Yǔ Liè,' 'Èr Jīng,' or 'Sān Dū.'
If so, how could the philosophical texts of antiquity
surpass the writers of today?
How could this be so?
Yet those who cling to the stumps,
play with useless things,
have ears but no eyes—
how could they admit this?
They revere the works of the ancients as divine,
yet call contemporary writings shallow;
they value the distant and disdain the near—
such attitudes have a long history.
Thus, a new sword by feigned inscription fetches a higher price,
an old square vessel is prized by a false title.
Because of this, though ancient writings are plain,
vulgar scholars say they surpass nature;
though modern works are like gold and jade,
common people compare them to rubble.
Ancient books are many,
but not all are fine;
they should be the mountains and abysses for the learner,
letting those who set their pens
discern, select, and hunt among them.
Yet, this is like the forests of Dōng'ōu
or Chángzhōu,
though catalpa and elm abound,
still they cannot be called majestic halls
or splendid mansions;
the swamps of Yúnmèng
and Mèngzhū,
though rich in fish and meat,
cannot be considered the sumptuous feasts
or rare delights of Yú and Dí.
Now, both ancient and modern poetry
possess meaning and principle,
each excelling in their differences.
Among scholars,
all possess virtue and conduct,
but one may alone excel in literature and the arts—
they cannot be treated as the same.
Among women,
all are graceful and beautiful,
but one alone may master a hundred skills—
they cannot be misjudged as identical.
If we consider songs on palaces and chambers,
how do Qí Sī's 'Road Chamber' odes
compare to Wáng Shēng's 'Luíngguāng' rhapsody?
In talk of hunting,
how does Shū Tián's 'Lú Líng' poem
compare with Sīmǎ Xiāngrú's account of 'Shàng Lín'?
In praise of sacrifice,
how do the pure and grand words of 'Qīng Miào' and 'Yún Hàn' compare
to the splendor of Táiguō's and Guō's 'Southern Suburb'?
On campaigns and conquests,
how do 'Chū Chē' and 'Liù Yuè'
compare to Chén Lín's 'Martial Army' for grandeur?
These examples make the point clear.
Recently, Xiàhóu Zhàn and Pān Ānrén both composed 'Restoring the Lost' poems,
modeled on 'Bái Huá,' 'Yóu Gēng,' 'Nán Gāi,' and 'Huá Shǔ' and their kind;
all the eminent scholars and men of talent who have judged literature
agree that among the three hundred ancient poems,
none can equal what these two worthies have written.
Moreover, in ancient times, everything was pure and simple;
now, nothing is without adornment and embellishment.
As times change and the world transforms,
such is the natural order of things.
As for Kāi-jǐn being beautiful and durable,
it cannot be said to be inferior to the rain cape;
splendid and sturdy chariots
cannot be said to fall short of rugged carts.
Writing is like speech;
if it enters into conversation,
then one becomes aware of
(a sound?)
When Hú and Yuè meet,
they ultimately do not understand each other.
So to instruct and admonish by this,
how can people comprehend it!
If one deems eloquence to be ease of comprehension,
then why does writing favor that which is hard to understand?
Just as boats and carriages replaced stepping through water,
so written characters succeeded knotted cords;
things that come later often surpass what came before,
and achievements follow each other in the thousands and tens of thousands;
it is impossible to enumerate them all.
People of the world all know this,
and delight in it more than before;
why, then, should literature alone fall short of antiquity?
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
To keep the ruler at peace and govern the people,
nothing excels ritual.
To pervade human relations,
it must indeed be detailed and complete.
Yet, in capping, marriage, drinking, and archery,
why must there be so much tedious minutiae!
Though human relations value ritual,
it is only necessary that it suffice to express ranks, authority, affection, and respect;
where is the need for such complexity in ascending, descending, bowing, and yielding?
For endless kneeling, rising, prostration, and obeisance?
In times past, when all under Heaven was at peace,
and all quarters were tranquil,
officials fond of antiquity
would sometimes practice these things;
even to the point of conducting examinations for months on end,
supervising by lash and cane,
laboring day and night,
neglecting sleep and food.
After years of study,
a single day would be spent on testing;
holding scrolls carrying out their duties,
scrutinizing written documents and conduct,
with punishments of demotion and exile
also among them.
Yet mistakes would still occur,
and the intent not be grasped.
To wish to make this the constant practice of the people,
is supremely difficult.
This is what Mòzǐ meant when he said, "Generations cannot exhaust such learning,
nor can one lifetime master it."
In antiquity, people consulted herders and woodcutters,
widely discussed children's songs,
and even the words of madmen
were considered.
As for the teachings of Mòzǐ,
they cannot be denied.
Yet in establishing laws and opening the way,
embracing all human affairs,
and furnishing the royal way,
he could not give a nuanced account;
that was his shortcoming.
As for his criticisms of lavish burials
and his censure of complicated rituals,
these should not be cast aside.
Since Jiàn’ān,
under the military and civil authority of Wèi,
funeral customs applied to the dead
have strived toward simplicity and frugality.
This is in accord with the Dao of Mòzǐ,
and is implementable.
In my view, now that disorder has been pacified,
and the court and realm are at ease,
what the king institutes
ought to follow the precedent set by rulers of the past.
Those with exhaustive study and broad learning can be appointed
according to their ability to balance reduction and addition,
unimpeded by stubborn fools,
and tasked with editing and settling the Three Rituals,
cutting and casting aside what is unnecessary,
arranging their origins and transmission,
uniting the institutions,
and classifying them by kind.
As for persistent and laborious debates
or where expressions differ but the meaning is one, retain these;
as for what cannot be regularly practiced, remove them.
Let there be no harm or loss;
in the end, one can summarize and select accordingly,
not allowing for concealment and obscurity
or for further stagnation to occur.
The materials for auspicious and inauspicious occasions—
sacrificial stands, beans, goblets, and wine vessels,
the styles of caps, robes, chariots, and uniforms,
the beauty of banners and insignia in distinguishing colors,
the ranks of palaces and houses, high and low,
the forms of court banquets and receiving visitors, host and guest,
the changes in rites of sacrifice, mourning, and burial,
the rules for suburban, ancestral, and collective sacrifices,
the rituals of state, harvest, mountains, and rivers—
all may be simplified and reduced,
striving always for conciseness and thrift.
Conciseness makes things easy to follow;
thrift reduces expenditure;
when things are easy to follow, there is no burden;
when little is spent, imposts are light.
When there is no burden, those charged with duties make no mistakes;
when imposts are light, those who have to raise and provide do not become harsh.
The etiquette of salutations and yielding,
the forms of ascending, descending, circling,
should suffice for expressing matters
and not be rendered trifling and minute.
Each heading and item should be set apart,
so as to be easily consulted and used.
Now the Five Rites are jumbled and confused,
their embellishments tangled and chaotic,
their branches split and leaves scattered,
their instances repeated and overlapping,
entangled with one another.
Even old scholars poring over them
are often troubled and stalled,
objections grow and differences proliferate without end,
various principles are stated together,
as years and months add up,
unless one is exceedingly meticulous
everyone falls into doubt and anxiety.
Hesitating at a crossroads,
beset by a thicket of doubts,
tormented in spirit and wrung in thought,
examining and reviewing precedents—
some spend a lifetime on this,
and still never achieve clarity.
The labor of governing it all is painful and intense,
yet nothing is resolved;
groaning as they sift and analyze,
worn out and defeated in argument,
their hair grows white while no progress is made,
years and months are wasted,
other professions are neglected,
later generations are all afflicted,
and truly it does not end.
The length of the commentaries
now exceeds the classic itself.
If one conforms with the mixed customs of the day,
sorts them according to type,
deletes the nonessential,
situates the main outlines,
examines the rules,
all will be as clear as sun and moon,
as distinct as the five colors set in order,
reducing a ten-thousandfold burden for students,
and ending the troubles of endless debate among scholars.
When those of the future who are enlightened see this,
they will surely applaud it more than the present lauds Zhōu.
This is akin to the reform that burned oracle-bones and abolished blood-sacrifice,
and should confront no difficulties,
except for a regretful attachment to the past,
lingering with the cart before departing the old cave-dwelling.
Yet, as for those who cling to constancy,
who finally hear of these ideas,
they will certainly be startled and wounded by the innovation,
and call them the ravings of a mad scholar.
The Three Kings did not inherit each other's music;
the Five Emperors did not copy each other's rites—
and yet their changes in customs and mores,
their methods of stabilizing rule and governing people, were all one in principle.
Some things were reformed, some continued,
adapting and improving where beneficial;
why must one insist on riding a boat to climb a mountain,
urging a horse to cross a stream,
or donning armor to enter the ancestral hall,
or heavy furs to stand the high summer heat?
If one claims that the ways of antiquity must never be changed,
then coffins should never replace firewood burials,
and clothing should not succeed nudity.
Bào Pǔzi said:
The orthodox classics are the deep sea of Dào and Yì;
the philosophical writings are the rivulets that add depth.
Looking up and comparing them,
they are like the splendid stars assisting the three celestial luminaries;
looking down and aligning them,
they are like woods and groves aiding Mt. Sōngyuè.
Though the ferries and paths are different,
they ultimately converge in the advance of virtue;
though they diverge in the first step,
they are unified in enlightening transformation.
Therefore, the insightful person gathers the origins to encompass the branches and leaves,
grasping the essentials to achieve unity.
The ancients lamented the difficulty of true talent,
thus they said a hundred generations follow in succession;
they did not discard the night-glowing treasure simply because uncut jade did not come from Kūnshān,
nor did they cast aside helpful words simply because the book was not written by sages.
Thus, the clumsy poetry of lanes and alleys,
the oaths and testimonies of armies,
though the language may be coarse or the examples humble,
and the text not even ten lines,
are still preserved in compilations,
ranked next to canonical decrees.
The sayings of the Hundred Schools,
are measured against virtue with the same standard.
Consider those who use water:
though the vessels are different, they equally extinguish fire;
as with those who use needles and moxibustion:
though the arts differ, they are equally effective in curing illness.
From the time of the Hàn and Wèi,
writings have become ever more abundant;
though their ideas are deeper than the dark abyss,
and their language richer than tumultuous waves,
applied, they can bring forth auspicious omens from heaven,
manifest good portents from the earth,
summon white pheasants from beyond the wilds,
and secure walled cities within the bounds of Hánxià;
they remove calamities and disorder nearby,
and bestow lasting blessings for generations to come.
Yet in times without sages,
people only value eloquent speech,
and thus cannot run fine horses for a thousand li,
nor weave the ways of recent days into the great books of antiquity.
Those who are shackled and bound,
confined in shallow narrowness,
busy themselves with trivial exegesis,
disparage what is extraordinary and belittle what is different,
deeming these things unimportant.
Some say petty doctrines are not worth viewing,
others claim wide learning confuses the mind,
yet do not realize that combined ounces can weigh as much as mountains,
and the gathering of tens can amount to billions,
that an array of colors makes brilliant embroidery,
and a harmony of sounds produces the sublime Sháo and Huò.
Some highly esteem the shallow writings of the Shī and Shèng,
and lightly regard the profound, rich, and abundant philosophical works,
taking earnest and exacting words as simple-mindedness,
and idle, flowery disputes as clever ingenuity.
So that truth and falsehood are inverted,
jade and stone confused,
and the majestic music echoes among mulberry groves,
while dragon-patterned robes are worn among plain clothes.
Such is the way of the world;
it is lamentable and sorrowful indeed!
Someone said:
"Though writings are abundant,
they only serve to let words fly and display rhetorical flourish,
yet do nothing to aid in right or wrong,
and are not equal to the wordless teaching of virtue.
Thus, Yán Huí and Mǐn Zǐqiān are ranked highest, and Yóu Rú and Xià Yǒu come next.
Of the four categories,
learning is fundamental and conduct is secondary;
then literary composition is certainly a supplementary matter,
yet you do not exalt its roots,
but only prize its branches —
is this proper?"
Bào Pǔzi replied:
"Virtue and conduct are things with substance,
and their higher or lower quality is easily discerned.
Writing is subtle and profound,
and its nature is hard to grasp.
That which is easily discerned is coarse;
that which is hard to know is refined.
Precisely because it is coarse,
there is a fixed standard for measure;
precisely because it is refined,
evaluation is difficult to unify.
Therefore, I set aside the easily seen coarseness,
to discuss the subtlety that is hard to know —
is this not permissible?"
Someone said:
"Virtue and conduct are the root;
writing is the branch.
Thus in the Four Categories,
literature is not placed first.
Accordingly, what is written on paper
is but dregs and remnants;
what can be passed down
is like the straw dog after the sacrifice.
The distinction of high and low,
is evident.
Tell me some outlines of what writing is."
Bào Pǔzi said:
"The fishnet may be discarded, but if no fish are caught,
then one cannot be without the net;
writing may be dismissed, but if the Way is not yet evident,
then one cannot be without writing.
As for the grand or concise structure of texts,
the varying density of style and analogy,
the greater or shorter reach of sources and flow,
and the deeper or shallower subtlety of its resonance —
if their difference is vast,
then, though one would speak in terms of what is beyond heaven or within a hair,
this would not suffice to express their distance;
if their mutual resemblance is considered,
then, though one speaks of the brilliance of the three lights,
it cannot match their myriad distinctions.
The sharp or dullness of swords and lead ingots from Lóngyuān,
does not suffice to compare their acuity or bluntness;
the lightness of swan feathers or the weight of piled gold,
does not suffice to compare their heaviness or lightness.
Purity and turbidity differ greatly,
each having its origin;
brightness and obscurity are not of the same category,
strength and weakness each have different natures;
yet common men see only those able to dip their brush and write on paper,
and so lump them all together.
Thus Bóyá longed for Zhōngzǐ,
and the man of Yǐng could not pursue what his tool could not cut.
So, though many carve and file,
yet only Bān Gǔ and Dì Lǐ have the name of supreme craftsmanship;
though there are many who play the qín,
only Kuí and Xiāng Yáng truly understood its depths;
with a thousand horses in the stables,
only the qíjì is valued above the rest;
among ten thousand beauties,
only Wēi Shī possesses unsurpassed grace.
There are indeed those few who far surpass the many.
Moreover, writing and virtue,
are as ten feet to one zhàng;
I have never heard them be called mere leftovers.
Heaven displays omens,
Tāng and Yú are celebrated by their writings;
the great man shines like a tiger,
the gentleman is as resplendent as a leopard;
Chāng Dàn fixed the sage's posthumous honor in a single word,
Zhōngní drew out the vitality of Zhōu;
all depend on writing.
The eight trigrams were applied to hawks and falcons,
the calendrical cycle came from the markings of sacred tortoises,
wherever there is writing,
even that which is low is still esteemed;
the hides of dogs and sheep
cannot compare.
Furthermore, the root is not necessarily always precious,
nor the branch necessarily always mean.
Just as the patterns of brocade begin as woven threads,
or pearls and jade reside among shells and stones,
clouds and rain arise from but inches of mist,
and rivers and seas begin from a mere trickle;
thus, though writing is younger brother to virtue,
it cannot be called a mere trifle."
Someone said:
“The endeavors of people today
are mostly inferior to those of antiquity,
whether in writing or composing texts;
this is no different.
Is it perhaps due to the decline of vital force and fate,
a law of nature?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“Among the teachings of the Hundred Schools,
though there is progress and innovation,
all stem from the thoughts of eminent scholars
and are shaped by the hands of accomplished men of talent.
Compared to the ancients,
they are not necessarily all diminished.
There are some whose thinking is vast and profound,
harmonious with the creators of the past;
within, they open up the unfathomable deep sources;
outward, they spread far-flung, inexhaustible currents.
Their forebears stood high,
their interpretations are marvelous;
their transformations are not confined by the squares and circles of rules and measures,
and their broad understanding is not obstructed by the constraints of a single path.
Thus, those with partial tastes, fond only of sour and salty flavors,
cannot recognize their taste;
those whose thoughts are limited
cannot grasp their spirit.
When the Yìng Lóng rises slowly,
looking back it soars above the clouds;
the sweat-blooded steed travels at a gentle pace,
breathing over a thousand lǐ;
would mole-crickets marvel at how it attains such heights without taking gradual steps?
Would handicapped nags complain that it did not surpass them by degrees?
As for those who hurry heedlessly through the discussions on poetry,
and turn about among the records and chronicles,
using commonplace feelings to contemplate what is extraordinary,
using narrow measure to fathom the boundless,
seeking the extremely subtle with a coarse approach,
or weighing the profound with what is most shallow,
even if they begin from childhood
and persist until their hair turns white,
still they will not attain it.
Those who delight in some work will certainly praise it as good;
but those who do not understand it
will inevitably disparage and condemn it—
this is the natural course of things.
Thus, that which they cannot comprehend they deem false and absurd;
they are fully sincere in this opinion,
and not necessarily acting contrary to their feelings or harming others.
Moreover, the common people always esteem the spirit and value the ancients, while carelessly belittling those of the same age:
even if presented with a horse swift as the wind,
they still say it cannot match the one Zàofù drove;
even if offered a treasure worth a walled city,
they still say it cannot compare with what moved the people of Chǔ to tears;
even if they have a peerless sword of decision,
they still say it cannot match what Ōuyě forged;
even if there is a medicine that can raise the dead,
they still say it cannot compare to what Héquè compounded;
even if there is a person far above his peers,
they still say he cannot match those recorded on bamboo and silk;
even if there is a book that benefits the world,
they still say it cannot compare to writings left from earlier dynasties.
Thus, Zhòngní was not esteemed in his own time,
and the Dàxuán was looked down on by its contemporaries.
The common scholars often say:
“Today’s mountains are not as lofty as mountains of the past;
today’s seas are not as vast as those of the past;
today’s sun is not as hot as the sun of former days;
today’s moon is not as bright as the moon of long ago”—
so how could they consent to believe that today’s men of talent
are not less than the dry bones of antiquity!
They value what they have only heard of,
and scorn what they have seen for themselves—
this affliction is not unique to a single age.
Those in the past who broke their qín and destroyed their strings
must truly have had this reason!
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Surveying the records of former ages,
down to near times,
the corruption of morals and decay of custom
was never more severe than at the end of the Hàn.
The court was monopolized by the clique of eunuchs,
playing with imperial power,
wielding the levers of state;
abolishing the upright and promoting the perverse,
harming benevolence and endangering righteousness;
crouching on the backs of those they hated,
willfully deaf and blindly ignorant,
banding together in wickedness,
recruiting fellow villains.
They hoarded wealth and amassed riches,
knowing no bounds,
yet could not distribute even the smallest coin
to rescue the desperately poor and honest.
In seeking office, none without abundant wealth could advance;
in lawsuits and cases, none without heavy bribes could win justice.
Those with high rank and great influence
wielded power enough to raise up the talented,
but could not utter even a word in favor
of those outstanding in the age.
All those they favored
did not go beyond the relatives of their wives and concubines;
their grace and kindness
never extended beyond their close associates and petty followers.
None took warning from the reproach of Zāng Wén usurping office,
nor emulated the selflessness of Jiě Hú abandoning private interests.
They handed out emoluments as if to compare with Wáng Lín,
and relinquished their offices as if following Fāng Huí.
Thus, when Lièzǐ said there was a sage in every house,
yet none received the aid due Zhèng Yáng;
highest ideals gathered in numbers,
but none found a sponsor like Bào Shēng.
Those who stood alone were suppressed and frustrated;
only favorites and sycophants were advanced.
This is why Fán Jī covered her mouth,
and Féng Táng grieved forever.
In prosperous times, most idly occupied their positions and fattened themselves,
obscured virtue and concealed the worthy,
envied those with merit and placed them in danger,
abhorred the honest and upright and estranged them,
shunned the loyal and forthright and cast them into calamity,
loathed those who stood out and rejected them.
The pliant and obsequious received favor and nurture;
the upright and angular suffered slander and rejection.
They reared jackals and wolves while exterminating qílín and yú;
planted thorny shrubs and cut down aromatic cinnamon and pepper trees.
Thus, those who were proud, unruly, unrestrained, drifting like spinning balls or floating duckweed were called magnanimous and great of character;
the petty and harsh, severe and secretly venomous
were called upright and principled;
those with a pleasing appearance, quick wits, but empty-hearted
were called wondrously perceptive and clear of mind;
the glib of tongue and petty debaters skilled in flattery
were called eminent in discerning and refined in style;
the rash, arrogant, and superficial
were called majestic and extraordinary;
those addicted to wine and lust, dull and unsuspecting,
were called natural and unpretentious;
those greedy and acquisitive, prone to seizing what is not theirs,
were called broad-minded and far above worldly matters;
those wild-haired, slovenly of dress, mingling indiscriminately
were called broadly benevolent and all-embracing;
those who rebelled against the classics, distorted the sages, followed perversity and disguised it as erudition
were called guests of Zhuāngzi and Lǎozi;
those mocking, sneering, and scorning propriety
were called possessing a carefree, elegant charm;
those who betray the square and embrace the round, agreeing with everyone for the sake of response
were called peerless and outstanding;
those who leaned on power and wealth, traded goods and followed well-worn tracks
were called perceptive and exceptionally adaptable;
those too lazy to read or write, yet eager for empty fame
were called accomplished in their work and lofty in ambition;
those who relied on powerful relatives and attained rank beyond their talent
were called peers of the Four Heroes;
those who bartered goods and alliances with influential houses to buy fame and rank
were called generous with wealth and valuing righteousness;
those who formed cliques and conspired for empty praise, acting contrary to their words
were called refined in forming friendships;
those using sorcery, heterodox arts, and invoking spirits
were called enlightened and divine;
those who practiced divination and petty prognostications, deceiving with promises of fortune or disaster
were called marvels of foreknowledge;
those who brandished spears on horseback with the strength of one man
were called generals-in-chief;
those who parroted hearsay and echoed the vulgar
were called outstanding talent and eminent scholars.
As for those whose character is brilliant and conduct lofty,
whose spirit is clear and discernment far-reaching,
who do not flatter with smiles to seek favor,
who do not twist their words to betray their hearts,
who endure frost and tread on snow,
whose sense of duty does not allow pursuing alliances lightly,
who base themselves on principle and act with uprightness,
standing forth with distinction, different from the common herd;
though the wind blows fiercely, their branches do not bend,
though their bodies are hard-pressed, their integrity does not change,
when advancing, they speak sincerely and debate justly,
pointing out faults and admonishing failings;
when retiring, they maintain honesty and block out selfishness.
Those who do nothing except what they know is right
are dismissed as naïve, foolish, and worry needlessly.
Rising early and sleeping late,
withdrawing from meals due to public duty,
being concerned with toils that harm or benefit,
exerting their utmost to govern,
they are called narrow-minded, ordinary officials.
As a result, enlightened and wise people retreat into seclusion,
the lofty and outstanding tie their purses and feign foolishness,
the humble and outcast strive to take flight and choose their perch,
those bound and restrained bend to circumstances and hide in court;
the wise are unwilling to reveal their secret calculations,
the courageous are unwilling to show their resolute boldness,
the loyal and outspoken retire,
the treacherous and vicious gain favor,
evil currents overflow, impossible to stem,
false ways open wide, impossible to block.
Thus it comes to the powerful oppressing their superiors and abandoning those below,
bandits and thieves are found everywhere,
eunuchs seize the authority of the rulers,
and three times out of nine, people die at the hands of base lackeys.
Loyal and worthy men, men of reputation,
are branded as factionalists,
imprisoned, hunted, executed, uprooted,
the world laments in grief,
the innocent and blameless,
shut their doors and yet meet disaster.
A faint smoke rises from the inner walls,
but sudden storms set the world ablaze;
a shallow rift appears on the skin,
and yet waves and torrents flood every corner of the earth.
A fortress of gold is slaughtered by common bandits,
a moat as broad as a river crossed on a single reed;
strong and sharp men see their reputation melt like ice,
summoned troops turn their spears and flee north;
sharp blades break through door screens and chambers,
people in barbarian dress rampage through the inner court,
weeds and millet grow in the temple hall,
thorns and wild grass flourish on the jade stairs,
clouds and towers turn into dens for foxes and hares,
mighty walls become paths for tigers and leopards,
the eastern quarters turn to ashes and dust,
the people perish in the blaze and sink amid fiery depths,
malignant households destroy the state,
incurring crimes written on bamboo and silk,
no good words from the noble historians,
no praise in bronze or stone.
How could this be?
It is because of men.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
In the waning days of Wú,
different eras suffered the same sickness,
knowing that past ills brought ruin to them,
yet unable to change their tune now.
Though the warning of disorder and destruction was not distant,
they still followed in the tracks of overturned chariots,
seeing the hedge thorns fight over the same clod,
forgetting the disaster of perishing together,
laughing at the lice and nits at ease,
unaware that calamity though different in form is equal in threat.
Seeing the boat of competition sink,
but not realizing that though routes differ, the drowning is alike.
I, living in the Jìn era, saw none of this,
but my teacher, Zhèng-jūn,
had personally witnessed it in detail;
he would often instruct me, saying:
In the late generations of Wú,
the sickness became even more severe;
the worthy found no employment,
the impure and filthy were cast aside,
rules and standards flew into disorder,
even enormous boats leaked freely.
In public examinations, those who gave lavish gifts came first;
in office, those with strong factions took the right side;
without wealth or status,
one might hope for nothing in a lifetime.
Those of virtue and lofty conduct,
treasured the heroic spirit yet were pressed down and submerged;
those of talent and strength,
once they caught the eye, soared to office.
The ruler was muddled above,
the ministers deceitful below,
without factions, one could not get by,
without rivalry, one could not advance,
the custom of forsaking the public good grew ever worse,
the way of uprightness and honesty was thus destroyed.
So a sparrow, taking the violent wind as its chance, soared to the heavens,
a rotten boat, trusted to rushing waves, sped like lightning;
mandarin ducks and phoenixes folded their six wings in the thorny bush,
a wild duck’s prow stagnated in muddy water, unable to rise.
Those who assisted in holding the reins,
those who governed the people,
if not close kindred of the empress-dowager,
then were flatterers and sycophants.
Advancing, they offered no loyal reproof to correct faults;
retiring, they didn’t dare hear lawsuits with fairness;
in empty talk, breath like frost and ice escaped their lips,
in their actions, they were muddied by filth and mire.
No one felt shame at the taunt of “corpse drawing salary,”
nor feared disaster for bringing on war;
they used slander and praise as if spinning silk,
replaced agriculture with wielding power and dispensing favors.
Their carriages and robes shone so brightly they could be mirrors;
their mansions attracted flocks of birds to settle.
Their shouts and commands were swifter than thunder and lightning,
misfortune and fortune came quicker than from spirits and ghosts;
their power shook lords of states,
their hoards made the public treasury rich.
Going out, they paraded with peacock hoods and guards;
entering, they wandered among ornate jade beams and painted pillars.
Their servants and pages numbered an army,
their closed doors turned home into a bustling market,
cattle and sheep crowded the fields and marshes,
ponds and estates spanned a thousand li.
They displayed the frugality of washing fur in ocean water,
thereby stealing the repute of Zhào Xuānpíngzhòng.
Inside, they venerated the reputation of Táo Kǎn and Wén Xìn,
while in fact carried the filth of Ānchāng Dǒng Dèng.
Though guests arrived, they never offered generous delicacies,
hungry scholars never gained relief of a single meal,
but gold and jade filled their halls,
their chambers overflowed with courtesans and concubines,
their merchant ships numbered in the thousands,
moldy grain filled ten thousand barns,
their gardens and parks rivaled the imperial Shanglin,
their mansions and lodges rivaled the Tàijí Palace,
meat from feasts was left for dogs and horses,
rare treasures piled up in the vaults.
In their dealings with scholars,
there was no bond even as thin as the reed’s membrane;
in attending to themselves,
they enjoyed the fattest share.
Some never opened a page of the statutes and laws,
but usurped the position of Grand Judge;
did not know where files and cases were placed,
but occupied pivotal posts;
did not know the names and titles of the Five Classics,
but received salaries for scholarly office;
were not familiar with the cycles of days and seasons on a single sheet of paper,
yet sat in academicians’ seats.
Their writing was never wild or free,
yet they received honor through judging disputes;
with downcast brows, wings drooping,
yet they filled the ranks appointed to present memorials of impeachment;
unable to distinguish the refined or crude among men,
yet were entrusted with ruling on merit and worth;
not knowing the strategic balance of Heaven, Earth, and Man,
yet towering in the highest seats of command;
repeatedly disgraced as defeated generals in retreat,
yet never losing the prominent title of vanguard;
unable to tell wheat from barley,
yet shamelessly enjoying favored offices that required close counsel.
They have the nature of fish but bear dragon’s markings,
seeming to be, yet not truly so,
glad to meet water,
but sorrowing at the sight of an otter;
though threatened with the might of swords and axes,
seduced by treasures enough to topple a city,
still one cannot take away a leaden tip from a rhinoceros or wild ox;
even if you hire a sorry nag to chase the wind,
it isn’t that they do not fear great punishment,
nor that they are not delighted by beautiful rewards,
rather their nature cannot be forced,
and there is nothing that can be done;
to wish to entrust to such men the harmonizing of the hundred agencies,
the grand management of all affairs,
is like placing a massive weight upon a boat a foot long,
seeking a thousand dippers of grain from a single bowl,
expecting a straw dog to bring the feats of Lü Jué,
or a chicken horse to achieve the eagle’s exploits;
such men are unusable,
and this is perfectly clear!
The ruler of Wú gave no thought to such matters,
nor did he increase his vigilance at dusk and dawn.
He entrusted weighty positions
to the flatterers, sycophants, and the mediocre.
The crisis then was more pressing than arrows on a drawn bow or a fully-loaded crossbow;
the signs of imminent ruin were as plain as the sun and moon,
but he claimed he stood as secure as towering mountains,
worthy to look up to as Táng and Yú of old.
His eyes grew weary from gazing at resplendent ornaments,
but he did not examine the gains and losses of administration;
his hearing was exhausted among lascivious music,
but he did not distinguish the truth and falsehood of his counselors’ words;
his silos of grain and bolts of silk were squandered on those who idly refused to compete,
but he did not succor soldiers who shivered from cold and hunger;
his heart delighted in those who captivated his affection,
but he gave no thought for the grave principles of the state's survival.
He slighted the source of rise and fall,
and neglected the weighty significance of ancestral temples.
Jhèng Jūn also said
his teacher, Mr. Zuǒ, lived in retirement at Tiānzhù.
When he ventured out, he did not seek offices or profit;
he befriended no nobles;
yet in his heart, he longed for a world in peace,
secretly grieved for his native land,
and so, beneath his thatched roof, he gave a long, drawn sigh
and said to his disciples:
“Hàn shall surely be restored to its glory,
and the yellow essence will once again arise;
the linchpin of government will revert to Tàiwēi,
the purple canopy will return to the head of the quail.
The order of Heaven will unite with all creatures,
the light will encompass the East and all Xià,
beneficent winds will reach beyond the Myriad Regions,
the deep, mysterious grace will suffuse all under Heaven.
Envoys will come through many interpreters,
tributes of rare woods will fill the halls,
majestic and grand will be their spectacle,
respected above and below.
To maintain peace and abide by institutions
may seem exceedingly easy,
but the five-stringed zithers hum with desolate tones,
and the southern winds sing no songs;
those above cannot attain the ease of self-restraint,
those below do not hear the song of well-being.
Dragons fly but do not alight,
deep-dwelling hornless dragons coil but do not leap;
Zhōuyú hides in darkness,
the crimson blossom puts forth teeth but does not yet bloom.
Yin and Yang clash in disorder;
cold and heat come in the wrong seasons;
the seven celestial governors proclaim omens of disaster,
valleys and ridges shift places,
the thunder of war chariots clatters amid turmoil.
In the moon of the dragon’s concealment,
frost congeals, and cold death looms in the season of bright summer.
The Jade Candles give no light,
aged wine does not overflow;
the sounds of suburb rites are only of conflict,
all life fails to thrive—for what other reason?
Truly because the Four Fiends are not removed,
the worthy Yuán Kǎi is not promoted,
those employed are not virtuous,
and the virtuous are not employed.
“Yet men of noble ideals and distant vision,
wearing coarse clothes but harboring jade within,
uphold tranquility and pure aims,
have no desire for outward things,
hide their path in deep pools,
find fulfillment in forsaking the world,
do not act without ritual,
do not appear at the wrong times,
are beset by hardship but are unruffled,
face poverty but do not repent,
take joy in Heaven and trust their fate,
regard glory and disgrace as one,
advance with no look of joy,
retreat with no display of grief:
these are they who would willingly accept death beneath a cracked and weathered window,
how could they hawk themselves in dazzling displays to pursue advancement,
or flaunt their priceless treasures
just to compete for the price of common stones?
The ways of Kǒng and Mò
in former times were not put into practice;
Mèng Kē and Yáng Xióng
likewise dwelt in distress,
possessing virtue but not opportunity—
it has ever been thus.
When the world lacks Lízhu, the discerning,
then black and white intermingle.
When times want for Guǎn Qīng,
good steeds are mixed with the ordinary.
Pebbles fill the golden coffer;
beautiful jades are abandoned to ditches;
Jiàngshí departs and is lost afar,
Zǐyù is neglected and none recognize him.
Alas,
how sad!
I was born in an inauspicious time,
