neither early nor late,
and will witness the transformation of Wú to Jìn,
and the southern people’s subjugation by the north.”
His words still ring in the ear,
and the Sūn clan’s funeral carriage had already passed by.
Bàopǔzǐ heard this and said:
“The words of these two gentlemen
are worthy as warnings for generations to come.
Therefore I record them here,
so that those who come after may know that Wú’s loss of state
was not something decreed by Heaven.
If we blindly conceal our nation’s faults,
never so much as censure a mote,
then Dǒnghú’s noble candor in writing loses all value,
and Jiǎ Yì will be reproached as too severe towards Qín.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
I have a friend called Master Qiánjū,
who admires Qǐnqiū’s contentedness without contest.
He thatched a hut on hard, stony ground,
devoted himself to literature and art,
but suddenly thought to study farming;
again and again he failed for years,
hunger showed plainly on his face.
Someone questioned him, saying:
“Heaven knows that rites are based on abundant granaries,
and kindness proceeds from ample wealth;
lofty virtue arises from surplus,
frugality is born of want.
Therefore, ten thousand coins are the poet’s pride,
and food and goods lead the Eight Policies.
To labor in the fields is the basis of matching the destiny set by Heaven,
plowing in pairs brings the unchanging joy.
As for the dwelling of the uncommon man,
in office, he flutters with wild swans and phoenixes;
in retreat, he seeks the simple joys of Táo and Bái;
if he serves, he must be kingly,
if he stays at home, it must be with riches.
Thus the people of old cut up the fertile earth to share its profit,
toiled with their limbs in sowing and reaping,
sowed beans generously,
grew splendid vegetables in abundance,
harvested millets till a thousand granaries brimmed,
accumulated ten thousands in their storehouses,
rode out with huntsmen for sport,
returned home with the food of kings.
And yet, when the ancient kings dwelled here,
if the sun soared too high, grain wilted and dust flew;
if clouds gathered thick, waters flooded the hills;
on land, not a single good shoot would sprout,
in water, no stalk would bear ears;
rank weeds and wild rice filled the granary bins,
the firewood and cookpots of the kitchen fell into neglect.
You delight in passively waiting for rabbits to hit the stump,
serenely without plans for advance or retreat.
I fear that what befell Shǒuyáng
will surely be seen again today;
what befell Dānshān
may soon come to pass.
People worry for your plight,
how can you seem so untroubled?
To see the signs and not act
makes understanding impossible;
resigned to the land and never moving
is the conduct of the masses;
is it that those who admire foul fish forget the scent of orchids,
or that those lost in delusion have changed their true nature?
How long, sir, before you awaken?
I, coarse fellow that I am, am perplexed,
and do not comprehend your way.
Crowns and robes cannot fend off spear and arrow,
ancient texts do not relieve hunger or cold.
Why not look at the fertile fields beyond the city walls,
labor with the country farmers at their noble work,
forsake the remote abstruseness of the Six Arts,
and reap a thousand chests to relieve the needy?”
Xiánjū Xiānshēng said:
"As for the deaf, one cannot regulate them by distinctions between Yǎ and Zhèng music;
as for the blind, one cannot demand that they distinguish cinnabar from lacquer;
as for the well-frog, one cannot speak to it about the vast ocean;
as for the common and vulgar, one cannot explain to them the classics and learning.
If you, sir, are familiar with the small tasks of the old farmer,
but have not yet understood the great awkwardness of facing a wall,
how is this different from picking up trifling sand and discarding Suí Hé,
turning to candlelight while turning your back on the bright sun?
What people like and esteem cannot be measured with a single stick;
what people pursue or abandon cannot be exchanged between one and another.
Those who desire to soar to Làngfēng and ascend Sōng and Huá
will surely not linger among mounds and hillocks;
if one's intention is to roam in the Southern Sea,
to float upon the blue expanse,
how could one have leisure to wander idly by muddy pools?
Thus, those who attune their ears to the purity of Jiǔsháo,
the sounds of the Bā people cannot please them;
those who cook great sacrifices and feast in square pavilions,
the taste of sour herbs cannot sweeten their mouths.
Kūnpéng swoops through the crimson sky in lofty flight,
while the wagtail proudly beats its wings in the bramble thicket;
high and low differ in their paths,
both having their limits of flight.
The alternation of the new and dark moon passes swiftly;
the morning fungus does not perceive it.
The mayfly flits in an instant of time,
the wild colt rests only after six months have passed;
the minnows and crucian carp frolic and expose their scales,
the spirit dragon is not to be used in the unfathomable depths.
If one’s actions are misguided and crossed,
how can one’s intentions be accomplished?
Though my food of grass and wild pears does not suffice,
yet it is enough for sumptuous feasting.
Therefore, Lièzǐ did not, because of his want,
covet the stipend of Zhèngyáng;
Céng Cān did not, because of his poverty,
exchange it for the wealth of Jìn and Chǔ.
"To gather subtle words from those who are about to fall—
that is the far-reaching martial prowess of Zhōu and Kǒng;
to toil ceaselessly for profit—
that is to be a criminal in the eyes of Mèng Sǒu.
Those who broaden their vision cannot take every divergent path;
those who strive to accomplish cannot simultaneously reap in both farming and study;
if the body is weary but the spirit content,
what harm is there in living simply?
Moreover, to dwell in barrenness leads to toil,
through toil, one ceases to pursue luxury, and thus purity is attained.
To dwell in richness leads to ease,
through ease, one ceases to pursue frugality, and so extravagance arises.
Purity
is where fortune gathers;
luxury
is where calamity rushes.
When fortune gathers,
even the slightest can become apparent,
and even the declining can be revived;
when calamity rushes upon one,
even the strong can be weakened,
and even the existent can perish.
These are things that come inevitably and unbidden,
that arrive of themselves without being called.
Therefore, if the gentleman wishes to correct the branches,
he must set straight the root;
if he wishes to stop the flow,
he must block the source.
Thus, when the merits of Dào and virtue are established,
the gates of extravagance are shut.
Jiāng Wàng possessed supreme virtue, so farmers no longer sowed,
Chónghuá was a great sage, so fishermen no longer laid their nets;
only then did the jade huáng mark the blessings of Yíngqiū,
and great achievements rose to heights of twentyfold;
why must one mock them for indolence,
or scrutinize their talent in selecting worthies?
When two men share their wealth,
the one who takes less is termed upright;
I now yield the abundance of the whole world,
dwelling instead in this remote and barren land,
forsaking the rich soils of Ānchāng,
and choosing the desireless life north of the city wall.
Truly, all things can be considered trivial,
so where could I go and not have enough?
The Northern Star, by not changing, is revered by all the stars;
the Five Sacred Mountains, by not moving, are honored among all peaks.
The cricket, though it often moves, is never esteemed;
birds and fish, if glutted with depth, will encounter harm.
I am about to clear the wild weeds of the Nine Classics yearly,
and sow the excellent grains of the Six Virtues;
let my fields be far from those of the gentlemen of rank,
and my harvest fill the space between Heaven and Earth.
Why should I take farming as my main task!
In ancient times, a man cast off his robes and abandoned wealth to stop a thief,
the Gēng clan used analogy to warn against greed,
Liú Guǎng scattered gold to avert disaster from his descendants,
Shū Áo chose barrenness to dispel the worry of desires,
Niú Quē, by carrying treasures, attracted robbers,
Táo Gǔ amassed wealth and brought calamity upon himself.
Gain and loss are clearly revealed;
how could one not take warning?"
At this, the questioner was subdued,
and after a long time, stood with mouth open, unable to speak,
bowed his head, unable to look up.
Sighing in regret,
he finally awakened to the words establishing immortality,
which do not pollute harmony with property,
and admired those who drop the curtain to their weaving,
who do not peer greedily into the gardens of others.
You call the sweets of rank-smelling chicks a treat for mandarin ducks and phoenixes,
and use the plan for cracking crabs to entrap a fierce tiger—
is this not narrow and crude!
How base,
your lack of early understanding!
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"In former times, as the Han fire waned in brilliance,
dragons and tigers battled,
the Nine Provinces were torn asunder,
and three families stood in stalemate with tripods.
There was a certain gentleman Lètiān,
who fled the land like a rolling bramble,
and drifted as far as Mín and Yì.
At first he dwelled in intimacy with Wén Xiū,
but in the end was recognized by Kǒngmíng.
His words lofty, his conduct upright,
he stood alone, not joining the crowd;
the people of his time held him in awe,
and none dared associate with him.
Even the power of the two nobles at the time
could not override the multitude;
thus this man was long pressed down in the shadows and among thorns,
as his hair turned gradually to white in old age,
yet he never changed from his coarse clothing.
At that time, though the ruler sought worthy men,
none heard or knew of him;
as for those on the path to office,
none recommended or advocated for him.
He secluded himself in the humble alleys near the martial precinct,
and hid away in grass-thatched houses of rope-hinged doors,
advancing only to put aside the affairs of statecraft,
and withdrawing, forgot even the tools of livelihood;
again and again he went without even wild fruits for food,
and in the morning had no plan for the evening meal.
At this time, an ordinary young noble came and asked him,
saying:
'I have heard that one who has the talents of Yī and Lǚ
does not long remain in poverty and lowliness;
one who holds the arts of Yī Dùn
does not long dwell in hunger and cold.
The accomplished value the ability to adapt;
the wise are proven by never being in want.
Thus, when Fàn Shēng went out, he overthrew Wú and subjugated Yuè,
as an assistant for an age;
when he returned, he amassed wealth in trade,
and accumulated thousands in gold.
Heaven allots poverty among the six extremes;
wealth is among the five blessings.
The Book of Poetry praises those who can add to it.
The Yì esteems gathering people together;
when the bait is fragrant, shàn and wěi fish come.
If the reward is great, the courageous and resolute exert themselves.
This is how Zhǎng Qīng untied the calf-nose and took up the vermilion banner,
how Qū Nì bowed beneath the mat and received mounds and soil,
how Bù Wéi dined upon the city of a hundred thousand households,
and how Zhāng Hóu escaped the distress of the prison.
Thus those who go down to the humble villages seize the hour of repentance and regret,
while those old women who are cast adrift in Fēng receive the reward of a thousand gold.
Sir does not have the ingenious strategies of Shào Bó,
but wholly devotes his keen thoughts to the Six Classics;
suddenly forsaking the tangible calamities of rice and length,
yearning for the empty fame of immortality,
ashamed to seek official salary by deceitful means,
and mortified to flaunt oneself for honor's sake.
Hoping for the hunts of Xī Bó,
awaiting the Yellow River's clearing.
Enduring the sallow look of Liè Zǐ,
distancing the spirit and abandoning the form,
how is this different from painting a splendid steed
to substitute for the labor of walking?
Pointing distantly at ocean water
to quench the parched thirst of the mouth;
casting a fish-net atop a precipitous mountain;
hanging a great coin at the tip of a tall tree;
even if one thinks he has found his place,
he still cannot escape eccentricity and emptiness.
Affairs have no accomplishments after one's demise,
and things cannot flourish contrary to their time.
Now, the realm within the seas is carved up,
heroes contend by might,
the likes of Xiàng Gōng surge to the heavens,
the cunning of Huá Xià act with license,
the slow and weak race like shooting stars to share the path,
jackals and wolves battle with open jaws for supremacy.
Those in power cast aside their cloaks to assert grievances,
men of integrity are covered with dust as they tread narrow ways,
true Confucians abandon imperial principles to practice the strategies of the Five Hegemons,
while erudite scholars forsake the Four Categories and focus anxiously on the monthly critiques.
Those whose baskets are truly laden
advance from the grassy wastes;
those lacking capital or footing
retreat from the court;
those clutching yellow and white
push through the golden gates and ascend the jade hall;
those reciting formulas and policies
make lifelong foes and are cast into the mud;
those whose gifts and bribes are ample
turn tiles and stones into jade disks;
those with scant pleas and support
see their fine dragons abandoned to the wilderness;
those with many political allies
soar with the raging wind to overtop the clouds;
those with narrow connections
drift with mud turtles in quiet waters.
A lump of clay cannot stem the boiling of Pénglǐ Lake,
how can one of singular virtue hope to reverse the errant tide?
Now you, sir, have no stores of even a dān of grain within,
nor means to present even a bundle of dried meat without.
Though you harbor brilliance like a dragon or phoenix,
and bear ornament like a tiger or leopard,
utter words like surging waves,
present them like brocaded embroidery,
yet you freeze and hunger within a clay-walled hut;
what method of distancing could call forth aid?
Why not float a light boat to entrust yourself to swift currents,
and, wielding a flying sail, go far away?
Trade rare goods between the North and South,
gather gold and jasper at Jiǔ Yí.
Travel far and achieve military exploits like Cuī Liè,
and obtain handsome offices in peaceful times?
Merely exhausting yourself in writing and composition,
can this truly result in a cicada's molting—a timely escape?
Suffering the body alone for the sake of a name,
this is what the teachings of Huáng Lǎo scoff at!”
Sir Lètiān replied:
“I have thoroughly studied the Six Arts,
and fully comprehended the Eight Inquiries.
In this, I am indeed wealthy.
When I raise my writing brush and unfurl brilliant diction,
virtue’s sound is inexhaustible,
in this, I am indeed noble.
I strive for benevolence, and benevolence truly arrives;
if I should forsake it, how could that be?
Dwelling in the deep abyss to nourish the spirit,
transcending all things to find self-contentment,
abandoning turmoil and dust on dangerous roads,
and purifying my spirit in profound silence.
Not peering through windows for distant vistas,
judging subtle words without confusion.
Even if one were to offer me terraces and tripods,
still I would firmly not change my course.
How could I, distressed by poverty, struggle with merchants for profit,
or, stung by hardship, vie for success against the petty and trivial?
If you, sir, know that trade and commerce can amass treasure,
so too can tilling the fields stave off hunger.
Yet, do you not know that the one chasing deer does not look back for the rabbit?
If the path is far, the arrival is necessarily delayed.
Consider how Grand Tutor (Shàng Fù) used his cleaver,
and in old age yet uttered extraordinary words;
the weight of ten thousand jun may not be moved
by a light wind;
when the music of Xiāo Sháo was not yet complete,
the spirit birds circled in patterned flight.
Thus, one who waits to ride the whirlwind and ascend to the heavens
does not despise being bent beneath mugwort and weeds;
he who gallops on orchid’s sinew to reach sixty thousand li
does not compete with a herd of stumbling donkeys upon the road.
The truly filial always fears disgrace and danger for their parents;
thus Zǐchūn trembled at descending from the hall.
The highest wisdom does not treasure wealth that is hard to obtain;
thus the sage-kings Táng and Yú cast aside gold and compared moral persuasion.
The wise see disaster before it comes;
a knowledgeable man, upon hearing profit, ponders its hazards.
Yet you, sir, urge me to drift downstream in a boat,
painstakingly seeking a damp-floored house,
encouraging me to use Sui pearls to shoot sparrows,
or to seize flesh by reaching into a tiger’s jaws;
lightly casting aside the body into the unpredictable,
seeking distant achievement through perilous risk,
forgetting the clear admonishments regarding hair and skin,
and seeking profits as elusive as the dry depths.
Suppose one burns carriages and overturns cliffs,
trees are uprooted, stones fly,
great waves rise like mountains,
and monstrous waves tower dauntingly,
a light craft is cast away like dust,
strength and intent are at odds,
sighs and lamentations attain nothing,
thus the wise discern subtle dangers beforehand.
In the past, Huí Xiàn was renowned for his pure hardship,
Chén Píng was spared danger by lacking gold,
Guǎnghàn perished due to greed,
Niú Quē, though laden with treasure, was reduced to ashes.
An ordinary man dies tragically because he harbors a jade,
the rich fox invites disaster for its fine fur.
Now you, sir, press me toward the career of thieves,
coax me with plans for inviting robbers,
offer me poisoned wine as if it were a welcome cup,
though your intention is for my long life and welfare.
Yet the true scholar regards the Three Graves as gold and jade,
the Five Canons as zithers and lutes,
discoursing and studying as bells and drums,
the Hundred Schools as reed pipes and ocarinas,
tasting the Way as words to sate hunger,
drinking in virtue so that righteousness is their intoxication,
exceeding the flow of the age by noble conduct,
surpassing past generations to propagate their names,
urging their steeds ahead on solitary paths.
What need is there for the filthy emotions of gain and riches?
Those who hoard much, have no true substance;
those who relish modesty, guard against excess;
those who keep the luminous gem soon are cut open;
those who heed overturned carts are certain to avoid ruin;
those who overload their boats, sink them;
those who covet victory, destroy themselves.
These are the aspirations of trivial men,
not what high virtue seeks.”
At this, the questioner’s thoughts utterly disintegrated,
and he requested to be placed among the lowest ranks of the disciple’s register,
to forever treasure the elixir of immortality’s good prescription.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The disciples discussed among themselves the precedence of benevolence and clarity,
each holding to what he had seen,
so they came to consult me.
I told them:
“The radiant image of the Three Luminaries is Qián,
the one who bears infinitely is Kūn;
Qián has benevolence and also clarity,
Kūn has benevolence but no clarity.
The sequence of low and high
is not merely a matter of distance!
Only sages
unite their virtue with Heaven.
Thus, Táng Yáo is crowned in the canons for his reverent clarity,
and Zhòngní leads the volumes for illuminating righteousness.
Illumination above
is the honored title of the High Sovereign.
The wise preserve themselves
as the utmost model of the noble.
Worms, flies, and crawling things
also possess benevolence.
Therefore, their loving intent is evident in nurturing,
and their sorrow in song and cry.
Yet, they enter pits and snares without suspicion,
step into nets and traps unawares.
When there is benevolence without clarity,
so all pursue disaster and fail to avoid its worsening;
with hidden sunlight one easily loses life;
constructing dwellings saves them from nests and holes;
selecting grains replaces poison and bitterness;
making clothing reform their nakedness;
building ships and boats lets them cross impassable rivers;
harnessing oxen and horses relieves them from backs burdened by walking;
establishing order and authority pacifies chaos;
making tools prepares for unforeseen trouble;
inventing writing governs officials;
instituting rites and codes refines customs and teaching—all
are the work of illumination,
not something one-sided men can fully explain.
If the mind does not depart from rén, yet the understanding does not manage the state,
then the disaster of peril and destruction
cannot be prevented or stopped—
this too can be known.
To weigh prosperity and decline before signs have appeared,
to probe opportunities when affairs are without form,
to indicate turns of fortune beyond what reason can show,
to ward off gradual harm at its roots—
these are the achievements of understanding.
To extend compassion to even insects,
to forgive offenses and not seek retribution,
to change the sacrificial animal upon seeing its terror,
to avoid treading where reeds are trampled—
these are the deeds of rén.
Thus, understanding is talent;
acting is conduct.
The conduct of sacrificing oneself for the accomplishment of rén can be pursued by effort,
whereas the profound insight to fathom the hidden is not easily gained.
The distinction between subtlety and coarseness,
is clearly set apart.
If one embodies the compassion of rén that cannot bear to harm,
but lacks the understanding to discern right and wrong,
then the mind is confused concerning true and false,
the spirit confounds red and purple,
thought and calculation do not distinguish,
and one cannot recognize good from evil.
If one does not look far to discern safety and danger,
then even one's own person will not be secure;
how can one have leisure to stand for and aid others!
In the past, Jī Gōng was not without love for friends,
yet wept and severed ties with kin;
Shí Shí in ancient times was not lacking in natural kindness,
yet sacrificed private feelings to serve the public.
This was because they clearly saw the nature of events,
and did not indulge momentary affections,
thereby becoming loyal ministers.
To decide by righteousness over affection,
to set aside rén to employ understanding,
to restrain rén by calculation—
rén may at times be set aside, but understanding must always be present.
Tāng and Wǔ seized power against the current for the sake of order—
this was truly not rén.
They responded to Heaven and changed the fate of the world
because of their understanding.
Xú Yǎn cultivated rén and attended court with his peers,
neglecting the outer defenses of city walls,
and lacking military preparations within,
lost his state and destroyed his family—
this is the disaster of lacking understanding."
A disciple said:
"Zhòngní lamented that rén is a heavy charge and the way is long,
and also said,
'If a person is not rén, what use are the rites?'
As for sageliness and rén,
how could I dare aspire!
Mèngzǐ said,
'Rén
is the home;
yì
is the path.'
If a person lacks a heart of compassion,
that is not rén.
The Three Dynasties gained the world through rén,
and lost it through lack of rén.
These are the maxims of sages;
manifest proofs in writings.
And yet, Master, you esteem understanding
but I have not seen the classical grounds for it.
As a foolish youth,
I am secretly confused."
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"The ancients said,
'To love rén but ignore learning—
such one's blindness is stupidity.'
You are close to this.
Formerly, during the era of the Six States devouring each other,
wolves and tigers contended by might,
treachery and power were valued above morality,
killing was exalted and yielding abandoned.
Mèng Shēng, then, sought to restrain greed and cruelty,
and to promote rén and yì—
how could he not earnestly and repeatedly praise rén alone?
Yet never has he uttered a single word
saying that rén surpasses understanding.
It is like in times of plague:
doctors and shamans are prized,
everyone, with one voice,
speaks only of medicines and therapies;
can it then be said
that the art of acupuncture and moxibustion
exceeds the way of long life and enduring vision?
Morever, I believe that matters of rén and understanding,
spread throughout all measures,
my aim is merely to illuminate principles clearly,
describe the broad outlines,
and present only one corner.
Yet you make use of them daily without recognizing,
and claim that understanding lacks authority!
The Qián says, 'Great understanding at the beginning and end,'
and the six positions are completed in their seasons.
Thus, Heaven is established with understanding;
nothing is not encompassed.
Kūn states, 'How great! All things depend on earth to live;'
this is the virtue of rén in earth—
merely sustaining and yielding.
The sequence of principle—
is it not manifest!
The Shī says,
'Bright, bright is Heaven above,
shedding light upon the earth below.'
'Brilliant, brilliant is the Son of Heaven,
his virtuous reputation is unceasing.'
The Yì says,
'The king, being enlightened, receives blessings.'
Mysterious aid comes from the spirits,
reaching to spiritual understanding.'
Here, understanding and spirit are of one nature—
truly not something
that pure rén
can hope to emulate.
Confucius said, 'Intelligent and spiritually powerful,'
he did not say 'intelligent and rén;'
He also said, 'In the past, the enlightened king governed the world,'
not, 'the rén king.'
The Annals state:
'Virtue is made perfect by understanding,'
not, 'Virtue is made perfect by rén.'
The Shū says, 'The sovereign is enlightened indeed,'
not 'rén indeed.'
Lǎozǐ, when praising the highest sage,
said, 'Enlightened, clear, and understanding in all directions;'
but when his school declined,
he said, 'When the Way is lost, then comes virtue;
when virtue is lost, then comes rén.'
The Yì says, 'The king faces south toward understanding,'
not, 'facing rén.'
If I desire rén,
rén has already arrived.
It also says, 'To practice rén lies with oneself;'
thus anyone can perform it.
But as for understanding,
how can it be forced!
Therefore, Mèngzǐ said,
whenever people see an infant about to fall into a well,
they all rush to save it.
From this it can be seen
that all possess a mind of rén,
only differing in degree,
whereas understanding varies greatly among people.
Long ago, Cuī Zhù did not kill Yàn Yīng;
Yàn Yīng called Zhù very unrén
yet possessing some rén.
Thus, even treacherous ministers and rebellious sons
can still possess rén."
The disciple further said:
"The Yì speaks of establishing the way of man,
stating 'rén and yì.'
Thus, nothing is greater for man than rén."
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"The reason for this saying
is that rén lies in conduct;
and conduct can be exerted by effort,
but understanding enters into the spirit,
and must be endowed by Heaven—
it cannot be instilled by teaching.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
That which weighs ten thousand jūn
must have begun with a speck,
that which soars and pierces the heavens
must start with a tiny point.
Thus the floods gather and the southern ocean embraces boundless vastness,
common increments accumulate and the Xuánpǔ attains the highest heavens.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
One who drives a swift chariot,
even if missing his shadow does not tire;
one who rides the wind and skims the waves,
even if crossing danger, does not topple.
Thus, when Yuán Kǎi divided the offices,
he fulfilled Heaven's accomplishments;
when Yī Lǚ cast off worldly duties,
he achieved the merits of revolution.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
A jeweled boat, a jade shuttle,
are useless for crossing rivers;
a golden bow, a jade string,
are powerless amid chaos.
Thus, those upright and pure yet lacking statecraft
are not tools for restoring order;
the refined scholar lacking governing strategy
is not the talent to aid and illuminate.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
Làngfēng and Xuánpǔ
do not rely on hills and mounds to be high;
Xuánlí and Jíelǜ
do not depend on jewels and jades for their beauty.
Thus, the outstanding and unique
cause even hidden orchids to startle with their fragrance;
those lofty in spirit and independent
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Ice and coal do not flaunt their ability regarding cold or heat,
and jǐn or yú do not prove their preciousness, yet their nature is plain to see.
Therefore, the junzǐ maintains self-respect,
unconcerned if none join him;
the perfect man dwells like a corpse,
his heart indifferent to praise or blame.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A sudden gale can topple mountains,
yet it cannot exert effort to pluck a hair;
fire can melt metal and stone,
yet it cannot use its brilliance to dry the wet.
Thus, Huái Yīn was skilled at war and defense,
yet clumsy in affairs of governance;
Jiàng Hóu secured the state and altar,
yet lacked eloquence in court debate.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those who pursue fame do not find giving up life difficult;
those who value their bodies do not let immediate desires entangle feelings.
Thus Jì Xìn willingly met death by ashes and did not regret it;
Yáng Zhū would not part with a single hair for the price of a nation.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Small fry do not understand the far course of the spiritual qiú;
wild ducks do not know that swans are not their peers.
Thus, yoked ploughmen mocked Chén Shèng for casting aside his ploughshare;
the shallow-minded sneered at Kǒng Míng for sitting with knees in arms.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The edge of pure jūn metal
is tested on rhinoceros and ox-horns;
the virtue of xuān and cí
is proven in manifest trials.
Therefore, if paired wrongly, prime talent and mediocrity are no different;
employed alike, a fine steed and a nag show no distinction.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A vessel that is not hū or guǐ,
must advance keenly yet retreat swiftly;
measure yourself against Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wáng,
though your time comes late, you arrive early.
Thus, the tired wren,
still does not fly beyond the tip of a mugwort;
a young mandarin duck, rising slowly,
looks back and glances over the blue sky.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When adversity ends, it is followed by prosperity;
at the height of darkness, clear brilliance shines at daybreak.
Therefore, one drooping his ears climbing Mǒou’s slope,
might yet gallop a thousand li on a swift track;
a coiling fish in the deepest abyss,
might leap among rainbows and soar high.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
He who is divided from his four limbs,
it is by his composed speech that his spirit stands out;
those broken by branch and leaf,
for them, chǎi and huì only increase their fragrance.
Thus, Yí Wū in shackles,
yet achieved unifying success;
Lord Yìng suffered hardship and humiliation,
yet accomplished meritorious entry into Qín.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When listeners are petty,
then equal interests turn to enmity;
when right and wrong travel separate roads,
then affairs differ and resentment arises.
Thus, the ugly grandmother with a swollen face
hates seeing Xī Shī's beautiful appearance;
Shāng Chén and Xiǎo Bái
once heard of Yán Zhōu’s retiring from farming.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If the pure conflicts with the impure,
the torturers grow ashamed;
when the strong and weak are classified apart,
the heavy-lifter is envied.
Thus, Huái Yīn rose to prominence,
yet commoners resented his surpassing them;
Wǔ'ān had towering merit,
yet Fàn Suī adorned his words to undo his business.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Incurable patients,
do not take bitter yet effective medicine;
rotten timber
does not accept the decorations of carving or inlay.
Thus, Bǐ Gān did not act for himself,
but cut open his heart for loyalty’s sake;
Tián Fēng spoke of hidden danger,
but died violently for his honesty.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The lonely paulownia from Yì Yáng,
cannot produce mournful sounds without strings;
the lone bamboo from Dà Xià,
without a player cannot issue clear notes.
Thus, when the position is low, Jì Lí cannot secure people’s works;
when power is slight, Yī and Zhōu cannot achieve perfect peace.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those who climb high must beware reaching the summit;
those who cross great depths meet disaster with an overloaded boat.
Thus, in western Qín, they longed for Lǐ Sī of Shàng Cài;
in eastern Yuè, they regretted Wén Zhòng’s overreaching.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Firmness and gentleness each have their inborn qualities;
integrity and flexibility have natural natures.
Thus, southern gold stands true through a hundred temperings;
the hero in danger does not lose his uprightness.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Without following the right way,
wealth and rank are not worth having;
forsaking benevolence and righteousness,
even longevity is not to be cherished.
Thus, Biàn Suí carried a stone to the abyss;
Zhòng Yóu gladly faced the blade.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
High and low cannot be made identical;
food from storage cannot change virtue through encouragement or discouragement.
Thus, Huì Shì lamented that too few followed his chariot;
Zhuāng Zhōu worried that too many got fish.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
To leave or to stay, there is difference as great as ice and coal;
to be restless or tranquil, as flying or submerged.
Thus, Mò Dí endured cocoons and callused feet, yet was cheerful;
Jī Sǒu, abandoning the world, was content.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those who fulfill their hearts, though their ties are shallow, their affection runs deep;
Those who oppose what is divine, though connected long, only grow more at odds.
So when sounds accord, one can be intimate at first meeting;
when ways differ, a lifetime together will lack love.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Yúhuáng and yìshǒu,
are fine vessels for crossing rivers;
but rowed by the Běi Dí,
they drift and founder in the current.
The sweat-blood horse,
is a steed of swift pace;
but if not driven by Zào Fù,
it tumbles on rough paths.
The Qingpíng and Hǎo Cáo swords,
are extremely sharp;
but if not wielded by Yǔ Yuè,
they bring harm to the user.
Well-trained soldiers,
instruments for quelling chaos;
but if not used by the wise,
they quickly bring disaster.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The order of Heaven keeps its supremacy unchanged;
to violate ritual invites swift and severe punishment.
Thus, the birds and beasts of Xuán Zhōu,
though able to speak, cannot be offered as noble sacrifices;
crickets and their like, with their bent legs,
though clinging to life, cannot participate in rites of benevolence and righteousness.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Slander cannot be quelled by clever words,
real grudges not dispelled by empty acts.
If you try to resolve them the wrong way,
and suppress them not by reason,
it is like clinging to ice to dispel cold,
or adding furnaces to ward off heat,
chasing light to flee from shadow,
or boring holes in a boat to stop leakage.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A wise ruler employing men,
does not allow them to go beyond their capacity;
a loyal minister in office,
does not dare to exceed his measure.
Appointing the unfit,
or falsely assigning duties,
is like putting boiling soup in an ice bowl,
or wrapping blazing fire in reed husks,
or hanging ten-thousand-jūn weights from rotten cords,
or overloading a small boat.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The fur-lined robe of leopard and otter,
is not for carrying firewood;
Nine turns with six changes
are not designed for the deaf;
high songs and distant echoes,
are not sung for the dense and foolish;
risking death to deliver results,
is not performed for those of petty virtue.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The wealth of the people is exhausted, yet their demands have no end;
their strength is spent,
but their labor does not cease;
to expect no resentment or complaint,
and always desire their peace,
is like severing roots to nourish branches,
slicing the back for the belly’s gain,
carving out the eye to increase vision,
gouging the ear to open hearing.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The law is never fixed,
but should follow what is timely and expedient;
yet achievement does not surpass the former,
since custom delights in frequent change;
it is like cutting down a tall horse to fit a short carriage,
or paring off the ankle to fit a bent shoe,
or breaking a long sword to fit a short scabbard,
or slicing a foot-long jade to fit a cramped case.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
The cultivated scales that still the ripples
do not leave the narrow confines of a remote valley;
the luán perches in lofty trees,
not in the low mounds of anthills.
The maxims of the Jiu Chóu
are not spoken by the mouths of the common and base;
the lofty calculations on golden tablets
do not arise from the ordinary hearts of the masses.
To see the branching of a hundred embraces
is enough to know that its root is not slight;
to behold the vastness and depth of one's writings
is enough to comprehend the profundity of the person.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Though the mulberry woods are lush and flourishing,
they do not relieve the chill of the cypress;
rich soil girds the city
but cannot brush away the dust from Qián Áo's sleeves.
Yet the silk for cocooning, padding, and fine cloth
is drawn forth of itself,
and the countless stores,
thus come into being.
Therefore, those who discern the distant value the root;
those who see only what is near focus on the branches.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Those coarse in body are tethered to form;
those keen in understanding attain the spirit.
Whoever traces the beginning to see the end
can find a thread to follow;
one who gains it yet not entirely comprehends
cannot rely on external causes.
Therefore, seeing heaven and earth by day
is not enough to be called wise;
discerning the slightest divide at night
is truly without peer.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Branches and algae may shine brightly in spring,
but cannot stay fresh for long apart from the trunk;
the fish capable of swallowing a boat
cannot abandon water and continue to live.
Thus, those whose fame exceeds their reality
surely lack enduring integrity;
those of high rank whose talent is insufficient
cannot escape inevitable defeat by enemies.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Those who endure the bitter pain of medicine and stone
thereby rid themselves of life-threatening illness;
those who bear the cold burden of armor
thereby defend themselves against the onslaught of arrows;
those whose conduct is pure and endure hardship
thereby achieve exceptional distinction;
those who accept the utmost words that go against their heart
thus avoid confusion from changing principles.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
If luán and fèng compete for grain in the courtyards,
they will be defiled by chickens and ducks;
if dragons and unicorns are mixed with livestock,
they will be gazed on just like the six domestic beasts.
Thus, Shāng Lǎo secluded himself in lofty places to bequeath his remote example to generations,
whereas Biàn Suí went to the depths to preserve a reputation apart from worldly things.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
If a deep well is not cleaned, mud will accumulate increasingly;
if good grain fields are not weeded, then shoots and weeds will run rampant.
If one studies without reflecting, obstacles and confusion will become plentiful;
if one debates without precision, ignorance will grow and success be lost.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
One could pile up ten thousand gold pieces in chests and cases,
but if, from frugality or want, none is used,
it cannot be known if one is any different from the poor.
If one harbors elegant talent in the mind
but does not set it forth in writing,
it cannot be known if there is any difference from the mediocre and base.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Nán Wēi and Qīng Qín,
paragons of beauty,
still required splendid adornment to increase their charm;
Huízǐ, Zǐyóu and Zǐxià,
though blessed with great natural gifts,
actually needed the books Fén and Gào to broaden their learning.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Scarlet curtains interwoven with nets,
ornate canopies giving deep shade,
thus conceal plain beauty;
red lacquer adds elegant finish,
dazzling stripes shine forth,
thus hiding deadwood beneath.
So when the Six Arts are fully cultivated, the base and vulgar are transformed into gentlemen;
when universal praise is gathered, the crude and ignorant are distanced from noble society.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
When lush forests darken and thicken,
birds of every kind gather together;
when the deep pool is broad and vast,
then schools of fish eagerly come.
When virtue flourishes and deeds are great,
many are drawn to it by heart;
when faults are overlooked and talents recognized,
both the distant and the near are brought together.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Though one traces the footsteps upon the highest peaks,
one cannot run free upon Lǚ Liáng;
though one glides over the waves and swims the depths,
one cannot climb the heights or scale the perilous.
Thus Lízhu can split a hair at a hundred paces,
but cannot distinguish the elegance or vulgarity of the eight musical tones;
Zǐyě may harmonize the wondrous notes of spiritual melodies,
but cannot point to white or black at arm's length.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
When the four senses are wide open,
then Xī Hé can receive the sun's light;
when a thousand fathoms make themselves empty,
then all streams flow in.
Thus, when the art of discernment is vast,
all that is strange and heard gathers fully;
when the brilliance of the palace torch blazes,
then worthies gather humbly;
when the tree of criticism is set up,
every fault becomes known;
when the drum of bold remonstrance is hung,
upright words are surely presented.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
All who can speak invariably praise Yáo,
yet Yáo's administration was not wholly perfect;
the world as one disparages Jié,
yet not all of Jié's deeds were lost causes.
Thus the withering of one branch
does not lessen the lushness of the forest;
the wormwood and wheat of winter
do not dispel the killing chill of the first frost.
Xī Shī had faults but could not lessen her beauty,
for her beauty was abundant;
Mómǔ had some small beauty but could not save her ugliness,
for her ugliness was severe.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Bodily being and reputation
are hard to achieve together;
achievement and spirit
are rarely both preserved.
Those who scatter their virtue
suffer and yet remain secure;
those who use their talents to fit the age,
find delight but court much danger.
Thus fierce birds, for their striking power, are caged or tethered;
birds of song, for their wit, are treasured and loved;
finest jade, for its patterns, is cut and carved;
the three golds, for their strangeness, are refined and melted;
sweet-smelling orchids and angelica, for their fragrance, are picked and harvested;
the resonant catalpa, for its sound, is felled for timber.
So the green tadpole, seeing transformation, ascends to the dark clouds;
the divine phoenix, out of season, returns to the cinnabar cave;
Zǐyǒng praises the grandeur of heavenly order;
Qī Yuán mourns the sacrificial victim, shrouded in embroidery.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
When ten thousand elk lower their antlers,
the fierce tiger retracts its fangs;
when a thousand birds and fish gather,
the raptor sharpens its talons.
Thus, when slander spreads across the kingdoms,
even Gōng Dàn could not stop it;
when calumny fills the roads,
Zǐchǎn could not block it off.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
The magnificence of imposed authority
is not augmented by powder and rouge;
the energies of the two solstices
cannot be increased by mere breath.
Therefore, those who possess truly outstanding abilities
do not strive for style to seem exceptional;
those with vulgar natures
do not care for passing praise to seek acceptance.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
The scales that manifest the demeanor of the phoenix
are remarkable only for their rarity;
the cries of fox and owl
are reviled for their abundance.
Therefore, though the talented fill the court,
those seeking worthies never grow weary;
though slanderers set themselves up as mighty,
the loyal and upright gnash their teeth.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Great strength is not exclusive to Mèng Bēn or Wū Huò;
grace and beauty are not found only in Zhèng Dàn and Máo Qiáng;
swiftness is the gift not solely of Huá Liú or Sù Sāng;
decisive courage is not unique to Shěn Lǘ or Gàn Jiāng.
Thus, those who can establish the works of a sage ruler
are not necessarily like Qiū of Eastern Lǔ;
those whose benevolence covers even the withered
are not necessarily Chang of the Western neighborhood.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
When the divine phoenix resounds at morning sun,
nothing is gained for creatures,
yet all listen with rapt attention downwind.
When the owl gathers by night upon the walls,
there is no loss of even a hair,
yet all plug their ears and notch their arrows.
Thus, when fine words go forth,
none, however distant, fails to be pleased;
when evil words arrive,
none, however near, is not annoyed.
It is like the sun and moon, never failing in their clarity,
and arrows, loosed and soon forgotten.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The shadow does not depart from the form,
a name does not leave the reality.
Thus, water that turns from its source
cannot flow on to the east at length;
flowers out of season
cannot retain their luster amidst ice and frost.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A beast with saw-like teeth,
though it crouches low, still inspires fear;
an insect wielding an axe,
though its mouth is intact and its form whole, inspires no awe.
Thus when a junzǐ wears coarse cloth,
he may be poor but must not be slighted;
when a xiǎorén wears tall caps and carriages,
he may reach prominence yet still cannot be esteemed.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A transcendent qílín ranges free beyond the bounds of the great wilds,
so it suffers no calamity of snares and pits;
the numinous cāng soars at the summit of Xuánpǔ,
thus avoiding nets and traps.
Why must one dwell in winding warrens and harbor constant fear?
Why must one hold reeds in the mouth and live in miserable dread?
Thus, those who serve at slaughter and butchery
are surely valued by those who raise stock and fodder;
those who supply the boiling cauldron with food
surely feel secure standing in the courtyard.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The discerning are praised for grasping meanings and transmitting echoes a thousand ages on,
thus grasping the traces of rise and fall.
The wise are cherished for their discernment, standing out in times of hardship,
and for drawing out the talents that set the age aright.
If one listens to a medley of sounds
yet asks for advice from mediocre craftsmen,
that is not the clear ear of Yánzhōu.
If one stifles the talents of distant geniuses
while consulting with common men,
this is not the rare insight of those who see alone.
Thus, to debate transcendent instruments with those who lack appreciation,
is like asking the blind to distinguish among five colors;
to plot the proving of virtuous men with jealous rivals,
is like asking the fox to judge the making of furs.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The lóngbó endures hardship at razor-sharp heights,
disdaining the toil of guarding a hole with its mouth;
the jíguāng hungers and thirsts on fields of ice and frost,
too proud to covet the well-salted flesh of sacrificial animals;
Gūzhú would not trade abstinence from grain for the riches of Lùtái,
Zǐ Lián would not exchange destitution for the abundance of the Copper Mountain.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When will is united, mountains and seas are not distant;
when the way departs, even inches are not near.
Thus some traverse and gather through hardships,
while others may dwell close yet never meet.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The splendid robes shine bright,
yet this is not the work of one sole dye;
the heights of Sōng and Dài
are not the result of one basketful of earth.
Thus when the nine sons accept their duty, prosperity flourishes;
when the forty-seven assume their charge, their accomplishments become manifest.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The emerald jiū has no wings, yet soars in the heavens;
the téngshé has no feet, yet dashes as lightning;
the turtle has no ears, yet well perceives with its head;
the earthworm has no mouth, yet raises its voice.
Thus, Gāo Yáo was mute yet matched the eloquent in achievement;
Jìn Yě, though blind, equaled Lí Zhū in sight.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Among those with high position, talent does not always match the office;
among those of fine praise, substance does not always fit the name.
Thus, saw-like teeth cannot chew;
a shovel-like tongue cannot discern flavors;
the ear of a jar cannot harmonize notes;
the nose of a shoe cannot distinguish scents;
the eye of a cauldron cannot gaze at the radiance of Wàngshū;
the leg of a bed cannot go on an ordinary journey.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A traveler cannot draw a strong bow and, in the moment, recognize the archery of Yǎng Yóu;
Yánzǐ could not control rein and whip and thus judge Dōngyě's defeat.
Thus, there are those who cannot play chess, yet by watching know win or loss;
there are those who cannot tune the strings, yet by listening comprehend Zhèng and Yǎ.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
That which shades ten thousand acres
must come from the ultimate heights;
waters that overflow the sky and surge over hills
must issue from the source of Bǎntóng.
Achievements that surpass an age
must rely on peerless persons;
stratagems that stabilize calamity
must come from hearts above the common.
So in a scorched moth's nest,
there are no wings to ride the wind;
in the midst of ditches and channels,
there are no precious stones that shine by night.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A sudden whirlwind burns chariots,
yet this is how the primeval fire grows more fierce;
but fireflies and candles, meeting it, are snuffed out instead.
Sweet rain and generous dew,
meant to nurture life to flourish,
yet, to withered wood that receives it, brings swifter decay;
scarlet wheels and ornate hubs,
a great treasure to talented men,
yet when controlled by thieves, bring about disaster;
abundant meals by the cauldron,
a reward for meritorious service,
but when given to the unworthy, lead only to gluttony and want.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The hide of an ox is made into armor,
serving for special troops' gear;
the kingfisher's green is cut for ornament,
to adorn noblewomen's heads;
though these started from the deep valley
and are now lifted to tall trees,
yet for such things,
it would be better to dwell in forest thickets
and keep life safe among the brambles.
Thus, the spirit turtle would rather trail its tail in the mud
than vie for the riches of the coffer;
the marsh pheasant is content pecking every ten steps,
to avoid the calamity of the chicken and duck.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Partial skill is not enough for all uses;
being long in one thing cannot remedy the many shortnesses.
Thus, the rooster knows the approach of dawn,
but cannot fathom the cycles of yīn and yáng;
the swan knows midnight,
but cannot fully know the movement of the sun;
the wood pigeon knows the coming weather,
but cannot understand the astronomical patterns;
how could creeping creatures know the location of hidden springs
or penetrate the earth’s topography?
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When prohibitions and commands are unclear,
stringent punishments are used to quell disorder;
when council deliberations are imprecise,
exhausting wars are waged to invade neighbors.
It is like sharpening a sickle to kill locusts,
felling trees to kill wood-borers,
eating poison to get rid of fleas and lice,
or demolishing houses to chase away sparrows and mice.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A sharp blade issues from blunt stone;
a bright fire from dark wood;
a precious pearl comes from a lowly oyster;
fine jade is found in ugly rock.
Therefore, one should not limit Chóng Huá by his parents,
nor measure Wèi Huò by his ancestors.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When one’s ambition is satisfied, the face is pleased;
when the mind is frustrated, the countenance is distressed.
If the root is rotten, the tip will wither;
if the source is shallow, the flow will be short.
When something exists inside, it must show outwardly;
what arises nearby will surely become manifest far away.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Lovely form and charming looks
may differ in appearance,
yet their delight is matched;
silk, bamboo, metal, stones,
with five tones and strange harmonies,
yet equally please the ear;
entwined nets, flying hooks,
lift nets, snares set low,
though their methods differ, the catch is the same;
erecting merit or composing writing,
though by different paths,
what is prized is unity.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Where gain is high, harm is deep;
where quality is fine, disaster is drawn.
Thus, southern birds are killed for their splendid feathers,
leopards in dens die for their patterned pelts,
sturgeon and carp collect and dark pools dry up,
deer gather and the lush forest is burned,
when gold and jade pile up, robbers come,
with fame and rank high, anxiety and blame increase.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When the commerce wind chills the night, the summer fan is cast aside;
when climbing dangerous heights, the light boat is abandoned;
when weapons are raised and turmoil abounds, the literati and scholars withdraw;
and when disorder subsides, then the warriors are dismissed.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
What is worth ten thousand pieces of gold
can be discerned in preference without seeing the object;
where branches twist and embrace,
you need not measure the tree to know its size.
So, when viewing great waves surging to the sky,
one knows they do not rise from a puddle of scum;
observing lush grass in wild profusion,
one knows it is not reared by pedants of clauses and phrases.
Bào Pǔzi said:
The cinnabar blossom and green grass
are not limited to the withered and bent trees;
the purple zhī, fragrant and fine,
is not confined to the barrenness of alkali soil.
Therefore, those who receive the mysterious jade tablet and proclaim accomplishment
are born at the gate of the four transgressions;
those who inherit the cyclical order from Wénzǔ
emerge from households of stubborn arrogance.
Bào Pǔzi said:
If one speaks well of dwelling,
then no distance is unresponsive;
if one bends what is straight and misses the mark,
then even the near will part.
Thus, in Sòng fields there were astray noblemen in retreat;
in the Yīn court, there were close associates fleeing abroad.
Four walls surround from beyond Shàoguǎng;
within the inner partitions, stags and horses change places.
Bào Pǔzi said:
Jīng Qīng and Zhū Hài
did not display courage among the timid and weak;
Mèng Bēn and Féng Fù
did not brandish spear and halberd among the rude and vulgar bands.
Heroic scholars and eminent men
do not embellish subtle arguments among the shallow and familiar;
broad-minded and great men
do not alter their daily interactions to scrutinize the common crowd.
Bào Pǔzi said:
Circling to pay respects and yielding
are not the deportment for resisting enemies;
donning armor and helmets
is not the ornament for the hall of state.
Dangling tassels and swaying pendants
are not suitable for wielding blades in competition;
walking by compass and square
is not fit to rescue from fire and drowning.
Bào Pǔzi said:
Heaven and earth nurture all things,
yet the many creatures do not recognize their grace,
because their benefit has no bounds;
the transformation of great men is divine,
yet the many commoners are unaware of what is bestowed,
because governance occurs before there is awareness.
Thus, what can be known is small,
what can be easily assessed is few.
Bào Pǔzi said:
É Yīng and Rèn Sì
are not foremost praised for weaving silk;
Tāng, Wǔ, and Hàn Gāo
do not court near praise for minor deeds.
Therefore, those whose gaze is fixed on the three luminaries
do not linger to reflect upon wells and valleys;
those who attune their ears to the music of Sháo and Huò
hardly have leisure to strain listening to tunes at the mulberry grove.
Bào Pǔzi said:
The surface of the skin is not always basis for arguing the inner;
outward appearance may not verify ability.
Zhòng Ní seemed like a homeless dog;
Gōng Dàn resembled coarse, unhewn timber;
Jiù Yáo’s face was like daubed color;
Yī Yǐn’s form was like withered bones;
as for Lóngyáng and Sòng Cháo,
they were like clay figurines crowned with glowing gems;
Jiè Rú, Dǒng, and Dèng
were like brocade and silk wrapped in dust and ashes.
Bào Pǔzi said:
Distinguished accomplishments cannot transform the deeply ignorant,
thus teaching takes no effect among the sons and younger brothers;
Xīn and Guǐ could not sway the supremely wise,
so vice does not taint the three virtuous men.
Bào Pǔzi said:
The utmost greatness cannot change everything,
and the utmost fineness cannot be taken away in all respects.
Therefore, frost and ice that chill and kill
cannot wither the flourishing of beans and wheat;
the burning heat and stifling shade
cannot melt the chill of snowy mountains;
storm winds sweeping the sea
cannot raise waves from hidden springs;
spring’s moisture fostering things
cannot make withered grasses bloom.
Bào Pǔzi said:
The treasure that weeps blood,
looks up to stones as mirrors to display its brilliance;
Shěn Lǘ and Mèng Láo
require the grindstone of Chǔ to gather their edge;
fine steeds daily await ownership by Wang Sun to travel far,
excellent material must await the shaping clamp to accomplish virtue.
Bào Pǔzi said:
When the luán and jí yuè birds roost,
though hungry and thirsty, they do not wish to be cooped in the cook’s cage;
riding the yellow heavenly deer,
though hidden and hungry, they do not enjoy the grass and fodder in the Zhuó Lóng stables.
Therefore the old man gathering cicadas
forgets all things in the fragrant forest;
the angler lets down his line,
suddenly taking the jade tablet at Southern Chǔ.
Bào Pǔzi said:
Square and round, forms at odds,
movement or repose, different in outcome.
Thus, the chaotic sphere is honored for persistent movement,
the Empress of Kūn is esteemed for tranquil steadfastness.
The seven directors and four seasons
range everywhere to accomplish merit;
the Five Mountains and Six Pillars
stand still to serve as supports.
Thus, Mò of Sòng and Shēn of Chǔ
set forth in chariots to preserve their states;
the hollow wood and Hú Míng
used non-action to mediate conflict.
Bào Pǔzi said:
Those who find meaning in fields and gardens,
though the body is deprived, their spirit is at ease;
those who put themselves in service for the relief of others,
their body may be at leisure, but their mind is wearied.
Thus, those who carry jars to water the garden
are happy compared to terrace dignitaries;
those who eat distasteful food and chew wild herbs
find goodness compared to feasting at tripods;
those wielding staff and leaving Bīn
are as the moon dwelling during the winter festival;
those who watch through the night for dawn
let toil and worry damage their lives.
Bào Pǔzi said:
The divide between benevolence and cruelty is as deep as heaven’s abyss;
the difference between goodness and unworthiness is as if between being and non-being.
The zōu yú treads lightly to walk on emptiness,
jackals and wolves pack together to work harm.
Lord Yú cast aside the seal of office to rescue the destitute;
Lord Huá yielded three offices to promote the worthy.
Lǐ Sī envied the talented and killed Hán Fēi;
Páng Juān chafed at inferiority and punished Sūn Bìn.
Bào Pǔzi said:
Only when one employs strengths
does no talent go to waste;
but if one only probes for faults,
nothing goes right in any matter.
Thus, light gauze and misty silk
are the finery of attire,
but cannot guard against flying darts;
the giant sword of Shěn Lǘ
is an excellent cutter,
but not suitable for picking out splinters.
Bào Pǔzi said:
Small imperfections cannot harm great vessels;
a minor fire or transient illness cannot hinder great talent.
The sun and moon bear specks and motes,
yet are not marred in their brilliance in the sky;
the Huáng Hé bears muddiness and filth,
but does not spoil its surging over mountains.
Obstacles in the woods are no reason to neglect Yí Wú;
confiscated land is no reason to slight Xiāo Hé;
the theft of a wife is no reason to abandon Xiàng Rú;
accepting gold is no reason to exclude Chén Píng.
Bào Pǔzi said:
Tigers and leopards cannot strike and bite in the roaring waves;
the flying snake cannot ascend on fogless days;
pursuing pheasants and rabbits, even phoenixes cannot match hawks and goshawks;
harnessed to a plow, even dragons and qilin cannot match a pair of oxen yoked together.
Thus, martial men and warriors
are useless in times of peace;
eminent scholars and extraordinary talents
are not valued in eras of competition by strength.
Bào Pǔzi said:
With both feet tied and a rope on their neck,
even qí lù horses are like crippled donkeys;
losing the forest and dwelling in a cage,
monkeys and wildcats become equal;
hiding swords without striking,
the Dragon Spring blade equals a lead knife;
when talents far exceed their duties,
the outstanding and the mediocre king come to the same.
If one seeks traces of a thousand li in a fettered steed,
or expects the deeds of master craftsmen from shattered materials,
and claims this is not delusion,
I do not believe it.
Bào Pǔzi said:
He who rejects tea and eats wormwood
certainly never knew the taste of sweetness;
he who casts aside jade and picks up stones
surely lacks the discernment for precious things.
Those who disparage Jiǔchéng and delight in northern rusticity,
I know they cannot summon divinities or present the flying phoenix;
those who discard the gifted and rely on ordinary people,
I know they cannot set the right order and reach great harmony.
Bào Pǔzi said:
Those who thoroughly understand the ultimate principle of access and obstruction
do not grieve in hardship;
those who grasp the destiny inherent in nature
do not lose themselves in pleasure along the Way.
Thus, confined in deep pools,
they abandon feelings of grievance and resentment;
shining in the emperor’s gates and halls,
they show no air of satisfaction.
To serve thrice and resign thrice,
such is the man.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Adversity and prosperity are bound to fate,
poverty and success are insufficient to judge a scholar;
gain and loss depend on circumstance,
striving or disgrace cannot be measured as talent.
The times and destiny cannot be attained by force,
encounters cannot be evade by cleverness.
Thus, Shangfù [Jiang Tàigōng]
was but an old woman's abandoned husband;
Hán Xìn
was a starving beggar child;
Xiāo Gōng [Xiāo Hé]
was a petty official clinging to the bushel measure;
Qíng Bù
was a condemned and exiled convict.
When they revealed the bearing of dragons among lizards and geckos,
when they folded the wings of phoenixes among flocks of little birds,
then those who were later called dragons
were thought merely kin to their kind.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The four auspicious beasts hide away,
thus becoming the signs of great peace;
the reclusive man esteems withdrawal,
thus becoming a treasure to a kingdom.
Why must one oversee the morning and bite the bit,
to be fettered by anxiety and responsibility?
What is useful for others is their use,
what is useless for me is my use;
one who preserves himself does not let reputation disturb his harmony,
one who cultivates life does not let things burden himself.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
He who assigns duties by measuring talent
does not demand achievements beyond the capacity of the vessel;
he who accepts responsibilities by assessing ability
does not resent being held accountable when his strength is exhausted.
Thus, to extinguish a lamp one need not trouble the vast sea,
to lift a weight of a few jin one need not employ Wū Huò.
Hauling firewood or transporting salt
should not tire the legs of a thoroughbred;
petty errands and trifling posts
are not worth bending the outstanding loner to serve.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A stream or brook,
cannot carry a great vessel;
a small measuring cup
cannot contain a thousand bushels.
A glowworm cannot match the faint light of the stars,
ordinary talent cannot distinguish the extraordinary instrument.
Thus, what creation has endowed
intelligence has its root and source.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The people of Yǐng admired the wanton croaking frogs below,
and slighted the harmonious music of the six pipes;
vulgar men delight in flowery praise that pleases the ear,
and loathe the good guidance that improves conduct.
Therefore, Sòng Yù abandoned his refined and spiritual talents,
while the wise man promoted his far-ranging and unique strategies.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Even mountains of precious jade,
cannot be without some flawed vessel;
even forests stretching a thousand li,
cannot be without some withered tree.
When discussing treasures, great beauty should not be abandoned for minor blemishes;
when speaking of the great, slight faults should not discredit vast merit.
He who betrayed his lord
was Liáng Píng,
yet he gave six marvelous strategies to secure his ruler;
the bandit chief Péng Yuè,
accomplished meritorious feats in establishing the dynasty.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The Five Sacred Peaks are lofty,
yet hiding flaws does not diminish their towering reach to the sky;
the seas are vast and boundless,
yet harboring impurities does not burden their limitless expanse.
Therefore, those with the nine virtues value magnanimity to win the masses,
Confucius fostered broad love to promote advancement.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Establishing virtue and keeping one’s word,
conducting oneself with unblemished integrity,
this is true wealth;
why must one pursue the honor of jade and silk?
Uplifting one’s aspirations,
neither lowering nor disgracing oneself,
this is true nobility;
why must one pursue the purple and blue robes of office?
The commonfolk cannot comprehend such measure,
the ordinary man cannot guess such scales and balances,
this is true height;
why must one soar to the clouds and tread upon the rainbow?
Those who question cannot fathom its deep current,
those who seek have not discerned its shortage,
this is true depth;
why must one plunge into river and sea?
If throughout the four seas there is sufficiency,
then even if a house has only a hanging chime of poverty,
there is no need to envy casting mountains or boiling seas.
Dwelling among birds and beasts,
one need not thirst for vermillion wheels and ornate hubs.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A hidden spirit awaits auspicious clouds to soar aloft,
a nesting swan relies on a strong wind to traverse the void,
the white-scaled fish must have Lady Jī’s reed to leap,
the white pheasant must await Dù Gōngdàn to arrive,
Jiang Lǎo met Xī Bó and cast his line at Shífān creek,
Hán Yīng met Emperor Gāo of Hàn to display his talent for quelling disorder.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
He who clarifies his spirit with the dark Unity
can forget his physical form;
he who elevates his virtue beyond external things
can leave wealth and rank behind.
Thus the crippled one—
marveled at creation, smiling with content;
the old straw-collector of the north
dwelt on Mount Sōngshān and found fulfillment there.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Rough reasoning cannot be entirely thorough,
one skilled in affairs cannot master them all.
Thus, the suspended stars shine yet may be covered,
mountains and rivers are impeded but may be moved,
gold and jade are hard yet may be softened,
solid ice is dense yet may be sundered.
Dù Gōngdàn could not tie himself to Bozhī, clinging to the precarious heights,
Confucius could not compete in acrobatics with those at the sheer cliffs of Lǚliáng.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Thunder cannot refine its sound
to match the concord of bells and stones;
the sun and moon cannot keep their radiance to themselves
to transform the favor of their partial light;
a great river cannot shorten its banks
to suit the wish of crossing swiftly;
the Five Sacred Peaks cannot lessen their steepness
to please those who would climb them.
Thus, a broad chariot cannot squeeze its track to pass easily on a narrow path,
a noble man cannot diminish his virtue to join the dust of base society.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Yin and Yang broaden creation and support all things,
the Three Luminaries universally illuminate what is clear and bright,
Sōng and Huá Mountains are vast because they conceal flaws,
the North Sea is called great because it holds much impurity,
great Confucians propagate the Way through promotion,
the man of distant calculation embraces many to include the multitude.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The shell of the spirit turtle
need not necessarily be used for battle;
the horn of the unicorn, talon of the phoenix
need not necessarily be prepared for combat.
Thus, the gifted do not lay aside their swords in times of peace,
nor do watchmen cease to prepare in times of apparent safety.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Southern gold is not debased by dwelling in obscurity,
beautiful jade is not sullied by residing in depth.
He who aspires to the Way does not change his purpose because of adversity and blockage,
he who upholds correctness does not compromise for lack of reward.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
One who has ascended the Xuánpǔ [Paradise Garden],
realizes the lowliness of humble hills;
one who has floated upon the Mínghǎi [Boundless Sea],
recognizes the narrowness of pools and ponds.
Only after examining the Nine Canons does one realize the restrictions of a mere wall,
only after hearing the Supreme Way does one understand the many confusions of attachment to custom.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The origin of chaos
has no clear and lucid flow;
the root of the finest hair
has no branching limbs;
the remnant of a tiny measure
retains no lasting heat;
within a crevice
there is no shining assemblage;
the bent and hooked have
no shadow of straightness;
upon what is irregular
there is no ordered arrangement.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Without seeing the brilliance of fine jade,
one does not realize how base pebbles are;
without viewing the elegance of tigers and leopards,
one does not know the coarseness of dogs and sheep.
Only after hearing the "White Snow" ninefold melody
does one understand the vulgarity of Bā men’s songs;
only after knowing the vastness of refined scholars
does one lament the ignorance of the unlearned.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A cracked jade cup,
is not as good as a whole vessel made of clay;
a fragment of fine-dyed silk,
does not compare to sturdy and whole leather-cloth.
Thus the lack of propriety in Lady Xiàjī,
is not as good as the purity of the outcast;
the many crimes of the rich and noble
are not as good as the path-following of the poor and lowly.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A fierce beast does not strike beyond its measure,
a hawk does not recklessly strike with its wings.
If in planning one does not weigh virtue within,
nor strength without,
it is like light feathers thrown in a great furnace,
or snowflakes cast in boiling cauldrons,
a morning fungus trying the sword of Gànjiāng,
a lamb or calf challenging the fierce tiger indeed.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When the Three Celestial Bodies are obscured in the heavens,
then the clear light is darkened on earth;
when roots and grasses overturn here,
then the branches and twigs wither there;
when the Dào is lost nearby,
then disaster befalls afar;
when government is in error above,
then the people suffer below.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those who are intent on distant matters may lose what is near;
those who govern the exterior may find trouble arises within.
One who covers his head will not necessarily keep his feet from getting wet,
nor will one who shields his belly necessarily prevent his back from being harmed.
Thus, when Qín first built walls to block the Hú, misfortune arose in the tent itself;
when Hàn Wǔ raised his banners ten thousand li away, the crisis began within his own court.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The worth of talent is not fixed,
nor is the use of tools unchanging;
those who pursue uprightness are praised for their fitness to the age,
those who are adaptive are esteemed for conforming to the times.
Thus, when black ice forms, the five bright gems are set aside,
when the great heat rages, fur coats and braziers are withdrawn;
when high-flying birds gather, then fine bows are drawn,
when cunning hares are many, then the lǔquè flees;
when weapons rise, warriors show their strength,
when the music of Sháo and Xià plays, scholars and gentlemen arise.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those who stir rapid currents towards the court’s flow
cannot neglect Wǔchéng and leap over Jīshí;
those who unfurl emerald leaves and flower with crimson blossoms
cannot discard the robust roots and abandon the spreading branches.
When the fount is ruined and roots lost,
it seldom escapes withering and dying;
when sages are betrayed and the canon abandoned,
order cannot be widely established.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The Four Rivers are distinct in their sources,
the Five Streams branch in their flow,
all tend downward to the sea,
by different paths reaching the same destination.
Colors are uneven yet all are splendid,
sounds differ yet all can be sorrowful,
fragrances are not one but all are sweet,
flavors are not equal yet all can be delicious.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Things are valued for fulfilling needs, yet their embellishments are pursued;
customs are transformed by virtue, yet speech strays from the source.
Thus, coarse cloth suffices to ward off cold,
one need not wear sable or fox;
pure simplicity can create things,
it does not lie in ornate disputation.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When the wind is emptied and the air calmed, the drifting tumbleweed stands firm as a mountain;
when the warp has been smoothed, all the threads are orderly.
Thus there has never been a case where the ruler delights in humility above and the people are arrogant below,
nor does the lord disdain treasure while customs are penurious.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Events may become manifest from faint causes,
and things may be well ordered nearby to reach distant results.
Thus, polishing the fishpond in the garden
attracts deep-sea fish from rivers and oceans;
enriching the forest in Cháoyáng
draws spiritual birds from crimson caves;
designing patterns on plates and bowls
brings jade dragons down from the dark heavens;
pouring ashes into a foot of water
causes Wàngshū to shift within the Supreme Ultimate.
So, when Jìn Wén turned his chariot for the valiant bugs,
his brave men went forth like clouds;
when Gōu Jiàn humbled himself before croaking frogs,
his troops faced death lightly.
As the nines are revealed, the swift heroes gather at the ding’s corner;
when dry bones are covered, the virtue of the threefold benevolence flourishes.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
In fertile soil reside grasses,
and in withered leaves lies hidden glory;
guiding customs by personal example,
then change occurs wordlessly.
Thus, Yǒu Táng used a deer’s robe to bring great peace;
Qí Huán curtailed extravagance by discarding purple vestments.
When the Zhānghuá palace was completed, the excess of rich dwellings became apparent,
but when the Lùtái was stopped, the influence of silent restraint prevailed.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The discerning
can perceive rise and fall from the fading echoes of ancient music;
the wise
can discern patterns from subtle signs before form emerges.
Thus, a man of Yuè saw in Qí Huán’s unsteady movement the harbinger of an illness not yet revealed;
Jīzǐ recognized the calamity of the Yin people’s Deer Terrace upon seeing ivory chopsticks appear.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The Two Principles cannot abolish spring and autumn and still produce a year;
an enlightened lord cannot abandon punishment or virtue and yet achieve good governance.
Thus, punishing the noble is the way to establish authority,
rewarding the humble is the way to encourage goodness.
If penalties reach those above,
then treachery is rooted out and cannot be used by the timid and weak;
if favors extend to those below,
then distant peoples are won over, something misers cannot achieve.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those who voyage the distant seas
must excel in discerning wind and weather,
thus ensuring safe passage and profit.
Those skilled in government
are always cautious with gains and losses,
thus enjoying enduring happiness.
What a foolish lord belittles
is exactly what a wise ruler values.
What a lost state discards
is what a well-ordered age adopts.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If the smallest error is made at a strategic moment,
it becomes great in the end;
if gains and losses are misjudged here,
then good and bad are confused there.
If right and wrong are jumbled together,
then the human order falls into disarray;
if merit and fault are not distinguished,
then productive works collapse.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler’s rewards are like spring rains, without excessive abundance,
and his punishments are as autumn frost, without out-of-season severity.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
One who keenly judges worth
will not lightly be deceived as to importance;
one who relies on law and regulation
cannot grant favors based on private feelings.
Thus, those who obtain others
are first those who have achieved it in themselves,
those who lose others
are first those who have lost themselves.
Never has one obtained oneself yet lost others,
nor lost oneself and still obtained others.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
An enlightened lord personally wields authority and grace,
not delegating the instruments of advantage;
a benighted ruler inverts sword and shield,
though honored in name, his power departs.
Thus, those who controlled rewards to win the masses—
this was how Tián Cháng usurped Qí;
those who monopolized power and fortune and commanded the court—
this was how Wáng Mǎng usurped Hàn.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Regular methods cannot cope with changes,
one path cannot respond to myriad needs,
carving marks on a boat cannot recover a lost sword,
gluing strings cannot harmonize pure melodies.
So, the emerald canopy is not raised on a clear day,
nor are red wheels used for crossing rivers;
if the taste is bland, add salt,
if the pot boils over, add water and reduce the fire.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Scarlet documents and iron contracts,
sacrificial animals and blood oaths,
cannot correct breaches of agreement,
so how could mere knotted cords suffice?
The five punishments, nine campaigns,
and whole-clan executions
are not enough to stop treacherous designs;
thus one cannot use only the qian transformation.
Therefore, the Shū has counsel for the importance of successive generations,
and the Yì embodies accommodation to circumstance.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those with insight to discern truth
cannot be deceived with falsehood;
those with deep wisdom
cannot be misled with the trivial.
Otherwise,
one would take a poisonous snake for the divine dragon,
a fox-owl for the qilin or phoenix.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
There are widespread praises that do not indicate true worth;
there are noisy denunciations that do not reveal true evil.
Thus, those who win favor by greeting and agreement
are inferior to those who discern works and test utility;
those who oppose and reject
are less than those who listen to words and examine achievement.
Then flatterers will not advance by empty talk,
nor will the capable be hindered by weakness or solitude;
the slow and lame will stop hoping for the great chariot,
while fine horses speed forward, their bells ringing like thunder.
Then why should achievements remain so great as to be unreachable,
and the Dào so remote it cannot be attained?
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Decayed wood with hollows
cannot resist a mountain-toppling wind;
a fissured cliff
cannot withstand surging waves that reach the sky.
Thus, the seven-hundred-year reign,
and thirty generations,
are not solely due to the achievement at Mùyè;
defeat by inverted spear,
disaster at the Deer Terrace,
did not begin with the first day of the sexagenary cycle.
Their strength lasted long,
and their downfall was fated earlier.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
To value what is distant and despise what is near
is the common way of people's feelings;
to trust the ears yet doubt the eyes
is an affliction of both ancient and modern times.
Thus, King Qín sighed over Hán Fēi's writings, imagining what manner of person he was;
Emperor Hàn Wǔ was stirred by the prose of Sīmǎng Xiāngrú, adopting sentiments not of his own age;
but when they finally obtained these men,
in the end they could not employ them fully.
Some believed slander and executed them;
some dismissed them into idleness and obscurity—
this is like Lord Yè’s fondness for counterfeit forms,
and losing his composure when seeing a real dragon.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If a luminous jewel does not shine at night,
then it is no different from gravel;
if the transformed Kūn is unable to soar to the skies,
then it is no different from a peach grub.
If the silken colt swallows its voice,
it becomes as one with the mute;
if outstanding talent is suppressed and stifled,
it is grouped with the mediocre.
Thus, loaches and eels profane the brilliant red dragon in the muddy depths;
dull and slow horses defile the fleet with whom they roam the open fields,
unable to discern that in stillness they seem alike,
but in movement they differ.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If gold and jade are cast by the roadside,
passersby will stop in awe;
if fine silks are thrown into the mire,
