those who see are startled and dismayed.
As for casting a person of transcendent character among the vulgar and commonplace,
discarding a vessel of statecraft in a constricted place of hardship,
while those who converse do not lament their frustration,
and the capable do not rescue them from distress,
some cherish their writings while neglecting their persons,
some use their strategies but forget their achievements.
This is a longstanding malady,
so it has always been.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If a spring does not reach to great depths,
it cannot create a river like Huái Shān;
if mountains do not soar to the sky,
there can be no clouds spanning heaven.
If wealth is not abundant,
its generosity cannot be widespread;
if talent is not far-reaching,
its words cannot be comprehensive.
Thus, on seeing tusks a yard long,
one knows they do not come from a mouth no wider than an inch;
on seeing branches a hundred fathoms high,
one knows they do not grow from the twig of a hair’s breadth.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The spirit phoenix rises from the cinnabar cave at dawn,
and gathers at Xuānqiū by dusk;
before midday’s shadow shifts,
it sweeps through the nine tiers of heaven,
rides the wind and treads the clouds,
without obstructions or hindrances—
all by the light and strength of its six pinions.
So for great talent and capacity,
these too are the six wings of a state.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Without a string, the flute of Qí Wèi would forget to return,
unable to sound resonantly afar;
the music of dust is raised,
unable to arouse sorrow without instruments.
Virtue that transcends and surpasses the world
cannot establish merit before the time is ripe.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Brilliant red and green algae
do not flourish on withered branches;
a mighty flow off the mountain
does not arise from a dried-up spring.
A fleeting flame in the night,
cannot show all forms of ten thousand things;
a will exhausted by pursuit of profit and power,
cannot make a fragrant wind that lingers through the ages.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A deep abyss, if not boring through to the earth,
cannot contain a dragon
who swallows a boat whole;
a lofty mountain, unless reaching to the heavens,
cannot conceal precious gems
nor spread clouds and rain;
establishing virtue without transcending the vulgar
cannot gain a fair reputation
nor manifest solid substance;
holding to aspiration but never leaving the crowd
cannot gain accomplishment
nor inscribe great achievement.
And so, ordinary people expect the benefit of cicada wings come morning,
and wish for the rewards of hills and mounds by evening;
it is like planting millet and grain
and waiting idly for a rich harvest.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
One whose conduct lacks highest distinction,
yet seeks the praise reserved for the extraordinary;
whose character lacks the root of principle and artistry,
yet busies himself with cliques and factionalism.
Wanting thereby to obtain purity and honor in the present age,
and spread virtue into the future,
is like lifting your robe to cross the open sea,
or standing on tiptoe to leap up to the ninefold sky.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A dragon made of clay, however brilliantly painted,
cannot respond to the summons of auspicious clouds;
a fashioned bird, however finely carved,
cannot ride the wind in flight;
a straw dog, though adorned with gold and emerald,
cannot chase shadows and vanish in a bound;
talent near at hand, though heaped with honors and riches,
cannot make heaven clear, nor lay earth smooth.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When poison is laid out,
there will be mice gnawed to the bone nearby;
when a bright fire burns in the night,
there are insects gathering dead at its base.
When livestock is plentiful,
the cauldrons await it;
a small talent tasked with great responsibility
will surely weep tears of blood.
The warnings of Sāng Huò are weighty,
and the discernment of Fàn Shū is clear.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The blue sea raises waves for ten thousand li,
yet cannot gather the dust atop a mountain peak;
a violent wind fells trees a thousand fathoms high,
yet cannot uproot a weak grass blade.
Marshal Zhì, brave as a tiger, and Wǔ Hǔ and Hǔ Kàn,
cannot intimidate mosquitoes or biting flies;
talent that crowns an age
cannot win over common custom.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
One of firm resolve
is master of achievement and reputation;
one who is not slothful
is teacher of all virtues.
If one climbs a mountain undeterred by hardship,
he will surely reach the summit;
if one gathers good without resenting adversity,
his noble fame will endure forever.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Although the hoarse magpie cannot live long,
needle and stone cannot be denied as instruments that save life;
although scholars are often poor and base,
books and classics cannot be denied as means for advancing virtue.
Though some sow without reaping,
farming and planting must not be abandoned;
though benevolence and righteousness may encounter calamity,
action and undertaking must not cease.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If what is carried is heavy and does not stop,
it will surely sink my boat;
to pursue without knowing when to retreat,
is to bring peril upon oneself.
If scorpions gather and attack the root,
though for a while there is safety and repose,
it surely portends disaster.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Dark clouds rise as dragons,
not by the call of newts or insects;
a mighty wind raises tigers,
not brought forth by foxes or weasels.
Thus, when the great receive their mandate,
those of surpassing worth congregate;
when jade and silk are sought in seclusion,
talents arise from fields and gardens.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Gold by its hardness may be broken,
water by its softness remains whole;
mountain by its loftiness is steep,
valley by its lowliness is at peace.
Thus, one who holds to the yielding avoids the calamity of striving for dominance,
while one who exalts others invites resentment.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Huái Yīn hid his courage in humiliation beneath another’s legs,
yet it did not harm his dragon’s leap nor tiger’s glare;
Lord Yìng concealed his brilliance when carrying mud-baskets,
yet it hindered not his soaring like a luán nor rising as a phoenix.
Some then sat facing south and called themselves sovereign,
some ruled over the highest altars of state.
Thus, those who rise and fall by turns
are like light swans soaring in emptiness;
those who bend and stretch by shifts
are talents awaiting their proper time.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The low-perched jiāo míng prefers not the shrill cry of the mouse to the sky;
the pure, hunger-enduring xuán chán would not desire the filthy satiety of the dung beetle.
Thus, Yù Kòu would not accept the gifts of Zhèng Yáng,
nor would Céng Sān value the treasures of Jìn and Chǔ.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A slight breeze cannot raise waves on the great sea;
a tiny hair cannot move a bell weighing ten thousand jun.
Thus, the thoughts of Huì from Qīyuán
gave rise to the sigh of discarding the axe;
the lament of Bóshì in mourning
produced the indignation of cutting the string.
A short song cannot bring about a grand and splendid harmony,
nor can force and power shift a mind that is aloof and indifferent.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Bears and tigers do not compete in speed with foxes,
nor do golden eagles rival small hawks in striking prey.
Thus, Zhāng Ěr’s fame for strength was eclipsed by guarding the gate,
and Zhū Hài’s valor was hidden while wielding the butcher’s knife.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A hanging fish is beguiled by fragrant bait,
and the caged tiger perishes because of the fox in the trap.
That which cannot be caught with a fishing line
must be a dragon or a horned serpent;
that which cannot be lured by trap or pitfall
must be a qilin or a phoenix.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those who soar through the clouds
are unaware of the filth of those who dwell in the mud;
those in high positions
seldom show compassion for the labors of the masses.
Yet a root that has rotted
cannot preserve the flourishing of its tree for a thousand days;
when the people are resentful,
even Yáo and Shùn cannot rely on the fortune of a lasting reign.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Any tree that takes root on a sacred mountain
will have the artisan and stonecutter rest his axe and chisel;
small fish living in the dragon pond
cause the fisherman to cease using his nets and traps.
If a mosquito gathers on an eagle's head,
then herons and cranes do not dare peck;
if a mouse dwells beside a tiger,
then wildcats and dogs do not dare glare askance.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Ling Cài remains silent,
and yet fortune and misfortune are made clear without form;
the spring frogs are noisy and loud,
and their ugly croaking afflicts the ear.
Therefore, sounds that are rare must echo greatly,
and words that are few must be trusted and well-known.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those whose custom is to sit with knees spread
resent those who move gracefully in circles;
those who let their hair loose
abhor the adorning of ceremonial hats.
Thus, the loyal and upright are pushed aside in a world where slander prevails,
and men of refinement find no place in societies that disdain integrity.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Lifting water cannot quench the heat of burning grass in a marsh,
gathering dust cannot stem the boiling torrent at the Zhǐzhù;
a small blade cannot cut down the woods on a great islet,
and one person’s rectitude cannot halt the faults of partisan cliques.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A thousand sheep cannot withstand a lone tiger,
ten thousand sparrows cannot oppose a single eagle.
Even if torches are clustered in the courtyard,
they cannot match even the last rays of Xīhé’s sunlight;
even if a hundred drums strike together,
it does not compare to the lingering rumble of thunder.
Thus, if commoners fill the bright halls,
they still cannot ensure the order of proper relationships;
while a solitary man of outstanding talent
is sufficient to make the roots of all affairs enduring.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Success achieved out of place
is like flowers blooming among forest weeds in the winter;
the hardship of upholding the Way
is like bamboo and cypress enduring frost.
Thus, those who discern fortune and adversity through their own insight
will not lose integrity or change their course, even if threatened by blades and swords;
how would they ever fawn or flatter to conform with the vulgar?
Those upright in body and steadfast in nature
will not deviate from their sincerity to follow the times, even if enticed with a fiefdom or a kingdom;
how would they ever take shortcuts to win acceptance?
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Even a thunderclap and a raucous chariot
cannot be heard by deaf ears;
radiant light brightens the heavens,
yet its rays cannot reach into the shadowy depths;
thick ice can chill and wither,
but cannot wilt the blossoms of a coltsfoot;
a crimson wind can melt stone,
yet cannot topple the trees of Mount Xiāo.
Therefore, supreme virtue cannot be moved.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If a bow's span and a crossbow's trigger
are drawn and the sharp arrow is nocked—
truly fearsome—
yet a brave pheasant will strike without wariness;
in dark governance and a chaotic state,
where the corrupt hate the upright and envy ability—
extremely dangerous—
yet the greedy still contend and do not shy away.
Thus, when sudden disaster descends, they remain unaware,
when calamity befalls, they are caught unprepared.
Therefore, what pleases the foolish
is precisely what grieves the wise;
what all talents strive after
is precisely what the truly wise forsake.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If wind does not cease, fans are useless;
if the sun does not set, candles do not shine;
if flowers do not fall, fruits do not form;
if the banks do not erode, the valleys do not fill.
When the Nine Provinces are pacified,
the achievements of Hán Xìn and Bái Qī are not recognized;
when wise rulers continue unbroken,
the merits of Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng cannot be made.
Therefore, only in times of illness and hardship is the great physician valued,
and only in chaos are the loyal and steadfast esteemed.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those who desire glory delight in many words of praise;
those who fear humiliation are sensitive to words of blame.
But those who have comprehended the essence and spirit,
whose fates are joined with creation,
who merge fullness and emptiness along a single branch,
who regard gain and loss as even as the turning of a finger,
for them, love and hate never take root,
poverty and prosperity cannot disturb their harmony.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Those whose minds are unmoved by reward or loss
are the purest;
those whose harmony is unsullied by gain or harm
are the most refined.
So vast is this that it cannot be measured by gourd or goblet,
so far-reaching that it cannot be sought by half-steps.
Rare sound makes for the greatest music,
scarcity of accord elevates what I value most;
the profound and the distant neither mingle with nor diminish vastness.
Life and death are great indeed,
yet they do not alter one’s resolve;
how, then, could trivial changes cause any distress?
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When the forest is dense, the artisan enters;
when pearls are fine, worms gnaw at them.
The stone with gold within is melted by fire,
the herb with medicinal value is plucked and dug,
the sharp blade is first to break,
the mournful string is quickest to snap.
To use things in order to fulfill oneself
is the treasure of the *zhēn rén*;
to have talent sought by the world
brings the calamity of skill.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If an archery target is set up, arrows will surely fly toward it;
when a fine reputation rises, slander and attack will follow.
Rare treasures, though stored in abundance, attract resentment even without cause;
when one’s capacity is full and pride arises, calamity comes unbidden.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A treasure worth a city
cannot be bought by the poor and destitute;
a talent above the world
cannot be recognized by the shallow and vulgar.
Yet a precious thing of a foot in length
does not become obscure because no one knows it;
a man of surpassing virtue
does not become lax in principle because he is unappreciated.
Content with fate, serene in destiny—
what need for complaint or resentment?
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A great roc has no use for the crow of dawn;
a mighty elephant has no skill in chasing or running.
Thus, Jiǎng Wǎn failed in small tasks
yet became a model at the Three Terraces;
Chén Píng struggled in managing his household
yet possessed grand strategy among the Six Geniuses.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Clarity and obscurity
are a matter of talent,
natural and unfeigned;
success and failure
depend on fortune,
arising from circumstance and beyond one’s effort.
Lǚ Shàng was not slow in awakening nor late in wisdom,
yet only after long years did he encounter his time;
Hán Xìn was not timid at first nor brave at last,
yet only after suffering danger and hardship was he able to rise.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A racing steed cannot make up for a misstep already taken,
a thousand gold pieces cannot redeem a flawed remark.
Therefore, it is better to guard against small faults than to strive to correct great ones;
it is better to speak little than to laboriously pursue much.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The devotion of the ardent knight to his country is as to his own home,
his service to the ruler is as to his own kin,
thus matters of disloyalty
do not constitute his crime.
The benevolent man's regard for others is as for himself,
his treatment of outsiders is as close as that of intimates,
thus grudges of unkindness
are not held as his fault.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
If the black ice is not yet formed,
and the white snow does not accumulate,
then the luxuriance of the green pine will not stand out;
if common customs do not grow decadent,
and religious teaching does not collapse,
then integrity's purity is not distinguished.
Dwelling in a perilous state and remaining lowly,
thus Zhuāng Lái stands tall in renouncing honor;
abiding in a chaotic land and enduring hunger and cold,
thus Zēng Liè is lauded for forgetting riches.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Heaven dwells on high and regards that which is lowly,
thus though its net is wide, nothing escapes;
spirits are intelligent and upright,
thus their way rewards the genuine and punishes the false.
For when favor and harmony flourish in the Nine Regions,
then the Seven Luminaries shine in the dark vastness;
when ruin and harm are manifest among things,
then the Two Forces are thrown into disorder among the four and eight.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Heaven's rank possesses inexhaustible honor,
no human rank surpasses the virtue of worth.
Therefore, though Zhòngní was a mere commoner, he is worshipped through a hundred generations;
though Xīn Guǐ held the sway of emperors, even servants and pages refuse comparison;
the elder of Shāng grew ever more humble in station, yet his reputation ever more honored;
Yōu and Lì bore heavier positions, yet their crimes all the more notorious.
Thus the life of the King of Qí
does not compare to the tomb of Liǔ Huì;
the palace of the King of Qín
is not as good as the gate of Kāngchéng.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Reflections and echoes cannot appear without form and sound,
accumulated blessings cannot be attracted without virtue.
Thus only after the governance of Táng Yáo for over seventy years
did the luminous star manifest its splendor;
only after Lord Yáng accumulated conduct
and the aged did not tire,
did the golden rain descend.
For journeys far, arrival is surely late;
favors given late, their return is always delayed.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Where principle is fully exhausted, one cannot demand surplus;
where one has attained the limit, one cannot ask for all-encompassing salvation.
Thus at the end of great tides,
they cannot sweep away floating duckweed;
after a strong wind,
it cannot lift the lightest dust;
the remnant force of a sturdy crossbow
cannot pierce silken mist;
the setting sun in the west
cannot shine upon the eastern mountains.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Although the suspended orb is dimmed by eclipse,
it cannot compare to the steady brilliance of a firefly’s flame;
though the Yellow River is muddied and turbulent,
it cannot be likened to the clear pool and pond.
Even when mountains collapse,
they are still loftier than small mounds;
even when the tiger is emaciated,
it is fiercer than the jackal and wolf.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Had Shénnóng not suffered nine illnesses,
the Way of the Four Classics would not have been transmitted;
had Great Yǔ not worn calluses,
the blessings of the dark jade would not have gathered.
Thus long worry is the root of deep joy,
brief toil the beginning of lasting ease.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Though golden hooks and cassia bait are precious,
they cannot lure the hidden fish of the nine depths;
though honor and rich salary are noble,
they cannot draw the recluse of no desires.
Thus in Lǚliáng dwells the one who stands like a swan,
by the banks of the river are those who labor at cutting sandalwood.
Jade and silk pile up in the alley of Zǐlíng in vain,
imperial chariots return empty from the gate of Master Xú.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Tastes in sight and hearing differ,
love and hate cannot be the same.
Birds, seeing Xī Shī, are startled and fly away;
fish and turtles, hearing the Nine Sháo music, dive deep.
Thus the dazzling hue of yuǎn-zǎo
cannot please the eyes of the naked villages;
the clear sound of the biànlíng
cannot delight the ears of Chu slaves.
The benevolence of Gǔgōng
cannot convince the Dí of the land of desire;
the eloquence of Duānmù
cannot resolve the bonds of horse-tethering peasants.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The swirling dancer’s grace
meets scorn in the land of those who squat naked;
the carpenter master of lines and rules
is resented in shops of crooked wood.
The greedy and gluttonous
loathe the pure whiteness of raw silk;
the frequenters of company
resent the solitary integrity of those of high principle.
Like the merchant-boy’s aversion for shared profit,
and an ugly woman’s harm to a national beauty.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
When the gentleman rises in the world,
he elevates the worthy and shares his rewards;
when the common man attains his ambition,
he flaunts his status and neglects the worthy.
Beneficence is lavished on flatterers and favorites,
the use of wealth is reserved for petty favors.
Not sharing peace with the wise,
and yet hoping for rescuers in peril;
not sharing joy with exceptional men,
yet wishing for sympathy in distress;
like disaster-fire spreading beneath the heavens,
and only then pleading for rain at the sacred mountains;
or when the great flood overtops the horizon,
chopping up boats at the gates to the east;
is it not too late?
Someone said:
"Heaven and earth form square and circle,
not by compass and rule;
the three stars shine forth,
not by polishing and grinding;
spring blossoms splendidly,
not by gradual dyeing;
the fragrance of chāi and huì,
not by being lent their scent.
To know the utmost truth,
value lies in innate nature.
Rarity is valued in principle by its being seldom seen,
beauty in speech lies in its not being commonplace,
but upon surveying families of writers through the ages,
few can achieve spontaneous grace with their brush,
most draw from the words of others.
Why is this?"
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Pure sound is prized for harmonizing refined tones,
valued writing lies in its subtle discernment and analysis.
Thus, though the Eight Sounds have differing forms, the bells and pitch pipes are in accord;
though embroideries and ornaments differ in pattern, the five colors are in harmony.
Even in halting phrases there are rulers and guests,
in beauty and ugliness, order and sequence.
Thus, the conductor has no fixed melody,
the master chef no set flavor.
Though timber is heaped on Mount Yù,
without the master carpenter it cannot become a fine utensil;
though books are without number,
without talent none can gather their essence.
Must one always search for wood a thousand li away
to build a grand hall?
Must the words of spirits and divinities
always appear in literary works!"
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Talent has clarity and turbidness,
thought, its length and brevity;
though together they make literature,
they differ by ten thousand qualities;
some are vast yet not deep,
some are fact-focused but dull in phrasing,
some ignore truth but are skilled in style;
this is the result of lopsided strength in one direction,
not the talent of all-rounded comprehension.
Dull in self-assessment,
yet forcibly coveting all fields,
and deviating from their aptitude to seek easy endeavors,
thus they cannot escape ridicule.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
The five flavors may conflict yet all are sweet;
the multitude of colors may clash yet all are beautiful.
As for the feelings of ordinary people,
they love what is similar and hate what is different,
valuing that which conforms to themselves,
and belittling that which follows a different path.
As for the nature of literary works,
it is especially difficult to examine and appreciate thoroughly;
if one simply considers what pleases the ear as excellent,
and what fits one’s own taste as delightful,
few understand the subtlety of flavors and the graceful elegance of the yǎ sòng's airs.
What is meant by “judging the saltiness and sourness of salt and plums,”
is failing to recognize that the great broth cannot be achieved by such analysis;
in discerning delicate and skillful details,
one becomes blinded to profound and deep grandeur.
Those works that are outstanding, extraordinary, grand, and unrestrained
are gathered beyond the bounds of the mysterious and the yellow;
those that are constrained and petty
are fettered within a confining enclosure.
The flapping of wings may be sharp or dull,
thus soaring and settling may be high or low;
racing ahead may be slow or fast,
thus advancing and hurrying may be distant or near.
The dull and the sharp cannot be harmonized by forcibly tuning the zither.
Literary works should value richness and abundance;
why must one insist that praise be as unanimous as from a single mouth!
If they cannot save customs from decline and flight,
or the path of the world from ruin and decay,
open the way for those who are perplexed,
relieve the shortages of the impoverished,
how is this different from spring flowers that are of no use as food,
or chái huì that cannot save one in the hardship of ice and cold?
Ancient poetry pointed out faults,
and thus was beneficial and esteemed;
modern poetry is mere empty praise,
and thus is harmful and despised.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Among those who wield the brush,
each has his own defect:
those who are profound suffer from excessive illustration and verbosity,
multiplying warnings and broad analogies,
wishing to discard them yet reluctant,
unconsciously succumbing to over-elaboration.
Those who are superficial suffer from prettiness without foundation,
with insufficient support from evidence and citations,
their surface glistens but their bones are exceedingly weak.
When the dazzling and resplendent vie each day for brilliance,
even the seven luminaries combine to show distinction;
when subtle and mysterious thoughts are profound,
one is compared to the unfathomable deep abyss.
In the affairs of men, there are no details left unaddressed;
in the kingly way, there is nothing so slight as to be neglected;
thus one can be base in station yet noble in speech,
and, after a thousand generations, shine all the more.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Tranquility, emptiness, and calm are
the foundation of spiritual clarity;
gentleness and firmness, the principles of yīn and yáng,
are the foundation of the two primordial forces;
towering cliffs and peaks
are the foundation of mountains and hills;
virtue, conduct, and learning
are the foundation of the jūnzǐ.
None can stand without a foundation.
Therefore, to achieve great height,
you must have a solid base;
to have luxuriant branches,
you must have deep roots.
When friends in one’s own village are not in harmony,
yet exert oneself to seek faraway connections;
when one’s record in office is unremarkable,
yet one desires out-of-turn advancement;
thus, even if you gain hollow praise,
it is like wild blossoms that shine through withering frost,
and before long shall fall and wither away.
Even if you unexpectedly seize great treasure,
carry dust and filth astride a carriage,
or, with few helpers, attempt to ride the surging waves to soar high,
you will only gaze back from a withered stump atop a dangerous height.
The sages and worthies are diligent
and exert themselves accordingly,
while the shallow-minded are fleeting and unconcerned,
disregarding such matters completely.
Accustomed to something, one forgets the stench of the fish market;
those who dwell among the naked do not perceive the shame of being unclothed.
Unless one retires from the world without regret,
or regards all things equally, whether smooth or blocked,
how can one cast aside what is near and easy to seek out what is remote and empty!
To correct this fault,
there is no other method
but to raise up the people from rocky crags,
and employ talent without regard to other considerations.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
A guest once jested with me, saying:
“Sir, you always pursue the One,
hiding your brilliance in the deep springs;
turning your back on the world and dwelling alone;
remote and aloof in your solitude.
Your plans are decisive yet hesitant,
your heart does not rest on scheming;
your position is firm but you are burdened by worldly ties,
yet none of this weighs upon your mind.
Bó Yáng put Dào and virtue first;
Zhuāng Zhōu crowned his works with wandering freedom;
thus they established lofty standards in the highest heavens
and made their fragrant name resound without limit.
Now you, sir, are nobly reclusive and never serve,
do not submit yourself to official employment,
yet write books on the Way of ruler and minister;
do not mingle in society,
yet compose treatises that satirize the vulgar and rescue the living;
greatly value uprightness and discipline,
yet append the arts of warfare and defense;
do not seek advancement or position,
yet write essays judging success and failure;
I am truly puzzled by this.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The relationship between lord and minister
is second only to heaven and earth;
those who possess the Way find happiness in it;
whether one enters or withdraws, the feeling is the same;
to be hidden or manifest depends on the times;
what one says is of little consequence.
Great men and jūnzǐ
respond to changing circumstances.
Lǎozi advocated non-action;
Guǐgǔ finally withdrew from the world;
yet both wrote books
all concerning the affairs of the world.
Must one be in such a position
before one may speak about such matters?
If a vessel is not made of jade and precious stones,
the jewelers of Chǔ and Hé do not weep;
if the substance is not a hidden dragon,
winds and clouds will not assemble.
I am of meager talent and shallow virtue,
unable to fit myself for governance;
yet whether I act or withdraw, my fate is much the same;
my actions are consistent and unified.
Is it necessary to attain high office
before one is allowed to discuss governing the state and serving the ruler,
and forbidden otherwise to speak of order and chaos?
I have always regretted that Zhuāng Zhōu belittled himself in word and deed,
shackled by worldly affairs;
though living in Qīyuán he spoke much extravagant talk,
loving to paint ghosts and monsters,
detesting depictions of dogs and horses,
narrow and petty in his loyalty and chastity,
belittling benevolence and righteousness.
This is like carving tigers and painting dragons—
how could you summon wind and clouds from them?
Though you paint countless boards,
you cannot rescue someone who is penniless.
The child’s bamboo hobbyhorse
cannot escape chafing the feet;
scholars’ desks piled high with writing
do nothing to ease their hunger.”
Another said:
“Yet what you have written
criticizes prevailing customs,
your words are sharp and upright;
I fear you will only incur the hatred of the powerful,
attracting rejection in your time,
and this is not the way
to spread your name and win reputation,
or to be esteemed.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Those who fashion tools are valued in times of pressing need,
yet do not consider the adornment of outward form as excellence;
those who compose words are esteemed for assisting instruction,
yet do not regard courting common approval as lofty.
If one merely flatters and is obsequious,
praising falsely and concealing faults,
how could this correct error or set right deviation,
or awaken the deluded and make up for shortcomings?
If, fearing lack of harmony, one abandons the sound of 'White Snow',
or, begrudging the difficulty of selling, devalues the price of a 'Jade Worth a Walled City',
I have no use for such things.
It is not that I cannot string together elegant phrases to please others,
nor that I do not know that forthright words often incur resentment,
but I cannot bear to violate my feelings and twist my writing,
mingling true and false in confusion.
I desire that mind and speech act in accord,
looking back unashamed before illumination,
and hoping there will be an appreciative listener in future times.
Favor and adversity follow fate;
success and failure depend on Heaven.
Why must one’s words be circulated or used in practice,
and glory reach one's own time?
Whenever a gentleman opens his mouth or sets brush to paper,
he must be on guard against confusion and delusion,
rectifying the tendency to conform blindly,
abrading away anything obscure and stained that drifts with the current.
Yet authors only deck out their writings in florid decoration,
spreading forth with contrived emptiness,
composing words difficult to verify and offering no benefit,
striving after the beauty of ornate and hollow speech.
Some are like writings on 'Hardness and Whiteness', or 'Effort and Practice',
or the discourses on 'Punishments and Names' by Gōngsūn,
which may range beyond Heaven and Earth,
or subtly probe the innermost spaces,
taking apart interlocked rings,
separating what is united and joining what is different;
denying the movement of a bird's shadow,
claiming chicken eggs have feet,
or that a dog can be made a sheep,
or offering the words of the great turtle and the long snake—
all merely to display cleverness and feign marvels to deceive the world.
How is this different from painting the granary at Àocāng to relieve hunger,
or gazing at the Milky Way to quench one’s thirst?
To speak of Kūnshān’s abundance of jade
does nothing to relieve Yuán Xiàn’s poverty;
to consult pharmaceutical ledgers
cannot cure a pressing illness;
for Mòzǐ to carve a wooden rooster to awe the heavens
is not as good as three inches of metal that can avert harm;
even Guǎn Qīng's casting of qilin steeds in gold
is not as useful as a common nag that completes its circuit.
Words as lofty as autumn in the high sky, if unfit for use,
I, Qiū, will not join in discussing them."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"I have always considered Wáng Zhòngrèn’s *Lùn Héng* of over eighty chapters
to be foremost among great talents.
A peer in the same school, Master Lǔ, once questioned me, saying:
'Jade and precious stones are prized for being rare,
while gravel is cheap for being common.
Thus, Fú Xī’s trigrams number less than ten, yet include and wrap up both Yí;
Lǎozi’s teachings are fewer than ten thousand words, yet fully embody the Way and its Virtue.
When Wáng Chōng writes books,
he fills boxes and stacks of volumes,
yet his assertions contradict each other,
sometimes Ru, sometimes Mohist,
his wording and meanings at odds,
and not entirely admirable.
As one says of the mugwort and weeds on the marsh’s edge,
they cannot compare to millet and grain from the fields.' "
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"Now, those who create are called sages;
transmitters are called worthies.
One only sees the quality of transmission and creation,
never having heard there is a fixed limit on how much or how little.
What you speak of is the gloom of denizens lurking in holes,
unaware that within the eight borders there is nothing outside;
those who guard a lamp in the night,
not recognizing the brilliance of the three lights;
those who swim in shallow, stagnant water,
thinking it equals the vastness of the southern ocean;
those trapped on an anthill,
not aware of the heights of Sōng and Dài.
The two principles are termed great
because they embrace the eight extremes,
extending endlessly with no boundary;
mountains and seas are considered abundant
because they gather in great breadth,
containing a medley of things.
If, as in your view,
what is rare is noble and abundant things despicable,
then the boundless dome would have no esteem for its vastness,
and things broad and capacious would not be valued for their support.
In the middle of a stream,
there are no fish big enough to swallow boats;
atop a single branch,
there are no wings spread wide as the sky;
on the tip of an anthill,
there is no forest of Fúsāng trees;
from a muddy pool,
one will not find the torrents of Xiānglíng.
The great ao turtle crowns Yíngzhōu,
surging waves reach beyond Fāngzhàng;
the mighty peach fills Dùlíng,
the Jìanmù rises in Dūguǎng;
the great shēnkūn lies within the heavenly pool,
the cloud-peng soars through the dark heavens.
The crash of thunder
cannot be made delicate in sound;
the tumult of the Yellow River
cannot be confined in its flow;
a fine steed chasing the wind
cannot be caught up with in its tracks;
the wild goose soaring its wings
cannot be made to fly low.
When the clouds are thick, the rain must be fierce;
when the bow is taut, the arrow flies farther.
Master Wáng’s learning is vast and talents broad,
how could one scrutinize them so lightly?
You say:
'Jade is valued for being rare;
stone is cheap for being common.'
Yet beneath the Xuánpǔ,
atop the Jīnghuá,
in the marsh of Jiǔyuán,
within the depths of Zhéfāng,
jade and jewels are heaped into mountains,
the luminous pearl glows and lights the heavens,
surely that is not without worth!
You also cite that the writings of Fúxī are not many,
but after the Duke of Zhōu elaborated on the Great *Yì*,
and added the rites and music,
Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
with further additions in ten chapters.
These surpass Fúxī,
and exceed Lǎozi;
should these all be denigrated?
If there are few words, the ultimate principle is incomplete;
when expressions are few, many matters are left unspoken.
Thus, it is essential to amass chapters and accumulate volumes,
so that the guiding threads are raised up.
Xīhé raises the light to usher in dawn,
Wàngshū shines its radiance through the night;
the five materials arise together but serve different uses;
myriad medicines blossom together but have various effects;
the four seasons come together and complete the year’s work;
the five colors combine to yield splendid brocade;
the eight tones harmonize for beautiful music;
varied words converge and the path of art and reason are distinguished.
With the resources of Yī Dùn amassed,
yet little of it is used,
how is that different from Yuán Xiàn?
With a mind lacking scales to measure,
writing meager and crude,
how is that any better than trivial pettiness?
Sounds are precious to those with understanding;
books are handed down for those with discernment.
The tuning of Gǔ Kuàng’s bells
may not find appreciation among contemporaries;
words of principle and lofty writings—
is it really because they do not win praise that they are lessened?
Moreover, the filth of the rivers and seas
is beyond reckoning,
yet does not diminish their depth;
the crooked trees on the Five Peaks
are beyond calculation,
but do not mar their lofty heights.
The jade disk of the rulers of Xià,
though it has the tiniest flaw,
its radiance and brilliance
suffice to make up for it.
Among words numbering in the thousands and tens of thousands,
though there are some that are not ornate,
suppose the ideas and meaning are lofty and far-reaching,
that is enough to outshine the rest.
Thus it is said:
the muddiness of the four great rivers
does not compare to the clearness of water in a jar;
the emaciation of an elephant
cannot be equated with the fatness of a lamb."
You also criticize, saying:
“Now entering, now leaving,
sometimes Rú, sometimes Mò.”
To utter words with the mouth
and to inscribe them on paper is to make a book.
Books are that by which words are substituted,
words are that by which affairs are recorded.
If one’s writing does not permit a mixture of subjects,
then in debate one should always uphold only one matter.
In antiquity, when the zhūhóu sought advice on governance,
and disciples inquired about rén,
Zhòngní answered them,
and his replies varied with each person.
This was because he adapted principles to circumstances,
and responded according to urgency.
It is like the myriad methods for treating illness:
the use of acupuncture and moxibustion does not always follow the same pattern;
one expels cold with warmth,
removes heat with coolness,
the sole aim is to save lives and preserve the body.
How could it be that visitors must always follow a single path, as in Qí and Chǔ,
and never change their road?
The wealth of Táo Zhū and Bái Guī did not consist in a single thing,
that is abundance;
the myriad life in Yúnmèng and Mèngzhū is all of different kinds,
that is vastness.
Thus the Huáinán Hóngliè
begins with Yuán Dào and Chù Zhēn,
and also contains Bīnglüè and Zhǔshù;
Zhuāng Zhōu’s writings
treat life and death as one,
and yet there are passages about fearing sacrifice, yearning for the tortoise, requesting grain to relieve famine.
If one were to discard the text because its statements are not uniform,
that would be like treating a pearl cataract by gouging out the eye,
treating moist numbness by amputation,
cutting the millet because of weeds,
or cutting down the tree because of withered branches.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“The words of a hundred schools,
though not all are elegant brushwork and sharp phrasing,
grand and splendid,
are nonetheless the deposit of talented scholars,
each uttered by one who pondered deeply.
The classic scriptures are the abyssal sea of dào and yì,
while the ‘masters’ writings’ are the deepening rivers and streams.
Look upward and compare them:
they are like the guiding constellations supplementing the three luminaria.
Look downward and set them beside each other:
they are like the forest and thickets supporting Sōng Yuè.
Yet students focus on only one occupation,
swimming in wells and ignoring the sea,
thus picking up and stumbling in the mud,
and sinking into the stagnation of immobility.
The ‘masters’ writings’ unveil profound vastness,
remote, distant, deep and secluded,
gathering unmeasurable sources,
raising up undiminished flows,
changing and transforming unconstrained by compass or square,
comprehensively connecting without falling into biased paths that stray from correctness.
Their style is lofty and austere,
of such height and depth as is hard to exhaust.
Thus, for those who are partial only to sour or sweet,
none can truly appreciate their flavor;
for those whose thought is limited in use,
they cannot discern the spirit within.
The ancients sighed at the difficulty of talent,
so that in a hundred generations, they succeeded one another,
not because unpolished jade is not produced on the slopes of Bǎntóng,
and thus they discard the shining treasures of night;
not because writings do not originate from the schools of Zhōu or Kǒng,
and thus dismiss words that aid in teaching.
It is like those who use water:
though the vessels may differ, putting out fire is the same;
or like those who practice acupuncture and moxibustion:
though their techniques differ, they attack illness all the same.
The narrow-sighted sort,
stubbornly cleaving to a single standpoint,
abandoning broad learning and refinement,
think but do not understand,
comparing the weight of grains with that of mountains and hills,
and believing that gathering hundreds and thousands could reach up to billions.
They are dazzled by the trivialities of poetry and rhapsody,
and ignore the profound beauty of the ‘masters’ discourses.
True and false are reversed,
jade and stone are mingled together,
as if playing grand music among the mulberry fields,
or comparing dragon embroidery to plain silk—
it is lamentable and moving,
and how could this be but one particular instance!
Someone says:
“Virtue and conduct
are the root;
writing
is secondary.
Therefore, in the four classes,
writing is not placed in the highest rank.
Thus, what is inscribed on paper
is the leftover dregs;
what can be transmitted
is like the straw dog after the sacrifice.
The difference between low and high
is available to criticism.”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“To discard the net before the fish is caught
is then to do without a net;
to abolish writing before the dào is practiced
is likewise to do without writing.
As to the broadness and narrowness of calligraphic traces and rhymed outlines,
the beauty or ugliness of composition and meaning,
the length or brevity of their sources and outcomes,
the depth or shallowness of what is contained or drawn forth,
their remoteness and distinction—
even from outside heaven to the tip of a hair,
it is not sufficient to illustrate the vastness,
and though the three luminaries shine brightly,
it does not suffice to compare the great and small.
The Longyuān sword and lead ingot
cannot describe their sharpness or bluntness;
swan feathers and accumulated gold
cannot express their lightness or heaviness.
Yet vulgar men see only the skill of manipulating brush and paper,
and immediately judge all by a single rule;
thus Bó Shì was always longing for Zhōngzǐ,
and the man of Yǐng held a standard too heavy to wield.
Those who carve and polish are plentiful,
but Bān and Dí monopolized the name of peerless hands;
those who play the qín are numerous,
but Kuí and Xiāng alone possess the reputation of pure sound.
There are thousands of horses in the stables,
yet Qílióu commands a price far above the herd;
beauties by the ten thousand,
yet Wēi and Shī alone possess beauty that surpasses the age,
far exceeding the many.
As for writing and virtue,
it is like ten chǐ and one zhàng;
to call one a mere appendage
is not what I have heard.
The Eight Trigrams arose from the flight of hawks and falcons,
the Liùjiǎ originated from the markings on the numinous tortoise’s shell.
Wherever writing is found,
though the root is esteemed, one need not immediately neglect it;
the branches need not always be despised.
It is as if in brocade, the colored patterns rely on the base cloth;
pearls and jade are presented in chiseled stone;
clouds and rain are generated from a mere inch of skin;
rivers and streams begin from a small source;
the principle truly is thus.
If so, then ‘upright critiques’ have gone astray.”
Again he said:
“The Yinglóng rises slowly,
turning its gaze as it soars among the clouds;
the sweating-blood horse moves at a gentle pace,
yet with a breath traverses a thousand lǐ.
Thus ants and termites find it strange that it ascends heights without climbing,
inferior nags are startled that it passes them without gradual advance.
To charge along amid discussion of poetry,
to circle within a single scripture,
using ordinary feelings to assess what is vastly different,
using narrow measures to gauge the boundless,
beginning from childhood,
arriving at the heights of purity,
this cannot be accomplished.
Furthermore, the world in general values the ancient and despises the present,
reveres what is heard but treats what is seen lightly.
Though in the same age there are steeds that pursue the wind and outstrip the scene,
still it is said they do not compare to those driven by Bólè.
Though there are uncut jades, flawless enough to besiege a city,
they are still deemed inferior to those that caused the artisan of Chǔ and Hé to weep.
Though there are swords that can split the horse and pierce the eagle,
they are still said not to match those forged by Ōuyě.
Though there are medicines that revive the dead and heal the rotten,
they are still deemed not equal to those compounded by Héquè.
Though there are men whose virtue crowns the group and who walk alone,
it is still said they do not compare to the ancients.”
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“Jī Shēng, with Guō Línzōng of Tàiyuán,
in the end was not respectful of the appointments of the Three Excellencies.
In study, there was no field he did not explore,
and his reputation was weighty among the ages,
further enhanced by his discernment of people.
To know men is to be wise;
truly a vessel of second-sage caliber.
Yet he lived in a declining age,
careworn and anxious,
with barely time to warm his mat,
his ambition resting in setting right and walking the Way,
much akin to Zhòngní.”
I replied:
“Wisdom and folly
reside in a single utterance;
a flaw in the crucial moment
confounds the pure jade Bái Guī.
In my view, the appraisal of the Yà Shèng
should not be lightly granted.
As for what is called the Yà Shèng,
he must truly possess subtle substance,
be unmatched in his generation,
leaving no room between himself and Zhōu and Kǒng.
How could such a person as this suffice to attain that rank!
Línzōng, outstanding and exceptional in his generation,
with discerning and penetrating insight,
judged by ordinary men,
is surely often raised above them,
yet in truth is still insufficient.
This man possesses quick wit and distinguished bearing,
adept at confronting others and skilled in self-use;
moreover, enthusiasts became his wings and feathers,
spreading his reputation to the four quarters,
and so he was able to carry this and be admired in troubled times,
promoted by those who believe rumor but do not verify the facts.
When praised even by a few words,
it carried the weight of a thousand gold pieces.
Wherever he traveled,
worthies and fools were stirred and tossed,
compared to the gathering of dragons and phoenixes,
and the appearance of strange auspices.
When he spoke, even the lingering sound became a model;
when he moved, the traces he left were imitated.
He could be called one who strikes the drum so well as to lift sun and moon—
but not a true recluse.
When he wished to join the court, the world was greatly chaotic;
when he wished to hide, he was overcome by frustration;
if he leapt forward, he feared disaster;
if he remained firm, he was not at ease.
Restless and unfixed,
pacing in distress and anxiety by the month,
and the people of the world chased after his brilliance but did not examine the substance,
played with his form but did not explore his spirit.
Even when his cap was ruined by rain,
he could still affect a look,
and did not perceive his deficiencies—
they were all such as these.
The common folk chase after fame,
to this extreme.
So although there were shortcomings,
no one dared to point them out.
Línzōng had learning and insight into people,
he was not without qualification.
Yet he could not avoid the reputation of overestimating the facts,
and was blind in self-assessment.
When some persuaded him to enter government service,
Línzōng replied:
‘By day I observe human affairs,
by night I study the patterns of Heaven.
What Heaven casts aside
cannot be sustained.
Now the course of fate is in the Yáo of Míngyí,
at the position of "do not employ";
it is a time for lingering in obscurity,
not an occasion for Heaven to favor appearances.
Though there is land in the plain,
I still fear what the turbulent sea may bring.
I am but a fish;
how much less could I brave the howling wind and ride the surging waves!
It is better to nurture my spirit amidst cliffs and valleys,
please my heart like Pénglǎo,
leisure and free wandering,
so to pass my years.’
Judging by Línzōng’s words,
he knew Hàn could not be saved,
which was surely beyond his talent to accomplish.
According to the pattern, he should have looked up to Shāngluò,
floated down upon the Five Lakes,
pursued Chāo Fù among high mountain peaks,
sought the fisherman at the blue waves;
if he could not unite himself with the hermits of the mountains,
and travel alone apart from the group,
then he should have vanished in remote pools,
concealed his scales and sealed his sack,
instead of journeying from west to east,
not letting his seat grow warm,
wishing to emulate the restless actions of Confucians and Mohists.
Sages are burdened for the world,
roaming the four directions,
yet even they, as retiring scholars,
are subject to blame and criticism.
Línzōng’s talents did not match the times,
his capacity was not unexcelled;
going out, he could not pacify the ruler or govern the people,
nor transform customs;
staying in, he could not wield the brush,
inherit and transmit the Six Arts;
his conduct was self-glorifying,
which was indeed excessive;
he gathered resounding fame,
and received many honors.
Yet in the end, advancing, he added nothing to order or disorder,
retreating, he left no trace in history.
Observed in decline and confusion,
as ice melts and grass droops,
he is no different from the common man.
For no reason, he drifted among billows,
knocked off his shoes amid dust and dirt,
travelled and gathered at the capital,
socialized with the eminent and noble,
his carriage wheels worn, his traveling chest damaged,
without leisure to open his home,
and so his fame shone brightly,
attracting admiration from Qín and Hú,
the byways crowded with red-wheeled chariots,
his halls filled with guests in scarlet sashes,
chariots jammed the streets,
carriages conveyed memorials in constant procession.
Truly, he was among the company of wandering knights,
hardly matching the ranks of the tranquil recluse.
Even in a world of the Dao where such things happened,
he could not again be included among the lists of pure and lofty men;
being a fine subject of Mìqiū,
yet cultivating such ways in chaotic times,
how could it be worthy of much?
Who would not say he was blind to the alternations of Heaven and man,
and obscured in measure of his own strengths and weaknesses?
He in vain turned away from the tranquil path,
and ultimately gained no benefit from it.
That he did not encounter ruin,
was but his good fortune.
To call this ‘worrying for the world and caring for the state,’
or aspiring to emulate the Sage Kings,
is like a crippled foot chasing a flying dragon horse,
or a quail pursuing a wild swan,
a mayfly trying to follow the giant péng-bird in the clouds,
a shrew compared to a great elephant.
“Thus Línzōng could be said to possess the talent to dazzle the vulgar,
but lacked the steadfast substance;
his observation met with nothing he could not understand,
and he nearly attained great usefulness;
outward display issued forth with eloquence,
but his spirit was empty within,
unable to bear weariness and agitation;
his words and actions conflicted,
his lips spoke of quiet withdrawal,
but his heart yearned for glory and profit;
he did not attain the state of the hidden bird in the Xuánpǔ,
nor the submerged spirit of the Nine Depths.
Self-display and self-advertisement,
are a disgrace to gentlemen and ladies alike.
Knowing its impossibility yet all the more imitating and emulating,
where is the capacity of a Yà Shèng?
Where could it be found?
Even if it is said he knows men,
the discernment of men
was difficult even for Yáo and Shùn to achieve,
and a trouble even for Master Ní.
In former ages, even comparing oneself to sun and moon,
knowing beginnings and seeing ends,
still sometimes went astray,
and did not always strike the middle path.
How much less in the case of Línzōng’s glow-worm insight,
grasping only half of right and wrong,
which is already not a little.
Thus, his name outweighed those of the age,
and his fame flourished after his passing.
So what he attained
was passed around by the world,
while what he failed at,
was unknown to any.
Though he sometimes selected unknown men from the grass and wilds,
and pointed to uncarved jade in the fields and gardens,
he still could not advance the loyal and brave into the court,
nor stand guard on the frontier,
nor deliver the oppressed from danger,
nor thwart the competition of seditious plans.
As Bàozi promoted Guǎn Shēng,
and Píngzhòng introduced Ráng Jū,
so Línzōng’s name was exalted at court,
venerated in his time,
among all the nobles and officials,
none failed to respect him,
his power could raise men of talent,
his words could uplift the downtrodden,
but he only nursed his illness in the capital,
gathering guests of distinction,
achieving nothing with it,
to remedy chaos and darkness;
he could only know men,
but would not recommend or promote them.
How is this different from one who knows fertile soil suits fine fields,
or straight timber makes pillars and beams,
but in the end does not plow or sow good grain,
nor cut it to use for construction?
How would this help feed the hungry,
or shelter those exposed to the elements!
His rejection of participation in recommendation and selection
was indeed lofty conduct,
but his constant busyness
was also his flaw.”
Jī Shēng also said:
“Línzōng existed as a model for his generation,
and after his death, his fragrant reputation will be broadcast forever.
Great scholars and outstanding men,
none ever pointed out his faults,
but I alone among the living criticize his shortcomings,
will this not make me a laughingstock to those who come after?”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“Why should this be so?
If what I say is true,
it should be passed down to later generations;
when the discerning in the future
recognize it, why should I care about few responses now?
Moreover, many former worthies also reproached him,
only Huáng Shēng excessively praised him.
Thus, Grand Tutor Zhūgě Wúxùn also said:
‘Línzōng, when in hiding, did not truly cultivate withdrawal;
when he appeared, it was not to benefit the times;
he really just wished to spread his name and nourish his reputation.
To argue with the populace in streets and alleys he considered wit,
to criticize superiors and slander the government he considered noble;
at the time it was valued by custom,
just like Guō Jiě and Yuán Shè who were also admired,
all following the trends of former times.
Those coming after, who sought fame,
could not examine according to the canons of sage kings,
nor discuss according to the conduct of ancient worthies;
they were merely confused by flowery reputation,
all competed to emulate him,
those who studied him feared they could not keep up,
those who discussed him filled the ears,
even average men did not realize,
how could mere children possibly understand?
’ Thus Línglíng Grand Administrator Yīn Fǔjūn Bóxù,
a man of high talent and firm discourse,
also said:
‘Línzōng entered into association with high ministers,
and traveled among all the states,
exalting private opinions to move the masses,
laying the burdens of slander and praise on the court.
When he favored something, it would soar like wind and pour like rain,
its value and appearance swiftly changed;
when he disliked it, it would be broken and cast down,
unfit for the company of gentlemen.
● As for the renowned worthies,
they withdrew into hiding in times of chaos,
concealing their brilliance and hiding their light;
this is by no means remote.
The gentleman practices the Way
in order to support the ruler,
in order to rectify customs;
if at the time the ruler cannot be supported,
and customs cannot be corrected,
Línzōng wandered about,
chatting idly in alleys and neighborhoods,
never restoring the decline of the world’s order,
and never alleviating the suffering of the weary people.
’ Further, the former Palace Attendant Zhōu Shēng Gōngyuǎn,
a heroic and celebrated scholar,
also said:
‘If one encounters a well-governed age and assists it,
it is called delighting in the Way;
if one encounters chaos and rescues it,
it is called being concerned for the Way;
if chaos cannot be rescued and one avoids it,
it is called preserving the Way.
Yú Shùn delighted in the Way,
Zhòngní was concerned for the Way,
Wēizǐ preserved the Way.
In the late Hàn when collapse neared,
the custom of the age was making connections;
Línzōng should have resolutely emptied his heart,
sought true gentlemen of kindred spirit,
and together set things aright;
yet he only busied himself as a hero among men,
not suitable for rescuing the world.
At that time, even the imperial attendants,
all kinds of people, merely sought to lodge themselves.
Those like Chén Fán and Dòu Wǔ,
even though they held high offices,
all valued Línzōng,
believed his words and discourse,
and used his praise or blame for their judgments;
in saving what was dangerous and changing customs,
was this not to be hoped for?
Yet Línzōng could not recommend any men of action,
could not establish the slightest benefit;
as for those who absconded and refused official posts,
he compared them to Cháo and Xǔ;
those who abandoned office and entertained guests,
he likened to Zhōugōng;
those who gathered disciples to avoid service,
he compared to Zhòngní;
those who abandoned kin and relied on magnates,
he likened to Yóu Xià.
Thus the world became dazzled by name and reality,
and the great disorder grew worse.
If we say that Línzōng did not know this,
then he cannot be called wise and discerning;
if we say that he knew and did not reform,
then how can he be said to have cared for the Way?
In former times, the Four Heroes were like Zhōugōng but could not become Zhōugōng,
now Línzōng is like Zhòngní but cannot become Zhòngní.
’” At this, the questioner sighed and lamented:
“Then this man is but one who avoids chaos,
not one of the highest accomplishment in reclusion.”
Bàopǔzǐ said:
“At the end of Hàn there was a certain Mí Héng,
aged twenty-three;
Kǒng Wénjǔ rated him as already past the age of understanding fate,
he attained the ninth rank,
and surpassed all in literary learning,
acclaimed by both young and old,
his name and position unique;
he was friends with Héng despite being a commoner,
and moreover recommended him at the Hàn court,
believing he should serve as a Gentleman of the Terrace.
He said:
‘Only when the mountains send down spirits,
do extraordinary men appear together.
Whatever his eyes once saw
he could recite by mouth;
whatever his ear caught in passing
he never forgot in his mind;
his nature was in accord with the Way,
his thoughts seemed inspired by god.
’ Such was his praise.
When Héng traveled to Xǔ,
from the highest nobles and national heroes on down,
Héng at first never addressed them by their titles,
but called all by their given names,
or called them by their surname as so-and-so’s child;
he called Kǒng Róng “Big Boy,”
and called Yáng Xiū “Little Boy.”
Only Xún Yù could still force himself to converse with him;
beyond these,
all were mere wooden clubs and clay figurines,
human in appearance but lacking humanity,
all fit only as wine jars and drinking bags.
At a great assembly of all officials,
Héng was present,
and suddenly frowned in sorrow,
sighing mournfully in frustration.
Someone reproached him:
‘Full of heroes and outstanding men, is this an occasion for lament?’
Héng glanced around at the throng and replied:
‘Amid these piles of corpses and coffins,
how can a humane man not be sorrowful?’
Cáo Gōng once ground his teeth wishing to kill him,
but still had no legal pretext warranting death,
and begrudged acquiring a reputation for slaying a scholar,
so demoted him to be a drum official;
Héng displayed no regret or shame,
tied horns to a pillar,
held his mouth to blow on it,
and produced a strange sound;
shaking the drumsticks and beating the drum,
listeners could not tell it was one person.
Moreover, his criticism grew fiercer,
utterly without concern;
soon he absconded to Liú Biǎo, Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Biǎo wished to write a letter to Sūn Quán,
who had by then secured Jiāngdōng,
with a million armored troops,
seeking a relationship as close as lips and teeth,
to together resist the Central States.
He ordered all the scholars to draft the letter,
but none could capture his intent.
He showed it to Héng.
After reading, Héng said:
‘If this is only to be shown to the knife-wielding attendants beside Sūn Quán,
then it will suffice;
but if Zhāng Zǐbù were to see it,
it would be a great embarrassment.’
He immediately tore it up and threw it to the ground.
Biǎo was disappointed and looked perplexed,
and said to Héng:
‘Is it truly so unsuitable?’
How I regret it!”
Héng requested paper and brush,
and immediately wrote a new draft.
Of all the many versions written by others,
Héng simply glanced at each,
and recalled them by heart as he wrote,
completing it and handing it to Biǎo.
Biǎo gave it back to his lord,
and someone compared the original drafts,
checking them together,
and not a single word was different,
which greatly amazed everyone.
Then Biǎo requested Héng to compose a new one;
Héng did so at once,
his hand never pausing,
and Biǎo greatly praised it and put it to use.”
Héng became ever more arrogant,
and the people of the entire province
all despised and resented him.
Even Biǎo could no longer tolerate it,
and wished to kill him.
Someone remonstrated, saying that Cáo Gōng was reputed for severity and cruelty,
yet could still endure and be tolerant;
while Héng possessed only an empty reputation from youth.
If he were killed suddenly,
then among the wandering scholars of the world,
none would again wish to set foot in Jīngchǔ.
Thus Biǎo sent him away.
Héng fled to Xiàkǒu,
relying on General Huáng Zǔ;
Huáng Zǔ treated him as an honored guest.
Huáng Zǔ’s eldest son, Huáng Shè,
often accompanied Héng,
passing once beneath a grave mound,
where they both read the epitaph aloud before departing.
After a long while,
Shè said:
“The inscription we saw earlier was excellent;
I regret not having copied it down.”
Héng replied:
“You only need to recall its outline;
even having read it but once, I still remember it.”
He then secretly wrote it out,
but at the end there was one character
where the stone was damaged,
making it unclear.
Héng supplied half a character,
saying:
“I suspect this should be a certain character,
but I fear it may not be precise.”
Shè reflected and deemed it plausible;
(text missing below).
Although his words and actions belittled others,
he persistently sought glory and distinction;
thus he soared at leisure above the Phoenix Groves,
unable to hide among the weeds and thistles.
Yet in cultivating himself he was contentious and critical,
confused but unaware of it;
thus when he spoke, he evoked resentment,
and wherever he stepped, he courted disaster.
With such skills as these,
how could he find a place in the world, or obtain a proper end?
Like the shriek of an owl or the cry of a fox,
all who heard could not abide it;
yet the sound itself did not change,
so what was gained by changing its dwelling place?
Xǔxià
is an ocean of talents and people.
Wénjǔ acts as its steward,
bearing enough responsibility to ensure his presence.
If even there he found no peace,
it is readily understood why.
It is like a man with a fatal illness
pleading for help from Yù and Yuè man physicians,
but to no avail.
Decayed wood and leaden ingots
cannot be shaped even by Bānshū or Ōuyě,
and again fleeing to the lands of Jīngchǔ,
in the end he fell into extreme misfortune.
This is indeed the result of Héng’s delusion and blindness.
He sought it but could not obtain it;
it was not that he could obtain it but did not use it.
Alas, you men of talent—
can you not take heed!
Jī Shēng said:
“What confuses me
is Héng’s empty reputation;
what you have critiqued
are Héng’s real faults.
How dare I not keep your guidance in mind,
and cast aside my staff at the proper measure!”
Bào Shēng spoke respectfully,
delighting in the books of Lǎo and Zhuāng,
and skilled in arguments of paradox and debate.
He maintained that in ancient times there was no ruler,
which was better than the present age.
Thus in his treatise, he wrote:
“Confucians say:
‘Heaven gave birth to the common people and established for them a ruler.’
But could it be that august Heaven, so earnest, also actually desired this and said so?
For when the strong oppress the weak,
the weak submit;
when the wise deceive the foolish,
the foolish serve them.
Because they submit,
the way of ruler and subject arises;
because they serve,
the people with little strength are thereby ruled.
Thus, the subjugation and service of men
arose from struggles between the strong and the weak, from measuring intelligence and folly.
That azure sky truly is without will;
in primordial chaos, namelessness is prized;
among all living things, finding satisfaction is joy.
Hence stripping cassia and carving lacquer
are not the wish of the tree;
plucking kingfishers and tearing out emeralds
are not what birds desire;
restraining reins and bits
are not the nature of horses;
bearing carts and hauling heavy loads
is not the pleasure of oxen.
The sprouting of trickery and cunning,
the misuse of strength that violates true nature,
the severing of the root of life
to decorate the useless,
catching flying birds for ornament and display,
piercing the noses of perfectly whole creatures,
binding the feet of those born to walk free—
surely these are contrary to the intent of all beings to live together.
To press into service the commoners,
to nourish those in officialdom,
making nobles’ stipends fat while the people grow ever more wretched.
If, having died, one could return to life,
one’s delight would be boundless;
but even so, it would not compare to never having died at all.
If one relinquishes rank and refuses salary
to fish for empty fame,
this is not as good as never having needed to yield in the first place.
Only when the world is in disorder do loyalty and righteousness shine;
only when the bonds between kin are not harmonious do filial piety and kindness become manifest.
In bygone ages,
when there were neither rulers nor subjects,
people dug wells to drink,
ploughed fields for food,
worked when the sun rose,
rested when the sun set,
wandering freely, unfettered,
open, content within themselves,
not competing or scheming,
neither honored nor disgraced,
the mountains lacked paths or tracks,
the marshes had no boats or bridges.
With rivers and valleys impassable,
none would encroach or conquer.
Since the people did not band together,
they did not attack one another.
Thus, lofty nests were unplundered,
deep pools unexhausted;
phoenixes and luans roosted in courtyards,
dragons swam together in ponds;
hungry tigers could be trodden upon,
vipers could be grasped;
crossing marshes, gulls did not fly away at men's approach,
entering forests, foxes and hares were unafraid.
As long as power and profit did not arise,
disasters and chaos did not begin;
armaments were unused,
walls and moats unbuilt;
all things existed in mysterious unity,
forgetting themselves within the Way;
epidemics did not spread,
and the people lived out their natural span.
Their hearts were pure and unadulterated,
scheming thoughts did not arise,
chewing their food contentedly,
patting their bellies as they wandered at ease.
Their words were without embellishment,
their conduct unadorned;
how then could wealth have been amassed by plundering the people?
How could cruel punishments have been devised as snares and traps?
When it came to the latter ages,
cunning and artifice arose from intelligence,
the Dào and Dé declined,
ranks between high and low were established,
elaborate rituals of ascending and descending, benefit and loss, proliferated,
adornments in ceremonial tassels and black and yellow robes appeared,
constructions of earth and wood rose to brush the heavens,
vermilion and green edifices were built with intricate complexity,
treasures were tirelessly sought from steep heights,
and pearls were distinguished in the depths.
Jade was amassed like forests,
yet this could not exhaust the transformations;
gold was piled up into mountains,
yet this could not suffice for their expenditures.
They wallowed in the realm of extravagance and excess,
while they betrayed the original foundation of the great beginning,
and grew ever more distant from the ancestral source,
increasing their opposition to simplicity.
When worthies are esteemed, the people compete for reputation;
when goods are valued, thieves arise.
When desirables are seen, the true and upright heart is thrown into disorder;
when status and profit are displayed, the paths of robbery and plunder open.
They create sharp and keen implements,
ever lengthening the afflictions of invasion and division—
crossbows are feared not to be strong,
armor feared not to be firm,
spears feared not to be sharp,
shields feared not to be thick.
If there were no violence and oppression,
all these could be discarded.
Therefore it is said:
If white jade is not destroyed,
who would call it a tablet or emblem?
If Dào and Dé are not cast aside,
whence would one seek humaneness and righteousness?
Thus those like Jié and Zhòu,
who succeeded in burning men and punishing those who remonstrated,
made jerky of lords,
pickled the regional chiefs,
split open men’s hearts,
broke people’s legs,
exhausted the evils of pride and excess,
and employed the cruel tortures of searing and roasting.
If such people had all been mere commoners,
even if their natures were fierce and extravagant,
how could they have carried such acts out!
Because their cruelty and desires were indulged at will,
and they butchered and divided all under Heaven,
this was due to their being rulers;
thus they were able to give full rein to their intentions.
Once ruler and subject are established,
evil increases daily among the multitude,
and all strive and suffer amid shackles and constraints,
toiling wholly in hardship and misery.
The ruler is anxious atop the ancestral temple dais,
and the people are harassed and troubled amidst affliction and suffering.
They are regulated with rituals and measures,
and disciplined with punishments and penalties,
which is like damming a source that rises to the sky,
diverting an unpredictable current,
blocking it with a handful of earth,
and obstructing it with the palm of one’s hand.”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied, “I have heard: when the primordial obscurity was sundered,
the turbid descended and the clear rose;
the heavens arched above and diffused their light,
spreading wide and settling below.
Qián and Kūn were fixed in their stations,
above and below thus took form.
Looking far to what is external,
Heaven is honored and Earth humble,
to manifest the structure of human relationships;
looking closely to the body,
the head, thighs, and arms
demonstrate the sequence of ruler and subject.
The system of devolution and restraint
has its origins from the start.
As for the Great Ultimate in its undivided chaos,
when the Two Principles had no established forms,
it was not yet equal to the division of black and yellow,
to the manifestation of the Seven Luminaries,
to the harmonizing of yīn and yáng,
and the myriad things each taking their kind.
To speak from most ancient times:
we also know that birds flock and beasts scatter,
birds nest and beasts burrow,
they eat hair and blood,
bind grasses for clothing,
inside there were not the ranks of close kin,
outside there were not distinctions of status or awe;
but it did not match having great houses to shelter the body,
fine rice and savory foods to eat,
brocades and silks for adornment,
to keep out cold and heat,
with a wise ruler presiding over affairs,
and good ministers and craftsmen serving the world.
Offices and tasks were established,
and the universe was harmoniously ordered.
When high and low are distinguished,
people admire reward and fear punishment;
when power and strength are evenly matched,
people contend and have no hesitation.
Thus sages were established,
receiving their commission from Heaven;
some made nets to hunt and fish,
some observed the stars to bore fire,
some tasted plants to select grains,
some built dwellings for shelter.
They prepared things for practical use,
eliminated harm and promoted benefit,
the people delighted and submitted,
serving and honoring them.
Thus the Way of ruler and subject came into being;
how could there be the principle of deceiving the foolish and oppressing the weak?
In the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors’ times,
the ways and teachings flourished,
clarity in rules for encouragement and prohibition,
virtue prevailing and punishments gentle,
songs of wise ministers arose,
and culture became broad and grand.
When the Great Stairs were at peace,
the seven celestial ordinances followed their patterns,
phoenixes trilled at the morning sun,
Qílín and Yú appeared in holy response,
tortoises and dragons displayed their markings at the river’s bank,
Jǐng Lǎo shone on the Celestial Path,
the imperial mandate resounded in the nine regions,
weapons of war were stored in the arsenals,
so that with ritual order rulers found peace,
and with music, punishments were set aside.
As for luxury, excess, madness, and violence,
these arise from people themselves;
is it necessarily because of rulers
that these must occur?
Yet Bào-shēng singles out only the crimes of degenerate ages,
without discussing the meaning of perfect governance—
why is this?
Besides, going back to ancient simplicity,
before it changed,
the people remained childlike;
the mind of calculation did not stir,
like infants,
wisdom had not yet sprouted;
it was not that they knew and chose not to act,
or that they desired but restrained themselves.
If people struggled over grasses and fields,
and families litigated over nesting grounds,
without magistrates above to judge wrongs,
but having heavy bands united below,
then private quarrels would exceed public wars,
and wood and stone would be sharper than spears and halberds.
Corpses would lie all over the fields,
blood would stain the roads crimson,
and after a long time without rulers,
nothing capable of chewing and breathing would remain.
As for the appearance of dragons tamed and phoenixes docile,
the River Chart and the Book from Luo,
the Qílín bearing armor in its mouth,
yellow fishes surging in waves,
red birds soaring and delivering tokens,
and threefold meetings of turning winds—
all happened in times with rulers,
and never appeared in ages without kings.
These auspicious signs
point to the mysterious apex,
sometimes marking tokens of dynastic change,
sometimes showing the prosperity of ideal rule.
If you say having rulers
does not accord with Heaven's intent,
then how could auspicious responses come—
who would cause them?
If you consider chaos and darkness as the highest good,
then Heaven and Earth should never have been separated;
if namelessness is supreme,
then the eight trigrams should not have been drawn.
Could it be that creation itself was in error,
and Tài Hào was in the dark?
True teachings honor only what is natural.
If I may ask: to know the mother but forget the father
—is that the nature of all living things?
Bowing and prostration in reverence
are only the latter adornments of the world.
Yet nature cannot be solely followed;
one must honor the father.
Ornamentation cannot be utterly discarded;
there must be bowing.
If all were either followed or discarded,
how could this suffice?
In ancient times, the living had no beams or houses,
the dead had no coffins or burial,
rivers had no boats or oars,
and land had no use for carts or horses.
People swallowed and ate poisonous things,
which led to their demise.
Illnesses had no medical techniques,
and wrongful deaths were without limit.
In later ages, the sages
reformed these ways and passed them down;
and to this day the people
rely on their profound benefaction.
The advantages of clever devices
are not easily overthrown.
Now suppose you were made to live in the mean caves and nests of old,
and the dead were abandoned in the wild fields;
when hindered by water, you would swim across;
when traveling mountains, you would go on foot bearing burdens;
you would discard cauldrons and tripods, eating raw and fetid food;
you would forgo acupuncture and stone needles and leave illnesses to nature.
Nakedness would be your adornment,
and you would not wear clothing;
when you met a woman, you would pair off
without need of a go-between.
You, sir, would surely say:
'It is not possible.
' How much less could we do without a ruler?
If the people of antiquity could truly be like wood or stone,
and if thick ice could freeze yet not be cold,
and if all sustenance were cut off yet they did not hunger,
then perhaps it could be so.
But as long as desires for food and clothing
dwell in their hearts,
that which they contend for is not always gold and jade,
nor do they always compete for honorable positions!
Even acorns and wild grasses can give rise to disputes,
and pigweed and coarse greens are enough
to bring about plunder.
For the nature of desire
sprouts at the very start of receiving breath,
and self-interest
is visible from the day the form is completed;
theft, murder, and mutual predation
arise naturally.
If you expect disorder not to come,
how is that possible?
When a sagely king presides above,
and all the ministers strive to fulfill their duties,
sitting in waiting for dawn,
breakfasting late into the morning,
inviting criticism to attack faults,
charging favorites and relatives to make corrections,
listening to the songs of the people to reflect and examine,
taking warning from footsteps behind to remain vigilant at night,
sending forth a clear wind to sweep away filth,
wielding autumnal severity to maintain order,
establishing strict and fine laws,
punishing all offenders without pardon,
sentencing and executing to warn against small crimes,
launching great campaigns to punish monstrous villains,
then still, it is like wolves and tigers blocking the road—
distressed that right order among men is not established,
anxious for the harm that tyranny will bring to families,
afraid that cunning and evil will bring ruin to the state.
Hence strict officials like hawks patrol to strike the unruly,
and ministers fierce as tigers wield weapons in the mountains,
yet the wild and the cunning
have never been absent from the world;
but if you let them loose,
so they are utterly unafraid,
then Dào Zhí will run rampant, robbing and killing,
while the upright and good stand idle with folded arms, awaiting disaster.
There will be no lord to whom complaints can be brought,
no power to whom one can turn for help,
and to hope for each family to be like Yí and Qí,
and every person to be Liǔ Huì—
