it is like carrying a pig and wishing there were no smell,
or wading through a river and wishing not to get wet,
or driving wild horses without bits and reins,
or sailing a light boat with no oar or rudder.
I have never seen such a thing as possible."
Bào Shēng objected again, saying:
"The ordering of Heaven and Earth
gave form to things through the two energies;
those who delight in yang float among the clouds;
those who love yin settle in rivers.
Following both softness and hardness, each responds to its nature;
according to the cycles, all transform and are born;
each clings to what suits it
—in origin, there is no high or low.
Once ruler and subject are established,
then changes and complications arise.
If there are many otters, the fish are alarmed;
if there are many hawks, the birds are disordered;
if officials are set up, then the people are burdened;
if much is supplied to those above, then the people below become poor.
When treasure and goods are hoarded,
and fine trinkets and grand halls are sought,
food is prepared by the square yard,
robes are embroidered with dragons,
within are gathered unwed women,
without many unmarried men,
rare treasures are distinguished and valued,
strange and grotesque things are held dear,
useless devices are made,
and desires are indulged without end.
They are neither ghosts nor gods—
from where comes all this wealth and strength?
When grain and silk are piled up, the people suffer hunger and cold;
when government posts are fully staffed, consumption and expense follow.
Palace guards are a multitude who eat doing nothing;
the people support idle men;
the people lack food and clothing,
struggling to provide for themselves,
how much more if taxes are imposed
and harsh labor added?
The people below cannot bear it,
frozen and hungry,
they break the law and it runs rampant—
it is because of this.
The king is burdened with cares above,
and officials below wear sorrowful faces;
they tread on the edge of danger,
fearing disaster may strike.
Fearing that the wise and brave are not employed,
he offers them high rank and heavy salaries as inducements;
dreading the unexpected outbreak of treachery,
he fortifies walls and deepens moats in defense.
Yet he does not know that high salaries impoverish the people and strengthen his ministers,
and severe fortifications add to the labor and sharpen the skills of attackers.
So when the gold from the Lùtái is distributed,
and the grain from the Great Granary is given out,
there is joy everywhere;
how much more if gold had never been piled up
and the people’s grain never seized at all?
If oxen rest in Táolín,
and horses are released in Huà Shān,
and shields and spears are put away,
and bows and arrows are placed in their cases,
people still believe this is great peace;
how much more if there had never been armies
nor any need to fight or garrison troops?
Thatched cottages and earthen steps,
no more weaving or gathering of wild vegetables,
sacks mixed together as curtains,
washing fur robes and wearing cloth quilts,
concubines clothed not in silk,
horses not fed on grain,
frugality guiding all,
all praised as fine things—
just as when Dào Zhí divided stolen wealth,
those who took the least yielded;
or like fish living on land,
breathing moisture on each other for comfort.
When none are pressed into public service,
and households pay no taxes,
they cherish their homes and delight in their work;
following the order of Heaven and the division of land,
within, there is enough for clothing and food,
without, there is no strife for power or profit.
Those who wield staffs and rob others,
do so not by human feeling.
When the law is only a model,
none among the people break it;
but as prohibitions and orders multiply,
thieves and bandits increase.
Is it that those earlier lacked a desire for profit, while now alone they are greedy and cruel?
It is only that if I keep myself pure and calm, the people will be upright;
if those below are weary and resentful, then cunning and trickery arise.
If things are left to their natural course,
there are still fears of violence;
if they are toiled without rest,
and plundered without end,
fields grow wild and granaries are empty,
the shuttle and loom stand idle,
food does not fill the mouth,
and clothes do not cover the body.
If you wish then that there should be no disorder,
how can it be done?
Thus, in seeking to rescue from disaster, disaster only grows deeper;
with ever-stricter prohibitions, the prohibitions do not cease.
Passes and bridges are set to prevent wrongdoing,
but corrupt officials use them to do wrong.
Weights and measures are established to check deception,
but evil men use them for their own deceit.
The reason great ministers uphold the endangered,
is because treacherous officials fear the ruler is not endangered.
Weapons and armor are used to pacify difficulties,
yet raiders and thieves exploit them to create disturbances.
All these are outcomes caused by those who govern.
When the people have something profitable,
they develop contentious hearts;
in the households of the wealthy and noble,
the stakes of profit are very high.
Moreover, when the common people contend,
it is no more than a trifling matter;
when an ordinary man vies in strength,
how much harm can be done?
There is no territory for him to covet,
no city walls from which to profit,
no gold or treasure he may desire,
no power or authority for him to compete for;
he lacks the means to gather followers,
and his might is insufficient to command outsiders.
How could this compare to the king, when roused in wrath,
deploying armies and mustering troops,
driving innocent people,
and attacking guiltless states?
The corpses then number in the tens of thousands,
and the flowing blood stains shields and reddens the wilds.
A tyrant without virtue,
there has never been an age without one;
when he indulges in cruelty and disorder,
under heaven there is no true state then,
loyal and worthy men are harmed within,
and the common people perish exposed beyond.
How could this merely be the peril of petty quarrels over trifles?
Reaching the point where fathers are made to serve their rulers,
and filial piety is abandoned for loyalty,
decrees are issued without regard for sovereigns—
these are of the same kind.
In ancient times, houses
were sufficient to shelter from wind and rain,
but now they are adorned with vermillion and purple,
and embellished with gold and jade;
the clothing of the ancients
sufficed to cover their form,
but now it is of black and yellow with elaborate embroidery,
of fine, brocaded silks;
the music of old
sufficed to regulate human feelings,
but now it is troubled by licentious sounds,
disturbing the soul and harming harmony;
in food and drink of old,
it sufficed to fill hunger and emptiness,
but now forests are burned and pools are drained,
and the lives of many creatures are slaughtered.
(Below are the words of critical rebuttal by Bào Pǔzǐ) “Can it be that, because a thing has faults, one should utterly reject it?
If Yú were above,
and Jì and Xiè assisted in affairs,
with humble palaces and light taxes,
employing the people according to the seasons,
exalting the pure practice of thrift,
and strictly forbidding extravagant feasts;
if plainness and simplicity
were honored and made manifest,
and those who disrupt order and oppress the people
were dismissed and punished;
then praise would arise and the common people would be at peace.
Why worry of fire and then demolish all houses,
or fear wind and waves and fill in all the great rivers?”
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
“Bào-shēng values the theory of the ancients that advocated having no sovereign,
but I have already refuted it.
What he has since replied to me
is too lengthy to include in full,
so I shall select his main ideas and address them one by one.”
Bào-shēng says:
“The ruler amasses hard-to-get treasures,
gathers rare and strange things,
adorns himself with useless luxuries,
and is never sated in his desires.”
Bào Pǔzǐ replies:
“Let me ask: of the emperors and kings, past and present,
did all amass hard-to-get treasures,
and gather rare and strange things?
There are those who did not do so.
I have heard that Táng Yáo, as ruler,
abandoned gold in the mountains;
Yú Shùn, when abdicating,
cast away jades into the valleys.
Their meals were plain, their clothing humble;
compared to the gatekeeper,
they never plunged to the depths to find pearls,
toppled cliffs to mine jade,
split stone to smelt gold and silver ore,
crossed the sea to gather kingfisher feathers,
or netted tortoise shell from remote regions,
or dug up cinnabar and azurite from Mín and Hàn;
this much is clear.
If not for distinctions in attire,
then the dignity of rank would not be evident;
if names and ranks were not different,
then the ritual articles would not have different numbers or grades.
Thus, Zhōu Gōng established the distinctions of noble and base, high and low,
set standards for mansions and dwellings,
determined their size and limits,
and regulated caps, canopies, banners, and flags,
establishing embellishments for ritual vessels;
regarding chariots, clothing, utensils,
determined measures of more or less;
for kitchens and sacrifices,
established categories of regulated meals.
In years of famine or disaster,
these were reduced or omitted.
Unending desires
do not exist in an age of true governance.
What you have criticized
can serve to denounce the crimes of Jié and Zhòu,
but is no decisive proof for refined discourse.
Bào-shēng says:
“The ruler's harem numbers three thousand—
is that truly Heaven’s intent?
When grain and silk accumulate, the people are left hungry and cold.”
Bào Pǔzǐ replies:
“The number of consorts for a king
was fixed by the sages.
The sages
possess virtue united with Heaven and Earth.
Their virtue in accord with Heaven and Earth—
how could that simply be arbitrary!
Is it merely to gratify and fill personal desires?
It is in order to assist the Six Palaces,
regulate yīn and yáng,
teach and honor sacrifices to the ancestral temple,
reverently perform the great sacrifices,
furnish the dark-colored ceremonial robes,
and extend the lineage’s branches.
Furthermore, according to the records of nine regions in the Zhōu canon,
and the treatises in the geography of the Hàn line,
the number of women in the realm
exceeds that of men.
That which kindred kings rely upon
is certainly not enough to suit the marriageable ones.
Jī-gōng, consider this:
it should be clear.
The emperor leads all ministers in tilling the fields,
the empress and consorts lead the noblewomen in weaving silk;
thus down to the common people,
farming tasks have quotas,
productive cultivation is rewarded,
and idleness punished.
One in ten is taxed,
to supply public needs.
Each household stores reserves for bad years,
each state accumulates grain for nine years.
All submit to the proper division of heaven and earth,
not depriving the people of their times,
corvée and taxes are light and rare,
so that none are hungry and cold.
With food and clothing sufficient,
ritual and deference arise among them.
In the era of Wén and Jǐng,
the people diligently farmed,
households were well supplied,
and the grains in the state granaries
piled up and rotted in uncountable amounts.
Yet commoners and gentry still enjoyed fine clothing and rich food,
and cattle and horses filled the marshlands,
for taxes were levied with moderation,
never to the harm of the people below.
By the end times,
officials lost control over agricultural quotas,
private pursuits turned toward trivial trades,
and the ways of growing grain were not extended,
while idle and itinerant people multiplied.
Thus, high and low alike transgressed,
and lawbreakers increased.
Now Bào-shēng places the blame on having a ruler.
As for censure beyond reasonable limits,
or criticism that agricultural quotas are not met,
or complaints about the ruler's three thousand cattle,
belittling the assessed acreage or the greater part,
as long as the harem adheres to the Rites of Zhōu,
and taxes and levies are not arbitrarily imposed,
all is acceptable.
But must there be no ruler at all!
If one day you rise late,
your tasks go awry.
If the deer have no warden,
they vanish into the woods,
how could order be maintained?
When there is nothing to unify all under,
the worthy have nothing to look up to,
and the wicked achieve their aims.
If loose meshes in a net still let some through,
can you do without a net entirely?”
Bào Shēng said:
"Human life is already burdened with clothing and food;
these matters are toil enough.
How much more so when further compounded by taxes and levies,
and weighed down by forced labor?
Hunger and cold come together;
people at the bottom cannot endure it.
Braving the law and violating prohibitions,
it is thus that they are compelled to live."
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"The spider spins its web,
yet fleas and lice are not starved.
Humans possess intelligence and skill,
employ all things under heaven,
eat their fill and clothe their bodies;
what hardship is there in this?
The trouble lies only in the wealthy lacking a mind to know limits,
the noble possessing endless desires.
Is it because of a single stumble
that one should never walk again for life?
And, considering the cruelty of Jié and Zhòu,
to imagine as if there were no sovereign—
when affairs are most overreaching
and taxes more oppressive than of old,
the people’s strength exhausted by trivial labors,
these are sources of hunger and cold
and may be criticized for that.
But to claim that the existence of corvée and taxes
brings chaos to the state,
then let me ask: in the peaceful times of Tāng and Yú,
in the age of virtuous governance by the Three Dynasties,
was it really that there were no taxes or labor levies to provide for those in office?
Did the sovereign and his ministers
personally till the fields to support themselves?
Bào Shēng merely knows when hunger and cold arrive together;
he cannot endure hardship resolutely,
and does not realize that when clothing and food are ample,
the people come to know honor and shame!"
Bào Shēng said:
"When the king treads on deep waters and walks upon the tail of a tiger,
such metaphors are insufficient to describe his peril.
He feigns sleep awaiting the dawn,
eats late each day after dusk;
so what fear is there of calamity striking him?"
Bào Pǔzǐ replied, challenging him:
"If assuredly one could be like this,
then truly he would be a sagely ruler.
The problem with kings
lies in arrogance and extravagance:
the worthy are not employed,
and those employed are not worthy.
Jiǎ Guǐ of Xià compared himself to heaven and sun;
Qín Shǐhuáng fretted over having the same posthumous title for ten thousand generations,
thus bringing ruin upon himself,
becoming a laughingstock for the ages.
If only they could truly fear danger and be vigilant by night,
widely accepting remonstrance and criticism,
seeking advice from commoners as Yáo did,
nourishing the old to elicit their words,
then what worry would there be that government would go astray?
What anxiety that a hundred offices would fail to flourish?
For in trembling wariness, order is established in human relations;
in indolence and neglect, treachery and villainy arise.
How much more so if there were no ruler—
could there be no disorder?"
Bào Shēng said:
"Kings esteem auspicious omens and marvels,
seeking out the hidden and the wild,
desiring thereby to exalt virtue and enhance prestige.
Yet the dazzling does not impress the unconquered;
white pheasants and jade rings—
what benefit are these to the common people?"
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"When the king’s virtue reaches heaven, there are heavenly omens;
when virtue reaches the earth, there are earthly responses.
If the shining star emits brilliance,
assisting the splendor of Wàngshū;
if the luminous crown contains keen discernment,
marking the sundials of Xīhé;
if numinous birds call harmoniously in the eaves and towers,
golden elephants shine radiant in the clear ponds—
could these be obtained through humble words
or enticed by lavish gifts?
Wáng Mǎng was cunning and treacherous,
harbored a mind of rebellion,
forged documents to feign peace,
deceived both court and country,
bestowed gifts upon distant lands
to induce them to send tribute of auspicious objects.
Can it be said, then, that this was always the way of antiquity?
When one sees a tail as long as ten fathoms,
he knows it cannot belong to a body only a foot in size;
when one beholds tusks many fathoms high,
he knows they cannot be borne by a mouth an inch wide.
Thus, the Queen Mother of the West’s envoys
signified the transformation of mysterious virtue,
with none too distant to come drawn in;
the repeated embassies from Yuèchāng
prove how beneficence reached far lands,
and that the king’s grace covered all without exception.
Remote territories cannot be subdued by force,
nor the Mānmò pacified by might.
Unless there is perfect governance,
how could such wonders come about?
On what grounds does Bào Shēng claim them to be useless?
The Zhōu court was not poor in jade, nor did it need the Queen Mother’s ring to consider itself wealthy;
nor was its cuisine frugal so as to crave the white pheasant from Yuèchāng to fill its kitchens.
That these things were prized
truly shows that such objects signify peace and prosperity.
When above there is no oppressive governance,
and below no one has lost their place,
all that crawls and flies
obtain their joy;
what greater mark of a well-ordered state could there be than this!
Who can match such beauty?
And yet you call them useless,
of no benefit to the people?
The origin is remote, the essence vast—
it is not easily perceived.
Are not Bào Shēng’s words
only fitting as they are?"
Bào Shēng said:
"Sovereigns fear unforeseen treachery and crime,
therefore they build fortified cities to guard against them."
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"Lords and kings erect fortifications—
the Dà Yì esteems this.
Yet if one does not discern the need for strongholds,
what is there to criticize?
When Yīn and Yáng began to function,
all things came into being,
and thus good and evil were present together.
The sage recognizes the naturalness of malefactors,
the difficulty of transforming the thoroughly foolish—
just as the spring sun cannot revive withered trees,
or blazing sunlight cannot melt metals and stones.
Flaunting one’s looks and carelessly storing treasures
entices wantonness and invites thieves;
thus they take as their model the hexagram “Kǎn” to
prepare for troubles before they emerge.
Multiple gates are signs of vigilance against the night,
and military discipline checks the threat of violent intruders;
to wish all this away—
what reasoning could there be?
The rhinoceros has its horn,
the phoenix its spur;
Heaven granted these things,
yet they are not used daily!
Bees and scorpions carry venom to defend themselves,
wise birds carry reeds to break traps,
the badger curves its burrow
to guard against surprise attacks,
water buffalo form ranks
to ward off tigers and leopards—
and yet Bào Shēng wants to cast aside armor and shields to resist sharp blades,
and to tear down walls and moats to block advancing troops.
Should armor truly be discarded, yet blades still not halted;
fortresses destroyed, but attacks keep assembling—
then even Gōngshū and Mò Dí
could not protect themselves.
Pray, from your perspective,
what would you have us do?"
Someone said:
"If a thing is not desirable enough,
even without strong cities or walls,
no enemy will come to take it."
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"As to what is desirable,
why must it be gold and jade?
Even the tip of an awl or a dagger,
fools contend over.
The great battle among the Yuè people
arose over who would claim a giant python;
the war between Wú and Chǔ
was triggered by a single mulberry leaf.
In times of famine,
people ate each other,
baring white hands and going barefoot.
As for times further past, there were Lord Fǔ and Zǐ Gāo;
closer to us, Yú Gōng and Shì Zhī—
they governed emotions and judged punishments,
splitting the hair and weighing the finest point.
Those who suffered punishment would stifle sobs and praise their rulers’ virtue;
even those who lost noses bore no grudge to the end.
Yet none of these were times without a ruler.
In the past there were orphans below, yet the Four Mountains did not shield them;
the worthy hidden in humble places, but all talents were raised up.
Some cast away the butcher’s knife and entered the golden gates;
others abandoned basket-weaving and tread upon jade halls.
Some forsook tending livestock and rose to high office;
others went from fugitives to grand generals.
Bó Liǔ took vengeance upon a foe,
and Jiě Hú recommended his enemy;
Fāng Huí knocked his head on the ground to introduce scholars,
Qín Xī sacrificed his life to promote the worthy.
May I ask, in those times,
was there or was there not a ruler?"
It is also said:
“Fields lie fallow and granaries stand empty,
all because there is a ruler.”
“Yet the ruler is not the tangled weeds choking the fields,
nor are ministers the sparrows and rats that deplete the storehouse.
If there are fallows and emptiness,
it ultimately arises from misfortunes passing through the household,
such as floods, droughts, pestilence, and plague,
leading to calamity and famine.
Is it truly in the levying of taxes
and governmental orders that it is so?
As for food, the very head of the eight political concerns,
it is called the people’s heaven.
Hòu Jì toiled in the fields himself,
Yǒu Yú plowed with his own hands;
in plentiful years, there was abundance of millet and rice,
our granaries held a hundred million,
the people ate of the stored grain.
The Bai Canal opened, expelling brine and turning saline earth into fertile soil;
Shào Fù raised the reservoirs at Yánglíng and piled up grain into mountains;
Shū Áo innovated at Qī Sī, and every household had aged millet;
Zhào Guò invented the skillful three-plow method, so Guān Yòu became prosperous;
Rèn Yán taught the people of Jiǔ Zhēn how to cultivate, and the common folk of Qián feasted abundantly;
were these not all times when there was a ruler!”
Bào Pǔ Zǐ said:
“No blessing is greater than having no insatiable desires,
no fortune richer than knowing when to stop.
Those who are full yet dwell in emptiness
are surely skilled in preserving themselves;
those who indulge in ease, comfort, and abundance
find it hard to guard against disaster.
As for the likes of Shàn Juǎn, Cháo Xǔ, Guǎn Hú, and their company,
all tread lightly on the clouds and things in high pursuit,
depending on dragons and phoenixes to hold themselves apart;
discerning hidden dangers amidst fragrant baits,
recognizing upturned carts on the road where hubs pass by,
avoiding perilous paths and traveling far to safety—
thus they could escape the fisher’s net of Zhān Hé,
truly adept at foreseeing subtle omens beyond appearances,
perceiving solid ice before frost,
moving fuel and bending chimneys before the fire rages,
securing boats and pulling in oars before the storm arises,
seeing danger to the nine oxen and sinking deep into the pond,
glimpsing dense thickets and swiftly passing by,
not building nests at the tips of reeds and rushes,
nor reclining on the crumbling cliffs of collapsing mountains.
These all had vessels vast and noble,
judged opportunities and understood outcomes,
went their own way beyond the crowd,
not pulled by common desires,
with spirits aligned with creation,
hearts detached from all things,
so that desire could not disturb their pure essence,
and nearness to reason could not corrode their clarity.
If one lacks such spontaneous nature,
it is truly hard to attain such extraordinary conduct.
Merely knowing that when one’s merit is accomplished, one must retire—
taking on the greatest labors yet accepting no reward;
when the crafty hare dies, the hunting hound is no longer needed,
when the high-flying birds are gone, the fine bow is set aside.
Reflecting on the bright mirror of Péng and Hán,
recalling the art of withdrawing;
seeing the hidden mechanisms among the Yuè clan,
discerning the worth of golden statues.
If Fàn Gōng sailed away to escape at the height of the sun,
Xuē Shēng resigned amidst chaos to preserve his purity;
the two Shū cast away their seals when at the height of success,
Tián Yù laid down his cords when time was running out.
Advancing, they avoided the reproach of arrogance;
withdrawing, they lacked the regret of hesitating too long.
Their refreshing example is enough to dispel the dust of a thousand generations,
their virtuous words enough to clear away the confusion of those to come.
Compared to displaying treasures,
is this not truly distant and rare!
Some with little wisdom fail in great schemes,
some with weak axles break under heavy burdens,
some, being right alone, fall into the opposition of the crowd,
some, in full loyalty, are exposed by those who see to all sides.
Some proposed high strategies and suffered the misfortune of Cháo Cuò,
some gave their whole heart and strength and met the fate of Wú Qǐ.
Thus, those with wide mouths and high palates—
even so, they could not escape.
The exile of Gōng Dàn,
the wanderings of Zhòng Ní,
Jiǎ Shēng demoted among the lowest officials,
Zǐ Cháng poisoned in innocence,
Yuè Yì pacified Qí,
Wǔ Yuán overthrew Chǔ,
Bái Qǐ expanded the borders with a hundred victories,
Wén Zǐ with nine stratagems dominated Yuè,
Hán Xìn’s merit overshadowed the world,
Qíng Bù destroyed his own family in service of the throne,
their glory did not last the turning of the sun,
disgrace had already come upon them.
Not evading such misfortune—
was this truly wise?
To be a minister is not easy,
nor is there but one path.
In short,
it all depends on choosing the right master.
I am not to be relied upon,
the evidence is as above.
Declining office and yielding to the worthy,
keeping pure and at peace,
with a fair name and solid virtue—
is there any greater good fortune!
Of those able to employ this method,
seldom one in ten thousand.
Good and ill arise from people,
how could one not reflect on this?
Words that offend the ear—
those who enjoy them are few;
offering advice in pursuit of glory
is to invite disaster upon oneself.
There is no time to prevent slander and defamation,
how certain can one be that honesty will always be received!
When arrows fly thick and fast, the young mandarin ducks beat their wings in confusion,
when pits and snares fill the path, the qilin and deer draw in their traces.
Feelings cannot reach their utmost,
desires cannot be completely satisfied.
The wise one regulates feelings by way,
uses strategy to disperse desires;
even those who advise on plans should employ loyalty,
how much more so when planning for oneself, and not with care!
So one who knows sufficiency is always satisfied,
one who knows not sufficiency is never satisfied.
The ever-content
attracts fortune,
the never-satisfied
summons disaster.
To value life greatly,
and yet seek to destroy it—
like the Song family pulling up shoots,
the Ying man stretching silks,
both in pursuit of quick gains,
actually hasten wilting and breakage.
To know how to advance and not retreat—
is this not the case?
A cart that runs but does not stop
seldom avoids overturning;
one who treads the waves without rest
rarely escapes drowning;
one who plays with blades without ceasing
will surely be wounded;
the one who hacks and strikes without pause
is doomed to dings and breaks.
To be full is to invite loss,
this is the law of nature;
the vessel of Zhōu's ancestral temple—
did it ever deceive us?
Thus, Yǎng Yóu’s archery,
made the passersby know by the twang of his bowstring;
Dōng Yě’s charioteering,
Yán Zǐ discerned its coming failure;
beneath the peak of success,
it is not easy to abide long.
Those who drink wine do not all descend into chaos,
yet many are ruined;
not all the wealthy and noble are in peril,
yet some are.
The wise judge matters by what lies beyond the visible,
hews wood at the very tip of the shoot,
utters high words not in the midst of rivalry,
discusses the mending of furs not among the pack of foxes.
The ancients feigned madness or folly—
was this for pleasure?
The times compelled it,
they had no choice.
Yet some, though fleeing deep into hiding, met upon the waves with peril;
some concealed themselves in darkness but were caught in fire;
as Gōng Shèng starved himself and met his end,
as Lǐ Yè tortured himself and swallowed poison;
all because there was some trace left,
their shadows were not extinguished.
If one could act as if treading ice,
stand as if dwelling in shade,
leave no trace in movement,
and in stillness be united with non-action,
how could such dangers arise?
All the more so for those who expose themselves to the world,
or beat the drum to parade their sharp tools!
Those who meet a bright age excel in aiding the realm,
those who face troubled times cannot even protect themselves;
for this, everlasting regret arises,
not for a single worthy alone.
I have heard that without excess there is no destruction,
and without overflow there is no loss.
Brilliance and splendor contain the omen of ashes,
spring grass is the beginning of autumn’s withering.
When the sun reaches its zenith, it begins to decline;
when the moon is full, it begins to wane.
Such is the sequence of the four seasons:
those who achieve success must recede.
If one takes far from things,
then one may build boundless heights and steep summits,
but collapse and ruin are then the only worries;
if one takes near from oneself,
then to indulge in fine food and delicious wine without restraint,
is to accumulate sickness and harm one’s nature.
How much more, if one’s lofty ambitions reach the clouds and still do not cease,
one’s power shakes rulers and is ever increased,
yet there is no end to it!
When a mosquito or gadfly falls from a mountain,
it only soars and flies;
should an ox or tiger fall,
it is smashed to pieces.
This shows that for great things,
one must not let them lose their proper place.
If one confronts wrongs with uprightness,
walks the straight path,
strikes against the established order,
and does not consider enmity or resentment,
then grievances grow deep and hatred accumulates.
If one sets aside the law to accommodate error,
accepts all as echoes,
spits out the strong and swallows the yielding,
twists and bends the rules and standards,
then loyalty and righteousness will be lost and defeated.
Those who dwell in such a place,
how can they avoid exhaustion?
Thus, those who preserve both their person and reputation are extremely rare,
while cases of broken limbs and overturned rice bowls are not lacking.
Yet when one enters, there are secluded orchid chambers,
vermilion curtains and brocade canopies,
embroidered mats spread through splendid halls,
brilliant beauty shining brightly on every side,
graceful bodies and soft voices,
pure songs and exquisite dances,
the skill of Sòng Cài,
the loveliness of Yáng’ē,
the mouth sings the melodious compositions of Biàn Líng Yán Lù,
the feet tread the seven-fold rhythms of Lùshuǐ,
knowing sounds delight the ear,
charming forms please the heart.
Secret banquets gather in succession,
fine wine never removed,
looking up to ascend ornate towers,
looking down to reflect on clear springs,
wandering among orchards of lush red and green,
frolicking in fragrant gardens of orchids,
colorful fish swim in abundance,
red birds fly in formation,
captive swans fall from the clouds,
silken lines draw up chub and carp,
distant treasures sought without effort gather together,
delights and luxuries arrive unbidden.
Going out, there are ruby wheels glinting along the road,
tall canopies meeting at the axles,
scarlet banners like clouds,
emblems and scepters blazing,
sweet delicacies and rare foods are presented,
arms and armor flashing brilliantly,
the favored are carried in the rear chariot,
fine flavors fill the accompanying carts,
pleasures of sight-seeing pursued to their limit,
the joys of hunting and fishing exhausted.
Praise for sage wisdom,
fills the ears as it enters;
words of flattery and delight,
come from many mouths in unison.
At such a time, in one’s mind,
the ancients are dismissed with contempt,
one claims Yī, Lǚ, Guǎn, and Yàn
are not worth considering.
How could one then perceive that exaltation and decline are the head and tail of each other,
joy and sorrow are morning and evening to each other,
and be willing to leave riches and honor,
to request retirement,
to turn away from vermilion gates and return to hills and gardens!
If a sage and enlightened one is above,
great worthies assist in governance,
all ministries advance only by him,
the multitudes prosper only by him,
he is high yet does not fear danger,
full yet does not worry about overflow—
such a one is beyond discussion.
Someone asked:
“Those of extraordinary talent,
why are some poor and some successful,
what is the reason for this?
When the outstanding are held back and depressed,
do they bear resentment?”
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
“When skills and accomplishments do not differ,
but some are suppressed and others exalted,
it is because there is no one who recognizes them.
Thus adversity and prosperity are due to the times,
success and failure are due to fate.
He who understands the times, what grievance has he with being hidden and obscure,
he who knows his fate, what regret for being lowly and exhausted!
Thus the sword of Shěn Lǘ and Tíng Jūn,
though an excellent and refined blade,
if not used for cutting,
cannot even slice through a mushroom;
the shell of the pearl oyster and the green luster of Lí Lǜ,
though treasures worth a city,
a if left in the mud,
are covered with tiles and pebbles.
Therefore, a thing may be precious without being appreciated as precious,
may be useful and yet not be used.
Ordinary and vulgar men,
dull in distinguishing things,
do not tell vermilion from purple,
cannot distinguish beans from wheat;
they simply regard the successful as the worthy,
yet do not know to what chance those succeed;
they call the unsuccessful inferior,
yet do not examine why those who keep to the Way are unsuccessful.
Suppose the hanging image did not match the sky,
then it could not spread great brilliance unbounded;
were Sōng and Dài not set on the earth,
they could not tower and soar to the clouds.
The rabbit’s speed comes from level paths,
the dragon boat gains swiftness from rushing currents;
flint and tinder do not ignite without Suìrén,
Chǔ gold is not sharpened without Ōuyě;
the beauty of blooming waits for spring to burst forth,
the wild goose waits for the strong wind to fly swiftly;
were the Four Peaks not clearly exalted,
Guān could never achieve office;
if Shū Yá did not recommend the worthy,
Yíwú would not have been highly regarded;
Ráng Jū relied on Píng Zhòng to rise far and high,
Huái Yīn rose through Lord Xiāo to spread his wings,
Jun born through Shèng Zhī's speech,
Qūnì relied on Wúzhī's recommendation,
Yuán Zhí rose by Lóng Yíng’s Zhūgě Liàng,
Gōngjìn was presented to Xìngbà by Hǔwò,
so their glorious names are inscribed in the imperial register,
and their achievements renowned in their time.
At the end of the Hàn and the last years of Wú,
this was not so.
When promoting gentlemen,
one always chose those who were personally attached;
in selecting men,
numerous partisans determined the decision;
but those attached to oneself were not necessarily fit for advancement,
yet because they agreed with one,
they could not be left out;
and those with many partisans were not necessarily outstanding in talent,
yet because public opinion was trusted,
they were deemed suitable.
Thus sometimes one believes these commonplace and vulgar men,
unable to cast off personal feelings;
others recognize the exceptional talents,
but cannot be impartial toward utmost fairness.
So the standards of selection were set aside,
and personal associations determined weight;
measures were abandoned,
and circle of friends determined status.
Among those then called “gentlemen of refined manners,”
holding the strings of government,
deciding promotion and demotion themselves,
praise and blame depended on their words,
few indeed escaped this burden.
All the more when the heart naturally harbors hatred for the independent,
envy those not of their party,
begrudge anyone greater than themselves,
and ignore those from humble origins!
Alas!
Those who are far from the common ways,
those who are unique and apart,
their failure to meet their match and stand shoulder to shoulder,
cannot be counted;
some are suppressed and stagnate amid swamps and marshes,
some stand in court only to be repelled and dismissed.
One may cultivate virtue, yet the Way does not prevail;
store up talent, yet the appointed time does not arrive;
some wait for the Huáng Hé to run clear, only for their teeth to be long gone;
some exhaust their loyal diligence yet are never recognized;
those who journey afar are not celebrated in their generation;
meritorious beneficence is not bestowed upon the people.
Rare treasures upon a mat,
covered in mud and mire;
the ability to benefit others,
in the end, finds no place to be employed.
Wielding a builder’s tool, but not encountering Wǔ Dīng;
holding a fishing pole, but not meeting Xī Bó.
From ancient times until now,
how could there be a limit to such things?
And to dwell alone in grief over this,
is it not rather narrow-minded!
Beholding the distant path,
and being ashamed to follow it;
knowing that the Way is blocked,
and yet not seeking to change it.
For those who regard success and failure as one and the same,
who entrust honor and disgrace to the natural order,
how could they harbor melancholy from being little known,
or let the endless sighs arise like a river’s flow!
If one suspects there is regret here,
then one has not yet understood the intent of the True Person.
It is as the young do not comprehend the old;
as the frog in the well does not understand the vast sea—
such has always been the way.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
“I have a friend, Xuán Bó Xiānshēng,
whose age was at the learning of wisdom,
yet already he had exhausted the scrutiny of the Six Categories,
and made a broad study of the Hé-Luò classics.
By day, he vied with Xī Hé for the last rays of sunlight;
by evening, he gazed at the lingering glow of Wàng Shū.
No path was too distant for his inquiry,
no topic too subtle to be explored.
He took the teachings of Confucians and Mòzǐ as his city walls,
and spiritual insight as his shields and spears.
Thus all who conversed with him looked up to him and presented their jade tokens;
literary scholars rose early to witness his writings.
But soon he awoke to the wisdom of not speaking,
perceiving that precise measurement brings no blame;
when understanding is attained, even the precious qúan and tí may be discarded;
when the Way is at variance, one’s voice goes unjoined in song.
Therefore, he honored Lǎozi’s admonition regarding excessive failure,
and pondered the teaching of the threefold silence of the Golden Man;
he reined in his sharpness, became like the taciturn Tán Táo,
composed writings with cinnabar-tipped brushes;
held gold in his mouth and jade in his bosom;
suppressing ornate eloquence,
throughout the day and far into night,
he would often speak not a single word.
One of his students stepped forward and said:
‘Teacher, you are always silent;
why should I, your humble disciple, speak at all?
It is no different from the manner of common men.
I venture that if a bell does not ring,
it is no different from a pile of bronze;
if a floating chime is silent,
it is indistinguishable from a heap of stones.’
Xuán Bó Xiānshēng replied:
‘My aim is only to preserve a distant reputation through ten thousand generations,
to seek understanding friends among those who come after;
how could I merely compete for recognition today,
or distinguish myself for but a single moment?
If a potter’s vessel is used to store wine,
though fine, it is unseen at the banquet;
when one’s status is low and yet his words are lofty,
though true, he is not believed.
Simply wagging the tongue and exhausting one’s voice,
how can that remedy one’s passing into oblivion?
The ancients at sixty laughed at those of fifty-nine;
not far from confusion and return—
only then do they realize the reason.
The hardness of jade,
the strength of gold,
the coldness of ice,
the heat of fire—
is there need to speak of these
for them to be manifest?
Moreover, the Eight Sounds and Nine Modes
cannot be free from defects of length or shortness;
Yǎng Yóu, even with a hundred arrows, could not fail to miss once—
there must be some lapses.
Those who sport by the river
often drown in its waters;
those who love lively debate
often let slip words from their mouths.
Bó Yá was careful in plucking the strings,
and so was never troubled by clumsy hands;
the Confucians are circumspect in their utterances,
and thus never suffer slander.
The shallow and superficial
are not thus.
They debate hurriedly over meaningless trifles,
argue over petty matters and waste words,
discuss at length the futile theory of ‘white horses are not horses,’
recite the unfounded criticisms of the various philosophers,
undermining instruction and increasing confusion,
yet call it profound and excellent;
abandoning the right canons,
they vie to cultivate heterodox studies.
Some argue victory or defeat of lips and tongues with those of dim insight,
and display elegant discourse before those without understanding;
when there is no worthy rival,
and no bystander to appreciate,
how is it any different from performing elegant music beside mere logs,
or displaying mysterious yellow fabrics before clay statues!
In vain their mouths become dry and breath is spent,
pounding tables and clapping hands;
their axes are blunted and the knotted wood remains unbroken,
their faces flush with anger and they become all the more discordant.
Hence, resentment shows in their features,
ugly words come from their mouths—
fleeting and shallow changes
arise thus among them.
Having already tarnished themselves with error,
it cannot be mended.
It is better to follow the principle that ‘great sound is rare and music is incomplete,’
to keep speech simple and await those with understanding.’
As for Bào Pǔzǐ,
his surname is Gě,
his given name Hóng,
styled Zhìchuān.
He was a native of Jùróng in Dānyáng.
His ancestor was Gě Tiānshì,
who, it is said, once ruled the world in ancient times.
Later his descendants became ranked lords among the feudal states
and thus kept Gě as their surname.
In earlier times, Hóng’s ancestor served as Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
his lord was ashamed to serve a national traitor;
he abandoned office and returned home,
and together with Zhái Yì, Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn, raised troops.
They intended to punish Wáng Mǎng,
but were defeated by him;
when an amnesty was declared, they were spared from disaster.
Thereafter, he feigned illness and withdrew from the world.
Because Wáng Mǎng considered his clan powerful,
he feared a future uprising,
and thus exiled him to Lángyé.
The lord’s son, Pǔlú,
gathered troops to assist Guāngwǔ,
and rendered great service.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Pǔlú as Chariot General.
Later, he was promoted to Grand General of Cavalry,
and ennobled as Marquis of Tóng County in Xiàpī,
with a fief holding five thousand households.
At the founding of the state,
the marquis’s younger brother Wén
accompanied the marquis on campaign,
and achieved many great victories.
Repeatedly, the marquis submitted petitions to commend Wén’s merit,
but since Wén had followed his elder brother unofficially,
he had no record of military title,
and so his achievements were not officially recognized.
The marquis said:
‘My brother braved arrows and stones with me,
wounded and scarred all over,
losing his right eye,
yet did not gain so much as an inch of reward.
I myself receive golden treasures and purple robes—
how can my mind be at peace?’
He thus submitted a memorial, asking that his own title be transferred to his brother.
The memorial reached the court, and
the Hàn dynasty, wishing to fulfill the marquis’s high principle,
granted special approval.
Wén declined,
but could not refuse entirely.
Upon receiving his rank, he moved to the capital,
and established his residence within the Cavalry General’s camp at Bówàng village.
To this day, the foundations and stone pillars remain.
He further divided his income and stipend to provide for his officials and soldiers,
giving to them as if they were like two lords.
The Cavalry General earnestly tried to stop him, but he did not comply.
The Cavalry General said:
‘This merely imposes a greater burden on the people—
what merit is there in such yielding?’
Wén then claimed another errand,
and crossed south over the Jiāng River to settle in Jùróng.
His sons and grandsons cultivated the fields by their own hands,
finding contentment only in their books.
Wén repeatedly sent envoys to persuade the Cavalry General to return,
but he never came back.
He even had people watch over the residence at Bówàng,
in hopes the Cavalry General might return,
so that for generations, there was no longer an inhabitant there.
Hóng's grandfather studied without limit,
investigated subtle and profound matters,
and reached great heights in literature and the arts;
in his era, none could rival him.
He possessed the talents to govern a state,
was benevolent in Wú,
and served successively as magistrate in Hǎiyán,
Lín’ān,
and the three counties of Shānyīn.
He entered the court as Vice Director of Personnel,
Censor-in-Chief,
Grand Administrator of Lúlíng,
Minister of Personnel,
Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince,
Palace Secretariat,
Grand Herald,
Palace Attendant,
Director of the Imperial Household,
General Assisting Wú,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wúshòu County.
Hóng’s father was renowned for his filial piety and brotherly affection,
his conduct was a model for the gentry,
all the books recorded his deeds,
and there was nothing he did not thoroughly examine.
He served as Officer of Five Offices in Wú,
Central Evaluator,
magistrate of Jiànchéng and Nánchāng counties,
Secretary of the Palace Secretariat,
Minister of the Court of Justice,
Assistant Army Protector of Píngzhōng, and
Grand Administrator of Kuàijī.
Before he could resign, the Jìn army moved downstream,
the western borders could not be defended,
and Bó Jiǎn, who possessed both civil and military talent,
won the praise of court and countryside.
All unanimously recommended you.
Thus, you were transferred to five commanderies to respond to alarms.
The Grand Commander provided five thousand personal troops,
put you in charge of conscripted armies,
and sent you to garrison the frontiers.
What Heaven destroys,
man cannot withstand.
The old ruler was reverently mourned,
the nine regions paid respects,
and you, with your former office,
went to take up the post of Palace Attendant.
Gradually, you were promoted to Senior Grand Master,
held the post of Chief Evaluator,
and served as magistrate of Féi Xiāng.
That county had twenty thousand households,
and was the most well-governed of the province.
Your virtuous influence was especially remarkable,
kindness spread and punishments were clear,
songs of praise filled the countryside,
and there were no traces of crime on the roads.
You did not cultivate public fields,
yet boundaries were as lively as a market.
Even the slightest gift
did not enter your gate;
paper and brushes for official use
all came from your private funds.
Punishments were rare and prohibitions effective,
transformation was achieved without words.
Due to illness, you resigned from office,
but were called by imperial edict to serve as Palace Secretary for the King of Wú.
Upright and firm in counsel,
advancing where appropriate, substituting where not,
you promoted the good and corrected wrongs,
so that the military and state were orderly.
You were transferred to Grand Administrator of Shàolíng,
and died in office.
As for Hóng,
he was the third son of your younger brother.
Born late,
he was especially doted on by both parents,
and was not early guided to books and history.
At age thirteen,
his beloved father passed away.
Thus deprived of household instruction,
he suffered hunger and cold, hardship and exhaustion.
He personally tilled and sowed,
rose before dawn and walked the dewy grass,
diligently following ancestral ways.
He frequently endured the devastation of war and fire,
so his forebears’ books were all lost.
In the idle moments after farming, there was nothing left to read,
so he carried his basket and traveled on foot to borrow books.
But even at those homes,
he seldom found complete volumes;
to make up for the lack, he spent his days chopping wood to supply paper and brushes,
settling near farmlands,
and wrote books by the light of firewood.
Because of these circumstances,
he could not engage early in the study of literature.
Paper was often in short supply;
whenever he wrote,
both sides of the page would be filled,
so few could read what he wrote.
At sixteen,
he began reading the *Jiào Jīng*, *Lún Yǔ*, *Shī*, and *Yì*.
Too poor to travel afar for teachers and friends,
he remained uninformed and ignorant;
his understanding was shallow, mind limited,
and so he could not fully grasp the greater meanings,
but only sought to read widely.
Of the multitude of books, there was none he did not memorize privately and grasp with precision.
What he had browsed through,
from the classics, histories, sayings of the Hundred Schools,
down to the brief miscellaneous writings,
amounted to nearly ten thousand volumes.
But as his nature was dim and apt to forgetfulness,
and lacking in literary talent,
his will wavered,
what he understood was shallow,
so he too did not escape confusion;
yet in writing, he could still cite sources
but never became a pure scholar,
nor one suited to be a teacher of transmission.
As for the Hé Luò diagrams and their commentaries,
he would look at them once and then desist,
unable to devote attention.
He took no delight in star charts, mathematics, the Nine Palaces, Three Chess, Tài Yī, or flying talisman methods,
having nothing to do with them.
Because these disciplines weary people and lack flavor.
In later years, he studied wind divination, observation of omens, the Three Origins, and Escape from the Armor,
and methods of Liù Rén and Tài Yī,
grasped their basic intent,
but did not study them in depth.
He also reckoned that all these skills mainly serve others,
and that they stem from the same impulse to rise in the world,
so it was not urgent to toil at them,
and it was better to read filial texts for their benefit,
so he abandoned them as well.
According to the *Bié Lù* and *Yì Wén Zhì*,
the collection then reached 13,299 volumes;
but since the era of Wèi,
all literature grew and multiplied,
doubling that of the past,
and so he realized how much he had not seen.
In Jiāngbiǎo, books were
generally incomplete;
previously he wished to visit the capital to seek out rare works,
but fell amid great chaos,
and returned halfway.
He often lamented and regretted this.
Now, with age nearing forty,
his early aspirations have waned,
so he only thinks of letting go again and again,
doing nothing and embracing non-action,
occasionally tilling wild marshes,
barely preserving his life.
His efforts at broad learning
thus declined daily.
As for Hóng’s character,
he was honest and rustic,
dull of nature and halting in speech,
ugly in appearance,
yet he never sought to defend or adorn himself.
His hats and shoes were filthy and worn,
his clothes sometimes ragged,
yet he did not always feel ashamed.
Worldly fashion
compelled frequent change:
sometimes wide collars and large sashes,
sometimes tight bodies and long sleeves,
sometimes long hems dragging the ground,
sometimes short so as not to cover the feet.
Hóng aspired to constancy,
not following the changing times.
In speech, he was direct and sincere,
utterly avoiding jest and mockery;
if not finding congenial people,
he would remain silent all day.
Thus, the people of his homeland all called him “the man who embraces simplicity.”
For this reason, when Hóng wrote books,
he adopted this as his style-name.
Hóng, by nature, was frail and weak,
and moreover often afflicted by illness.
Poor and without carriage or horses,
he could not bear to travel on foot,
nor was travel to his liking by temperament.
He also lamented the miserable customs of the times:
abandoning the essential to chase the trivial,
and socializing beyond proper bounds.
Thus he took up the brush and remained idly at home,
keeping to a quiet, humble gate with nowhere to follow or hasten to.
As for those of influence and power,
although he resided nearby,
none ever made his acquaintance.
His clothing did not ward off cold,
his house did not escape leaks,
his food did not satisfy his hunger,
and his reputation did not go beyond his door;
yet he could not be troubled by this.
Being poor, he had no servants;
his fences and enclosures broke down,
brambles filled the courtyard,
weeds and wild grass blocked the steps, remnants of rain lingered;
pushing through brush to leave the house,
parting grass to enter the room.
Critics held that his aspirations were lofty yet he neglected the near and showed no understanding,
in truth, it was due to his want of attendants.
Not versed in courtly approaches, from the first he did not seek out officials.
Only for mourning great losses,
or visiting the sick and afflicted,
did he try to rouse himself,
forcing himself to attend without fail,
but as he was mostly ill and seldom well,
he was often unable to carry through
and was frequently reprimanded by critics.
Hóng accepted blame without concern.
As long as his mind had no excess desires
and his illness made his heart averse,
he looked only to not shame himself;
what cause had he to seek understanding from others?
Only those of clear discernment
could be understanding of his sincere and simple ways,
for it was not to cultivate lofty detachment.
Most men of the world value ease in closeness,
delighting in secrecy and intimacy.
Hóng believed that it is extremely difficult to truly know people,
something even sages find hard.
Superficial ties are muddled and mixed;
outwardly harmonious but inwardly estranged,
yielding no benefit and rather bringing harm.
Though unable to sever all ties as Zhū Gōngshū did,
he always aimed for clarity and careful understanding,
and thus conducted himself.
For this, too, he was much resented but did not change.
Those who rushed after attainment
and stood on the margins of power,
all detested Hóng for being different from themselves
and found fault with him,
claiming that he was arrogant and contemptuous of the world.
Yet as for Hóng's character,
he acted faithfully by his heart,
and regarded both praise and blame as if unheard.
If there was trouble with those close by,
he saw some relying on their strengths to disparage others' weaknesses.
Hóng, ashamed to call himself even a minor scholar,
whenever he spoke with others,
always gauged what they knew and spoke accordingly,
never forcing them toward things they had not heard.
When discussing or debating with scholars,
he would present the main threads;
if he encountered those shy of exposing their faults,
and unwilling to openly discuss their meaning,
he would only broadly state his direction and intention,
so as to provoke their realization,
without laboring the discussion
or causing them to lose their own way.
For those who could reflect in silence,
retaining details and pondering,
often enlightenment would come of itself.
If he judged them unfit for discussion,
even if asked,
he would always decline, saying he did not know,
thus avoiding the fault of verbose replies.
Hóng's nature was deeply averse to seeking favor from officials;
from youth to old age,
he had aided several friends who were suppressed,
and when he had no choice,
he would make intercession to those in authority.
But these people never knew of Hóng's concern for their plight.
He could not bear to see them suffer injustice,
but acted quietly on their behalf only.
As for others, though personally close
and in power,
if they felt no sympathy for Hóng,
he would never use a word, even half a character,
to trouble them in the slightest.
Only when food and necessity were exhausted,
and he needed to procure herbal medicine, would he call upon friends,
and sometimes received help;
neither refused such aid.
When accepting others' assistance,
he would always wait until long after to repay them,
in ways unnoticed by them.
Of those not his kind, he would never rashly accept gifts or offerings.
If Hóng had stores of food for ten days,
he would share them with those in need;
if he lacked even for himself,
he would not take from his own share.
He did not make a show of fastidious conduct,
nor practice petty, ostentatious honesty.
When villagers and others praised him as good and upright,
sometimes,
they would bring wine and food to visit Hóng;
even if not of his circle,
he did not refuse them.
If he had occasion to repay them,
he would not do so immediately.
Hóng once said Shǐ Yún would not eat with his brothers,
and that Huá Shēng kept his chambers clean for intimate guests;
such are insincere acts to seek reputation,
not the broad measure fit for court and temple.
Hóng especially despised the unrighteous,
those who do not labor in the basic work of farming or weaving,
yet seek illicit profit contrary to right.
Those who influence local affairs
sell official recommendations for thanks;
those with authority
wield their seals and orders to demand bribes.
Some take gifts from criminals,
or use their position to wrong upright families.
Some provide refuge for fugitives,
and host those who have fled the law;
some coerce laborers,
disrupting public service;
some seize money and goods by force,
seeking high prices;
some take over markets and shops,
robbing the people of their profit;
seizing others' fields,
usurping the estates of the weak and orphaned.
They prowl anxiously within official quarters,
watching for opportunities to exploit and oppress,
boasting to wives and concubines at home,
and fishing for fame and position outside.
To such people
he would never extend friendship.
Thus common people resented Hóng's loathing,
and naturally distanced themselves.
So in his alley, there were no traces of carriages or horses,
and no guests of different mind in his hall,
so that nets for sparrows could be set in his courtyard,
and the seats were covered with accumulated dust.
From the time Hóng understood the world until near old age,
he never spoke of others’ faults,
nor discussed others' private matters;
this was entirely natural to him.
Even if servants or commoners had their faults,
or shameful affairs,
he never joked about them.
He never commented on the superiority or inferiority of persons,
nor enjoyed censuring or praising others’ friendships.
If compelled by elders or superiors to comment,
he would reply only when absolutely necessary;
and if obliged to discuss people,
he would mention only their merits.
When discussing writings,
he would point out only what was good in them,
never singling out their flaws,
and thus bore no resentment for criticism or praise.
At times, a nobleman would ask about officials or commoners,
how this or that person fared;
as for those pure, lofty, and capable,
Hóng would indicate their merits;
as for the greedy, violent, or obtuse,
he would only say he was not acquainted with them.
Because of this Hóng was sometimes criticized
for being too protective of others,
for not clearly judging right and wrong,
and for not drawing clear distinctions;
yet Hóng never dared to change.
He often saw the people of the world eager to judge others,
categorizing and comparing,
without necessarily being correct;
thus their praise and blame,
sanctions and dismissals,
often missed the standard.
though not necessarily virtuous;
those criticized bore deep resentment,
as if it were a blood feud.
This increased Hóng's caution,
so that he no longer spoke of scholars.
Even regarding members of his own clan,
he would leave both praise and blame to the family at large,
not lightly judging their worth.
Some reproached Hóng,
and Hóng replied:
“For my own person, I am myself;
as for principle, it should be easy to understand.
Suppose someone were to ask me
to compare myself to the ancients,
or among contemporaries to seek out my peers,
I truly cannot know myself
—with whom could I be matched?
All the more if it is not myself,
how could they seize upon me and judge me?
At the end of the Hàn, custom was corrupted,
and factions divided regions.
The followers of Xǔ Zǐjiāng
pronounced judgments with their tongues.
They quarreled and disputed,
turning clans and families into enemies.
Thus, among the men of Rǔnán, there was no stable estimation of worth, but only the ‘monthly judgments’.
Wèi Wǔ-dì deeply hated this as well,
and wished to take their heads;
thus you fled in terror,
nearly to the point of slaughter and extermination.
The warnings of former times are not distant;
from them, a lesson can be taken.
Moreover, people are not easily understood;
even fathers and elder brothers do not fully know their sons and younger brothers.
Those like me—are they truly so?
Those unlike me—are they truly not so?
Some begin but do not finish.
Táng Yáo, Gōngdàn, Zhòngní, and Jì Zǎ,
all harbored regrets at not wholly attaining it.
How, then, can one trust the petty, narrow judgments and fleeting insight of ordinary people
to lightly appraise the worth of others?
Is this not marketing the great wisdom of sage and worthy for a pittance?”
Formerly, during the Dà’ān era,
Shí Bīng rebelled,
and in the land of six provinces,
trees shook and leaves fell,
opposing the rightful and banding with traitors.
The Grand Commandant of the righteous army invited Hóng to be Captain of Troops,
entreating him repeatedly.
Since his homeland feared the enemy,
the disaster seemed deep and the worries great.
The ancients spoke of responding swiftly in emergencies;
also, fearing military law,
he dared not follow his own inclinations.
Thus he recruited several hundred men
and advanced with the various armies.
Once, attacking a lieutenant of the rebels,
on the day of victory,
coin and silk were piled like mountains,
and treasures and curios covered the ground.
The soldiers all let their troops loose to loot and gather wealth,
forming a continuous stream.
Hóng alone ordered his men
not to leave the ranks without cause.
A soldier who picked up spoils from others
Hóng at once executed to serve as a warning.
Thus none dared drop their arms,
and indeed, several hundred hidden rebels
rose up and wounded the troops.
The soldiers all scattered,
lost their order;
all man and horse were burdened,
no heart for battle remained.
This led to panic and chaos,
with the dead and wounded strewn everywhere,
barely recovering from disaster.
Only Hóng's troops remained disciplined and ready,
suffering no losses or injuries.
In rescuing the army from great collapse,
Hóng was of great merit.
Later, in a separate battle, he beheaded a rebel subcommander,
taking many armored heads,
and reported his victory to headquarters.
Thereupon, the Grand Commandant promoted Hóng to General Fubó,
and in accordance, granted him a hundred bolts of cloth.
The other generals mostly hoarded it,
or sent it home,
but Hóng distributed it among his officers and soldiers,
and also gave it to impoverished acquaintances.
Of the ten remaining bolts,
he directly purchased meat and wine,
to feast his officers.
At that time, he privately enjoyed a day's worth of fine praise.
When the matter settled,
Hóng laid down his spear and removed his armor,
and went directly to Luòyáng,
wishing to search widely for uncommon books,
caring not at all for battle merits.
He secretly admired Lǔ Lián, who refused the gold of Liáochéng,
and Bāo Xū, who would not accept rewards for preserving Chǔ,
and admired the principle of retiring after success.
Just then, great chaos erupted in the capital,
and the northern road was blocked.
Moreover, Chén Mǐn rebelled in Jiāngdōng,
cutting off the way home.
Just then, an old friend, Jiǎngjūn Dào of Qiáo State,
was appointed Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
He petitioned for Hóng to become Staff Officer.
Although not pleased by it,
as it enabled him to retreat south,
he forced himself to accept.
He was ordered to proceed first to urge on the troops,
but later Jūn Dào was killed,
so Hóng remained in Guǎngzhōu.
On several occasions, he was invited by regional commanders,
but always refused.
He ever thought that wealth and rank can come gradually, but never suddenly;
amid the petty matters in between,
there is enough to exhaust a man.
Moreover, high position and influence
are like being a guest in a foreign inn;
since they are not permanent,
and when they depart, they cannot be retained.
Those resounding are cut off;
those brilliant are destroyed;
like the flowers of spring,
wither away in an instant.
Acquiring them does not bring joy,
nor losing them sorrow.
Regrets abound in myriad ways,
anxieties and fears unending,
unspeakable in words.
It is not worth pursuing.
Moreover, measuring myself, my nature is steadfastly indolent and my talent is quite meager;
with such indolence restraining my paltry ability,
even if I bowed my head and knelt,
running to and fro in dust and wind,
I could hardly attain great name and rank, or avoid disaster and burdens;
how much more could I possibly achieve?
It would be better to follow Sōngqiáo’s path,
relying on myself alone,
not dependent on others.
I plan to climb the famed mountains,
and take nourishment to cultivate my inner nature.
This is not idleness;
for if one concurrently manages affairs,
unless abandoning worldly matters completely,
how can one cultivate the lessons of profound tranquility?
Knowing is truly difficult;
one should not begrudge questions or discussions with others.
Therefore my carriage and horses
do not pass through realms of wealth and influence;
the letters I write
do not reach the homes of those in office.
Again, within the grove of scholars,
though I cannot withdraw completely,
when guests call upon me,
my intention cannot refuse them;
they hinder my pursuits,
preventing me from being single-minded.
Then I sigh, saying:
‘There is no Dao in the mountains and forests.
Yet the ancients who cultivated the Dao
all necessarily entered mountain forests;
truly wishing to avoid distant noise and tumult,
so their minds are not disturbed.
Now I will fulfill my true intent,
leaving home and village,
going to Sōngyuè,
to follow the path of Fāngpíng and Liáng Gōng.’”
Of the previously composed Zǐshū inner and outer chapters,
fortunately I have already put in the effort,
and so I have arranged and compiled them again,
simply to show posterity, that is all.
When Hóng was fifteen or sixteen years old,
the poems, fu, and miscellaneous writings he composed
he then believed could stand in their age,
but upon reaching his early twenties,
he reviewed them more carefully,
and found that many did not meet his own expectations.
My talent had not necessarily increased,
but only that what I had read was somewhat broader,
thus I recognized distinctions between the beautiful and the ugly.
Therefore, I made significant selections,
discarding ten and retaining not even one.
Now, apart from the Zǐshū I composed,
I have only a few miscellaneous works left, about a hundred volumes,
and these are still not fully revised and perfected in principle,
most are filled with anguish and indignation,
and I have not had leisure to review or protect them again.
When others complete their compositions,
they immediately call it satisfactory,
but my talent is dull and my thoughts slow,
I truly cannot do so.
Whenever I write and revise a single character,
it always improves upon itself,
but I suffer from laziness,
nor can I review the many things I have written several times each.
When Hóng was over twenty years old,
he calculated that composing trifling short pieces
hindered his daily efforts,
and he decided instead to establish a doctrine of his own,
and so drafted the Zǐshū.
At that time, encountering military chaos,
I endured flight and dispersal,
and some works were lost,
as I was constantly on the road,
I did not again take up the brush for more than ten years,
until the middle of the Jiànwǔ era,
at which time I finalized and authored twenty juàn of the “Inner Chapters,”
fifty juàn of the “Outer Chapters,”
a hundred juàn of inscriptions, praises, poems, and fu,
thirty juàn of military dispatches, proclamations, memorials, missives, and records,
and additionally compiled other works not listed among common folk,
as the Shénxiānzhuàn in ten juàn,
and also compiled those of noble reclusion,
as the Yǐnyìzhuàn in ten juàn, and again excerpts from the Five Classics, Seven Histories, sayings of the Hundred Schools,
military affairs, methods and techniques, brief miscellaneous essentials, three hundred and ten juàn,
with a separate catalogue.
The Inner Chapters discuss the arts of immortals, alchemy, supernatural beings and transformations, nurture of life and longevity, exorcising evil and averting disaster,
belonging to the Daoist school;
the Outer Chapters speak of human gains and losses,
the appraisal of worldly affairs,
belonging to the Ruist (Confucian) school.
Hóng saw the “Diǎnlùn” self-preface of Wèi Wéndì,
which did not yet touch on matters such as board games and swordplay,
and intended to briefly explain what I know,
but in reality my skills are not even a few practical talents,
and it is not fitting to falsely praise myself.
Now I will fully recount
what I am not familiar with.
Hóng’s natural disposition is pure but dull,
and has few amusements or pleasures;
since letting my hair hang at my temples,
whether tossing tiles or rolling balls by hand,
I could not match the other children,
never have I fought cocks or ducks,
chased dogs or horses,
when seeing others gambling and playing games,
I never even glanced at them.
Even when forced to watch by being dragged along,
I was utterly unmoved in spirit,
like sleeping in daylight.
Thus even to this day, I do not know how many lines are on a chessboard or the names of chūpú dice.
I also thought these are mere trivial pastimes,
they scatter the mind’s intent and waste one's days,
for those in office they diminish governmental affairs,
for scholars they disrupt learning and recitation,
for ordinary people they make them neglect farming,
for merchants they cause loss of goods and wealth.
When victory and defeat are not yet decided,
they argue and contest in the marketplace,
the heart is agitated within,
the countenance troubled without,
they call this pleasure,
yet in truth it consumes and emaciates them,
destroying integrity and the sense of shame,
stirring up strife and competition,
seeking to take others’ valuable possessions,
and secretly forging enmities and resentments.
In former times, Sòng Mǐngōng and Wú Tàizǐ brought upon themselves the calamity of being dashed to pieces,
inciting rebellion and chaos,
the overthrow and extinction of seven states,
nearly toppling the imperial court.
This serves as a warning for a hundred generations,
and its lesson is clear.
Whenever I see those playing games,
they gradually become angry and agitated,
hands and feet come to blows,
they heap insults and abuse on each other,
break off friendships and ruin companionships,
which often happens.
Their resentment is not in great matters,
nor is it in small matters,
but it frequently brings about regret and shame,
and is not worth pursuing.
Even though Zhòngní cautioned about sleeping in the daytime,
when compared with me,
I do not actually regard him as superior for having chosen midday sleep.
And why is this?
Daytime sleeping is merely unprofitable but does not bring worry of resentment,
or the mutations of contests and disputes;
sages even wore out their book bindings three times through devoted study,
being diligent in their classical pursuits,
as for those of ordinary or mediocre talent,
how could they possibly excel in all alike?
Of all games, none compare to reading a single scroll of writing,
therefore, because I am fundamentally unenthusiastic, I do not pursue them.
This is what the common people are familiar with.
In youth, I once studied archery,
but my strength was too little to draw strong bows,
just like Yán Gāo’s bow.
I thought that archery, being included among the Six Arts,
furthermore can defend against bandits and repel thieves,
and is useful for hunting birds and beasts,
so I practiced it.
In former days with the army,
I once personally shot at a pursuing horseman,
and at the twang of the bowstring he fell,
killing two bandits and one horse,
whereby I escaped death.
I also once learned the sword and shield, as well as the single sword and double halberd,
and mastered the oral formulas and essential techniques,
using them to take men in service,
and came to possess secret methods,
their skill excelled to the miraculous.
If with these techniques I were to face someone unacquainted with them,
I could win a complete victory single-handedly,
going wherever I wished unhindered.
Later on, I also learned the art of the seven-foot staff,
which allows one to enter among drawn blades,
and seize great halberds,
but this too is a marginal and unnecessary study.
Knowing this is like knowing the horn of the qílín or the talon of the fènghuáng,
when would one ever need to use it?
Beyond this,
I have understood little.
From youth, Hóng had a steadfast intention,
resolved never to seek office,
often reading the biographies of Cháo Xǔ, Zǐzhōu, Běirén Shíhù, the Two Jiāngs, the Two Yuáns, Fǎ Zhēn, and Zǐlóng,
always putting down my books and stepping forward,
and admiring their conduct.
I determined to refine and master the Five Classics,
compose a Zǐshū in one collection,
so that later generations would know me as a man of literature and scholarship, nothing more.
Afterwards, when the prefectures and the chariot and cavalry general summoned me,
I refused them all.
When recommended to the Liángyá Wáng chancellor’s office,
though I raised righteous troops before,
after the bandits were pacified,
I made no preparations to present myself at the government office,
nor made claims for merit,
and never sought reward.
The Jìn Wáng obeyed Heaven and submitted to the people,
put down disorder and restored order,
reestablished imperial governance on the verge of collapse,
repaired the ruined ancestral temples,
considered the overdue rewards of the former dynasty,
and did not grant them to motivate the present.
According to regulation, Hóng followed them,
in a year of gēngyín,
an imperial edict conferred on me the title of Guānzhōng Marquis,
with an income of two hundred households in Jùróng.
Inwardly I thought that having fought the bandits to save my native land,
my efforts are not worthy of being recorded,
the golden and purple bestowal
was not my original desire.
I had always wished to emulate Lǔ Lián from afar,
or follow Tián Chóu as a nearer example,
and submit a petition resolutely declining,
in order to fulfill my humble aspiration.
But there happened to be a broad edict,
denying any exceptions.
In former times, Zhòng Yóu refused what he ought to accept in order to hinder good,
when the barbarian invaders were not yet pacified,
the realm was troubled,
and the state needed to clarify reward and certain punishment,
to make manifest its laws.
How could a lesser man like me dare, for a bit of personal purity and timid resolve,
to resist the great decree of public affairs?
Thus I relinquished my intentions and respectfully accepted the imperial order.
After Hóng had written the chapter “Self-Narration,”
someone questioned him, saying:
“In former times, Wáng Chōng, in his sixtieth year,
when his path was exhausted and all hope severed,
feared that his very person and name would perish together;
therefore, he set down a record to conclude his writings.
Now you, sir, are in the prime of your establishment,
encountering an era of virtuous governance.
You are about to accept bundles of silk from Shēn Gōng,
to ride the rush-wheeled chariot of Mù Shēng;
to dazzle as the fivefold brilliance at court,
and distinguish your fame like Kūn Wú.
Why do you resent that your fragrance has not been spread abroad,
and instead strive after the concerns of the aged philosopher?”
Hóng replied:
“The Two Forces are endlessly remote,
and man dwells as if but a sojourner;
the morning mushroom flourishes in brilliance,
yet before hours have shifted, it withers and perishes;
it is like the spring flower’s fleeting glory—
before ten days have passed, it withers and falls.
Even the tempest that rushes through the night,
and lightning flashing in sudden glare,
are not necessarily swifter.
Neither is mature age; it is like a shooting star trailing smoke,
or yellowed hair passing like an arrow through a crack.
How much more those who have not even sprouted and already their sheaths have fallen,
or who wither in the mist, opposing the autumn—what of these?
Thus, Xiàngzǐ gave voice to the sigh of the unharvested ear,
Yáng Wū grieved for early death.
Looking far back over antiquity,
among those of surpassing virtue,
some leapt like dragons in literary talent,
others crouched like tigers in feats of arms,
their high merits recorded in the halls of alliance,
their virtuous melody pervading pipes and strings—
though their form and vessel have sunk,
having melted into the deep earth,
yet fine tales of them float and are carried day after day;
thus, though a thousand or hundred generations pass,
they remain dignified as before.
As for me, dull and unworthy,
mired and constrained in mediocrity,
my abilities unsuited to the times,
my conduct at odds with the world—
when I speak, my voice jars with common custom;
when I walk, my steps clash with the multitude.
Within I have no support from the likes of Jīn Zhāng,
without, I lack friends who would dust off their caps for me.
Though the path is even,
my feet are not those of Qílín;
though the six directions are wide,
my wings are not the great Péng bird’s.
Above, I cannot soar as the eagle to assist the state,
below, I have no means to honor my kin and bequeath a name.
My virtues are not entrusted to a worthy historian,
nor my repute cast in bell or tripod.
Therefore, amid composing these writings,
I have made this chapter of self-narration;
though it brings no aid to fortune or failure,
yet I may depend on those to come who might record it!”
